%===========================================================================
\phantomsection\section*{The point}
\label{sec:point}
%===========================================================================

Here's the whole thing before any of the careful parts. I'm going to start with one small picture,
take it apart, and keep asking what each piece means, as far down as I can get before I hit
something that holds or something I can't get under. I'll tell you which. Then I'll put it back
together at the end and you can check whether it still stands.

One warning about how this went, because it explains the shape of everything after it. Most of the
time I had the hunch first and found the names later. Over and over, somebody had been here before
me. Sometimes that made my day. Sometimes it pissed me off. You'll see both.

\subsection*{Two computers that end up the same}

Put two computers on a table. Hand each of them the same list of a thousand numbers.

The first one sorts it. It compares, swaps, walks the list again and again until nothing is out of
order. Then it does one more thing: it walks the whole list front to back and checks that every
number is no bigger than the one after it. That check could have failed. It passes. Then it tidies
up after itself, wipes its scratch work, and leaves the sorted list in memory.

The second one never looks at your list. Somebody typed the sorted version into it earlier, same
thousand numbers, same order, and it puts them in memory.

Now wait until both are done and look inside. Same bits in memory. Same bits on the screen. Set it
up right, and you can, and it's the same everything, down to the last bit. One of them found
something out about your list and stood behind it. The other one is holding identical bits and found
out nothing. Wheel them out on a cart, swap them, wheel them back, and ask me which is which. I
can't tell you. You can't tell me. And the part that bugs me most: built the ordinary way, neither
machine can tell you either.

Sure, while they ran they were different. One did thousands of comparisons, the other did a copy.
But the runs are over and the runs are gone, and nobody was being sloppy. Ordinary computers are
built to forget how their bits got there, on purpose. Later in this chapter there's the sentence
where a physicist said so in 1961, and why he said it costs heat.

Who cares? Anybody who's been handed a sheet that says ``all tests passed.'' Anybody who's looked at
an inspection sticker on a windshield: the sticker looks the same whether somebody checked the
brakes or somebody sold the sticker. An audit, a proof, a ledger, an AI that sounds very sure of
itself: every one of them is a pile of bits that could have come out of either computer, and the
question that matters is the one the bits can't answer. Did something establish this, or did it just
print it?

I'm going to call the difference \emph{established}. The first machine established that your list is
sorted. The second has the same answer and established nothing. The rest of this chapter is me
taking that one word apart.

\subsection*{Look harder}

The obvious answer is: just look harder. Don't look at the end, look at everything. So make the
computers as lookable as computers get. Scale them up to the size of a warehouse, every wire a
lamp that's lit or dark, every switch something you can walk up to and touch. Nothing hidden in a
chip too small to see. Put both of them side by side and walk the floor.

While they run, sure, you'd see the difference. One has a whole wing lighting up, comparing and
swapping, and the other just copies. But they finish. The comparing wing goes dark. Now walk the
floor and look at every single lamp. The sorted list is spelled out in lit and dark lamps in both,
the same pattern, and everything else is dark in both, because both cleaned up.

There is no lamp anywhere that says ``a check ran here and passed.'' Not hidden. Not encrypted. Just
not there. You can see everything there is, and the thing I'm after isn't one of the things there
is. Looking harder doesn't help, because the problem isn't that you can't see enough. It's that
nothing was kept.

That's the shape I want you to carry through the rest: it's not a visibility problem, it's a keeping
problem.

\subsection*{Computed, stored, established}

Three words that get used like they're one.

\emph{Computed} is about the steps. The first machine computed the sorted list. The second didn't.

\emph{Stored} is about the bits. Both machines stored it.

\emph{Established} is neither, and that's the whole problem. It isn't the steps, because they're gone. It
isn't the bits, because they're identical. It's something like this: the first machine has a right
to lean on ``this list is sorted,'' because it ran a test that could have failed, the test passed, the
test was about this very list, and then the question got closed. The second machine has the same
sentence and no right to it. That's a true fact about the two of them, and it's written down
nowhere, in either one.

Four words I'll hold still from here on. A \emph{check} is the test, the thing that could say no. A
\emph{commit} is the closing, the question shut for good. The \emph{record} is whatever stays behind to say
so. And \emph{established} is all three, about one thing.

People say ``a right to lean on it'' about a lot of things that turn out to be vibes, so I had to find
out whether this one was anything. So I went looking. Here's what I ran into.

\subsection*{The clerk who forgets everything}

The picture everybody passes around is a person with a pencil, a strip of paper and a short list of
rules, and that's what a computer is. It's worth going back to the source, Alan Turing's 1936
paper, and seeing how far he actually takes it.

He takes it a long way. Back then a ``computer'' was a job, a human doing sums by hand, and Turing
modelled that person. He's careful with the person's mind: whatever the clerk knows, beyond a
handful of states, has to go down on the paper. Then he goes all the way. He imagines the clerk
getting up, walking off, forgetting everything, and coming back later. To pick up where he left
off, the clerk leaves himself ``a note of instructions,'' and Turing says that note \emph{is} the clerk's
state of mind, as far as the computation is concerned. Marks on paper and a note. That's the whole
state.

My two computers are sitting right inside that. Suppose the clerk didn't write the note. Somebody
slipped it under the door, in the right form, with the right instructions. He comes back, reads it,
carries on, and every mark he makes from then on is exactly what he'd have made if he'd written it
himself. Turing's model can't tell the clerk who did the work from the clerk who was handed a note
saying he did. It was never asked to. Turing wanted something you could check without crawling into
anybody's head, and a note on a desk is about as checkable as it gets. That's why the paper still
works ninety years later. It's also why there's no place in it for the thing I'm after.

So the founding picture of computing is a man who leaves his desk, forgets everything he was doing,
and trusts a sticky note. I relate to him deeply.

And now the question nobody needs answered to follow the argument, which is exactly the kind I
can't leave alone: who were those clerks? Real people. Before machines took the word, a
``computer'' was a job title. In the late 1800s the Harvard Observatory hired rooms full of women to
do the arithmetic of the sky, cataloguing stars by hand for a fraction of a man's wage, and some of
them found things the astronomers who hired them had missed. Rooms like that ran artillery tables in
both world wars. So when Turing modelled ``the computer,'' he was modelling somebody's actual
afternoon. Does that change the argument? Not a bit. But it changes the picture, for me anyway: the
sticky note was always a person trusting another person's work, and the question of whether the
work behind it was really done is older than any machine.

\subsection*{Information doesn't have it either}

My next guess was information: one machine got some, the other didn't. That one died fast. Claude
Shannon, who turned information into a number in 1948, says on his first page that the meaning of a
message is ``irrelevant to the engineering problem.'' His number measures how many messages you
\emph{could} have sent, not what the one you sent did, which is exactly right for building telephone
lines and exactly no help to me. Same message out of the same set, same number, for both computers.
He'd give them the same number if one of them got hit by lightning and came out right by luck.

Fine, look at the one message instead of the set. In the 1960s some people (Ray Solomonoff, Andrei
Kolmogorov, Gregory Chaitin, separately) worked out how to measure the information in one string:
the length of the shortest program that prints it. Same two computers, same string, same number. And
then there's the thing in that theory I keep going back to and standing on, to see if it creaks.
Running a program can't add this kind of information. What comes out can't hold more than what went
in plus the program, give or take a little. Leonid Levin, who proved a general version of this, has
a one-liner for it that's too good not to repeat: you can torture an uninformed witness all you
want, you won't get information about the crime.

Which means, as far as information goes, sorting your list told you nothing. The sorted list holds
nothing that ``your list, plus the word \emph{sort}'' didn't already hold.

And it turns out logic says the same thing in a different coat. The standard logic of knowing, the
one Jaakko Hintikka worked out in 1962, has a property people call logical omniscience: if you know
some facts, you automatically know everything that follows from them. So by that logic, once you
knew every number on your list, you already knew whether it was sorted. Hintikka flagged the problem
himself, in the same book, and people have been trying to fix it since. The fix that comes closest
to me is Sergei Artemov's, from 1995: you only get to know a thing if you've built an actual
justification for it, and the justification rides along with the claim. That's a reason traveling
with the claim, which is almost a record. But it's a way of writing things down and reasoning about
them. Nothing in it steps, and nothing in it pays.

So the two most careful accounts I could find, one about bits and one about knowing, say the same
thing: the sort added nothing.

And yet you know something after the sort that you didn't before. You can read the smallest number
off the first slot. You can stop worrying. Something happened. That's the clue, and it's the first
solid thing I've got: whatever
\emph{established} is, it isn't new bits. It's the same bits, \emph{settled}.

\subsection*{The guy who got closest}

Somebody had that clue before me, and he's the closest neighbour I've found, so he gets the most room
and the hardest push.

Charles Bennett, a physicist at IBM, wrote a paper in 1988 that starts where I just ended up:
information isn't the same as value. His example is an almanac of where the moon and planets will
be every day for a hundred years. It has no more information than the equations it was calculated
from, but it saves you doing the calculating. So the value is the work. He called the amount of
work a thing carries its \emph{depth}.

Was this my idea, already done, by a guy at IBM? The only way to find out was to find where it
parts from mine, because if I couldn't find that place I'd just be renaming his idea. And it's one
word: \emph{plausibly}. Depth is the amount of work a thing was \emph{plausibly} made with. Bennett says
straight out that you can't know how a message actually came to be; for all you know it came from
flipping coins. Depth is read off the finished thing, the way a fossil's age is read off the
fossil.

Bring the two computers back. The sorted list in the first one has some depth. The identical list in
the second has exactly the same depth, because depth looks at the list and nothing else. A
photocopy of a deep thing is just as deep. Depth tells you \emph{some} work was done, somewhere, by
someone. It's not a record that \emph{this} machine did it, and it's not a receipt for what doing it
cost.

So Bennett's standing right next to the line, on the other side of it, and as far as I can tell he
got his own question right. He asked how much work a thing embodies. I'm asking who has the right to
lean on it and what they paid to get there. His answer lives in the object. Mine, if I've got one,
has to live in the machine.

\subsection*{Statues that walk off}

If it isn't in the information, maybe it's in the knowing, so I went and read the philosophers.
And there it was again: people had been arguing about the difference between having the right
answer and knowing it for a couple thousand years.

Plato's version is a joke about statues. There was a story that the sculptor Daedalus made statues
so lifelike they'd walk off if you didn't tie them down. Plato says true opinions are like that:
they wander off, and they're not worth much until you tie them down with the reason why. Once
they're tied down, they're knowledge, and they stay put. Knowledge tied to a reason, and knowledge
that stays. Of everybody I'd have bet on to hand me that shape, Plato wasn't on the list.

Then in 1963 a philosopher named Edmund Gettier broke the tidy version in three pages. Smith and Jones are up for the same job. Smith has good reason to think
Jones will get it, and he's counted the coins in Jones's pocket: ten. So Smith figures, fairly, that
the man who'll get the job has ten coins in his pocket. Then Smith gets the job, and, unknown to
him, Smith also has ten coins in his pocket. True, believed, backed by a reason. Not knowledge. He
was right by luck, because his reason was about the wrong pocket.

That's the push that matters for a machine. Checking one pocket and committing to a claim about
another is right by luck. So whatever a machine commits to, the check underneath has to be about
\emph{this very claim}, and I'd better say exactly what that means, because it carries a lot of weight
later.

A check is about this very claim when four things hold. It tests the same property the commit names,
not a cousin of it. It tests that property on the same thing the commit names, not the thing next to
it. Nothing has written to that thing between the check and the commit, so it's still the same
edition the check looked at. And the check is honest: it says yes when the property is true and no
when it isn't, on every value it could ever be handed, not just this one. Break the first three and
you're Smith with his ten coins. Break the fourth and the check is just a rubber stamp. Later in the
book I build a machine whose step won't let a commit through unless the first three hold, and whose
checks come with a proof of the fourth.

And here's where I went further than this chapter needs, because the obvious next question is:
does anything fix Gettier? People tried for years. The first patch is ``no false steps in the
reasoning'': Smith's mistake was believing Jones would get the job, so rule that out. Then a
philosopher named Alvin Goldman, crediting Carl Ginet, came back with barns. You're driving
through a county that, unknown to you, is full of fake barns, just painted fronts propped up to look
like the real thing. You look at the one real barn in the county and think ``that's a barn.'' True. Believed. Good
reason, your own eyes, and no false step anywhere. And still you were lucky: if you'd glanced at
the next one over you'd have believed the same thing and been wrong. Every patch gets a new barn,
and as far as I can tell the arguing hasn't stopped. Which tells me something I'll keep: whether a
check was good isn't only about this one case. It's about what the check would have done on the
cases next door. Hold on to that, because it's the next section.

\subsection*{What ``could have failed'' means}

I keep saying the first machine's test \emph{could have failed}. Take that apart, because it's the
piece everything else hangs off.

The machine is deterministic. Given your list, the check was always going to pass. So in what sense
could it have failed? In this sense: if your list had been out of order, the check would have said
no. That's a claim about a different list, not about chance. Run the second machine on a scrambled
list and it prints the same sorted list anyway, because it never looked. Run the first on a
scrambled list and its check catches it. The first machine's answer follows the truth about your
list; the second machine's would be the same either way.

Here's the shape. A check is a question asked of every possible input, and it splits them into two
piles: the ones it says yes to and the ones it says no to. ``Could have failed'' just means the no
pile isn't empty. A check that says yes to everything has an empty no pile, and it establishes
nothing, however long it runs and however official it looks. A philosopher, Robert Nozick, made a
version of this a condition for knowing, in 1981: you know a thing only if, had it been false, you
wouldn't believe it.

Push on it once more, because this is where it really gives. ``Could have failed'' is a fact about the
\emph{procedure}, about what the check would have done on other lists. It isn't a fact about the end
state at all. Look at the first machine's memory when it's done: a sorted list. Nothing in those
bits says ``and whatever made me would have caught a mistake.'' That's the warehouse again, every
lamp visible and none of them saying it. The one thing that makes the first machine's answer
worth more is exactly the kind of thing an end state can't hold. The only way a machine can own it
is to write something down at the moment the check passes, and to have that something mean what it
says. More than anything else in this chapter, that's why I ended up needing a record and not just
a better answer.

One more thing that tripped me up and then didn't. Rig a check to pass only on your one list. Is
that cheating? No. It's a perfectly honest check of a different claim, ``this is that exact list,''
and it has a big no pile: every other list. It establishes exactly that and nothing more. What a
check establishes is whatever it's honest about.

\subsection*{Settled, whether it's true or not}

Then I ran into Charles Sanders Peirce, writing in 1877, and he said the thing I'd been running
together without noticing. The point of inquiry, he says, is to get out of doubt and settle on a
belief. And when someone objects that surely what people want is a \emph{true} belief, he answers like a
guy who's watched a lot of arguments end: ``as soon as a firm belief is reached we are entirely
satisfied, whether the belief be true or false.''

That's funny, and then it isn't, because he's right. Settling and being right are two different
events. A question can be closed on a wrong answer, and once it's closed it acts closed. Peirce cares
a lot about which ways of settling hold up (science wins, for him, because it has to answer to
something outside any one person), but the settling itself, the question snapping shut, is there
every time, and it never comes with a guarantee.

Karl Popper said it from the other side. Every test, he says, has to stop somewhere, at some
statement somebody decides to accept, and nothing in the evidence forces you to stop there instead
of one step further. You stop when you're satisfied. His picture is a jury: the verdict is a
decision about what happened, and the jury deciding it doesn't make it true. Science, for him, is a
building on piles driven into a swamp, and the piles stop where somebody's satisfied they'll hold,
not where the ground gets firm.

That swamp sent me further down, because it's the oldest problem in the book and it doesn't have a
bottom. Ask why you believe something and you get a reason. Ask why you believe the reason and you
get another one. Sextus Empiricus wrote down the ancient version, credited to someone called
Agrippa, and in the 1960s a follower of Popper's, Hans Albert, gave it a name with a joke in it: the
Münchhausen trilemma, after the baron who claimed he pulled himself out of a swamp by his own hair.
Every chain of reasons does one of three things. It goes on forever. It loops back on itself. Or it
stops somewhere, because somebody decided it stops. People have argued for a very long time about
which of the three to live with. So ``when do I actually know, and when am I done checking?'' doesn't get a clean answer
from anybody. What you can do is be honest about where you stopped and why. That's a lot of what
the rest of this book is: every place it stops is written down, with its name on it, so you can
decide whether you'd have stopped there too.

Lay those two on top of each other and here's what shows through. The check is one act. The stopping
is another. The check can run as long as you like and it never \emph{makes} you stop; at some point
something decides, and the deciding is its own event. That's the second machine's whole trick: it
skipped the check and kept the answer.

And a logician said the part I didn't expect a logician to say. Per Martin-Löf, whose ideas sit
underneath the kind of proof checker that checks this book, says a proof isn't an object, it's an
act, and once it's done it's done, \emph{irrevocably}. You could say that's true of everything that ever
happened. Fine. But it's the two computers again: the first machine's check happened, irrevocably,
and the machine right now carries no trace of it. The past can't be undone. The \emph{record} of it can
be lost, unless something keeps one. That gap is where this book lives.

\subsection*{Turns out computing already had a word for it}

Here's the slightly embarrassing part. Computing already has a word for this and uses it every
day. Anyone who's used a database has seen it: COMMIT.

A database does a pile of tentative work, and then there's one moment, the commit, written to a log,
after which the change counts. Jim Gray, who more or less built the theory behind that, opens his
1981 paper on it by saying the idea comes from contract law, and his example is a wedding. People
negotiate, somebody asks, two people say ``I do,'' and from then on it's binding. If it was a mistake
you don't erase it; you do another transaction to fix it, the way a bad contract gets a second
contract and not a time machine.

The wedding was a philosopher's example first. J. L. Austin, lecturing in 1955, said ``I do'' doesn't
\emph{describe} a marriage, it \emph{makes} one, and sayings like that aren't true or false. They can misfire
(the wrong person says it, a step gets skipped) but they can't be false. That's a commit exactly.
Writing the commit record doesn't report that a question got closed. Writing it \emph{is} the closing.
And a commit can't be false, only misfire: committed without the check, committed about the wrong
pocket. Gettier and Peirce again, from a third direction.

Robin Milner, building a proof checker in the 1970s, ran out of memory, so he decided to keep only
the finished theorems and throw the proofs away, like a teacher rubbing out the blackboard to make
room. The obvious worry is forgery: if the proofs are gone, what stops someone just writing a
theorem down? His answer was beautiful. Theorems got their own type in the programming language, and
the only way to make one was through the rules of logic. You couldn't forge one because the language
wouldn't let you build it any other way. He named that language ML, for Meta Language. I wanted to
call my machine the meta machine. I'm choosing to treat that as a coincidence and not a sign, which
is more restraint than I usually manage.

Bitcoin is the loud modern version. Its records can't be changed without redoing all the work that
came after them, and a computer that drops off the network and comes back trusts the longest chain
as the story of what happened while it was gone. That's Turing's clerk again, coming back to a note.
The difference is that the clerk's note costs nothing to forge and Bitcoin's costs a mountain of
work. It's the clearest case I know of somebody making a settled fact expensive to fake, and they got
there by paying for a search, not by putting a price on the settling.

And Bitcoin wasn't first. Pull on its footnotes: three of the eight
references in the paper that started it point to Stuart Haber and Scott Stornetta, who in 1991
worked out how to stamp a document with a time nobody could fake later, by chaining each stamp to
the ones before it. A company built on their idea has been printing a short fingerprint of its
chain in the classified ads of the New York Times, once a week, since 1995. Think about that for a
second. To make a record nobody could quietly rewrite, they put it somewhere a million people would
keep a copy of without even meaning to. That's the same move Zurek describes the world making with
a measurement, and I'll get to him at the end.

There are more fences like these: logs that can't quietly change, certificates you can check. Later
in the book I take five of
them apart. I lean on all of them. They work. I want that said plainly, because the next thing isn't
``they're broken.''

The next thing is where they sit. The database's commit is bits in a log, kept by a database
program, on a machine whose own step will overwrite those bits the moment some instruction says to.
Milner's guarantee is a type checker; it holds inside programs written in his language and nowhere
else. Bitcoin is a protocol on ordinary computers that will do whatever they're told. Every one of them is a program or a rule, on top of a
machine that can't tell my two computers apart. The machine underneath keeps nothing and charges
nothing for what got settled.

The obvious comeback: so put the rule one level lower, in the operating system, or what security
people call a reference monitor, the small always-on piece everything has to pass through. Yes.
Exactly that. A monitor that wouldn't let any program raise its record without paying would be doing
the thing I'm talking about. In this book's words it would be \emph{implementing} the model, and I'd
count that as agreement. What I care about isn't who builds the fence. It's what the fence has to
obey, wherever it's built, and whether that's forced or just a good idea.

\subsection*{What settling looks like}

The next chapter ends with a pile of things sorted into buckets. Settling a question is that, plus
one more thing.

Picture every state the machine could be in as a field of dots. A yes-or-no question about the state
splits the field into two rooms: yes and no. That's a sorting, the smallest one there is. And
remember the no pile: if one of the rooms is empty, there's no sorting at all, just a field. Now the
extra thing that makes it a settlement: once the machine is in the yes room, \emph{no step it can take
leads back out}. The door opens one way. A settled question is a sorting plus a door that only
swings in.

At its best, what goes through the door is a relation: these numbers are in this order, these two
things belong together. There's a chimpanzee named Sultan, later in the book, who fitted two short
sticks into one long one and reached the food. Nothing new got added to the cage. Two sticks became
one tool. That's what I'd want the door to be for.

But the door doesn't care, and this is the honest edge of the whole picture. Hook the door to a
check that says yes to everything and the machine walks through, settled, and wrong. Settled whether
true or false, like Peirce said. A door that only swings one way tells you a question was closed. It
doesn't tell you it was closed right. Price and correctness are two different books, and I keep
both, separately.

\subsection*{Why it has to cost}

This is the part I'm proudest of, because once you've picked a record that stays, the choosing stops
and the counting takes over. And the counting is chairs.

Take any machine with a finite number of states. Its step is a function: give it a state and a move,
it gives you back one state. Pick a yes-or-no reading of the state and make it permanent: no step
ever turns a yes back into a no. Now suppose some step takes a state that reads no and lands it on
one that reads yes. Then that step has to land two different states on one. It \emph{merges}.

Do it with chairs. Draw a box on the floor, three chairs inside, one chair outside by the door. Four
people, one per chair: the four states the machine could be in. The three inside already read yes.
One step moves everybody at once, each to the chair the rule sends them to. Nobody inside may leave,
because yes is permanent. The person by the door has to come in, because this is the step that flips
them to yes. Now finish the move, one person per chair. You can't. Four people, three inside chairs:
somebody shares. Maybe the newcomer ends up on a lap, maybe two insiders squeeze onto one chair;
either way, two people end on one chair, and from where everyone's sitting you can't tell which two.
That's the pigeonhole principle, which is old and not mine, and the checked version, with exactly
those three conditions (finite, permanent, one flip), is in the chapter ``Why the toll isn't
arbitrary.'' No physics in it anywhere. Counting.

(How old is it? Older than you'd guess. A French Jesuit, Jean Leurechon, used it in 1622 to argue
that two people somewhere must have exactly the same number of hairs on their heads, which is the
kind of thing you can be completely sure of and never check. Its first proper name came two
centuries later, from Dirichlet, who called it the drawer principle; the pigeons came later still. Is 1622 the bottom? I can't
tell you. History is like that: it's where you start digging, not where you stop.)

Turn it around and it gets better. A \emph{reversible} computer, one where every step can be run
backwards, never merges anything, because a step you can undo never puts two people on one chair.
Bennett, the same Bennett, showed in 1973 that any computation can be done reversibly if you give it
room to keep its history while it works. But give a reversible computer a finite memory and, however
much it computes, it can never raise a flag that stays up. It can always back up to before the
flag. Settling needs exactly the kind of step a reversible computer refuses to take.

Now the physics, as an assumption with its name on it. Rolf Landauer, at IBM, 1961, said that a step
that can't be run backwards, that merges, ``requires a minimal heat generation.'' That's the rule
people call Landauer's principle. On a finite machine, settling something for good takes a merge,
and if Landauer's right, a merge costs. So on that assumption, establishing something for good can't
be free.

And here's the rest of his sentence, the one I promised at the start. That heat, he wrote, ``serves
the purpose of standardizing signals and making them independent of their exact logical history.''
That's my two computers, in 1961. Ordinary machines spend their merges, and their heat, on
\emph{forgetting how the bits got there}, on purpose, so a 1 is a 1 no matter what path made it. That's
why the sorter and the copier end up identical, and why the comparing wing goes dark. And the very
same kind of step, a merge, is what it takes to close a door for good.

So here's the deepest thing I can say about settling, and I'll say it carefully, because it's easy
to say it bigger than it is. Not every forgetting settles anything: wiping a scratch pad closes no
question. But on a finite machine, every settling forgets. The step that closes a question for good
lands two states on one, somewhere, maybe not where you happen to be standing, and afterward nothing
can tell which one it was. A verdict keeps the decision and lets go of the arguing. An ordinary
computer pays for the forgetting and keeps nothing to show for it. What I want to know is what a
machine looks like that pays for the same forgetting and keeps the receipt.

Every assumption in that is a way out, and you should know where they are. Give the machine
unlimited memory and it never has to merge; it can write its history down forever, and the chapter
on the toll builds exactly that machine. Let the flag come back down and the chairs lose their grip.
The merge the counting finds might happen among states the machine never actually visits, and then
Landauer, who cares about what's actually possible, might charge nothing; there's a section on
exactly when that bill comes to zero. And Landauer's principle is physics, not math. A group in Lyon
measured the heat of erasing one bit in a tiny bead held by a laser, in 2012, and it has serious
critics too, the philosopher John Norton among them. So the counting is proved and the price is an
assumption, and I never let those two swap places.

\subsection*{Somebody got there first, goddamn it}

Bennett also says looking can be free. His famous move with Maxwell's demon (the whole story's later
in the book) is that you can write down which side of a box a molecule is on without paying
anything, as long as you write on a blank page. What costs is wiping the page to make room for the
next one.

I'd been sitting on this idea that \emph{committing} is what costs, not learning, and I thought: this
one's mine, I finally had an original thought. Then I found Carlo Rovelli's 2024 paper, ``The
Thermodynamic Cost of Choosing.'' Nope. Somebody got there first, goddamn it. A real physicist, with
a real paper, saying that making a choice that sticks costs at least the same heat Landauer charges
for erasing a bit. He even quotes a German saying, \emph{Wahl ist Leiden}, to choose is to suffer, and at
that point what are you going to do but laugh.

And then, taking him apart properly, it got good, because he seems to contradict Bennett. Bennett
says measuring can be free; Rovelli says any measurement costs. So which is it? Look at what Rovelli
calls a choice. A coin in the air hasn't chosen anything; it has to hit the ground and stop. And
then the sentence I'd put on my wall: ``stabilization must be irreversible, otherwise it is not
stabilization.'' Bennett's free measurement is one that could still be undone; that's \emph{why} it's
free. Rovelli's choice is one that's been made to stay; that's why it costs. The way I read them,
they're standing on opposite sides of the same door: learning on Bennett's side, committing on
Rovelli's. (Bennett's demon still pays in the end, when it wipes the page.) Neither of them puts it
that way, so push on it. But if it holds, it's the best sign I've got that the line I keep drawing
between knowing and settling isn't something I made up.

So he's my closest neighbour, and here's the difference, exactly. His is physics: a price in heat,
at a temperature, for a choice that sticks. Mine is a rule in a model of computation: a charge in
the machine's own count, on the step that flips a permanent reading on, with no temperature anywhere
in it. Same instinct, different place. I'll take it. It's annoying to be second. It's worse to be
alone and wrong.

\subsection*{What the Thiele Machine is}

So here's what I built, and which parts I was pushed into and which parts I chose, because you
should know which is which.

The Thiele Machine is a model of computation, the way Turing's machine is: math you can reason
about, not a box you can buy. It has a few parts. A state. A step that moves the state. A record: a
yes-or-no reading of the state that says whether something's been established. A charge on each kind
of move, added up on a counter that only climbs. One rule, which I call the toll: the step that
flips the record from no to yes has to cost at least one mark on that counter. And a window, what an
outside observer gets to see, which is there because the two computers already showed you the
problem: the usual window, the bits, can't see the record. The toll's first name, the one I gave it
before I understood it, is No Free Insight.

One what, and why one? One mark, in the model's own count. One because it's the least a whole-number
count can charge and still not be free, and the toll only says \emph{not free}. The model doesn't say a
mark is worth a joule or a dollar; whether it's worth anything physical is Landauer's assumption,
named, and nowhere else. And one is just the floor: Part II shows that if you charge merges by how
much they squeeze together, the price grows with the logarithm of the squeeze, roughly how many
times a step halves the number of states it can tell apart.

What was I pushed into? That on a finite machine, a record that never comes down can only be raised
by a merge: counting, proved. That merges cost: physics, assumed. What did I choose? To put the
count \emph{inside the step}, as part of what a step is, instead of in a log off to the side. Nothing
forces that. It's my claim about where the account belongs, and the rest of the book is the case for
it.

About the name. I named it after myself, on purpose. Half of that is a joke and half of it is a
stake in the ground. Turing got a machine, so here's mine. The longer story,
meta machines and all, is in the next chapter.

The names work the way Turing's do, and I'm going to be a little annoying about them. \emph{The Thiele
Machine}, capital letters, is the model and nothing else. \emph{A Thiele machine}, lower case, is any
particular system proved to fit the model, the way one rule table is a Turing machine; a two-box toy
on a sheet of paper counts. A Thiele machine is \emph{Thiele-complete} when the machine under the record
can compute anything a Turing machine can while still keeping the record and paying the toll. And a
\emph{universal} Thiele machine is one fixed machine that runs other machines as guests, with each
guest's record kept and its toll collected by the host's own step, not by the guest's good manners.

\subsection*{The two computers, put back together}

Here's the two-computer story again, rebuilt as Thiele machines, with the record and the counter
written out, so you can watch it instead of taking my word. The prices are the ones on the smallest
machine I build later: one mark each to check, to commit, and to certify (raise the record), and
nothing for ordinary work like moving numbers around.

\begingroup\small
\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.205\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.097\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.097\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.097\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.097\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.097\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.097\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{step} & \textbf{sorter does} & \textbf{record} & \textbf{counter} & \textbf{copier does} & \textbf{record} & \textbf{counter} \\
\midrule
\endhead
\bottomrule
\endlastfoot
start & nothing yet & no & 0 & nothing yet & no & 0 \\
1 & sorts (lots of ordinary steps) & no & 0 & copies in the typed list & no & 0 \\
2 & checks ``sorted'' on this list, this edition: passes & no & 1 & (no check) & no & 0 \\
3 & commits to ``sorted,'' about this list, this edition & no & 2 & tries to commit: nothing checked, refused & no & 1 \\
4 & certifies & \textbf{yes} & 3 & tries to certify: nothing committed, refused & no & 2 \\
\end{longtable}
\endgroup

At the end, the bits on both machines are still the same sorted list. Everything else differs. The
sorter's record is up and its counter reads 3. The copier's record is down, and it's paid 2 for two
refusals, because on that machine a refused attempt still costs what it costs. Nothing the copier
can do raises its record without first running a check of that very claim that passes. And no
outside window that only shows the list can tell you which is which; the difference is all in the
part the window doesn't show. Walk that warehouse now and there's finally a lamp that's lit in one
and dark in the other.

Now the honest half. Take away the small machine's rules and keep only the bare toll, and the copier
has an easier move: pay one mark, flip the record to yes, done. The toll is satisfied. The receipt
is real. It's a receipt for nothing. The bare toll prices the closing of the door, not the check
behind it.

\subsection*{What putting it in the step buys}

So here's the hardest objection, and I'd rather make it myself. You defined a flag and a charge,
then proved the charge gets paid when the flag goes up. That's your definitions agreeing with each
other.

On the bare model, that's fair, and the copier's receipt for nothing is the proof. What makes the
record mean \emph{established} is the small machine's step, which won't let a commit through unless a
check of that very claim passed, in the four-part sense from Gettier's pocket. And what it proves
isn't about one program. It's this: on \emph{every} list of instructions anybody can write, starting
clean, if the record is up, then somewhere earlier a check of exactly that claim, about exactly that
edition, passed; then a commit of the same claim; then the certificate; with nothing touching the
thing between the check and the commit.

That ``every'' is the whole answer to what the step buys. A log kept by a program gives you a fact
about that program: if the program's right, the log's right. The database's guarantee holds for work
that goes through the database. A rule in the step gives you a fact about every program the machine
can run, the buggy ones and the hostile ones too, because there's no way to run anything on it that
isn't a string of its steps. That's what moving the rule down a level changes. Not what can be
computed. \emph{Which} programs the guarantee covers: this one becomes every one. Most of the rest of the
book is how far that ``every'' goes and where it stops.

\subsection*{What it isn't}

It isn't more computing power. Anything a Thiele machine computes, an ordinary computer computes
too. The book proves that over any machine at all, an honest record is a switch the machine's own
events flip once and nothing flips back; it watches the computing, it doesn't add to it. It isn't
faster. It isn't quantum. It says nothing about which problems are hard.

And an ordinary computer can keep a record like this. Give a Turing machine a spot for the record
and a track for the counter, write its rules so it never sets the spot without bumping the counter,
prove that, and it \emph{is} a Thiele machine, not a counterexample. What an ordinary universal computer
can't do is make its own step enforce a record \emph{for the programs it runs}. When it runs another
program, that program's record is just data on its tape, and a buggy program can flip it for free,
because the host's step has no opinion about it. That gap, between the machine doing the stepping
and the program it runs, is where the databases and the proof checkers and Bitcoin built their
fences, and it's the gap the universal Thiele machine later in the book closes, for the programs of
the small machine it's built on.

\subsection*{What's proved, what's argued, and what I just believe}

Every claim in this book has a status and I'll tell you which, every time. Here's the whole list at
once, so you know what I'm on the hook for.

Checked by a proof assistant, with every assumption printed, for any system with the named parts:
anything that obeys the toll pays at least one mark to get from not-established to established
(short enough that you'll prove it yourself on paper in Part II). On a finite machine whose record
never comes down, the step that raises it merges, which is the chairs; with merging priced, the toll
follows, and the price is an assumption with a name. Finding out can be free: you can learn
something from a step that merged nothing and cost nothing, so the toll lands on committing, not
learning. A window that shows a paid state and an unpaid one as the same can't price the step
between them exactly, however clever it is. And over any machine, an honest record is a one-way
switch on an event, with two choices left free: the price list and which event.

On the smallest machine I could build, six instructions on two counters: everything in the table
above, for every program, not just that one. A raised record always went through a passing check,
then a commit, then a certificate, of exactly the same claim about exactly the same edition. Nothing
gets into its list of checked facts without a check writing it. The cheapest certificate costs
exactly three marks. It's Thiele-complete, because it does everything Marvin Minsky's two-counter
machines do, and Minsky proved those can compute anything a Turing machine can. And a host built on
it is a universal Thiele machine for its programs: its own step collects every guest's toll. A
machine from somewhere else can come in as a guest and keep its computation and its toll, but not
its own price list.

Argued, not proved: that an account of computation \emph{should} carry what was established, and what it
cost, in how it steps. That's what the proofs are there to test, and it's a claim about what
matters, which no proof checker can check.

Guessed at, with the ways to kill it written down: that the event worth recording is certification,
because its records are the ones that get copied and relied on all over the place (the pointer
conjecture, Part III).

Not proved, and I'll say so every time it's tempting: any physical price for one mark, anything
about real hardware that was ever switched on, or anything about which problems are hard.

\subsection*{At the bottom: what I suspect and can't prove}

This is underneath the proofs, so read it with the lights on. None of it is a theorem, and I'm not
going to dress it up as one. It's why I care, and I'd rather you know that going in than catch me
sneaking it in later.

Physics has a word for the moment a question closes: \emph{measurement}. And the people who thought
hardest about it keep describing it in this chapter's shape. Before a measurement, it could go
either way. After, it's settled, and the result gets copied out into the world, the light and the
air, so many times that it can't be taken back and everybody who looks agrees. Wojciech Zurek has
spent decades on how that copying works. Rovelli's coin has to hit the ground.

Niels Bohr said seeing anything at that scale depends on an apparatus that works irreversibly, like
permanent marks on a photographic plate: a door that swings one way. John Wheeler went further and
said every physical thing gets its existence from yes-or-no questions answered and registered, and
boiled it down to ``it from bit.'' And Peirce, way before any of them, said the kind of settling worth
trusting is the kind that has to answer to everybody.

Lay that next to everything above and the parts line up: a check that could have come out either
way, a result that's now settled, a price paid in forgetting, a record that stays. I suspect that
isn't a coincidence. I suspect the event this book prices on a machine is the same kind of event
physics calls a measurement, showing up in a different place. That's as far as I'll take it here,
and it's a suspicion, not a finding.

Now let me point the biggest gun I can find at it, and that's John Bell. In 1990 Bell wrote a short,
furious essay against the word ``measurement,'' with a list of words he said have no place in a
physics that wants to be precise. On the list: system, apparatus, environment, irreversible,
information, and measurement, which he called the worst of all. I used half of them in the last few
paragraphs without even trying. Bell would have taken my suspicion apart in an afternoon, and he'd
have been right to, because every piece of it leans on words physics hasn't pinned down. Nothing in
this book proves any of it. The proofs are about models and machines, and whenever physics shows up
in them it shows up as an assumption with a name on it. The suspicion is why I went looking. It
isn't what I found.

\subsection*{Where this goes}

So here's the picture, put back together. Two machines can hold the same bits and differ in what
they've established, and you can't see it even walking the floor between them, because it was
never kept. The difference isn't information; information theory says the sort added nothing new.
It isn't depth; depth belongs to the bits, and a copy has just as much. It's an event: a check that
could have said no, about this very claim, then a question closed for good, with no promise the
answer's true. The could-have-said-no part lives in the procedure, not in the end state, so only a
record can carry it. On a finite
machine, a record that never comes down can only be raised by a merge, a kind of forgetting, the
same kind ordinary computers pay heat for so their bits forget where they came from. If Landauer's
right, that costs. The Thiele Machine puts the record and the charge in the step itself, and what
that buys isn't more computing. It's a guarantee about every program instead of one.

Every time I thought I'd found something new on the way down, somebody had a name for part of it
already. Fine. I think the part nobody had put together is that last sentence, and the rest of the
book is me trying to break it. First where I came from, then the word I couldn't define when I
started, structure. Then the smallest thing that could carry the bill, on a sheet of paper, with one
rule I'll hand you without a reason, and then the chapter where I find out whether I had to pick it.
If it breaks there, the book ends there. I'd rather know.

\clearpage

%===========================================================================
\phantomsection\section*{Before the book: the short version}
\label{sec:shortversion}
%===========================================================================

\emph{The book in one paragraph.} The Thiele Machine is an abstract model of computation: a
state, a step rule, a counter that only climbs, a rule that the step turning a certification
reading from no to yes costs at least one unit on that counter (I call that rule the toll,
and its first name, the one I gave it before I understood it, is No Free Insight; Part II
builds it), and a window that says what an observer sees. Here's what's proved,
in Coq (a proof assistant: software that checks every step of a proof), with every premise
printed. Any system that follows the toll pays something to get from uncertified to
certified. On a finite machine whose certificate is never taken back, the certifying step
merges states, so the toll follows from pricing merges, with Landauer's principle (the
physicist's rule that forgetting costs heat) as a named premise. A measurement that forgets
nothing can be priced at zero. A window that shows a certifying step and a quiet one as the
same can't price certification exactly. Over any base machine, an honest permanent record is
a latch on an event (a switch the event flips once and nothing flips back). And no procedure
a substrate can represent decides which programs admit a shortcut, given a recursion theorem (the fact
that a program can act as though it held its own code). A substrate is the model's bare
shape, a kind of state and a rule for stepping, with whatever extra pieces a given theorem
asks for; here the extra pieces are programs written as states and that recursion theorem.
All of that is about the model: any system with the named pieces. Two builds carry the
model, and both are Thiele machines in the sense a few pages on pins down. The small one, six
instructions on two counters, is where commitments are earned and universality is proved.
The big one is what I mean every time I say ``my machine'': a fifty-one-instruction
machine in Coq, a runner extracted from it as ordinary code, and hardware in Kami (a Coq
library for describing circuits) refined instruction by instruction. On it, leaning on a
structural fact costs at least the index bits it commits to (roughly, how many times it
halves its list of possibilities), under the hypotheses of one representation theorem; the
recursion theorem is proved for its twelve-instruction guest (a small fragment it runs as
data), as it is for the lambda calculus L, and on the full machine it is a premise about a
chosen class of program transformations (asked of every transformation it is false there,
and that is proved too); and an integer
check on eight counters implies that a fixed moment matrix is positive semidefinite, and so
Tsirelson's bound, the ceiling quantum mechanics puts on the score of a two-player game
(Part IV builds the game, the matrix and the check from zero). Not proved: a physical price for one mark,
any separation of complexity classes, that certification is the event worth recording
(that's a conjecture), or anything about a powered-on board, since none was.

I didn't invent a machine. I found one. That's how I see this work, and I'll be straight
about the difference between that conviction and a theorem before I do anything else.

That sentence walks straight into one of the oldest fights in mathematics, so here's a short
trip into it first. G. H. Hardy, in \emph{A Mathematician's Apology} in 1940, came down on
the found side about as hard as anyone ever has: mathematical reality, he wrote, lies outside
the people who study it, and the theorems they like to call their creations are really just
notes on what they saw there. Leopold Kronecker supposedly split the difference: God made the
whole numbers, and everything else is the work of people. Supposedly, because push on that
line and it gets thin fast. It comes down through Heinrich Weber, in a memorial piece written
after Kronecker died, pointing back to a lecture from 1886, and that's the only source anybody
cites. A great line with one witness. (The first chapter of Part II stops early on to ask how
many witnesses a claim ought to need. The answer is more than one.) So does any of this
settle whether I found the Thiele Machine or made it up? No. A proof checker doesn't settle
it either; Coq checks a proof the same whether you think the theorem was out there waiting or
you think you built it. That's why it's labelled a conviction. What it changes is how I hold
the thing: like something that was already there, which means I can be wrong about its shape
and the shape won't care.

What the Thiele Machine is. An abstract model of computation. A machine the way Turing's
machine is a machine: mathematics you can reason about, not a device. It isn't a CPU, an
instruction set, a graph, or category theory; those are things I built with it, or things it
can carry. The model is small. A state. A step rule. A counter that only climbs. A rule for
which steps have to pay. And a window: what an observer is allowed to see. Like a Turing
machine, it's a precise way to say what a computation is. Unlike a Turing machine, it
computes nothing new. It adds what a computation \emph{establishes}, and what establishing it
cost. The event it accounts for happens on any computer, whether anybody keeps track of it
or not. What Turing's model doesn't have is a place for the record of that event, or
anything that enforces one. A Turing machine can be programmed to keep the record, and then
it obeys the toll and it's a Thiele machine in its own right. But when it runs some other
program's record as data on its tape, nothing in its own step enforces it
(Section~\ref{sec:machine-vs-program}). The event's physical cost comes in only under
Landauer's premise, with its name on it. The record exists only if something keeps it, and
keeping it, priced, is what the model adds.

What this book is. An argument, made with that model, about what an account of
computation should preserve. The usual account describes a computation by what it reads and
writes. I think that account is a shadow, and that there's another axis, holding what the
computation established and what that cost. Here's the argument in five steps, each with
where it stands.

\emph{Holding a sorting costs something; standing behind one might.} That's Part I: one word,
structure, pushed on with you through as many of the people who wrestled it before me as I
could reach. It finds three
different acts that people run together. Building and storing a sorting you can read back
costs work and space. Forgetting where things came from costs heat, if Landauer is right.
And standing behind a sorting, vouching for it, is a third act that nobody I read had put a
price on. Whether it has one is the question the rest of the book takes up.

\emph{Establishing is not free.} If the step that turns uncertified into certified has to pay,
every run from uncertified to certified has paid. Proved, for any system that follows that
rule, whatever its states and steps. And the rule isn't arbitrary: on any system with
finitely many states, a certificate nothing takes back can only be switched on by a step that
merges two states. That part is pure counting, proved. If merging is charged for, the way Landauer's
principle charges for it in its worst case, the rule follows. That part is proved with the
charge as a named premise, its critics named, and every premise refusable with a
counterexample built. Learning isn't what costs: a measurement that forgets nothing can be
priced at zero by an honest price list, and an observer still learns from it. Proved. What
can't be free, on those premises, is committing to what you learned in a record the machine
can't take back.

Two more things belong to that step. First, which steps a price on merging has to charge:
exactly the ones that merge. Every step that writes a record nothing takes back is one of
them, and on a finite machine a step that switches a certificate on escapes the price only
when the same step switches one off somewhere else. The tidier guess, that the priced steps
are exactly the permanent records, is false, and three states show it. No theorem picks out
a wider class of events every account must price. With one mark per halving, the step that
writes a permanent record costs at least the base-two logarithm of how much it squeezes
together (how many times it halves the number of states it can tell apart), and the same
bound holds in bits of Shannon entropy, the standard measure of information. Proved, with
the price as a premise. Second, where the machine I built stands, which is a Part IV fact
and not a Part II one. A small finite piece of it, eight states seen through a narrow window, is such a machine, and the machine runs it
paying exactly what that finite machine charges; one of those charges, two for a jump, is
the program's own choice, which the machine's price list allows and doesn't force. The full
machine isn't one: every step that raises its certified flag merges states and costs at
least one, but an ordinary jump can merge states too and cost nothing. So the full machine
doesn't price every merge, and that's a theorem too (Section~\ref{sec:witness}).

\emph{A window can hide what was paid.} Two runs can look identical through the usual window
and differ in what they established and paid, and nothing reading only the window gets the
difference back, so no price read off the window charges the certifying step exactly. Proved, for any
window with such a pair; and the machine I built has such a pair for both windows you'd
point at it.

\emph{Leaning on a fact takes a paid history.} A computation is entitled to lean on a structural
fact when it holds the object, a checked relation, and a paid event on its record. Defined,
for the model, with a counting fact beside it: narrowing a list of rivals down takes at least
the yes-or-no questions that name the survivors. The cost floor that ties those questions to
steps a run actually paid for is proved on my machine (Part IV), for shortcuts that hand over
their receipts (the record of what they paid), under a list of hypotheses printed in full.
Entitlement is a license to lean on a claim, not a proof that the claim is true.

\emph{So the axis belongs in the step.} An account of computation should carry what was
established and what it cost as part of how it steps, not as something bolted on after.
Proposed. This is the conviction the proofs are there to test. What's proved around it: over
any base machine, an honest record is a latch on an event, with two free choices, the
price list and the event; no procedure a substrate can itself represent decides which
programs admit a shortcut, given a recursion theorem, by the same self-referring trick, the
diagonal, that put a hole in Gottlob Frege's foundations for arithmetic (Part I tells that
story); and which event deserves the record is a conjecture, with its refutations listed.

Certification is one point I could pin down. It gave me a law I could state, a machine I
could build and run, and proofs I could put in front of someone who didn't share my
intuition. It's one witness in a larger argument about structure and observation. It isn't
the argument.

How the book is laid out. Part I is the picture: how I got here, and what structure is.
Part II is the axiom: the smallest thing that could carry a bill, and why its one rule
isn't arbitrary. Part III is the logic: the counter, the windows, entitlement, insight, the
latch, the diagonal, five real systems, and a conjecture. Parts I to III never use my
machine; every claim in them is about any system with the pieces it names, and the pictures
are toys. Part IV builds twice. First the smallest honest machine I could make: two
counters, six instructions, a table of checked facts, a ledger and a flag. On it a raised flag
provably went through a passing check, a commitment and a certification of the same claim, in
that order, and it computes everything Minsky's two-counter machines can, so whether it halts
is undecidable. Then the big build, one try, in three materials, as the witness for everything
before it: its state and fifty-one instructions, the claims a module of it can carry, what
insight and entitlement look like on it, and where each Part III result has a machine instance.
The big build prices every commitment and doesn't enforce that one was earned; the small one
is where earned commitments and universality are proved. Part V is
the chain from the proof to a chip, with each link labelled proved, tested, or trusted, and
the sentence that no board was ever powered on. Part VI is how to check all of it and how
to break it. The vocabulary I had to learn is at the back.

One more thing before the book starts, because people get it backwards. I used language models to
write the code and the proofs in this project, and I trust language models about as far as
I can throw them, which is exactly why every formal declaration is checked by a proof
assistant that doesn't care who or what wrote it. Coq rejects a wrong proof the same whether
a tenured professor or a model hands it over, and it accepted these, with none of my own
axioms anywhere in them, re-checkable by the procedure in Part VI. Being self-taught and
using modern tools didn't make this looser. It's the reason I made a machine check the
formal corpus, and then built an auditor to read over the checker's shoulder for every way I
might have cheated, on purpose or by accident (Part VI says what it looks for). It doesn't
trust me either. Good.

I think there's something foundational here. The results in this book have statements,
premises, and proof terms. The larger claim is a conjecture, not a theorem. I built the
machine so that the work could be done in public, with something firmer than my confidence
to argue over.

%===========================================================================
\phantomsection\section*{Let me be straight with you}
\label{sec:straight}
%===========================================================================

\emph{What this project is.} An argument about what an account of computation should preserve,
made with an abstract model built to carry it. Its central proposal is that what a
computation established, and what establishing it cost, belong in how it steps. The working
form of that proposal is structural entitlement: a computation is entitled to lean on a
structural fact when it holds the object, a checked relation, and a history that earned
it. The model, its laws, and the instructions of any one build are different things, and I
keep them apart. The generic
flag-raising step pays to set a flag; it checks nothing. A claim that something is actually
\emph{true} needs explicit witnesses and a checker proved sound, and some results here are of
that kind; the generic accounting law isn't one of them. It's a law about marks.

\emph{The proved core, in three steps.} Anything that follows the toll pays something to get from
uncertified to certified. A window that shows two states as the same, when they disagree on
the counter or on some other question, can't answer that question on every state. Those two
are about any system with the named pieces. The third is checked on my machine, in Part IV: a
checker that only sees the bare window, where a named pair of the machine's states collides,
can't be both sound and complete about the claim that separates them. All three are
statements about named laws and named windows. An ordinary machine can keep a richer encoding, or enforce the same invariant
through its own transition table. What I'm proposing is about why the extra distinctions
matter. It isn't a theorem that every Turing-equivalent system lacks them.

\emph{Substrate versus scaffolding.} Two layers run through the book, and confusing them makes
the theorems quietly stop meaning what they say. The \emph{substrate} is the shape: a kind of
state and a rule for stepping. Different theorems ask that shape for different extra pieces,
and the pieces aren't the same. The universal floor (the ``pays something'' result above)
asks for a certification reading and the toll on it. The counter's uniqueness (only one
count fits a chosen start and price list) asks for a starting value and a schedule of
increments; Part III gives the argument, a short induction that works for any system with
those two pieces, and the checked theorem is stated for my machine and sits in Part IV
(Section~\ref{sec:witness}). The diagonal asks for a way to write programs as states and a recursion theorem for
the transformations the substrate can express, and needs no toll at all. ``Substrate-level''
doesn't mean one fixed plug that every theorem shares. A theorem only gets to use the parts
it asks for. Ask it what it needs and it'll tell you, and whatever else is lying around the
workshop isn't the theorem's. So each result is stated over exactly the extension it uses. The substrate with the extension a theorem names is what I
mean by \emph{the model}, and the name Thiele Machine belongs to the model. The \emph{scaffolding} is
everything that holds the shape up so you can touch it, and when I say \emph{my machine}, \emph{the
machine I build} or \emph{the build}, this is what I mean: its state record (registers, memory, a
program counter, a graph of groups and arrows, the certification readings, the counters),
fifty-one instructions and their prices, a reference kernel (the machine's definition in
Coq), the guest it runs as data, an extracted runtime, the Kami hardware, a simulator
harness. The build fills in several extensions at once and borrows, for any one theorem, only
the extension that theorem names. Let that line blur and a theorem stated over one extension
starts reading as if it carried premises it never uses. ``Substrate'' never means the build,
and it never means the side of a simulation doing the stepping; for that I say ``the machine
doing the stepping,'' as against ``the program it runs.''

So here's how the book keeps the two apart. Parts I to III are about any system with the
pieces each result names, and their pictures are toys you can hold (two boxes on a sheet of
paper, chairs in a room, a row of dots), not my machine. My machine first appears in Part IV.
Every Part III claim that has a machine instance gets that instance in Part IV or V, with
its own checked name, and Part III says so in one sentence at most. When the origin story,
a few pages on, says the shape ``was the substrate the entire time,'' it means this layer, the model's shape,
and not any piece of the build. Same story with two more of its words. When it says ``the
machine'' about the thing it named the Thiele Machine, or calls that thing a meta machine, it
means the model; ``my machine'' is the build, and the build doesn't show up until Part IV.
And when it lists what the model asks for (a state, a step, a ledger, a window), read the
ledger and the window as two of the extra pieces: a result asks for them only if it uses
them.

Part IV has two pieces of scaffolding, not one, and I'd rather you know that up front. Section~\ref{sec:smallest}
builds the smallest honest machine I could: two counters, six instructions, a table of checked
facts, a ledger and a flag. Earned commitments are proved there (a raised flag was checked,
then committed, then certified, on the same edition, with nothing in between), and so is
universality, through Minsky's two-counter machines and a halting result borrowed from the Coq
undecidability library. Then comes the big build of fifty-one instructions, which is what ``my
machine'' and ``the build'' mean everywhere else in this book. It prices commitments without
enforcing them: its check commits to nothing and its commit doesn't look for a check (Section~\ref{sec:machine-claims}
shows where). Neither one is the model. The small one shows the model fits in six
instructions; the big one shows how much a single build can carry while the toll holds.

The names again, this time with every part pinned down, because I'll hold to them for the rest
of the book. \emph{The Thiele Machine}, with
capitals, is the model and nothing else. \emph{A Thiele machine}, lower case, is any particular
system proved to be an instance of the model's core definition, a certification system with
its five parts and its toll (Definition~\ref{def:certsys}), the way one rule table is a Turing
machine. The toys on paper in Part II count, the same way trivial Turing machines do. Both of
my builds count too, each with its toll proved, and Part IV names the theorems. A Thiele
machine is \emph{Thiele-complete} when its base is Turing-universal, so it carries the record
and pays the toll while computing anything a Turing machine can. The small machine is proved
Thiele-complete. Whether the big build is, I haven't proved, and nothing in this book
depends on it. A \emph{universal} Thiele machine is one fixed machine that runs any machine of a stated
class as a guest, with the guest's record kept and its toll collected by its own step. Part IV
builds one: its guests are the small machine's programs, so every computation runs on it, and
a machine from elsewhere comes in with its computation and toll kept but not its exact
prices.
And the chip of Part V isn't a Thiele machine at all. It's hardware that implements one, the
big build, inside bounds Part V states, the way a laptop implements a Turing machine.
Push on that last comparison, because it's looser than it sounds, and the looseness is the
point. Does a laptop implement a Turing machine? Not exactly. Turing's tape never runs out,
and a laptop's memory does; strictly, a laptop is a very large machine with finitely many
states, and it behaves like a Turing machine only on computations that fit. Nobody minds,
because the bound is known and most computations people care about fit inside it. That's the
same deal the chip gets. The words ``inside bounds Part V states'' aren't fine print. They're
the whole difference between implementing a model and being one.

\emph{What ``new model of computation'' means here.} It adds something to how a machine runs:
structure it keeps, and an account of what that structure cost. It doesn't add computable
functions. It's an abstract model the way the Turing machine is, but it doesn't hand you a
new primitive to compute with; whatever base machine sits under it still does all the
computing. When I say ``shadow'' I mean the particular window I name, not
every way a conventional machine could store things. Enforcing the law, storing it, and
letting an observer see it are three separate questions, and the book keeps them separate.

Which leaves a fair question hanging: if it computes nothing new, does it even get to call
itself a model of computation? I think so, and not only on my say-so. Computer science has
long kept models that compute exactly what Turing's does and differ only in what they count,
how long a step takes, what reaching into memory costs, because the counting is the reason
to have them. Part III lays the toll over a register machine of that kind, and over a Turing
machine and a lambda calculus, and none of them computes one function more afterward
(Section~\ref{sec:latch}). What each of them gains is a record and a bill.

\emph{What this project is not.} Not a solution to P versus NP, and not a complexity-class
separation of any other kind. Not a theory of everything. Not a claim that computation is
physics, or that physics is computation. Not a physics result: the game result (the
integer check and Tsirelson's bound from the short version) is pure mathematics, and
Landauer's principle enters only as a premise with its name on it, never as something
derived. Not a quantum computer or a claim about quantum behaviour. Not a verified chip; a
verified model with a chain of trusted and tested links below it. Not a claim to priority on any idea in
it. Not finished; the open questions are listed at the end.

\emph{What I do and don't know about prior work.} I came to this with no formal training in the
fields it turned out to need, and I've read what I could reach, with every tool I had. The
prior-work map below is orientation, not scholarship: for each piece of this book, who did
the thing it leans on, and what, if anything, this development adds. I'd welcome correction
on any row.

There's a law about rows like these, and it's a joke that keeps turning out true. In 1980 the
statistician Stephen Stigler proposed that no scientific discovery is named after the person
who first found it, and then credited the idea to the sociologist Robert K. Merton, who had
been writing about fights over scientific priority since 1957. So Stigler's law is an example
of itself, which is either the best joke in the history of science or a very tidy accident.
Is it a law? No. It's a pattern, not a theorem. But this book has already tripped over it
once, in the opening chapter: the pigeonhole principle wears Dirichlet's name, not
Leurechon's. And I put my own name on a machine. By Stigler's law, that makes it
somebody else's. The table below is my best attempt at finding out whose.

What I compare each time is what a result is \emph{about}. Landauer's bound is about heat, a
physical cost under a thermodynamic model. No Free Lunch (an optimisation result, in the
list below the table) is about averages over a whole spread of problems. The toll is a floor on one kind of step, the step that turns a
certification reading on. Exact pricing adds a second rule on top: never charge more. So the
comparisons are about the shape of each result. They aren't claims about who got somewhere
first, and they don't show that certification is the only event worth pricing.

The right-hand column uses words the book only builds later (the latch, the fibre, the
guest, the integer gate, the matrix test), so read it as a list of places to go, not as
something you're meant to follow yet.

Everything in the right column is stated with its premises in the body of the book, and
everything in the middle column is cited where it's used. The table is the short form. The
long form is Appendix~\ref{sec:whats-mine}, which takes each row, says what was
already known with sources, and sorts what's added into new result, new proof,
mechanization, implementation, synthesis, or conjecture. Most of the right column is
mechanization, implementation, and synthesis.

A few more labels I went and looked up don't get a row, because nothing in the book leans on
them. They're neighbours, and I list them so you can see why I don't think the toll is one
of them in a hat. Each is a claim inviting correction.

\begin{itemize}
\item Linear logic (Girard 1987) treats an assumption as a resource that gets used up. It
constrains what a program, or a proof, may consume. The toll constrains the model's step
function instead. Same instinct, different layer.
\item Foundational proof-carrying code (Appel 2001) checks safety proofs against the smallest
trusted base it can: a logic plus the machine's semantics. Here no proof rides along with
the program. The step rule writes the receipts as the run goes.
\item Session types (Honda 1993) constrain how programs talk to each other so the conversation
can't go off script. The toll is about what one computation has paid to establish.
Different problem.
\item No Free Lunch (Wolpert and Macready 1997): averaged over every problem, whatever an
optimiser gains on some problems it gives back on others. That's an average over a whole
problem space, and the edge is paid for elsewhere. The toll charges one step in one run,
with no refund anywhere.
\item Kolmogorov complexity (Kolmogorov 1965): the structure in an object is the length of the
shortest program that prints it. That's a property of a finished string, with no steps and
no moment of paying. The toll is a law about a step.
\item Cook and Levin (Cook 1971; Levin 1973): checking can be cheap while finding looks
expensive, and whether finding is really harder is the open P-versus-NP question, a gap in
how difficulty grows with size. The toll puts a fixed floor under the one step that
commits, however easy or hard the finding was.
\item The thermodynamic cost of choosing (Rovelli 2024): settling a binary choice at temperature
T gives off at least kT ln 2. That's the closest thing to the toll I've found, because it
charges a commitment rather than an object or an average. But it's physics, indexed to a
temperature. The toll charges the commitment in a model of computation, with no
temperature in it. Closest neighbour, not the same chair.
\item CerCo, the Certified Complexity project of Amadio and coauthors, builds a verified C compiler that carries the object
code's execution cost back up to annotations on the source. There the cost decorates the
program and survives compilation. Here it lives in the model's step rule.
\end{itemize}

And then the silly question that list raises, which I'm going to chase anyway: why is an
optimisation theorem named after lunch? Wolpert and Macready borrowed an old saying, ``there
ain't no such thing as a free lunch,'' and the saying is older than almost everyone who gets
credit for it. American saloons in the 1800s put out a free lunch for anyone who bought a
drink, and the drink paid for the lunch. A Washington newspaper was already saying in 1909
that somebody has to pay for a free lunch; a newspaper fable by Walter Morrow had the whole
line in 1938; Robert Heinlein's 1966 novel \emph{The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress} squeezed it
into TANSTAAFL; and Milton Friedman put it on the cover of a book in 1975. People usually
credit Heinlein or Friedman. Neither coined it. Stigler's law again, at lunch. Here's what it
changes. No Free Insight sounds like a cousin of the saying, and the sound misleads in one
way. The saloon's lunch was paid for somewhere else, in the price of the beer, and that's
