Wolpert and Macready's shape: a gain here, handed back over there. The toll isn't that.
Nothing gets paid somewhere else. The step that raises the flag pays, on the spot.


\part{The picture}

%===========================================================================
\section{How I got here}
\label{sec:origin}
%===========================================================================

What I am is curious, past the point of good sense.

I pick a thing up and cannot set it down until I have turned it over enough times to see how it holds together, and this time it did not let go.

I am not a programmer and I was never formally taught any of this.

I was not trying to build a formally verified CPU.

I would not have known what one was if it bit me.

I was trying to build a 3D renderer.

There was no plan behind it.

Just a pull to make something real with my own hands, and the kind of stubbornness that will not let a thing go until it stands up on its own.

I have worked on it in off hours every day since.

Once I started digging in, two things came clear fast. I knew nothing about computers, and the field was already saturated, every obvious road paved and crowded. So I needed an angle nobody else was standing on, and the angle I had was not a strategy, it was just the only way my head works. I did not know what compositional meant. I had never heard of category theory. I called the thing I was building digital DNA, because that is what it felt like in my hands, and I thought about it in the only language I had: gravity pipes and directions and vectors, things that were linear and somehow not linear at the same time, structure that flowed and joined and came apart without my owning one proper word for any of it. I built a custom rendering pipeline out of those intuitions, by feel, throwing out pieces that did not sit right even when I could not have told you the rule they were breaking. And then, the way I always do, I went looking for what I was actually doing, and found out it already had a name. An old one. A deep one. What I had been reaching for in the dark was composition. It was category theory, a whole field I had never once heard of, sitting there describing the exact shapes I had been shoving around. The moment that landed, the rendering pipeline stopped being a rendering pipeline and started turning into a categorical engine, and I started swallowing the real theory as fast as I could find the words for things I had already built.

The method underneath was crude and it held. I wrote a long structured spec in JSON (a plain-text format for describing data) as a context document, fed it to Copilot, and had it build one Python file per concept, one at a time, each with its own tests, and I would not move to the next until I could watch the current one actually run. Category. Object. Morphism. Functor. Monoidal product. It came together in pieces and never in chapters, the way a picture resolves out of static instead of getting drawn in left to right. The Yoneda lemma (a result buried deep in category theory) was the piece that made the rest snap into place, the night I quit borrowing other people's runtimes and started writing my own around it, with Z3 (a constraint solver out of Microsoft Research) wired into the middle.

Then within weeks I found out the engine I had built to draw pictures was general enough to run a physics simulation on the exact same primitives, without my rewriting any of it. I wrote Newton's laws as a program in it, half expecting nothing, and it ran. I want to be careful about what that was and what it was not, because this is exactly the kind of thing that gets misread. It was not me deriving physics, and I am not claiming the machine explains gravity. It was the compositional structure being general enough to express a physics simulation the same way it had expressed a renderer, and that generality is what told me the structure was the point and the pixels never were. Somewhere in those weeks I crossed from debugging why one pixel would not show up to understanding that I had quietly built a categorical computing engine, and that the rendering had only ever been the first thing I aimed it at. The pixel did eventually show up, for what it is worth.

I kept going, because by then I could not not keep going. I built a small custom language for describing scenes (the name for that is a domain-specific language, a DSL), then a program that read the language and caught my mistakes in it (a linter), then a way to type commands at the whole thing from a terminal (a command-line interface, a CLI). The night the engine first ran a program declaratively, meaning I told it what should happen and let it work out the how instead of my spelling out every step, I told my wife, Julie, I thought I was onto something. She said okay.

Then I hit a wall, and it is the wall this whole document is about. Z3 could settle the small questions and fell over on the exact ones I needed answered, which left me staring down an infinite hallway of guess-and-test with no proof waiting at the end of it, ever. One night, not even working, I was watching a video about Flatland, the old story about a creature living in two dimensions who cannot so much as picture a third. And it landed on me sideways, all at once, the way the real ones always do. I said it out loud: I get it now. There is another axis. Classical computation only ever sees what it can read and write off its own surface, and there is a whole direction it is blind to, not because it is broken but because it was never built with an eye that points that way. I opened a new repo that same night and called the thing in it the Thiele Machine. The name began as a working title and became the name of the model. It carries the larger claim plainly: the machine treats structural state as part of computation.

What survived the whole trip from there to here is not the code. Not one line of it. By the time the Coq proofs finally landed, every line of that first renderer had been thrown out and rewritten at least twice, probably more, and good riddance to all of it. What survived was a single architectural commitment I made early and never once let anyone talk me out of: structure is the state itself, the actual thing the machine runs on, not a metaphor laid over some realer state underneath. Category theory was the first language I found for that structure. It is not what the model is. The model asks for a state, a step, a ledger, and a window, and category theory appears nowhere in that list. It lives on in the build. The \code{Category} structure that came together in that first week and first ran morphisms correctly at two in the morning is, in different words and different syntax, the same object the partition graph is in the machine I ended up with (the graph of groups, and arrows between them, that Part IV builds). I did not write that code, not then and not now. I directed the models and refused everything they handed me until the morphisms composed the way the shape said they had to. The morphisms in that early code were objects that remembered where they came from; the morphisms in the machine I ended up with are objects that remember where they came from and that you can walk up to and challenge. The receipt grew teeth. But the shape itself never moved. The shape was the substrate the entire time, and everything else, every renderer and language and proof, was me slowly learning to see what I had already built. By the shape I mean structure held as state. Not category theory. Category theory was just the first language I had for it.

Formal verification was a graveyard of dead ends further on. The hardware came after that. Every step pulled back to show another layer underneath that I had not known was there, and I mean that as plainly as it sounds: I did not know what a Turing machine was when I started, I did not know what Coq was, I did not know most of the words in this document existed. I learned each one the same way, by walking face-first into a wall that needed it and not being let past until I had it. The needing always came first. The learning came after, dragged along behind the needing because it had no say in the matter.

Large language models were my hands the whole way through, and I want the division of labor exact, because it is the thing people most want to get wrong about work like this. The hands had nothing like this to draw on: no reference implementation, no prior project to point at. The ideas, the architecture, the direction, the demand that the thing be true: those are mine, all of them, no asterisk. The symbol-pushing, the actual Coq and the actual math, the models produced and the proof checker judged. The proofs compile or they do not. I refused every one that did not. Coq is an obedient idiot. It checks the proof matches the statement. It does not check that the statement means what you think it means. A theorem can claim ``every cat that is also a prime number has whiskers'' and the proof can be three characters long and Coq will nod and stamp it. So I read every statement. The proofs you can't fake. The statements you can fake by accident, which is the more dangerous failure mode. I refused both kinds. However the symbols got onto the page, the argument on it is checkable by reading, and it would be exactly as right or as wrong if a million monkeys had typed it. The monkeys could not have refused.

A word on what I actually do, because it is stranger than the usual split and it runs under everything after it. I do not write code or math by hand. I do not pick constants. I do not grind through derivations. I have never written a line of code on paper or in a notepad in my life. What I do is see, and direct, and refuse. When I take hold of an idea it does not stay a point. It opens up. It becomes a shape I can blow up and turn over and take apart, lay across another shape to find where the two of them touch, run forward and then back to where it started, zoom into until it is the only thing in the world and pull back until it is one dot in a field of other dots, and the whole time it stays wired to everything I have ever connected it to, the right connections and the wrong ones both, all of them live at once. I am not reading that field neutrally, the way a search would. The thing doing the looking is me, the whole of me, my gut and my mood and my stubbornness picking what lights up and which way I move through it, and that is the part you cannot lift out without turning me back into a search engine. So I see where a thing has to fit, the shape it is obligated to have, usually well before I could write it down in a single symbol. Then the model gives me the symbols, the proof checker takes them or throws them back, and I refuse anything that will not compile or does not match the shape I am holding. That refusal is the one thing in this entire document that is mine and only mine: the demand that it be true, and the throwing-out of everything that wasn't.

I am telling you all of this because it is not background color, it is the engine. I did not come up through anywhere that hands you a foundation and says trust us, this part is settled. No professors, no colleagues, no field full of authority to lean back on when a claim got heavy. From the outside that is a deficit. From the inside it is the whole reason any of this is solid: when I meet a claim I either find the proof or I do not believe it, and that goes double for my own, because my own are the ones I most want to wave through. It is how I am built. It is the only way I know to hold a thing and actually trust that I am holding it.

So everything in here gets built from the ground up, and not as a courtesy to you. I build it because I do not believe I understand a thing until I have built it with my own hands, watched it stand up on its own, and tried to knock it over. I built this document the exact way I built the machine, brick by brick, refusing each brick until it held weight. That includes the parts you already knew cold before you opened this. I did not skip them for you, and I could not skip them for me.

The vocabulary I had to go look up to do any of this sits at the back of the book, so the argument comes first. If a word stops you, it is there. If you already know this material, you never have to open it. But if you catch something in the basics that is wrong, I want to know, and I mean that as a real ask and not a polite one. Nothing in here is correct just because I wrote it. Especially the parts I wrote.

\textbf{On the name.} I wanted to call it the meta machine. Then Facebook bought the word ``meta'': a company renaming itself after a term for self-reference and draining it of any in the same motion. So I went one level up, where this machine already lives. The most meta move available, for a machine that runs on meta-level reasoning, was to put my own name on the cover and take the word back. That's the whole of it, a meta move on a meta machine. It happens to be my dad's name too, and my wife's now. So I asked them before I did it. They said go ahead.

%===========================================================================
\section{What structure is}
\label{sec:structure}
%===========================================================================

One word. That's this whole section, and I'm aware of how that sounds, so here's the word
and you can decide whether to stay. Structure.

I used that word for most of my life without once looking at it, which I suspect is true of
most people and most words, and it's fine, right up until you do something stupid. The
stupid thing I did was build a machine that keeps a running bill, and the bill has one rule I
couldn't talk it out of. You can arrange things however you like for whatever price you
name, including free. But the moment you ask the machine to \emph{vouch} for an arrangement, to
put its own name on the claim that these things belong together, there's a charge, and it
isn't zero. How much, charged in what, why I picked that and not something else, and whether
I had any business picking it at all: that's all later, and some of it I'm still not sure
of. What I was sure of, standing there with the thing built, was that I'd made something that
charges for standing behind structure and I could not have told you what structure was. It
didn't care. It can't nod along the way a person does. It needed the word to hold still, and
the word had never held still for anyone, least of all me. (The machine itself stays off the
page until Part IV, on purpose. Until then, the one rule is all of it that matters, and I'd
rather you met the rule in a toy you can hold than in a machine you'd have to take on trust.)

So I went looking at the people who'd wrestled it before me. Some of them have been dead two
thousand years and are still, I'd bet money, better at this than I am. I used everything I
had: language models, more than one, books, libraries, my own gut, anything in reach. I don't
know if I found enough. I never do. There's always another shelf behind the one I was
reading. And being dead and famous is not the same as being right, so I pushed on each of
them, and what follows is what I could reach, pushed on as hard as I know how. The one thing
I'm asking is that you push on it with me, out loud, at your own kitchen table, because the
first time through I was the only one checking, and that's not enough people.

The order I ran into them was a mess. Category theory came first, because I'd built one by
feel before I knew it had a name, and everything else came in whatever order the next
question dragged it in. I'm going to put them in the order they happened instead, because
that's the order where each one leans on the last. And none of it is an oracle. History is where
I start, not where I stop. It gets retold, smoothed over, and now and then made up outright
(there's a drowning coming up that never happened), so every piece of it is a lead to check,
and I check the parts I lean on.

\subsection{A string, a square, and a drowning that didn't happen}

Start with the oldest one, and start by doing it. Take a string. A guitar string, a rubber
band over an open box, anything that twangs. Pluck it. Now press it down exactly at the
middle and pluck half. That's the same note, an octave up, the one that makes a round sound
like a round. Press at a third of the way along and pluck the long side: that's the fifth,
the second note of every bugle call you've ever heard. Half. Two thirds. Small whole numbers,
and your ear says yes before your brain does. About twenty-five hundred years ago, in the
south of Italy, the followers of a man named Pythagoras are credited with finding exactly that, and it's as true
in your kitchen tonight as it was on their hillside.

Here's what they did with it, as best anyone can tell. Nothing survives that's surely from
Pythagoras's own hand. The earliest fragments are from a later member, Philolaus, and scholars
argue over those. Mostly what's left is Aristotle, one to two centuries later, writing in his
\emph{Metaphysics} about them the way you'd write about the neighbours' religion, and he says they
took the elements of numbers to be the elements of all things: everything is number. Not that everything can be counted. That the parts of numbers are the parts of all
things.

Stop and ask what I asked. What does that even mean? Is a chair a number? Does a chair have
a number tucked inside it somewhere? Aristotle doesn't say, and he's reporting a belief he
doesn't hold. So don't take it on his word, or theirs, or mine. But before you push on it,
know what it was holding up, because you can't test a load-bearing wall without knowing what
sits on it. These weren't people doing math for fun on weekends. They were a brotherhood,
with rules about what you could eat and when you had to keep quiet, and that plucked string
was their scripture. Halve the string, hear the octave: to them that was proof that under the
mess of the world there were whole numbers in clean ratios, that the cosmos was a chord and
they'd heard it. ``Everything is number'' wasn't a slogan. It was what they'd organized their
lives around. Which is exactly the kind of sentence you should be suspicious of, mine
included.

Now push, and push where they loved most: the square. Draw one, with a side one unit long,
any unit you like, and draw the line from one corner to the opposite corner. Call that the
diagonal. If everything is number, then the diagonal is some whole number of parts long when
the side is some whole number of parts, so the diagonal divided by the side is a fraction, a
whole number over a whole number. Cancel anything the top and bottom share, the way
four-sixths becomes two-thirds, until they have no common factor left. I'll call the top $p$
and the bottom $q$, and the letters are purely so I don't have to keep writing ``the top'' and
``the bottom.''

You need one fact about squares, and it's the one Pythagoras is famous for. The square built
on the diagonal has exactly twice the area of the square built on the side. If you want to
see it rather than believe it, cut a square along both diagonals into four triangles and
arrange them around; it's a five-minute job with scissors. So $p$ times $p$ is twice $q$
times $q$. People write ``times itself'' as a small raised two, so that's $p^2 = 2q^2$, and that
is the only piece of notation in this argument.

Twice anything is even. So $p$ times $p$ is even. An odd number times itself is always odd
(three times three, five times five, try a couple), so $p$ itself must be even: it's two
times something, and I'll call that something $r$. Put it back in. Two $r$ times two $r$ is
four times $r$ times $r$, and that equals twice $q$ times $q$. Halve both sides: two times $r$
times $r$ equals $q$ times $q$. So $q$ times $q$ is even, so $q$ is even too, by the same step
as before. But you already cancelled everything the top and bottom had in common, so they
can't both be even. The argument has eaten itself, and when an argument eats itself the
thing you supposed at the start is false. There is no such fraction. The diagonal of a square
can't be named by any ratio of whole numbers, ever. Aristotle reaches for this very argument in
his \emph{Prior Analytics} as his example of proof by contradiction (suppose the diagonal can be
measured, and odd numbers come out equal to even ones), and you just did it with a pencil.

There's a story that's been told for two thousand years: that a member of the brotherhood
named Hippasus let this secret out, and his brothers took him to sea and drowned him for it.
I went and checked, because it's a good story and good stories are the ones to check. The
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy's entry on Pythagoreanism finds no ancient writer who
connects Hippasus to this discovery at all. It's a legend. But notice that the legend exists.
Somebody, long after, felt that a man \emph{should} have been drowned for this. That's how much
was riding on it. To them, the diagonal wasn't a math problem. It was the end of the world.

So the claim is dead, and you killed it, not me. Now the question that matters: what's left?
Look at your square again. The diagonal is still there. It still stands in a perfectly
definite relation to the side; you drew it, and nobody drowned. That relation was real before
anyone tried to put a number on it, and it stayed real after the number failed. The relation
came first. The number, when there is one, is a name for the relation, and sometimes there
isn't a name. I'm going to keep that, and I want you to keep it too, because you're going to
watch the same move get made again and again as this book goes on: somebody says ``everything
is X,'' and it's true enough to do real work with, and it sounds right when you pluck it, and
then somebody draws the diagonal. I don't know yet whether the thing I built survives its own
diagonal. That's a real question, and I'll get to it.

\subsection{Shapes poured into nothing}

About a century and a half after the brotherhood, Plato, in a dialogue called the \emph{Timaeus}, tried to
build the whole physical world out of geometry. Fire, air, water and earth were four
regular solids (the pyramid, the eight-faced one, the twenty-faced one, and the cube), and the
faces of those solids were built from exactly two kinds of right triangle. You can make one
of each in a minute: cut a square from corner to corner for the first, and cut an equilateral
triangle from a corner to the middle of the opposite side for the second. Everything else, in
Plato's story, was a receptacle, a featureless medium that takes on shape the way wax takes a
seal. Structure, for Plato, is shape laid into something that has no shape of its own.

Why did he care? He wanted a world made on purpose, by a craftsman working from a plan, and
triangles were the plan. Is it true? No, but not for the cheap reason. You can't refute a
claim about what things are made of at the smallest scale by picking one up; the smallest
scale is exactly where your hands don't reach, and Plato knew that. What sank it is that it
made no prediction anyone could check and the people who eventually did reach that scale,
two thousand years on, found atoms, and atoms aren't triangles. The idea was a guess with no
way to lose, until it lost. But push on it and two things survive. One: structure is something \emph{laid in}, and the stuff it's laid into doesn't carry it
by itself. That's a real idea, and I'd ask you to keep it loosely for now, because later I'll
have to ask whether the state a machine holds is the wax or the seal. Two: Plato broke his own
claim, in a later dialogue called the \emph{Parmenides}, with an objection that Aristotle later
nicknamed the third man, and it's the most useful mistake in this section. Take all the large
things. Plato says they share one thing, Largeness. But Largeness is itself large, so now
there's a further thing that all the large things \emph{and} Largeness share, and that one is
large too, and it never stops. Try it with any property you like; it runs away every time.
The lesson, and I think it's right though Plato never quite accepted it himself: the
structure of a collection is not one more member of the collection. The plan isn't a brick.
Hold on to that one. It'll come back in a place you won't expect.

\subsection{Prove it from what you and I both accept}

Around 300 BC, in Alexandria, Euclid wrote the \emph{Elements}, and the thing to take from it is
not the geometry. It's the method, and the method is the whole reason I trust anything in
this book, so give me a paragraph on it. He starts with definitions (``a point is that which
has no part''), five postulates (things he asks you to grant, like ``a straight line can be
drawn from any point to any point''), and five common notions (things nobody argues with, like
``things equal to the same thing are equal to each other''). Then he derives everything else,
four hundred and sixty-five propositions, from only those, in order, each meant to use nothing but
what came before (he sometimes leans on things he never stated, and later geometers filled
those in). Not ``trust me.'' Not ``it's well known.'' Here are the rules you and I both accept;
now watch. If you've ever been in an argument that ended with ``well, that's just your
opinion,'' Euclid is the man who found a way out of that room, and I'm not embarrassed to say
I learned the way out from someone dead for two thousand three hundred years. Four hundred and
sixty-five times he does the same trick, and the trick is everything.

And then there's the one rule Euclid seems almost embarrassed by, and it's a hole worth falling into. His
fifth postulate, the one about parallel lines, is long and awkward next to the others, and for two
thousand years people tried to prove it from the rest so it wouldn't have to be assumed. Proclus
tried. Mathematicians in Persia and the Arab world tried. In 1733 an Italian priest named Girolamo Saccheri spent a
whole book assuming it was false so he could watch the contradiction arrive, and he got pages deep
into what is now a perfectly good geometry before declaring that it was repugnant and stopping. A
century later three people, separately, took the step he wouldn't: drop the postulate, and you
don't get nonsense, you get other geometries that hold up just as well. Farkas Bolyai begged his
son János to stay away from the problem, warning that it had swallowed years of his own life; the son went in anyway
and came out with one of those geometries. Here's the part I keep: they found something real by
refusing to believe one of the rules everyone accepted, and checking what happened without it.
That's the push, two thousand years long.

What is structure, to Euclid? Whatever the starting rules force. And when are two shapes the
same? Here's the one you can do: cut out two paper triangles and lay one on the other. If
they coincide, they're equal. That's his fourth common notion, and it's how he proves his
fourth proposition, by picking up one triangle and setting it down on another. Sameness is
coinciding under a move. Keep that; it's about to get very general, and I didn't see that
coming either.

\subsection{The statue and the bronze}

Aristotle, Plato's student, pulled the forms down out of heaven and put them inside things,
which was a bit rude to his teacher and also, I think, correct. His example, from the
\emph{Metaphysics}: a bronze statue is bronze plus a shape, and being made of bronze is no part of
what it is to be a statue. The same shape in marble makes a different statue with the same form.
Matter and form, and form is what the thing \emph{is}.

Push on it. Is that true? Take anything on your desk. Could the same thing be made of
something else? A coffee cup, sure. A sandwich, no; a sandwich made of wood is a sculpture of
a sandwich, and if you've ever tried to eat one you know the difference matters. So the claim
doesn't hold everywhere. It holds exactly where the material was never doing the work, and
that's a sharper thing than Aristotle said: structure is what survives a change of material,
in the places where the material didn't matter. Why do I care? Because the machine I keep
mentioning and not describing gets built more than once, in more than one material, and I'd
like it to be the same machine every time, and I don't get to just say it is. That's a
promise I make in Part IV (Section~\ref{sec:onemachine}) and have to keep in Part V (Section~\ref{sec:chip}), and Aristotle is the one who told me what the
promise means.

\subsection{Where things are, without numbers}

In 1679 Gottfried Leibniz, who co-invented calculus and had opinions about everything, wrote
to the physicist Christiaan Huygens asking for something that didn't exist: a way to reason
about \emph{where} things are directly, the way algebra reasons about \emph{how much}, without ever
laying down coordinates. He called it the analysis of situation. Try it yourself. Describe
where the furniture is in the room you're sitting in without using a single number. ``The couch
is against the wall. The table is between the couch and the window. The lamp is next to the
chair.'' You just did it, and what you used was relations between places and nothing else.
Huygens wrote back that November and was not impressed. It took roughly two hundred years for
Leibniz's idea to become a field, and the field is called topology, and Huygens is remembered
for other things.

What survives the push is the same thing that survived the square, coming at you from the
other side. Position is a relation among places. The numbers you lay on top are a
convenience, and they're a convenience you can take away and still have the room. I'll be
honest about why this one landed for me: the thing I built keeps track of which things
belong together, and I spent a long time thinking that was a list of numbers before I
understood it was a relation that the numbers were merely naming. Leibniz had that in 1679.
Huygens told him no. I'd like to think I'd have sided with Leibniz. I probably would have
sided with the famous guy.

\subsection{Naming a thing by saying when two are the same}

In 1884, in a short book called \emph{The Foundations of Arithmetic}, Gottlob Frege noticed
something you can check in your head right now. ``Line $a$ is parallel to line $b$'' and ``the
direction of $a$ is the direction of $b$'' say exactly the same thing. There is no fact in one
that isn't in the other. But the second sentence has a new object in it, a \emph{direction}, that
the first one doesn't. Where did it come from? From the sameness. Once you can say when two
things count as the same, you've earned the right to name the thing they share. Frege used
exactly this move to say what a number is: the number of things in a pile is whatever every
pile you can match up with it, one to one, has in common. That's a residue with teeth: a
sameness relation lets you name a new object.

Now push, because Frege pushed too hard, and it cost him. In his big system he also assumed
that any condition you can state picks out a collection, the collection of everything that
satisfies it. In June of 1902, a young Bertrand Russell wrote him a short letter. Consider
the collection of all collections that are not members of themselves. Is it a member of
itself? If it is, then by its own rule it isn't. If it isn't, then it qualifies, so it is. Do
it in your head; it flips every time you look at it, like one of those drawings that's a vase
and then two faces and then a vase. Frege's floor had a hole in it, and he knew it the day he
opened the letter, and his second volume was already at the printer. The repair came from
Ernst Zermelo in 1908 and it's the one mathematics still stands on: you may only cut a
collection out of a collection you were \emph{already given}. You don't get to sort ``everything.''
You sort a pile. I'll tell you now that this rule shows up again, later, in a place where I
had to obey it or fall through the same hole, and I'll point at it when the book gets there.

Frege's reply is worth hearing, because it's the best example I know of how to lose. He wrote
back within days. He didn't hide it or argue around it. He said, more or less, that arithmetic was
tottering, and in an appendix to the volume that was about to come out he wrote that hardly
anything worse can happen to a scientific writer than having a foundation give way right after the
work is finished. Then he tried to fix it. If I'm wrong about something in this book, and I'd bet
I am somewhere, that's how I'd like to take it.

\subsection{Choose the changes, keep what survives}

By 1872 there were too many geometries. Euclid's, and ones where parallel lines meet, and
ones with no such thing as distance, and nobody could say what made them all geometry rather
than a pile of unrelated hobbies. Felix Klein, twenty-three years old and taking up a
professorship at Erlangen, published an answer in a program paper that people still call the
Erlangen program. Pick a set of allowed changes: rotations, stretches, whatever you decide.
Then a geometry is the study of the properties that \emph{stay the same} under those changes. Pick
a different set of changes and you get a different geometry on the very same page. Euclid's
is the one where you may slide and turn a shape but not stretch it. And here's the part I'd
underline if this were my book, which it is: in Klein's scheme any group of changes can define
a geometry. The choice is free. Nobody tells you which changes to allow.

You can do this one at your desk. Take any drawing and ask what's still true after you turn
it upside down (lengths, angles), after you stretch it (not lengths anymore, but which lines
cross which), after you crumple it (almost nothing but what touches what). Three answers,
three structures, one drawing. The residue: structure is what survives a chosen set of
changes, and ``chosen'' is doing real work in that sentence. There's no structure of a thing
from nowhere. You have to say what you're allowed to do to it first. I didn't know that when
I started, and I'd been saying ``the structure of'' things for years.

\subsection{An invariance comes with a bill}

In 1918 Emmy Noether, who wasn't allowed to hold a professorship because she was a woman and
for a while lectured under a male colleague's name, proved something that physicists still
treat as close to holy. Take a physical system whose laws can be written the way most of
physics is written, as ``of all the paths the system could take, it takes the one that makes a
certain total smallest'' (the total is called the action, and that's all I'll say about it
here). For such a system, every continuous symmetry of the laws comes with a quantity that is
conserved. If the laws don't care \emph{where} you are, momentum is conserved. If they don't care
\emph{when} it is, energy is. A symmetry isn't decoration. It has a consequence downstream that
you can measure with instruments. I can't hand you this one to do at the table; the proof
needs calculus I'd have to build first and I'd lose you and probably me, and the ``written
as an action'' condition is doing real work that I'm not going to unpack here. What I can hand you is the
shape. Structure, once it's really there and the setting is the right kind, has consequences
you can measure. I'll admit that's the sentence that made me think a machine could carry a
bill for structure in the first place, and I'll also admit I don't yet know whether that
hope was reasonable. Noether makes it reasonable to ask. She doesn't make it true, and
nothing I build in this book is a system with an action.

\subsection{All of mathematics as structures}

Starting in the 1930s, a group of young French mathematicians began publishing a vast
treatise under one made-up name, Nicolas Bourbaki, as if he were a single person. He wasn't.
He also applied for membership in the American Mathematical Society and was turned down,
which I find comforting. Their goal was to rebuild all of mathematics on one idea: a
structure is a set of elements ``whose nature has not been specified,'' together with one or
more relations on them that satisfy stated axioms. They believed three kinds of structure
were the mothers of all the rest: algebraic, order, and topological.

Push on it, and here's what the historian Leo Corry found when he went through the entire
treatise looking for the place where this formal definition of structure actually does any
work: it ``plays no actual role in the presentation of theories within the treatise.'' Outside
the chapter that defines it, almost nowhere. And I found no argument in their writing for why
the mother structures number three. And the chapter on category theory,
which they announced, never appeared. Why? The thing their definition left out was the \emph{maps},
the ways of carrying a structure from one set to another, and it turned out the maps were
where the weight was. So I keep two things from Bourbaki. The right thing: relations on
elements whose nature doesn't matter, which is Aristotle's bronze in different words. And the
warning: a structure stated without its maps won't carry the work. I learned that one the
slow way, and the origin story you just read tells it.

\subsection{A set with some named relations}

What mathematical logic eventually settled on, with Alfred Tarski giving the field its name,
``the theory of models,'' in 1954, is almost boring, and the boring ones are the ones that
last. A structure is a set, called the domain, plus whatever relations and functions a
chosen vocabulary names on it. Pick the vocabulary (Klein again: you choose), and a structure
is anything that gives those names a meaning. Now I want to say ``the smallest one,'' and the
word ``smallest'' has no meaning until I say what I'm measuring, so here is the ruler: count
the vocabulary. One name, taking one thing at a time, with two possible answers. That's a
domain with one yes-or-no property named on it. One question, put to each thing. Two honest
limits, and I'd rather give them to you than have you find them. A vocabulary with one named
constant (``this one, here'') is exactly as small by my ruler and it doesn't sort anything, so
``smallest that sorts'' is the claim, not ``smallest.'' And one question only splits the domain
into two groups when some things answer yes and some answer no; if they all agree there's
one group and nothing was sorted. With those limits said, and with the ruler said: by the
count of names, the smallest structure that sorts anything is one question. Someone with a
different ruler (fewest symbols to write down, say, or least information) might land
somewhere else, and I'd want to see where. Keep it. It's about to turn into the whole
section.

\subsection{The structure is in the arrows}

This is the one I met first, backwards. I'd built it by feel, in a rendering engine, as
``digital DNA,'' and only went looking for its name after the thing already ran. In 1945
Samuel Eilenberg and Saunders Mac Lane published a paper that founded a field now called
category theory, and they said in plain words that it was a continuation of Klein, which I'd
have loved to know at the time. The move: stop asking what a thing is, and ask how it's
carried. A category is some objects and
some arrows between them, where arrows can be followed one after another and every object has
a do-nothing arrow to itself, plus two rules that make the following dependable: following
three arrows in a row gives the same result whether you pair up the first two or the last
two, and the do-nothing arrow really does nothing when you tack it onto either end. That's
the whole definition, and I know it sounds like nothing. The two rules are the part people
skip, and they're the part you'll watch me have to prove later. What a thing \emph{is} is how it
maps. For now the residue is the one Bourbaki missed: structure lives in the maps. Whether the thing I built honours that, you'll be able to
judge when I build the category in front of you, from scratch, later in this book.

\subsection{Structure is the part that compresses}

Play this one with me. I write ``th'' and you guess the next letter. You said ``e,'' and you were
right. Now ``the q'': you said ``u.'' Congratulations, you just measured the structure of English.
In 1948 Claude Shannon measured it properly, in a paper that founded information theory, and
found that about half of written English is ``determined by the structure of the language.''
It's the reason a zip file of a long letter is so much smaller than the letter.
Be careful what that says. It does not say that every other letter is fixed by the ones
before it; you just guessed ``e'' after ``th'' and you could have been wrong (think ``than''). It
says that, on average and over long stretches, about half of what's written could be
rebuilt from the rest: the text is roughly twice as long as the choices in it. And he said
why that matters in one line that I'd frame if I framed things: the structure ``allows one to
make a saving in time.'' The more you can predict, the less you have to read.

Thirty years later Jorma Rissanen turned that saving into a price. His idea is called the
minimum description length principle, and it says: the best model of some data is the one
that makes the total description shortest, where the total is the length of the model \emph{plus}
the length of the data once the model has explained what it can. A model is paid for in bits.
It's worth stating only if it saves more than it costs. Peter Grünwald, in a tutorial you can
find online, adds the footnote that keeps this honest: the price of a model depends on the
code you chose to write it in, so the price itself needs a principle behind it, and nobody
hands you that principle for free.

That's a lot of ``length of'' to swallow in one paragraph, so do one with me, with
numbers small enough to check on the back of an envelope. Every number in it comes from a
code I'm about to make up on the spot, and I'll say every rule of the code out loud, because
Grünwald's footnote is the whole point: change the rules and every number moves.

Here's the data. A row of thirty-two digits, each a 0 or a 1, and you and I agree in advance
that the row is thirty-two long, so nobody has to spend anything saying so:

\[\texttt{0101010101010101 0101010101010101}\]

(The space is only there to rest your eyes.) Now the code. Every description starts with one
digit that says which kind of description follows: 0 means ``here's the row, written out,'' 1
means ``here's a pattern, then the exceptions to it.'' Each digit is one yes-or-no answer, one
bit, which is what Shannon's unit is. Written out, the row costs that first digit plus the
thirty-two digits themselves: thirty-three bits, and there's no model in it at all. A pattern
description goes like this. First five digits giving the length of a little block, anything
from 1 to 32, because five yes-or-no answers can pick out one of thirty-two lengths. Then the
block itself. The rule is ``repeat the block until you have thirty-two digits.'' Then five digits
for how many places the row disagrees with the pattern (up to thirty-one, which is plenty here), and
five more digits for each of those places, saying which of the thirty-two it is.

Do it for the row above. The block is $\texttt{01}$, two digits long. So the model costs 1 (which
kind) plus 5 (the block's length) plus 2 (the block): eight bits. Then what's left to say
about the data once the model has said its piece: the row disagrees with ``repeat 01''
nowhere, so that's five digits saying ``zero exceptions'' and nothing else. Five bits. Total,
thirteen, against thirty-three for writing it out. The pattern pays for itself, with twenty
bits to spare. That's Rissanen's sentence happening on paper: a model is worth stating when
it saves more than it costs.

Now spoil the row. Flip two of its digits anywhere you like. The model doesn't change, eight
bits, but now the leftover says ``two exceptions, here and here'': five plus five plus five,
fifteen. Total twenty-three. Still cheaper than thirty-three; the pattern still pays, it just
pays less, because the data has more to say that the model can't. Flip four, and the total
is $8 + 5 + 4 \times 5 = 33$, a dead tie. Flip five and it's thirty-eight, and now writing the
row out is cheaper than explaining it, and by Rissanen's rule you shouldn't state the pattern
at all, even though it's still sort of there if you squint. So ``is there structure here?'' has
turned into a question with a number on each side, and a break-even point you can find
yourself: somewhere between four and five spoiled digits, in this code.

And now change the code, because I promised you'd see the numbers move. Say I'd used six digits
for each exception's place instead of five (wasteful, but nobody stopped me). Then four
spoiled digits cost $8 + 5 + 4 \times 6 = 37$, and the tie is gone; the pattern stopped paying
one spoiled digit sooner. Same row, same pattern, different verdict, and the only thing that
changed was a convention I chose. That's Grünwald's footnote, and it's why I won't let you
take any of those numbers anywhere else. They're the price of a description in one made-up
code, a length of a written-down message, and nothing more. They are not the charge I opened
this book with. That charge, when the book finally states it, is on one step a machine
takes, not on how long anybody's description is, and if the two ever turn out to be related,
that has to be shown, not assumed from both of them being counted in whole numbers.

Now push, because this is where ``structure means information'' gets born, and it's wrong, and
it's an easy thing to believe. Flip a fair coin two hundred times and write down the string.
Almost always, there's no shorter way to say that string than to say the whole thing. You can
watch it happen in the little code above, cut to thirty-two digits: a coin-flip row disagrees
with ``repeat 01'' in about sixteen places, which would cost eighty-odd bits to list,
and even the one block guaranteed to fit with no exceptions, the whole row used as its own
block, costs $1 + 5 + 32 + 5 = 43$. The written-out row at thirty-three wins, and no pattern
earns its keep. Nikolai
Vereshchagin and Paul Vitányi, in a 2004 paper on exactly this question, put it without
mercy: every bit of a string like that is ``meaningless information, random noise.'' Maximum information. Zero
structure. So in this sense structure is the part that compresses, the part where the ``th''
tells you about the ``e,'' and most information and most structure are different things. Hold
that one tightly, because if you built something that charged for information, you'd be
charging for the wrong thing, and for a while I wasn't sure which one I'd built.

And now notice that the word just changed meaning on you, and on me, and I'd rather point at
it than let it slide. Shannon and Rissanen and Vereshchagin mean \emph{regularity}: a pattern that
lets you say something shorter. Tarski, a few pages back, and Halmos, coming up, mean a set
with named relations on it, and
those two are not the same thing. Here's the test, and you can run it: number a thousand
objects, flip a coin for each, heads goes in group one, tails in group two. That's a perfectly
good sorting in the set theorist's sense, every object in exactly one group. And the list of
who went where is a thousand coin flips, which is to say it compresses about as well as a
thousand coin flips, which is to say not at all. Feed it to a code built like the little one,
with the fields widened to fit a thousand, and you get the coin-flip row again, only longer: no block earns its keep, the written-out list wins, and by
Rissanen's rule there's no pattern worth stating. By the set theorist's rule, the sorting
\emph{is} the structure, and it's every bit as much a sorting as ``evens in one group, odds in the
other,'' which compresses to almost nothing. Same kind of object, wildly different
description lengths. So the two meanings don't even rank things the same way: one asks ``is
there a sorting?'' and the answer is yes for both; the other asks ``does a short rule say who
went where?'' and the answer is yes for evens and odds and no for the coins. Structure in the
set theorist's sense, none in Rissanen's. I'll keep both meanings, and I'll try to say which
one I'm using, and when I slip you'll know what to look for.

\subsection{The four parts of every computer}

In 1936 Alan Turing described the machine that every computer you've ever touched is a
version of, and he did it before any of them existed. It's the clerk with the pencil from the
opening chapter, written down as a machine. Write down its parts; there are four.
A tape, divided into squares. A head that reads one square at a time and can write on it and
move left or right. A finite list of states the head can be in. A table of rules: in this
state, reading this symbol, do this. That's all, and two different things are true about it
that get run together. Every other formal recipe for ``a procedure'' that anyone has written
down since computes exactly what this one does; those are theorems, proved one pairing at a
time, and Turing proved the first of them himself. That it also captures everything a person
could ever carry out by rote, everything ``computable'' in the plain-English sense, is a
claim, called the Church-Turing thesis, and nobody has proved it, because the plain-English
side isn't a mathematical object. Turing himself kept those two apart in the 1936 paper, and
so will I. There's a third claim that gets stacked on top, and it's a different kind again:
the physical Church-Turing thesis, that every device you could build out of real stuff
computes no more than this machine does. That one is a claim about physics, not mathematics.
Nobody has built a device that breaks it. Your laptop, your phone, every server in every data
center compute nothing a Turing machine can't; what differs between them is speed, space,
energy, and cost. Hold on to that last word. Cost is where this book lives.

Now do the thing I did, and do it honestly. Look through those four parts for a place that says ``these squares belong
together.'' I couldn't find one. Any grouping has to live in the table, as a rule, or on the
tape, as marks, which is to say as bytes like any other bytes. Maybe you can find a slot I
missed. I'd want to know. I looked for a long time and I kept not finding it, and not finding
something is weaker than proving it isn't there, so I'll be careful about what I claim from
that.

In 1972 David Parnas, a software engineer, wrote a short paper that every programmer should
be made to read and most haven't, on how to cut a program into modules. He took one small
program and cut it two ways. Both worked. But one was easy to change later and the other
wasn't, and the easy one could be ``much less efficient'' if talking between modules cost
anything. His point: a module is ``a responsibility assignment,'' a decision about who answers
for what, and how you cut decides what every later change costs. If you've ever maintained
someone else's code, you've paid Parnas's bill, probably at two in the morning. What survives
the push: a division is a commitment, not a caption. It changes what the work costs. It is not
a label stuck on afterwards. I'd like to say the thing I built understood that from the
beginning. It didn't. I did, eventually.

\subsection{Laying them all down}

Now lay every one of those on top of the others and see what shows through. Here are the
seven things I think I see. Be clear about what
this is: it's my overlay, the places where I see the sources agreeing, and not a thing the
sources proved together. They didn't; some of them never met, and some of them disagree
(Bourbaki left out the maps that Eilenberg and Mac Lane built everything on; Shannon's
structure and Tarski's are two different words, as I just showed you). You've pushed on each
source yourself by now, so you're in a position to tell me if I'm seeing things.

A list of seven slogans would be easy to nod at and impossible to check, so I'm going to
carry one thing through all seven and let you watch each one add to the one before it. The
thing is the square you drew for the Pythagoreans, side, diagonal and all. Draw a few more
on the same sheet: one small, one big, the small one again but tilted, and one stretched
out into a long rectangle. You'll want a pile.

Structure is about relations among things, not the things. The diagonal, the bronze,
Leibniz's room, Bourbaki's unspecified elements, Tarski's named relations, the arrows. On
your sheet, what makes a square a square was never the ink. It's that the four sides match
and the corners are square, and that the diagonal stands to the side the way it does whether
or not any number names it. Every one of those is a relation among parts. But on its own
this first thing is too loose to use, because a sheet of paper is drowning in relations:
this square is left of that one, this one is nearer the coffee ring. Which relations count?

Structure is what stays the same under a chosen set of changes. Euclid's triangles laid
together, Klein's allowed moves, Noether's symmetry, Frege's direction that every parallel
line shares. That's the answer the first thing was missing. The relations that count are the
ones that survive the moves you've decided to allow. Slide the small square across the
sheet, turn it, and the diagonal still stands to the side exactly as before; ``left of the
coffee ring'' doesn't make it across. The second thing is a filter on the first.

The same structure can be carried by different stuff. The statue in marble. Two sets that
answer the same vocabulary the same way. This is the second thing again with one more change
allowed: swap the material. Cut the square out of cardboard, or lay it out in string on the
table, and if the relations survive, it's the same square in every way you agreed to care
about. Aristotle's bronze turns out to be one more thing you agreed not to look at, and the
wooden sandwich is what happens when the material was never on that list.

The first act of structure is a sameness that sorts a pile you were already given. Euclid's
first common notion, Frege's direction, Tarski's one question, and Russell's letter saying
you must start from a pile. This is where the overlay stopped being a list for me and turned
into a shape, so slow down here with me. Look at your pile of drawings and say: two of them
count as the same when an allowed move carries one exactly onto the other. Watch what
happens to the pile. It falls into groups. The small square and its tilted twin go together;
the big one sits on its own; the rectangle sits on its own. And it falls cleanly, nothing
half in one group and half in another, for a reason you can check. Klein's allowed moves
always come with three guarantees: doing nothing counts as a move, every move can be undone,
and two moves in a row is again a move. Those three are, word for word in different
clothes, ``everything is the same as itself,'' ``if this matches that, then that matches this,''
and Euclid's first common notion, ``things equal to the same thing are equal to each other.''
So the second thing, sameness under chosen moves, \emph{is} a sorting of the pile the moment you
ask which drawings it calls the same. Frege did it with lines and parallels. Tarski's one
question does it in the crudest way there is, by cutting the pile in two. And the pile has to
be there first, because a sameness has to be a sameness among something; that's Russell's
letter, and Zermelo's repair.

Adding structure rules possibilities out. Every one of Euclid's postulates is a door closed.
Half of English is already decided. A conserved quantity limits where a system can go. On
your sheet: once the small square and its tilted twin are in one group, you've given up the
right to answer any question the moves respect differently for the two of them. Tell me the
side of one and the diagonal of the other isn't an open question any more. A sorting is a
bundle of doors closed at once.

Held structure gets used without re-deriving it. Shannon's saving in time. Rissanen's
compression. Parnas's one-module-at-a-time. Leibniz, who hoped his algebra of position would
spare people a great many fruitless tries. This is the fifth thing paying out. The doors you
closed are doors you never have to check again: know which group a drawing is in and you know
everything the group shares without getting the ruler out, the same way the row of
$\texttt{01}$ never needed writing out. With one catch that I'll need a whole section for:
it only pays if you kept the sorting somewhere you can read it back.

And structure is always relative to a chosen frame. Klein's group. The vocabulary. The code
you compress against. Parnas's criteria. Nobody gets to say ``the'' structure of a thing
without saying from where, and I do it constantly, so watch me for it. On your
sheet: allow stretching as one of the moves and the rectangle walks over and joins the
squares; allow only slides and turns and it doesn't. Same pile, same ink, different groups,
because I chose different moves. The groups were never in the paper. They were in the paper
and the choice, together.

So here's how I think they hang together. Relations are what structure is made of. The
chosen moves pick which relations count, and a change of material is just one more move.
Asking which things the moves call the same sorts the pile. The sorting closes doors, and
closed doors are what you get to skip later. And because the moves were chosen, all of it is
relative. Read that way, the fourth thing sits in the middle: it's where the first three
turn into something you can write down, and where the last three get their start.

That's my reason for starting the next section with a sorting, and I want to be exact about
what kind of reason it is, because it's mine and not theirs. None of these people said
``start with a partition.'' Klein would tell you to start with the moves, Eilenberg and Mac Lane
with the arrows, Shannon with the probabilities. What I can actually point at is narrower. In
the framings about when two things are the same shape or the same kind (Euclid laying one
triangle on another, Klein's moves, Frege's directions, Tarski's question) there's a moment
where somebody decides what counts as the same, and that decision, written down, is a sorting
of a pile. In Shannon, Rissanen and Noether I can't find that moment as cleanly, and I'm not
going to bend them until I do. So the overlay doesn't prove that a sorting comes first. It
shows me where the framings I trust most keep putting their first foot down, and I'm putting
mine there too.

I looked for a framing that denies any of the seven and didn't find one, which could mean
there isn't one or could mean I didn't look where it lives. If you know of one, I'd like to
see it.

\subsection{The smallest piece}

Now the sentence I wanted to say at the top and had no right to until here, and even here I
have to split it in two, because half of it is a textbook fact and the other half is me. The
piece of structure I'm going to start from is a partition.

The textbook half: a partition and an equivalence relation are the same object. That's Paul
Halmos, \emph{Naive Set Theory}, 1960, section seven, and you could read that section before
dinner. Here it is in words. Take
any pile of things. An equivalence relation on it is a way of saying ``these two count as the
same'' that behaves the way sameness should: everything is the same as itself; if $a$ is the
same as $b$ then $b$ is the same as $a$; and if $a$ is the same as $b$ and $b$ the same as
$c$, then $a$ is the same as $c$. Every such relation sorts the pile into groups, the things
that count as the same go together, and every sorting into groups hands you back a relation,
``same group.'' Do one and then the other and you land where you started, in both directions.
So a partition and an equivalence relation are one object seen from two sides, and that's the
fourth thing on the overlay, the sorting of a given pile, now with a name and a page number.

Here it is in the exact form, since this is the first place the book uses one. A \emph{set} is a
pile, $x \in X$ means ``$x$ is in the pile $X$,'' and a \emph{relation} on $X$ is any rule $\sim$
that, for each pair of things, says whether $x \sim y$ holds. A few more marks show up below,
and each is a word in disguise. $S_1, \ldots, S_k$ are the buckets, numbered one to $k$. A
cap, $S_j \cap S_l$, is ``what the two buckets share,'' a cup, $S_1 \cup \cdots \cup S_k$, is
``everything in any bucket,'' and $\emptyset$ is the empty pile. And curly braces with a colon,
$\{\, y \in X : y \sim x \,\}$, mean ``the pile of every $y$ in $X$ for which $y \sim x$
holds''; the theorem writes that pile $[x]$, the things that count as the same as $x$.

\begin{definition}[Equivalence relation, partition]\label{def:equiv-partition}
A relation $\sim$ on a set $X$ is an \emph{equivalence relation} when it is reflexive
($x \sim x$), symmetric ($x \sim y$ implies $y \sim x$), and transitive ($x \sim y$ and
$y \sim z$ imply $x \sim z$). A \emph{partition} of $X$ is a collection of non-empty subsets of $X$,
the blocks, such that every member of $X$ lies in exactly one block. Spelled out for blocks
$S_1, \ldots, S_k$: each $S_j$ is non-empty, no two share a member ($S_j \cap S_l = \emptyset$
when $j \ne l$), and together they cover everything ($S_1 \cup \cdots \cup S_k = X$).
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Sameness and sorting are one object]\label{thm:equiv-partition}
Every equivalence relation on $X$ determines a partition, whose blocks are the classes
$[x] = \{\, y \in X : y \sim x \,\}$; every partition determines an equivalence relation,
``$x$ and $y$ lie in the same block''; and the two constructions undo each other.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The classes are non-empty ($x \in [x]$ by reflexivity) and cover $X$. If $z$ lies in $[x]$ and
in $[y]$, then $z \sim x$ and $z \sim y$, so $x \sim y$ by symmetry and transitivity, and then
$[x] = [y]$ by transitivity again; so the blocks don't overlap. ``Same block'' is plainly
reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. Going relation to partition to relation returns
$x \sim y$ exactly when $x$ and $y$ share a class, which is the original relation; going
partition to relation to partition returns the original blocks.
\end{proof}

This is textbook mathematics (Halmos, section 7), and the book uses it as a foundation, not
as a contribution.

And the smallest structure that sorts, by my ruler in Tarski's setup, the one question, is
the same object a third time. Put a yes-or-no question to every thing in the pile. The ones that say yes are one
group and the ones that say no are the other. Going the other way, a two-group partition
becomes a question the moment you point at one group and call it ``yes.'' The only thing a
question has that the partition doesn't is which group got the label. So the set theorist's
first step and the logician's first step are the same step, and nobody has to pick a side,
which is a relief, because it's an argument you can lose with yourself for a long time.

That's the textbook half. Now mine, and hold it looser, because Halmos says nothing about
``smallest'' or ``first'' and I'd be lying if I let his page number carry my sentence. In what
I'm going to build, the order goes: a pile, then groups in the pile, then whatever connects
one group to another, and the groups come first because a question needs something to be
about and a connection needs somewhere to land. That's an order for \emph{my}
construction. It is not a law that every account of structure has to start by sorting. You
could start with an ordering instead (``this one comes before that one''), or with arrows
between the things themselves and no groups at all, and people do, and nothing I've shown you
rules that out. So the honest sentence is: a partition is where I chose to start, it is the
smallest start by the ruler I gave you, and I chose it because it's the first thing that can
be right or wrong about a pile and the last thing I could take away without everything I
build on it coming down. If you have a smaller start by a ruler you can state, I want to see
it. It would change this book.

\subsection{Buckets}

So here's the smallest piece, done once, for real. Take everything in front of you and sort
it into buckets: nothing in two buckets, nothing left on the floor. That's the whole of the
definition. It's the thing you do with a kindergartner and a pile of blocks, and I am aware
that I've just marched you past Pythagoras, Plato, Euclid, Frege and Noether to arrive at a
pile of blocks. Keep the blocks anyway. They're about to cost you something.

Ten blocks. Red ones in one bucket, square ones in another, everything else in a third. Now a
red square turns up, as they do, and you've got your first crisis: it belongs in two buckets
and the rule says one. So this isn't a partition yet, and you have to decide which bucket
wins. That decision is the whole thing. A partition is a pile of small rulings like that one,
and once you've made them all, the pile is holding a fact it wasn't holding a minute ago. The
formal version says the same thing with fewer words and more squiggles, and you've already seen
it: it's the definition of a partition a few pages back (Definition~\ref{def:equiv-partition}). Non-empty
buckets, nothing in two, nothing on the floor.

Here's the part that isn't kindergarten. Why would that fact cost anything? Watch what it does to one question. Before the buckets, ``are
these two in the same group?'' means working it out: go find the first one, go find the
second one, apply the rule to each, compare. After the buckets, it's a glance: read the first
one's bucket, read the second one's bucket, done. And the glance costs the same when the pile
goes from ten blocks to a billion. That's Shannon's saving in time and Parnas's
one-module-at-a-time, the sixth thing on the overlay, showing up in a kindergarten.

Now push on it, because that paragraph sells more than it should, and I want you to see
where. The partition didn't give you the glance. A \emph{table} gave you the glance: a written-down line
for each block saying which bucket it went in. The partition is the fact; the table is one
way of holding the fact so it can be read back fast, and you had to build the table, and
you have to store it, and it has to be the kind of thing you can read in one look (a bucket
number, say, and not a list of every block in the bucket that you'd have to search through
again). Anybody who's used a database has met this table; it's what an index is, and an
index is a thing you build, store, and keep up to date, not a thing you get for free. Take the
table away and keep the partition and you're back to working it out. And
sometimes there was never a search to save: if the rule is ``evens here, odds there,'' you can
answer ``same group?'' by looking at the last digit of each, no buckets needed. So the honest
residue is smaller than the sentence I wanted: holding a sorting in a form you can read back
is worth something, and building that form cost something, and those are already two
different events. Building the table, storing it, checking that it's right, and deciding to
\emph{rely} on it are four different things. The question this book is about lives in the gap
between the third and the fourth, and nothing in the kindergarten has shown you yet that
there's a charge in that gap. It's shown you there might be a place for one.

So who, in everything I read, says what the bill is? I found three answers that come close,
and I'll be exact about how close, because this is the edge of what I know. Rolf Landauer, in
1961, and Charles Bennett after him, say that any step which takes two possible situations
and makes them one, erasing a bit or merging two paths a computation could have taken, has to
push some disorder out into the world, which in a real machine means heat. That's not a
metaphor; it's the one place where a fact about information turns into a fact about your
electricity bill, and it's been measured. Is sending blocks to buckets a step of that kind?
Push, because it depends on what you keep. If you keep each block and write its bucket next
to it, you've lost nothing; you can read the block right back off the pair, and Bennett's
whole point in his 1973 paper was that a computation which keeps its inputs can be run
without any such step at all. If instead you throw the block away and keep only the bucket
label, then two different blocks can leave the same label behind, and that is a many-to-one
step, the kind Landauer charges for. Both are things people call ``sorting into buckets.'' Only
the second loses a distinction. So the bucket by itself doesn't hand you a Landauer bill; the
\emph{forgetting} does, when there is forgetting, and whether a given machine forgets is a
question about that machine, which has to be answered on the page and not waved at here.
Rissanen says a model is paid for in the bits it takes to state, and Grünwald says the price
depends on the code. Parnas says a bad cut is paid for later, at two in the morning. And
that's where it stops. I couldn't find anyone who says that the moment you \emph{vouch} for a
grouping, the moment you stand behind ``these belong together'' instead of just arranging them
that way, has a price of its own. That could mean nobody says it. It could mean I didn't find
the person who does. I honestly can't tell you which.

So that's where I am at the end of one word. Holding a sorting in readable form is worth
something and cost something, forgetting where things came from costs heat, and standing
behind a sorting is a different act from either, and nobody I found has priced it. You can
walk back through all of that and tell me where it breaks. Maybe there's no such bill. Maybe
I'm about to spend a book chasing a charge that nobody owes, which would be an extremely me
thing to do. The next section is me trying to find out whether that charge is real on any
machine at all, not mine, any machine, and if the answer comes back no, you should stop
reading there. I would have stopped writing there too.


\part{The axiom}

%===========================================================================
\section{A record and a toll}
\label{sec:toll}
%===========================================================================

I left you with a question I couldn't answer: something pays for the glance, and I couldn't
find anyone who says the moment of vouching for a grouping has a price of its own. Before I
go looking for that price in anything complicated, I want to try the opposite. Build the
smallest thing that could possibly carry such a bill, on paper, with a pencil, write the bill
into its rules, and see what follows from it. If nothing follows in something with five
parts, nothing is going to follow in something with five thousand, and I'd rather find that
out on page one than on page four hundred.

But first the word, because I've got a new one and I don't trust it either. Record. Receipt.
Certificate. Vouch. People have been making marks that other people are supposed to rely on
for a very long time, and I wanted to know what they thought they were doing, and what it
cost them, and whether any of them ever said the thing I need said. So, same deal as before:
here's what I could reach, pushed on with you, and I'll tell you where the search ran out.

\subsection{Clay, seals, and seven witnesses}

Start about five thousand years ago, in the Near East, with people who counted sheep with
little clay tokens. To send a count across a distance without the courier changing it, they
put the tokens inside a hollow clay ball, pressed the shapes of the tokens onto the outside
while the clay was soft, and sealed it. The archaeologist Denise Schmandt-Besserat has
spent a career on these; the ball is called a bulla. Here's the push, and you can do it with
a cookie tin: the thing that makes it a record isn't the tokens, it's that the outside shows
what's inside and you have to break it to get in. Opening it destroys it. Tampering shows.
That's a real idea and it will show up again in a form you won't expect: a record is worth
something only if it can't be silently undone.

Now law, which is where people get serious about who's allowed to say what happened. The
book of Deuteronomy, chapter nineteen: nobody is convicted on the word of one witness; it
takes ``two or three.'' The Roman jurist Gaius, writing in the second century, says a will the
praetor will honour is one sealed by seven witnesses. Seven. Why did they care that much?
Because one person can lie, and a will moves a fortune, and the dead man can't object. So
the record isn't the paper. It's the number of independent people who have put their own
seal, their own name, their own risk, next to the claim. Try it: write ``paid five dollars,
signed A'' on a napkin and ask a friend to forge it. Takes them ten seconds. Now require two
other people to initial it at the moment of payment and each keep a copy. Your forger needs
two accomplices or has to match two copies held in two other pockets. The claim didn't change.
What stands behind it did.

Which brings me to seals, and the medieval historian Michael Clanchy, whose book is called
\emph{From Memory to Written Record}. England between the Norman Conquest and the early 1300s was
learning to trust writing instead of trusting people who remembered, and the lesson was
painful: seals were forged, charters were forged, and historians today have a whole craft of
telling real charters from fake ones because the fakes are so many. A seal is only as good as
whoever holds the stamp. Keep that one too, because in 2011 a certificate authority called
DigiNotar found out, at the cost of its existence, that a mathematically perfect signature is
worth exactly what the custody of the key is worth, and intruders had taken control of the
machines that signed. Nine
hundred years, same failure. I find that oddly comforting.

And then the obvious next question: if seals could be forged, what caught the forgeries? Not
the seals. The most famous forged record in European history is the Donation of Constantine,
a document in which the emperor Constantine supposedly handed rule over Rome and the western
empire to the Pope. It was most likely written in the eighth century, some four hundred years
after Constantine died, and it was leaned on for centuries. Around 1440 a scholar named
Lorenzo Valla took it apart by its Latin: the language belonged to a much later age, and it
used words, ``satraps'' among them, that no Roman of Constantine's day would have used for his
officials. (Valla wasn't even
first; Nicholas of Cusa had already called it a forgery. Valla's is the version people
remember, which is a pattern that keeps turning up.) Look at what kind of check that was.
Not ``is the stamp real'' but ``could these words have been written when they say they
were.'' A record can pass the first and fail the second, which is a hint that what I keep
calling one thing, a record, is doing more than one job.

\subsection{Two columns and a stamp}

Here's the one I'd never have guessed mattered. Bookkeeping. Around 1300, the ledger of a
Florentine company called Farolfi, kept at its branch in Provence, shows the earliest complete example anyone
has found of a trick merchants were working out: write every transaction twice, once where the money came
from and once where it went, and the two columns have to balance. Genoa's public accounts of
1340 do it. And in 1494 a friar named Luca Pacioli printed the method in a mathematics book,
and it spread. That's double-entry bookkeeping, and it's easy to take it for just a tidy
habit.

Do it for one day. Keep two columns of every dollar that moves, and total them at night. Now
have a friend secretly change one entry in one column. The totals disagree; you catch it. Now
have them change the matching entry in both columns. The totals agree. You've caught nothing.
Push on that and you've found what double entry actually is: a trap for slips, not for
careful liars. Pacioli knew. The scholar Forrester reads him as reporting that in many places the
books were taken to the local consul to be authenticated before a single entry went in. The
stamp is a witness again, from outside. The two columns are the discipline; the stamp is the
claim that someone other than you will stand behind the fact that these books, and not some
others, are the books. Keep both halves separate in your head. One is a method. The other is a
commitment.

And then I found the place where this got turned into a motto. The Royal Society, founded
in London in 1660 and still running, picked as its motto \emph{Nullius in verba}: take nobody's
word for it. (Where did they get it? From somebody's words, naturally. It's half a line of the
Roman poet Horace, from a verse letter to his patron, saying he isn't bound to swear by the
words of any master. So the society that takes nobody's word for it took its motto from a poet
and cut the line to fit. That's not a contradiction, and it's a nice picture of the method:
borrow what's useful, say whose it was, and don't swear by it.) The historian Steven Shapin wrote a paper about what that meant in practice,
and the answer is more interesting than the slogan. Robert Boyle, pumping the air out of a
glass globe to see what happens to a candle or a bird, had three problems: the machine, the
report, and the witnesses. He solved the third by having gentlemen present who'd sign their
names, and the second by writing the report so richly that a reader who wasn't there could
picture the scene and count as a witness anyway. Shapin calls that virtual witnessing, and he
notes, dryly, that the air pump was very expensive, seventeenth-century big science. So there
\emph{was} a cost. It just wasn't a cost of declaring the fact. It was the cost of the instrument
and of getting enough people into the room. Hold on to that distinction. It's going to turn
out to be the whole question.

\subsection{A demon, and the step that pays}

Now the strangest entry, and the one that gets closest. In 1867 the physicist James Clerk
Maxwell, in a letter to a friend, imagined a ``very observant and neat-fingered being'' sitting
at a tiny door between two halves of a box of gas, letting fast molecules through one way and
slow ones the other, so that one side heats up and the other cools with no work done, which
is supposed to be impossible. The being got called Maxwell's demon, and physicists have been
arguing about it for a hundred and fifty years, which should tell you something.

Szilard's one-molecule engine, in 1929, made information part of the accounting.
The tempting move is to put the whole bill on finding out which side the molecule is on.
Bennett pulled that apart from restoring the memory for another round: measuring onto a
blank record can, in principle, be thermodynamically reversible, and resetting an unknown
record is a different operation. That does not make a real measuring device free to build
or run. It says that learning and resetting do not carry the same unavoidable entropy
cost, and I'm about to pick a step to charge, so I need that distinction before I do.

Bennett's version of the rule, in a 2003 paper you can read, is that what must cost is ``the
erasure of a bit or the merging of two computation paths.'' Erasing, or taking two possible
