by thinking; it's by playing with the four dots. Run MEASURE \emph{twice}. The first copies the
hidden bit onto the display. The second adds the hidden bit in again, and adding a bit twice
with a light-switch add gets you back where you were: the display is blank again. Check the
arrows: 10 to 11 to 10. The display went full and then blank, and nothing merged, and the
price was zero both times. So a display that was blank before the first MEASURE \emph{can} be put back to blank for
free, by a second MEASURE. Just not by WIPE.

What's the difference? MEASURE \emph{consults the hidden bit} when it clears the display. It knows
what's written there, because it has access to the thing it was copied from, and so it can
undo the copy instead of erasing it. WIPE doesn't look. It sets the display to 0 regardless,
and ``regardless'' is exactly the many-to-one. Bennett has the general form of this in the 2003
notes: erasing one of two copies that you \emph{know} match is reversible, because you're not
destroying information, you're removing a duplicate. And it goes further than Bennett in
work that came after him: del Rio and colleagues in 2011 showed that the cost of erasing a
system depends on how much the eraser already knows about it, down to zero and in the
quantum case past zero. The bill for clearing a record is sent to whoever clears it, and it's
smaller the more they know. Try it with a card under a cup and a sticky note: write the
colour on the note, then erase the note \emph{without lifting the cup} (two possible notes become
one blank: a merge) versus lift the cup, check the note matches, and then erase (nothing
unknown was destroyed). Same blank note. Different bill.

\subsection{The smallest machine that teaches for free, and the one that can't}

Two more small facts, and then the point. The demon measures what you learn by comparing the
start to the end, but an observer's very first look already rules things out before any step
runs, so the fairer question is: after that first look, can a \emph{step} teach you more, for
free? Yes, and the demon still does it. And the smallest machine
that can is three states in a ring: U goes to V, V goes to W, W goes to U, and the window
shows ``true'' only at W. Start with candidates \{U, V\}; both show false. Take one step. From U
you now see false; from V you now see true. One step told them apart, and a ring forgets
nothing, so a zero price meets the halving rule, and the file takes it.

Two states can't do it, ever, with any arrows, and this is the one that needs no price
premise at all. If a machine has only two states and you can't tell them apart at the first
look, then the window shows the same thing on both, and those two are \emph{all the states there
are}, so the window shows the same thing everywhere, forever, and you never learn anything.
Try to draw a counterexample. You'll draw the
same two dots a few times and give up, and the giving up is the proof. Three is the smallest
number of states on which two states that look alike at the first look can come apart at a
later look, and that's what teaching is.

\begin{theorem}[Three states are the minimum for free teaching]\label{thm:three-states}
Call a machine a \emph{free teacher} when it has a cost satisfying the halving price, a list of
candidates with no repeats containing the actual start, and a run of cost 0 after which the
observer knows strictly more than after the first look, $|K(\Omega, t, s_0)| <
|K(\Omega, [\,], s_0)|$. There is a free teacher with exactly three states, and there is none
with two or fewer.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Three: the ring $U \to V \to W \to U$ with the window true only at $W$, candidates
$\{U, V\}$, one step, cost 0 (a ring is a bijection, so cost 0 satisfies the halving price).
Two or fewer: two candidates that agree at the first look are, on a two-state machine, all
the states there are, so the window takes one value everywhere and no later look can
separate them. This half never uses the price at all.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{free\_incremental\_narrowing\_with\_three} and
\code{no\_free\_incremental\_narrowing\_below\_three} (KnowledgeNarrowingMinimal.v), and the
demon-against-the-first-look form as \code{demon\_refutes\_incremental}.

\subsection{What the toll prices, said at last}

Now I can say, more precisely than I could two sections ago, what the mark in Section~\ref{sec:toll} is a mark
for. Not for learning. What you know can be narrowed at no cost, with nothing merged, on
some machines under some honest price lists, and the demon is one. Not for
looking, not for copying, not for finding out. The mark
is for the one thing in Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} that couldn't be done without merging, on a machine with finitely
many states: raising a flag that stays up. Learning is the demon writing on a blank pad, which merges nothing. What the demon
pays for is the wipe, a step with a shared chair. The mark in Section~\ref{sec:toll} is paid for the same
reason, because raising a flag that stays up also has a shared chair, but it's a different
step: the demon machine has no flag, and its file prices merges, not commitments. Same
chair. Different room.

So ``No Free Insight,'' the name I gave the toll before I understood it, is narrower than it
sounds, and I'd rather tell you the narrowness than let the name do work it hasn't earned.
Insight in the sense of \emph{finding out} can be free. The insight the toll prices is the kind
you've \emph{committed to}, written into a record the machine can't silently revise. Whether that
narrower thing deserves the name is a fair thing to argue about; I kept the name because it's
the question I started with, and because the narrowing is the finding, not a retreat.

It also tells you how to read a bound that's coming. Section~\ref{sec:entitlement} counts what it takes to narrow a
list of candidates down to a shorter one: at least as many yes-or-no questions as it takes to
point at the survivors among their rivals, a counting fact that holds for anything with a
list in it. Turning that count into a \emph{bill}, saying a run actually paid that many marks, is
a different claim, and when the book makes it, for any system with a counter in Section~\ref{sec:entitlement} and on the
machine I build later in Section~\ref{sec:machine-claims}, the payment goes in as a hypothesis: a decision tree (a branching chart of yes-or-no questions, which Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}
builds) no deeper than the number of paid steps the run took is handed in, along with the
lists themselves. This section is the reason it has to go in that way. The narrowing alone
doesn't force anyone to pay; the demon just showed you a narrowing that cost nothing. So
wherever narrowing gets a price in this book, the payment is a premise, and I'll keep calling
it one.

And one more boundary. This whole section is about a machine that's finite and deterministic
and a watcher who crosses candidates off a list. There's no quantum anything in it. People
sometimes reach for ``observation collapses the state'' when they hear ``watching narrows
things down,'' and I want to head that off: the narrowing here is bookkeeping in the watcher's
list, the machine never notices, and the result would be the same if the watcher were a
filing cabinet. In 2010 a group in Tokyo (Toyabe, Sagawa, Ueda, Muneyuki and Sano) did
run a real demon, a tiny particle walked up a staircase of potential by feedback on what a
camera saw, and the energy it gained
was paid for by the information the camera took, with no violation of anything. The demon is
real, it works, and it pays. Where it pays is the part that took a century.

What I still owe: everything so far says ``at least one mark'' and I've been keeping the marks
on the side of the page, a running total you tally as you go. What happens when the machine
keeps that total itself, inside its own state, where a step could in principle reach in and
change it? That's the counter, and it's the next thing I have to build.


\part{The logic}

%===========================================================================
\section{The counter}
\label{sec:counter}
%===========================================================================

Everything so far has kept the marks on the side of the page. You played the toy, you made a
tally as you went, and the tally lived in your hand and not in the machine. That's fine for a
toy. For anything that's going to run on its own, with nobody tallying, the total has to live
somewhere the machine can reach, which means the machine can, in principle, reach it. So
this section is about what a counter has to be before you're allowed to call it a receipt.
Not the counter of some particular machine: the counter of \emph{any} machine whose state carries
a running total that every step bumps by whatever a price list says that step costs. Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s
five parts don't need one (there the total was a sum you did on the side), so this is one
piece added to the five, and the facts below are about anything that has it. I'll give
you the answer first, because it's short, and then spend the section on why each word is
there: a receipt is a total that lives in the state, that only climbs, that equals the sum
of what was charged, and that nothing else could have been.

\subsection{A stick, split down the middle}

The oldest receipt I could find that you can still hold is a piece of wood. From about 1100,
under Henry the First, until 1826, the English treasury recorded what it was owed on tally
sticks: a strip of hazel, notched across with cuts of set widths (a thumb's width for a
hundred pounds, a swollen barleycorn for a pound, a bare cut for a penny), then split lengthwise so that each half carried the
same notches. The payer kept one half, called the stock, which is one story for where the word
stockholder comes from. The treasury kept the other. When the time came to settle, you laid the two halves
together, and only the two original halves fit, because wood splits along a grain nobody can
copy. Add a notch to your half and the other half shows a gap where the partner should be. Try
to remove a notch and you find that wood can't be uncut. When they finally stopped using them,
the clerks burned centuries of old tallies in the furnaces under the House of Lords,
overheated the flue, and burned down the Palace of Westminster, which I mention because it's
the best fact I picked up for this book and because it tells you how many of them there were.

Do it: notch a strip of card once for every coin you hand a friend, split it, keep half each.
Try to cheat, either direction. The three things you'll find are the three things I want.
The total is the notches, added up, and nothing else (I'll call that conservation). You can
add a notch but you can't take one away (it only climbs). And two halves that were notched
together must agree; a half that disagrees is a forgery, and the wood says which one (there
is only one honest count). The treasury didn't have the words. They had the stick.

\subsection{Why it has to climb}

Start with the second property, because it's the one that does the most work and the one
people fight hardest. Why can't the counter ever go down?

Because of what the toll is for. The floor it buys, back in Section~\ref{sec:toll}, says a run from NO to YES
costs at least one. That
sentence is a \emph{floor}: it says the run paid at least this much. If the counter could come back
down, a run could pay the toll, get its flag, and then take the payment back, and the floor
would be a floor on nothing; ``this run cost at least one'' would be true of a run that ended
having cost nothing. So a counter that can fall is an accountant you can lean on to revise the
books, and a floor stated in terms of it isn't a floor. The counter only climbing is not a
flourish. It's what makes ``at least'' mean something. (In Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s abstract theorem the total is
a sum of whole numbers and climbing comes for free; this paragraph is about why a total
\emph{stored in the state}, where a step could in principle write it, has to be designed so that
no step ever lowers it.)

The same rule turns up in two places that have nothing to do with each other, pointing in
opposite directions, and that's a big part of why I trust it. In 1978 Leslie Lamport asked how
a set of computers that pass each other messages, with no shared clock, could ever agree on
what happened before what. His answer is a counter per machine with two rules: add one before
you do anything, and when a message arrives carrying the sender's count, jump your own counter
above it (never below your own). Those counters, he showed, respect cause and effect: if this
caused that, this has the smaller number. And they do it ``with no actual timing mechanism,''
his words; they're not clocks at all. Try it with three people passing notes and you'll see
it work in two minutes, and then let one of them reset their counter to zero after reading a
note, and watch a reply come out numbered \emph{before} the note it replies to. A counter that
goes down can't be leaned on for order.

Where did Lamport get it? In the notes he keeps on his own papers, he says the timestamps came
from an earlier note by Paul Johnson and Bob Thomas on keeping copies of a database in step,
whose algorithm wasn't quite right: it let things happen in an order that broke cause and
effect. What let him see the fix, he says, was special relativity, which teaches that there's no
one order of events everybody agrees on, only the order of what could have caused what. And he
passes on a line from Jim Gray, the same Gray as the commit at the start of the book: Gray had
heard two opinions of the paper, that it was trivial and that it was brilliant. Lamport's
answer is that he can't argue with the first and isn't inclined to argue with the second.
And what's under the relativity? His account stops there, so the chase does too. What it changes is only the picture, and the picture is a good one: a number that's
allowed to climb and never to fall is enough to write ``this came after that'' with no clock
anywhere.

Now the other direction. In 1949 Alan Turing, and in 1967 Robert Floyd, each asked how you
prove a program \emph{stops}. The answer, both times: find a quantity that goes \emph{down} on every step
and can't go down forever (a whole number that can't go below zero, say). If every step
lowers it and it can't fall forever, the steps can't go on forever. Up-only gives you order.
Down-only gives you stopping. They're not the same rule (one needs the jump-above-the-message
step, the other needs a floor it can't fall below), but they're the same shape seen from the
two ends: a one-way quantity is something you can build on, and a two-way quantity is a
number that happens to be written down somewhere.

And the real-world case where a counter was allowed to go down, and got gamed exactly there:
Ethereum, one of the largest blockchains, charges ``gas'' for every step of a program, and for
years it \emph{refunded} gas when a program freed up storage. Someone noticed you could fill
storage when gas was cheap, hold it, and cash the refunds when gas was dear, and a token was
built to do exactly that, and the real work in a block could reach nearly twice the block's
stated limit. In 2021 a change called EIP-3529 cut the refunds sharply (none for
self-destruct, a smaller one for clearing storage, and a cap of one fifth of the gas used).
The written reasons are the gas token and those overfull blocks. I read both as the same
lesson: a counter that goes down was being leaned on at the place where it went down.
Ethereum comes back in Section~\ref{sec:models} as one of five small models of systems people actually run, and
it's the only one of the five that prices a write at all, and it's instructive that the part
they had to fix was the part that could fall.

\subsection{Conservation: the total is the charges and nothing else}

The first property sounds too obvious to state. The counter after a step is the counter
before plus what that step was charged. Add up a whole run and the middle values cancel out,
the way a sum of differences collapses to last minus first, and the total is the sum of the
per-step charges. Why state it?

Because it's the property that fails quietly. Say a machine charges one for raising a flag,
and also, somewhere in its error handling, forgets to add the charge when the step fails
halfway through. Or charges two in one code path and one in another for the same move. Or
has one step that writes the counter directly. Then the counter is \emph{mostly} the sum of the
charges, and ``mostly'' is the whole gap between a receipt and a note that says ``trust me, about
this much.'' Conservation is the sentence that there is no ``mostly'': every step, every outcome,
every error, adds exactly its charge, and a step that fails is charged the same as one that
succeeds, because the charge is on the attempt. For a machine built the way I'm describing,
that sentence is the rule the counter is updated by, so it can't fail by definition. What can
fail is the claim that a real machine \emph{is} built that way, and checking that means going
through every move it has, the failure branches included, one at a time, which is dull and is
the whole job. The run-long form, counter at the end equals counter at the start plus the sum
of the charges, then follows from the one-step rule by the cancelling sum; it's below. It's
the kind of theorem that looks boring and is the one you'd most want if you were going to
rely on the number.
One thing it doesn't say: that every mark bought something. The ledger is exact about what
was spent, not about what the spending was worth; whether a mark bought a real narrowing is
Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}'s question, and it needs a witness on top of the ledger entry.

\subsection{Only one honest count}

Here's the property that surprised me by being provable at all. Suppose you fixed the
schedule: this move costs one, that move costs zero, and so on, for every move. And suppose
someone else keeps their own books: their own function from states to totals, which starts at
zero and, on every step, goes up by exactly what the schedule says. Could their books disagree
with the machine's counter, somewhere, on some state you can actually get to?

No. And the proof is the tally stick. Both totals start at zero. On every step both go up by
the same amount. So on every state you can reach by steps from the start, they're equal.
That's it; it's an induction, the one-step-at-a-time argument from Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s floor.
The mathematician's word for this is \emph{initiality}: the counter is the one bookkeeping that
all the others, if they're honest about the schedule, turn out to be. Given the schedule, the
count is forced. Two things about that sentence I had to be careful with, and they're worth
saying before the symbols. It doesn't assume the other books climb: climbing follows from the
schedule, since the schedule never charges a negative amount, so ``only one honest count'' and
``it only climbs'' aren't two separate demands on the other bookkeeper. And it holds on
\emph{reachable} states only. A state you can't get to from the start is one where it says nothing
about whether the other books agree, which is the right thing for a receipt to say.

Here are the properties exactly. First the piece being added to Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s five, a counter and a
price list, and then the two facts about it. The counter gets the Greek letter $\mu$ (mu),
which is what the checked work calls it.

\begin{definition}[A counter kept by a price list]\label{def:u06-counter}
A \emph{counter machine} has a set of states, a set of moves, a step function
$\mathrm{apply}$ that takes a state and a move, a start state $s_\mathrm{init}$, a
schedule $c$ giving each move a cost in $\mathbb{N}$, and a counter $\mu$ from states
to $\mathbb{N}$, such that $\mu(s_\mathrm{init}) = 0$ and
$\mu(\mathrm{apply}(s, i)) = \mu(s) + c(i)$ for every state $s$ and move $i$, with no
exceptions. A \emph{run} of a list $t$ of moves from $s$ applies them in order, and
$c(t)$ is the sum of their costs. A state is \emph{reachable} when it is the start or is
$\mathrm{apply}(s, i)$ for a reachable $s$ and some $i$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Conservation]\label{thm:conservation}
In a counter machine, for every state $s$ and every list $t$, $\mu$ at the end of the run of
$t$ from $s$ equals $\mu(s) + c(t)$. In particular $\mu$ never decreases along a run.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Induction on $t$. For the empty list both sides are $\mu(s)$. For a list $i$ followed by $t'$,
the one-step rule gives $\mu(\mathrm{apply}(s, i)) = \mu(s) + c(i)$, and the induction
hypothesis from $\mathrm{apply}(s, i)$ adds $c(t')$. Since every $c(i) \ge 0$, the counter
never falls.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Only one honest count]\label{thm:initiality}
In a counter machine, let $B$ (for ``books'') be any function from states to $\mathbb{N}$ with
$B(s_\mathrm{init}) = 0$ and $B(\mathrm{apply}(s, i)) = B(s) + c(i)$ for all $s$ and $i$.
Then $B(s) = \mu(s)$ for every reachable state $s$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By induction on why $s$ is reachable. At the start both are 0. If $s = \mathrm{apply}(s', i)$
with $B(s') = \mu(s')$, then $B(s) = B(s') + c(i) = \mu(s') + c(i) = \mu(s)$, the last step
by the counter's rule.
\end{proof}

Those two proofs are the whole of it, and they're about any counter machine. There's no
Coq statement of them over arbitrary states, so here they're argued, on
the page, where you can check every line. The checked statements are about the machine I
build later, which is one of these: Section~\ref{sec:state} goes through every move it has and checks the one-step
rule on every branch, and Section~\ref{sec:witness} gives the run form and the uniqueness under their checked
names.

I want to flag what initiality does \emph{not} do, because the word sounds grander than the fact.
It doesn't pick the prices. The schedule is an input: somebody decided that raising the flag
costs one and adding two numbers costs zero, and nothing here says that decision was right
(Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} is where I argued the floor isn't arbitrary; the rest of a schedule has to be defended by
whoever writes it). It doesn't turn marks into anything physical. And it isn't the category
theorist's ``initial object,'' though the word is borrowed for a related reason.

There \emph{is} a universal property nearby, and I'll say exactly how far it reaches so the
borrowed word doesn't reach further. Take any other machine that understands the same
moves (call it the \emph{target}), and pick a state of it to start from. Walking a list of moves
through it, one at a time, is the one and only way to send lists to its states that starts
where you said and keeps in step as the list grows by one. Programmers call that walk down a
list, one item at a time, a \emph{fold}, and I'll borrow the word. That's an induction on the list from its
end, the same shape as the proof just above, and it never looks at the other machine's
reading or its prices, which tells you how much the toll is doing here: nothing. It's a fact
about \emph{lists of moves}, not about states.

Coming down from lists to the states of the machine running them is where it gets
interesting, and where the borrowed word stops. Two different lists can leave a machine in the
same state. If they leave the target in two different states, there's no single place
to send that state. That's the whole obstruction, and it's exact: the map from states exists
on the reachable ones precisely when equal states always come from lists that agree on the
other side (and the readings agree). Call that the \emph{descent} condition, because it's what
lets the fold come down from lists to states. A toll plus a reading that agrees doesn't force
it to happen. A machine that keeps its whole history as its state obeys any toll you like and
still never comes down. So the fold is unique on lists, and that's what the word ``initial''
earns. It doesn't make anybody's states initial among everything that obeys the toll, and I
won't say it does. The checked statements (the fold, the descent condition, and three
example targets that show where its edges are) are written for the machine I build later, so
they're Section~\ref{sec:witness}'s.

\subsection{The toll is an old trick with a new name}

Now a thing that sounds like a let-down and isn't. It would be nice to have a new kind of
cost argument. This isn't one. The toll is a case of a technique that
algorithm people have used since 1985 and that physicists had, in a different costume, in
1892, and I'd rather tell you it's old than let you think I invented it.

The trick is called the potential method, and here's the whole of it. Give every state a
number, call it the potential, that measures how much ``owing'' is stored up in that state.
Then look at each step and ask: does the cost of the step, plus the change in potential it
causes, ever come out negative? If it never does, you've got a bound: any run costs at least
the amount the potential \emph{dropped} from start to finish, because the drop had to be paid for
by the steps along the way. Robert Tarjan and Daniel Sleator used it in 1985, going the other
way (potential as prepaid credit, to bound a run from above), to analyse data structures that
are occasionally expensive and usually cheap; and the decreasing-function idea underneath it
is the one Aleksandr Lyapunov used in 1892 to prove that a system settles down. Do the coin
version: a stack of coins, PUSH adds one and costs one, POP-ALL removes them all and costs as
many as it removed, potential equals the number of coins. PUSH costs one plus one potential;
POP-ALL of k coins costs k and drops the potential by k, net zero. So any sequence from an
empty stack costs at most twice the number of pushes, however many expensive pops are in it.
That's the method. Three lines.

Push on that 1892 for a second, because a date like that hides a lot. Lyapunov wrote the idea up
as his doctoral thesis, in Russian. A French translation came out in 1907. The English one came
out in 1992, a hundred years after the original, and it was translated from the French: a
translation of a translation. So for most of the twentieth century a reader with only English
met the idea secondhand or not at all. Did the algorithm people of 1985 get it from him? I can't
tell you, and nothing here needs them to have. Whether anybody walked from one to the other on
purpose is a question I'd like answered. What it changes is the picture: the same
idea, a number that only goes one way along a run, turned up in a thesis about whether a moving
system settles down and in a paper about data structures, close to a century apart.

Now point it at the flag. Potential: one if the flag is down, zero if it's up. A step from
down to up drops the potential by one, so for the step's cost plus potential change to be
non-negative, the step has to cost at least one. That's the toll, exactly, and the two are the
same statement: the toll holds for a machine if and only if every step has non-negative
amortized cost under the flag potential (``amortized cost'' is just that sum, the step's cost
plus the change in potential). Then the universal floor from Section~\ref{sec:toll}, ``any run from NO to YES
paid at least one,'' is just the potential method's standard conclusion, the drop in
potential from one to zero, and every system with the five parts that obeys the toll is an
instance (the checked record carries the toll as a field, so that's every certification
system). Two more facts fall out of the same picture. Under the toll, a run raises the flag
at most as many times as its total cost; each raise uses up a unit and a unit isn't used
twice. And if you demand the upper-bound version too, that the potential before a step covers
its cost plus the potential after, then the two together hold exactly when raising the flag
costs exactly one, everything else costs zero, and the flag never comes down; that's the
sharpest version of
the schedule, and notice that Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s toy doesn't meet it: the toy's VOUCH move, played from
YES, makes a mark
although it raises nothing, which the floor allows and the exact version forbids. (These
two theorems let the price depend on the state as well as the move's name, which is wider
than Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s per-name cost; a per-name cost is a special case.) Two older tools sit beside
these, named for completeness: running a list of moves in a ``writer'' that accumulates a
number returns the final state and the run's cost (\code{run\_writer\_is\_run\_and\_cost}), and a
per-move schedule is a ``grade'' fixed before the run (\code{run\_graded\_is\_run}); neither
embeds those frameworks' full type systems, and the files say so. The writer is the move
Danner and Licata make in their cost semantics, a translation that carries a cost alongside
a program's result (Danner, Licata and Ramyaa, ICFP 2015; Danner and Licata, \emph{Journal of
Functional Programming}, 2022). The grade is Katsumata's: a computation carries its resource
as a grade, and the grades compose as the computations do (``Parametric effect monads and
semantics of effect systems,'' POPL 2014). Orchard, Liepelt and Eades put grades into the
types of a working language (``Quantitative program reasoning with graded modal types,'' ICFP
2019). Read against them, the counter is a grade carried in the state by the step rule, not
in a type. And what does that difference even mean? A cost that lives in a type gets checked
before the program runs, by whoever checks the types; a cost that lives in the state gets
written during the run, by the step itself. Same number, different moment of truth. Whether
mine is an embedding of their frameworks or something weaker is a question this book leaves
open, and I'd love for someone who knows those frameworks better than I do to settle it.

Exactly, for any certification system with states $S$, moves $I$, step, per-name cost, and
reading:

\begin{definition}[Potential, amortized cost]\label{def:potential}
A \emph{potential} is a function $\Phi : S \to \mathbb{N}$. A step has \emph{non-negative amortized
cost} under $\Phi$ when $\mathrm{cost}(i) + \Phi(\mathrm{step}(s, i)) \ge \Phi(s)$. The
\emph{flag potential} is $\Phi_\mathrm{cert}(s) = 1$ if $\mathrm{cert}(s) = \mathrm{no}$ and $0$
if it reads yes.
\end{definition}

Defined as \code{amortized\_nonneg} and \code{cert\_potential} (CostSemanticsComparison.v).

\begin{theorem}[The toll is the potential method]\label{thm:potential}
(1) The toll holds exactly when every step has non-negative amortized cost under
$\Phi_\mathrm{cert}$. (2) For any $\Phi$ with non-negative amortized cost and any run $t$ from
$s$, $\mathrm{cost}(t) + \Phi(\mathrm{run}(t, s)) \ge \Phi(s)$. (3) Hence, under the toll,
a run from a no-state to a yes-state costs at least $1 - 0 = 1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Check the four combinations of the reading before and after: only no-to-yes has
$\Phi_\mathrm{cert}$ dropping, by one, so the inequality there is exactly
$\mathrm{cost}(i) \ge 1$; in the other three it holds for any cost. (2) Induction on the run,
adding the per-step inequalities so that the middle potentials cancel. (3) Apply (2) with
$\Phi_\mathrm{cert}$, which is 1 at the start and 0 at the end.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{a2\_iff\_nonnegative\_amortized\_cost}, \code{potential\_telescoping}, \code{nfi\_by\_potential},
and \code{certification\_system\_is\_potential\_method} (CostSemanticsComparison.v), with the
state-dependent-cost results \code{flips\_le\_cost} and \code{a2\_and\_aara\_iff\_exact}
(CostFrameworks.v).

So what's new, if the method isn't? Only where it's pointed. The potential method is a way of
proving things about costs. What this book adds is a claim about \emph{which} potential, the
flag, and about what happens to that claim when you can only see a window of the state. The
method is Tarjan's. The reading is mine, and I'm about to find out what it can and can't
survive.

\subsection{What the counter is, said once}

A receipt is a total that lives in the state, only climbs, equals the sum of the charges on
every path including the failures, and is the only such total for its schedule. Each of
those four, counting ``lives in the state'' as the one the others are about, had a home
before this book: the stick, Lamport's clocks and Floyd's ranking
functions, the telescoping sum, the induction. None of them is physics. None of them says
what the charges should be. What they say is that once you've chosen the charges, the
counter isn't a second opinion; it's the arithmetic. And the toll on top of it is the
potential method with the flag as potential, which is to say a trick from 1985 wearing the
question from Section~\ref{sec:structure}.

Here's one thing the counter can't do just by existing: if you can only see \emph{part} of the state, can you
tell what the counter is? Can you even tell, from outside, which step paid? The stick works
because you can lay the two halves together. What if you're only ever shown one half, through
a window, and the window doesn't show the notches?

One piece of that has a short answer, and I'll give it now so the next section can start
from it. A window, for now, is just the part of the state an outside observer is shown (Section~\ref{sec:narrowing}'s
display was one, and Section~\ref{sec:windows} is about windows in general). Call a window \emph{counter-complete} when
some rule, applied to what the window shows, returns the counter on every state;
\emph{flag-complete} likewise for the flag. Say a window \emph{forgets the counter} when changing the
counter and nothing else never changes what the window shows, and likewise for the flag.

The short answer: a window that forgets the counter is never counter-complete, whatever else
it shows, and a window that forgets the flag is never flag-complete. Take any state and make
two copies of it, one with the counter set to 1 and one with it set to 2, everything else
held still. The window shows the same thing for both, so any rule gives the same answer for
both, and one of the two answers is wrong. The flag is the same argument with yes and no. On
the stick: a window that shows you the wood's colour and its length but not the notches can't
tell you what's owed, and staring harder at the colour won't help. (The argument needs a
state space where the counter can be changed on its own, the rest held still; that's what
``forgets'' quietly assumes. The machine I build later is such a space, and Section~\ref{sec:witness} has its checked
version, with the machine's own full window.)

Be careful what that doesn't say. It says neither part can be dropped. It doesn't say a
window showing both is the smallest window that works, because nothing here orders windows,
so there's nothing for it to be smallest in. And it's about reading the counter back, not
about which step paid. That second question is harder, and it's the next section's.

%===========================================================================
\section{Windows and shadows}
\label{sec:windows}
%===========================================================================

I left you with the stick split in half and asked what happens if you can only ever see one
half through a window that doesn't show the notches, and with a harder question under that
one: can you tell, from outside, which step paid? This section is about windows. It's a
section where the mathematics is so small that I'm going to state it in
full and then spend most of the pages on what it's \emph{not}, because the smallness is the
trap: the fact is a one-liner and people keep trying to climb over it with cleverness, and
you can't, and seeing why you can't is the content.

\subsection{A cave, and the people who got good at it}

You've probably heard a version of this, so let me tell it carefully, because the version
that usually gets told is the wrong half. In the seventh book of the \emph{Republic}, Plato has
Socrates describe prisoners chained in a cave since childhood, facing a wall, with a fire
behind them and people carrying objects along a walkway between the fire and their backs.
All the prisoners have ever seen is the shadows on the wall. To them, Socrates says, the
truth would be nothing but those shadows. That's the part people remember, and it usually
gets used to say ``the real world is hidden from us,'' which is a thing Plato did believe and
which is not what I need from the story.

Here's the half that matters for this book, and it's one line further on. The prisoners,
Socrates says, hand out honours to whoever is quickest at spotting the shadows as they pass
and best at guessing which comes next. Read that again. The prisoners \emph{get good at it}. They
build a whole science of shadows, with experts and prizes, and it works, on shadows. What
they can't do is say anything about a carried object that leaves no mark on the wall. Not
because they're stupid. Because the information isn't on the wall. Skill inside a window
doesn't reach past the window, no matter how much skill. That's the fact. Plato dressed it as
a lesson about education, and it is one, but strip the dressing and it's a sentence about
functions, and it's going to be the whole section.

\subsection{The shadow of a cube}

Do this one tonight with a lamp. Hold a cube face-on to the light: its shadow is a square.
Now hold up a square of card the same size: same shadow. A person who sees only the wall
can't tell you whether what's casting the shadow has any thickness at all. Ask them, and
they'll tell you, truthfully, that they can't know, and if they're honest they'll also tell
you that no amount of staring at that square will change it.

Now turn both a quarter turn. The card's shadow collapses to a line. The cube's stays a
square. Now the wall-watcher knows. What changed? Not their cleverness. The \emph{window}. A
second look from a different angle is a bigger window than one look, and it was bought with
a turn and a second look. Edwin Abbott told this as a novel in 1884, \emph{Flatland}: a sphere
visits a world of flat shapes and the only thing the flat shapes can see is a circle that
grows and shrinks as the sphere moves through their plane; from one slice they can't
reconstruct a sphere, and from the sequence of slices over time, they can start to. The
escape from a window is never ``think harder.'' It's always ``a different window,'' and a
different window always costs something: a turn, a second look, time.

Who was Edwin Abbott? Not a mathematician by trade. He was headmaster of the City of London School
for twenty-four years, a clergyman, and the author of more than forty books, a Shakespeare
grammar among them. He put \emph{Flatland} out under the name ``A Square.'' His full name was
Edwin Abbott Abbott, two A's, and people like to read the pen name as a joke on that, A squared;
nice if true, but take it as a lead. Here's the part I like best, from a sketch
of his life on the geometer Thomas Banchoff's pages: \emph{Flatland}, by far the most read thing
he wrote, isn't mentioned at all in his obituary in the London \emph{Times} or in his entry in the
\emph{Dictionary of National Biography}. The official record of the man was a window too: it
showed the headmaster and the grammarian and left out the one book people still read. That
changes nothing in the argument. It's the argument, acted out by an obituary. (\emph{Flatland} already turned up once in this book, in Section~\ref{sec:origin}.)

\subsection{The whole fact, in one paragraph}

Here's the mathematics, and I promise it's all of it. You have a set of states, the real
things. You have a window, which is a function that takes a state and gives you what you can
see of it: the shadow, the slice, the half-stick without notches. And you have a question
about the state, which is also a function: it takes a state and gives an answer. The thing
you want is a \emph{decoder}: a rule that takes what you can see and gives the right answer to
the question, every time. When does one exist?

Think about two states that cast the same shadow. The decoder sees the same shadow for both,
so it gives the same answer for both. So if the question has \emph{different} answers on those
two states, the decoder is wrong on at least one of them, and there's nothing it can do about
it, because it never saw the difference. That's the whole fact. If a decoder exists, then the
question must already give the same answer on every pair of states that look the same through
the window. Mathematicians call the set of states that cast one particular shadow the \emph{fibre}
over that shadow (think of the shadow as a point on the wall and the fibre as the bundle of
all the things that could have cast it), and the sentence is: a decoder exists only if the
question is constant on every fibre. That's the theorem just below, and the ``only if'' is the
direction that bites. The other direction, ``if the question is constant on
fibres then a decoder exists,'' is true too, but it needs you to be handed, for every possible
shadow, one actual state that casts it, so you can look up the answer there, and the handing
is not free either, since someone has to supply a representative for every shadow. (You can always fill a gap with a default
answer. The default doesn't recover what was really there.)

Exactly. Let $S$ be any set of states, $V$ any set of views, $w : S \to V$ a window, and
$q : S \to A$ a question with answers in any set $A$. A \emph{decoder} is a function
$d : V \to A$ with $d(w(s)) = q(s)$ for every state $s$. The question is \emph{constant on
fibres} when $w(s) = w(s')$ implies $q(s) = q(s')$.

\begin{theorem}[Decoders need constant fibres]\label{thm:fibre}
If a decoder exists, the question is constant on fibres. Conversely, if the question is
constant on fibres and you are handed, for every view $v$, a state $r(v)$ with
$w(r(v)) = v$, then $d(v) = q(r(v))$ is a decoder.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If $w(s) = w(s')$ then $q(s) = d(w(s)) = d(w(s')) = q(s')$. Conversely,
$d(w(s)) = q(r(w(s)))$, and $r(w(s))$ has the same view as $s$, so by constancy its answer is
$q(s)$.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{decoding\_requires\_fiber\_constancy} and \code{selected\_representatives\_give\_decoder}
(ObservationPolicy.v), for arbitrary types.

Try the smallest case, by hand, because it'll keep coming back. A state
is a pair: a position, 0 or 1, and a hidden flag, up or down. The window shows the position
only. Two moves from (0, down): one sets the position to 1 and raises the flag; the other
sets the position to 1 and leaves the flag alone. Both land on position 1. Now write down
every possible decoder from ``what I see'' to ``is the flag up'': there are exactly four
functions from two positions to two answers. Check each against both results. None of the
four gets both right, because both results show position 1 and one has the flag up and one
doesn't. That exhaustive check is the theorem on this example; the general statement is the
one-line argument above, and that's what's checked. There's no fifth function hiding
somewhere.

\subsection{People who found this on their own}

The fact is so plain that it got discovered separately in every field that has to deal with
seeing part of something, and I want to lay them beside each other, because that's the kind
of evidence I trust: not that one smart person said it, but that people who'd never met kept
walking into the same wall.

In 1956 Edward Moore, working on the small switching machines that became computer
hardware, asked when an experimenter who can only feed a machine inputs and watch its
outputs can tell two of its internal states apart. His answer gave a precise meaning to
``indistinguishable from outside,'' and a theorem with a sting in it: even when every pair of
states can be told apart by \emph{some} experiment, there are machines where no single experiment
tells you which state you started in. What you can always do is run an experiment after
which you know which state you're in \emph{now}. In 1960 Rudolf Kalman,
whose filter is in the navigation of aeroplanes and phones, asked the same question for continuous
systems, called it \emph{observability}, and gave a test (a matrix rank, which you can compute)
for whether watching the output over time pins down the internal state. His unobservable
states are exactly a fibre: states whose difference never reaches the output, and, this is
the part people miss, never will, however long you watch. More samples of the same window
only repeat the same fibre. Try it on a car: if your only instrument is the speedometer, two
cars driving side by side at the same speed read the same forever, and nothing on that dial
will ever tell you which mile marker either one started at. Swap the speedometer for an
odometer and you can recover both. Same car, different window.

Where did Kalman's filter go first, before aeroplanes and phones? Toward the Moon. In the autumn
of 1960 Kalman called an acquaintance, Stanley Schmidt, at NASA's Ames Research Center, and came
to visit, not knowing what Schmidt's group was working on. The group, a branch with eight people
doing the analysis, was stuck on how a spacecraft going around the Moon and back could work out
where it was from what its crew could measure through an optical sight: a few angles to the Earth
and the Moon. That's a window problem with a capsule in it. The state is position and velocity,
the view is a handful of angles, and the job is to keep a running best guess at the state from a
sequence of views. Kalman presented his new filtering paper to them, and with real work (their
problem wasn't linear and his theory was) it fit, and it went into the feasibility studies for
navigating Apollo. Schmidt and Leonard McGee, telling the story in 1985, call it a fortunate
sequence of events and say the solution might have gone undiscovered but for that meeting. What
it changes: it shows the limit from the useful side. The filter didn't make the angles show more.
It made a sequence of views, over time, pin down the state, and it can only do that when the state
is observable from those views, which is Kalman's own condition. The odometer, not a cleverer
speedometer.

In 1977 Patrick and Radhia Cousot built a whole discipline of program analysis, called
abstract interpretation, on throwing information away \emph{on purpose}: run the program over
coarse descriptions of its values instead of the values, and accept that the answer you get
has to be true of \emph{every} real value the coarse description could stand for. That last
clause is fibre constancy as a design rule. And in 1970 Ted Codd, inventing the relational
database, made programs independent of how the data is stored, and the relational systems
that followed gave users \emph{views}, deliberately partial windows onto the stored data. A
decade after Codd, Bancilhon and Spyratos set out the view-update problem: if a user changes what they
see through a view, which of the many underlying states that cast that view should the
database move to? Several are legitimate. The fibre, from the writing side.

And Parnas, from Section~\ref{sec:structure}, hid things on purpose: a module is characterised by the design decision
it \emph{hides} from its callers. Hiding is a window. The caller can't later read back what was
hidden, including the things it later wishes it could check, and that's the price side of
the coin whose benefit side Parnas was selling. None of these people were doing philosophy.
They were trying to build filters, databases, compilers, and modules, and the wall is the
same wall in each.

\subsection{The clerk with two photographs}

Now point it at the counter, because that's why this section is here. Suppose you want to
bill for raising the flag, exactly: at least one mark for every step that raises it, and
nothing for a step that doesn't. And suppose the person doing the billing is a clerk who
sees only a \emph{window} on the state, a photograph before the step and a photograph after.
The clerk's bill is a function of the two photographs. Can the clerk bill exactly?

Not if the window has the wrong kind of blind spot. Here's why, and it's the cube again.
Suppose there are
two steps that give the clerk the same before-photo and the same after-photo, and one of them
raised the flag and the other didn't. (The two-move toy above is exactly such a pair; so are
``a stamp goes onto a document inside a closed drawer'' and ``someone opens and closes the
drawer.'') The clerk has one bill for that pair of photographs. If the bill is at least one,
it overcharges the step that didn't raise the flag. If it's zero, it undercharges the step
that did. Any bill that never misses a raise bills something that wasn't a raise, and no
bill from those photographs is exact. The fix is the plain one: put the flag in the
photograph. If the window shows the reading, then ``one when the reading goes from down to
up, zero otherwise'' is exact, and such a window has no pair like the one above. That's enough.
It isn't the only way: a window can hide the flag and still have no colliding pair, in
which case a bill from the photographs can be exact; what the file proves the other way is
only that a colliding pair rules exact pricing out. And ``exact'' here has a definition: at least
one on every step that raises the flag, nothing on any step that doesn't. That's all the
clerk's problem needs, and the bill ``one for a raise, zero otherwise'' meets it
(\code{step\_price\_is\_exact}). So it's exact about \emph{which} steps get charged. It isn't exact about \emph{how much}, and it
doesn't pick out one bill: ``two for a raise, zero
otherwise'' meets it too. Pinning the bill down takes one more demand, a ceiling: over any
run, the total never exceeds the number of raises. With the floor and that ceiling there's
exactly one bill left, one per raise and zero otherwise; that's an if and only if, proved for
any system whose bill is decided step by step (\code{exact\_commitment\_pricing\_characterization},
CommitmentPredicateAdequacy.v). These are stated for any states, any steps,
any window; they're the cube theorem with a price in place of a decoder.

Same clerk, now in symbols, so you can check every word I just used. Take the five parts
of Section~\ref{sec:toll} with a window $w : S \to V$, and say a step $(s, i)$
\emph{raises} the flag when $\mathrm{cert}(s) = \mathrm{no}$ and
$\mathrm{cert}(\mathrm{step}(s,i)) = \mathrm{yes}$. A \emph{price} is any function of a state and
a move. It \emph{meets the floor} when every raise costs at least one, and \emph{never overcharges}
when every non-raise costs zero; together, it is \emph{exact} (about which steps are charged;
the amount is pinned only by the whole-run ceiling above). A \emph{window price} is one computed
from the two photographs only: $\mathrm{price}(s, i) = b(w(s), w(\mathrm{step}(s, i)))$ for
some bill $b : V \times V \to \mathbb{N}$. A \emph{collision} is two steps $(s_1, i_1)$ and
$(s_2, i_2)$ with $w(s_1) = w(s_2)$ and $w(\mathrm{step}(s_1, i_1)) = w(\mathrm{step}(s_2,
i_2))$, the first a raise and the second not.

\begin{theorem}[No exact window price across a collision]\label{thm:shadow-price}
If the window has a collision, every window price that meets the floor charges at least one
on some step that is not a raise; so no window price is exact. If instead the reading is a
function of the view, $\mathrm{cert}(s) = r(w(s))$ for some $r$, then the window price
``one when $r$ goes from no to yes, zero otherwise'' is exact, and the window has no collision.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Across a collision both steps get the same bill $b(v, v')$. The floor makes it at least one
because the first step is a raise; the second step, not a raise, pays it. If the reading is
$r$ of the view, the window price reads the raise directly, and two steps with the same
photographs either both raise or both don't, so there's no collision.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{shadow\_floor\_overcharges}, \code{shadow\_cannot\_price\_exactly},
\code{window\_showing\_reading\_prices\_exactly}, and \code{window\_showing\_reading\_has\_no\_collision}
(ShadowPricing.v), for arbitrary types.

So the exact price of raising the flag lives in the step itself, or in a window that shows
the flag. A window that contains a pair like that one can't carry it. Whether a particular
machine has such a pair, for a particular window, has to be checked machine by machine and
window by window; the theorem only tells you what a pair does once you've found one.

\subsection{The three escapes, and what each one costs}

Suppose you're the person outside, and you want to be convinced that a run paid. The window
you've got doesn't show the counter. Here's how bad that is, in the smallest setting I can
build. Take a counter machine from Section~\ref{sec:counter}, give its states a position and a flag as well, and give
it a window that shows the position and nothing else. Now take two runs from the same start,
with the position at 0, the flag down and the counter at 0. Run $A$ makes one move that
raises the flag, costs one, and lands at position 1; its counter reads 1. Run $B$ makes one
move that does nothing but step to position 1, at cost zero; its counter reads 0. Call the
pair of photographs, position 0 then position 1, the \emph{transcript}. Both runs leave exactly
that transcript. A \emph{verifier} is a rule that takes a transcript and says accept or reject.
It is \emph{sound} when every transcript it accepts comes only from states where
the claim holds, and \emph{complete} when every transcript from a state where the claim holds is
accepted. The claim is ``the counter is 1.''

No verifier on these transcripts is both, and the proof is three lines. Suppose one were both.
Run $A$ ends with the counter at 1 and leaves the transcript, so completeness says the
verifier accepts it. Now soundness, on that same accepted transcript: every state that leaves it satisfies the
claim, and run $B$'s does. So run $B$'s counter is 1. It is 0. That's the cube again, with a
verdict in place of an answer: a verifier sees only what the window kept, and two states that
the window can't tell apart get one verdict between them.

Now dress the transcript up. Take any richer kind of transcript, with a way to squash one
down to its bare photographs, and say a verifier on the rich ones \emph{only looks at the bare
part} when two rich transcripts that squash to the same photographs always get the same
verdict. If some rich transcript left by run $A$ and some rich transcript left by run $B$
squash to the same photographs, then no verifier that only looks at the bare part is sound
and complete either: it gives those two the same verdict, completeness makes that verdict
accept, and soundness then lies about run $B$. Notice what that needs. The pair has to survive
into the richer kind of transcript; a design whose extra part tells $A$ from $B$ doesn't meet
the premise, and the argument says nothing about it. So it doesn't classify every transcript
design. What it says is that a verifier that only reads what the bare window keeps fails on
that pair.

What can you do? Here are three things that work, and nothing says they're the only
ones; as far as I can tell, cryptography uses all three. Each rests on something you have to trust, and I'll say
what, because ``a price'' in the counter's sense is not what any of them costs.

You can be shown the \emph{whole state}. Then there's nothing to decode; you read the counter off
the state. The price is trust: you have to believe the state you were shown is the state
there was.

You can be shown a \emph{commitment}: the ordinary window plus one extra bit that is set when,
and only when, the claim holds (here, that the counter reads exactly one).
Reading that bit gives a verifier that is sound and complete for that claim, \emph{if} the bit is
binding (set only when the claim holds) and honest (set whenever it holds). The trust is in
those two ``ifs,'' which are a contract about who can set the bit. The contract can be met,
and a bit anyone can set breaks it, which is the one-line version of why an unsigned log is
just another window. Nothing in that picture has a hardness assumption in it; whether a real
commitment scheme meets the contract is a question for cryptography, not for this book.
In 1999 Bruce Schneier and John Kelsey worked out how to make a log that an intruder who
takes over the machine can't quietly rewrite, and the honest scope in their paper is the
honest scope here: it protects what was written \emph{before} the break-in, through keys, and
nothing after.

Or you can \emph{ask}. Interaction: the outside party gets to put a question and gets an answer
that pins the thing down. The price is the honesty of the answerer; a liar's answer is
another shadow. Moore's experimenter chose inputs; the zero-knowledge proofs of Goldwasser,
Micali and Rackoff in 1985 are the refined form, where a verifier is convinced by a
conversation designed to cut exactly the line between true and false and nothing else, with
a mathematical guarantee against a cheating prover. I mention zero-knowledge to say what I'm
\emph{not} claiming: the asking in this section is one round, with one fixed question (``tell me
your counter''), and nothing in it models a cheating prover; the honesty is assumed, not
enforced. That's a toy of the real thing, and I'm not going to let the real thing's
reputation stand behind the toy.

The real thing even has a cave in it, which after Plato I can't resist. In a paper for the 1989
CRYPTO conference called ``How to Explain Zero-Knowledge Protocols to Your Children,''
Jean-Jacques Quisquater and Louis Guillou, with their families on the byline and Tom Berson,
told it as Ali Baba's cave: a ring-shaped tunnel with a magic door at the back that opens only
for a secret word. Peggy goes in down one side while Victor waits outside; then Victor walks to
the fork and shouts which side she should come out of. If she knows the word, she always can. If
she doesn't, she gets away with it only when Victor happens to call the side she went in. Play
it at the table with a coin for Victor's shout: one round, a cheat gets through half the time;
twenty rounds, about one time in a million. And here's the part that belongs in this section. In
the way the story is usually told, Victor ends up convinced, but a video of the whole thing
convinces nobody else, because a staged run, where the two agreed beforehand which sides he'd
shout, makes exactly the same recording. The recording is a window, and the real run and the fake
one cast the same shadow. That's the cube in the cryptographers' favourite bedtime story, and it's
why the real thing has to ask live, many times, against a prover who might be lying: everything
my one round leaves out.

Each escape is a window with something added: the whole state, a bound bit, an honest
answer. None of them is ``a smarter verifier on the old window.'' Cleverness lives on the
wrong side of the projection. What's true of any machine is the cube. The machine I build
later has pairs like these, and checked versions of all three escapes; they're stated on it,
so they're Section~\ref{sec:witness}'s.

\subsection{What this isn't}

Three things people reach for, and I'd rather take them off the table now.

It isn't mysticism. Nothing here says the window is false or the state is unknowable. The
wall is a function, the objects are its inputs, and the only claim is that the function isn't
one-to-one on the thing you asked about. A richer window recovers it. Plato's prisoners could
have turned around.

Somebody always says Rice's theorem at this point, so let me say it first. It isn't Rice's
theorem, though it rhymes with it. The logician Henry Rice, in 1953, proved
that no program can
decide any interesting property of what another program \emph{does} from its code, and a cousin
of the fact here is that a run which hasn't halted yet looks, so far, exactly like one that
never will. But Rice is about what's \emph{computable}. The cube is about what's \emph{there}. The
cube theorem holds for a toy with two states and nothing to compute; the obstruction is
missing information, not missing cleverness, and I'd be overclaiming if I let the famous
theorem lend its weight to the small one.

And it isn't ``with enough data you can recover anything.'' Kalman's unobservable states stay
unobservable for all time. The question is never how much of the window you've got. It's
which window.

So: the counter lives in the state, and whether anyone outside can read it depends entirely
on what they're shown, and a window with a pair like that in it can't price the flag
exactly, not with any rule, ever. Which raises the question I've been pushing in front of me since the
buckets. Fine, the flag went up and was paid for and I can see it in the right window. What
does that \emph{entitle} me to? A paid flag is a paid flag. What's the claim behind it, and when
am I allowed to lean on it?

%===========================================================================
\section{Structural entitlement}
\label{sec:entitlement}
%===========================================================================

I keep writing the word ``vouch'' and then taking it back. Let me stop doing that and say what
it would take. A reading went from NO to YES, the toll charged the move that did it (Section~\ref{sec:toll}),
maybe the reading stays up (Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} says what it costs to make it stay), and the right window
shows it (Section~\ref{sec:windows}).
Now: what is a later step \emph{allowed to do} because of that? That's a different question from
``is the thing true,'' and the gap between those two is the subject of this section, and I'd
argue it's the subject of most of the arguments people have about evidence, so give me the
long way round.

\subsection{The coin that moved}

Here's an experiment you can run on a friend, and I'd ask you to actually run it, because
the feeling of it is the point. Put a coin under one of three cups while they watch. Say,
cup one. Send them out of the room. Move the coin to cup three. Then, and this is the trick,
put a \emph{second} coin under cup one. Bring them back and ask: ``Is there a coin under cup one?''

They say yes. They're right; there is. And they have a reason: they watched you put it there.
True, and believed, and justified by what they saw. And it's not knowledge, and you can feel
that it isn't, because their reason points at a coin that left. The coin that makes them
right is not the coin they're thinking of.

That's a three-page paper from 1963 by Edmund Gettier, ``Is Justified True Belief Knowledge?'',
which broke a definition people had leaned on since Plato, in about the time it takes to
read it. The definition, which people read into Plato's \emph{Theaetetus}, was that you know something when it's
true, you believe it, and you've got good reasons. Gettier's two cases, and the cups, show a
belief that passes all three tests and still isn't knowledge, because the reasons and the
fact aren't connected; they just happen to agree. Bertrand Russell had a related case in 1948:
somebody looks at a stopped clock at the one moment it happens to be right, and they're right
about the time, and they know nothing.

Is 1963 the bottom? Not even close, and 1948 isn't either. The Stanford Encyclopedia's entry on
the analysis of knowledge, which is where I'd send you to check me, gives a case from the
eighth-century Buddhist philosopher Dharmottara: you're looking for water on a hot day, you see
water ahead, it's a mirage, and when you get there you happen to find water under a rock. And one
from Peter of Mantua, in the fourteenth century: Plato is running right next to you, you take him
for Socrates, so you believe Socrates is running, and Socrates is in fact running, in Rome, where
you can't see him. Older still? Maybe. This is where the trail goes cold, which isn't the same as
where it ends. What it changes is how much
I trust the shape. People in different centuries, languages and traditions kept building the
same trap by hand: a reason that points at one thing, and a truth that happens to be sitting on
another.

What's missing is a wire from the reason to the fact. Ask your friend what they'd need, to
be \emph{entitled} to ``there's a coin under cup one,'' and they'll tell you: lift the cup. Not
``remember putting it there.'' Lift it, now, and look. That lifting is an event, it happens on
the record, and after it the reason and the fact are the same object.

\subsection{Plato nearly had it}

Who was Theaetetus, though? The dialogue is named for a real person, and that side of it
usually gets left out. He was a mathematician. In the dialogue he's a teenager, and he tells
Socrates that his teacher Theodorus had been showing them, one case at a time, that the side of a
square of area three, or five, and so on up to seventeen, can't be named by any fraction: the
Pythagoreans' diagonal from Section~\ref{sec:structure}, done again case by case. The young man's
idea was to stop going one case at a time and find one word for all of them. Euclid's tenth book,
on lengths that share no common measure, is thought to be largely his work, and he's credited with
being the first to study the eight-faced and twenty-faced solids, two of the four Plato built air
and water from. The dialogue opens with him being carried home to Athens from the army at Corinth,
badly wounded and sick with the dysentery going round the camp, barely alive; the usual date is
369 BC. And the conversation itself has come down as a record. Euclid of Megara (not the geometer) says he
took notes as soon as he got home, filled them out later, and had Socrates correct them whenever
he came to Athens, and he has the result read aloud. So the dialogue about what turns a true
belief into knowledge survives as a checked record of what was said. That changes nothing in
the argument. I just like that the book about knowledge is named for the man who took the diagonal
and made it general.

I want to be fair to the \emph{Theaetetus} here, because it's easy to be quick with the ancients
and they deserve better. Socrates, in that dialogue, doesn't just say ``true belief
plus reasons.'' He tries three different senses of what the ``account'' behind a true belief
could be: a statement you can say aloud; a list of the thing's parts; and, third, the mark
that sets this thing apart from everything else it could be confused with. He tries each,
and each fails, and the dialogue ends with nobody knowing what knowledge is, which is one of
the more honest endings in philosophy. But the third sense is the one I'd underline. An
account as \emph{the thing that distinguishes}: the test that gives the real case a value no rival
gives. He couldn't make it work because he had no way to say what the account had to be
attached \emph{to}. Two and a half thousand years later, here's this book's guess: the thing it
has to be attached to is a state, and the account is an object sitting in it. I'm not claiming
that settles Plato. I'm claiming he was pointing at the right thing, and that's my reading of the
dialogue, which you can check against it in an afternoon.

Push on that once more, because Socrates gives his own reason for dropping the third account,
and it isn't the one I just gave. If the account means \emph{knowing} the mark that sets the thing
apart, then knowledge has been defined as true belief plus knowledge of something, and the word
you were trying to define is back inside its own definition. A circle. Does a check get out of
it? It gets the word out: a test that ran and found the mark isn't defined in terms of knowing.
Whether the test was any good is still a real question, and it's the question the rest of this
section puts a price on. So I'd say the circle moves rather than vanishes. It moves somewhere you
can look at it, which is the most I'd claim.

\subsection{The shape, said once}

So here's what I mean by entitlement, and it has three parts, and I'll try to earn each.

A run is entitled to a claim when three things are present. First, an \emph{object}, carried in
the state: a grouping, a relation between groups, a counter, a package of constraints. Not a
belief; a thing you could print. Second, a \emph{checked relation} between that object and the
claim: a test that was actually run, with its result on hand, not ``a test exists.'' Third, an
\emph{event on the record} that says this object was put there and paid for, so that anyone
auditing the run can point back at the moment the claim was marked.

Said as a definition, so the rest of the section has something to point at:

\begin{definition}[Entitlement]\label{def:u08-entitlement}
A run is \emph{entitled} to a claim when three things are on hand: an \emph{object} carried in the run's
states; a \emph{checked relation} between that object and the claim, meaning a test whose result is
on the record, not a test that merely exists; and a \emph{paid event}, a move of the run at which
the object was put in place and which the price list charged at least one. In a certification
system (Definition~\ref{def:certsys}) a move that takes the reading from no to yes is such a
move, because the toll charges it. This is the book's word, not a Coq definition.
\end{definition}

Without the third part, the object may be sitting right there and the claim may be true, and
the run still hasn't \emph{earned} it. That's the cups: the coin is under cup one; the reason is
disconnected from it; nobody lifted the cup. Put it on Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s sheet of paper, the one with the
NO box, the YES box and the tally line, and grow the toy by one thing: the state is now the box
you're in plus whatever is written on the sheet beside it. Next to the boxes, write a note:
``coin under cup one, checked.'' Writing the note is a WORK move, and WORK costs nothing. The note is an object, it's
on the paper, and it might even be true. What it doesn't have is a crossing on the record: no
move took the reading from NO to YES when the note went down, and there's no mark under the
line for it. The note is raw data, forged in one write, and any system with the five parts
lets you write one, because nothing in the five parts says what an ordinary move may put in
the state. A note put down by the move that crosses has a receipt, and the receipt is the
event. One limit on that word ``receipt'': the crossing records that something was paid for at
that moment. What the crossing move actually looked at before it crossed is up to whatever
the move does, and the five parts don't say.

And here's the part to hold on to. Nothing in the five parts makes a later move \emph{read} the
reading. The step function is handed the state and a move name, and it's allowed to ignore
the YES box completely; plenty of systems will. So when I say a run is \emph{entitled}, I mean what
someone auditing the run may conclude from the reading and the receipt. The system doesn't
have to enforce it, and unless somebody builds it to, it won't.

The engineering version of this was already built, in 1997. George Necula's
\emph{proof-carrying code}: when you ship a program to a host that doesn't trust you, you ship a
\emph{proof} with it that the program obeys the host's safety rules, and the host \emph{checks the proof that arrived} before running anything. Not your reputation. Not ``a proof exists
somewhere.'' The one in the box. A quarter century earlier Stephen Cook's certificates had the
same bones, from Section~\ref{sec:toll}: a claim comes with a witness that's cheap to check, and the checker
checks \emph{that} witness. And David Hume, in 1748, arguing about miracles, laid out the thing
the receipt replaces: he weighed testimony against evidence, and said a wise person believes
in proportion to the evidence, and the whole of his argument is a method for how much to
trust a witness when you have no receipt. The move in this book is to stop weighing. A claim
on the record is either backed by its object and its paid event, or it's testimony from
outside, and a run that leans on testimony hasn't earned anything.

Three things entitlement is \emph{not}, which people reach for. It isn't permission: an access
control system says who may write to what, and that's granted from outside and says nothing
about truth; a process with permission to write the note still has no entitlement. It isn't
``true, therefore usable'': that's the cups. And it isn't ``sound by luck'': a shortcut that gives
the right answer because the inputs happened to cooperate is the stopped clock. The count
below has one condition aimed at it, and I'll tell you what the condition says and how much it
actually catches.

\subsection{What narrowing costs: count the rivals}

Now the number, because a book about a bill has to say how much. Here's the idea in a form
you can do with three playing cards. Shuffle cards marked 1, 2, 3 face down. Sort them using
only questions of the form ``is this one bigger than that one?'', and count the questions.
There are six orders the cards could be in. Each question has two answers, so after one
question you've split the six into at most two piles, after two questions at most four, and
you need to get down to one. Four is less than six, so two questions can't always do it, and
three can, and you can draw the tree of questions on paper and see it: six leaves, three
deep. The number of questions you need is at least the base-two logarithm of the number of
possibilities you started with, rounded up: that's log2 of 6, which is a bit under 3, rounded
to 3. Donald Knuth, in the volume on sorting of \emph{The Art of Computer Programming}, gives this
as the lower bound for all comparison sorting, and the shape of
the argument is just: a tree f questions deep has at most 2 to the f leaves, so it can't tell
apart more than 2 to the f cases.

And then the obvious next question: is the floor always the price? Try five cards. There are 120
orders, log2 of 120 is a bit under 7, so you need at least seven questions, and seven is enough,
though not by the obvious method. Finding the way is a good evening with a deck of cards (Knuth
has it, under the name merge insertion, from Lester Ford and Selmer Johnson in 1959). Now twelve
cards. They can be in 479,001,600 orders, log2 of that is about 28.8, so the count says at least
29. Ford and Johnson's method takes 30, and in 1965 Mark Wells showed that nothing does better:
twelve cards need 30. The floor was 29. The price is 30. So the count is a floor and only a floor;
it never promises the floor can be reached, and the bound later in this section has to be read
exactly the same way.

Ralph Hartley in 1928, before Shannon, measured information exactly this way: the logarithm
of the number of possibilities, no probabilities, just a count. That's the measure here, and
I'll say plainly it's Hartley's and not Shannon's: there's no distribution over the list,
only the list's length.

Now put it on a run. Say a run comes with a list of states that are ``still on the table,''
the candidates, and a shorter list, with some ruled out. Call the first the prior and the
second the posterior, and I want you to hear those as \emph{a list you could print}, not ``the
space of possible worlds.'' Picture the ruling-out as observations, each observation that
ruled something out being one branch point in a tree like the card tree. And here's the claim: if that tree is no
deeper than the number of paid steps the run took, and the tree has enough leaves to cover
the narrowing in a way I'll spell out in a moment, then the counter rose by at least log2 of
the prior's length minus log2 of the posterior's length. At least as many marks as \emph{index
bits} the list lost, where the index bits of a list are the yes/no questions it takes to point
at one entry of it, the card count again. That's the bound.

``Paid step'' needs its own sentence. It means a step the price list charges at least one for.
In a certification system the toll guarantees that every crossing of the reading is one; a
price list is free to put a floor under more steps than that (a look, a send, a check), and
the count takes every paid step there is. The tree is a bare shape, branches and leaves with
nothing written on them, and ``no deeper than the number of paid steps'' is a count along the
run that happened. It isn't a walk down the tree. A paid step doesn't have to have asked any
question at all.

Notice, too, what the bound does and doesn't say about the run. It takes the two lists, the
tree and the covering as given. It doesn't say the run produced the posterior from the prior;
nothing in it reads the lists off the run. What it says is that, given lists, a tree and a
covering that someone supplies, the paid steps of the run cover the rounded drop in list
length. That's Section~\ref{sec:narrowing}'s warning come due: watching can narrow for free, so the payment can't be
dug out of the narrowing. It goes in as a premise, the tree's depth against the paid steps,
and I'll keep calling it one.

\subsection{What ``narrower'' buys: a stronger test}

Before the count, one link that's pure logic, and Plato's third account is the whole of it.
Take a list of candidates and an observation, a function that says what each candidate looks
like from outside. The list's \emph{membership test} accepts an observation when some candidate on
the list shows it. Shrink the list, and the test can only get pickier: anything the short
list's test accepts, the long list's accepts too. The word for that, and it runs backward
from English, is \emph{stronger}: the stronger test is the one that lets \emph{fewer} things through.

Pickier, though, isn't the same as strictly pickier, and the cards show the gap. Take all six
orders as the prior, and as the posterior the three where card 1 sits left of card 2:
1-2-3, 1-3-2 and 3-1-2. First observation: ``is 1 left of 2?'' Every survivor says yes, and
the removed 2-1-3 says no, so the prior's test accepts yes and no, the posterior's only yes.
Strictly stronger. Second observation, same two lists: ``is the first card a 3?'' Now 3-1-2
says yes and the other two survivors say no, and among the removed orders 3-2-1 says yes and
2-1-3 says no. Both tests accept yes and no. Same strength, even though three orders are gone.
What made the difference is a removed candidate whose observation \emph{no survivor shares}. That's
Plato's mark, the thing that sets this case apart from everything it could be confused with,
turned into a function. Narrow the list and keep one distinguishing removed candidate, and
the test is strictly stronger; narrow it without one, and the test may not have moved at all.

\subsection{The count, exactly}

Here are the words and the count, for any system with Section~\ref{sec:counter}'s counter. A \emph{list} is a finite list
of candidates, repeats allowed, and $|\Omega|$ is the length of the list $\Omega$, repeats
counted. $\lceil \log_2 x \rceil$ is the base-two logarithm of $x$ rounded up: the smallest
$k\in\mathbb{N}$ with $2^k \ge x$. At $x=0$ this index-bit count is defined to
be $0$ as well; the notation $\lceil\log_2 0\rceil=0$ here is a convention for empty
lists, not the real logarithm of zero. And $a \mathbin{\dot{-}} b$ is subtraction on whole numbers that stops at
zero, so $3 \mathbin{\dot{-}} 5 = 0$.

\begin{definition}[Decision tree]\label{def:u08-dtree}
