A \emph{decision tree} is a leaf, or a branch with two subtrees. Its depth is $0$ for a leaf and
one more than the deeper subtree for a branch; its leaf count $L(T)$ is $1$ for a leaf and the
sum of the two counts for a branch. Nothing is written on a tree: no question, no answer, no
candidate.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[A tree is no wider than two to its depth]\label{lem:u08-tree-width}
For every decision tree $T$, $L(T) \le 2^{\mathrm{depth}(T)}$, and so
$\lceil \log_2 L(T) \rceil \le \mathrm{depth}(T)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Induction on the tree. A leaf has one leaf and depth $0$, and $1 \le 2^0$. A branch with
subtrees of depths $d_1, d_2$ has at most $2^{d_1} + 2^{d_2} \le 2 \cdot 2^{\max(d_1, d_2)}$
leaves, which is $2$ to its own depth. The second half: $L(T) \le 2^{\mathrm{depth}(T)}$ means
$\mathrm{depth}(T)$ is one of the $k$ with $2^k \ge L(T)$, and the rounded-up logarithm is the
smallest of them.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{decision\_tree\_leaves\_le\_pow2\_depth} and \code{decision\_tree\_log2\_up\_leaf\_bound}
(MuShannonBridge.v). Both are stated over the tree type alone, a leaf or a branch, with
nothing about any machine in them.

\begin{theorem}[Paid narrowing, counted]\label{thm:u08-count}
Take a system with a counter $\mu$ and a price list $c$ that obey conservation
(Theorem~\ref{thm:conservation}): each step raises $\mu$ by exactly its charge. Let $\Omega$ and
$\Omega'$ be lists with $|\Omega'| > 0$, let $T$ be a decision tree with
$|\Omega| \le L(T) \cdot |\Omega'|$ (the tree \emph{covers} the narrowing), and let $t$ be a run from
$s$ ending at $s'$ in which at least $\mathrm{depth}(T)$ steps are charged at least one each.
Then
\[
\lceil \log_2 |\Omega| \rceil \mathbin{\dot{-}} \lceil \log_2 |\Omega'| \rceil \;\le\; \mu(s') - \mu(s).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The rounded-up logarithm respects order, so the covering gives
$\lceil \log_2 |\Omega| \rceil \le \lceil \log_2 (L(T) \cdot |\Omega'|) \rceil$. It is also
subadditive on products of positive numbers,
$\lceil \log_2 ab \rceil \le \lceil \log_2 a \rceil + \lceil \log_2 b \rceil$, because
$2^{\lceil \log_2 a \rceil} \cdot 2^{\lceil \log_2 b \rceil} \ge ab$. So
\[
\lceil \log_2 |\Omega| \rceil \mathbin{\dot{-}} \lceil \log_2 |\Omega'| \rceil \;\le\; \lceil \log_2 L(T) \rceil \;\le\; \mathrm{depth}(T),
\]
the last step by Lemma~\ref{lem:u08-tree-width}. By hypothesis at least $\mathrm{depth}(T)$
steps of the run were charged at least one, and no step is charged less than zero, so the sum
of the charges is at least $\mathrm{depth}(T)$. By conservation that sum is
$\mu(s') - \mu(s)$.
\end{proof}

Argued here for any system with a counter that obeys conservation. The tree half is the
checked lemma above; the rest is arithmetic on three whole numbers, the two lengths and the
leaf count, and on the counter. Notice what's missing from the hypotheses: anything tying the
lists to the run. That's the honest shape of the bound.

Three honest small prints, all of them visible in the statement. Both logarithms round up
separately, and the subtraction stops at zero, so when the prior and the posterior round up to
the same number of index bits (four candidates narrowed to three, say) the bound says nothing.
The lists are plain lists, not sets, so ``index bits'' is a difference of rounded list lengths
with repeats counted; a list can get shorter by dropping a duplicate without losing a single
candidate, and ``a candidate was ruled out'' and ``the list got shorter'' are two different
claims. And the difference isn't the number of questions anyone asked.

The covering condition, $|\Omega| \le L(T) \cdot |\Omega'|$, is the nearest thing the count
has to an anti-stopped-clock clause, and I have to be exact about how near. Picture each
survivor standing for a little crowd of the candidates that were dropped, a crowd no bigger
than the tree has leaves. Then the condition says every candidate in the prior fits in some
survivor's crowd. That limits how much can be deleted per leaf you paid for. It doesn't say
why anything was deleted. So the condition rules out deleting too much for the tree you've
paid for. It doesn't rule out deleting for no reason. A run can satisfy every hypothesis of
the count and have ruled nothing out on purpose; the count prices the size of the drop, not
the honesty of it.

\subsection{What you've got}

A paid flag is not a true claim; Section~\ref{sec:windows} left it at ``a paid flag is a paid flag,'' and Section~\ref{sec:insight} will say
it flatly. What a paid flag with an object and a checked relation behind it gives you is
\emph{entitlement}: anyone auditing the run may treat the claim as established, and can point at
the event where that became legitimate. (Nothing in the five parts makes the system itself
read the flag; I said that above and I'm saying it again because it's the sentence most likely
to get lost.) Entitlement costs at least the index bits of narrowing it commits to, given
lists, a tree and a covering somebody supplies, and given a run that paid for the tree's
depth. The cups say why entitlement and truth are different. Plato says what the checked
relation has to do: distinguish. Necula says how to build it. Hartley says what to count.

The machine I build later has all of these pieces at once, and Section~\ref{sec:machine-claims} puts this whole section on
it, every hypothesis written out, with one worked member you can count by hand. Before any of
that, I owe you the word the toll is named after, the ``insight'' in ``No Free Insight'' (Section~\ref{sec:narrowing}),
because I've been using it as if it meant one thing.

%===========================================================================
\section{What insight is}
\label{sec:insight}
%===========================================================================

I named the rule in this book ``No Free Insight,'' and the name ran ahead of any careful account
of what insight is. The book has been narrowing it ever since: not learning (Section~\ref{sec:narrowing}), not
looking, not copying. It's time to say what's left, and to say it in a way that someone who
studies actual insight, in actual heads, wouldn't laugh at. So who are those people, and what
did they find? Here's what I ran into, pushed on as I go, because the founding stories of a field
get retold like any other stories, and a retold story is a lead to check.

\subsection{Sultan and the sticks}

In 1913 the psychologist Wolfgang Köhler went to Tenerife to run a research station with a
colony of chimpanzees, and the First World War then kept him there until 1920 with
nothing to do but watch them.
The famous one is Sultan. Food is outside the cage, out of reach; two sticks are inside, each
too short, but one fits into the end of the other. Sultan tries each stick, fails, sulks,
plays with the sticks, and then, by Köhler's account, at a moment you can see, joins them and
reaches the food. Köhler's word was \emph{einsichtig}, which came into English as ``insight,'' and
the whole school of psychology he belonged to, the Gestalt school, said that's what thinking
is: not stacking up tries until one works, but a \emph{restructuring}, the moment two sticks stop
being two sticks and become one tool. Karl Duncker gave the human version, in German in 1935
and in English in 1945, five years after he died at thirty-seven; he'd spent his last years
working with Köhler at Swarthmore. You can set it up yourself: a candle, a box of tacks, matches,
and the task of fixing the
candle to the wall. Almost nobody sees that the \emph{box} is a shelf, until they do. And then he found that if you hand people the box \emph{empty}, with the tacks poured out beside it, they
solve it far more readily. Same objects. What changed was which relation among them was on the table.

I like both of these for the same reason: the insight didn't add an object. Sultan had both
sticks the whole time. The box was there the whole time. What arrived was a \emph{relation}, which
is to say a piece of structure in Section~\ref{sec:structure}'s sense, and the arrival was sudden. Hold that, because
it's going to turn out that the thing the toll prices also arrives in one step, and at its
best it's also a relation.

\subsection{It isn't a feeling}

But here's the finding I'd hand anyone who thinks insight is a feeling, and it comes from
someone who measured it. In the 1980s the psychologist Janet Metcalfe asked people to solve
problems while rating, every fifteen seconds, how ``warm'' they felt, how close to the answer.
On ordinary problems, algebra for instance, the warmth climbs steadily and peaks at the
answer, which is what you'd expect. On \emph{insight} problems, riddles of the candle-box kind, the
warmth stays flat, flat, flat, and then the answer arrives, and if anything the people who
felt warmest beforehand were \emph{more} likely to be wrong. The feeling of being close is not a
gauge of being close. Try it yourself: write a number from one to seven every fifteen seconds
while doing a long sum, then while doing a riddle, and compare the curves.

And the most famous insight story there is fits Metcalfe uncomfortably well. Archimedes, asked
whether a goldsmith had cheated the king on a crown, gets into a bath, sees the water rise, and
runs home naked shouting ``eureka,'' I've found it. That comes from Vitruvius, writing about two
centuries later. Is it true? Galileo, at twenty-two, in 1586, thought the method as Vitruvius
tells it was too crude to catch a clever goldsmith, and wrote a little tract, \emph{La
Bilancetta}, proposing a balance weighed in air and in water instead, which he thought was
probably what Archimedes actually did, since it rests on Archimedes's own results. So the eureka
is a legend, wrapped around a real man and probably a real problem. Notice what the legend kept:
the bath, the shout, the running home naked. The feeling. What it got shaky is the part that
would count as the check, the test that could have caught the goldsmith. The bit everybody
remembers is the bit that tells you least.

So any account of insight that keys on the sensation, the ``aha,'' is keyed to something that
the data says is unreliable. Whatever insight is, it isn't the feeling of having it. That's a
relief, because a system of states and moves doesn't have feelings, and a word that only
meant a feeling would be cheating if I hung it on one. The version this book can price has to be keyed to an \emph{event}, and the
question is which.

\subsection{What happens when a computation learns}

Here's the split, and I'll say what the toll does with each part, and then I'll say who
decided the split, because it wasn't me. Keep Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s sheet of paper in front of you: the NO box,
the YES box, the tally line, and the three moves STAY, WORK and VOUCH.

The first thing: \emph{raw observation}. Something comes in and gets written down. A counter
ticks. Nothing is claimed about what it means, nothing is marked as resting on it, and the
reading doesn't move because of it. Later moves can read what it wrote, but that reading is a
move of its own. This is the demon's pad in Section~\ref{sec:narrowing}, and it's what the statistician Dennis Lindley
measured in 1956 as ``the information an experiment provides,'' the expected drop in your uncertainty: a real quantity,
and a quantity about what was \emph{seen}. It can be free. The toll says nothing at all about a
move that doesn't cross from NO to YES, so a price list may charge it zero: on the paper,
STAY and WORK cost nothing, and Section~\ref{sec:narrowing}'s watcher narrowed a whole row of candidates without paying
a mark. ``Can be'' is the honest word. A price list is allowed to charge for looking anyway, and
whether looking costs anything in the physical world is a different question that this sheet
of paper doesn't touch.

Lindley's measure has a back story, and it runs through Bletchley Park. I. J. Good, who was Alan Turing's main
statistical assistant at Bletchley Park in 1941, wrote in 1979 that Turing had worked out the
expected weight of evidence an experiment would give, to judge one of the codebreaking
procedures before running it, and so partly anticipated Lindley by about fifteen years, in work
that stayed secret. Turing measured evidence in \emph{bans}, logarithms to base ten, with a tenth
of one called a deciban, and the name came from the town of Banbury, where tens of thousands of
the sheets used in that procedure were printed. It's the same base-ten unit other people call the
hartley, after the Hartley from the last section. And Good adds that Turing didn't know the
logarithm he was using had already appeared in 1878, in a paper by Charles Sanders Peirce, the
same Peirce from the opening chapter, who'd called it the weight of evidence. Peirce is as far
back as Good takes it. What it changes: nothing in the argument, but it shows how well trodden this
first kind of thing is. For a century and a half careful people have measured what an
observation tells you, and every one of those measures is about what was seen. That's the side
of the line the toll leaves alone.

The second thing: \emph{certified insight}. Some move turns the reading from NO to YES. Here is
where the toll lives. In any system with the five parts that obeys the toll, that move costs
at least one mark, and every run that starts at NO and ends at YES pays at least one somewhere
along the way, which is Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s universal floor. What's being charged for, at its best, is
exactly the Gestalt thing: a relation, committed to. Not two sticks; one tool, claimed. ``At
its best,'' because Section~\ref{sec:toll} was careful about what YES means: the flag is up, and nothing more. A
crossing that writes down which relation it's committing to carries Sultan's tool with it. A
bare crossing, VOUCH on the paper, commits to no relation at all, and it pays exactly the
same.

The third thing isn't a kind of event. It's an observation about the price: it's \emph{flat},
whatever is certified. Say the YES state also shows something striking, a deep relation, a
result nobody could have guessed, Sultan's two sticks become one tool. The toll charges the
crossing at least one. It doesn't charge the striking crossing more, because the floor's proof
never looks at anything but the reading before and after. On the paper: VOUCH from NO makes
one mark whether you were thinking of Duncker's box or of lunch. Meaning is not cost. The
depth of what's certified adds meaning. It doesn't add a mark.

The candle box has a footnote that says the same thing from the other side. In 1962 Sam
Glucksberg ran Duncker's problem with money on it: some people were told they could win five or
twenty dollars depending on how fast they solved it. With the tacks in the box, the people
chasing the money did worse than the people who weren't. With the box empty, the money made no
clear difference. Paying more didn't buy the insight, and on the hard version it got in the way.
That's a fact about heads, not about records, and I won't push it further than that. But it's a
nice mirror for the paper. On the paper a deeper crossing isn't charged more, and in Glucksberg's
room a bigger prize didn't bring the crossing sooner. In neither place does the price measure the
depth.

Here they are, exactly, for any certification system (Definition~\ref{def:certsys}). Runs are
written as lists, the way Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s proof wrote them: $[\,]$ is the empty run, and $i :: t$ is the
run that starts with move $i$ and carries on with the run $t$.

\begin{definition}[Certified insight event, raw observation]\label{def:u09-events}
In a certification system, a step from state $s$ by move $i$ is a \emph{certified insight event}
when it turns the reading on: $\mathrm{cert}(s) = \mathrm{no}$ and
$\mathrm{cert}(\mathrm{step}(s, i)) = \mathrm{yes}$. A move $i$ is \emph{raw observation} when no
step by it, from any state, is a certified insight event.
\end{definition}

\begin{remark}[What the toll prices, and what it doesn't]\label{rem:u09-three}
Read off Definition~\ref{def:certsys} and Theorem~\ref{thm:universal-floor}; there is no further
Coq theorem at this generality. (1) The toll puts no bound on the cost of a raw-observation
move; on Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s board STAY and WORK are raw observation and cost $0$. (2) Every certified
insight event is charged at least $1$, by the toll, and every run from a state reading no to
one reading yes has total cost at least $1$, by the universal floor. (3) The price is flat:
the floor's proof uses nothing about the end state but its reading, so adding any hypothesis
about what else the end state shows leaves the bound at $1$ and cannot raise it. A system that
wants to charge more for a deeper certification has to write that into its price list, move
by move; the toll doesn't do it for anyone.
\end{remark}

So the account comes down to two facts and a warning. Looking can be free. Turning the reading
on can't. And putting something remarkable behind the reading doesn't make it cost any more.

Who decided the split? Not the costs alone. The toll prices exactly one thing, the crossing.
A price list is free to put a floor under more moves than that (a look, a send, a check) and
free to leave other moves at zero, so the sorting into raw observation and certified insight
is by whether the reading moves, and that sorting is this book's. The part that's \emph{forced} is
the floor under the crossing, and Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} is the argument for it; anything a price list charges
beyond that is a choice, and any concrete machine owes you its whole table so you can see
which choices it made.

\subsection{Test, then commit, and nothing forces the second to follow the first}

The philosopher Karl Popper said a theory earns its standing by being \emph{exposed}: you make a
conjecture, you try to kill it, and what survives a real attempt counts for something, where
``real'' means the test could have failed. His word for that earned credit is \emph{corroboration}. I've leaned on that idea through this whole book, and here's
where a certification system has a version of it, and here's where the version is weaker
than Popper and I have to say so.

Add a fourth move to the paper: CHECK. It looks at something (a sum, a coin under a cup, a
formula against a row of values), and it can come out pass or fail, and it doesn't move the
box. Charge it whatever you like; charging it on the attempt, pass or fail, fits Popper,
because what made his test count was that it was really run and could have failed. That's
the test. It's raw observation in the sense above,
because it never turns the reading on. VOUCH is the commit. So the honest protocol is two
moves: test, then commit, and the costs are separate, one for the checking work and one for
the crossing.

But nothing in the five parts makes the second move wait for the first. The step is handed
the current state and a move name; the toll looks only at whether the reading crossed. Play
VOUCH from NO with no CHECK anywhere before it, and you land in YES and make one mark, the
same box and the same mark as the player who checked first. The two tally lines differ by
exactly what the CHECK was charged, and if you charged it nothing they don't differ at all.
The mark for the crossing is the same mark either way. The receipt says a commitment was paid
for. It does not say it was earned. Popper's corroboration needs the test; the toll doesn't.

You can build a system that makes the commit wait. Let CHECK leave a mark in the state when it
passes, and write the step so VOUCH only crosses when that mark is there. That's a design,
written into the step function, and it's a perfectly good one. Nothing in the five parts or
the toll asks for it. That's a real gap between the word and the bare system, and the only
honest thing is to leave it visible: the toll prices the commit, and whether the commit was
preceded by a test is a fact about the run, or about a design somebody chose, not a guarantee
of the five parts.

\begin{remark}[Nothing makes the crossing wait]\label{rem:u09-no-wait}
Read off Definition~\ref{def:certsys}; there is no Coq theorem. The toll constrains
$\mathrm{cost}(i)$ for moves that cross, and nothing else; the step function is any function
of the current state and the move. So a certification system may have a move that crosses
from a state no check has touched, and the toll still holds. On Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s board extended with
CHECK, the run $[\mathrm{VOUCH}]$ from NO crosses with one mark, and so does
$[\mathrm{CHECK}, \mathrm{VOUCH}]$. Making a crossing depend on an earlier check is a
condition on the step function, which a particular system can impose and the definition does
not.
\end{remark}

\subsection{What the word means}

So: insight, in the sense this book prices, is a relation committed to, in a move that flips a
reading from off to on, and that move costs at least one mark, in any system with the toll,
for any relation, whatever its depth. (And one edge from the paper: a bare crossing that
commits to nothing pays the same mark, so ``a relation committed to'' is what the crossing is
at its best, not what the toll guarantees.) Three boundaries, each from a different place.
From Metcalfe: it isn't a feeling, and a system's version has to be an event. From the proof:
the price is flat; a shallow commit and a deep one both cost at least one, and cost is not
depth. A system can pay heavily to check a claim that turns out trivial, and Duncker's box
is one small commit. And from the two-move protocol: a paid flag proves nothing on its own.
Price and correctness are separate books.

Which leaves a suspicion I'd have in your place. Everything so far has been one reading on one
sheet of paper, with a rule I chose and a count I bolted on. Is the shape of that record
something I picked, or is it what any honest record has to look like, on any machine at all?
That's the next section: take \emph{any} machine that steps, bolt a record onto it, and see what
shape it's forced into. How a concrete machine hangs actual claims on its parts, formulas and
labels and where they sit in the state, comes in Part IV.

%===========================================================================
\section{Records over any base: the latch}
\label{sec:latch}
%===========================================================================

For the whole book so far I've been building up a thing with a flag and a counter, and a
fair reader is entitled to suspect that the whole apparatus is special pleading for one
machine, the one I keep promising to build. So here's the section that answers the suspicion
with no particular machine in it at all, and sees what's left. Take \emph{any} machine that steps deterministically: a Turing
machine, a register machine (a few numbered boxes that each hold a whole number, and a
program that adds, subtracts and jumps), a lambda calculus (Alonzo Church's way of computing by nothing
but plugging expressions into expressions; Section~\ref{sec:diagonal} builds one), anything. Call it the base. Now bolt a record onto it, under rules I'll state,
and ask: what can the record be?

The answer is one shape, and I'll show you the shape first because it's a thing you can
build from a cup and a die.

\subsection{A cup and a die}

Put a cup upside down on the table. The rule: the first time a coin lands in front of it,
turn it right side up. There is no rule for turning it back over. Now roll a die, and put a
coin down on every six. Roll twenty times. The cup turns over on the first six and stays
turned over. Write down which roll did it. That number, the roll that turned the cup, is
where the record happened, and the cup afterward is the record.

That's a \emph{latch}. Electrical engineers have had the circuit since 1918, when William Eccles
and Frank Jordan applied for a patent on a two-valve arrangement that holds whichever state you last put it
in; it became the flip-flop, and the registers and caches in the device you're reading this on
descend from it. The simplest version has one input, ``set,'' and the rule \emph{new state = old state or set}: once set, it stays set, and there's no reset wire. The cup is that circuit:
a flip-flop with its reset wire cut off.

(Eccles and Jordan didn't call it a flip-flop. Their 1919 paper calls it a \emph{trigger relay}.
Where the newer, sillier name came from I can't source, so I'll leave it at that.)

Is a flip-flop with its reset wire cut off only a picture, or did anybody ever build one on
purpose? Somebody did, and for a reason that's very close to this book's. In the mid-1950s Wen
Tsing Chow, an engineer at the Arma division of the American Bosch Arma Corporation in Garden City,
New York, was asked by the United States Air Force for a more flexible and secure way to hold
the fixed numbers, the targeting constants, inside the guidance computer of the Atlas missile.
What he and William Henrich patented (filed in 1957, granted in 1962, under the plain title
``Storage matrix'') was a grid with a connection at every crossing, where you set the numbers by
taking out the connections you didn't want, physically or by burning them out with too much
current. The word \emph{burn} is right there in the patent, and people still say they burn a
chip. The descendants are called programmable read-only memories, PROMs, and a fuse blown in
one stays blown: there's no current you can send to grow it back. A whole memory built out of
cups with no reset wire, because somebody wanted numbers nobody could quietly change later. Does
that prove anything here? No. The theorem below doesn't care what a cup is made of. But it's
good to know the shape wasn't invented for a sheet of paper. Somebody needed it, for stakes a
good deal higher than a die.

Now the claim, stated loosely and then exactly: \emph{every honest record over any base is a cup with no reset wire, turned by some event the base passes through.}

\subsection{What ``honest'' has to mean}

Here's where the content is, and I'll give you the five rules, because the theorem is only as
strong as they are.

A machine \emph{extends} a base when there's a map from the big machine's states down to the
base's, and that map starts in the base's start states, reaches every one of them, moves in
step with the base (one step up top is one step down below, through the map), and agrees
about halting. The big machine may carry as much hidden state as it likes beyond the base.
That's the ``any base'' part: the base doesn't get to see the extension, and the extension
doesn't get to change what the base does.

The extension carries a \emph{record}, a yes/no reading, and a \emph{ledger}, a counter. It's an
honest extension when five things hold. One: the record's next value depends only on the
base's current state and the record's current value. (I'll call this \emph{driven by the computation}. It says the record answers to what the machine is doing, not to a clock on the
wall or someone's hand.) Two: the ledger never goes down (Section~\ref{sec:counter}). Three: the step that turns the
record on costs at least one; that's the toll (Section~\ref{sec:toll}). Four: once on, the record stays on;
that's permanence (Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}). Five: some run from a start state actually reaches a step that
turns the record on; otherwise the record is decoration.

Here are the words exactly. On/off is true/false, $\lor$ is ``or'' (on when either side is
on), and $\mathrm{next}^k$ is $k$ steps.

\begin{definition}[Base, record-carrying machine, cover]\label{def:u11-base}
A \emph{base} $B$ is a set of states with a step function $\mathrm{next}_B$, a set of starting
states, and a halting predicate. A \emph{record-carrying machine} $M$ is a set of states with a step
function $\mathrm{next}_M$, a set of starting states, a \emph{record} $\mathrm{rec}$ from states to
Booleans, a \emph{ledger} $\mu$ from states to whole numbers, and a halting predicate. The cost of a
step is $\mathrm{cost}(m) = \mu(\mathrm{next}_M(m)) \mathbin{\dot{-}} \mu(m)$. A \emph{cover} of $B$
by $M$ is a map $\pi$ from states of $M$ to states of $B$ that sends starting states to starting
states, has every starting state of $B$ as the image of some starting state of $M$, commutes
with the steps, $\pi(\mathrm{next}_M(m)) = \mathrm{next}_B(\pi(m))$, and agrees about halting:
$m$ halts exactly when $\pi(m)$ does.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Honest extension, latch]\label{def:u11-honest}
$M$ with cover $\pi$ is an \emph{honest extension} of $B$ when, for every state $m$:
(R1, driven by the computation) there is one function $f$ with
$\mathrm{rec}(\mathrm{next}_M(m)) = f(\pi(m), \mathrm{rec}(m))$; (R2, ledger)
$\mu(m) \le \mu(\mathrm{next}_M(m))$; (R3, toll) if $\mathrm{rec}(m)$ is off and
$\mathrm{rec}(\mathrm{next}_M(m))$ is on, then $\mathrm{cost}(m) \ge 1$; (R4, permanence) if
$\mathrm{rec}(m)$ is on, so is $\mathrm{rec}(\mathrm{next}_M(m))$; and (R5, a reachable write)
some starting state $m_0$ and some $k$ have $\mathrm{rec}(\mathrm{next}_M^k(m_0))$ off and
$\mathrm{rec}(\mathrm{next}_M^{k+1}(m_0))$ on. An \emph{event} is a function $h$ from base states to
Booleans, and its \emph{latch} is the step $(b, r) \mapsto (\mathrm{next}_B(b),\, r \lor h(b))$. $M$
\emph{factors as the latch of} $h$ when, for every state $m$ (reachable or not),
\[
(\pi(\mathrm{next}_M(m)),\ \mathrm{rec}(\mathrm{next}_M(m))) = (\mathrm{next}_B(\pi(m)),\ \mathrm{rec}(m) \lor h(\pi(m))).
\]
\end{definition}

Now the theorem. Under those rules, the base state and the record move \emph{exactly} as a latch:
the record switches on at the first base state where some event holds, and never off, and
the event is read off the extension's own rule by asking it what it does when the record is
off (stated exactly below). Everything else the extension carries, all the hidden
state, shows up only in its ledger; it can't leak into the record's behaviour.

I promised the content was in the definition, and here's what that means: the proof is a
short case split on whether the record is already on, and it uses only \emph{two} of the five
rules, ``driven by the computation'' and ``permanent.'' The ledger, the toll, and the reachable-write clauses play no part in it. A
latch is what you get from ``answers only to the base'' plus ``never comes back down,'' full
stop. The other three rules matter for the \emph{converse}: for any base and any event the base can reach, the latch of that event, priced at one unit per write, \emph{is} an honest extension.
Put the two together and you've got: honest records are exactly
latches. One shape, no others, over any base.

\begin{theorem}[The record is a latch]\label{thm:u11-latch}
Let $B$ be any base and $M$ an honest extension of it through $\pi$, with $f$ the function of
(R1). Then $M$ factors as the latch of the event $h(b) = f(b, \mathrm{off})$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The base half of the equation is the cover's step clause. For the record, split on
$\mathrm{rec}(m)$. If it is on, permanence (R4) makes the next value on, and
$\mathrm{on} \lor h(\pi(m))$ is on. If it is off, (R1) makes the next value
$f(\pi(m), \mathrm{off}) = h(\pi(m)) = \mathrm{off} \lor h(\pi(m))$. Only (R1), (R4) and the
cover are used; (R2), (R3) and (R5) are discarded.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{record\_axis\_is\_latch\_holds} (StructuralRecordAxis.v), with the definitions
\code{BaseMachine}, \code{BaseCover}, \code{computation\_driven}, \code{HonestBaseExtension} and
\code{latch\_factorization} (StructuralCoreAnyBase.v), and the clauses (R2) to (R5) as
\code{ledger\_carried}, \code{rc\_a2} (StructuralCore.v), \code{record\_permanent} and \code{reachable\_record\_write}
(StructuralCoreCover.v).

\begin{theorem}[Every reachable latch is an honest record]\label{thm:u11-converse}
Let $B$ be any base and $h$ any event. Let $\mathrm{Latch}_h$ have states $(b, r, x)$, starting
states $(b, \mathrm{off}, 0)$ with $b$ starting in $B$, step
$(b, r, x) \mapsto (\mathrm{next}_B(b),\ r \lor h(b),\ x + \delta)$ with $\delta = 1$ when $r$
is off and $h(b)$ is on and $\delta = 0$ otherwise, record $r$, ledger $x$, halting as $b$
halts, and cover $(b, r, x) \mapsto b$. Suppose some starting $b_0$ and some $k$ bring
$\mathrm{Latch}_h$ from $(b_0, \mathrm{off}, 0)$, in $k$ steps, to a state whose record is
still off and whose base state satisfies $h$. Then $\mathrm{Latch}_h$ is an honest extension
of $B$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(R1) holds with $f(b, r) = r \lor h(b)$. (R2): each step adds $0$ or $1$. (R3): a step that
turns the record on has $r$ off and $h(b)$ on, so it adds $1$. (R4): $\mathrm{on} \lor h(b)$ is
on. (R5) is the supposition. The supposition asks for the first time $h$ holds on some run;
any run from a start that reaches an $h$-state has such a first time, though the file states
only the first-time form.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{latch\_core\_honest} (RecordAxisDiscrimination.v).

A reversible base needs one more thing to carry a record, and the files say exactly what. If
the base never merges two states, keep every earlier record value in a growing history beside
the latch, and the whole step merges nothing either; but on a finite state space a permanent
record can't be written by a step that merges nothing at all. A step that merges nothing is
called \emph{injective}: no two states go to the same next state. And $r :: H$ is the history $H$
with $r$ put on the front, as in Section~\ref{sec:insight}.

\begin{theorem}[Records on reversible machines]\label{thm:u11-reversible}
(1) Let $B$ be a base whose step is injective. The machine with states $(b, r, H, x)$, step
$(b, r, H, x) \mapsto (\mathrm{next}_B(b),\ r \lor h(b),\ r :: H,\ x + \delta)$ ($\delta$ as in
Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-converse}), starting states with $r$ off, $H$ empty and $x = 0$, has an
injective step, and under the supposition of Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-converse} it is an honest
extension of $B$. (2) On a finite state space, a single injective step with a permanent
reading never turns that reading from off to on.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Equal images have equal base parts, so equal base states by injectivity; equal histories
$r :: H$, so equal records and histories; and equal ledgers once the equal $\delta$ is
subtracted. Honesty is the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-converse} with the history carried
along. (2) is Theorem~\ref{thm:perm-flip-merges} of Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} with a single move.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{history\_latch\_injective}, \code{history\_latch\_honest} and
\code{finite\_reversible\_cannot\_write} (RecordAxisDiscrimination.v), the last from
\code{permanent\_flip\_is\_not\_injective} (PermanentCertification.v).

So a base that never merges can still carry a record, if it's allowed to grow a history that
never ends. A finite one can't. On a finite machine the record's first write is a merge, and
Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} already put the price on that.

\subsection{Both rules do work: the toggle and the clock}

A theorem with two hypotheses should have two counterexamples, one for each hypothesis
dropped, and it does, and they're the two ways a record goes wrong in the world.

Drop permanence. Take a base that just counts, and a record that flips at every step: on,
off, on, off. It's driven by the computation; it's not permanent; and it's not a latch of
any event. This is a \emph{toggle}, a piece of working state. A record you
can revoke is working state wearing a record's clothes, and if a revocation has to stick,
that's a \emph{second} latch (``revoked''), which is how certificate revocation lists actually work:
you add an entry; you never delete the certificate. The pair theorem (stated below) covers two
latches that can each read the other; do it with two cups where the
second only turns over on an even roll \emph{if the first is already up}, and you'll see the
second can never turn before the first.

Drop ``driven by the computation.'' Take a base that counts, and a record that switches on at
the fifth tick of a \emph{hidden clock}, whatever the base is doing. It's permanent; it's not driven by the computation. This is a \emph{timestamp}. A timestamp is not evidence; it says \emph{when}, not \emph{what happened}, and a record switched by an outside
party or a clock records the party or the clock, not the computation. Try it with the die:
play twenty rolls with the rule ``turn the cup after roll seven no matter what,'' and notice
you've recorded nothing about the dice.

The file proves exactly the facts I named for each: the toggle is driven, not permanent and
not a latch; the clock is permanent and not driven. That each also keeps the other rules (the
ledger is the step count, the first switch-on costs one, a run reaches it) is true by
inspection, and isn't a separate theorem.

So: permanent but undriven is a clock, driven but impermanent is a toggle, and a record is
the thing that's both. That's the whole discrimination, and I think it's the most useful
three-sentence thing in this book for looking at systems other than the one I build, which is
why it's here.

The pair theorem and the two counterexamples, exactly. The base for both counterexamples is the
counter: states are whole numbers, the step adds one, every state is a starting state, and
nothing halts. Two more bits of shorthand: $\lnot r$ is $r$ flipped, and a statement in
square brackets, like $[k = 5]$, reads on when it's true and off when it isn't.

\begin{lemma}[Two records are two latches]\label{lem:u11-pair}
Let $c_1, c_2$ be two records on $M$, with cover $\pi$ onto a base $B$, such that: there is one
function $F$ with $(c_1(\mathrm{next}_M(m)), c_2(\mathrm{next}_M(m))) = F(\pi(m), c_1(m), c_2(m))$;
the ledger never goes down; a step that turns either record on costs at least one; and each
record is permanent. Then there are $h_1, h_2$ with
$c_1(\mathrm{next}_M(m)) = c_1(m) \lor h_1(\pi(m), c_2(m))$ and
$c_2(\mathrm{next}_M(m)) = c_2(m) \lor h_2(\pi(m), c_1(m))$ for every $m$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Take $h_1(b, r_2)$ to be the first part of $F(b, \mathrm{off}, r_2)$ and $h_2(b, r_1)$ the
second part of $F(b, r_1, \mathrm{off})$, then split on each record as in
Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-latch}.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{record\_pair\_is\_two\_latches\_holds} (StructuralRecordAxis.v).

\begin{lemma}[The toggle]\label{lem:u11-toggle}
Let the toggle have states $(n, r)$, step $(n, r) \mapsto (n + 1, \lnot r)$, every state
starting, record $r$, ledger $n$, cover $(n, r) \mapsto n$ onto the counter. It is driven by
the computation, with $f(b, r) = \lnot r$; it is not permanent; and it factors as the latch of
no event.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
At $(0, \mathrm{on})$ the next record is off, which breaks permanence; and any latch gives
$\mathrm{on} \lor h(0) = \mathrm{on}$ there.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{toggle\_not\_permanent} and \code{toggle\_not\_latch} (StructuralRecordAxis.v).

\begin{lemma}[The clock]\label{lem:u11-clock}
Let the clock have states $(b, k, r)$, step $(b, k, r) \mapsto (b + 1, k + 1, r \lor [k = 5])$,
every state starting, record $r$, ledger $b$, cover $(b, k, r) \mapsto b$ onto the counter. It
is permanent and not driven by the computation.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Permanence: $\mathrm{on} \lor x$ is on. Not driven: the states $(0, 5, \mathrm{off})$ and
$(0, 0, \mathrm{off})$ have the same base state and the same record, and their next records are
on and off, so no $f$ of the base state and the record can give both.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{toggle\_computation\_driven}, \code{toggle\_not\_permanent}, \code{toggle\_not\_latch},
\code{clock\_record\_permanent} and \code{clock\_record\_not\_driven} (StructuralRecordAxis.v). ``Driven'' is a condition on every
state, reachable or not, and that is what the clock's proof uses.

\subsection{Is there only one such machine? No. One structure, two free choices.}

Here's a sentence that's tempting and wrong, and the way it's wrong is more interesting
than the sentence: ``there's only one honest way to carry a record.'' Three different things
get squeezed into that breath, and I'll pull them apart.

First claim: given the toll and a fixed price list, is there one way to keep the books? Yes;
that's Section~\ref{sec:counter}'s initiality, and it assumes the price list.

Second claim: is every honest extension of a base \emph{the same machine}, charges and all? No,
and the counterexample is embarrassing in its simplicity. Take any honest extension and add
one more coin to the bill on every step, whatever the step is. Now walk the five rules. The
record still answers only to the base and its own value (R1); the bill never touches it. The
ledger still never goes down (R2); it climbs faster, if anything. The step that turns the
record on still costs at least one (R3), because the toll is a \emph{floor} and a surcharge only
raises the price. Once on, the record stays on (R4), and the same run still reaches the write
(R5). So the billed machine is honest, and it isn't the machine you started with: wherever
the original sat still for free, the billed one pays a coin a tick for sitting still. Do it
with the cup and the die. Charge a coin for every roll, six or not. The cup turns over on the
same roll as before. You've changed the bill and nothing about the record. A machine that
charges for CPU time is honest and isn't the one that doesn't.

But the billed machine isn't a different \emph{structure}. It's the same machine with a different
price list. So the claim worth keeping is sameness \emph{up to the price schedule}: compare two
machines by their record, their halting and their steps, through their maps down to the
base, and don't compare charges. Fix which event the record is, and the bill stops mattering;
a flat surcharge, or any surcharge that depends on the current state, sits on the same
structure. That's the first free choice. The walk above is the whole argument, and it's
argued here, not checked over an arbitrary base: the checked statements, the exact uniqueness
refuted and the uniqueness up to schedule proved, are written for the machine I build later,
with its own certification reading as the record, and they're Section~\ref{sec:witness}'s.

And then the second free choice, and this one still surprises me. \emph{Which event} is the record?
Nothing in the five rules picks it. The converse above already says so, if you read it
twice: for any event the base can reach, the latch of that event, priced at one unit per
write, is an honest record. Do it with the die. One cup turns over on the first six. Another
turns over on the first one. Both are cups with no reset wire; both are honest. Roll a one
first, and until a six turns up the two cups disagree about whether anything has been
recorded. So \emph{which permanent reading counts as the record} is a second thing nobody forces
on you. The price list is one free choice. The event is the other. That second choice is the
question Section~\ref{sec:pointer} is about: what, if anything, makes certification the event worth recording,
rather than ``the ledger passed one'' or anything else.

\begin{corollary}[The event is a free choice]\label{cor:u11-event-free}
Let $B$ be any base and $h_1, h_2$ two events, each meeting the supposition of
Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-converse}. Then $\mathrm{Latch}_{h_1}$ and $\mathrm{Latch}_{h_2}$ are both
honest extensions of $B$. If some starting base state $b$ has $h_1(b)$ on and $h_2(b)$ off,
then one step from $(b, \mathrm{off}, 0)$ leaves the first record on and the second off.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Honesty is Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-converse} applied twice. The step is the latch's own rule:
$\mathrm{off} \lor h_1(b)$ is on and $\mathrm{off} \lor h_2(b)$ is off.
\end{proof}

Argued from \code{latch\_core\_honest} (RecordAxisDiscrimination.v) applied to each event; the
corollary itself is not a separate Coq statement.

Now let the cup wobble. Say whatever turns it over sometimes does and sometimes doesn't, with
odds you could write on a card. Does fixing the price list fix the odds? No, and the
counterexample is two cups with the same price tag and differently loaded coins. Here's the
setup, said carefully. Let a record be a single bit that moves at random: from each value, a list of weighted next values, every weight positive,
never empty, never leaving on once on, and with the write from off to on charged at least one.
Call two such records \emph{the same schedule} when the same moves are possible and every move is charged the same, and \emph{the same in probability} when the weighted lists are equal.

\begin{theorem}[The schedule doesn't fix the probabilities]\label{thm:u11-probabilistic}
(1) There are two honest probabilistic records with the same schedule that are not the same in
probability. (2) There is an honest probabilistic record that no deterministic latch on its
current value describes.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) From off, one record moves to off or on with weights $1$ and $1$, the other with weights $1$
and $2$; from on, both stay on with weight $1$; both charge $1$ for the write. Same possible
moves, same charges, different weights. (2) The first record moves from off both to off and to
on, while a latch $r \lor h(r)$ gives one value.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{schedule\_determines\_probabilities\_refuted} and
\code{deterministic\_latch\_handles\_branching\_refuted} (ProbabilisticRecord.v), with the definitions in
ProbabilisticRecordCore.v. These are finite-weight models on one bit with no base underneath;
they say nothing about any particular machine.

Third claim: is there one state space, up to renaming, that every honest record-carrier has
to have? I don't claim it. Nothing needs it.

\subsection{Bases from outside, and a relation I have to be honest about}

The theorem is stated for any base, and the checked work instantiates it on three models of
computation that other people built: a small Turing machine (any program); a register machine
of the kind Cook and Reckhow described in 1973, with unit-cost indirect addressing (any
program); and a lambda calculus (call-by-value, meaning an argument is worked out before it's
plugged in, and made deterministic by letting a term with no step left to take step to
itself). On each, the latch form holds, by the one generic theorem applied to that base
(the checked names are listed with the formal statement below). So a register machine
with an honest record is a register machine plus a cup. So is a lambda calculus. (There are two
more instances, both machines I build later: the small one, where the flag is shown to be a latch
directly, in Section~\ref{sec:smallest}, and the big one, in Section~\ref{sec:witness}.)

Here are the three bases explicitly. A base needs a state, a next-state function,
a set of starting states and a halting predicate; the latch theorem asks for nothing
else about its instruction vocabulary.

\begin{definition}[Three concrete bases]\label{def:u11-concrete-bases}
The \textbf{tape base} has a finite Boolean list $t$, a head index $h$, a program counter
$q$ and a natural-number cost field. Reading beyond the list returns false. Writing
at $h$ extends the list with false cells if needed, then changes that cell.
Moving right increments $h$ and extends the list through the new head position.
Moving left decrements a positive $h$; at $h=0$, it prepends a false cell and keeps
the head at zero. A fixed finite program contains these instructions:

\begingroup\small
\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.482\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.482\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Instruction} & \textbf{Next state} \\
\midrule
\endhead
\bottomrule
\endlastfoot
Write a bit & Perform the write and advance $q$ by one. \\
Move left or right & Perform the move and advance $q$ by one. \\
Branch to $j$ & Set $q:=j$ if the current cell is true; otherwise advance $q$ by one. \\
Halt & Leave the entire state unchanged. \\
ClaimTapeIsZero with parameter $\delta$ & Advance $q$ by one and do nothing else. \\
\end{longtable}
\endgroup

An out-of-range program fetch is Halt. Every state is allowed as a starting state,
and halting means the fetched instruction is Halt. The cost field is preserved by
every instruction in this base. In particular, its ClaimTapeIsZero instruction
neither erases the tape nor charges the cost field; the name supplies no extra
semantics.

The \textbf{random-access base} has a register function $X:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$ and a
program counter $q$. For a fixed finite program its instructions are:

\begingroup\small
\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.482\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.482\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Instruction} & \textbf{Next state} \\
\midrule
\endhead
\bottomrule
\endlastfoot
Constant $(i,c)$ & Set $X(i):=c$. \\
Add $(i,j,k)$ & Set $X(i):=X(j)+X(k)$. \\
Subtract $(i,j,k)$ & Set $X(i):=\max(0,X(j)-X(k))$. \\
Indirect load $(i,j)$ & Set $X(i):=X(X(j))$. \\
Indirect store $(i,j)$ & Set $X(X(i)):=X(j)$. \\
Positive branch $(j,a)$ & Set $q:=a$ if $X(j)>0$; otherwise advance $q$ by one. \\
Jump to $a$ & Set $q:=a$. \\
Halt & Leave the entire state unchanged. \\
\end{longtable}
\endgroup

Each register-writing instruction advances $q$ by one; its operands are evaluated
in the old state, and all other registers are preserved. A fetch outside the program
also leaves the state unchanged. Starting states have $q=0$ and arbitrary register
contents. A state is halted when it fetches Halt or is outside the program.
Unit cost here concerns instruction counting, not the certification ledger.

The \textbf{lambda base} uses the terms and weak call-by-value rule defined in
Definition~\ref{def:u12-L}. To compute its next state, first try to reduce the function
part of an application. If that part cannot step and is an abstraction, either
substitute an argument that is already an abstraction or take a step in the
argument. If neither applies, the term cannot step. Variables and abstractions
cannot step by themselves, and there is no reduction under an abstraction.
The base leaves a term unchanged when it cannot step and calls precisely those
terms halted. Every term is allowed as a starting state, including open terms.
\end{definition}

These definitions make the examples instances of the base record. Applying the
latch theorem to them does not assert universality, an execution-time bound, or
a simulation between the three bases.

There's also a relation defined between bases, \emph{weak base equivalence}: two bases are
equivalent when some correspondence covers their start states both ways, related states agree
on an observation and on halting, and one step on one side is matched by some number of
steps, possibly zero, on the other. That ``some number of steps'' is the \emph{stuttering} idea
Leslie Lamport (the same Lamport as Section~\ref{sec:counter}'s message counters) put forward in 1983: a fine-grained machine and a coarse one shouldn't count as
different because one takes three ticks to do what the other does in one. The relation
carries no cost; a machine that multiplies huge numbers in one step and a Turing machine
differ in price, not in records. It's proved to be an equivalence relation, and the latch
form is preserved across it.

There is a limit to that statement. The ``preserved across it'' proof throws away its equivalence hypothesis; the latch holds
on every base regardless, so the preservation is true for a boring reason. And nowhere in the
checked work are \emph{two} of the bases actually related by this relation. The relation is
defined, it's an equivalence, and it is not used to connect the Turing machine to the
register machine to the lambda calculus, or any of them to the machines in Part IV. It would be
easy to read that list as if it did. What's proved is that each base, separately,
carries a latch. That's the honest sentence.

\begin{definition}[Weak base equivalence]\label{def:u11-weak-equiv}
Bases $B_1$ and $B_2$, with observations $o_1$ and $o_2$ into one common set, are \emph{weakly equivalent} when some relation $R$ relates every starting state of each to some starting state
of the other, and any related $x$, $y$ have $o_1(x) = o_2(y)$, the same halting, some $n \ge 0$
with $R(\mathrm{next}_{B_1}(x), \mathrm{next}_{B_2}^n(y))$, and some $n \ge 0$ with
$R(\mathrm{next}_{B_1}^n(x), \mathrm{next}_{B_2}(y))$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Outside bases, and the relation]\label{thm:u11-four-bases}
(1) Weak base equivalence is reflexive, symmetric and transitive. (2) If two bases are weakly
equivalent, Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-latch} holds over one exactly when it holds over the other.
(3) Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-latch} holds over each of the three bases in
Definition~\ref{def:u11-concrete-bases}, for every fixed program where the base has one.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Reflexive with equality as $R$ and one step against one. Symmetric by reversing $R$.
Transitive by composing the two relations; a step on the first base is matched by $n$ steps on
the second, and those $n$ steps by some number on the third, by induction on $n$. (2) and (3)
apply Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-latch} directly. In (2) the equivalence hypothesis is discarded.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{weak\_base\_equiv\_refl\_holds}, \code{weak\_base\_equiv\_sym\_holds},
\code{weak\_base\_equiv\_trans\_holds} (through \code{weak\_match\_left\_runs} and \code{weak\_match\_right\_runs}),
\code{weak\_equiv\_preserves\_record\_latch\_holds} and \code{record\_axis\_is\_latch\_on\_tm\_holds}
(CrossBaseGranularity.v), \code{record\_axis\_is\_latch\_on\_ram\_holds}
(CrossBaseGranularityRAM.v) and \code{record\_axis\_is\_latch\_on\_l\_holds} (CrossBaseGranularityL.v), with
the definitions in CrossBaseGranularityCore.v.

\subsection{Records with more than two values}

A cup has two positions. Some records have more: a counter of how many checks passed, a level
that only rises. The same reasoning goes through one threshold at a time. For each value $a$,
``the record has reached $a$'' is a yes/no reading, and each of those readings is a latch. What
doesn't go through is squeezing the whole record into one cup. ``Rises'' needs one word: the
values come with an order $\le$, ``is at or below,'' which needn't compare every pair (that's
what makes it a \emph{partial} order), and $[a \le x]$ is the yes/no reading ``$x$ has reached $a$.''

\begin{definition}[A growing record]\label{def:u11-growing}
Let the record take values in a set $A$ with a partial order $\le$ decided by a Boolean test. A
record $\rho$ on $M$, with cover $\pi$ onto a base $B$, is an \emph{honest growing record} when: there
is one function $f$ with $\rho(\mathrm{next}_M(m)) = f(\pi(m), \rho(m))$; it grows,
$\rho(m) \le \rho(\mathrm{next}_M(m))$; the ledger never goes down and every step that changes
$\rho$ costs at least one; and some run from a starting state reaches a step that changes it.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Growing records are families of latches]\label{thm:u11-growing}
(1) For every honest growing record there is an $h$ with
\[
[a \le \rho(\mathrm{next}_M(m))] = [a \le \rho(m)] \lor h(a, \pi(m), \rho(m))
\]
for every value $a$ and state $m$: each threshold is a latch, whose event may read the current
value. (2) The thresholds determine the value: if $[a \le x] = [a \le y]$ for every $a$, then
$x = y$. (3) For a growing record, charging every change is the same as charging every threshold
that switches on. (4) One latch is not enough: a three-valued record that climbs
$0 \to 1 \to 2$ over a one-state base, each climb charged one, is honest, and no single Boolean
latch with a decoding from the base state and the latch reproduces it. (5) A chain of distinct
$k$-bit words, each word's set bits contained in the next one's, has at most $k + 1$ members.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Take $h(a, b, x) = [a \not\le x] \wedge [a \le f(b, x)]$. If $a \le \rho(m)$ already, growth
and transitivity give $a \le \rho(\mathrm{next}_M(m))$; otherwise the equation is the definition
of $h$. (2) Antisymmetry, with $a = x$ and $a = y$. (3) Growth plus antisymmetry turn ``the value
changed'' into ``some threshold switched on,'' and back. (4) Over one base state, a latch and a
decoding can produce at most two values, and the record takes three. (5) Each strict step up the
chain adds at least one set bit, and there are only $k$ bits.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{growing\_record\_decomposes\_holds}, \code{thresholds\_determine\_record\_holds},
\code{record\_price\_iff\_threshold\_price\_holds}, \code{one\_latch\_refuted} and \code{chain\_needs\_bits\_holds}
(GrowingRecord.v), with the definitions in GrowingRecordCore.v. The order need not be finite;
(5) is the finite-memory bound.

\subsection{What the base being free buys you}

The reason this section exists is to answer the suspicion I started with. The record isn't
special pleading for one machine. Over any base, under rules you can read, a record that
answers to the computation and never comes down is a latch on an event, and the proof
doesn't care what the base is. What a particular machine adds is not the latch; it's a
\emph{choice of event} and a \emph{choice of price list}, and both are choices. The surcharged cup
shows the first: the bill can change and the record not notice. The two cups on one die show
the second: the rules are happy with either event. Any machine I build will have to make both
choices, and whether its choice of event is the right one is an open question, and I'll get
to it. Before that, the question every machine with a record has to face, and that no amount
of good design makes go away. A record is worth keeping because something later leans on it
instead of working the thing out again: that's Section~\ref{sec:structure}'s glance, reading a block's bucket off the
table instead of applying the rule from scratch. Call any move like that a \emph{shortcut}, and
call it \emph{sound} when it gives the answer the long way would have given. So: can a machine
\emph{decide}, from inside, whether its own shortcuts are sound? That's a wall,
and it's the same wall Gödel and Turing hit, and I have to show you that it's there before
I show you anything that pretends to be on the other side of it.

%===========================================================================
\section{The diagonal}
\label{sec:diagonal}
%===========================================================================

In Section~\ref{sec:structure} I said you'd watch the same move get made again and again as the book went on:
somebody says ``everything is X,'' it's true enough to do real work with, and then somebody
draws the diagonal. I owe you the diagonal itself now, because Section~\ref{sec:latch} just handed a record to
\emph{any} system that steps, and the next thing anyone wants from a system with a record is for
it to tell sound shortcuts from unsound ones by itself. Before I let anything claim that, I
have to show you the wall every such claim runs into, and then show you exactly where a
system with a record stands relative to the wall. Not on the far side. Nobody's on the far
side.

\subsection{Five names and a table}

Do this first, with a pencil, because the whole family of arguments is this one trick and
you should own it. Write five friends' names down the left of a page. Next to each name,
write a five-digit string of zeros and ones, anything you like. Now build a new string: its
first digit is the \emph{opposite} of the first digit of the first row; its second digit is the
opposite of the second digit of the second row; and so on down the diagonal. Look at what
you've made. It differs from row one in position one, from row two in position two, from
every row at that row's own position. So it's nobody's string. Your table of five missed
something.

With five rows and five digits that's a cute fact. Georg Cantor's point, in 1891, was that
it works for \emph{any} list, however long, even infinite: hand me a complete list of all infinite
strings of two symbols, I'll walk the diagonal flipping as I go, and I'll hand you back a
string that's on no row. So there is no complete list. There are more such strings than there
are places on any list, and that's where ``some infinities are bigger than others'' comes
from. (He wrote the two symbols as m and w, not 0 and 1, and that paper wasn't even his first
proof of the fact; the 1874 one was harder. The diagonal was him finding the easy way.)

Now look at what the argument \emph{did}, because it's going to do the same thing again and again,
in new clothes, and I want you to recognise it each time. (Not every name below is a
flipped diagonal in the table sense. Kleene's theorem is the tool that makes the diagonal
buildable, Rice's is the general form, and Thompson's is an attack that uses the same
trick.) There was a table: rows are the things being
listed, columns are questions, each cell says ``does row i do column j.'' There was the
diagonal: the cells where a thing is asked about \emph{itself}. There was a flip: something with no
fixed point, like turning yes into no, applied along the diagonal. And the thing that got
refuted was \emph{the assumed object}, the complete list. Nothing outside the assumption was
touched. Table, diagonal, flip, and the assumption eats itself. Hold those four.

\subsection{The same move, again and again}

Russell, 1902, from Section~\ref{sec:structure}: the collection of all collections that don't contain themselves.
That's Cantor's flipped diagonal with ``contains'' as the table, and Russell said as much; he
got there by running Cantor's argument on a supposed collection of everything. What got
refuted was the assumed object, the collection of everything, and Zermelo's fix was to stop
assuming it.

Jules Richard, 1905: some English phrases define real numbers (``the ratio of a circle's
circumference to its diameter''); there are only countably many phrases, so list the numbers
they define in order; run Cantor's diagonal down their decimal expansions and you get a real
number no phrase defines, except that you just defined it, in the phrase that describes the
diagonal. The lesson that came out of that one is the lesson this whole
section turns on: keep apart the language a system \emph{talks in} and the language you use to
talk \emph{about} it. Mix them and the diagonal bites you.

Richard's paradox has a cousin small enough to do at the table, and it comes with a footnote I
can't resist. Russell, the first to put it in print, in 1906, credited it to G. G. Berry, a
junior librarian at the Bodleian Library in Oxford. A paradox that has outlived empires, and it
came from the library desk. In the version in \emph{Principia Mathematica} it's about syllables. Take
the phrase ``the least integer not nameable in fewer than nineteen syllables.'' There are only
so many phrases shorter than nineteen syllables, so they name only so many numbers, so some
least number is left over, and the phrase picks it out. Now count the phrase: the, least,
in-te-ger, not, name-a-ble, in, few-er, than, nine-teen, syl-la-bles. Eighteen. In eighteen
syllables it has named the number that can't be named in fewer than nineteen. Same lesson as Richard's, in a smaller coat: ``nameable'' is a word about the
language, used inside the language, and that's where the bite is.

Kurt Gödel, 1931, with an improvement by Barkley Rosser in 1936: the big one, and I'll say exactly what it says because it's misquoted more
than any theorem alive. Take any consistent formal system with a mechanically checkable list
of axioms that can do a bit of arithmetic. Then there are sentences it can neither prove nor
refute. The engine is a lemma that lets you build, for any property you can write down, a
sentence that the system proves \emph{equivalent} to that property holding of the sentence's own
code number. Apply it to ``not provable'' and you get a sentence equivalent, inside the
system, to its own unprovability. Table: sentences by code. Diagonal: a sentence about its
own code. Flip: provable to not-provable. Two cautions the Stanford Encyclopedia stresses and
I'll repeat: the sentence doesn't literally ``say'' anything about itself, it's provably
\emph{equivalent} to a claim about its code, which is less mystical and more exact; and the
theorem doesn't say the sentence is unknowable, it says \emph{this one system} can't settle it.

And how did the world take it? Mostly, at first, it didn't. Gödel, twenty-four years old,
announced the first theorem during a round-table discussion on the last day of a conference in
Königsberg in September 1930, and by the account of Solomon Feferman, one of the editors of
Gödel's collected works, the room met it with general incomprehension. Except for one man. John
von Neumann pulled Gödel aside to talk about it, kept thinking about it, and a couple of months
later saw that the argument gave something more: a consistent system of this kind can't prove
its own consistency. He wrote to Gödel with it in a letter dated 20 November 1930. Gödel had
already got there. His paper had reached the journal three days earlier, with that
second theorem announced in it, and von Neumann left the credit with Gödel. It's the
``somebody got there first'' shape from the opening chapter, with one difference: here the man
who got there second was von Neumann.

Alan Turing, 1936: and here the historical record is not the story you usually hear. The
usual story is that Turing proved the halting problem undecidable. Joel David Hamkins and
Theodor Nenu went back to the 1936 paper and found that the word ``halting,'' the modern
statement, and the self-referential proof everyone teaches are all, strictly, absent from
it. What Turing proved undecidable were two other questions about his machines (whether a
machine prints infinitely many digits; whether it ever prints a given symbol). The second is
\emph{equivalent} to halting and the first is strictly harder, and the name ``halting problem'' came later, probably from Martin
Davis. The textbook version is still right as mathematics, and here it is, on two index
cards. Card A is the Checker: hand it any program card and it announces ``halts'' or ``runs
forever.'' Card B is the Contrarian: ``Hand me to the Checker. If it says I halt, run forever.
If it says I run forever, stop.'' Hand B to A. Either answer is wrong. There's no Checker.
Table: programs by programs. Diagonal: a program run on itself. Flip: halt to loop.

Stephen Kleene, 1938, and this is the one that turns the paradox into a tool, so slow down.
Everything above needs the self-referring object to \emph{exist}: Gödel's sentence has to be
buildable, the Contrarian has to be able to ``hand me to the Checker.'' Kleene's second
recursion theorem says: for any transformation of programs you can compute, there's a
program that behaves exactly as if it had been handed its own source code. Any program may
be written as though it already had a copy of itself in hand. He stated it almost in passing, in a paper
on something else, and proved it in two lines, and Yiannis Moschovakis calls it a little
gem, and it's the reason ``programs that print their own source'' exist in
every programming language (they're called quines, after the philosopher; try ``Print the
following twice, the second time in quotes: `Print the following twice, the second time in
quotes:''' and obey it). Self-reference in computation isn't a paradox. It's a construction.
The paradoxes happened only when someone assumed an \emph{unrestricted} collection or language;
the theorem happens when you build the self-referrer honestly.

And where does the word quine come from? Not from the philosopher himself. Douglas Hofstadter
coined it in 1979, in \emph{Gödel, Escher, Bach}, in honour of Willard Van Orman Quine, who had
made a long study of self-reference that works indirectly. Quine left a sentence you can take
apart at the table, from a 1962 essay on paradox. Here it is, all of it: ``yields falsehood when
preceded by its quotation'' yields falsehood when preceded by its quotation. Do what it says.
Take the part in quotation marks, put a quoted copy of it in front of itself, and look at what
you've built: it's the whole sentence, word for word. So the sentence says that it itself is
false. That's the liar paradox, but look at how it got there: no ``this sentence'' anywhere, no
pointing at itself, just an instruction to quote and copy, the same move as the print-twice
instruction above. That's Kleene's trick in plain English, and it's why the paradox and the tool
look so alike. The paradox is what you get when the copy asserts something about its own truth.
The tool is what you get when the copy just does something.

Henry Rice, 1953, whom you met briefly in Section~\ref{sec:windows}: the general form. Any property that depends only on what a program \emph{does}
(not how it's written), and that's true of some programs and false of others, has no
algorithm that decides it for all programs. ``Does this program halt'' is one such property.
``Does this program ever output 7'' is another. ``Does this program contain an if-statement''
isn't, because that's about the text. One standard proof goes straight through Kleene.

And the one that's actually an attack: Ken Thompson, in his Turing Award lecture, published in 1984.
Build a compiler that, when it compiles the login program, plants a back door, and when it
compiles \emph{a compiler}, plants both habits into that one too. Then delete the trick from the
source. The compiled compiler still carries it, and recompiling a clean source with the
poisoned binary re-plants it, forever. Reading the source never reveals it. A locksmith
teaches an apprentice to cut a spare for every town-hall key and to teach \emph{that} to every
apprentice they train, and never to write it in the manual; years later the manual is
spotless and every locksmith in town cuts the spare. That's the recursion theorem with a
knife in it, and his moral was that you can't trust code you didn't write entirely yourself,
which is a sentence I'll come back to in Section~\ref{sec:coq} when I tell you what the trusted base of this
book is.

And Thompson wasn't first either, and he said so. Pull on the lecture's acknowledgment the way
the opening chapter pulled on Bitcoin's footnotes: he writes that he first read of the
possibility in an Air Force critique of the security of an early implementation of Multics, a
time-sharing system from the 1960s, and that he couldn't find a more specific reference to it,
and he asks anyone who can to send him one. The critique is Paul Karger and Roger Schell's 1974
security evaluation of Multics, which already described a trap door planted in a compiler that,
because the compiler is written in its own language, keeps itself alive. So the knife was in the
drawer ten years before the lecture. Then the obvious next question: is there any way out, or is
``trust no binary you didn't build'' the bottom? There's a partial answer, and it took a while.
David A. Wheeler, in a 2005 paper and a 2009 dissertation at George Mason University, worked out
\emph{diverse double-compiling}: compile the suspect compiler's source with a second,
independently made compiler, use the result to compile that source again, and compare the
output bit for bit with the suspect binary. If they match, the binary really is what its source
says, unless both compilers were poisoned in the same way. The trust doesn't vanish. It moves,
from one compiler to the claim that two unrelated ones weren't rigged together. That's the shape
of every stopping point in this book: you don't reach the bottom, you reach a place where you can
say exactly what you're trusting.

Bill Lawvere, 1969, showed all of these are one theorem in disguise: if a set can be mapped
onto all the functions from itself to some target, then every function on the target has a
fixed point; so if the target has a function with no fixed point (a flip), no such covering
exists. Cantor, Russell, Gödel, halting, as instances of one shape. Noson Yanofsky retold it
in 2003 without the category theory. I mention it because ``it's the same wall'' is a claim I
make below, and I want you to know it's fair at the level of \emph{proof shape}, and that every
instance has its own boundary of \emph{who counts as a decider}, and that boundary is exactly
where most overclaims live.

\subsection{What it doesn't say}

Before I point this at a system with a record, the four wrong turns, because they're the
ones people take.

``Gödel shows minds aren't machines.'' John Lucas argued it in 1961 and Roger Penrose revived
it twice. The standard replies, as far as I can tell, have held up: the Gödel sentence is true \emph{only if the system
is consistent}, so a human who ``sees'' its truth has to know the system is consistent, which
is the hard part; and nobody can build the Gödel sentence of a system they can't specify, so
humans might be machines too complicated to diagonalise. The theorem has a conditional in it
and the argument drops the conditional.

And here's the part that's easy to miss: Gödel himself didn't go as far as Lucas. In a lecture
on the day after Christmas in 1951, at a meeting of the American Mathematical Society at Brown
University, he drew from his own theorems only an either-or. Either the human mind, even inside
pure mathematics, infinitely surpasses the powers of any finite machine, or there are problems
about whole numbers, of a certain simple kind, that no proof the human mind can conceive will
ever settle. Feferman, writing about that lecture, says Gödel privately believed the first half
and still stated only the disjunction, because he didn't have a knock-down argument against the
machine side. Gödel wrote soon afterward that he meant to publish the lecture, and never did; the
text sat among his papers until after his death. So the man whose theorem gets quoted for
``minds aren't machines'' stated an either-or and left the deciding to whoever came next. That's
the conditional again, kept, by the person with the most right to drop it.

``Undecidable means unknowable.'' No. Two senses share the word: a problem with no single
algorithm correct on every instance, and a sentence independent of one particular system.
Neither means nobody can know a given answer. Any single instance is decidable, trivially:
for any one program, one of ``say yes'' and ``say no'' is right. What's ruled out is one
\emph{inside} procedure that's right on \emph{every} case.

``Everything interesting is undecidable.'' Rice is about behavioural properties over \emph{all}
programs. It says nothing against checking the text, nothing against deciding for specific
programs, nothing against analyses allowed to say ``I don't know,'' nothing against finite-state
model checking or type checking. Real compilers are limited by cost and by choosing to be
sound-but-incomplete, not by the diagonal.

``Self-reference is a paradox.'' It's a theorem with a construction. Kleene, quines, Thompson.

\subsection{Now point it at the record}

Here's the question Section~\ref{sec:latch} left open, with nothing in it but what Parts I to III have built. A
system steps; a record rides along and latches on an event (Section~\ref{sec:latch}); when the event is a
certification, Section~\ref{sec:entitlement} said the reading, with its object and its paid event behind it, is what lets an
auditor treat a claim as established, and for a claim that a shortcut is sound, that's what
makes the shortcut \emph{admissible}. So: can a system like that have, as one of its own programs, a procedure that
correctly decides, for every program, ``does this program admit a sound shortcut''? That
would be autopilot. Hand it any program and it says yes or no, and it's always right.

That's the question in plain words, and the checked statement is narrower, so here it is
before the proof. In the theorem, ``admits a shortcut'' is any property of programs with two
features: two programs that behave alike agree on it, and there's one program that has it
and one that doesn't. That's all the argument gets to look at. The diagonal doesn't see
soundness. Each system that wants the wall picks its own property, and whether that
property lines up with being entitled to soundness in Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}'s sense is a separate fact about that system,
checked one system at a time if it's checked at all. A procedure that returns soundness
records for some programs, or only for restricted inputs, or with outside evidence, is not
what the wall rules out.

The answer is no, under premises. The proof is the two index cards, and I'll give you the
premises because they're the whole content. Suppose there were such a decider, one that says yes
exactly when a program admits a shortcut. Build the
flip: ``if the decider says yes about me, behave like a program that admits no shortcut; if
it says no, behave like one that does.'' If the system has a recursion theorem (a program
can be handed its own code), and if that flip is one of the transformations the system can
carry out, and if ``admits a shortcut'' depends only on behaviour (two programs that behave
the same agree on it), and if there's at least one program each way, then there's a program
that behaves exactly like its own flip, and whatever the decider says about it is wrong.
Both cases close in a line each. That's \code{structural\_shortcut\_undecidable}, stated for \emph{any}
substrate with those fields. (A substrate here is the bare shape with exactly the pieces
this theorem asks for: programs, a run that may fail to give back a state, a counter, an
encoding of programs as data, a notion of ``representable'' transformation, and the recursion
theorem for those. Nothing about what the states are made of. The smallest checked
instance is the nat family below.) It's Rice's trick one floor over, and I should be careful
with that. Rice's theorem is stated for the functions Turing machines compute. This wall is
the same diagonal with different premises: it carries its own recursion theorem and its own
list of representable transformations, and it picks the property. So it isn't a corollary
of Rice as Rice stated it, and it doesn't separate anything from classical halting. And
here's something about its proof that I want you to have: it never touches the counter,
the toll, or the step relation. It uses the recursion theorem, representability of the flip,
the two witnesses, and extensionality, and nothing else. (The file's header calls the
substrates it covers ones that respect the toll, which reads as if the toll were needed. The
proof uses neither the toll nor the counter's climbing. It's the diagonal, clean.)

Here's the setting and the wall, with every word pinned down so you can poke at it.

\begin{definition}[Substrate]\label{def:u12-substrate}
A \emph{substrate} has a type of states, a type $\mathrm{Prog}$ of programs, and a run map that
takes a program and a state and either gives back a state or gives nothing. It has a counter
$\mu$ on states and a step relation along which $\mu$ never decreases; an encoding
$\mathrm{enc}$ of programs as states with a decoder $\mathrm{dec}$ such that
$\mathrm{dec}(\mathrm{enc}(p)) = p$; and a predicate $\mathrm{Rep}$ on maps
$f : \mathrm{Prog} \to \mathrm{Prog}$, the transformations the substrate counts as its own.
Two programs are \emph{equivalent}, $p \simeq q$, when $\mathrm{run}(p, s) = \mathrm{run}(q, s)$
for every state $s$. The last field is the \emph{recursion theorem}: for every $f$ with
$\mathrm{Rep}(f)$ there is a program $p$ with $p \simeq f(p)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Shortcut predicate]\label{def:u12-shortcut-predicate}
