three numbers in one), and to do arithmetic on the exponents by multiplying and dividing
with the second bin as scratch space. It is as slow as it sounds. Exponentially slow. A
two-counter machine doing your taxes would finish sometime after the sun doesn't. But
``universal'' is a claim about what's \emph{possible}, not about what's pleasant, and on that
claim two bins of pebbles are as strong as anything.

Who cares? Minsky did, because the question then was where the edge of computation sits and
how little machinery reaches it. You should, because it means the base of this chapter's
machine hides nothing: if it can compute everything with plus one, minus one and a jump,
then nothing about the record can be smuggling computing power in through some instruction
I made fancy. And I care because it's the smallest universal base I know of that is
already in a Coq library, so the hard part (proving that its halting question is
undecidable) is someone else's checked work and not my say-so.

And the pebbles aren't only my picture. They were somebody's actual machine, the same year.
In one issue of the Canadian Mathematical Bulletin, September 1961, Z.~A. Melzak described a
computer made of distinguishable holes and an unlimited supply of pebbles, with one
three-place operation, and a few pages later Joachim Lambek trimmed it to two moves: put a
pebble in hole $X$; take one out of hole $X$ if there's one to take. He called it an
\emph{infinite abacus}, and early on he writes ``Our method is probably not new,'' which is
a hard sentence to beat. He also tells anybody who distrusts infinity not to worry
about all those holes, since any one computation only ever uses finitely many of them. Is
that two inventions or one? Lambek says his was a modification of Melzak's, so call it one
and a half, with Minsky's as a separate find the same year. And then Lambek went somewhere
you wouldn't guess: in 1986, with Philip Scott, he wrote a book showing that typed lambda
calculi and a certain kind of category are essentially the same thing. Pebbles to category
theory in one career, which is the trip this Part takes too, in four sections instead of
twenty-five years. Does any of it change the argument? No. The library and I use Minsky's
version and Minsky's name. But a bare machine that several people reach for in the same year
looks less like anybody's invention and more like a shape that was sitting there.

One word clash, before it bites. Minsky's machine is usually called a \emph{counter machine},
and its bins are \emph{counters}. Section~\ref{sec:counter} also had a counter: the ledger $\mu$, the number that only
climbs. Same word, two completely different things, and I'd love to say I set that up on
purpose. In this chapter, \emph{counter} means one of Minsky's two bins, called $A$ and $B$, and
the climbing total is always \emph{the ledger} $\mu$.

\subsection{The machine}

Here's the whole state. I'll say each piece in words first.

\begin{itemize}
\item Two counters, $A$ and $B$. Each holds a whole number, with no upper limit.
\item A \emph{version} for each counter, also a whole number with no limit. It starts at 0 and goes
up by one every time its counter is written. Think of it as the counter's edition number:
a new value is a new edition.
\item A \emph{line number}, which instruction comes next, counting from 1 the way Minsky does.
\item A \emph{fact table}: a list of facts. A \emph{fact} is three things stuck together: a property, a
counter, and a version. ``$A$ is even, as of edition 3'' is a fact. The table has room for
sixteen. Why sixteen? It's a pick, with no derivation behind it, and what the pick costs is
in the last subsection of this chapter, the one on what the machine doesn't do.
\item A \emph{channel}: either empty, or holding one fact. This is where a commitment sits.
\item A \emph{trap}: one bit, down at the start. When it goes up, the machine has refused something,
and it stays up.
\end{itemize}

Everything above is the \emph{core}, the part the base moves. Outside the core sit the two
pieces from the model: the ledger $\mu$ and the flag. The machine never reads either of
them to decide what to do next. That's not a promise, it's how the step is written, and it
shows up as a theorem below.

The properties a fact can name come from a tiny fixed language with three words: \emph{is zero};
\emph{is even}; and \emph{is at least $n$}, for any whole number $n$ you like. Each one comes in two
forms. There's the \emph{checker}, a little program that computes yes or no: compare with 0,
look at the last bit, compare with $n$. And there's the \emph{meaning}, the plain arithmetic
statement the checker is supposed to be checking: the number is 0; the number is two times
something; $n$ is less than or equal to the number. Why both? Because a checker is code, and
code can be wrong in ways that look right, and ``the checker says yes'' is only worth
anything once somebody has proved it says yes exactly when the meaning is true. That proof
is one line per property, and it's the first block below.

Now the six instructions.

\begingroup\small
\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.242\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.344\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.344\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Instruction} & \textbf{What it does, when the trap is down} & \textbf{Cost} \\
\midrule
\endhead
\bottomrule
\endlastfoot
INC $c$ & Adds one to counter $c$, adds one to its version, goes to the next line. & 0 \\
DEC $c$ $j$ & If $c$ is above 0: subtracts one, adds one to its version, jumps to line $j$. If $c$ is 0: just goes to the next line. & 0 \\
HALT & Nothing. A program that reaches it stops. & 0 \\
CHECK $p$ $c$ & Runs the checker for $p$ on $c$'s value. If it says yes and the table has fewer than sixteen facts, writes the fact ($p$, $c$, $c$'s current version) into the table and goes to the next line. Otherwise, trap. & 1 \\
COMMIT $p$ $c$ & Looks in the table for exactly the fact ($p$, $c$, $c$'s current version), field by field. If it's there, puts it in the channel and goes to the next line. Otherwise, trap. & 1 \\
CERTIFY & If the channel holds a fact, goes to the next line, and the flag goes up. Otherwise, trap. & 1 \\
\end{longtable}
\endgroup

The first three are Minsky's machine, plus a HALT so a program can say it's done. The last
three are the record's. Read them as a chain: you can only certify with a commitment in the
channel, you can only commit to a fact in the table, and the only way into the table is a
check that passed. Three links, and each one costs.

One of what? One unit of $\mu$, the same unit as Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s toll. Why one and not ten? Because one
is the smallest positive whole number, which is honestly the whole defence, and Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} is the
section where I tried to do better than that for the flag. The zeros matter just as much:
computing is free on this ledger. Plus one, minus one and jumping around cost nothing at all.
Only the three acts that make a claim cost, and each of them costs whether it passes or traps.
Failing is not a discount.

\textbf{The version rule.} Here's why versions exist, with numbers. Start with $A = 4$, version 0.
CHECK \emph{is even} $A$ passes, and the table gets the fact (\emph{even}, $A$, 0). Now INC $A$: $A$
becomes 5, and its version becomes 1. Now COMMIT \emph{is even} $A$. The machine looks for
(\emph{even}, $A$, 1), the claim about the current edition. The table only has (\emph{even}, $A$, 0).
No match. Trap. The old fact is still sitting in the table, still true about edition 0,
and completely useless for committing to anything about edition 1. A fact is about one
edition of one counter, and an edition never comes back, because versions only go up and
never wrap. That's the whole trick against stale evidence: you can't check a number, change
it, and then commit to the check.

Notice what \emph{isn't} a write. DEC on a counter that's already 0 doesn't change the counter, so
it doesn't change the version. It's a test that happens to move the line number.

\textbf{The fact table.} Facts go in and never come out. Nothing erases them and nothing
overwrites them. When the table is full, a seventeenth CHECK doesn't push an old fact out to
make room; it traps. That's a choice with a bill attached, and I'll put the bill in the
section on what this machine doesn't do.

\textbf{Traps.} Any failure puts the trap up and changes nothing else. Once it's up, every
instruction leaves the core alone. A stored program stops at a trap. But I also prove
things about \emph{any} list of instructions, not just programs, because an adversary doesn't
have to run my programs; they can feed the machine whatever they want. For those lists, an
instruction after a trap is still charged its cost, and still changes nothing.

Now the exact version.

\begin{definition}[Properties, checker, meaning]\label{def:u34-props}
A \emph{property} is one of: $\mathsf{Zero}$, $\mathsf{Even}$, or $\mathsf{Ge}(n)$ for a whole
number $n$. The \emph{checker} $\mathrm{eval}(p, v)$ computes yes or no: $v = 0$ by equality,
evenness by the parity function, $n \le v$ by comparison. The \emph{meaning} $\mathrm{holds}(p,
v)$ is the arithmetic statement: $v = 0$; there is an $m$ with $v = 2m$; $n \le v$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[The checker says what it means]\label{lem:u34-eval}
For every property $p$ and every whole number $v$, $\mathrm{eval}(p, v) = \mathrm{yes}$ if
and only if $\mathrm{holds}(p, v)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Split on the three properties. Equality with zero returns yes exactly at zero; comparison
with $n$ returns yes exactly when $n\le v$. For evenness, the parity checker returns yes
at $0$, no at $1$, and the same answer at $v+2$ as at $v$. Induction in steps of two gives
yes exactly at $0,2,4,\ldots$, the numbers $2m$. Those are precisely the three meanings.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{eval\_iff} (EarnedCore.v).

\begin{definition}[Core, state, claim, start]\label{def:u34-state}
A \emph{core} $k$ holds two counters $A$, $B$ and their versions (whole numbers), a line number,
a fact table (a list of facts, a fact being a triple of a property, a counter and a
version), a channel (empty or one fact), and a trap bit. Write $\mathrm{val}(k, c)$ and
$\mathrm{ver}(k, c)$ for counter $c$'s value and version. A \emph{state} $s$ is a core, written
$\mathrm{core}(s)$, with a ledger $\mu(s)$ and a flag $\mathrm{cert}(s)$. The \emph{claim} $p$ of
$c$ in $k$ is the fact $(p, c, \mathrm{ver}(k, c))$. The table's room is 16. The start
$\mathrm{start}(a, b)$ has counters $a$ and $b$, versions 0, line 1, an empty table, an
empty channel, the trap down, $\mu = 0$ and the flag down. A state is \emph{clean} when its
table and channel are empty and its flag is down.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Instructions, costs, the step]\label{def:u34-step}
The instructions are INC $c$, DEC $c$ $j$, HALT, CHECK $p$ $c$, COMMIT $p$ $c$ and
CERTIFY, with effects on a core with the trap down as in the table above. Passing any
check, commitment or certification requires the trap to be down. With that condition, CHECK
passes when $\mathrm{eval}(p, \mathrm{val}(k, c)) = \mathrm{yes}$ and the table holds fewer
than 16 facts, COMMIT passes when the claim $p$ of $c$ is in the table, and CERTIFY passes
when the channel holds a fact; a failing one sets the trap and changes nothing else. On a
core with the trap up, every instruction changes nothing. Costs: CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY
cost 1, the rest 0. One step on a state is
\[
\mathrm{exec}(s, i) = \big(\,\mathrm{cexec}(\mathrm{core}(s), i),\ \ \mu(s) + \mathrm{cost}(i),\ \ \mathrm{cert}(s) \lor \mathrm{fires}(\mathrm{core}(s), i)\,\big),
\]
where $\mathrm{cexec}$ is the core's step and $\mathrm{fires}(k, i)$ is yes exactly when
$i$ is CERTIFY and passes at $k$. For any list $t$ of instructions (a \emph{trace}),
$\mathrm{run}(t, s)$ applies them in order and $\mathrm{cost}(t)$ adds their costs. A
\emph{program} is a list of instructions numbered from 1; a program run fetches the instruction
at the line number and executes it, and stops when the trap is up, the line holds HALT, or
the line holds nothing.
\end{definition}

Defined as \code{cexec}, \code{exec}, \code{run}, \code{total\_cost}, \code{run\_prog}, \code{start} and \code{Minimal.EarnedCore.clean\_start}
(EarnedCore.v).

Read the step line slowly, because the rest of the chapter leans on its shape. The core
moves by its own rule and nothing else. The ledger adds the cost. The flag becomes ``it was
up, or this is a CERTIFY that passed.'' The core's move doesn't mention $\mu$ or the flag
anywhere. The base is blind to the record by construction.

A worked run, the shortest one there is. The program: CHECK \emph{at least 0} $A$; COMMIT \emph{at
least 0} $A$; CERTIFY. Start anywhere, $\mathrm{start}(a, b)$ for any $a$ and $b$. Line 1:
every whole number is at least 0, the checker says yes, the table is empty so there's room,
and the fact (\emph{at least 0}, $A$, 0) goes in. $\mu = 1$. Line 2: the claim about $A$'s
current edition is (\emph{at least 0}, $A$, 0), and it's right there. Into the channel. $\mu =
2$. Line 3: the channel holds a fact, the flag goes up. $\mu = 3$. Line 4 has no
instruction, so the program stops. Three paid acts, in order, and a flag that can tell you
which fact it stands on. It's the dumbest possible claim (a number is at least zero, stop
the presses), and that's fine, because the point is the chain, not the claim.

\subsection{It computes everything two counters can}

First the base, because if the base can't compute, nothing else here matters.

\begin{definition}[Two-counter program, compile, window]\label{def:u34-minsky}
A \emph{two-counter program} $M$ is a list of instructions, each either $\mathrm{MINC}\ c$ or
$\mathrm{MDEC}\ c\ j$. A configuration is a triple (line, $a$, $b$). One step of $M$: if
the line holds no instruction, $M$ has \emph{stopped}; MINC adds one to $c$ and goes to the next
line; MDEC subtracts one from $c$ and goes to line $j$ if $c$ is above 0, and goes to the
next line if $c$ is 0. $\mathrm{mrun}(n, M, x)$ is $n$ steps from $x$, staying put once
stopped. The \emph{compile} of $M$ replaces each MINC $c$ by INC $c$ and each MDEC $c$ $j$ by DEC
$c$ $j$. The \emph{window} of a core $k$ is the triple (line number, $\mathrm{val}(k, A)$,
$\mathrm{val}(k, B)$).
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Step for step]\label{thm:u34-simulation}
For every two-counter program $M$ and every core $k$ with the trap down: $M$ has stopped at
$\mathrm{window}(k)$ if and only if the program $\mathrm{compile}(M)$ has halted at $k$;
and if $M$ steps from $\mathrm{window}(k)$ to $y$, then one program step of
$\mathrm{compile}(M)$ from $k$ lands on a core with window $y$ and the trap still down. So
for every $n$, $n$ program steps of $\mathrm{compile}(M)$ from $k$ land on a core whose
window is $\mathrm{mrun}(n, M, \mathrm{window}(k))$, with the trap down.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Look up the instruction at the line. If there is none, both sides stop. If it's MINC $c$,
the compiled INC $c$ adds one to $c$ and goes to the next line, which is exactly the
window's move (the version also moves, but the window doesn't show versions). If it's MDEC
$c$ $j$, split on whether $c$ is 0, and both sides do the same thing in each case. Neither
instruction can trap. The run statement is induction on $n$, one step at a time.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{simulation\_step} and \code{simulation\_run} (EarnedCore.v).

\begin{theorem}[Halting matches]\label{thm:u34-halting}
For every two-counter program $M$ and whole numbers $a$, $b$: $M$ stops after some number of
steps from $(1, a, b)$ if and only if the program $\mathrm{compile}(M)$ halts after some
number of program steps from $\mathrm{start}(a, b)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The start has window $(1,a,b)$ and its trap is down. Apply
Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-simulation} after any number $n$ of steps: the two configurations
still have the same window, the trap is still down, and one is stopped exactly when
the other is halted. The same $n$ witnesses termination in either direction.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{halting\_correspondence} (EarnedCore.v).

Now the part that isn't mine. Proving that halting is undecidable for two-counter machines
is real work, and it's already done, checked, in a shared Coq project called the Coq
Library of Undecidability Proofs (presented by Yannick Forster, Dominique Larchey-Wendling
and coauthors at CoqPL 2020). The two-counter result in it is Larchey-Wendling's, reached
from his and Forster's work on Minsky machines (CPP 2019) by way of FRACTRAN. Their two-counter machine has the
same two instructions as Minsky's, with the same rule for zero. So the only thing I have to
prove is that their machine and my INC/DEC fragment are the same machine, step for step,
and then borrow their theorem.

One honest wrinkle about what ``undecidable'' means in that library, because it isn't the
textbook sentence. Every function you can write in Coq is a program, so ``decidable'' there
means ``some Coq function answers it.'' Coq by itself can't prove that \emph{no} Coq function
answers a question without an extra assumption about what programs are. So the library
says the strongest thing it can without one: if anything decided this, then the questions
on which a single-tape Turing machine \emph{doesn't} halt could be listed by a program, which is
the classic thing that can't be done. That's their convention, and the theorem below
inherits it exactly.

\begin{theorem}[Halting is undecidable for this machine]\label{thm:u34-undecidable}
The library's two-counter machine agrees with the INC/DEC fragment: its step, its stop, and
its termination match those of the compiled program, so a library problem $(P, a, b)$ halts
if and only if the compiled program halts from $\mathrm{start}(a, b)$. Consequently, the
question ``does program $P$ halt from $\mathrm{start}(a, b)$?'' is undecidable in the
library's sense: a decider for it would make the complement of single-tape binary Turing machine
halting enumerable.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The agreement is a case split on the library's instruction at the current line, and then
induction along the run, ending in Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-halting}. The compile map is then a
reduction from the library's two-counter halting problem, which the library proves
undecidable, and the library's own lemma carries undecidability across a reduction.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{mm2\_step\_iff}, \code{mm2\_stop\_iff}, \code{mm2\_terminates\_iff}, \code{mm2\_halting\_iff} and
\code{earned\_core\_halting\_undecidable} (EarnedCoreLinks.v), the last applying the library's
\code{MM2\_HALTING\_undec}.

What that buys, and what it doesn't. It buys: the base of this machine is a universal
machine in Minsky's sense, and nobody (in the library's sense) can predict in general what
it'll do. What it doesn't buy is a fast machine, or one where your input arrives
conveniently. The counters start holding $a$ and $b$, given directly; there's no encoding
layer in my files. Minsky's prime-power packing is how you'd get from ``any Turing machine''
to ``two counters,'' and that construction is his and the library's, not something I
re-proved.

Is ``given directly'' just a convenience, or does it bite? It bites, and somebody found
exactly where. In 1972 Rich Schroeppel, in a short memo from the MIT AI Lab, proved that a
two-counter machine started with $n$ in one counter and zero in the other can't compute
$2^n$. So the packing Minsky needs is precisely the thing two plain counters can't do for
themselves. Hand the small machine its inputs straight and there are functions of them it
can't compute; hand it the inputs already packed and it computes anything a Turing machine
can. That's no contradiction with the undecidability above, which ranges over every program
and every starting pair, packed ones included. The base hides nothing. It just needs its
input pre-chewed, and the chewing is somebody else's.

\subsection{It's a certification system, and the flag is a latch}

Now the record. Three facts first, all of them read straight off the step line.

\begin{theorem}[Ledger, toll, permanence]\label{thm:u34-toll}
For every state $s$ and instruction $i$, $\mu(\mathrm{exec}(s, i)) = \mu(s) +
\mathrm{cost}(i)$, and for every trace $t$, $\mu(\mathrm{run}(t, s)) = \mu(s) +
\mathrm{cost}(t)$. If $\mathrm{cert}(s)$ is down and $\mathrm{cert}(\mathrm{exec}(s, i))$ is
up, then $i$ is CERTIFY, it passes at $\mathrm{core}(s)$, and $\mathrm{cost}(i) \ge 1$. If
$\mathrm{cert}(s)$ is up, so is $\mathrm{cert}(\mathrm{exec}(s, i))$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Read the ledger component of Definition~\ref{def:u34-step}: it adds exactly
$\mathrm{cost}(i)$. Repeated substitution along a trace gives the sum of its costs,
or, equivalently, induction on the length of the trace does. The flag's new value is
its old value or $\mathrm{fires}(\mathrm{core}(s),i)$. A false-to-true change therefore
requires that event, whose definition requires a passing CERTIFY. CERTIFY costs $1$.
An already true flag stays true under the same disjunction.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{mu\_conservation}, \code{mu\_conservation\_trace}, \code{only\_certify\_certifies}, \code{a2} and
\code{cert\_permanent} (EarnedCore.v).

That third clause in the middle is Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s toll, for this machine. Which means this machine \emph{is}
one of the things Section~\ref{sec:toll} was about, and Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s theorem applies to it without my lifting a finger.

\begin{theorem}[An instance of the certification system]\label{thm:u34-instance}
The states, the instructions, the step $\mathrm{exec}$, the cost and the flag, with the toll
of Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-toll}, form a certification system (Definition~\ref{def:certsys}). So
the universal floor (Theorem~\ref{thm:universal-floor}) holds here: if
$\mathrm{cert}(s_0)$ is down and $\mathrm{cert}(\mathrm{run}(t, s_0))$ is up, then
$\mathrm{cost}(t) \ge 1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Take the state and instruction sets of Definitions~\ref{def:u34-state} and
\ref{def:u34-step}, their step and cost, and the flag as the reading. These provide the
five data fields of Definition~\ref{def:certsys}. Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-toll} supplies its
one required rule. Applying Theorem~\ref{thm:universal-floor} gives the claimed bound.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{earned\_cs} and \code{earned\_core\_floor} (EarnedCoreLinks.v); \code{earned\_core\_floor} is
\code{universal\_nfi\_any\_substrate}, the checked name of Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s theorem, applied to \code{earned\_cs}. The
same floor is proved directly, without the link, as \code{nfi\_floor} (EarnedCore.v).

Then Section~\ref{sec:latch}. Section~\ref{sec:latch} said: take any base, and any record that answers only to the base and never
comes back down, and the record is a latch. This machine has a base: a program together
with a core, stepping by the program step. And it has a record, the flag, with the ledger
riding along. So the question is whether it's an \emph{honest} extension in Section~\ref{sec:latch}'s five-rule
sense (Definition~\ref{def:u11-honest}), and if it is, Section~\ref{sec:latch} does the rest.

\begin{theorem}[The flag is a latch of the base]\label{thm:u34-latch}
Let the base have states (program, core), stepping by the program step, starting at
$\mathrm{start}(a, b)$'s core for any $a$, $b$, and halting when the program has halted.
Map each (program, state) to (program, core). Then the machine, run as a closed machine on
(program, state), is an honest extension of that base, and so its flag factors as the latch
(Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-latch}) of the event ``the next instruction is a CERTIFY that passes.''
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The rules of Definition~\ref{def:u11-honest} one at a time. Driven by the computation: the
next flag is the old flag or ``the next instruction is a passing CERTIFY,'' which is a
function of the base state and the old flag (that's the step line). Ledger: $\mu$ only adds.
Toll: Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-toll}. Permanence: Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-toll}. A reachable write: the
three-line program of the worked run raises the flag from a start. Section~\ref{sec:latch}'s theorem then gives
the factorization.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{earned\_core\_honest} and \code{earned\_core\_is\_latch} (EarnedCoreLinks.v), the latter
by \code{record\_axis\_is\_latch\_holds}; the step-level facts are \code{cert\_latch} and \code{base\_blind}
(EarnedCore.v).

So far, nothing new. The toll, the floor and the latch are things Part III already promised
about any machine of this kind. The next subsection is the part Part III couldn't give.

\subsection{Commitments are earned}

Here's the shape before the words. Pick any run from a clean start, any list of instructions
at all, chosen by somebody who'd love to cheat. Look at the moment a COMMIT would pass.
Then, somewhere earlier in that run, there's a CHECK of exactly the same claim that passed
and paid, at the same edition of the counter, and between that CHECK and now, nothing
touched the counter. Not ``probably.'' Not ``on the programs I wrote.'' On every list of
instructions anybody can write.

To say ``nothing touched it'' exactly, one word.

\begin{definition}[Untouched]\label{def:u34-untouched}
A list of instructions $\mathit{mid}$, run from a state $s$, leaves counter $c$
\emph{untouched} when, for every way of splitting $\mathit{mid}$ as $t_1$, then $i$, then
$t_2$, executing $i$ at the core reached by running $t_1$ from $s$ leaves both
$\mathrm{ver}(\cdot, c)$ and $\mathrm{val}(\cdot, c)$ as they were.
\end{definition}

Defined as \code{untouched} (EarnedCore.v).

\begin{theorem}[A commitment was checked first]\label{thm:u34-commit-earned}
Let $s_0$ be clean and $\mathit{pre}$ any trace after which COMMIT $p$ $c$ would pass. Then
$\mathit{pre}$ splits as $\mathit{pre}_1$, then CHECK $p$ $c$, then $\mathit{mid}$, where:
the CHECK passes at the core reached by $\mathit{pre}_1$; CHECK $p$ $c$ and COMMIT $p$ $c$
each cost at least 1; $c$'s version after $\mathit{pre}_1$ equals its version after
$\mathit{pre}$; and $\mathit{mid}$, run from just after the CHECK, leaves $c$ untouched.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
COMMIT passes, so the claim $(p, c, \mathrm{ver}(c))$ for the current version is in the
table. By the no-forging invariant (Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-no-forging} below), that fact was
written by a passing CHECK $p$ $c$ at some point $\mathit{pre}_1$, with the version $c$ had
then; since it's the current version too, the two versions are equal. Versions never go
down, and any instruction that changes a counter's value also raises its version, so an
instruction in $\mathit{mid}$ that touched $c$ would have left $c$'s version higher at the
end than at the CHECK. It isn't. So nothing in $\mathit{mid}$ touched $c$.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{earned\_commitment\_provenance} (EarnedCore.v).

\begin{theorem}[A raised flag was checked, then committed, then certified]\label{thm:u34-cert-earned}
Let $s_0$ be clean and $t$ any trace with $\mathrm{cert}(\mathrm{run}(t, s_0))$ up. Then
for some $p$ and $c$, $t$ is
\[
\mathit{pre}_1,\ \ \mathrm{CHECK}\ p\ c,\ \ \mathit{mid}_1,\ \ \mathrm{COMMIT}\ p\ c,\ \ \mathit{mid}_2,\ \ \mathrm{CERTIFY},\ \ \mathit{post},
\]
where the CHECK passes at its state, the COMMIT passes at its state, the CERTIFY passes at
its state, $c$ has the same version at the CHECK as at the COMMIT, and $\mathit{mid}_1$ leaves
$c$ untouched.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The flag starts down, so some first instruction raised it, and by
Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-toll} it's a passing CERTIFY. A CERTIFY passes only with a fact in the
channel, the channel starts empty, and only a passing COMMIT puts a fact there, so some
earlier COMMIT $p$ $c$ passed. Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-commit-earned} at that COMMIT gives the
CHECK, the equal version, and the untouched stretch.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{earned\_certification\_provenance} (EarnedCore.v).

And the failure side, so you can see the refusals are clean and not half-done:

\begin{theorem}[Unearned steps trap and change no claim]\label{thm:u34-failures}
If COMMIT $p$ $c$ would not pass at a core $k$, executing it puts the trap up and leaves the
channel and the table as they were. If CERTIFY would not pass at a state $s$, executing it
puts the trap up and leaves the flag as it was.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If the trap is already up, the core is unchanged and its trap remains up. Otherwise,
the failed COMMIT takes the failure branch of the instruction table: set the trap,
leave every other core field alone. A failed CERTIFY takes the same branch, and its
$\mathrm{fires}$ value is false. The flag update is then its old value or false,
which leaves it unchanged. The instruction's charge still applies to the ledger.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{unearned\_commit\_traps} and \code{uncommitted\_certify\_traps} (EarnedCore.v).

Read Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-cert-earned} once more for what it \emph{doesn't} say. Between the CHECK
and the COMMIT, the counter is untouched. Between the COMMIT and the CERTIFY, it isn't
promised anything. You can check $A$ is even, commit to it, add one to $A$, and then
certify. The flag goes up, and what it stands on is a commitment about the edition that was
current when you committed. The certificate is historical: ``this was checked and committed
about this edition,'' not ``this is still true.'' I think that's the right meaning for a
certificate (a birth certificate doesn't expire when the baby grows), but it's a meaning,
and you should know which one you're getting.

\subsection{What a passing check means}

Provenance says a CHECK happened. It doesn't yet say the CHECK was \emph{right}, and that's a
separate question with a separate proof. A machine could have a perfectly ordered chain of
check, commit, certify, all standing on a checker that says yes to everything. So: what does
a fact in the table actually tell you about the counter?

\begin{theorem}[Checker soundness]\label{thm:u34-soundness}
Let $s_0$ be clean and $t$ any trace, and let $k$ be the core of $\mathrm{run}(t, s_0)$. For
every fact $(p, c, v)$ in $k$'s table with $v = \mathrm{ver}(k, c)$, the property holds of
the counter's current value: $\mathrm{holds}(p, \mathrm{val}(k, c))$. In particular, if
COMMIT $p$ $c$ would pass at $k$, then $\mathrm{holds}(p, \mathrm{val}(k, c))$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Carry one sentence through every instruction: every fact in the table has a version no
higher than its counter's, and if its version equals its counter's, its property holds of
its counter's value. A clean start has an empty table, so the sentence holds there. A
passing CHECK adds a fact at the current version, and the checker said yes, so by
Lemma~\ref{lem:u34-eval} the property holds. A write raises one counter's version, so every
old fact about that counter falls strictly behind and the second half no longer applies to
it. Nothing else changes a value or a version. The sentence holds after every instruction,
so it holds at the end. The part about COMMIT is the case where the claim is in the table at
the current version.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{checker\_soundness} and \code{committed\_claim\_holds} (EarnedCore.v), through the
invariant \code{sound} and its one-step form \code{sound\_step}.

So a live fact means exactly this: one of three arithmetic properties holds of one counter's
current value. Not ``the program is correct.'' Not ``the number is interesting.'' The property,
of the value, now. That's all ``checked'' means on this machine, and it's enough to be true.

\subsection{Nothing gets forged}

The proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-commit-earned} leaned on an invariant I promised to show you.
Here it is. The fear it answers: could some clever sequence of instructions get a fact into
the table without a CHECK writing it? A DEC with a funny jump target, a COMMIT after a trap,
something I didn't think of? The answer is checked one instruction at a time, which is the
only way I trust myself to answer it.

\begin{definition}[Earned fact; no forgery]\label{def:u34-earned}
After a trace $t$ from $s_0$, a fact $f = (p, c, v)$ is \emph{earned} when $t$ is $\mathit{pre}$,
then CHECK $p$ $c$, then $\mathit{mid}$, where the CHECK passes at the core reached by
$\mathit{pre}$, $f$ is exactly the claim $p$ of $c$ at that core, and, if $f$ is live at the
end ($v$ equals $c$'s version after $t$), $\mathit{mid}$ leaves $c$ untouched. The trace has
\emph{no forgery} when every fact in the table after it is earned.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[No forging]\label{thm:u34-no-forging}
For every core $k$, instruction $i$ and fact $f$ in the table after executing $i$ at $k$:
either $f$ was already in $k$'s table, or $i$ is CHECK of $f$'s property and counter, it
passes at $k$, and $f$ is the claim it writes. Consequently, if a trace has no forgery, so
does that trace followed by any one instruction; and from every clean start, every trace
has no forgery.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The first part is a case for each of the six instructions: only a passing CHECK adds
anything, and it adds exactly its claim. For the second, a new fact is earned by the CHECK
that just wrote it; an old fact stays earned, and if it's still live after the new
instruction, its counter's version didn't move, so the new instruction didn't touch the
counter and the untouched stretch grows by one. A clean start has an empty table, which has
no forgery, and the step carries it along any trace.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{facts\_step}, \code{no\_forging\_step} and \code{no\_forging} (EarnedCore.v).

\subsection{A full table traps}

Sixteen facts of room, and no eviction. Two halves to prove: nothing ever leaves, and
nothing ever overflows.

\begin{theorem}[Bounded table, no eviction]\label{thm:u34-bounded}
Every instruction keeps every fact already in the table. If the table holds 16 or more
facts, CHECK $p$ $c$ puts the trap up and leaves the table as it was. If the table holds at
most 16 facts, it still holds at most 16 after any instruction.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
With a raised trap no instruction changes the table. With the trap down, only CHECK
can change it, and a successful CHECK adds one fact without removing an entry.
Success requires a previous length strictly below $16$, so the new length is at most
$16$. At length $16$ or greater that branch is unavailable: CHECK raises the trap
and preserves the table. Every other instruction preserves it as well.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{facts\_keep}, \code{full\_table\_traps} and \code{facts\_bounded\_step} (EarnedCore.v).

Why trap instead of making room? Because ``making room'' means deciding which fact dies, and a
fact that can die is a fact whose absence you have to explain later. A table that only grows
is a history you can read back, and the provenance proofs above lean on exactly that. The
bill for it is real, though, and it's in the last subsection of this chapter, the one on
what the machine doesn't do.

\subsection{The window can't see the record}

Section~\ref{sec:windows} was about windows: a view of a state that shows some of it, and the theorem that a window
which can't tell two states apart can't price the step between them exactly
(Theorem~\ref{thm:shadow-price}). Here's the smallest pair I could build where the window is
Minsky's view of the machine (line number and the two counters) and the record is
everything else.

Run two traces from $\mathrm{start}(0, 0)$. The \emph{earned} run is CHECK \emph{is zero} $A$; COMMIT
\emph{is zero} $A$; CERTIFY. The \emph{idle} run is DEC $A$ 0, three times. In the idle run, $A$ is 0
every time, so each DEC just goes to the next line and writes nothing. Both runs end on line
4, with $A = 0$ and $B = 0$, both versions 0. Through the window, identical. One of them has
paid 3, holds a fact, could commit again, and has its flag up. The other has paid nothing,
holds nothing, can't commit, and its flag is down. Two photographs, same picture, different
people.

\begin{theorem}[Same window, different record]\label{thm:u34-separation}
The earned run and the idle run from $\mathrm{start}(0, 0)$ end at cores with the same
window and the same versions of $A$ and $B$, and with different ledgers, different flags,
different tables, and different answers to ``would COMMIT \emph{is zero} $A$ pass.''
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
In the earned run, CHECK adds $(\mathsf{Zero},A,0)$, COMMIT puts that fact in the
channel, and CERTIFY raises the flag. The ledger is $1+1+1=3$. No counter is written.
In the idle run each DEC sees zero, so it advances the line without writing a counter
or raising a version. Its three costs are zero and it adds no fact or commitment.
Thus both final windows are $(4,0,0)$ with versions $(0,0)$. The earned table contains
the current zero claim and the idle table is empty, giving the stated difference in
whether another COMMIT would pass, as well as in the ledger and flag.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{receipt\_separation} (EarnedCore.v).

\begin{theorem}[No window oracle]\label{thm:u34-no-oracle}
There is no function $g$ from windows to whole numbers with $g(\mathrm{window}) = \mu$ at the
end of every trace from $\mathrm{start}(0, 0)$. Likewise there is no function from windows to
yes or no that gives the flag at the end of every such trace, and none that gives whether
COMMIT \emph{is zero} $A$ would pass.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Such a $g$ would have to give both 3 and 0 on the one window the two runs of
Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-separation} share. The same for the flag and the commit right.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{no\_mu\_oracle}, \code{no\_cert\_oracle} and \code{no\_commit\_oracle} (EarnedCore.v).

This is Section~\ref{sec:windows}'s shape, made of pebbles: the record lives off the window. Anybody who only
watches the counters and the line number, which is everything Minsky's machine \emph{is}, can't
tell you what was paid, what was committed, or whether the flag is up. Not because they
looked carelessly. Because it isn't there to see.

\subsection{The exact price is three}

Section~\ref{sec:toll} said a raised flag costs at least one. On this machine that's true and too modest. A
raised flag needs a CERTIFY, a CERTIFY needs a COMMIT, a COMMIT needs a CHECK, and each of
those is its own instruction costing one. So at least three. One of what: three units of
$\mu$, one per paid act, each one the ``one'' I picked back in the table. And three isn't a
guess that happens to hold; it's the number of links in the chain.

\begin{theorem}[The minimum price of a certificate]\label{thm:u34-min-price}
If $s_0$ is clean and $\mathrm{cert}(\mathrm{run}(t, s_0))$ is up, then $\mathrm{cost}(t)
\ge 3$ and $\mu(\mathrm{run}(t, s_0)) \ge \mu(s_0) + 3$. For programs: if the flag is up
after $n$ program steps from $\mathrm{start}(a, b)$, then $\mu \ge 3$ there.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-cert-earned} finds a CHECK, a COMMIT and a CERTIFY at three different
places in $t$, each costing 1, and every other instruction costs at least 0. The ledger
statement is Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-toll}. A program run is the run of the instructions it
actually executes, so the program form follows.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{certified\_run\_min\_cost} and \code{program\_certified\_min\_cost} (EarnedCore.v).

\begin{theorem}[Three is tight]\label{thm:u34-tight}
For all whole numbers $a$ and $b$, the program CHECK \emph{at least 0} $A$; COMMIT \emph{at least 0}
$A$; CERTIFY, run for 4 program steps from $\mathrm{start}(a, b)$, ends with the flag up,
$\mu = 3$ exactly, and the program halted.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Every natural number $a$ satisfies $a\ge0$. The first instruction therefore adds
$(\mathsf{Ge}(0),A,0)$ to the empty table and charges $1$. No counter changes, so
the second instruction finds that same fact, puts it in the channel and charges $1$.
The third finds the channel occupied, raises the flag and charges $1$. The line is
now $4$, beyond the three-instruction program. The fourth program step stays there
and adds no charge. The final ledger is exactly $3$ and the program is halted.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{min\_cost\_tight} (EarnedCore.v), with the program named \code{witness}.

That's the worked run from the start of the chapter, now as a theorem. The floor is 3 and
something pays exactly 3, so 3 is the price, not a bound with slack in it.

And that's every piece of the model, standing on six instructions: a base that computes
everything two counters can, a ledger that's exact, a toll the universal floor applies to, a
flag that's a latch of the base, a window that can't see the record, and a commitment that
can't happen unless a check of the same claim, on the same edition, came first and was
right. Every result above is closed: Coq reports no assumptions for any of them. The base
file uses nothing but Coq's standard library, so you can check it with nothing else
installed; the link file adds only the book's own abstract records and the library of
undecidability proofs.

\subsection{One machine that runs them all}
\label{sec:universal-host}

The small machine raises its flag only by checking, committing and certifying, and it pays
for that. The next question is whether one machine can stand in for all of them, the way
Turing's universal machine stands in for every Turing machine. Here's what I mean by that. A
\emph{universal Thiele machine} is one fixed machine that runs any machine of a stated class
as a guest, with the guest's record kept and the guest's toll collected by its own step, not
by a convention some program running on it has to keep.

So I built a host. It carries a guest inside its own state: the guest's program as data, the
guest's counters, its table, its ledger, its flag. The host has one extra move, run one guest
step. In that one move it looks at the guest's flag, takes the step, looks again, and if the
flag went from down to up, the host's own copy of that flag goes up in the same move, and the
host pays for it.

\begin{definition}[The host]\label{def:u34-host}
A \emph{guest} is a program $P$ of this chapter's machine together with a state $g$ of it
(Definition~\ref{def:u34-step}). A \emph{host state} $h$ has six parts: its own core
$\mathrm{core}(h)$, its ledger $\mu(h)$, its own flag $\mathrm{own}(h)$, the guest program
$P(h)$ held as a list of instructions, the guest state $g(h)$, and the \emph{mirror} $m(h)$, a
yes/no copy of the guest's flag. The host has two kinds of move. $\mathrm{OWN}\ i$ runs the
instruction $i$ on the host's own core, costs what this chapter's machine charges for $i$,
and raises $\mathrm{own}$ exactly when that machine's flag would rise. $\mathrm{GSTEP}\ b$
costs $b$. If the host's core is trapped it does nothing else. Otherwise it moves the host to
its next line and, if the guest's next instruction costs at most $b$, runs that instruction
on $g(h)$; in the same move the mirror becomes $m(h) \lor (\lnot\mathrm{cert}(g(h)) \land
\mathrm{cert}(g'))$, where $g'$ is the new guest state. The host's reading is
$\mathrm{own}(h) \lor m(h)$. The universal program is $U = [\mathrm{GSTEP}\ 1;\ \mathrm{OWN}\
(\text{INC } A);\ \mathrm{OWN}\ (\text{DEC } A\ 1)]$: one guest step, then two moves that
bring the host back to its first line.
\end{definition}

Every instruction of the small machine costs at most one, so $\mathrm{GSTEP}\ 1$ runs every
guest instruction there is. Why charge the budget $b$, and not the cost of whatever
instruction got fetched? Because charging the budget keeps the price a function of the move
alone, which is what the certification system of Part II asks for: you read the price of a
host move off the move, the way you read the small machine's prices off its table, without
peeking inside the guest. The bill for that is easy to see. A host that steps a free guest
instruction, an INC say, still pays one for the move.

\begin{theorem}[The host runs any guest]\label{thm:u34-universal}
(1) If the host's core is not trapped, then after $n$ moves $\mathrm{GSTEP}\ 1$ the guest state
is the guest program's own run of $n$ steps from $g(h)$, the guest program is unchanged, and
the host is still not trapped. (2) If the host's core is at line 1 and not trapped, then $3n$
steps of the program $U$ leave the guest exactly where $n$ steps of its own program put it.
(3) For every two-counter program $M$ and inputs $a$, $b$: $M$ halts from $(1, (a, b))$ exactly
when the host program made of $\mathrm{OWN}$ moves of the compiled $M$ halts, from a host
whose core starts at $(a, b)$, whatever guest that host carries.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Induction on $n$: a host that isn't trapped stays untrapped through a guest step, and with
budget 1 the guest step is the guest's own step. (2) One pass of $U$ is a guest step, then
INC $A$ and DEC $A$ back to line 1, so it is (1) once per pass. (3) A host program made only
of $\mathrm{OWN}$ moves is the small machine, core for core, and
Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-halting} does the rest.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{universal\_simulation}, \code{universal\_program\_simulation} and
\code{host\_thiele\_complete} (UniversalThiele.v).

\begin{theorem}[The copy is the record]\label{thm:u34-mirror}
Say a host state $h$ \emph{agrees} when $m(h) = \mathrm{cert}(g(h))$. Every host move takes an
agreeing state to an agreeing state, so every host trace and every stored host program
does too, and a freshly loaded host agrees. In particular, if $h$ agrees and is not trapped,
the mirror after $n$ moves $\mathrm{GSTEP}\ 1$ is the guest's flag after $n$ steps of its own
program.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
One move at a time. An $\mathrm{OWN}$ move touches neither the mirror nor the guest. A trapped
$\mathrm{GSTEP}$ touches neither. An untrapped one sets the mirror to the old mirror or the
crossing, and the guest's flag is a latch (Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-toll}), so if the old mirror
equalled the old flag, the new mirror equals the new flag. The last sentence is this
together with Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-universal}.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{record\_agreement\_step}, \code{record\_agreement},
\code{record\_agreement\_program}, \code{hload\_agrees} and \code{simulated\_record}
(UniversalThiele.v).

\begin{theorem}[The host's step collects the guest's toll]\label{thm:u34-host-toll}
(1) If $h$ agrees, is not trapped, and the guest step that budget $b$ allows takes the guest's
flag from down to up, then the mirror is down before $\mathrm{GSTEP}\ b$ and up after it,
the host's ledger rose by exactly $b$, and $b \ge 1$. (2) In the run of (1) of
Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-universal}, if the guest's flag goes up between its steps $n$ and $n + 1$,
the mirror goes up between the host's moves $n$ and $n + 1$, and that move costs 1. (3) For every
host trace $t$, $\mu(g(\mathrm{run}(t, h))) + \mu(h) \le \mu(\mathrm{run}(t, h)) +
\mu(g(h))$: the host's ledger grows at least as fast as the guest's.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) The guest's flag rises only on a passing CERTIFY (Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-toll}), which costs
1, and the budget let it run, so $b \ge 1$; the mirror was the guest's flag, so it was down,
and the move sets it to the crossing. (2) is (1) at the matching move. (3) Induction on $t$: a
guest step that runs costs the guest at most the budget the host paid, and every other move
leaves the guest's ledger alone.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{toll\_enforced\_by\_host\_step}, \code{every\_guest\_crossing\_is\_a\_host\_crossing},
\code{host\_pays\_for\_guest}, \code{host\_cost\_covers\_guest} and \code{simulated\_cost}
(UniversalThiele.v).

\begin{theorem}[No free host certification]\label{thm:u34-no-free-host}
If the mirror is down at $h$ and up after a host move $i$, then $i$ is $\mathrm{GSTEP}\ b$ with
$b \ge 1$, the host was not trapped, the guest's next instruction was CERTIFY, and the guest's
flag went from down to up in that move. A trace made only of $\mathrm{OWN}$ moves leaves the
mirror and the guest state exactly where they were. And the host's own flag rises only by an
$\mathrm{OWN}$ CERTIFY that passes on the host's core.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
An $\mathrm{OWN}$ move copies the mirror unchanged, and a trapped $\mathrm{GSTEP}$ does too, so
the rise is an untrapped $\mathrm{GSTEP}\ b$ whose guest step crossed; a crossing is a passing
CERTIFY, which costs 1 and needed the budget. The own flag moves by this chapter's step line.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{no\_free\_host\_certification\_step}, \code{no\_free\_host\_certification},
\code{no\_free\_host\_certification\_program}, \code{guestless\_runs\_leave\_mirror} and
\code{own\_record\_only\_by\_certify} (UniversalThiele.v).

\begin{theorem}[The host is a Thiele machine]\label{thm:u34-host-instance}
For every host state and move, if the host's reading goes from no to yes, the move costs at
least 1; the same holds for the mirror alone and for the own flag alone. So the host read
through $\mathrm{own} \lor m$, the host read through $m$ alone, and the guest class are
certification systems (Definition~\ref{def:certsys}), and any host trace that raises the
host's reading costs at least 1.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The mirror's half is Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-no-free-host}; the own flag's half is the small
machine's toll on the host's core. The trace form is Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s universal floor.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{host\_toll}, \code{host\_own\_toll} and \code{host\_mirror\_toll}
(UniversalThiele.v), and \code{host\_cs}, \code{host\_mirror\_cs}, \code{guest\_cs} and
\code{host\_nfi} (UniversalThieleLinks.v).

\begin{remark}[Two guests, run]\label{rem:u34-host-runs}
Load the guest CHECK \emph{is zero} $A$; COMMIT \emph{is zero} $A$; CERTIFY; HALT with both
counters at 0. After two moves $\mathrm{GSTEP}\ 1$ the mirror is down; after three it is up,
the guest's flag is up, the host's own flag is still down, and the host has paid 3. Under the
program $U$ the mirror is down at host step 6 and up at step 7, with 3 paid. The guest
CERTIFY; CERTIFY traps on its first step: after five moves $\mathrm{GSTEP}\ 1$ the mirror is
down, the guest is trapped, and the host has paid 5 for nothing.
\end{remark}

Checked as \code{demo\_certifies}, \code{demo\_program\_certifies} and \code{demo\_forgery\_fails}
(UniversalThiele.v).

That copy can't be faked. The proof walks every host move there is, and the copy only rises
in a guest step where the guest itself ran CERTIFY and passed. A host program that never
touches the guest leaves the copy exactly where it was. The copy always equals the guest's
flag, the host's ledger always grows at least as fast as the guest's, and a three-instruction
loop runs any small-machine program one guest step per pass. Since the small machine already
runs every two-counter program, the host runs every computation, and every guest's toll is
collected by the host's own step, not by a convention someone has to keep.

Why make such a fuss about a proof that walks every host move? Because the first universal
machine had bugs. It's the machine in Turing's 1936 paper that reads another machine's
description off its tape and does what that machine would do, and nobody gets to call Turing
careless. In 1947 Emil Post, in an appendix to a paper on a problem of Thue, pointed out that
the construction leaned on a convention it hadn't earned, and he patched a small defect in
how the universal machine writes out each complete configuration. Around the same time Donald
Davies, who joined the National Physical Laboratory in 1947, where Turing was designing a
computer, worked through the universal machine's tables and found more mistakes. (It's the
same Davies who later named the \emph{packet} in packet switching.) His corrections were finally printed in Jack Copeland's collection
\emph{The Essential Turing} in 2004. People like to call them some of the first bugs ever written,
in a program for a computer that didn't exist yet, which is a lovely claim and a hard one to
check, so take it as a lead and not a fact. What it changes here: a universal machine is
exactly the kind of construction where a careful person leaves a hole, and the host's
theorems are checked by Coq one move at a time, which is the kind of check that catches
Davies's kind of slip. It doesn't catch a definition that says the wrong thing. That's why the
definition is on the page, for you.

Here's what that covers, said plainly, a sentence at a time. The guests are this chapter's
programs, every one of them, from every state. That's the stated class. It's the same kind of
class Turing's universal machine has: a fixed instruction set, and a finite program held as
data. The guest program sits in the host's state as a list of instructions, not packed into
one number; packing it would add bookkeeping and nothing to the record argument. A Thiele
machine from somewhere else comes in through the two-counter encoding. It keeps its
computation. It keeps its toll: a raise still costs at least one. It doesn't keep its own
price list. As a guest it pays one for each CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY and nothing for
counting, and the foreign machine's reading has to be computed into a counter and checked
with this machine's three properties. Picture a clerk who'll stamp anybody's receipt, as long
as it's copied onto his forms and billed at his rates. A compilation that keeps every foreign
price exactly is not proved. And here's why the extra move is the point. A plain two-counter
host could interpret guests too. But then the guest's record would be data the host's program
updates by convention, which is exactly the Turing machine's position from the front matter.
Here the mirror, the crossing test and the charge are in the host's step rule, so
Theorems~\ref{thm:u34-host-toll} and~\ref{thm:u34-no-free-host} hold for every sequence of host
moves, including ones that never run a guest.

\subsection{What it doesn't do}

Here's where it falls short, in plain words, because a small machine is only honest if its
edges are as visible as its middle.

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{The check price is flat.} CHECK costs 1 whether it's asking ``is this 0'' or ``is this at
least a billion.'' The property language is fixed and each property is one evaluation, so
``pays for its work'' here means that flat price, not a price that grows with how hard the
question was. A machine that charged by the difficulty of the check would be a different
machine, and I haven't built it.
\item \textbf{DEC on zero isn't a write.} It doesn't change the counter, so it doesn't change the
version. That's the right call for versions (nothing changed), but it means DEC on zero is
a free way to move the line number without leaving any mark. The idle run in the window
section uses exactly that.
\item \textbf{After a trap, a trace still pays.} On programs, a trap stops the run. On arbitrary
traces, instructions after a trap are each charged their cost and none of them changes the
core. I chose to keep charging so that the ledger stays the plain sum of what was issued
(Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-toll} has no exceptions); the price of that choice is that a trapped
machine can still be billed for nothing.
\item \textbf{``Checked'' means three properties and nothing more.} Is zero, is even, is at least $n$.
A live fact means one of those holds of one counter's current value. It doesn't mean the
program is correct, or that anything follows from the property, or that the property was
worth checking.
\item \textbf{The certificate is historical.} Between the COMMIT and the CERTIFY, the counter can
change, and the flag still goes up. The flag says a claim was checked and committed about
an edition, not that the claim is still true.
\item \textbf{Sixteen checks per run, ever.} Facts never leave and the table holds sixteen, so a run
gets at most sixteen passing CHECKs in its whole life, and the seventeenth traps. A
certificate needs only one, so this costs nothing for the theorems, but it's a hard wall
for any program that wants to keep checking forever.
\item \textbf{The clean start matters.} Provenance, soundness, no forging and the price of three are
all stated from a clean start. Hand the machine a table pre-loaded with facts nobody
checked, and of course none of that follows. The theorems are about what the machine
produces, not about what you smuggle in at the door.
\item \textbf{The host keeps a guest's toll, not its prices.} The universal host of the last
subsection runs this machine's programs. A machine from elsewhere gets in through the
two-counter encoding with its computation and toll intact and its own price list replaced
by this machine's.
\item \textbf{Slow, and fed directly.} Universality is Minsky's, with the inputs placed straight in
the counters. Getting from an arbitrary Turing machine to two counters goes through his
exponential packing, which is not in my files.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{What comes next}

The next section opens a much bigger build. It carries far more than this one: memory and
registers, modules and the arrows between them, a two-player game and its check, and
eventually hardware. I'll introduce all of it there, from scratch, and I won't lean on any
of it before then.

But I want one thing said plainly before you meet it, so it doesn't surprise you later. The
big build prices commitments. Its toll on the flag is there and proved, and every paid step
is on its ledger. What it doesn't do is \emph{enforce that a commitment was earned}: in it, the
act that checks a claim commits to nothing, and the act that commits doesn't look for a
passing check (Section~\ref{sec:machine-claims} shows exactly where). Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-cert-earned}, the one that says a
raised flag was checked, then committed, then certified, on the same edition with nothing in
between, is a theorem about \emph{this} machine, the small one. The earned version lives here.

So Part IV has two machines, and neither of them is the model. Both are Thiele machines in
the front matter's sense, instances of the certification system with the toll proved: this
one as \code{earned\_cs} (Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-instance}), the big one as
\code{thiele\_cert\_addr\_system} (UniversalCertificationCost.v), whose toll is
Theorem~\ref{thm:u17-nfi}. This one is also Thiele-complete. Its base is a two-counter
machine, so it computes whatever a Turing machine can while it carries the record and pays
the toll (Theorems~\ref{thm:u34-simulation} and~\ref{thm:u34-halting}). And a host built on it
is a universal Thiele machine for its programs: it runs any of them as a guest and collects
the guest's toll in its own step (Section~\ref{sec:universal-host}). Whether the big one
is Thiele-complete I haven't proved, and nothing in this book leans on it. The small one shows the
model whole, with earned commitments, on the least I could build. The big one shows how
much a single build can carry while the toll still holds, and where it stops short. If you
ever find yourself wondering whether a property of the big one is the model's or just the
build's, this chapter is the one to hold it up against. Six instructions. If the model
needs more than that, the big one is where it'll show.

%===========================================================================
\section{One machine, built three times}
\label{sec:onemachine}
%===========================================================================

That was the small machine: six instructions, the whole model, earned commitments and
all, on the least I could build. Now the big one, which I'll call the big build, and which
is the test bench where I find out how much a single machine can carry while the toll still
holds. From here on, through the hardware, everything is about it. When I say ``my machine'' or
``the machine'' from now on, I mean exactly one thing: that build, with its state record, its
fifty-one instructions and the price of each, written down in Coq and then turned into a
hardware design. The six-instruction one keeps its own name, the small machine. Not a toy,
not ``any system.'' This one, warts included. I want to say three
things about it before I show you a
single field, because the way people misread a concrete machine is to mistake it for the
idea.

First: this is one try. The theorems of Part III quantify over any states and any steps;
the thing in Part IV is one particular choice of states and steps, with sixteen registers
and a hundred and twenty-eight words of memory and fifty-one instructions, and every one of
those numbers was a decision I made, some of them for reasons and some of them because I
had to pick something. Because those theorems are stated for any states and any steps, none
of them mentions these numbers. If you built a different machine that obeyed the toll, it
would be a different try at the same idea, and the latch theorem in Section~\ref{sec:latch} says its record
would have the same shape underneath. Section~\ref{sec:smallest} is exactly that: a different try, much smaller,
and its record is a latch. One difference I'll keep saying out loud: this build prices
commitments but doesn't enforce that they were earned. That guarantee is the small
machine's (Section~\ref{sec:smallest}), and Section~\ref{sec:machine-claims} shows where this one stops short of it.
The plainest sign is a name the two machines share. CERTIFY in the small machine traps
unless a commitment is waiting; CERTIFY here (Section~\ref{sec:isa}) raises the flag with
nothing required before it.
It's still a Thiele machine, an instance of the certification system with its toll proved
(\code{thiele\_cert\_addr\_system}, UniversalCertificationCost.v, with
Theorem~\ref{thm:u17-nfi} as the toll). And the hardware at the end isn't a second one. It
implements this one, inside bounds Section~\ref{sec:chip} states.

Second: why build one at all, if the abstract theorems are the point? Because an abstract
theorem about ``any machine'' is checked against nothing until there's a machine to check it
against, and an abstract statement can be wrong in ways nobody notices until it meets one. The
concrete machine is where the abstract claims get \emph{instantiated}, and each one meets it in a
place I can name now. Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s universal floor becomes a theorem about these fifty-one
instructions (Section~\ref{sec:isa}, and its whole ladder in Section~\ref{sec:witness}). Section~\ref{sec:counter}'s counter rule becomes a statement about
one field of the state (Section~\ref{sec:state}, with the run forms in Section~\ref{sec:witness}). Section~\ref{sec:windows}'s windows become two states that
look the same and aren't (Section~\ref{sec:separation}), and the clerk's collisions and the verifier's escapes become
named pairs (Section~\ref{sec:witness}). Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}'s entitlement and Section~\ref{sec:insight}'s insight land in Section~\ref{sec:machine-claims}, after Section~\ref{sec:claims} has shown what a
claim on this machine physically is. Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}'s finite-room merge argument becomes a statement
about a finite window onto this machine, because the whole record is not finite (Section~\ref{sec:state} says
why, Section~\ref{sec:witness} builds the window). Section~\ref{sec:narrowing}, Section~\ref{sec:latch}, Section~\ref{sec:models} and Section~\ref{sec:pointer} land in Section~\ref{sec:witness} too, and Section~\ref{sec:diagonal}'s diagonal comes
home in Section~\ref{sec:interpreters}. Each of those places names the Part III claim it instantiates and points back
to it rather than arguing it again. When an instantiation goes through, it's evidence the
abstract statement means what I think. When one doesn't, the abstract statement is the thing
under suspicion, not the machine. A machine is how a person who thinks in shapes checks that
the shapes close.

Third: I built it three times, in three materials. Once as a mathematical object in Coq, a
step relation on a record of twelve fields, where every theorem about the machine lives;
I'll call that version the \emph{kernel}, because it's the reference definition the other two are
held up against. Once as
a hardware model in a language called Kami, which is Coq again but shaped like a circuit,
with a proof, instruction by instruction and under stated side conditions on the hardware's
state, that the hardware's step, read back through an abstraction function, lands on the
same state as the kernel's step. And once as the thing that
falls out the far end of that model: Verilog, the language chips are described in, which a
tool chain turned into a file that would configure a real programmable chip, if I owned
one, which I don't. Aristotle's bronze from Section~\ref{sec:structure}: the statue in three materials, and the
promise that it's the same statue is a promise I have to keep in Section~\ref{sec:chip}, not assert here.

How hard is a promise like that to keep? There's a machine that answers better than I can,
and it's older than any of this. Between 1846 and 1848 Charles Babbage drew a calculating
engine, his Difference Engine No.~2, and never built it. The drawings sat for about a
hundred and forty years, until the historian Allan Bromley proposed building it and the
Science Museum in London did, with its curator of computing, Doron Swade, running the
project. The first thing they had to decide was what ``build it'' meant. The drawings had
dimensions that disagreed from one view to the next, mechanisms left out, a whole assembly
that did nothing, and one error in the carrying of tens that would have stopped the engine
from working at all. Swade's own account is blunt about it: built exactly as drawn, they
didn't expect it to work. So they set two rules. Every change had to be a solution Babbage had
used somewhere else in his own designs, and every change had to come back off, so the machine
could be returned to exactly what the drawings show. The calculating section did its first
full error-free table, the seventh powers, on 29 November 1991, twenty-seven days before
Babbage's two hundredth birthday, and the printer was finished in 2002. Eight thousand parts,
five tons.

You'll find it said that the errors were planted on purpose, to trip up anybody who stole the
plans. It's a good story, and good stories are the ones to check. Swade's account lists the
errors one by one and gives them no such motive; he calls the gap one of engineering
completeness, not of principle. So it goes on the shelf next to Hippasus until somebody shows
the letter where Babbage says so.

What does that change here? Swade had to answer the question Section~\ref{sec:chip} has to
answer: when the thing in the new material had to differ from the drawing, in what sense is
it the same machine? His answer was to write down every difference and keep each one
reversible. Mine is a proof, step by step, under side conditions that are written down. Different
tools, same promise, and it breaks the same way, through a difference nobody wrote down.

What the next eleven sections are, in the order you'll meet them, after the small machine
in Section~\ref{sec:smallest}. Section~\ref{sec:state} is the state: the
twelve fields and what each promises. Section~\ref{sec:isa} is the instruction set and the cost schedule, all
fifty-one, in a table, with the twelve that are never free picked out. Those two are the
reference chapters: every name the rest of the machine's story uses is handed over there
first. Section~\ref{sec:category} is the category, built from scratch, with the two laws I made you wait for in
Section~\ref{sec:structure}. Section~\ref{sec:claims} is about the claims a module can carry: a formula, a label, and the step that checks
one against the other. Section~\ref{sec:separation} is two states that look the same and aren't. Section~\ref{sec:receipt} is a receipt,
worked through in four acts. Section~\ref{sec:machine-claims} puts Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}'s entitlement and Section~\ref{sec:insight}'s insight on the machine. Section~\ref{sec:witness}
is the machine as the \emph{witness} for the rest of Parts II and III, where the remaining
forward pointers land on named theorems. Section~\ref{sec:interpreters} is the interpreter and the guest, where the
diagonal from Section~\ref{sec:diagonal} comes home. Section~\ref{sec:chsh} is the two-player game and its check, built from zero. Section~\ref{sec:landauer}
is the accounting against physics and the hierarchy of what costs more. Then the machine
leaves the page: Section~\ref{sec:chip}, in Part V, is the third material, the proof turned into a chip, and
the place where the same-statue promise gets kept or broken.

And one rule for all of them: no sentence about what the machine does stays on the page
unless I've read the step rule it describes. Where I've simplified, I say so. Where a
comment in the source and the rule next to it disagree, I follow the rule. The machine is
the one thing in this book I can be \emph{exactly} right about, because it's written down, and
being exactly right about it is the only way the abstract parts earn their keep.

%===========================================================================
\section{The state record}
\label{sec:state}
%===========================================================================

A state of the machine is a record with twelve fields. I'm going to give you all twelve,
because the whole of Part III was about ``the state'' as an abstract thing and you've earned
the right to see what one looks like when it's written down. Then I'll tell you what \emph{isn't}
in it, which turns out to be as informative, and then the one piece of structure that the
rest of the book hangs on, the partition graph.

\subsection{The twelve fields}

Here they are, in the order they appear in the source, with what each one is for. A few
instructions get named in passing, by the names the source gives them (the ones in capitals).
All fifty-one are in Section~\ref{sec:isa}'s table with exactly what they do; here each one gets a few words
the first time it shows up, enough to follow the field it touches.

The \emph{partition graph}: the modules (the groups from Section~\ref{sec:structure}, each owning a range of addresses),
the arrows between them, and two counters that hand out fresh identifiers and only ever go
up. Its own record is below.

Four \emph{control and status words}, held together in a small sub-record: the \emph{assertion channel}
(the record calls this field the certification address, \code{csr\_cert\_addr}, and the rest of
the book just says assertion channel), one of the machine's two certification
readings, holding the checksum
(the sum of the character codes) of the most recent property asserted on an arrow (the name
says address and the contents say fingerprint; it's nonzero after an assertion unless that
property's checksum is zero, and each assertion overwrites it rather than adding to it, so a
later one can put it back to zero); a general status word, which no step writes; an error code, which every
fault in the kernel sets to one (the hardware has a richer set of codes, and the kernel's
comment lists them, but the kernel writes one and lets the hardware tell faults apart); and
a heap base, used by two instructions that address memory relative to it, which no step
writes either.

The \emph{registers}: a list of sixteen natural numbers, read and written through an index taken
modulo sixteen, so an out-of-range register name wraps rather than faults.

The \emph{data memory}: a list of a hundred and twenty-eight natural numbers, addressed modulo a
hundred and twenty-eight, same wrapping rule.

The \emph{program counter}: a natural number.

The \emph{counter} from Section~\ref{sec:counter}, which the source calls mu: a natural number, no upper bound in the
type. It starts at zero, and every step raises it by exactly the instruction's cost (Section~\ref{sec:isa}),
so no step lowers it. This is the field the whole book is about, and it has no ceiling,
which matters for Section~\ref{sec:witness} and I'll flag it there.

A \emph{mu tensor}: sixteen numbers, a flattened four-by-four grid, which one instruction adds
into. I'll tell you what it's for in Section~\ref{sec:landauer}, and I'll tell you now that only one instruction ever
writes it. Don't confuse it with the little tensors the modules carry inside the
graph (below): the one in the record is global and REVEAL (an instruction that discloses a
count of bits and pays for them) adds into it, while each module's own is written by a
different instruction, TENSOR\_\allowbreak{}SET.

The \emph{error flag}: a bit that, once set, stays set; no step ever writes it back to false.
The faults that step on pass through a function that ors the new value with the old, and
the faults that jump to the trap address set it to true outright, so either way there's no
path back. A latch, in Section~\ref{sec:latch}'s sense (Definition~\ref{def:u11-honest}), on the event ``something
went wrong.''

A \emph{logic accumulator} and a \emph{mode word}, which I include because they're in the record and
not because they do anything: no step of the machine changes either. They mirror two
registers in the hardware, which gives them starting values (the mode word boots at one;
the kernel's starts at zero), lets you read them back, and never writes them either. The
mode word's comment says zero is ``Turing mode'' and one is ``Thiele mode,'' and there's a
constant defined that the comment says unlocks operations, and no step rule reads it. Two
fields and a constant that are scaffolding, honestly labelled.

The \emph{witness counts}: eight counters for the two-player game of Section~\ref{sec:chsh}, two for each of the
four ways the referee can ask the question, one for ``the players agreed'' and one for ``they
didn't.'' Exactly one instruction writes them, CHSH\_\allowbreak{}TRIAL, one round of the game (the five
instructions that run the game's check, the CHSH\_\allowbreak{}LASSERT family, read them).

And the \emph{certified flag}: the top-level yes/no reading of Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s certification system
(Definition~\ref{def:certsys}), the other of the two readings,
set by exactly one instruction (CERTIFY) and never cleared by any.

That's the state. Every value written into a register or a memory word is truncated to
sixty-four bits on the way in; the kernel's word is sixty-four bits wide. (The one
exception is XOR\_\allowbreak{}SWAP, which swaps two registers and so only moves values already in the
register file.) The other
numeric fields, the counter, the program counter, the tensor entries, the witness counts and
the assertion channel, are plain natural numbers with no truncation. (The hardware's datapath
word is thirty-two. That's a difference I'll have to account for in Section~\ref{sec:chip}.)

Here is the record written out, with the two sizes and the word.

\begin{definition}[The state record]\label{def:u16-state}
A \emph{state} $s$ is a record with twelve fields, in this order: the partition graph
$\mathrm{graph}(s)$ (Definition~\ref{def:u16-graph}); the control and status words, a record of four
natural numbers $(\mathrm{certaddr}, \mathrm{status}, \mathrm{errcode}, \mathrm{heapbase})$;
the registers $\mathrm{regs}(s)$ and the data memory $\mathrm{mem}(s)$, each a list of
natural numbers; the program counter $\mathrm{pc}(s) \in \mathbb{N}$; the counter
$\mu(s) \in \mathbb{N}$; the global tensor, a list of natural numbers; the error flag
$\mathrm{err}(s)$, a boolean; the logic accumulator and the mode word, both in $\mathbb{N}$;
the witness counts, eight natural numbers $\mathrm{same}_{xy}$ and $\mathrm{diff}_{xy}$ for
$x, y \in \{0, 1\}$; and the certified flag $\mathrm{cert}(s)$, a boolean. No field's type
bounds a number or fixes a list's length.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Registers, memory, and the word]\label{def:u16-access}
The sizes are the literals $R = 16$ and $M = 128$. Write $w(x) = x \bmod 2^{64}$ for the
64-bit truncation. Reading register $r$ returns entry $r \bmod R$ of the register list, or
$0$ when the list is too short. Writing $v$ to register $r$ puts $w(v)$ at position
$r \bmod R$; on a list of length $R$ it changes that entry and no other. Memory reads and
writes are the same with $M$ in place of $R$. Every register and memory write in the step
rules goes through these two writers, with one exception: XOR\_\allowbreak{}SWAP exchanges two register
entries as they are, without truncating.
\end{definition}

Checked as \code{REG\_COUNT}, \code{MEM\_SIZE}, \code{word64}, \code{read\_reg}, \code{write\_reg}, \code{read\_mem},
\code{write\_mem}, and \code{swap\_regs} (VMState.v); \code{word64} is written as a bitwise and with
sixty-four ones, which is the remainder mod $2^{64}$.

Here's the width difference in one sum. Add $2^{32} - 1$ and $1$: the kernel stores
$w(2^{32}) = 2^{32}$, since that's below $2^{64}$, and a thirty-two-bit word wraps the same
sum to $0$. The counter is the sharper case. In the kernel it has no width at all; in the
hardware it's a thirty-two-bit word. So the step-by-step hardware correspondence carries a
premise that the old counter plus the step's cost is below $2^{32}$ (the refinement lemmas
in ChshRetire.v and CouplingFaults.v, for example), and a run whose counter outgrows
that is outside what's proved there (Section~\ref{sec:chip}).

How much can a difference in width matter? There's a famous answer, and it's worth the
detour. On 4 June 1996 the first Ariane 5 rocket lifted off and broke apart about forty
seconds after its engines lit. The inquiry board, chaired by the mathematician Jacques-Louis
Lions, traced it to one conversion in the inertial reference software: a sixty-four-bit
floating-point number, an alignment value called BH that's tied to horizontal speed, squeezed
into a sixteen-bit signed integer. On Ariane 4, where the software came from, that value
could never get big enough to overflow, because of how that rocket flew in its first forty
seconds. Ariane 5 flew differently. The value got too big, the backup unit failed on it, the
main unit failed the same way about seventy milliseconds later, and the function doing the
converting didn't even serve a purpose on Ariane 5; it was kept for commonality with the old
rocket. The board's report says the assumption that made the conversion safe had been agreed
on and never exposed to outside review.

Push on what that changes for a counter that's a natural number in one material and
thirty-two bits in another. A width premise that holds on one machine is a fact about how
that machine gets used, not about the code, and it travels with the code without anybody
noticing. The only defence I know is the dull one: write the premise into every statement that
needs it, where the next person will trip over it. That's what ``below $2^{32}$'' in each
hardware lemma is for, and it's why a run that outgrows it is said, out loud, to be outside
what's proved.

The counter's rule, which Section~\ref{sec:counter} stated for any machine whose counter is kept by a price list
(Theorem~\ref{thm:conservation}), holds on this one exactly.

\begin{theorem}[Conservation on this machine]\label{thm:u16-conservation}
For every state $s$ and every instruction $i$,

\[
\mu(\mathrm{apply}(s, i)) = \mu(s) + \mathrm{cost}(i),
\]

where $\mathrm{apply}$ is the step function and $\mathrm{cost}$ is the schedule of Section~\ref{sec:isa}
(Definition~\ref{def:u17-cost}). No premise is needed: it holds on every state, reachable or not, and on
every branch, the faulting ones included.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Coq's proof is a case split over the fifty-one instructions and, inside each, over the
branches of the step (success, latch, trap). In every branch the new counter is written as
