the old counter plus the instruction's cost, either through one of the shared state
builders or, for PNEW, PSPLIT, PMERGE and CERTIFY (the steps that create a module, split
one, merge two, and raise the certified flag), written out in the rule. Each case closes by
computation. This is the one-step rule of Section~\ref{sec:counter}'s Definition~\ref{def:u06-counter} with the concrete schedule.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{vm\_apply\_mu} (MuLedgerConservation.v).

\begin{remark}[The error flag latches, argued from the rules]\label{rem:u16-err-latch}
If $\mathrm{err}(s)$ is true then $\mathrm{err}(\mathrm{apply}(s, i))$ is true for every $i$.
The argument is a reading of the rules, not a named theorem: every rule either copies the
flag, sets it to $\mathrm{err}(s) \lor \mathrm{true}$ through \code{latch\_err} (VMStep.v), or, on
a trap, sets it to true. No rule writes false.
\end{remark}

\subsection{What isn't in it}

Three things people assume are in a machine state and aren't in this one, each on purpose.

There's no \emph{program} in the state. The step relation takes the instruction as an argument;
the program lives outside, and a runner fetches from it by program counter. So ``the state''
never knows what it's about to do, which is the right design for a thing whose theorems
quantify over all instruction sequences.

There's no \emph{output} in the state. The one instruction that emits a payload to the outside
world, EMIT, leaves the payload outside the Coq state entirely; what the state keeps is the
charge, at eight marks per character plus one more (the floor, which Section~\ref{sec:isa} explains), added
into the counter with every
other charge, and only as part of that total. It can't tell you that anything was sent,
let alone what it said, because the same total can come from other instructions.

And there's no \emph{heap} as a separate thing. Heap access is the base word plus an offset into
the same hundred and twenty-eight words of data memory. One memory.

Also absent, and this one is subtle: the record doesn't fix the \emph{lengths} of the register
and memory lists. They're plain lists in the type. That the register list has sixteen entries
and the memory a hundred and twenty-eight is proved as a separate invariant, not enforced
by the record. I mention it because ``sixteen registers'' is a theorem about reachable states,
and the type would let you write a state with three. (The invariant is \code{eg\_size\_permanent}:
every step keeps both lengths, from a state that has them.)

\begin{lemma}[The two lengths are kept]\label{thm:u16-sizes-kept}
Let $s$ be a state with $|\mathrm{regs}(s)| = 16$ and $|\mathrm{mem}(s)| = 128$. Then for
every instruction $i$, $|\mathrm{regs}(\mathrm{apply}(s, i))| = 16$ and
$|\mathrm{mem}(\mathrm{apply}(s, i))| = 128$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Case split over the instructions and their branches. A step either keeps the two lists as
they are or writes them through the register writer, the memory writer, or the swap. Each
of those rebuilds the list as the part before position $k$, one new entry, and the part
after it, with $k = r \bmod 16$ or $a \bmod 128$; since $k$ is below the length, the result
has the same length.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{eg\_size\_permanent} (EventGeneralization.v), stated there as ``the size reading is
permanent'': if the reading holds before a step, it holds after.

One scope note on all of this. Everything the book proves about the kernel machine is a
statement about this record and the step rules, nothing more. What a real run has beyond
them, the program text, the stream an EMIT sends, the files a runner writes, lives in the
runner, the trace and the hardware's test harness, not in the state.

\subsection{The partition graph}

This is the field that carries Section~\ref{sec:structure}'s buckets.

The graph has four parts: a next-module counter, the list of modules, a next-arrow counter,
and the list of arrows. The two counters only go up (where they start is a few paragraphs
down); an identifier is never reused, so a deleted module's number is dead forever. A
\emph{module} has three parts. A region, the list of addresses it owns. A list of strings the
source calls axioms, which are labels no step reads (Section~\ref{sec:claims} shows what the steps do with them); no step writes a
nonempty list into one either, so every module on a reachable state carries the empty list.
And its own four-by-four tensor, sixteen numbers, zero by default (the comment says ``flat
space''; Section~\ref{sec:landauer}). An \emph{arrow} is a source module, a target module, a coupling (a list of pairs of
cells, one from each side, plus a label), a bit that marks it as an identity arrow, and a
cost field the comment says records what was paid to certify it, which under the step rules
is always zero because the asserting step never writes it. That last one is a field with a promise in its comment that the rules don't keep.
The module layer and the arrow layer are separate things: two states can agree on every
module and differ in their arrows, which is exactly what Section~\ref{sec:separation} builds.

\begin{definition}[Partition graph, module, arrow]\label{def:u16-graph}
A \emph{partition graph} $G$ is a record $(n_G, \mathrm{mods}_G, a_G, \mathrm{arrows}_G)$: a
next-module number $n_G \in \mathbb{N}$, a list $\mathrm{mods}_G$ of pairs (identifier,
module), a next-arrow number $a_G \in \mathbb{N}$, and a list $\mathrm{arrows}_G$ of pairs
(identifier, arrow). A \emph{module} is a triple (region, axioms, tensor): a list of natural
numbers, a list of strings, and a list of natural numbers, sixteen zeros by default. An
\emph{arrow} is a record (source, target, coupling, identity, certcost): two module identifiers,
a coupling made of a list of pairs of natural numbers and a label string, a boolean, and a
natural number. Adding a module to $G$ gives it identifier $n_G$, puts it at the front of
the list, and raises the counter to $n_G + 1$; the arrow list is copied unchanged.
\end{definition}

Checked as \code{PartitionGraph}, \code{ModuleState}, \code{MorphismState}, \code{CouplingData}, and
\code{graph\_add\_module} (VMState.v).

Now the regions, and here's the design decision, because there's a cheaper one. The cheap
way to give modules regions is to let every module own the prefix of memory from zero up to
its size, so two modules of size four own the \emph{same} four cells; that's enough for every
theorem about the counter and useless for anything about locality, and it isn't what Section~\ref{sec:structure}'s
buckets said. The kernel says what the buckets said: \emph{nothing in two buckets}. A region is a
run of consecutive addresses, a base and a length, and it lies inside the hundred and
twenty-eight words that exist; the regions of distinct modules are pairwise disjoint; and the
step that creates a module, PNEW, \emph{traps} (jumps to a fixed error address and raises the
error flag; Section~\ref{sec:isa} has the details) if the range it asks for overlaps a range some other module
owns (unless it's exactly a range a module already owns, in which case nothing changes and
nothing's charged beyond the declared cost), or runs past the end of memory. Splitting a
module, PSPLIT, gives its first half to one child and the rest to the other, in place.
Merging two modules, PMERGE, requires their ranges to touch end to end, and traps otherwise.
And all three trap when the machine is out of module numbers, which is a story of its own
below.
Every step preserves the properties, so from a state with no modules, every reachable
state has disjoint, contiguous regions (\code{vm\_reachable\_regions\_disjoint}, with the
preservation theorems under it), each inside memory (\code{vm\_reachable\_partition\_in\_bounds}).
Those are invariants proved about reachable states; they aren't part of the record type, the
same way the list lengths aren't.

Two properties and a theorem, then, with nothing left to the imagination. Write $[b, b + n)$ for the list
$b, b+1, \ldots, b+n-1$, and $\mathrm{reg}(m)$ for a module's region.

\begin{definition}[Disjoint and contiguous regions]\label{def:u16-regions}
A graph $G$ has \emph{disjoint regions} when, for any two entries of $\mathrm{mods}_G$ at
different positions in the list, no address lies in both regions. A list $r$ is
\emph{contiguous} when $r = [\mathrm{hd}(r), \mathrm{hd}(r) + |r|)$, where $\mathrm{hd}(r)$ is
its first element ($0$ for the empty list); the empty list is contiguous. $G$ has
\emph{contiguous regions} when every module's region is contiguous. A state $s'$ is \emph{reachable
from} $s$ when it arises from $s$ by zero or more steps of the step relation.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The regions stay a partition of addresses]\label{thm:u16-regions}
(1) If $\mathrm{graph}(s)$ has disjoint regions and $s$ steps to $s'$ on any instruction,
then $\mathrm{graph}(s')$ has disjoint regions. (2) The same holds for contiguous regions.
(3) If $\mathrm{graph}(s)$ has no modules and $s'$ is reachable from $s$, then
$\mathrm{graph}(s')$ has disjoint and contiguous regions.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) and (2) are a case split over the step relation. Steps that leave the module list alone
(every instruction other than PNEW, PSPLIT and PMERGE; TENSOR\_\allowbreak{}SET does change a module, but
only its tensor) keep both properties trivially; so does every trap, since a trap keeps the
old graph. A successful PNEW has passed the conflict test, so the new range meets no
existing region except one it equals, and in that case the graph is unchanged; the new
range is $[b, b + n)$ by construction. PSPLIT removes one module and adds its first half
and its rest, two disjoint subsets of the removed region, and on a range $[b, b+n)$ they are
$[b, b + \lfloor n/2 \rfloor)$ and $[b + \lfloor n/2 \rfloor, b + n)$. PMERGE removes two
modules and adds one region inside their union, so disjointness survives without any test;
contiguity of the joined region is exactly what the adjacency test checks, and without it
the step traps. (3) is induction on the number of steps, starting from the fact that a graph
with no modules has both properties.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{vm\_step\_preserves\_regions\_disjoint}, \code{vm\_step\_preserves\_regions\_contiguous}, and
\code{vm\_reachable\_regions\_disjoint} (VMStep.v), with the per-operation lemmas
\code{graph\_pnew\_preserves\_regions\_disjoint}, \code{graph\_hw\_psplit\_preserves\_regions\_disjoint},
\code{graph\_hw\_pmerge\_preserves\_regions\_disjoint}, \code{graph\_hw\_pmerge\_preserves\_regions\_contiguous}
and \code{psplit\_halves\_of\_range} under them. Nothing in these statements mentions the hundred
and twenty-eight words of memory; staying inside them is a separate theorem, which needs the
well-formedness condition below and comes right after it.

Now an honest limit on the word ``owns.'' Nothing in the kernel enforces ownership. LOAD,
STORE, HEAP\_\allowbreak{}LOAD and HEAP\_\allowbreak{}STORE take an address and read or write that cell without looking
at any module's region. The regions are read by the instructions that make and reshape
modules (PNEW, PSPLIT, PMERGE) and by the two that build arrows from regions (MORPH keeps
only the coupling pairs whose ends lie inside the two ranges; MORPH\_\allowbreak{}TENSOR compares ranges),
and no other step rule reads one. Locality, a program touching only its own module's cells,
is a check the hardware's partition table makes, and the kernel doesn't (Section~\ref{sec:chip}).

A few edge cases the definitions settle that no theorem names, since you'll find them if
you play: splitting a module that doesn't exist (after its number is taken modulo sixty-four)
adds two \emph{empty} modules, using up two module numbers; merging two that don't exist passes
the adjacency check (the empty list is a run) and adds one empty module, using up one;
and the creating step reads its region as ``first listed address, then the count of distinct
addresses,'' so asking for cells 5 and 3 gets you 5 and 6, not 3 and 5. The hardware's
encoding carries base and length, and the kernel reads lists that way to match.

The well-formedness condition is three clauses: every module identifier is below the next
counter, every arrow identifier is below its counter, and every arrow's two ends name
modules that exist. Every step preserves it, and so does a whole run
(\code{vm\_step\_preserves\_well\_formed\_graph}, \code{run\_vm\_preserves\_well\_formed\_graph}). That's the
reason PSPLIT and PMERGE delete every arrow that touches a module they remove: an arrow
left behind would name a module that's gone, and the third clause would fail.

\begin{definition}[Well-formed graph]\label{def:u16-wf}
A graph $G$ is \emph{well formed} when three things hold: every identifier in $\mathrm{mods}_G$
is less than $n_G$; every identifier in $\mathrm{arrows}_G$ is less than $a_G$; and for every
arrow in $\mathrm{arrows}_G$, its source and its target each appear as an identifier in
$\mathrm{mods}_G$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Well-formedness is kept]\label{thm:u16-wf}
(1) If $\mathrm{graph}(s)$ is well formed and $s$ steps to $s'$ on any instruction, then
$\mathrm{graph}(s')$ is well formed. (2) If $\mathrm{graph}(s)$ is well formed, then for any
fuel $k$ and any program $P$, the graph of the state reached by running $P$ from $s$ for at
most $k$ steps, fetching each instruction by program counter and stopping when the counter
leaves the program, is well formed.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) is a case split over the step relation. Adding a module uses the counter as the new
identifier and then raises it, so every identifier stays below the counter; the same holds
for arrows. The steps that add an arrow (MORPH, COMPOSE, MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ID, MORPH\_\allowbreak{}TENSOR) take its
ends either from modules they have just looked up or from arrows already in the graph, whose
ends exist by the third clause; when a lookup fails they latch an error and keep the graph. MORPH\_\allowbreak{}DELETE only removes. PSPLIT and PMERGE first delete every arrow
whose source or target is a module about to be removed, then remove it, so the third clause
cannot break; a PMERGE that traps keeps the old graph. (2) is induction on the fuel, using
the function form of (1) at each step.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{vm\_step\_preserves\_well\_formed\_graph} (VMStep.v) for (1), and
\code{vm\_apply\_preserves\_well\_formed\_graph} with \code{run\_vm\_preserves\_well\_formed\_graph}
(SimulationProof.v) for (2). Both are proved for the partition rules of this chapter:
ranges, the overlap trap, the adjacency trap, and the two traps of the next part.

\subsection{Inside memory, and sixty-four numbers}

Two more promises about the buckets, and both are about running out.

The first is memory. There are a hundred and twenty-eight words, numbered 0 to 127, and a
module that owns cell 200 owns a cell the machine doesn't have. So PNEW looks at every
address in the range it's about to claim and traps if any of them is 128 or more. Ask for
cells 120 to 127 from the initial state and you get a module of eight cells, the last eight
words of memory. Ask for cells 126, 127 and 128 and the step traps: the error flag goes up,
the program counter jumps to the trap address, the counter is charged the declared cost
anyway, and the graph is exactly what it was. Ask for the empty range and there's nothing to
check, so the empty range is never past memory.

The second is module numbers, and it's the one I find a little funny, because sixty-four
turns out to be a lifetime allowance and not a parking lot. Every module number comes from
the graph's counter $n_G$, which only goes up, and no number is ever handed out twice: PSPLIT
gives its two halves two fresh numbers and retires the old one, and PMERGE gives the joined
module a fresh number and retires both. So $n_G$ counts every module number the run has ever
issued, and a split followed by a merge that puts the cells back exactly where they started
has still spent three. The hardware's partition table has sixty-four slots, so the kernel's
rule is: a step that needs $k$ fresh numbers runs only when $n_G + k \le 64$, and traps
otherwise. PNEW needs one (and asks for it even when the range is one a module already owns,
so on a spent budget every PNEW traps), PSPLIT needs two, PMERGE needs one. A run from the
initial state can make sixty-four module numbers in its whole life. The extracted runner
starts its counter at one (next part), so it gets sixty-three.

That has a nice side effect. PSPLIT and PMERGE read their module operands modulo sixty-four,
which is how the hardware's six-bit slot field reads them. If a module numbered sixty-four
could exist, the operand 64 would land on module 0 and module 64 couldn't be named at all.
No such module exists: every number issued is below sixty-four, so reading a live module's
number modulo sixty-four gives the number back, and every module can be named by its own
number. An operand of 64 or more still names the module whose number is the remainder, so
PSPLIT of 64 splits module 0. That's arithmetic on the operand, not a module hiding behind
another one.

Try the budget with a pencil, because the arithmetic is the point. Start from the initial
state, module counter at zero. PNEW on cells 0 and 1: one module, counter at one. Then split it
and merge the two halves straight back, again and again, so the same two cells end up exactly
where they started every time. Each round trip spends three numbers, two for the split and one
for the merge. Write the counter down after each trip: 4, 7, 10, and on. How many trips before
something traps? The split needs the counter plus two to be at most sixty-four, and the merge
needs the counter plus one. After twenty trips the counter reads sixty-one. The twenty-first
split asks for sixty-three and gets it; the twenty-first merge asks for sixty-four and gets
it; the counter sits at exactly sixty-four. The twenty-second split would need sixty-six, and
traps. Twenty-one round trips, the same two cells the whole time, and that run can never make
another module. Not even with PNEW, which needs one more number too.

\begin{definition}[A partition in bounds]\label{def:u16-bounds}
A graph $G$ is \emph{in bounds} when it is well formed (Definition~\ref{def:u16-wf}), every address
in every module's region is less than $128$, $n_G \le 64$, and no identifier appears twice in
$\mathrm{mods}_G$.
\end{definition}

Checked as the definitions \code{partition\_in\_bounds}, \code{regions\_in\_memory} and
\code{module\_ids\_distinct} (VMStep.v).

\begin{theorem}[The partition stays in bounds]\label{thm:u16-bounds}
(1) If $\mathrm{graph}(s)$ is in bounds and $s$ steps to $s'$ on any instruction, then
$\mathrm{graph}(s')$ is in bounds. (2) If $\mathrm{graph}(s)$ is well formed, has no
modules and has $n \le 64$, and $s'$ is reachable from $s$, then $\mathrm{graph}(s')$ has
disjoint, contiguous regions, every address in every region is less than $128$, its next
module number is at most $64$, it has at most $64$ modules, and every module identifier $m$
in it satisfies $m \bmod 64 = m$. (3) The same holds for the step function, and for a bounded
run of a program from such a state.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) A case split over the step relation, one part at a time; a trap keeps the old graph, so
only successful steps need an argument. \emph{Memory:} a successful PNEW passed the memory test;
PSPLIT's two halves are pieces of a region already inside memory; PMERGE's joined region is
the two old regions laid end to end. \emph{The counter:} each step that takes fresh numbers checked
that it had room for them, and no other step touches the counter. \emph{Distinct numbers:} a new
module gets the counter as its number, and well-formedness says every existing number is
below the counter, so the new one is different from all of them; removing modules can't
create a repeat. Well-formedness itself is Theorem~\ref{thm:u16-wf}. (2) $\mathrm{graph}(s)$ is in
bounds (no modules, so nothing to check but the counter), and induction on the steps with (1)
carries it to $s'$. Then $s'$ has distinct module numbers, all below $n \le 64$, so there are at
most sixty-four of them, and each one is below sixty-four, so taking it modulo sixty-four
changes nothing. The disjoint, contiguous regions are part (3) of Theorem~\ref{thm:u16-regions}.
(3) The same case split, on the function.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{vm\_step\_preserves\_partition\_in\_bounds} for (1), with its parts
\code{vm\_step\_preserves\_regions\_in\_memory}, \code{vm\_step\_preserves\_modules\_bounded} and
\code{vm\_step\_preserves\_module\_ids\_distinct}, and \code{vm\_reachable\_partition\_in\_bounds} for (2), using
\code{modules\_count\_bounded} and \code{module\_id\_mod\_64}, with the two tests \code{module\_room} and
\code{region\_in\_memory} (all VMStep.v).
For (3), \code{vm\_apply\_preserves\_partition\_in\_bounds} and \code{run\_vm\_partition\_in\_bounds}
(SimulationProof.v). The chip makes the same two tests and traps the same way (Section~\ref{sec:chip}).

\subsection{Where a run starts}

I've been saying ``reachable,'' so here's the starting state, the kernel's \code{init\_state}:
every register and memory word zero, program counter zero, counter zero, the tensor
zeros, the error flag down, the certified flag down, the assertion channel zero, the witness
counts zero, and a graph with no modules and no arrows. The module counter starts at zero
and the arrow counter at one. These are conventions of this initialization. The theorems
about reachable states start from this state, or from any state with no modules. Three other
initialization conventions used by the implementations differ from this one: the library's
\code{empty\_graph} starts both counters at one; the extracted runner starts both at one (Coq can
turn its definitions into an ordinary program, here in the language OCaml, a step called
\emph{extraction}, and the runner is that program, the one the demonstration in Section~\ref{sec:receipt} drives); and
the standalone copy of the kernel starts both at zero. That copy is one long file,
ThieleMachineComplete.v, that carries its own copy of the machine so the whole build can be
read top to bottom; a test checks that its definitions match the kernel's text, which is a
test and not a proof. When I say ``initial'' below I mean the kernel's.

Four starting conventions that disagree about counting from zero or from one sounds like
carelessness, and maybe some of it is. It's also one of the oldest arguments in programming,
and it has a famous referee. In 1982 Edsger Dijkstra wrote one of the numbered notes he
circulated to colleagues, EWD 831, titled ``Why numbering should start at zero.'' His case goes
through ranges first. Of the four ways to write ``2 up to 12'' with less-than signs, he picks
the one that takes the bottom in and leaves the top out, $2 \le i < 13$: two ranges that meet
end to end then share one number written once, and the length is just the top minus the
bottom. Start a sequence of $N$ things at zero and it's $0 \le i < N$, and each thing's number
is how many things came before it. He reports that programmers on the language Mesa, which
allowed all four conventions, found the other three a steady source of clumsiness and
mistakes, and he points out that FORTRAN starts at one.

Does that settle it? It settles which convention is tidier, by an argument you can check. It
doesn't settle which convention somebody else's code used, and that's the trap: Minsky numbers
lines from 1 and the small machine follows him, the big machine's program counter starts at 0,
and the four initializations above split between 0 and 1. And look where the book already took
his side without saying so. The regions are written $[b, b + n)$, bottom in, top out, and
that's why PSPLIT's two halves, $[b, b + \lfloor n/2 \rfloor)$ and
$[b + \lfloor n/2 \rfloor, b + n)$, meet at a number written once, with no plus one or minus
one anywhere. Is zero the right place to start counting? I can't tell you. Dijkstra's note
doesn't claim to either; it shows which way makes fewer mistakes, which is a different and
more useful thing.

\begin{definition}[The initial state]\label{def:u16-init}
The initial state $s_0$ has graph $(n, \mathrm{mods}, a, \mathrm{arrows}) = (0, [\,], 1, [\,])$;
all four control and status words $0$; registers sixteen zeros and memory a hundred and
twenty-eight zeros; $\mathrm{pc} = 0$; $\mu = 0$; the global tensor sixteen zeros; the error
flag false; the logic accumulator and the mode word $0$; all eight witness counts $0$; and
the certified flag false.
\end{definition}

\begin{corollary}[What every run from the start keeps]\label{cor:u16-from-init}
For every state $s'$ reachable from $s_0$: the graph of $s'$ has disjoint, contiguous
regions, each inside memory; it is well formed; it has at most sixty-four modules, each
numbered below sixty-four; and $|\mathrm{regs}(s')| = 16$ and $|\mathrm{mem}(s')| = 128$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
$s_0$ has no modules, so part (3) of Theorem~\ref{thm:u16-regions} gives the regions. The graph of
$s_0$ is well formed because all three clauses are about empty lists, and
Theorem~\ref{thm:u16-wf} carries it along every step. Its module counter is $0 \le 64$, so part
(2) of Theorem~\ref{thm:u16-bounds} gives memory, the count and the numbers. The lengths hold at
$s_0$; each step of the relation lands on the value of the step function (the bridge between
the two, which Section~\ref{sec:isa} states as Lemma~\ref{thm:u17-bridge}), so
Lemma~\ref{thm:u16-sizes-kept} carries them.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{init\_state} (MuInitiality.v) for the values. The corollary is the four
theorems instantiated at $s_0$; no single Coq name packages it, and the step ``the empty
graph is well formed'' is checked for the library's \code{empty\_graph} (\code{empty\_graph\_well\_formed},
VMState.v) rather than for this graph, whose counter starts at zero instead of one.

\subsection{The size constants}

Sixteen registers, a hundred and twenty-eight words, sixty-four module slots, a region
size of sixteen. All four are definitions with literal values, and it's easy to read the first two as
parameters. They aren't: the proofs unfold the literal and compute with it
(\textnormal{\texttt{unfold REG\_COUNT; lia}} and its cousins appear throughout), no file binds either as a
variable or hypothesis, and no theorem is stated for other values. The proofs are about
sixteen and a hundred and twenty-eight. Retargeting means editing one definition \emph{and}
every tactic that computes on the literal, which the hardware side's own comment admits for
its table sizes. The sixty-four is the module-number budget of the last part, the one the
partition rules check, and the same number the hardware's table has slots for; the split and
merge rules still write their operand reduction as ``mod 64'' with the literal. The region-size
constant is used nowhere at all.

\begin{remark}[The four constants]\label{rem:u16-constants}
The kernel defines $R = 16$ (\code{REG\_COUNT}), $M = 128$ (\code{MEM\_SIZE}), $64$ (\code{NUM\_MODULES}) and
$16$ (\code{REGION\_SIZE}), each as a literal in VMState.v. $R$ and $M$ enter the semantics
through $r \bmod R$ and $a \bmod M$ (Definition~\ref{def:u16-access}), the initial lists
(Definition~\ref{def:u16-init}), and one cap: MORPH reads at most $M/2 = 64$ coupling pairs from
memory. $M$ also enters through PNEW's memory test, and \code{NUM\_MODULES} through the
module-number test of PNEW, PSPLIT and PMERGE (Definition~\ref{def:u16-bounds} and Section~\ref{sec:isa}). The
operand reduction of PSPLIT and PMERGE writes $m \bmod 64$ with the literal, not the
constant, and \code{REGION\_SIZE} appears nowhere else. Every theorem in this chapter that mentions
a size is about these values and no others.
\end{remark}

\subsection{What the record promises, and what it doesn't}

It promises: a counter that's a natural number, a flag that's a bit, an error that latches, a
graph whose regions don't overlap and stay inside memory on any reachable state, at most
sixty-four module numbers per run, and sixty-four-bit truncation on
every register and memory write. It doesn't promise: what the program is, what was emitted, that the lists have
their intended lengths (that's a separate invariant), that the axiom strings mean anything,
or that the per-arrow cost field records anything. And it's one choice of record. The
abstract theorems needed only ``a state, a step, a reading, a cost,'' and this is one way to
fill those in, with twelve fields, two of which are scaffolding.

Next: what you can \emph{do} to one of these. Fifty-one things.

%===========================================================================
\section{The instruction set and the cost schedule}
\label{sec:isa}
%===========================================================================

Fifty-one instructions. I'm going to give you all of them, because a reader who's been told
``the machine charges for certification'' deserves to see the whole price list and check that
nothing else is charged for in secret, and because the table is the thing that makes Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}'s
argument (Theorem~\ref{thm:toll-derived}: finiteness, permanence and merge pricing force the
toll) checkable on \emph{this} machine: here are the steps, here are the prices, go and see which
ones merge. Three things to know before the tables.

Every instruction carries a declared cost, which I'll write d, chosen by whoever writes the
program; it can be zero. The counter rises by exactly the instruction's cost on every path,
success or failure, because the cost is on the attempt (Section~\ref{sec:counter}'s conservation,
Theorem~\ref{thm:conservation}, checked on this machine as Section~\ref{sec:state}'s
Theorem~\ref{thm:u16-conservation}, \code{vm\_apply\_mu}).
(A housekeeping fact about every theorem name below: the rows are step \emph{relations}, but the
theorems are stated on \code{vm\_apply}, the function that computes a step, and \code{vm\_step\_vm\_apply}
is the bridge. If the relation says one state steps to another on an instruction, the
function returns exactly that state.) Thirty-nine instructions cost exactly d. Twelve cost at least one more than d, and those
twelve are the cost-positive class; the predicate that picks them out is called
\code{is\_cert\_setterb}, and its own comment says it is not the literal ``sets csr\_\allowbreak{}cert\_\allowbreak{}addr''
predicate (csr\_\allowbreak{}cert\_\allowbreak{}addr is the source's name for the assertion channel): it marks the positive-cost policy. In the step rules only \emph{two}
instructions actually flip a certification reading (one sets the assertion channel, one sets
the flag), and I'll point at them. For the channel, the fact is \code{morph\_assert\_step\_sets\_supra\_cert\_iff}:
from a clear channel, one step leaves it nonzero exactly when that step is a MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT on
an arrow that exists, with a property whose checksum isn't zero. For the flag it's the one
line in CERTIFY's rule. The class is wider than the flippers, which is a design
choice I'll defend after the tables.

Register names wrap modulo sixteen and memory addresses modulo one hundred and twenty-eight,
and every value written to a register or a memory word is truncated to sixty-four bits
(Section~\ref{sec:state}).

And how to read the tables. In the cost column, \emph{S d} means d plus one: S is Coq's name for
``the next number,'' which is the most Coq way possible of saying plus one, and that plus one
is the floor. The fault column says what a failure
does. TRAP jumps to a fixed trap address, 3840 (0xF00 in hexadecimal; it's the chosen trap
vector, a design pick that nothing derives), and sets the error code and the error flag.
LATCH steps on to the next instruction, sets the error code and the flag, and changes
nothing else. The last column says whether the instruction is in the cost-positive class.

Where does that S come from? It's older than Coq by about a century. In 1888 Richard Dedekind
published a little book whose title asks what numbers are and what they're for, and in 1889
Giuseppe Peano published a booklet, written in Latin, which is usually counted as the first
statement of the axioms for the whole numbers that people still teach: there's a first number,
and every number has a next one, and a few rules about how ``next'' behaves. The two were
worked out independently, and the axioms often go by both names. (Peano's booklet is also
where the sign $\in$ that you met in Section~\ref{sec:structure} is usually said to come from.)
Coq builds its whole numbers exactly that way, out of zero and ``the next one'' and nothing
else, so inside Coq the number three really is S (S (S O)), the next of the next of the next
of zero. What that changes here is small and I like it: the floor on the twelve positive
instructions isn't a ``plus one'' slapped on a price list. It's one application of the
smallest step the number system has. You can't charge less than one S and still charge
something.

Here is the shape of a step, exactly, before the tables fill it in.

\begin{definition}[Instructions, step relation, step function]\label{def:u17-step}
An \emph{instruction} is one of fifty-one constructors, each with its operands and a declared
cost $d \in \mathbb{N}$. The \emph{step relation} $s \xrightarrow{i} s'$ is an inductive
relation on states with one rule per outcome of each instruction: one rule for an
instruction that cannot fail, and a success rule and a failure rule for one that can. The
\emph{step function} $\mathrm{apply}(s, i)$ is a total function from a state and an instruction
to a state. A \emph{run} from $s$ on a program $P$ (a list of instructions) with fuel $k$ fetches
the instruction at position $\mathrm{pc}$ of $P$, applies it, and repeats, stopping after
$k$ steps or when $\mathrm{pc}$ falls outside $P$. The program is never part of the state.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[The relation computes the function]\label{thm:u17-bridge}
For all states $s$, $s'$ and every instruction $i$: if $s \xrightarrow{i} s'$ then
$\mathrm{apply}(s, i) = s'$. In particular the relation is deterministic: if
$s \xrightarrow{i} s_1$ and $s \xrightarrow{i} s_2$ then $s_1 = s_2$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Invert the step: each rule of the relation names a right-hand state, and the matching branch
of the function computes to the same record once the rule's side conditions are
substituted. Determinism follows because both results equal $\mathrm{apply}(s, i)$.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{vm\_step} (VMStep.v), \code{vm\_apply}, \code{run\_vm}, \code{vm\_step\_vm\_apply} and
\code{vm\_step\_deterministic} (SimulationProof.v). Coq states this direction only; that every
value of the function is also a step of the relation is not a named lemma. Theorems stated
on the function therefore cover every state the relation reaches.

\subsection{Group 1: partition (4)}

\begingroup\small
\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.224\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.159\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.159\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.159\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.159\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Instruction} & \textbf{Effect} & \textbf{Cost} & \textbf{Fault} & \textbf{Positive} \\
\midrule
\endhead
\bottomrule
\endlastfoot
PNEW region, d & Claims a range of cells as a fresh module. & d & TRAP on overlap with another module's range, on a cell past memory, or with no module number left & no \\
PSPLIT module, left, right, d & Replaces the module with two holding the first half and the rest of its range. & d & TRAP with fewer than two module numbers left & no \\
PMERGE m1, m2, d & Replaces two modules with one holding the joined range. & d & TRAP unless the ranges touch end to end and a module number is left & no \\
PDISCOVER module, evidence, d & Steps on. The evidence is not attached to anything. & d & none & no \\
\end{longtable}
\endgroup

The table is a diet version, so here's what it left on the plate. PNEW claims the range from the first listed address for as many
cells as there are distinct addresses, and traps if any cell of that range is past the
hundred and twenty-eight words of memory. If some module owns exactly that range, nothing
changes; otherwise a fresh module with no axioms is added; and a PNEW that traps leaves the
graph unchanged. All three take fresh module numbers from a budget of sixty-four per run
that is never refunded (Section~\ref{sec:state} tells that story): PNEW asks for one, PSPLIT for two, PMERGE for
one, and each traps when the budget can't cover it. PSPLIT and PMERGE remove every arrow
touching a module they remove. Both take their module operands modulo 64 first, which always
names the module itself (Theorem~\ref{thm:u16-bounds}); the odd corner, an operand of 64 or
more, is in Section~\ref{sec:state}.
PSPLIT accepts its left and right operands and ignores them, and a missing module splits into
two empty ones. PMERGE's joined range starts from the lower base.

The three rules that reshape modules, exactly. They use the region notions of Section~\ref{sec:state}
(Definition~\ref{def:u16-regions}).

\begin{definition}[PNEW, PSPLIT, PMERGE]\label{def:u17-partition}
For a list $r$, let $\bar r$ be $r$ with repeats removed (first occurrences kept) and
$q(r) = [\mathrm{hd}(\bar r), \mathrm{hd}(\bar r) + |\bar r|)$. A range $q$ \emph{conflicts} with
$G$ when some module's region shares an address with $q$ without having the same set of
addresses. Write $n_G$ for the graph's next module number; $G$ \emph{has room for} $k$ when
$n_G + k \le 64$. A \emph{trap} keeps the graph, sets the error code to $1$, sets the error flag,
and sets $\mathrm{pc}$ to $3840$. Every branch below adds the instruction's cost to $\mu$,
and every branch that does not trap sets $\mathrm{pc}$ to $\mathrm{pc} + 1$.

PNEW $r$: if $G$ has no room for $1$, or some address of $q(r)$ is $128$ or more, or $q(r)$
conflicts with the graph, trap. Otherwise, if some module's region has the same addresses as
$q(r)$, keep the graph; if not, add a module with region $q(r)$, no axioms, and a zero tensor.

PSPLIT $m$: if $G$ has no room for $2$, trap. Otherwise let $m' = m \bmod 64$ and $\rho$ the
region of $m'$ (empty if $m'$ is absent). Delete every arrow whose source or target is $m'$,
remove $m'$ if present, then add a module with the first $\lfloor |\rho|/2 \rfloor$
addresses of $\rho$ and another with the rest. Its two region operands are not read.

PMERGE $m_1, m_2$: let $m_j' = m_j \bmod 64$ and $\rho_j$ their regions (empty if absent).
If $G$ has no room for $1$, or neither $\rho_1 \rho_2$ nor $\rho_2 \rho_1$ (concatenation) is
contiguous, trap. Otherwise delete every arrow touching $m_1'$ or $m_2'$, remove both, and
add one module whose region is $\rho_1 \rho_2$ if that is contiguous and $\rho_2 \rho_1$ if
not.
\end{definition}

Checked as \code{step\_pnew}, \code{step\_psplit}, \code{step\_pmerge}, \code{pnew\_region}, \code{region\_conflict},
\code{module\_room}, \code{region\_in\_memory}, \code{pnew\_ok}, \code{pmerge\_ok},
\code{partition\_step\_state}, \code{graph\_hw\_psplit}, \code{graph\_hw\_pmerge}, \code{pmerge\_adjacent},
\code{pmerge\_region}, \code{psplit\_left} and \code{psplit\_right} (VMStep.v), with \code{graph\_pnew} and
\code{graph\_add\_module} (VMState.v).

\subsection{Group 2: logic and certification (3)}

\begingroup\small
\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.224\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.159\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.159\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.159\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.159\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Instruction} & \textbf{Effect} & \textbf{Cost} & \textbf{Fault} & \textbf{Positive} \\
\midrule
\endhead
\bottomrule
\endlastfoot
LASSERT freg, creg, kind, flen, d & The checking step (Section~\ref{sec:claims} takes it apart): reads a formula at the address in register freg and two witness rows at the address in register creg, checks the first satisfies and the second falsifies (a tautology has no falsifying row, so it can't pass), and that the length operand matches the length word in memory. On success, steps on; nothing else changes. & flen times 8, plus S d & TRAP on a failed check, a header mismatch, and always when kind is false (the unsatisfiability path is not implemented). & yes \\
LJOIN c1reg, c2reg, d & Steps on. Does not compare the certificates or touch any status word. & S d & none & yes \\
MDLACC module, d & Steps on. The comment says it charges for looking up a module. & d & none & no \\
\end{longtable}
\endgroup

About LASSERT's price: the declared length has to equal the length word in memory, so
declaring a smaller formula only gets you trapped (\code{lassert\_honest\_cost}; its corollary
\code{lassert\_honest\_mu\_cost} says a successful LASSERT is charged the length actually read,
times eight, plus the floor). The eight is a pricing convention. Nothing says each unit
is a byte or that the charge counts physical information. So a formula whose header says two
units, checked with declared cost zero, costs $2 \times 8 + 1 = 17$, and a declaration of
zero units for the same formula costs $1$ and traps.

\begin{theorem}[A successful LASSERT pays for what it read]\label{thm:u17-lassert-honest}
Let $s \xrightarrow{i} s'$ with $i$ = LASSERT with operands $f, c$, kind $k$, declared
length $\ell$ and declared cost $d$. Let $h(s, f)$ be the length word the checker reads from
the formula header at the address held in register $f$. If $\mathrm{pc}(s') \ne 3840$, then
$\ell = h(s, f)$ and

\[
\mu(s') = \mu(s) + 8\,h(s, f) + d + 1.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The rule's success test is the conjunction of ``$h(s, f) = \ell$'' and the satisfying and
falsifying checks; when the test fails the rule sets $\mathrm{pc}$ to $3840$. So a step that
lands elsewhere passed the test, which gives $\ell = h(s, f)$. The counter equation is then
conservation (Theorem~\ref{thm:u16-conservation}) with $\mathrm{cost}(i) = 8\ell + d + 1$.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{lassert\_honest\_cost} and \code{lassert\_honest\_mu\_cost} (StateSpaceCounting.v). The
premise is about the landing address: a success whose next address happens to be 3840 is
outside the statement. Two more names sit nearby and are about a different object.
\code{lassert\_cost\_from\_component\_floors} and \code{lassert\_cost\_is\_its\_formula} (MuCostDerivation.v)
concern a separate model of a constraint, with a state count before and after and a
description length: its total is defined as
$\log_2 \Omega - \log_2 \Omega' + \mathrm{bits}$, and the two theorems say that this total
is that sum and that any charge paying at least each term pays at least the total. Both hold
by unfolding the definition; neither is about the machine's schedule.

MDLACC's name is short for minimum description length, Rissanen's idea from
Section~\ref{sec:structure}, the one you worked on a row of thirty-two digits: a model's bill
is the bits to write the model down plus the bits to write the data given the model. The step
doesn't know any of that. It charges its declared d and steps on, with no graph change and
no register read. If a program uses it to enter a description-length bill, the number is
whatever the program declared, and nothing checks it against a description.

All fourteen step on; thirteen write one register and XOR\_\allowbreak{}SWAP writes two; none touches the
graph or the status words; none faults. Cost d for every one; none is in the positive class.
None can move the assertion channel either: over any run of the instructions the source
calls classical, which includes all fourteen, the assertion channel ends where it started
(\code{classical\_trace\_preserves\_cert\_addr}). Arithmetic doesn't mint certified structure.

LOAD and STORE above, and the heap pair in the next group, take any address and touch that
cell. None of them looks at a module's region (Section~\ref{sec:state}), so the kernel doesn't enforce the
locality the regions suggest; the hardware's table does (Section~\ref{sec:chip}).

What the cells leave out. CHSH\_\allowbreak{}TRIAL, given four bits, bumps the ``same'' or the ``different''
counter for the setting pair x y, and that's all it records: the witness counters keep only
same and different per setting pair, so no marginals are recorded, and the inequality is not
checked here. CERTIFY run again on a certified state still costs. REVEAL adds its bits to
entry (operand mod 16) of the global mu tensor in the record; the operand is called module
but acts as a direction index, not a module slot, and the cert operand is not checked. Each
supplied moment of the last three checks comes in the instruction as a same/different pair
of counts.

On success every CHSH\_\allowbreak{}LASSERT variant only steps on: neither certification reading changes.
Success is visible only as ``no trap.'' The check happened, and nothing was committed; Section~\ref{sec:machine-claims}
puts that next to Section~\ref{sec:insight}'s test and commit. (The source defines a marker word for a passed
check, and no step writes it.) CHSH\_\allowbreak{}TRIAL, in the same group, never moves a certification
reading from any state and costs its declared d, which may be zero; Section~\ref{sec:machine-claims} sorts it as raw
observation in Section~\ref{sec:insight}'s sense (Definition~\ref{def:u09-events}), with the theorem. Because no
marginals are kept, the checks are zero-marginal conditions (the bridge to the physics,
\code{zero\_marginal\_column\_contractive}, is Section~\ref{sec:chsh}'s).

What the G345 variant checks: the base
column check on the eight counters; each supplied moment $\gamma_3, \gamma_4, \gamma_5$,
given as a same/different pair, strictly between $-1$ and $1$; and a list of strict
positivity tests on integer polynomials in the counts and the supplied pairs, three for a
two-by-two block and four for the leading minors of a four-by-four matrix (Sylvester's test
for positive definiteness). All of it is integer arithmetic.

Sylvester's name on a test about matrices fits in a way I enjoy, because the word
\emph{matrix} is his. In 1850 James Joseph Sylvester used it for an ``oblong arrangement of
terms'' out of which you cut square blocks and take their determinants, and \emph{matrix} was
already an old word for the place something grows from. That's exactly what the test does:
it cuts the top-left square blocks out of the big grid, one row deep, two, three, four (the
leading minors), and asks each one's determinant to be positive. Was he the first to state the
test? The name doesn't settle that; names stick to people for all kinds of reasons, and I'd
treat this one as a lead.

And notice the tests are \emph{strict}: positive, not ``at least zero.'' That's not fussiness,
and you can see why at the table. Take the two-by-two grid with $0$ and $0$ on the top row
and $0$ and $-1$ on the bottom. Its top-left block is $0$ and its whole determinant is $0$:
both at least zero. But the grid isn't positive semidefinite, because pushing on the second
direction alone gives $-1$. With ``at least zero,'' looking at only the top-left blocks
misses that; you'd have to check every square block on the diagonal. With strict signs the
top-left blocks are enough, and they certify strictly positive (definite) blocks, which is the
version of the shortcut that's sound. How those blocks add up to the nine-by-nine conclusion
in the remark below is Section~\ref{sec:chsh}'s and Appendix B's argument, not this table's.

\begin{remark}[What a passing G345 step gives]\label{rem:u17-g345}
Let $s$ have $\mathrm{err}(s)$ false, let $i$ be CHSH\_\allowbreak{}LASSERT\_\allowbreak{}1AB\_\allowbreak{}G345 with declared cost $d$
and pairs $(a_3, b_3), (a_4, b_4), (a_5, b_5)$, and let $s' = \mathrm{apply}(s, i)$. If
$\mathrm{pc}(s') = \mathrm{pc}(s) + 1$ and $\mathrm{err}(s') = \mathrm{err}(s)$, then the
nine-by-nine level 1+AB moment matrix built from the four correlators of $s$'s counters,
with $\gamma_1 = \gamma_2 = 0$ and $\gamma_j = (a_j - b_j)/(a_j + b_j)$ for $j = 3, 4, 5$,
is symmetric and positive semidefinite. Section~\ref{sec:chsh} and Appendix B carry the matrix
and the argument; the check itself is \code{q1ab\_g345\_full\_integer\_check\_kernel} (VMStep.v) and
the implication is \code{chsh\_lassert\_1ab\_g345\_no\_trap\_implies\_npa\_psd\_q1ab}
(QuantumPartitionPSD\_\allowbreak{}1AB.v).
\end{remark}

\subsection{Group 7: arrows (7)}

Every one either succeeds or latches an error; none traps.

\begingroup\small
\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.224\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.159\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.159\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.159\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.159\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Instruction} & \textbf{Effect} & \textbf{Cost} & \textbf{Fault} & \textbf{Positive} \\
\midrule
\endhead
\bottomrule
\endlastfoot
MORPH dst, src\_\allowbreak{}mod, dst\_\allowbreak{}mod, coupling\_\allowbreak{}idx, d & Adds an arrow between two modules, with a coupling read from memory; identifier to dst. & d & LATCH if either module is missing & no \\
COMPOSE dst, m1, m2, d & Adds the composite arrow when the first's target is the second's source; identifier to dst. & d & LATCH if undefined & no \\
MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ID dst, module, d & Adds a fresh identity arrow on a module. & d & LATCH if the module is missing & no \\
MORPH\_\allowbreak{}DELETE id, d & Removes that one arrow. No cascade. & d & LATCH if missing & no \\
MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT id, property, cert, d & Writes the property's checksum into the assertion channel. The other flipper. & S d & LATCH if the arrow is missing & yes \\
MORPH\_\allowbreak{}TENSOR dst, f, g, d & Adds the tensor product of two arrows (Section~\ref{sec:category}). & d & LATCH if undefined & no \\
MORPH\_\allowbreak{}GET dst, id, selector, d & dst := source, target, pair count, or identity flag (selectors 0 to 3; else 0). & d & LATCH if missing & no \\
\end{longtable}
\endgroup

And the leftovers from this table. MORPH reads a coupling block from memory (a count, then pairs,
then a label) and keeps only the pairs whose ends lie in the two modules' regions. MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ID's
arrow has an empty coupling and the identity flag set, and every call makes a fresh one.
MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT's checksum is the sum of the property string's character codes, and it
overwrites whatever the channel held; the cert operand is never read. MORPH\_\allowbreak{}TENSOR adds its
arrow only when both arrows and all four of their end modules exist, both source regions are
disjoint, both target regions are disjoint, and modules owning exactly each union exist.

MORPH\_\allowbreak{}GET reads the graph, and so does TENSOR\_\allowbreak{}GET in group 5 (it reads a module's tensor).
The source still files both under the classical instructions, because neither writes the
graph, a channel, the certified flag or the witness counters. Keep that in mind in Section~\ref{sec:separation}.

\begin{definition}[Classical instructions]\label{def:u17-classical}
The \emph{classical} instructions are twenty-nine of the fifty-one: the fourteen of Group 3; the
eight of Group 4; and MDLACC, READ\_\allowbreak{}PORT, WRITE\_\allowbreak{}PORT, HEAP\_\allowbreak{}LOAD, HEAP\_\allowbreak{}STORE, TENSOR\_\allowbreak{}GET and
MORPH\_\allowbreak{}GET. The other twenty-two are not classical: PNEW, PSPLIT, PMERGE, PDISCOVER, LASSERT,
LJOIN, EMIT, REVEAL, TENSOR\_\allowbreak{}SET, CHSH\_\allowbreak{}TRIAL, CERTIFY, the five CHSH\_\allowbreak{}LASSERT variants, and
MORPH, COMPOSE, MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ID, MORPH\_\allowbreak{}DELETE, MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT and MORPH\_\allowbreak{}TENSOR. For a list $t$ of
instructions, $\mathrm{run}(t, s)$ applies them to $s$ in order with the step function, with
no fetching by program counter.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Classical runs move nothing that certifies]\label{thm:u17-classical}
Let $t$ be a list of classical instructions and $s$ any state. Then
$\mathrm{graph}(\mathrm{run}(t, s)) = \mathrm{graph}(s)$,
$\mathrm{certaddr}(\mathrm{run}(t, s)) = \mathrm{certaddr}(s)$, and
$\mathrm{cert}(\mathrm{run}(t, s)) = \mathrm{cert}(s)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
First one step: for each classical instruction, every branch of its rule copies the graph,
the control and status words' address field, and the certified flag from the old state. The
three with two branches (JNEZ, TENSOR\_\allowbreak{}GET, MORPH\_\allowbreak{}GET) copy them in both. Coq checks this by a
case split that closes by computation. Then induction on $t$.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{is\_classical\_opcode}, \code{classical\_trace\_preserves\_graph},
\code{classical\_trace\_preserves\_cert\_addr} and \code{classical\_trace\_preserves\_certified}
(ClassicalConservativity.v). The class is a choice of the file, not a closure property:
PDISCOVER is left out although its step changes nothing, and READ\_\allowbreak{}PORT is in although it
costs at least one. The same three equalities hold when the program runs by program counter,
jumps and all (\code{classical\_opcodes\_preserve\_structure\_run\_vm}); Section~\ref{sec:witness} states that form.

The classical view can't recover the flag either. Take the four fields a classical observer
sees, the program counter, the counter, the registers and the memory, and map a list of
states to the list of those four-field snapshots. No function on the snapshot lists gives
back the certified flag of the last state, for every list:
\code{no\_classical\_certification\_decider} (WitnessPreservationImpossibility.v). The proof is two
hand-built states that agree on all four fields and differ in the flag; they're records the
type allows, not states shown reachable from the start. Section~\ref{sec:separation} does the same with the graph.

Four plus three plus fourteen plus eight plus seven plus eight plus seven: fifty-one.

\subsection{The schedule, read as a whole}

Four cost shapes. Thirty-nine instructions cost exactly their declared d, which may be
zero. Eight cost d plus one, the floor: LJOIN, CERTIFY, MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT, and the five
CHSH\_\allowbreak{}LASSERT variants. Three cost a payload plus the floor: EMIT (eight per character),
READ\_\allowbreak{}PORT and REVEAL (their bit count). And LASSERT costs the formula length times eight
plus the floor. The twelve with a floor are exactly the positive class; that much is read
off the definitions, and the theorems are one line each: \code{cert\_setter\_cost\_pos}, if the
predicate holds, the cost is at least one; \code{cert\_setter\_cost\_above\_declared}, it's at least one
more than declared; and \code{non\_cert\_setter\_cost\_is\_declared}, if the predicate fails, the cost is
exactly what was declared.

\begin{definition}[The schedule]\label{def:u17-cost}
For an instruction $i$ with declared cost $d$, the cost $\mathrm{cost}(i)$ is:
$8\ell + d + 1$ for LASSERT with declared length $\ell$; $8|p| + d + 1$ for EMIT with
payload $p$ of $|p|$ characters; $b + d + 1$ for READ\_\allowbreak{}PORT and REVEAL with bit count $b$;
$d + 1$ for LJOIN, CERTIFY, MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT and the five CHSH\_\allowbreak{}LASSERT variants; and $d$ for
each of the other thirty-nine.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[The positive class and the setter class]\label{def:u17-floor}
The \emph{positive class} is the twelve instructions in the first four cases of
Definition~\ref{def:u17-cost}: LASSERT, EMIT, READ\_\allowbreak{}PORT, REVEAL, LJOIN, CERTIFY, MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT
and the five CHSH\_\allowbreak{}LASSERT variants. The \emph{setter class} is five of them: LASSERT, LJOIN,
EMIT, REVEAL and MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The floor]\label{thm:u17-floor}
If $i$ is in the positive class, then $\mathrm{cost}(i) \ge d + 1 \ge 1$. If $i$ is outside
it, then $\mathrm{cost}(i) = d$, and with $d = 0$ the instruction is free.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Case split on $i$. Each of the twelve has a $+1$ in its cost, so the cost is at least one
whatever $d$ is. The other thirty-nine cost $d$ by definition.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{instruction\_cost}, \code{is\_cert\_setterb}, \code{cert\_setter\_cost\_pos} and
\code{cert\_setter\_cost\_above\_declared} for the first sentence and \code{non\_cert\_setter\_cost\_is\_declared}
for the second, with \code{declared\_mu\_delta} reading the declared cost $d$ off any instruction
(all VMStep.v), the setter class \code{cert\_addr\_setterb} (AbstractNoFI.v) and the payload length
\code{payload\_bit\_length\_ascii} (VMStep.v). Examples of the second sentence at work:
\code{morph\_can\_be\_free}, \code{morph\_compose\_cost\_zero}, and the PNEW, PSPLIT and PMERGE cases inside
\code{partition\_free\_but\_certification\_nonfree}. One example runs a whole program at zero:
\code{blind\_program} (StructuralAdvantage.v) is a ten-instruction search loop of LOAD\_\allowbreak{}IMM, ADD,
SUB, JNEZ and JUMP, every one at declared cost zero, and \code{blind\_program\_total\_cost\_is\_zero}
says its costs sum to zero.

Now the design choice. Only two of the twelve flip a reading: CERTIFY sets the flag and
MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT sets the assertion channel. The other ten are in the class because they're
\emph{checks or emissions}: LASSERT and the CHSH family check and charge for the checking (Section~\ref{sec:insight}'s
Popper point: charge the attempt, pass or fail); EMIT, REVEAL and READ\_\allowbreak{}PORT move information
across the machine's boundary and charge per bit; LJOIN is a join of certificates that does
nothing yet and charges the floor anyway. The toll of Section~\ref{sec:toll} (Definition~\ref{def:certsys}) needs
only the two flippers to be priced. The schedule prices more. That's allowed, Section~\ref{sec:latch}'s billed
machine says so (the toll is a floor, and a surcharge only raises the price), and it's a
choice I'd defend this way: the things that cost
at least one are the things that claim to have \emph{looked at or sent} something, and I'd
rather the machine never let a look or a send be free than argue about which looks matter.
You can disagree. The flippers are two; the floor is on twelve; both numbers are in the
table.

And more things to watch doesn't mean a bigger floor. If an instruction triggers several of
the events you want priced, one mark covers all of them; the floors don't add unless you
write a rule that makes them add.

\begin{theorem}[The joint floor is the least]\label{thm:u17-joint-floor}
Let $E_1, \ldots, E_n$ be yes/no tests on instructions, and let $J(i) = 1$ if some $E_j(i)$
holds and $J(i) = 0$ otherwise. For any cost function $c$ from instructions to
$\mathbb{N}$: $c(i) \ge 1$ for every $j$ and every $i$ with $E_j(i)$ if and only if
$J(i) \le c(i)$ for every $i$. So $J$ is the least cost meeting all the unit floors at once.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If $c$ meets every floor and some $E_j(i)$ holds, then $c(i) \ge 1 = J(i)$; if none holds,
$J(i) = 0 \le c(i)$. Conversely, if $J \le c$ and $E_j(i)$ holds, then $J(i) = 1$, so
$c(i) \ge 1$.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{joint\_floor\_is\_least} (ObservationPolicy.v). It's stated for any instruction
type, not only this machine's.

A second thing you'll notice: the arrow-building instructions are free at d equals zero.
MORPH, COMPOSE, MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ID, MORPH\_\allowbreak{}DELETE, MORPH\_\allowbreak{}TENSOR, MORPH\_\allowbreak{}GET all cost d
(\code{morph\_compose\_cost\_zero} and its siblings), and so does PNEW. Building structure is free.
\emph{Asserting} it is not. In Section~\ref{sec:insight}'s terms (Definition~\ref{def:u09-events}), building never turns a
reading on, so it sorts with raw observation, and asserting is certified insight; Section~\ref{sec:machine-claims} lays
the tiers out on the machine.
Notice what that does to a tempting sentence: a zero-cost PNEW changes the graph, so ``every
change to the structure costs something'' is false for this machine. What costs something is
vouching.

And here's what the table makes checkable, all on this machine, all over the fifty-one
cases, one sentence per fact. One step that takes the assertion channel from zero to nonzero
costs at least one (\code{no\_free\_certification}). The same holds for the flag
(\code{no\_free\_certification\_certified}). Either one raises the counter by at least one
(\code{certification\_requires\_positive\_mu}). And over a whole run, a start with the channel
clear and an end with it set means the run contained a positive-cost instruction and the
counter rose by at least one (\code{no\_free\_certified\_insight}). One detail in that last
one: the instruction it finds comes from a narrower list than the
twelve, a five-member predicate called \code{cert\_addr\_setterb} (LASSERT, LJOIN, EMIT, REVEAL
and MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT), of which only MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT writes the channel. So the theorem says which
kind of instruction was in the run, and \code{morph\_assert\_step\_sets\_supra\_cert\_iff} is the finer
fact about which one moved the channel. Those are Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s universal floor
(Theorem~\ref{thm:universal-floor}), landed on fifty-one constructors; Section~\ref{sec:witness} lines up the whole
ladder of its instances.

Here are those facts exactly. Write $\mathrm{certaddr}(s)$ for the assertion channel,
$\mathrm{cert}(s)$ for the certified flag, and $\Sigma(p)$ for the sum of the character
codes of a string $p$.

\begin{theorem}[Only CERTIFY touches the flag, and it stays set]\label{thm:u17-certified}
For every state $s$ and instruction $i$: $\mathrm{cert}(\mathrm{apply}(s, i))$ is true if
$i$ is CERTIFY, and equals $\mathrm{cert}(s)$ otherwise. Hence (1) if $\mathrm{cert}(s)$ is
true, so is $\mathrm{cert}(\mathrm{apply}(s, i))$ for every $i$; and (2) if
$\mathrm{cert}(s)$ is false and $\mathrm{cert}(\mathrm{apply}(s, i))$ is true, then $i$ is
CERTIFY, $\mathrm{cost}(i) \ge 1$, and $\mu(\mathrm{apply}(s, i)) \ge \mu(s) + 1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Case split over the fifty-one instructions and their branches: CERTIFY's rule writes true,
and every other rule copies the flag. (1) follows because both cases give true when the old
value is true. (2): the old value is false and the new one true, so the second case is
impossible and $i$ is CERTIFY with cost $d + 1$; the counter claim is conservation.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{step\_certify} (VMStep.v), \code{vm\_apply\_certified} (PrimeAxiom.v),
\code{certification\_reading\_permanent} (EventSwapTheorem.v) for (1), and
\code{no\_free\_certification\_certified} with \code{no\_free\_certification\_certified\_mu}
(AbstractNoFI.v) for (2). The run form is \code{kernel\_certified\_implies\_positive\_mu}
(PrimeAxiom.v): if a run fetched by program counter starts with the flag down and the
counter at zero and ends with the flag up, the counter at the end is positive.

\begin{theorem}[Only MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT touches the channel]\label{thm:u17-channel}
For every state $s$: (1) if $i$ is not a MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT, then
$\mathrm{certaddr}(\mathrm{apply}(s, i)) = \mathrm{certaddr}(s)$. (2) For
$i$ = MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT with arrow $k$, property $p$, certificate $c$ and declared cost $d$: if
arrow $k$ is in the graph, the step sets $\mathrm{certaddr}$ to $\Sigma(p)$ and changes
nothing else but $\mathrm{pc}$ and $\mu$; if it is not, the step leaves $\mathrm{certaddr}$
alone, sets the error code to $1$ and the error flag to true, and changes nothing else but
$\mathrm{pc}$ and $\mu$. In both cases $c$ is not read and
$\mu(\mathrm{apply}(s, i)) = \mu(s) + d + 1$. (3) If $\mathrm{certaddr}(s) = 0$, then
$\mathrm{certaddr}(\mathrm{apply}(s, i)) \ne 0$ if and only if $i$ is a MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT whose
arrow is in the graph of $s$ and whose property has $\Sigma(p) \ne 0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) is a case split over the other fifty instructions and their branches; each copies the
address field, including the faulting branches, whose error writer changes only the error
code. (2) is the two rules read off. (3): if $i$ is not a MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT, (1) keeps the channel
at $0$; if it is and the arrow is missing, (2) keeps it at $0$; if the arrow is present, the
new value is $\Sigma(p)$, which is nonzero exactly when the right side says so.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{non\_morph\_assert\_preserves\_cert\_addr} and \code{morph\_assert\_step\_sets\_supra\_cert\_iff}
(RevelationRequirement.v), \code{step\_morph\_assert\_ok} and \code{step\_morph\_assert\_bad} (VMStep.v),
and \code{ascii\_checksum} (VMState.v). The channel is overwritten, not added to: a later
MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT with $\Sigma(p) = 0$ on an existing arrow puts it back to zero. No step rule
reads the channel or the flag.

There's no gap between paying and flipping. The rule that writes the flag or the channel is
the same rule that adds the cost; it's one step, and there is no state in between where the
reading has moved and the charge hasn't landed. A simulator that did these as two separate
operations could get the order wrong; this machine has no order to get wrong.

\begin{theorem}[No free certification on this machine]\label{thm:u17-nfi}
(1) If $\mathrm{certaddr}(s) = 0$ and $\mathrm{certaddr}(\mathrm{apply}(s, i)) \ne 0$,
then $\mathrm{cost}(i) \ge 1$. (2) If $\mathrm{cert}(s)$ is false and
$\mathrm{cert}(\mathrm{apply}(s, i))$ is true, then $\mathrm{cost}(i) \ge 1$. (3) In either
case, $\mu(\mathrm{apply}(s, i)) \ge \mu(s) + 1$. (4) If $\mathrm{certaddr}(s) = 0$ and
$\mathrm{certaddr}(\mathrm{run}(t, s)) \ne 0$, then some $i$ in $t$ is in the setter class
with $\mathrm{cost}(i) \ge 1$, and $\mu(\mathrm{run}(t, s)) \ge \mu(s) + 1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1): every instruction outside the setter class leaves the channel alone, so $i$ is in the
setter class, and each of its five members has a $+1$ in its cost. (2) is part (2) of
Theorem~\ref{thm:u17-certified}. (3) is conservation with (1) or (2). (4): the channel is $0$
at the start and nonzero at the end, so some step of the run takes it from $0$ to nonzero;
by (1) that step's instruction is a setter with cost at least one, and since the counter
never falls, the end counter is at least one above the start.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{no\_free\_certification}, \code{no\_free\_certification\_certified} and
\code{certification\_requires\_positive\_mu} (AbstractNoFI.v), and \code{no\_free\_certified\_insight}
(InsightTaxonomy.v). Here $\mathrm{run}$ applies the list in order, as in
Definition~\ref{def:u17-classical}. Three neighbours say the same thing in other shapes.
\code{thiele\_nfi\_pc\_indexed} (AbstractNoFI.v) is the setter half of (4) for a run fetched by
program counter with fuel: if such a run ends with the channel set from a clear start, the
program contains a setter. \code{partition\_refinement\_nonfree} (PartitionRefinementNoFI.v) is (4)
under a name that says what it is for: going from no certified claim to one is a strict
refinement, and it isn't free. And \code{partition\_free\_but\_certification\_nonfree} (same file)
packages the contrast of this section in one statement: PNEW, PSPLIT and PMERGE each cost
zero at declared cost zero, none of the three is in the setter class, and any run that takes
the channel from clear to set raises the counter by at least one.

One more fact the theorems lean on, about the per-arrow cost field of Section~\ref{sec:state}: there is a
function that writes a value into that field of one arrow, and
\code{graph\_certify\_morphism\_lookup} (VMState.v) says that after it the arrow reads back with the
new value and everything else the same. No step rule calls it, and every arrow a step
creates starts with zero there, so on every state reachable from the initial state the field
is zero. That last sentence is read from the rules; no theorem states it.

\subsection{What the chip has}

The hardware encodes forty-seven of the fifty-one. The four it doesn't are the four
CHSH\_\allowbreak{}LASSERT\_\allowbreak{}1AB variants: they exist in the kernel and in the hardware-side abstraction
function, but the hardware assigns them no opcode byte and the CPU has no reference to them.
(The Python side does number them, 47 to 50, which is 0x2F to 0x32 in hexadecimal: the
generated opcode table thielecpu/generated/generated\_\allowbreak{}core.py and the assembler script
scripts/forge.py. Neither Coq nor the hardware gives them a byte.) The test that checks
kernel-against-hardware parity, which compares the OCaml extraction's opcode names with the
ones defined in the hardware's type file, allows \emph{at most} four missing, with a comment
naming these four; it does not check that it's exactly these four. I'd rather you know the
test's shape than assume it's tighter than it is. Everything else in the table has a byte,
and the bytes are Section~\ref{sec:chip}'s.

One rule for reading everything above: where a comment in the step file and the step rule
next to it disagree, the book follows the rule, because the rule is what the proofs are
about.

That's what you can do. Next: the arrows, which the table has treated as seven opcodes and
which are, underneath, a piece of mathematics I didn't know existed when I built them.

%===========================================================================
\section{What a morphism is}
\label{sec:category}
%===========================================================================

Category theory, from scratch. I didn't know what it was when I started this project; Section~\ref{sec:structure} and
Section~\ref{sec:origin} have the story of building it by feel, as ``digital DNA,'' and finding out after the thing
already ran that it had a name and a founding paper. So this section is me explaining the mathematics I accidentally used, with the
two laws I made you wait for in Section~\ref{sec:structure}, and then holding my own machine up against those laws on
the arrows it actually stores, including the one case where the obvious rule for identities
breaks them. That case is the most useful paragraph in here, and it's near the end.

\subsection{Objects, arrows, and a quiet promotion}

A category is the part of mathematics that takes the relationships between things as
seriously as the things, and then quietly decides the relationships matter more. Two
ingredients. Objects: the things. Arrows: the relationships between them. That's the entire
inventory, and it looks thin until you notice what got promoted. In most of mathematics the
objects are the citizens and the maps between them are second-class traffic. A category
turns that around. The arrows are first-class, and nearly everything you can say inside a
category you say by pointing at arrows, not by reaching inside objects. That's the Eilenberg
and Mac Lane move from Section~\ref{sec:structure} (1945, ``a continuation of Klein''): stop asking what a thing is,
ask how it's carried.

And where did they get the word? Not from mathematics. They borrowed \emph{category} from the
philosophers, from Aristotle and Kant, and \emph{functor} (a map from one whole
category to another, which turns up much later in this book) from the philosopher Rudolf
Carnap, and then gave both words exact meanings none of those philosophers had in mind. So
Aristotle walks back into this book without being asked: the man who put the form inside the
bronze lent his word to the field that keeps track of forms by their arrows. Does that change
the laws? No.
It's a reminder that a word can start in philosophy and arrive in mathematics with a precise
meaning bolted on, which is the thing I've been trying to do with \emph{established} since the
first page.

The objects can be anything, which is both why the theory reaches so far and why it feels
slippery the first time through. Sets. Vector spaces. Shapes. The theory doesn't care what
the objects are made of; it cares how they connect. Here, the objects are \emph{modules}, the
named pieces a partition cut the state into (Section~\ref{sec:state}), and the arrows are claims about how two
pieces relate. Why modules and not cells or registers? Because a claim about a relationship
has to attach to something the machine can name and keep, and a module is the one thing in
the state an arrow's two ends can be: you can read an arrow's source and target back
(MORPH\_\allowbreak{}GET), and with selector two, the number of pairs in its coupling.

Arrows also go by the name \emph{morphisms}, and the words are interchangeable; I'll use both. An
arrow runs from one object to another, written f from A to B. The thing everyone imports
from school and has to set down is the assumption that an arrow is a \emph{function}. It needn't
be. An arrow is whatever the category accepts as a structure-respecting way to get from A to
B, and here it's something more pointed than a function: a morphism is a \emph{claim}, ``these two
modules are related, and here is the kind of relation,'' with the evidence stapled on.

\subsection{The two laws, and why each}

Section~\ref{sec:structure} gave you the definition in one breath. Here it is slowed down: two ingredients first,
then the two rules Section~\ref{sec:structure} said you'd watch me have to prove. Together they're the whole
definition, and the rules are the part people skip.

\emph{Composition.} If there's an arrow f from A to B and an arrow g from B to C, there must be a
composite arrow from A to C, written g after f. Why? Because relationships have to chain. A
to B, B to C, therefore A to C. Picture three dots in a row, A, B and C: f hops from the
first to the second, g from the second to the third, and the composite takes the whole
stride from A to C in one. Without that, every multi-hop path has to be named
individually, and the structure collapses into a pile of unconnected pairs. A category
without composition is a phone book without a search function. In the machine, COMPOSE
builds the long arrow.

\emph{Identity.} Every object has a do-nothing arrow to itself. Why bother? Because every object
needs a self-loop, even the boring ones: a module with no connections still has to exist
somewhere in the framework, and ``the arrow that does nothing'' is how you say ``this thing,
unchanged'' in a language that only speaks in arrows. On the drawing it's a small loop on A, leaving A
and arriving back at A. MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ID builds the loop.

And the two rules that make following arrows dependable, the ones Section~\ref{sec:structure} named in a sentence
and left for here. \emph{Associativity}: following three arrows in a row gives the same result whether you
pair up the first two or the last two. Why? Because parenthesisation shouldn't matter. Both
spell the same three-hop path. If they came out different, two programs that built the same
chain in different orders would produce two different morphisms, and that's a bug: the chain
is the thing, how you assembled it is not. \emph{Identity laws}: tacking the do-nothing arrow onto
either end of an arrow gives back the arrow. If the self-loop \emph{changed} things, it wouldn't be
the self-loop.

That's a category. Objects, arrows, composition, identities, associativity, identity laws.
Six words and you've got the whole of Eilenberg and Mac Lane's definition.

\begin{definition}[Category]\label{def:u18-category}
A \emph{category} has a collection of objects; for each pair of objects $A$, $B$ a collection of
arrows $f : A \to B$; for each $f : A \to B$ and $g : B \to C$ a composite
$g \circ f : A \to C$; and for each object $A$ an identity $\mathrm{id}_A : A \to A$. These
satisfy associativity, $h \circ (g \circ f) = (h \circ g) \circ f$ whenever the composites
are defined, and the identity laws, $f \circ \mathrm{id}_A = f = \mathrm{id}_B \circ f$ for
every $f : A \to B$.
\end{definition}

This is the textbook definition. No Coq file in the tree states it as a structure and proves
the machine is an instance; what Coq checks is the list of laws below, each on its own.

\subsection{What a coupling is}

Now the evidence stapled to the claim. In the machine, a morphism carries \emph{coupling data}: a
list of pairs of cells, one from the source module's region and one from the target's, plus
a label. A pair (a, c) says: cell a in the source is related to cell c in the target. That's
the \emph{relational content} of the arrow, the actual record of which parts of one module
correspond to which parts of another. What the pairs mean is up to the programmer: ``B
refines A, and here's which cells map to which''; ``A is correlated with B at these pairs''; ``A
simulates B, these transitions correspond.'' The kernel enforces the composition rule on the
pairs. The interpretation is yours.

Composition on couplings is \emph{relational composition}, the thing you learned without a name
when you learned that ``a is a parent of b'' and ``b is a parent of c'' gives ``a is a grandparent
of c'': a pair (a, c) is in the composite exactly when there's some middle cell b with (a, b)
in the first coupling and (b, c) in the second. That's \code{relational\_compose\_spec}, and the
machine's kernel function is proved to be that function (\code{kernel\_relational\_compose\_same}).

Who put a name on that move first? People older than you'd guess. Augustus De Morgan, writing
on the logic of relations around 1860, took the ``is'' out of the old syllogism, put a general
relation in its place, and composed two relations to get the conclusion. The example that
gets quoted from that tradition is ``$x$ is the lover of a servant of $y$,'' which is
relational composition with better gossip. When exactly he read that paper to the Cambridge
Philosophical Society, and on which pages it was printed, the sources disagree, which is a
small reminder that history is where you start digging. Then in 1870 Charles Sanders Peirce,
the same Peirce from the opening chapter, carried Boole's algebra of logic over to relations,
with composition as one of its basic operations, and he's usually counted as the real founder
of the theory. So COMPOSE's rule is older than computers, older than categories, older than
Turing's clerk: a nineteenth-century logician's product of relations, run on lists of cell
numbers. Does that change the proof? No. It changes how old the move is, not whether it
holds on this machine. That's what Coq is for.

And here's a thing I'd never have seen without the laws. The identity arrow in this machine
doesn't carry its identity in its coupling. The cheap guess for an identity coupling is the
\emph{empty} list, and the empty relation \emph{annihilates} under composition: compose anything with
``no pairs'' and you get ``no pairs'' back, not the thing you started with
(\code{relational\_compose\_empty\_l}, \code{relational\_compose\_empty\_r}). The coupling that \emph{would} act as an identity is the
diagonal, every cell of the region paired with itself, and that's proved to work on both
sides (\code{morph\_id\_left\_coupling}, \code{morph\_id\_right\_coupling}); but storing a diagonal means listing every cell
of the region in every identity arrow, so the machine stores a \emph{flag} on the record instead,
and COMPOSE honours the flag: if both arrows are flagged, the composite is flagged too, and
stored exactly the way MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ID stores an identity; if only the first is flagged, the
composite's pairs are the second's; if only the second, the first's; else the relational
composition (\code{graph\_compose\_morphisms\_coupling}, four cases). The flag is load-bearing.
That's why MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ID stores an empty coupling and sets the flag, and why MORPH\_\allowbreak{}GET has a
