selector for the flag. (The lemma that says the identity arrow is an identity,
\code{graph\_add\_identity\_coupling}, proves only the flag. It doesn't prove the coupling is
diagonal, because it isn't.)

Here are the objects exactly.

\begin{definition}[Coupling, relational composition, diagonal]\label{def:u18-coupling}
A \emph{coupling} is a finite list of pairs of natural numbers. Its \emph{relational composition} with
a coupling $S$ is
\[
R ; S = [\,(a, c) \mid (a, b) \in R,\ (b', c) \in S,\ b = b'\,],
\]
listed in the order the pairs of $R$ and then $S$ are visited. The \emph{diagonal} of a list
$X$ of cells is $[(x, x) \mid x \in X]$. Two couplings are \emph{equivalent}, $R \equiv S$, when
they contain the same pairs: $(a, c) \in R \iff (a, c) \in S$ for all $a, c$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Stored arrow and the composition rule]\label{def:u18-compose-rule}
A stored arrow has a source module, a target module, a coupling with a label, an identity
flag, and a cost field. Storing an arrow removes duplicate pairs from its coupling and sets
its cost field to 0. MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ID on an existing module $A$ stores the arrow from $A$ to $A$ with
the empty coupling (no pairs, label ``empty'') and the flag on. COMPOSE of stored arrows $f$
and $h$, when the target of $f$ equals the source of $h$, stores a new arrow from the source
of $f$ to the target of $h$. If both are flagged, the new arrow is flagged and has the empty
coupling, the same record MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ID stores. Otherwise its flag is off, its label is the label
of $f$, a semicolon, and the label of $h$, and its pairs are
\[
\begin{cases} \text{pairs of } h & \text{if only } f \text{ is flagged,}\\ \text{pairs of } f & \text{if only } h \text{ is flagged,}\\ \text{pairs of } f \;;\; \text{pairs of } h & \text{if neither is.} \end{cases}
\]
If either arrow is missing or the target and source differ, COMPOSE builds nothing.
\end{definition}

Checked as the definitions \code{relational\_compose}, \code{diagonal}, \code{coupling\_equiv}
(CategoryLaws.v), and \code{empty\_coupling\_data}, \code{graph\_add\_morphism}, \code{graph\_add\_identity},
\code{graph\_compose\_morphisms} (VMState.v); \code{kernel\_relational\_compose\_same} says the kernel's
copy of relational composition is the same function, and \code{graph\_compose\_morphisms\_coupling}
(CategoryBridge.v) says the stored composite's flag is the two flags anded together and its
pairs are equivalent to the four-case rule (equivalent rather than equal because storing
removes duplicates).

Here's why ``equivalent'' and not ``equal,'' at the table. Let $R$ be two pairs, (1, 2) and
(1, 3): cell 1 is related to cell 2 and to cell 3. Let $S$ be (2, 5) and (3, 5): both of
those are related to cell 5. Compose by the definition, walking $R$'s pairs in order and
matching each against $S$. (1, 2) meets (2, 5) and gives (1, 5). (1, 3) meets (3, 5) and gives
(1, 5) again. The list is (1, 5), (1, 5): two copies of one fact, because there were two
middles, 2 and 3, on the way from 1 to 5. Store it and the duplicate goes, leaving (1, 5)
once. Same pairs, different lists. So the book compares couplings by which pairs they hold,
and two routes to one place count as one place.

\subsection{What Coq checks, exactly}

I promised in Section~\ref{sec:structure} you'd watch me prove the two rules. Here's what's proved, with the
hypotheses, and you can decide whether it's enough.

On \emph{coupling lists}, with ``the same'' meaning ``hold the same pairs, order and repeats
ignored'' (\code{coupling\_equiv}): composition is associative (\code{relational\_compose\_assoc}, with
nothing assumed; the kernel-record forms \code{coupling\_data\_compose\_assoc}, \code{morph\_compose\_assoc\_coupling},
\code{morph\_graph\_compose\_assoc}, which are stated on the pair lists stored in the records, and
none of which mentions the identity flag or the composite a COMPOSE actually builds). The diagonal is a left identity when every pair's source lies
in the region, and a right identity when every target does. Composition respects the
equivalence on both sides. The empty list absorbs. And on the \emph{tensor} side (two arrows side
by side, pairs appended), there's an interchange law when the cross terms vanish, and append
is associative with the empty list as unit (\code{tensor\_bifunctor}, \code{monoidal\_coherence}).

On \emph{the stored records}: what COMPOSE builds is the four-case rule above; what MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ID
builds is flagged identity; a new arrow gets the next identifier and old ones are untouched;
a composite's certification-cost field is zero. Associativity and both identity laws hold on
the stored arrows themselves, flag and all, which is the next part's whole job. And the
hardware's COMPOSE step produces
exactly the state the kernel's does, whole state, coupling and label included
(\code{driven\_step\_compose}, under the hardware well-formedness invariant). That last one is
closed, with no axiom behind it; the whole-machine version, every opcode under its side conditions
(\code{driven\_step\_wf}), uses one standard extensionality axiom at the hardware layer, which Section~\ref{sec:coq}
will account for.

The laws on couplings, exactly.

\begin{theorem}[Laws of relational composition]\label{thm:u18-coupling-laws}
For all couplings $R$, $S$, $T$, $R'$, $S'$ and every list of cells $X$:
(1) $(a, c) \in R ; S$ if and only if there is $b$ with $(a, b) \in R$ and $(b, c) \in S$.
(2) $(R ; S) ; T \equiv R ; (S ; T)$.
(3) If every pair $(a, b)$ of $R$ has $a \in X$, then $\mathrm{diag}(X) ; R \equiv R$; if every
pair has $b \in X$, then $R ; \mathrm{diag}(X) \equiv R$.
(4) If $R \equiv R'$ and $S \equiv S'$, then $R ; S \equiv R' ; S'$.
(5) $[\,] ; R \equiv [\,]$ and $R ; [\,] \equiv [\,]$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Unfold the definition: a pair of the output comes from some $(a, b)$ in $R$ and some
$(b', c)$ in $S$ that passed the test $b = b'$, and every such match produces one. (2) By (1)
on both sides, each says there are $b$ and $b'$ with $(a, b) \in R$, $(b, b') \in S$ and
$(b', c) \in T$. (3) By (1), $(a, c) \in \mathrm{diag}(X) ; R$ means $a \in X$ and
$(a, c) \in R$, and the hypothesis makes the first part automatic; the right case is the
mirror. (4) and (5) are (1) again.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{relational\_compose\_spec} (item (1), an if and only if), \code{relational\_compose\_assoc},
\code{relational\_compose\_diagonal\_left}, \code{relational\_compose\_diagonal\_right},
\code{relational\_compose\_compat}, \code{relational\_compose\_empty\_l} and \code{relational\_compose\_empty\_r}
(CategoryLaws.v). The record-facing forms are the same statements about the pair lists
stored in records: \code{coupling\_data\_compose\_assoc} (CategoryLaws.v), and
\code{morph\_compose\_assoc\_coupling}, \code{morph\_graph\_compose\_assoc}, \code{morph\_id\_left\_coupling},
\code{morph\_id\_right\_coupling} (CategoryBridge.v). \code{morph\_graph\_compose\_assoc} takes three stored
arrows whose targets and sources line up and concludes (2) for their stored pairs. None of
these mentions the identity flag or the arrow COMPOSE actually stores; the laws on stored
arrows are Theorem~\ref{thm:u18-stored-laws} below.

\begin{theorem}[Tensor on couplings]\label{thm:u18-tensor}
Let $R \otimes S$ be the list $R$ followed by $S$. Then $(R \otimes S) \otimes T =
R \otimes (S \otimes T)$, $[\,] \otimes R = R$ and $R \otimes [\,] = R$, as lists. And if
$F ; G' \equiv [\,]$ and $G ; F' \equiv [\,]$, then
$(F \otimes G) ; (F' \otimes G') \equiv (F ; F') \otimes (G ; G')$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The first three are facts about appending lists. For the last, by (1) of
Theorem~\ref{thm:u18-coupling-laws} a pair of the left side comes from one of four combinations, and the
two cross combinations are empty by hypothesis.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{monoidal\_coherence} and \code{tensor\_bifunctor} (CategoryMonoidal.v).

\subsection{Where the laws meet the stored arrows}

Now the paragraph I said was the most useful. The associativity theorem above is about
\emph{coupling lists}. The question that matters is whether the laws hold for the arrows COMPOSE
actually stores, flag and all, and the flag hides a trap you can walk into with three arrows.
Take two identity arrows on module A (two calls to MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ID give two arrows, each flagged),
call them i1 and i2, and an arrow f from A to B with a nonempty coupling P.

Here's the wrong neighbour first, because the border is drawn by both sides. The obvious
rule for the flag is ``a composite is never an identity; if the first arrow is flagged, take
the second's pairs.'' Under that rule, i1 composed with i2 takes i2's pairs, the empty list,
and gets built with the flag \emph{off}. Compose that with f: neither is flagged now, so it's the
relational composition of the empty list with P, which is empty. Compose the other way, i1
with (i2 with f): i2 with f gives P, then i1 with that gives P again. Empty on one side, P on
the other. Under the obvious rule associativity breaks the moment two identities meet, the
mirror case breaks too (an arrow g from B to A with pairs Q, followed by the composite of i1
and i2, gives the empty list instead of Q), and the composite of two identities is an arrow
from A to A that is an identity for nothing. A book that proved the laws on pair lists and
let that stand on the records would be proving the laws somewhere the machine doesn't live.

The machine's rule passes the flag along (Definition~\ref{def:u18-compose-rule}): two
flagged arrows compose to a flagged one. Run the same three arrows through it. i1 composed with i2
is a flagged identity on A. That composed with f: only the first is flagged, so take f's
pairs, P. i1 with (i2 with f): i2 with f has pairs P and the flag off, i1 is flagged, so P.
Same both ways. And g followed by the composite of i1 and i2 gives Q, and so does g followed
by i1, then i2. The flag is the whole difference.

``Same'' needs pinning down, further than feels necessary, because a stored arrow carries more
than the laws care about. COMPOSE always stores a \emph{new} arrow under a fresh identifier, so
``i1 followed by f equals f'' can't mean the same identifier; it means a new arrow that is f
in every way the machine can act on. Its labels don't match either: the two bracketings
above store ``empty;'' in front of f's label once and twice. Labels are names for a person
reading the graph, and MORPH\_\allowbreak{}GET has no selector for one. And a flagged arrow's pairs are
never read by COMPOSE, so there's nothing to compare there. So two stored arrows are \emph{the
same arrow} when they have the same source, the same target, the same flag, and, when the
flag is off, the same pairs. With that, the laws hold on the stored arrows, with two side
conditions that carry weight: the graph has to be well formed (so the arrows being composed
are still where they were after each COMPOSE adds one), and an identity arrow has to go from
an object to itself. MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ID only builds those, and a separate invariant says nothing else
ever gets the flag.

\begin{definition}[The same stored arrow]\label{def:u18-stored-same}
Two stored arrows $x$ and $y$ are \emph{the same arrow}, $x \cong y$, when they have the same
source, the same target and the same flag, and, if the flag of $x$ is off, their pairs are
equivalent (Definition~\ref{def:u18-coupling}). Labels, identifiers and cost fields are not
compared.
\end{definition}

Checked as the definition \code{stored\_arrow\_equiv} (CategoryBridge.v).

\begin{theorem}[The category laws on stored arrows]\label{thm:u18-stored-laws}
Write $xy$ for the arrow COMPOSE stores from stored arrows $x$ followed by $y$, each COMPOSE
run in the graph the previous one left.
(1) If $i$ and $j$ are flagged and the target of $i$ is the source of $j$, then COMPOSE of
$i$ and $j$ succeeds and stores the arrow from the source of $i$ to the target of $j$ with
the flag on, the empty coupling and cost field $0$.
(2) If the graph is well formed and $f$, $k$, $h$ are stored arrows with the target of $f$
the source of $k$ and the target of $k$ the source of $h$, then the four COMPOSEs that build
$(fk)h$ and $f(kh)$ all succeed, and $(fk)h \cong f(kh)$.
(3) If $i$ is flagged, its source equals its target, and its target is the source of a
stored arrow $f$, then COMPOSE of $i$ and $f$ succeeds and $if \cong f$.
(4) If $i$ is flagged, its source equals its target, and the target of a stored arrow $f$ is
the source of $i$, then COMPOSE of $f$ and $i$ succeeds and $fi \cong f$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
COMPOSE of two stored arrows whose ends match always succeeds, stores the composite under
the next arrow identifier, and leaves every other identifier where it was. (1) is the first
case of the rule. (2) Well-formedness says every stored identifier is below the next one, so
$f$ and $h$ are still found after the first COMPOSE on each side. Both composites go from the
source of $f$ to the target of $h$, and both carry the flag exactly when all three of $f$, $k$,
$h$ do. If the flag is off, at least one of the three is unflagged, and there are seven
cases, one per pattern of flags; in each, item (1) of Theorem~\ref{thm:u18-coupling-laws} turns both
sides into the same membership condition. With none flagged it's associativity on pairs;
with only $k$ flagged both sides are the pairs of $f$ composed with the pairs of $h$; with
two flagged both sides are the third arrow's pairs. (3) If $f$ is flagged, so is $if$, and
both go from the source of $f$ to its target, so there is nothing more to compare. If not,
$if$ has the pairs of $f$ with repeats removed, which the equivalence ignores. (4) is the
mirror.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{graph\_compose\_identities\_is\_identity} for (1), \code{graph\_compose\_assoc\_stored} for
(2), \code{graph\_compose\_left\_identity\_stored} for (3) and \code{graph\_compose\_right\_identity\_stored}
for (4) (CategoryBridge.v), with \code{graph\_compose\_stored}
and \code{composite\_record} underneath.

\begin{theorem}[Every stored identity is the identity of its object]\label{thm:u18-canonical}
Call a graph's identity arrows \emph{canonical} when every flagged arrow in it has its source equal
to its target and no pairs. (1) If a state's identity arrows are canonical and it steps on any
instruction, the new state's are canonical. (2) If $\mathrm{graph}(s)$ has no arrows and $s'$
is reachable from $s$, then the identity arrows of $\mathrm{graph}(s')$ are canonical.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) A case split over the step relation. MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ID stores an arrow from a module to itself with
no pairs. COMPOSE stores a flagged arrow only when both inputs are flagged, and then from the
source of the first to the target of the second, with no pairs; when both inputs are
canonical, those four ends are one object. MORPH and MORPH\_\allowbreak{}TENSOR store the flag off.
Deleting an arrow, or the cascade when PSPLIT or PMERGE removes a module, only removes arrows.
Every other step leaves the arrow list alone. (2) A graph with no arrows has nothing to check,
and (1) carries it along each step.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{identity\_arrows\_canonical} (the definition),
\code{vm\_step\_preserves\_identity\_arrows\_canonical} for (1), and
\code{vm\_reachable\_preserves\_identity\_arrows\_canonical} with
\code{vm\_reachable\_identity\_arrows\_canonical} for (2) (CategoryBridge.v). The initial state has no
arrows, so on every reachable state every flagged arrow meets the side condition of (3) and
(4) in Theorem~\ref{thm:u18-stored-laws}, and the identity laws hold for every identity arrow a
program can build. The chip's COMPOSE follows the same rule: two flagged arrows give a flagged
arrow whose coupling descriptor holds no pairs and the label ``empty'' (Section~\ref{sec:chip} has the chip).

So the stored arrows obey associativity and both identity laws, up to the sameness of
Definition~\ref{def:u18-stored-same}. Calling the whole thing a category in the full sense would
still take more: a Coq structure that packages the objects, the arrows and that sameness and
proves the laws once as an instance, and an account of a category whose objects and arrows
come and go as modules are split and merged. Neither is in the tree, and nothing above claims
either. The laws are each a theorem on their own.

Three more things Coq doesn't say, smaller. Nothing proves composition is defined on exactly
the right pairs beyond ``the first's target equals the second's source'' by number; a
mismatch gives the error branch. Nothing in the law files mentions that splitting or merging
a module deletes every arrow touching it, so an arrow's lifetime is bounded by its modules';
that's in the step rules (Section~\ref{sec:state}) and not in the laws. And the per-arrow field the comment says
records what was paid to certify it is never written (Section~\ref{sec:state} again), so ``a composite's cost
field is zero'' is a theorem about a field that's always zero.

\subsection{Why this isn't just extra state}

Here's the question I chewed on longest. If you can bolt extra registers onto an ordinary
machine and stash arrow identifiers in them, why does the arrow layer matter?

Because extra registers have no provenance. You can write 42 into register 5 and call it an
arrow. The machine checks: does arrow 42 exist in the graph, put there by a MORPH or a
COMPOSE that actually ran? MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT looks the arrow up and fails, setting the error flag,
if it isn't there. Existence is all it checks; it doesn't compare the source and target
against anything (you can read those back with MORPH\_\allowbreak{}GET), it stores a checksum of the
property string, overwriting whatever the channel held, and doesn't check what the property says, and it never reads the certificate
operand you hand it. And it costs at least one even when it fails. Building the chain, by
MORPH and COMPOSE and MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ID, is free at zero declared cost. Asserting it into the
assertion channel never is. You can build for nothing; you can't vouch for nothing. The
graph is structure the machine holds outright, and Section~\ref{sec:separation} shows two states that
differ in nothing \emph{but} that graph.

\subsection{Two small facts that matter later}

Failing arrow instructions still charge; the cost is on the attempt, like everything else.
And MORPH reads its coupling \emph{from memory}: a count word (capped at sixty-four, half the memory size, so a garbage count can't send the reader past the end of memory), then pairs,
then a label, and it drops every pair whose ends don't lie in the two regions. With zeroed
memory the count is zero and the coupling is empty, which matters for Section~\ref{sec:receipt}.

\begin{definition}[Loading a coupling from memory]\label{def:u18-load-coupling}
For a MORPH whose coupling block starts at word $b$, between modules with regions $X$ and
$Y$: let $k = \min(\mathrm{mem}[b], 64)$, read the pairs
$(\mathrm{mem}[b+1], \mathrm{mem}[b+2]), \dots, (\mathrm{mem}[b+2k-1], \mathrm{mem}[b+2k])$,
read a length-prefixed label starting at word $b + 1 + 2k$, and keep only the pairs $(a, c)$
with $a \in X$ and $c \in Y$.
\end{definition}

Checked as the definition \code{load\_coupling\_from\_mem} (VMState.v), with the cap
\code{serialized\_coupling\_pair\_count} (64 is half the memory size). Two Python tests outside Coq exercise
it with real data. One is the Python test
\code{test\_morph\_loads\_nonempty\_coupling\_from\_memory} (tests/test\_\allowbreak{}categorical\_\allowbreak{}opcodes.py), which
drives the extracted runner of Section~\ref{sec:state}. Its program writes the count 1 and the pair (0, 1) into
words 80 to 82, runs PNEW twice, once on cell 0 and once on cell 1, and then a MORPH from module 1 to module 2
with its coupling block at word 80; the test asserts that the error flag is down, that the
first arrow's identifier is 1, and that its stored coupling is exactly $[(0, 1)]$. The other,
\code{test\_morph\_reads\_upper\_half\_memory} (tests/test\_\allowbreak{}rtl\_\allowbreak{}morph\_\allowbreak{}opcodes.py), runs the hardware in
co-simulation, puts the pair (1, 2) at word 80, in the upper half of memory, makes modules on
cells 1 and 2, and expects $[(1, 2)]$. These are tests, not theorems. The laws of
Theorem~\ref{thm:u18-coupling-laws} hold for every list, so they cover nonempty couplings like these;
that the hardware's MORPH produces the same state as the kernel's is \code{driven\_step\_morph}
(GraphReconstructionBridge.v), under the hardware invariant and with both modules present
and nonempty.

So the machine has modules, arrows between them, and pairs of cells stapled to the arrows,
and Coq has checked the laws those pairs obey, on the lists and on the stored arrows, with the
identity flag carried through the one case where the obvious rule would break them. What none of it has yet is anything a module can be said to \emph{claim}. A coupling says
which cells correspond. It doesn't say anything is true about them. That's next.

%===========================================================================
\section{Claims a module can carry}
\label{sec:claims}
%===========================================================================

Here's the gap Section~\ref{sec:category} left open. Back in Part III, Section~\ref{sec:windows} ended by asking what the claim behind a
paid flag even is, and Section~\ref{sec:insight} answered that insight, at its best, is a relation committed to in
one priced step (Definition~\ref{def:u09-events} and the remark after it), talking about the
claim as if it were a thing. On a sheet of paper it can't be; the paper has a NO box and a
YES box and nothing to hang a claim on. The machine has plenty. Section~\ref{sec:state} gave it a state record
with a graph of modules in it, each owning a range of cells; Section~\ref{sec:isa} gave it fifty-one
instructions, two of which turn a certification reading on; Section~\ref{sec:category} gave it the arrows. Time to
make the claim a thing. The buckets in Section~\ref{sec:structure} were a sorting of a pile into groups, and I
promised the sorting would cost something, and then the whole middle of this book turned out
to be about raising a flag, and you'd be within your rights to ask what the flag has to do
with the buckets. Here's the link, and it's the oldest link in this book: a group is a thing
you can \emph{say something about}. ``Everything in this bucket is red.'' ``This region of memory
holds a sorted list.'' A group with nothing said about it is a label, and labels are cheap
because labels promise nothing. Calling a group ``module A'' commits you to exactly zero about
what's inside it. Structure that earns the name starts one step later, when you hang a claim
on a group and make the group answer for it.

\subsection{A question with a definite answer}

Two words, so I can say that cleanly, and both are in every logic textbook; I'm giving them
to you because the book promised no unexplained jargon, not because they're hard.

A \emph{predicate} states a precise condition on a thing. That gives the claim a meaning;
it does not, by itself, give an algorithm for deciding it.
``Is this number bigger than five'' is a predicate about a number. ``Does this region hold a
sorted list'' is a predicate about a region of memory. A predicate is the shape a claim takes
once its truth conditions are precise. The finite formulas used here can be checked
by the procedures below; that is an additional fact about these formulas. Notice what that rules out: ``this
code is well written'' isn't a predicate until you say what you'd check.

A \emph{formula} is a predicate built out of smaller yes-or-no pieces wired together with ``and,''
``or,'' and ``not.'' Take three switches, call them x1, x2, x3, each up (true) or down (false),
and the formula ``(x1 or x2) and (not x1 or x3).'' It comes out true exactly when at least one
of the first pair is up and, at the same time, at least one of the second pair is. George
Boole worked out in 1847 that you can do arithmetic on claims this way, treating ``and'' like
multiplication and ``or'' like a kind of addition, and that's the whole reason a machine can
check a claim at all: a formula is something you \emph{evaluate}, by plugging in switch positions
and turning the crank.

Why multiplication? Try it at the table. Write 1 for up and 0 for down, and multiply: one
times one is one, and anything times zero is zero. That's ``and'' to the letter: the product
is up only when both are. Then the stranger thing Boole noticed. Say ``x and x'' about one
switch and you've said nothing new; it's just x. In numbers that's $x \times x = x$, and he
made it a law of his system, and it's a law ordinary numbers mostly break. Which numbers
equal their own square? Try a few. Two times two is four, no. A half times a half is a
quarter, no. Zero, yes. One, yes. That's the whole list. So when Boole wrote his bigger book
in 1854, \emph{The Laws of Thought}, he asked you to imagine an algebra whose letters take the
values 0 and 1 and nothing else. Every switch in this section lives in that algebra.

And the 1847 book has a backstory worth a detour. Boole was largely self-taught and spent
about fifteen years as a schoolmaster, and what pulled him back to logic, early in 1847, was a
loud public quarrel between Augustus De Morgan and the Scottish philosopher Sir William
Hamilton over who had first thought of a small technical idea in the old logic of
syllogisms. Two well-known men fighting over credit, and a schoolmaster watching from the side
picks up the subject and writes the little book this paragraph is about. Few people remember
what the quarrel was over. Every switch in this section runs on what the bystander wrote.

Then push on it, because Boole's ``or'' isn't quite the switches' ``or.'' His plus only made
sense for things that can't both hold at once, so ``x or y'' with both of them up had no
meaning in his system. In 1864 William Stanley Jevons, in a book called \emph{Pure Logic},
read ``or'' as ``either or both,'' which gives ``x or x is x,'' the same trick as before, and he
wrote to Boole saying plus ought to work that way. Boole wouldn't have it, since it broke the
tie to ordinary algebra his whole system stood on. The switches above use Jevons's ``or'': the
first clause is true when x1 and x2 are both up. Does that change anything about the checker?
No; the crank turns the same way on every formula in this book. It changes the picture: the
``or'' the switches use is the one the man who invented the algebra turned down.

Do it. Set x1 up, x2 down, x3 up. First clause: x1 is up, so true. Second clause: not x1 is
false, but x3 is up, so true. Both true, so the formula is true: that choice of switch
positions is called a \emph{satisfying assignment}, and you just found one. Now set x3 down
instead. Second clause: not x1 is false, x3 is false, so the clause is false, so the formula
is false. That's a \emph{falsifying assignment}. You've now done everything a checker does. The
checker has no cleverness in it; it has a formula, a row of switch positions, and a crank.

\subsection{Hang it on a group}

Now take a group of memory cells and say: ``the values in this group make this formula true.''
That's a constraint hung on a group, and the formula can carry real content: every value
here sits between zero and a hundred; this region encodes a satisfying assignment to the
formula sitting over in that other region; this region is sorted. Tony Hoare, in 1969, built
a whole way of reasoning about programs out of exactly this move: attach a claim to a \emph{point}
in a program (``whenever execution reaches here, this is true''), and reason forward from
claim to claim. Robert Floyd had done it two years earlier on flowcharts. Their claims were
checked on paper by the person writing the proof. The machine's version is a formula and two
rows in memory, checked by a step while it runs, and I'll be straight about it: the check
names no module and no region. The machine has the pieces. It doesn't join them.

And is two years earlier the bottom? Not even close, and the next step down is a paper this
book already leaned on. In June 1949, at a Cambridge conference held for the new EDSAC
computer, Alan Turing gave a talk three pages long, ``Checking a large routine,'' the same note
the counter chapter used for stopping (Section~\ref{sec:counter}). Stopping was the second half
of it. The first half is this section's move, twenty years before Hoare: the programmer should
make ``definite assertions which can be checked individually,'' and the correctness of the
whole should follow from them. His example program computes a factorial using nothing but
addition, and his picture for why you'd bother is one you can do on the back of an envelope.
Add up a long column of four-digit numbers and hand someone only the total, and they have to
redo the whole sum at one sitting, because the carries tie every column to the one before it.
Hand them the total of each column as well, and the job falls apart into small checks they can
do one at a time. That's a claim hung on a point in the middle of the work, so the person
checking never has to hold all of it at once. The paper got its due mostly later: in 1984
F. L. Morris and C. B. Jones republished it, with its misprints corrected, as an early program
proof by Alan Turing. Does any of that change the machine? No. It changes the date on the idea,
and it tells you something I like: the first person to ask how you'd check a program put the
claims in the middle of it, not at the end.

And here's the thing I most want you to see, because it's where ``structure'' and ``cost''
finally touch. A claim hung on a group \emph{rules things out}. Before the constraint, the cells
could hold anything. After it, they can only hold values that make the formula true. That's
the fifth item on Section~\ref{sec:structure}'s list, ``adding structure rules possibilities out,'' made concrete:
a formula on a region is a partition of all the ways the region could be filled into ``allowed''
and ``not,'' and the checked assignment is the proof that the allowed side isn't empty.

\subsection{A label is not a check}

Now the part I'm going to belabour, because it's the single most common way to fool
yourself with a machine like this.

Section~\ref{sec:state}'s state record stores, next to each module, a list of strings it calls axioms.
You'd think you could write ``sorted'' in a list like that and see what happens. Go looking
for the step that reads that list and tests memory against it, and there isn't one. Nor does
any step write it: every module the steps create starts with an empty list and keeps it, and a
merge or a split removes the modules it acts on, lists and all, and makes its new modules with
empty lists. A function that appends
to the list exists in the Coq model, and no step calls it. So the list is a field the machine
carries and nothing more. It's a label, and one a program can't even write. Whatever you put
in it would cost nothing and prove nothing, and you should hear that from the person who built
the thing. Try it with a card: write 5, 2, 9 on it, and underneath write
``sorted.'' Hand it to someone and have them check each neighbouring pair. The second check
fails. The label sat there the whole time.

\begin{remark}[What the steps do with the label lists]\label{rem:u10-labels}
Each module in the state carries a list of strings, its axiom list. Read off the definition
of the step function: no rule reads any axiom list. A step that makes a new module gives it
the empty list, and one asked for a range that is already a module's returns that module
unchanged. The steps that split and merge modules delete the modules they act on and create
their new modules with empty lists. Every other rule leaves the lists of existing modules as
they were. The helper that appends to a list (\code{graph\_add\_axiom}, with
\code{graph\_record\_discovery} built on it, both in VMState.v) is called by no rule. So along any
run, every module's list is either the list it had at the start or empty. This is an inspection of the definitions (\code{vm\_apply} in
SimulationProof.v, \code{graph\_pnew} in VMState.v, \code{graph\_hw\_psplit} and \code{graph\_hw\_pmerge} in
VMStep.v), not a named theorem.
\end{remark}

A \emph{check} is different. The machine has one step whose whole job is to read a formula from
memory, read two rows of switch positions from memory, and turn the crank. Section~\ref{sec:isa}'s table lists
it as LASSERT, in one row; here's what the row leaves out. The formula is
stored in a fixed layout: a word saying how long it is, a word for the number of switches, a
word for the number of clauses, and then the clauses, each a list of signed numbers (plus
for the switch, minus for ``not the switch,'' zero to end the clause). The two rows sit back to
back with each other, at a separate address that a second register holds: first a row that's
supposed to satisfy the formula, then a row that's supposed to falsify it. (The step also
carries a flag for which kind of certificate it's checking, and one setting of that flag
always traps. I'm describing the setting that does the work.) The step checks both. If the
first row doesn't satisfy, or the second
row doesn't falsify, or the length written in the instruction doesn't match the length
written in memory, the step \emph{traps}: it jumps to a fixed error address, sets an error flag,
and leaves memory, registers, and the modules exactly as they were. If both rows check, it
goes on to the next instruction.

Two things about that step that I think are the right design and want to defend. First, it
charges whether it passes or fails: the formula's length times eight, plus its declared cost,
plus one, every time.
You pay to check, not to be right; Popper again. (The eight is a pricing convention, not a
byte count; the file says so.) Second, and this is why there are \emph{two} rows: a formula that
\emph{every} assignment satisfies rules nothing out, so a satisfying row alone proves nothing
about structure, and the falsifying row is the cheap proof that the formula isn't that kind
of formula, that it's a real constraint with a real ``not allowed'' side. The source's name for
what the second row stops is ``tautology inflation.'' Try ``x1 or not x1'': write out both rows
and you'll find no falsifying one exists, so the step would refuse it. And the empty formula,
with no clauses at all, is the simplest tautology, and it's refused too.

Here is the check, exactly as the step runs it. In the symbols, $\lor$ is ``or,'' $\land$ is
``and,'' and $\lnot$ is ``not,'' the same three words the switches used.

\begin{definition}[The formula check]\label{def:u10-check}
Let $m$ be data memory, $f$ the value of the instruction's first register and $b$ the value of
its second. The formula words are $w_j = m(f + j)$ for $0 \le j < 3 + m(f)$: $w_0$ is the
length written in memory, $w_1 = v$ the number of switches, $w_2 = q$ the number of clauses,
and from $w_3$ on come the literals, each read as a signed 32-bit number, with $0$ closing a
clause. An assignment $a$ maps switch numbers to words, and switch $x$ is up when
$a(x) \ne 0$. $\mathrm{Sat}(w, a)$ scans the literals in order, keeping a count of closed
clauses: it is true as soon as the count reaches $q$; it is false if a clause closes with no
literal made true by $a$ (a positive literal $x$ is true when $x$ is up, a negative literal
$-x$ when $x$ is down), or if the words run out first. The satisfying row is
$a_1(x) = m(b + x)$ and the falsifying row is $a_2(x) = m(b + v + x)$. For the checking step with
kind flag $k$ and declared length $\ell$, the check \emph{passes}, written $\mathrm{ok}$, when
$m(f) = \ell$, $k$ is the satisfiable kind, $\mathrm{Sat}(w, a_1)$ is true, and
$\mathrm{Sat}(w, a_2)$ is false.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[What the check step does]\label{thm:u10-lassert}
Let $i$ be the checking step with kind $k$, declared length $\ell$ and declared cost $c_0$, and let
$s' = \mathrm{apply}(s, i)$. Then $s'$ has the same graph, registers, memory, certified flag
and assertion channel as $s$, and $\mu(s') = \mu(s) + 8\ell + c_0 + 1$. If $\mathrm{ok}$, the
program counter advances by one and the error flag is unchanged. If not, the program counter
becomes the fixed trap address $3840$ and the error flag is set.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
This is the checking step's case of the step function, read field by field: $\mathrm{ok}$ is a pure
function of $s$, and each field of $s'$ is written as stated. The counter line is
conservation for this instruction, whose price is $8\ell + c_0 + 1$.
\end{proof}

Checked as the checking step's case of \code{vm\_apply} (SimulationProof.v) and the rule \code{step\_lassert}
(VMStep.v), with the check as \code{lassert\_exec\_ok} and \code{lassert\_check\_ok} (VMStep.v) over
\code{check\_model\_binary\_fn} and \code{check\_countermodel\_binary\_fn} (CertCheck.v). The pieces are named
in \code{vm\_apply\_lassert\_pc} (DagRestriction.v) and \code{vm\_apply\_mu} (MuLedgerConservation.v); on a
step that doesn't trap, the declared length equals the one in memory, \code{lassert\_honest\_cost}
(StateSpaceCounting.v).

\begin{remark}[Why a tautology cannot pass]\label{rem:u10-tautology}
Argued from Definition~\ref{def:u10-check}; there is no separate Coq theorem. If the check
passes, the scan with $a_1$ reaches $q$ closing zeros, so the words hold $q$ complete
clauses. The scan with $a_2$ sees the same words and the same closing zeros, so it can only
fail at a clause that closes with no true literal: $a_2$ makes some clause false. Hence a
formula that every assignment satisfies, such as $x_1 \lor \lnot x_1$, never passes, and
neither does the formula with $q = 0$, which the scan accepts for every row.
\end{remark}

And third, which is subtle and easy to get wrong: \emph{this step doesn't turn either reading on.}
It checks, and it changes nothing it checked. Its evidence is in the run: the program counter
kept going and the error flag stayed off. Turning a reading on is a \emph{different} step,
MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT, which puts a property on an arrow (Section~\ref{sec:insight}'s ``commit''), or CERTIFY, the bare step
that raises the certified flag (Section~\ref{sec:isa} has both), and nothing forces either to be adjacent to the
check. A flag raised by the bare step carries no check at all. Check and commit are two acts
with two prices, and the machine, correctly I think, refuses to pretend they're one. What
that does to Section~\ref{sec:insight}'s test-then-commit protocol on this machine is Section~\ref{sec:machine-claims}'s to show.

\subsection{Who checks the checker}

A fast checker that might be wrong just moves the trust somewhere else, and in 2005 Henk
Barendregt and Freek Wiedijk gave this worry a name, the de Bruijn criterion, after the
logician who insisted on it: a proof system is trustworthy when its proofs can be checked by
a checker \emph{small enough that a person can audit it}, independent of whatever clever tool
produced the proof. Euclid had the instinct: five postulates you can hold in your head, and
everything else meant to follow from them. The machine's checker is of that kind. In the
chip I build at the end of the book it's a controller with three phases (idle, read the
formula's header, scan) that walks the formula word by word. The proofs hold it up against the kernel (Section~\ref{sec:onemachine}'s name for
the machine's reference definition in Coq, the step function every proof in this part is
about), and they show its word-by-word scan returns the same answer as the kernel's
two checks, as long as the formula declares at least one clause, its words
hold an end-of-clause zero for every clause it declares, and every word fits in thirty-two
bits. It also proves that the hardware step and the kernel step agree on the counter always,
and on the program counter whenever the check passes. ``The hardware step'' there is Coq's
model of it, which keeps every field as a whole number with no thirty-two-bit bound; on the
chip's own registers the agreement needs the counter to stay below $2^{32}$, and
Section~\ref{sec:chip} states it with that premise (Theorem~\ref{thm:u25-lassert}). The same
theorem pins the kernel's
error flag to the check's outcome, unchanged on a pass and set on a fail.
That's a fact about the hardware and it's Section~\ref{sec:chip}'s to show; I mention it here so you know the
checker isn't a black box, and so you know where to find the trusted base, which is short and
listed in Section~\ref{sec:coq}.

The question in this subsection's title is older than any checker, and its most famous
wording isn't about what you'd guess. ``Who will guard the guardians?'' gets quoted about
governments and police and, lately, proof assistants, and it often gets pinned on Plato. Push
on that. Plato's \emph{Republic} has the worry, sort of: in Book III, Glaucon says it would be
absurd for a guardian to need a guardian, which is close in words and opposite in mood, a man
calling the question silly. The Latin, \emph{quis custodiet ipsos custodes}, is from the Roman
satirist Juvenal's sixth satire, and it's a joke about a husband. His friends tell him to bolt
his wife in and set guards on her; the line asks who'll watch the guards, since she'll start
with them. And it gets better. In 1899 an Oxford undergraduate, E. O. Winstedt, found extra
lines of that satire in a medieval manuscript in the Bodleian Library, lines the other copies
lack, partly overlapping the familiar ones, and the famous question sits in that tangle.
Scholars have argued ever since about whether those lines are Juvenal's at all. So the most
quoted sentence about trusting the checker comes with a doubtful source of its own. Does that
change anything here? No. De Bruijn's answer is still the only one I know that works: you
never get rid of the last guard, you make the last guard small enough to watch yourself.

The two hardware facts, stated so their premises are in view. Two words first: a \emph{hardware snapshot} is the chip's whole state at one tick of its clock, written the way Coq's hardware model keeps it, with whole numbers and no thirty-two-bit bound, and $\alpha$ reads off which
kernel state that snapshot stands for. Section~\ref{sec:chip} builds both, and nothing else in this part of the
book leans on them. (Yes, these are theorems about a chip I have never held in my hand. Section~\ref{sec:chip}
is very upfront about that.)

\begin{theorem}[The chip's scan is the kernel's check]\label{thm:u10-hw-scan}
(1) Let the formula words be $w_0, w_1, q$ followed by literal words $u$, and let $g_1$, $g_2$
be the two rows. If $1 \le q$, $u$ contains at least $q$ zeros, and every word of $u$ is below
$2^{32}$, then the hardware scan of $u$ returns
$\mathrm{Sat}(w, g_1) \wedge \lnot \mathrm{Sat}(w, g_2)$. (2) For every hardware snapshot $h$
and every checking instruction $i$, write $\alpha(h)$ for the kernel state the snapshot stands
for. There is a kernel state $s'$ that the kernel's step relation reaches from $\alpha(h)$
under $i$ such that: $\mu(s')$ equals the hardware counter after the model's step, with no
bound on its size; if
$\mathrm{ok}$ holds at $\alpha(h)$, the hardware program counter after the step equals that of
$s'$; and the error flag of $s'$ is unchanged when $\mathrm{ok}$ holds and set otherwise.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Induction on the literal words, with an invariant that ties the scanner's three bits
(current clause met by the first row, current clause met by the second row, some earlier
clause already missed by the second row) and its clause countdown to where the two kernel
scans stand. (2) Composes three lemmas about the hardware model:
the kernel step exists, the two counters agree, and the program counters agree on a pass.
Section~\ref{sec:chip} goes through both.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{hw\_scan\_certcheck} (LassertSpec.v), from \code{hw\_scan\_spec}, and
\code{logic\_engine\_equivalent\_lassert} (LogicEngineEquivalence.v).

So the little checker in the chip and the check the proofs talk about give the same verdict,
as long as the formula meets those three conditions, and the model of the chip's counter
moves the way the kernel's does, which on the chip itself holds below $2^{32}$.

\subsection{Where, not just how much}

Last piece, and it's the one that the counter in Section~\ref{sec:counter} can't give you. The counter is a total.
Two different runs can end at the same total having checked different things in different
places. ``Did this run check the sorting constraint before it used the sorted list'' is not a
question the total can answer, any more than a grocery total of twenty-three dollars and forty
cents can tell you whether you bought milk. The itemised receipt can. The run gives you the
itemised receipt: which step ran, what it charged (the checked work reads a ledger off the
run, one entry per step, and the entries add up to the counter's rise), and
whether the error flag came on. A run somebody else hands you needs its own evidence before
you trust that receipt.

The itemised receipt has a history, and it's the history of exactly this gap. James Ritty ran a
saloon in Dayton, Ohio, and believed some of his staff were pocketing money. On a steamboat
trip to Europe in 1878 he watched a mechanism that counted the turns of the ship's propeller,
and wondered whether something like it could count the money instead. In 1879 he and his
brother John patented a ``Cash Register and Indicator,'' and they sold a version under the
wonderful name Ritty's Incorruptible Cashier. The first model was this book's counter
(Section~\ref{sec:counter}) with brass on it: press a key, the amount goes onto a dial showing
the day's running total. No drawer, no paper. At closing time you hold the dial up against the
cash. And that's all a total can do. It tells you \emph{that} the money is short, never which
sale went missing or who rang it up. The paper came later. The patents passed to other owners
and in 1884 to John H. Patterson's National Cash Register Company, and the story told about
that company is that it added a paper roll: one copy kept for the shop's own books, one handed
to the customer. That last part I only have from histories of the company and of the machine,
so hold it the way you'd hold any company's story about itself. The order is right either
way: first a total that can tell you something's wrong, then a list that tells you where. A run
gives you the second kind.

And the rule I named No Free Insight back in Section~\ref{sec:narrowing} has a \emph{where}. ``Structural gain'' is what I call it when
some step of a run takes the assertion channel from clear to set, the machine-wide reading
that says some label was asserted on some arrow. The shallow question is whether the channel
was clear at the start and is set at the end, and you settle it by holding the first state
next to the last. The machine isn't built for the shallow question. It's built for \emph{which step}. Walk
the run and find a step where the assertion channel went from clear to set; there's always
at least one such step when the channel is set at the end and was clear at the start, and
that step cost at least one, and the cost can sit nowhere else. In the checked work the
located version is a predicate on runs, \code{structure\_addition\_in\_run}, which says some step is
such a step. The gain
has a location. The location has a price. That's No Free Insight, said with the claim behind
it finally in view: a formula in memory, checked by a small auditable checker, and a label
asserted on an arrow by a step you can point at.

The located gain, exactly, with $\mathrm{run}(n, p, s)$ the run of program $p$ from $s$ with
fuel $n$ (Definition~\ref{def:u17-step}) and $\mathrm{addr}(s)$ the assertion channel, which
Section~\ref{sec:isa} writes $\mathrm{certaddr}(s)$.

\begin{definition}[Structural gain, located]\label{def:u10-gain}
The run $\mathrm{run}(n, p, s)$ has a \emph{structural gain} when some step it executes goes from a
state with $\mathrm{addr} = 0$ to a state with $\mathrm{addr} \ne 0$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The gain has a place and a price]\label{thm:u10-gain}
(1) If $\mathrm{addr}(s) = 0$ and $\mathrm{addr}(\mathrm{run}(n, p, s)) \ne 0$, the run has a
structural gain. (2) The run has a structural gain exactly when, at some step it executes
from a state whose channel is $0$, the instruction at the program counter is an assertion step
that names an arrow in the current graph and carries a label of nonzero checksum. (3) Each such
step costs at least one. (4) If $p$ contains no assertion step, no run of $p$ has a structural
gain.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Induction on the fuel. At each executed step either the channel turns nonzero, which is
a structural gain, or it is still zero and the rest of the run starts again from a clear
channel; a run that stops with the channel still zero ends at zero, which contradicts the end.
(2) From a state with channel $0$, one step makes the channel nonzero exactly in the stated
case, by part (3) of Theorem~\ref{thm:u17-channel}; then induction on the fuel. (3) The
assertion step is priced at its declared cost plus one (Definition~\ref{def:u17-cost}), and
any step that takes the channel from $0$ to nonzero costs at least one
(Theorem~\ref{thm:u17-nfi}). (4) follows from (2).
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{supra\_cert\_implies\_structure\_addition\_in\_run},
\code{structure\_addition\_in\_run\_iff\_morph\_assert\_bridge\_pattern},
\code{morph\_assert\_step\_sets\_supra\_cert\_iff} and \code{non\_morph\_assert\_trace\_has\_no\_structure\_addition}
(RevelationRequirement.v), with the price from \code{no\_free\_certification} (AbstractNoFI.v).

\begin{remark}[Clear at the start and set at the end is the stronger reading]\label{rem:u10-gain-converse}
The converse of (1) fails, argued from part (2) of Theorem~\ref{thm:u17-channel} and not
checked as a theorem: a run can set the channel and later run an assertion whose label has checksum $0$,
which writes $0$ back. That run has a structural gain and ends with the channel clear. So the
shallow question (first state against last) and the located one (which step) can come apart,
and the files answer the located one.
\end{remark}

One more boundary and then I'll stop. A satisfying row and a falsifying row prove that the
formula can be met and isn't trivial. They don't prove the formula \emph{means} what the label
next to it says. ``sorted'' in the axiom list and a checked formula in memory are two things
with no wire between them, and wiring them is a job for a proved encoding, which is a
separate piece of work. The step checks the formula. The label is still a label.

So: what a flag could stand for is a formula, which the machine can check in one step and
which a different step can mark with a label. Nothing in the machine joins the two, or either
to a module. The check is separate from the commit, and the commit has a place in the run.

Notice where everything in this section lives. The formula and its two rows sit in memory, the
labels sit on the modules, the arrows that get asserted sit in the graph. Memory an ordinary
computer has. The graph it doesn't. Which raises a question I can't dodge: if somebody looks at
this machine the way they'd look at an ordinary computer, reading registers, memory, the
counter, the program counter, the error flag and the certified flag, and nothing else, can
they even tell whether the graph is there? Two states that look the same to that reader and
differ in exactly the part that carries the claims: that's Section~\ref{sec:separation}.

%===========================================================================
\section{Two states that look the same}
\label{sec:separation}
%===========================================================================

Section~\ref{sec:windows} said: a window that doesn't show a thing can't recover it, because two states that look
the same through it have to get the same answer (Theorem~\ref{thm:fibre}, decoders need constant
fibres). Section~\ref{sec:windows}'s own pairs were about the flag and its
price, and they're Section~\ref{sec:witness}'s to show. This section's pair is about the graph. Here it is, and
it's smaller than you'd think, and then a caveat that has to go with it, and then a second
pair, built on a step, whose caveat is smaller.

Said without the word ``fibre'': anything that only looks through a window has to give the same
answer to two states the window shows the same. Think of identical twins and one passport
photo. A border guard who goes only by the photo waves both of them through or neither, and no
amount of staring at the photo changes that. If the two need different answers, the photo was
the wrong thing to be looking at.

\subsection{The pair}

Take two states. Both have an empty register file and empty memory, program counter zero,
counter zero, error flag down, certified flag down, all eight witness counters zero, a
sixteen-zero tensor, and \emph{no modules at all}. They agree on every one of those. Both have
the fresh-identifier counters at one. In the first state, the arrow list holds one arrow:
source module zero, target module zero, empty coupling, identity flag on, cost field zero,
and its own number is zero. In the second state, the arrow list is empty.

That's it. Six fields an ordinary observer reads (registers, memory, counter, program
counter, error, certified): identical. The rest of the record: identical. One list with one
entry versus one list with none. The theorem is \code{categorical\_separation}: there exist two
states that are \emph{computationally equivalent} (agree on those six) and \emph{categorically
distinct} (different arrow lists). The proof is reflexivity six times and one \code{discriminate}
on a list with an entry against a list without. It's as short as a Coq proof gets.

Two things the same in everything you look at and still two things: philosophy has an old
fight about exactly that, and it's worth a detour, because it tells you which side of the
fight this theorem stands on. Leibniz said it can't happen, not for real things. There are no
two individuals indiscernible from each other, he wrote to Samuel Clarke in 1716, and he told a
story to go with it. A clever gentleman of his acquaintance, talking with him in front of the
Electress Sophia in the garden at Herrenhausen, thought he could find two leaves perfectly
alike. She dared him to. He ``ran all over the Garden a long time'' looking, and it was ``to no
purpose.'' You can run his search tonight with a handful of anything, leaves or coins or grains
of rice: look hard enough and every pair differs somewhere. Then in 1952 Max Black pushed back
with a universe you can't build at the table. Nothing in it but two iron spheres, the same
size, the same colour, the same everything, some distance apart. Name a difference between
them. There isn't one, and there are still two of them. People have argued about Black's
spheres ever since, and I'm not going to settle it.

Here's why I don't have to. Leibniz's claim is about \emph{every} property a thing has. The
theorem above is about six. The two states aren't indiscernible in his sense at all: one has an
arrow and the other doesn't, and Coq tells them apart with a single \code{discriminate}. They're
indiscernible to a window, which is a much cheaper thing, and it's the thing that matters for a
machine, because an observer of a machine only ever gets a window. Leibniz's gentleman would
always find his difference if he could look at everything. It doesn't help him if all he's
allowed to look at is six things about each leaf.

\begin{definition}[Equivalent and distinct]\label{def:u19-equivalent}
Machine states $s_1$ and $s_2$ are \emph{computationally equivalent} when they have equal
registers, memory, counter $\mu$, program counter, error flag and certified flag. They are
\emph{categorically distinct} when their arrow lists differ.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[The separation pair]\label{def:u19-pair}
Let $s_A$ and $s_B$ both have empty registers and memory, program counter 0, $\mu = 0$, error
and certified flags false, all four control and status words 0, logic accumulator and mode
word 0, all eight witness counters 0, the tensor of sixteen zeros, and a graph with no
modules, next module number 1 and next arrow number 1. The arrow list of $s_A$ is the single
entry numbered 0: source 0, target 0, empty coupling with empty label, identity flag on, cost
field 0. The arrow list of $s_B$ is empty.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Categorical separation]\label{thm:u19-separation}
There are states $s_1$ and $s_2$ that are computationally equivalent and categorically
distinct; $s_A$ and $s_B$ are such a pair.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The six fields are equal field by field, by construction. The arrow lists are a list with
one entry and the empty list, which are different constructors.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{categorical\_separation} (PartitionSeparation.v), with the definitions
\code{computationally\_equivalent} and \code{categorically\_distinct} from the same file; the named
copies of the two states are \code{separation\_A} and \code{separation\_B} (ShadowProjection.v).

From it, the corollaries you'd expect. Any observer whose verdict depends only on the six
fields gives the same verdict on both (\code{classical\_observer\_cannot\_separate}); any yes/no
test of that kind can't tell them apart; any function that factors through the six-field
projection is constant on the pair (\code{no\_classical\_separation}); and the
difference survives a probe step, an ADD of nothing to nothing: after it the arrow lists
still differ (\code{shadow\_separation\_theorem}, \code{shadow\_strictly\_lossy}). ADD is a classical
instruction, one that writes a register and nothing in the graph, which is why it makes a
boring probe. And the plain statement that two distinct states can have equal shadow is the
last of the four parts of the degenerate-projection theorem; its parts two to four are the
quotient theorem just below, and Section~\ref{sec:witness} says what its first part is.

\begin{definition}[The shadow]\label{def:u19-shadow}
The \emph{shadow} of a machine state $s$ is the six-field record
$\mathrm{sh}(s) = (\text{registers}, \text{memory}, \text{program counter}, \mu,
\text{error flag}, \text{certified flag})$. It drops the graph, the control and status words,
the witness counters, the mode word, the logic accumulator and the tensor.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The shadow separation theorem]\label{thm:u19-shadow-separation}
There are states $s_1$, $s_2$ and an instruction $p$ with (1) $\mathrm{sh}(s_1) =
\mathrm{sh}(s_2)$, (2) the arrow lists of $s_1$ and $s_2$ differ, and (3) the arrow lists of
the states after one step by $p$ from $s_1$ and from $s_2$ differ. Moreover, for every type
$T$ and every function $f$ from states to $T$ such that $\mathrm{sh}(s) = \mathrm{sh}(s')$
implies $f(s) = f(s')$, $f(s_A) = f(s_B)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Take $s_A$, $s_B$ and $p$ = ADD into register 0 from registers 0 and 0 at cost 0. (1) and
(2) are Theorem~\ref{thm:u19-separation}. For (3), ADD changes registers, program counter and $\mu$ and
leaves the graph as it was, so each graph after the step equals the graph before. The last
part applies the hypothesis on $f$ to (1).
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{shadow\_separation\_theorem}, \code{shadow\_strictly\_lossy} (the same three facts with
the shadow equality written out) and \code{no\_classical\_separation} (ShadowProjection.v); the
yes/no version is \code{classical\_bool\_test\_indistinguishable} and the observer version
\code{classical\_observer\_cannot\_separate} (PartitionSeparation.v).

\subsection{The window is a quotient}

Here's another way to say what the pair shows. The shadow
is a map that sorts every state into a bin, one bin per six-field record. Two states share a
bin exactly when they agree on the six fields; that's all a bin is. A window that reads only
the shadow can only ever answer ``which bin,'' so it's blind to everything that varies inside
a bin. The pair says the graph varies inside a bin. That's what ``the window forgets the graph''
means, said precisely.

\begin{theorem}[The shadow is a lossy quotient]\label{thm:u19-quotient}
(1) $\mathrm{sh}(s_1) = \mathrm{sh}(s_2)$ exactly when $s_1$ and $s_2$ agree on registers,
memory, program counter, $\mu$, error flag and certified flag. (2) Let $s_1$ and $s_2$ have
equal shadows, equal graphs and equal control and status words. Then for every list of classical
instructions run in order from each, the two final states have equal shadows. (3) There are
distinct states with equal shadows.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Two records are equal exactly when their fields are. (2) By induction on the list: each
classical instruction computes the shadow, graph and control and status words of its result
from the shadow, graph and control and status words of its input, so agreement on those three passes
from step to step. (3) is $s_A$ and $s_B$.
\end{proof}

Checked as parts (2) to (4) of \code{degenerate\_projection\_theorem} (TuringClassicalEmbedding.v),
which are \code{shadow\_proj\_kernel\_is\_eq\_on\_classical\_shadow}, \code{classical\_run\_preserves\_shadow\_compat}
and \code{shadow\_strictly\_lossy}. Part (2) needs the equal graphs and control and status words, and the
file says why: MORPH\_\allowbreak{}GET and TENSOR\_\allowbreak{}GET are classical but read the graph, and the heap
instructions read one of the control and status words, the heap base. So a classical run is
a function of the bin together with the graph and those words, not of the bin alone.

\subsection{The caveat}

Now the caveat. The first state has an arrow
whose source and target are module zero, and \emph{there is no module zero}; the module list is
empty. So the first state is not well-formed by Section~\ref{sec:state}'s three clauses, and since every step
preserves well-formedness, it's not reachable from the initial state. (There's a second
reason, independent of the first: both states have an empty register file and an empty
memory, and every reachable state has sixteen registers and a hundred and twenty-eight
words.) The theorem is about the \emph{type} of states, not about states a run can get to. The pair is as simple
as a pair gets, as a type-level pair. As a claim about what a running machine can do, it says
nothing.

\begin{remark}[Why neither state of the pair is reachable]\label{rem:u19-unreachable}
Let $Z(s)$ say that $s$ has exactly 16 registers and exactly 128 memory words. No step turns
$Z$ from true to false, and the initial state has $Z$ true, so every state reachable from it
has $Z$ true. Both $s_A$ and $s_B$ have empty registers and memory, so $Z$ is false for both,
and neither is reachable.
\end{remark}

Checked as \code{eg\_size\_permanent} (EventGeneralization.v), with the initial state's sizes from
its definition (MuInitiality.v). The other reason in the text, the arrow whose ends name a
module that doesn't exist, rests on Section~\ref{sec:state}'s well-formedness clauses and is not restated here.

Does that gut it? No, and here's why not: the type-level pair is enough for the \emph{shape} of
the claim (the projection is many-to-one on the type, full stop), and a second pair
exists below, built on a step from the initial state, with no caveat of that kind. But it's a real distinction
and I'd rather you have it than find it.

\subsection{A step the shadow can't see}

Here's a pair built on a step, and it's the strictness theorem. Start where every run starts:
the initial state of Definition~\ref{def:u16-init}, with no modules and the next module number
at zero. Take one step: create a module on address zero (PNEW on the single cell zero, which
is inside memory, owned by nobody, with module numbers to spare, so no trap). The fresh-module
counter goes from zero to one. Now consider every \emph{classical} run from the same start: any
sequence of steps, each by one of the twenty-nine opcodes the source calls classical (Section~\ref{sec:isa}
lists them in Definition~\ref{def:u17-classical}: arithmetic, loads, stores, jumps, the heap, the
ports, and MORPH\_\allowbreak{}GET and TENSOR\_\allowbreak{}GET, which read the graph and write nothing), in any order the
program's jumps pick. None of them touches the graph, so after any such run the fresh-module
counter is still zero. One structural step changed a thing no classical run can change.

And it isn't a trick of the starting point. Stop a classical run anywhere, at any state it
reaches from the initial state, and the same PNEW is a step from there too, raising the
counter by one, while every classical run from there keeps it put. The state PNEW lands in has
a graph that no classical run from the initial state ever has. Nothing here is hand-built:
every state in the theorem is one the machine reaches.

\begin{definition}[Classical reachability]\label{def:u19-classical-reach}
A program is \emph{classical} when each of its instructions is one of the twenty-nine classical
opcodes. A state $s'$ is \emph{classically reachable} from $s$ when a chain of zero or more steps
leads from $s$ to $s'$ and each step is by a classical instruction; the steps can come in any
order, so a run whose jumps revisit instructions counts. Running a list means applying the
step to each instruction in order; the program-counter runner with fuel $F$ fetches the
instruction at the program counter $F$ times, following jumps.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Strictness, and with it conservativity]\label{thm:u19-strictness}
Let $p$ be PNEW on the region $[0]$ at cost 0. (1) For every state $s$ classically reachable
from the initial state $s_0$ (with $s = s_0$ allowed): $s$ is reachable from $s_0$; $p$ is a
step from $s$; that step raises the next module number by one and leaves the error flag as
it was; every state classically reachable from $s$ has the next module number of $s$, and
so does the state the program-counter runner reaches from $s$ on every classical program
with any fuel; and the graph after $p$ differs from the graph of every state classically
reachable from $s_0$. (2) At $s_0$ itself: after $p$ the next module number is 1, and every
classical program run by the program-counter runner from $s_0$, with any fuel, ends with next
module number 0. (3) For every state $s$ and every classical program, running it from $s$ as
a list, or under the program-counter runner with any fuel, leaves the graph, the assertion
channel and the certified flag as they were in $s$; so does every classically reachable
state.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(3) By induction on the list, on the fuel, or on the chain of steps: the program-counter
runner either stops or fetches an instruction of the program, which is classical, and no
classical instruction writes the graph, the assertion channel or the certified flag. (1) A
state classically reachable from $s_0$ therefore has $s_0$'s graph: no modules and next
module number 0. Memory has a hundred and twenty-eight words in every reachable state, so
cell 0 is inside it, no module overlaps it, and a module number is free, so PNEW does not trap
and adds a module, raising the next module number by one. Reachability holds because each
classical step is a step. Every state classically reachable from $s_0$ has next module number
0, and the graph after $p$ has 1, so the graphs differ. (2) is (1) at $s = s_0$ with the
program-counter half of (3).
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{pnew\_step\_separates\_thiele\_from\_classical\_reachable} (TuringStrictness.v; the
step is \code{separating\_pnew\_step}), \code{pnew\_step\_separates\_thiele\_from\_classical\_at\_init} for (2),
and \code{pnew\_step\_separates\_thiele\_from\_classical}, the existential form with the initial state
as witness. For (3): \code{classical\_opcodes\_preserve\_structure} (lists),
\code{classical\_opcodes\_preserve\_structure\_run\_vm} (the program-counter runner) and
\code{classical\_reachable\_preserves\_structure} (chains of steps), all in ClassicalConservativity.v,
with \code{classical\_reachable\_vm\_reachable} for reachability. \code{thiele\_strictly\_extends\_classical}
states (3) for both runners together with the separation of (1).

The standalone copy of the kernel has its own witness for the strictness shape, and that one
is on a hand-built base: the step is MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ID on module zero and the probe is MORPH\_\allowbreak{}DELETE of
arrow zero; after the identity arrow is built the probe succeeds, and after any classical run
it fails (\code{morph\_delete\_probe\_separates\_thiele\_from\_classical\_tc}, ThieleMachineComplete.v,
base \code{probe\_base\_state\_tc}). Same shape, different instruction, and the reachable version
above is the one I lean on.

\subsection{Three things the windows drop, each on its own}

The graph isn't the only thing riding along beside the ordinary fields. There are three: the
counter, the certified flag, and the graph. Each one can differ between two states while
everything else you'd look at holds still, including the other two. Five pairs of states show
it, one per claim. Four of them are one instruction away from a clean start, with CERTIFY on
at least one side. The fifth is the separation pair from the start of this section.

Write $Z_0$ for the clean start: everything empty or zero, no modules, no arrows. It is a
hand-built state, not the machine's initial state.

\begin{theorem}[Each of the three is independent of the others]\label{thm:u19-independence}
None of the following functions exists. (1) A function from (memory, registers, program
counter) to $\mu$, correct on every state. (2) The same, to the certified flag. (3) A
function from (memory, registers, program counter, $\mu$) to the certified flag. (4) A
function from (memory, registers, program counter, certified flag) to $\mu$. (5) A function
from (memory, registers, program counter, $\mu$, certified flag) to the graph.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Each is the same argument: two states with equal inputs and different outputs would force the
function to give two answers on one input. The pairs, all but the last one step from $Z_0$:
(1) and (2) CERTIFY at declared cost 0 ($\mu = 1$, flag on) against PNEW of the empty region at cost
0 ($\mu = 0$, flag off), both at program counter 1 with memory and registers untouched;
(3) CERTIFY at declared cost 2 against PNEW of the empty region at cost 3, both with $\mu = 3$,
flag on against flag off; (4) CERTIFY at declared cost 0 against CERTIFY at declared cost 1, both
flagged, $\mu = 1$ against $\mu = 2$; (5) $s_A$ and $s_B$.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{thiele\_state\_three\_component\_independence} (NecessityAbstract.v), the first
four parts being \code{mu\_ledger\_mutual\_independence} and the fifth
\code{graph\_not\_recoverable\_from\_P\_full}. In this kernel version the PNEW witnesses add a module,
so the graph differs inside pairs (1) to (3), and the graph is not among the inputs held
fixed there. The standalone copy of the machine has the stronger form, with the graph added
to the inputs of (1) to (4): the PNEW witnesses are replaced by JUMP to 1 at cost 0 and at
cost 3, which move only the program counter and $\mu$
(\code{mu\_ledger\_full\_pairwise\_independence}, with the records \code{FullStrictShadow},
\code{FullCostShadow} and \code{FullCertShadow}, ThieleMachineComplete.v). The agreement of that copy
with the kernel is tested, not proved.

Two things to keep beside this. First, it's a fact about the certified flag, not about any
flag you might put in its place. Replace the flag with an arbitrary reading that, once true,
stays true and that some step turns on, and the independence can fail: ``the registers and
memory have their full sizes'' is such a reading, and it's a function of (memory, registers,
program counter). That's checked as \code{mutual\_independence\_not\_event\_generic} and
\code{three\_component\_indep\_not\_event\_generic} (EventGeneralization.v). Second, the step that
sets the flag is itself a place where states run together: CERTIFY sends a state with the
flag off and the same state with the flag on to one and the same result, so the step by
CERTIFY is not one-to-one (\code{vm\_certify\_merges}, FiniteCertMachine.v). That's Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}'s room of
chairs on the real machine (Theorem~\ref{thm:perm-flip-merges}, a permanent flip merges).

The same shape answers a narrower question: which of these fields could a description that
sees only the ordinary part of the state recover? None of the three that matter here. Write
$\mathrm{fg}(s)$ for (program counter, $\mu$, registers, memory) and $\mathrm{bare}(s)$ for
(program counter, registers, memory).

\begin{theorem}[Three fields no bare window recovers]\label{thm:u19-irrecoverable}
(1) No function $\varphi$ of $\mathrm{fg}(s)$ equals the certified flag of $s$ for every $s$.
(2) No function of $\mathrm{bare}(s)$ equals $\mu$ for every $s$. (3) No function of
$\mathrm{fg}(s)$ equals the assertion channel of $s$ for every $s$. Equivalently, for
each given $\varphi$ the corresponding equation fails at some state.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Each uses two states that agree on the window and differ on the field. All six have program
counter 10, registers $[42, 0, 0, 0]$ and memory $[0, 0, 0, 0]$. (1) $\mu = 5$, certified
against uncertified. (2) $\mu = 0$ against $\mu = 1$. (3) $\mu = 5$, assertion channel 0
against 1. A $\varphi$ would have to give both values on one input.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{cert\_not\_function\_of\_forget}, \code{mu\_not\_function\_of\_bare\_observable} and
\code{cert\_addr\_not\_function\_of\_forget}, with the per-$\varphi$ forms
\code{no\_classical\_a2\_cert\_predicate}, \code{no\_classical\_mu\_separation\_predicate} and
\code{no\_classical\_cert\_addr\_predicate} (ProjectionNonExistence.v); the witnesses are
\code{trace\_witness\_A} and \code{forget\_witness\_uncert}, \code{mu\_separation\_witness\_zero} and \code{mu\_separation\_witness\_one}, and
\code{cert\_addr\_witness\_zero} and \code{cert\_addr\_witness\_one}. The names are bigger than the statements. The first says the
toll's flag can't be read off the bare window; it doesn't say the toll can't be stated on a
Turing machine (it can: Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s certification system, Definition~\ref{def:certsys}, is exactly
that). The third is about the
assertion channel; the property the diagonal uses on this machine (Section~\ref{sec:interpreters}) is a different one, bounded-run
equality with a reference program, and the file's comment linking the two overstates it.

\subsection{What the pair doesn't prove}

The obvious move is to reach for more room: bolt on a register, a tape region, any extra
slot, and surely an ordinary machine wriggles out. By hand, with no Coq statement behind it,
it doesn't: the same collision rebuilds one size up, with the added slot dropped from what
the observer reads. Bolt on another, then? Same collision, one size up again. Is there a size
where it stops? Only one that I can see: the window that reads every slot. That isn't a window
any more, it's the whole state, and the pair has nothing to say about it. Any window that
drops something the rest of the state doesn't already pin down has a pair hiding in what it
drops, which is Section~\ref{sec:windows}'s point about windows, not a fact about my machine.
That cuts both ways. The pair also says nothing about whether an
ordinary machine can hold the graph. It can, encoded on tape. A projection that sends
different graphs to the same place can't give the graph back on every state, and that's all
it says. It doesn't rule out an encoding that keeps the whole state, and it doesn't make
these particular opcodes necessary in every model. What a faithful simulation owes the
counter is a question about the simulator's own step rule, and the next subsection is
about that.

\subsection{The machine versus the program it runs}
\label{sec:machine-vs-program}

One more theorem belongs here, because it says what the pair \emph{means} for the rest of the
book. Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s universal floor was stated for any certification system. Now take any such system
that \emph{simulates} my machine: it has a decoding of its instructions into mine, an embedding
of its states into mine, its step commutes with mine through the embedding, and its
certification bit reads my certified flag through the embedding. Then two things hold for
any run of the base system from uncertified to certified: it paid at least one (that's just
the universal floor), and the \emph{embedded} run on my machine ends certified
(\code{thiele\_represents\_simulating\_cert\_system}). My machine itself is such a system, with the
identity as the embedding (\code{thiele\_self\_simulating}), and that's the only such construction
in the tree apart from some generalised variants.

Why does that matter? Because it separates two things people run together: \emph{the machine
doing the stepping} (what the machine is) and \emph{the program it runs} (what runs on it). The
floor is a property of the machine doing the stepping, and it transfers to anything that
faithfully runs on that machine. The pair in this section is a fact about the machine's state
space, not about any program.

Here's the picture I keep for it. Play Monopoly on the counter of a real bank. The game has a
bank of its own, with its own rules, and one of them is printed in the rules sheet: the Bank
never goes broke, and if it runs out of money the Banker may issue more by writing on any
ordinary paper. Inside the game that's fine; the players agreed to it. The real bank's teller,
standing right there, has no opinion about any of it. Push a thousand in Monopoly money across
her counter and her ledger doesn't move, because her rules are about her money, not the
game's. The real bank is the machine doing the stepping. The game is a program it happens to be
hosting. A rule that lives in the game holds as long as the players keep to it. A rule that
lives in the bank holds whatever the players do.

(And since the game is on the table: its box told an origin story for decades, that an
out-of-work salesman named Charles Darrow invented it during the Depression. The board is
older. Elizabeth Magie patented The Landlord's Game in 1904, with a square track, railroads and
a square that sends you to jail, and described it as a practical demonstration of the system
of land-grabbing. Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers in 1935, and the company bought
Magie's patent for a few hundred dollars. A story told by the company selling the product is a
lead to check, every time. It changes nothing about banks. It's a good reminder of who writes
the story on the box.)

A fixed machine can enforce an invariant in its own transition table, and that includes a
Turing machine. Give its tape a ledger track and a certification cell, and write a table
that never sets the cell without bumping the ledger: that machine obeys the toll in its step
relation. It's an instance of the abstract certification system, not a counterexample to it.
What it doesn't do is enforce the toll on the programs it runs. A universal machine
simulating another carries the simulated certification bit as data on its tape, and a buggy
guest can flip that bit without paying, because the host's step has no opinion about it. My
machine is in exactly that position when it simulates something else. The kernel's theorems
