are about the designated reading of the machine doing the stepping. That's a statement about
which reading a step rule prices. It isn't a claim that Turing machines can't price one. (The
floor for a certification system with no embedding into mine at all is
\code{universal\_nfi\_any\_substrate}, and the assumption receipt for
\code{thiele\_represents\_simulating\_cert\_system} is empty.)

Computing ran into this exact gap in hardware, and how it got out is worth the detour. In 1974
Gerald Popek and Robert Goldberg asked when a machine can run guests, a whole operating system
inside another, efficiently and safely. Their answer is one sentence you could check against any
instruction set. Call an instruction \emph{sensitive} if it reads or changes the machine's own
settings, the things the host has to keep for itself, and \emph{privileged} if running it
outside the host's own mode makes the machine stop and hand control to the host, which is
called a trap. For the kind of machine they modelled: if every sensitive instruction is
privileged, a host can be built. The guest runs at full speed, and whenever it touches
something that matters, the machine itself stops it and lets the host decide. That's a host
whose step has an opinion.

Then the obvious next question: did the machines people actually bought pass the test? The most
common one didn't. In 2000 John Scott Robin and Cynthia Irvine went through every instruction
of Intel's Pentium and found seventeen that are sensitive and not privileged; POPF, which loads
the processor's flags, is the one usually pointed at. A guest could run them and the host would
never hear about it. The fixes came two ways: VMware rewrote the guest's code on the fly so the
troublesome instructions never ran as written, and in the middle of the 2000s Intel and AMD
added hardware support so they'd trap. Does that change anything here? Not the theorem. Popek
and Goldberg were after speed and isolation, not a record and a price, so their result isn't
mine and mine isn't theirs. It changes the picture, though. The universal host of
Section~\ref{sec:universal-host} sits where they'd want a host to sit, for the small machine's
programs: the host's own step collects each guest's toll. And an industry learned the same
lesson the expensive way: a rule binds the guest only if it lives in the step underneath.

The smallest checked version of ``a ledger beside an ordinary machine'' is a Turing machine
configuration with a counter next to it, where each step adds one, plus one more if it writes
a nonblank symbol. The counter doesn't disturb the machine.

\begin{theorem}[A counter beside a Turing machine changes nothing]\label{thm:u19-tm-lift}
Let a Turing machine with transition table $\delta$ step a configuration $c$ to
$\mathrm{tm}_n(\delta, c)$ after at most $n$ steps (stopping when $\delta$ has no entry). Pair
each configuration with a counter, and step the pair by stepping the configuration and adding
the step's charge. Then for every $n$, $\delta$ and pair $(c, m)$, the configuration part
after at most $n$ steps of the pair is $\mathrm{tm}_n(\delta, c)$. In particular this holds
from $(c, 0)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By induction on $n$. For $n = 0$ both sides are $c$. For $n + 1$, if $\delta$ has no entry at
$c$, both runs stop and both sides are $c$. Otherwise the pair steps to $(c', m')$ where $c'$
is exactly the Turing machine's next configuration, whatever $m'$ is, and the induction
hypothesis at $(c', m')$ finishes it.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{thiele\_simulates\_turing\_gen} and \code{thiele\_simulates\_turing}
(ProperSubsumption.v). The ``Thiele'' in those names is a local record, a Turing configuration
and a number; it is not the machine of this book, and the file says not to cite it as the
machine simulating Turing machines.

And one honesty: the simulating-system record has a cost-preservation field (the base charges at
least what my machine would), and the theorem never uses it. It's there for a stronger
statement that hasn't been made.

Here it is exactly. A certification system is Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s, Definition~\ref{def:certsys}: states, moves,
a step, a cost per move, a certified bit, and the toll as a field.

\begin{definition}[A system that simulates the machine]\label{def:u19-simulating}
A \emph{simulating system} is a certification system $\mathcal{B}$ together with a decoding $d$
from its moves to machine instructions and an embedding $e$ from its states to machine
states, satisfying three premises: the step commutes, $e(\mathrm{step}_\mathcal{B}(s, i)) =
\mathrm{apply}(e(s), d(i))$ for all $s$, $i$; cost is preserved upward,
$\mathrm{cost}_\mathcal{B}(i) \ge \mathrm{cost}(d(i))$ for all $i$; and the certified bit is
reflected, $\mathrm{cert}_\mathcal{B}(s) = $ the certified flag of $e(s)$ for all $s$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The machine represents any system that simulates it]\label{thm:u19-represents}
Let $(\mathcal{B}, d, e)$ be a simulating system, $s_0$ a state of $\mathcal{B}$ and $t$ a
list of its moves. If $s_0$ is uncertified and the run of $t$ from $s_0$ ends certified, then
the total cost of $t$ in $\mathcal{B}$ is at least 1, and the machine run of the decoded list
$d(t)$ from $e(s_0)$ ends with the certified flag on.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The first part is the universal floor (Theorem~\ref{thm:universal-floor}) applied to $\mathcal{B}$ by
itself. For the second, by induction on $t$ using step commutation, the embedding of
$\mathcal{B}$'s final state is the machine's final state on $d(t)$ from $e(s_0)$; reflection
turns ``$\mathcal{B}$'s final state is certified'' into ``that machine state has the flag on''.
Cost preservation is not used.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{thiele\_represents\_simulating\_cert\_system} (UniversalCertificationCost.v), with
the record \code{SimulatingCertificationSystem} (its fields \code{scs\_step\_commutes},
\code{scs\_cost\_preserved}, \code{scs\_cert\_reflects}), the run lemma \code{scs\_run\_embed}, and the identity
instance \code{thiele\_self\_simulating}. The floor for a system with no embedding at all is
\code{universal\_nfi\_any\_substrate}.

One limit on all of this, so it isn't read as more. Certification is one event. Other kinds
of observable a machine might carry would each need their own event, their own evidence and
their own cost law, and nothing here supplies those. And stacking several such predicates
side by side gives a list of bits and nothing more: no topology, no metric, and no
independence between them beyond what Theorem~\ref{thm:u19-independence} proves for its
three named fields.

So: two states, same shadow, different graph, at the type level in two lines and from the
initial state in one step. The graph is the thing the ordinary windows drop. Next, what a
run that uses the graph looks like on a receipt, in four acts.

%===========================================================================
\section{The receipt in four acts}
\label{sec:receipt}
%===========================================================================

Four short acts with one receipt. They show the difference between an arrow that lives in
the graph and a register that holds its number, and they show the trace recording what an
assertion attempt cost, even when it fails. None of this vouches for a receipt somebody
else hands you, and none of it makes a property label true. I'll say what each act costs,
and under each act I'll name what's checked, because the four acts \emph{together} are a script
that runs (a small Python demonstration that asserts its own numbers as it goes, and a test that
runs it end to end), and the individual facts are the theorems.

That's the kind of demonstration I trust: it doesn't just print numbers, it checks them,
so if one ever drifts the script fails out loud instead of quietly printing something else.
Fair warning: this is one of the most bookkeeping-flavoured stretches of the book, a receipt read line
by line. Keep a pencil handy. Every number in it can be added up by hand.

\subsection{Act 1: the attempt costs, even when it fails}

Run the assertion step on an arrow number that doesn't exist. The demonstration does it on a
machine that has built no arrows at all, asserting arrow ninety-nine with the property
``two-hop'' and declared cost zero. Any arrow number at or above the arrow counter is absent, because
well-formedness (Section~\ref{sec:state}) puts every arrow's number below the counter. What happens: the error flag latches on, because the lookup failed; the
assertion channel stays at zero, because failure doesn't activate it; and the
counter goes up by one anyway, because the declared cost was zero and the floor is one.

What's checked: the failing branch of the assertion rule sets the error code, latches
the flag, steps the program counter and charges the cost, and changes nothing else
(\code{step\_morph\_assert\_bad}); the counter rises by at least
one on any assertion, any state, any argument (\code{morph\_assert\_mu\_pos}); the exact cost is
declared cost plus one (\code{morph\_cost\_morph\_assert}); and from a clear channel, the channel
becomes nonzero \emph{if and only if} the instruction is an assertion, the arrow exists, and the
checksum is nonzero (\code{morph\_assert\_step\_sets\_supra\_cert\_iff}), so a missing arrow leaves it
clear. The machine charges for the failed existence check. That's what the assertion
guarantees and all it guarantees: it checks the arrow exists, stores a checksum of the
property string, and leaves the certificate operand unread.

Exactly, with $i$ = MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT on arrow $k$ with property $p$, certificate $c$ and
declared cost $d$:

\begin{theorem}[A failed assertion still pays]\label{thm:u20-assert-bad}
(1) If the graph of $s$ has no arrow numbered $k$, then $\mathrm{apply}(s, i)$ agrees with
$s$ on every field except four: $\mathrm{pc}$ becomes $\mathrm{pc}(s) + 1$, $\mu$ becomes
$\mu(s) + d + 1$, the error code becomes $1$, and the error flag becomes true. In particular
$\mathrm{certaddr}$ and the graph are unchanged. (2) For every state $s$,
$\mathrm{cost}(i) = d + 1$ and $\mu(\mathrm{apply}(s, i)) \ge \mu(s) + 1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) is the failure rule of MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT, read through the bridge (Lemma~\ref{thm:u17-bridge}):
it builds the next state from $s$ with the error writer, which changes only the error code,
and the latch, which sets the flag. (2): the cost is the definition
(Definition~\ref{def:u17-cost}), and the counter claim is conservation
(Theorem~\ref{thm:u16-conservation}) with that cost.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{step\_morph\_assert\_bad} (VMStep.v), \code{morph\_cost\_morph\_assert} (CategoryBridge.v)
and \code{morph\_assert\_mu\_pos} (InsightTaxonomy.v). The if-and-only-if is part (3) of
Theorem~\ref{thm:u17-channel}, \code{morph\_assert\_step\_sets\_supra\_cert\_iff}. That an arrow number at
or above the counter is absent is read from the second clause of well-formedness
(Definition~\ref{def:u16-wf}); no lemma states it on its own, and the demonstration's machine
has no arrows at all, so its case needs nothing.

\subsection{Act 2: build the chain}

Run the demonstration's program. Three PNEWs, each claiming a cell of its own (cells one,
two and three, declared cost one each), which make modules A, B and C. Under Section~\ref{sec:state}'s rules
overlapping ranges trap, and so do ranges past memory, so the three claims have to be
different ranges inside the hundred and twenty-eight words, and they are.
Then MORPH f from A to B and MORPH g from B to C, declared cost two each. Then COMPOSE h from
f and g, declared cost one. Then MORPH\_\allowbreak{}GET into register zero the source of h and into
register one its target, declared cost zero each. The modules are numbered one, two and
three because the runner the demonstration drives starts its module counter at one; in the
kernel's own initial state they would be zero, one and two (Section~\ref{sec:state}). The arrows are numbered one,
two and three either way, since both start the arrow counter at one.

When it finishes, register zero holds 1, which is A, and register one holds 3, which is C.
Registers ten, eleven and twelve hold the three arrow numbers, and h, arrow three, from A to
C, sits in the graph. The counter reads eight: 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 1, and nothing for the two
MORPH\_\allowbreak{}GETs. The demonstration asserts all of that. Had every declared cost been zero, the
counter would read zero; each of these instructions charges what it declares.

Do the sum yourself before you trust mine. Write the eight instructions down the left side of a
sheet, the declared cost of each beside it, and add the column. Then do what Turing asked for
in 1949 (Section~\ref{sec:claims}) and write a running total after every line, so a mistake can
only hide in one line at a time. Eight instructions and a total of eight, by the way, is a
coincidence and not a clue: change one declared cost and they part company.

One detail from Section~\ref{sec:category} that matters here: MORPH reads its coupling from memory, a
count word then pairs. With zeroed memory the count is zero, so f and g have \emph{empty}
couplings, and if you MORPH\_\allowbreak{}GET the pair count of h you get zero. The chain is built; the
relational content is empty, because nobody wrote any. That's the honest state of Act 2 on
a blank machine. If you want pairs, write a coupling block first.

What's checked: the success branches of MORPH, COMPOSE, MORPH\_\allowbreak{}GET and their selector
function; each costs its declared cost (the six cost lemmas in the bridge file); arrow
construction can be free at zero (\code{morph\_can\_be\_free}, \code{morph\_compose\_cost\_zero}); and a run
that contains none of the five instructions in the setter class (LASSERT, LJOIN, EMIT, REVEAL,
MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT) leaves the assertion channel exactly where it was
(\code{structural\_trace\_preserves\_cert\_addr}). No named theorem gives the register values or the
total for this exact program: the total is the sum of per-step costs the lemmas fix, and the
register values come from running it.

Here is the channel fact Act 2 rests on, exactly. Write $\mathrm{run}(t, s)$ for applying
a list $t$ of instructions to $s$ in order (Definition~\ref{def:u17-classical}).

\begin{theorem}[Building leaves the channel alone]\label{thm:u20-structural}
Let $t$ be a list of instructions none of which is in the setter class (LASSERT, LJOIN,
EMIT, REVEAL, MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT), and $s$ any state. Then
$\mathrm{certaddr}(\mathrm{run}(t, s)) = \mathrm{certaddr}(s)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For one step: every instruction outside the setter class copies the address field on every
branch, by a case split that closes by computation. Then induction on $t$.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{structural\_trace\_preserves\_cert\_addr} (InsightTaxonomy.v), on top of
\code{thiele\_non\_cert\_addr\_setter\_preserves} (AbstractNoFI.v). Act 2's program uses PNEW, MORPH,
COMPOSE and MORPH\_\allowbreak{}GET, none of them setters. The theorem is about applying a list in order;
the demonstration's runner fetches by program counter, and for a straight-line program with
no jump and no trap the two orders are the same. That step is read from the program, not
checked. The costs are fixed one instruction at a time: MORPH, COMPOSE, MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ID,
MORPH\_\allowbreak{}DELETE, MORPH\_\allowbreak{}TENSOR and MORPH\_\allowbreak{}GET each cost exactly their declared $d$
(\code{morph\_cost\_morph} and its five siblings, CategoryBridge.v), and so does PNEW, by the
definition of the schedule.

\subsection{Act 3: assert}

Run the same program with one more instruction after the COMPOSE: the assertion on h, with
the property ``A-to-C-two-hop'', a certificate string the step never reads, and declared cost
four. It succeeds, because h exists. The channel moves to the checksum of the property, which
is the sum of its character codes, nonzero. The counter goes up by five, four declared plus
the floor, and reads thirteen. The demonstration also runs a smaller probe to show the floor
on its own: one PNEW at cost one, a MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ID at cost zero, and an assertion at declared cost
zero. The assertion still charges one, and the counter reads two.

Why does the property string need a non-NUL byte? (NUL is the character whose code is
zero.) Because the channel stores a plain byte sum. The empty string sums to zero, and so would an all-NUL string, leaving the channel at
zero: the step succeeds and nothing was activated. Any string with a non-NUL byte works. And
because the step writes the checksum unconditionally, an assertion whose property sums to
zero, made after a good one, writes the channel back to zero. The channel holds the
fingerprint of the latest assertion, not a running record of all of them. ``A-to-C-two-hop''
is just a label, and I'd ask you to hear ``just a label'' with Section~\ref{sec:claims} in your ear: the step
doesn't check that h is a two-hop path. It checks that h exists.

What's checked: the success branch (\code{step\_morph\_assert\_ok}); the if-and-only-if above; and
the machine's form of Section~\ref{sec:insight}'s point that certified insight isn't free
(Remark~\ref{rem:u09-three}): any flip of either reading (the channel or the flag) from off to
on costs at least one and raises the counter by at least one (\code{certified\_insight\_nonfree};
parts (1) to (3) of Section~\ref{sec:isa}'s Theorem~\ref{thm:u17-nfi}, which Section~\ref{sec:machine-claims} files under Section~\ref{sec:insight}'s tiers). And one
thing it does \emph{not} do, which the demonstration prints out so nobody misses it: the
assertion sets the \emph{assertion channel}, not the certified \emph{flag}. Those are two different
readings set by two different instructions (Section~\ref{sec:isa}), and this act sets one of them.

\begin{theorem}[A successful assertion]\label{thm:u20-assert-ok}
(1) If the graph of $s$ has an arrow numbered $k$, then $\mathrm{apply}(s, i)$ agrees with
$s$ on every field except three: $\mathrm{pc}$ becomes $\mathrm{pc}(s) + 1$, $\mu$ becomes
$\mu(s) + d + 1$, and $\mathrm{certaddr}$ becomes $\Sigma(p)$, the sum of the character
codes of $p$. The certified flag is not touched. (2) For any state $s$ and any instruction
$j$: if $\mathrm{certaddr}$ goes from $0$ to nonzero, or the certified flag goes from false
to true, across the step $\mathrm{apply}(s, j)$, then $\mathrm{cost}(j) \ge 1$ and
$\mu(\mathrm{apply}(s, j)) \ge \mu(s) + 1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) is the success rule read through the bridge. (2) is parts (1) to (3) of
Theorem~\ref{thm:u17-nfi}, put together as one statement about either reading.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{step\_morph\_assert\_ok} (VMStep.v) and \code{certified\_insight\_nonfree}
(InsightTaxonomy.v). With Act 3's numbers: $8 + 4 + 1 = 13$, and
$\Sigma(\text{A-to-C-two-hop})$ is nonzero because the string has a non-NUL character.

The trace now records a successful existence check and what it cost. The counter can't go
down. The total by itself doesn't say which assertion happened or where; for that you need
the trace (Section~\ref{sec:claims}'s grocery receipt). And keeping honest books is a different job from catching
an adversary who hands you a different history (Section~\ref{sec:windows}'s escapes).

\subsection{Act 4: equal observations can hide different graphs}

Two programs and one probe. Program A is Act 2's program: the three PNEWs, the two MORPHs, the
COMPOSE and the two MORPH\_\allowbreak{}GETs (the demonstration appends a HALT, which the runner stops
at). When it ends, register zero holds 1, register one holds 3, the counter reads eight, the
error flag is down, and the graph holds three arrows.

Program B never runs MORPH or COMPOSE. It makes three modules the same way, claiming the same
three cells, but declares their costs as two each, six in all. Then it loads the two values
straight into registers with LOAD\_\allowbreak{}IMM, register zero gets 1 and register one gets 3, at
declared cost one each. Six and one and one make eight, so the counter matches. B's graph has
three modules and no arrows, because PNEW and LOAD\_\allowbreak{}IMM never add an arrow. Its registers hold
the numbers one and three, a claimed source and a claimed target, and the numbers are tokens,
not graph entries.

The demonstration compares four values: register zero, register one, the counter and the
error flag. For A they are 1, 3, 8, down. For B they are 1, 3, 8, down. Same. That's a
fingerprint, and a weaker one than Section~\ref{sec:separation}'s pair, which agrees on all six shadow fields. B is a
different program from A in other ways, and the demonstration doesn't look at them: registers
ten, eleven and twelve hold the arrow numbers in A and zero in B, and B is shorter, five
instructions against A's eight.

Now the probe. Append MORPH\_\allowbreak{}DELETE of arrow one, declared cost zero, to each program. In A,
arrow one is f, the first MORPH built, so the delete succeeds. In B there is no arrow one,
and the delete fails and latches the error. The demonstration asserts both outcomes.
MORPH\_\allowbreak{}DELETE reads the graph, and the graph is the one thing a LOAD\_\allowbreak{}IMM can't forge.

There's a horse in this act, if you squint. In Germany in the early 1900s a mathematics teacher
named Wilhelm von Osten showed off a horse called Clever Hans, who answered arithmetic
questions by tapping a hoof, and got them right, in front of crowds. Same answers out as a horse
that could count: that's Program B's matching fingerprint. Then the psychologist Oskar Pfungst
stopped looking at the answers and started changing the conditions, and published what he
found in 1907. Put blinders on Hans, or have him asked by someone who didn't know the answer,
and the arithmetic fell apart. Hans was reading the questioner: tiny, unintended movements of
the head and body as the hoof reached the right number. That's the probe. Pfungst didn't argue
with the answers. He asked a question the answers couldn't fake, one that needed the real thing
to be there, the way MORPH\_\allowbreak{}DELETE needs an arrow to be in the graph. And the part
of the story I like best: nobody was lying. Von Osten was never persuaded by Pfungst and kept
showing his horse. A matching fingerprint doesn't need a cheat behind it, which is why you want
a probe and not an accusation.

What's checked, and here I have to be careful, because it's tempting to point at Section~\ref{sec:separation}'s
separation theorem as if it covered these two programs, and it doesn't: that theorem is one
abstract pair of states, not Program A and Program B, and the equal fingerprint for these
programs is pinned by the script, not by Coq. The conservativity theorem doesn't cover B
either, because B uses PNEW, and PNEW isn't a classical instruction: it adds modules. What
Coq proves is the general shape, and the probe's half of it lives in the standalone copy of
the kernel (Section~\ref{sec:state} says what that copy is). From any state whose arrow list is empty, MORPH\_\allowbreak{}DELETE finds nothing
(\code{graph\_empty\_morphisms\_delete\_fails\_tc}), and when the delete finds nothing the error flag
goes up (\code{morph\_delete\_no\_morphism\_err\_tc}). B ends with an empty arrow list. For the
classical case: in the standalone kernel's base state, any classical run followed by
MORPH\_\allowbreak{}DELETE of arrow zero ends with the error flag up (\code{classical\_trace\_fails\_morph\_delete\_probe\_tc}),
and after a MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ID the same probe ends with it down (\code{morph\_id\_step\_passes\_morph\_delete\_probe\_tc}); the pair
is packaged as the strictness witness (\code{morph\_delete\_probe\_separates\_thiele\_from\_classical\_tc}). In the kernel proper, the
classical half is \code{classical\_trace\_preserves\_graph}, which says a run of classical
instructions leaves the graph exactly as it was. So Act 4's \emph{point} is a theorem. Act 4's
\emph{numbers} are a script.

The probe's half, exactly. Write $\mathrm{del}(G, k)$ for removing arrow $k$ from graph $G$;
it fails when no arrow in $G$ has number $k$.

\begin{lemma}[The probe fails on an empty arrow list]\label{thm:u20-probe-fails}
(1) If the arrow list of $G$ is empty, $\mathrm{del}(G, k)$ fails for every $k$. (2) If
$\mathrm{del}(\mathrm{graph}(s), k)$ fails, then for every declared cost $d$, the step from
$s$ on MORPH\_\allowbreak{}DELETE of arrow $k$ at cost $d$ ends with the error flag true.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
(1): removal first asks whether some arrow has number $k$; on the empty list the answer is
no. (2): the step function's failure branch sets the flag to its old value or true, which is
true.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{graph\_empty\_morphisms\_delete\_fails\_tc} and \code{morph\_delete\_no\_morphism\_err\_tc}
(ThieleMachineComplete.v, the standalone copy of the kernel). In the kernel proper the same
fact is the failure rule \code{step\_morph\_delete\_bad} (VMStep.v).

\begin{theorem}[One step the classical instructions can't match]\label{thm:u20-strictness}
There are a state $s_0$ and instructions $u$ and $q$ such that the error flag of
$\mathrm{apply}(\mathrm{apply}(s_0, u), q)$ is false, while for every list $t$ of classical
instructions the error flag of $\mathrm{apply}(\mathrm{run}(t, s_0), q)$ is true.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Take $s_0$ with one module, numbered $0$, no arrows, the arrow counter at $0$, the error flag
down; $u$ = MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ID on module $0$ at declared cost $0$; and $q$ = MORPH\_\allowbreak{}DELETE of arrow $0$ at
declared cost $0$. After $u$ there is an arrow $0$, so $q$ succeeds; this part Coq checks by
computing. A classical run keeps the graph (Theorem~\ref{thm:u17-classical}, in the standalone
copy's form), so the arrow list is still empty, and Lemma~\ref{thm:u20-probe-fails} gives the
flag.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{morph\_delete\_probe\_separates\_thiele\_from\_classical\_tc}, with its halves \code{morph\_id\_step\_passes\_morph\_delete\_probe\_tc} and
\code{classical\_trace\_fails\_morph\_delete\_probe\_tc} (ThieleMachineComplete.v). The classical class there is
the standalone copy's own predicate, with the same twenty-two exclusions as the kernel's.
Program B uses PNEW, which is not classical, so B is outside this theorem; what covers B is
Lemma~\ref{thm:u20-probe-fails}, because B ends with an empty arrow list.

\subsection{What the receipt is}

The counter is what the schedule added up to: with the demonstration's declared costs (one
per PNEW, two per MORPH, one for COMPOSE, four plus the floor for the assertion), thirteen,
of which the assertion's five is the only part that touched the assertion channel, and the
floor's one is the only part the toll forced. The graph carries the structure the shadow
leaves out. The trace tells you where things came from, as long as whoever reads it has a
history they can trust, which is Section~\ref{sec:windows}'s question, the one its three escapes answer, and not
this act's to close.

Said plainly, in three sentences. The receipt tells you what was paid, and on which line. It
doesn't tell you the lines happened the way it says unless you trust whoever hands it to you.
And it doesn't make any label on it true.

And one rule the acts have to respect: MORPH\_\allowbreak{}DELETE removes one arrow and nothing else, but
PSPLIT and PMERGE delete every arrow touching the modules they remove. An arrow's life is
bounded by its modules'. In the four acts no module is split or merged, so nothing
cascades; in a longer program, it would.

That's one receipt, read act by act, with the price of every line on it. What the receipt
doesn't do on its own is tell you what anyone is \emph{entitled} to conclude from it, or sort what
happened in it into the kinds of learning Section~\ref{sec:insight} separated. Those were Part III's questions,
asked about any system with the pieces. The next section asks them of this one.

%===========================================================================
\section{Insight and entitlement on the machine}
\label{sec:machine-claims}
%===========================================================================

Section~\ref{sec:receipt} left a receipt on the table and two questions beside it: what does a receipt like that
entitle anyone to conclude, and which of the things on it were learning and which were
commitment? Those are Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}'s and Section~\ref{sec:insight}'s questions, and in Part III they were about any system
with the right pieces: a reading, a toll, a counter, a price list. They got by with cups,
three playing cards and a sheet of paper with two boxes on it, because that's all the claims
needed. The machine of Section~\ref{sec:state} to Section~\ref{sec:receipt} has every one of those pieces
at once, and more of each than the paper ever did: two readings instead of one, fifty-one
moves instead of three, a declared price on every move, and a counter that lives inside the
state. So this is where the two chapters meet something that runs. Some of their claims land
cleanly. Some land with conditions the paper never had to mention, because the paper had
nothing to hide them in, and I'll say which as they come. And the machine has one thing the
paper couldn't: a theorem with a long name and a longer hypothesis list, which is what
entitlement looks like when somebody actually has to check it.

\subsection{The two readings, and who writes them}

Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s paper had one reading. The machine keeps two that look alike, and I'm going to use them
by name. (I'll call them readings and not marks: since Section~\ref{sec:toll} a mark has been one tally on the
bill, and I'm keeping it that way.) One is the \emph{certified flag}. Only CERTIFY sets it, nothing
ever takes it down (that part is proved), and it carries no object and no check; it's a bit.
The other is the \emph{assertion channel}. Only MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT writes it, and what it writes is a
number worked out from the property's label, the sum of its character codes. A later
assertion writes over it, an assertion with an empty label writes a zero, which is the same as
clearing it, and nothing proves the channel stays set. Each sentence from here on says which
of the two it's about.

And here's the part to hold on to: no step of the machine reads either one. Every rule that
mentions them sets them or leaves them alone. Section~\ref{sec:entitlement} warned that nothing in the five parts makes a
later move read the reading; this machine is a case where nothing does. So when I say a run
is \emph{entitled}, I mean what someone auditing the run may conclude from the reading and the
receipt. The machine doesn't enforce it.

Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}'s note on the paper (the one beside Definition~\ref{def:u08-entitlement}) has a machine
version, and Section~\ref{sec:category} already showed it: 42 written into a register and called an arrow is a note,
raw data forged in one write, and the machine's assertion step looks the arrow up and refuses
one that isn't there. For entitlement, what matters is what the assertion leaves behind: a
paid event, charged at least one, and one reading on the whole machine, a number worked out
from a label. (It doesn't record which arrow it named.) An asserted arrow has a receipt, and
the receipt is the event. One limit on that word ``arrow'': the assertion step checks only that
the arrow exists. Whether the run built it or started with it depends on where the run
started.

Here are the two readings as symbols, and the one more bit that shows up below: the \emph{error
flag}, which a step raises when it can't do what it was asked, and which stays up once raised
(Remark~\ref{rem:u16-err-latch}).

\begin{definition}[The two readings]\label{def:u08-two-marks}
A state $s$ of the machine carries a Boolean $\mathrm{cert}(s)$, the \emph{certified flag}, and a
whole number $\mathrm{addr}(s)$, the \emph{assertion channel} (Section~\ref{sec:state}'s field, which Section~\ref{sec:isa} writes
$\mathrm{certaddr}(s)$), and a Boolean $\mathrm{err}(s)$, the error flag. Write
$\mathrm{apply}(s, i)$ for the state after instruction $i$ (Definition~\ref{def:u17-step}). The
\emph{checksum} of a label $\ell$ is $\Sigma(\ell) = \sum_{x \in \ell} \mathrm{code}(x)$, the sum of
its character codes; it is zero exactly when every character has code zero, and in particular
for the empty label.
\end{definition}

Who writes them, Section~\ref{sec:isa} already proved, over every instruction and every branch, and I won't
state it twice: Theorem~\ref{thm:u17-certified} for the flag and Theorem~\ref{thm:u17-channel}
for the channel are the home of every sentence above about who sets what. The one thing to
add is that the flag's permanence also holds for the machine's unbounded step, the one that
keeps every number exactly instead of cutting it to sixty-four bits
(\code{vm\_apply\_u\_certified\_permanent}, VMUnboundedLedger.v).

\subsection{Insight on the machine}

Section~\ref{sec:insight} sorted what happens when a computation learns into raw observation, which can be free;
certified insight, which the toll prices; and the observation that the price is flat whatever
is certified (Definition~\ref{def:u09-events} and Remark~\ref{rem:u09-three}, argued there for any
certification system). On the machine each of those gets a theorem, and the flat price gets a tier of
its own, because the machine has a thing to certify that's striking enough to tempt anyone
into thinking it should cost more.

The first thing, \emph{raw observation}, on the machine. Something comes in and gets written down.
A counter ticks. Neither certification reading moves because of it. Later steps can read what
it wrote, and one of the machine's own checks does, but that reading is a separate, paid step.
In the checked work the free case is the trial step, CHSH\_\allowbreak{}TRIAL (one round of a two-player game
I build in Section~\ref{sec:chsh}), and it's charged whatever its instruction declares, which can be zero. An
input read isn't free: READ\_\allowbreak{}PORT is on the cost floor. And ``free'' here is a fact about this
machine's price list, not a claim that looking costs nothing in the physical world.

The second thing, \emph{certified structural insight}. Some step turns a certification reading from
off to on: the certified flag raised, or the assertion channel set by a property asserted on
an arrow. On this machine that's a theorem over every one of its instructions
(stated exactly below: any step that takes either reading from off to on costs at least
one and raises the counter by at least one). Section~\ref{sec:insight}'s Gestalt reading of what's being charged
for, a relation committed to, fits the assertion channel, which stores a number worked out
from a property on an arrow. The certified flag by itself commits to no relation at all,
which is Section~\ref{sec:insight}'s bare crossing, and I'll come back to that.

The third thing, \emph{certified game-witness insight}. The run is certified \emph{and} what it
certifies is a result from that game, the one I haven't built yet, a result that no single
fixed strategy can produce: a score above two, when I get there. (That's a statement about
the tallies the machine kept: with those counts, no one fixed strategy gives them. Ruling out
every model where the answers were settled in advance by some shared hidden plan, which
physicists call hidden-variable models, would need a different argument and enough trials,
and that isn't what's checked.)
It gets its own tier because the thing certified
is so striking, and I'll tell you what the proof says about it, because it's humbling. The theorem for this tier
takes the hypothesis that the end state shows that score above
two, and then its proof \emph{discards that hypothesis} and uses only the second thing's
fact: that the certified flag went from off to on somewhere in a run, which costs at least
one. (The run is taken in list order, from a state where the flag starts off.)
The price of a certified game witness is the price of a certified anything: at least one.
The game adds meaning. It doesn't add cost. That's Section~\ref{sec:insight}'s flat price, landed. The three things
are collected as one theorem (its name is in the trail below), and I'd rather you know that
its third part is its second part lifted from one step to a whole run, for the certified flag
only, with the game hypothesis dropped.

Here are the three, exactly. The two readings are the certified flag $\mathrm{cert}$ and the
assertion channel $\mathrm{addr}$ of Definition~\ref{def:u08-two-marks}; $\mathrm{apply}(s, i)$
is one step, $\mathrm{cost}(i)$ is the price list's charge for $i$
(Definition~\ref{def:u17-cost}), and $\mu$ is the counter. The step that raises the flag is
CERTIFY and the one that writes the channel is MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT. For lists, $[\,]$ is the empty
list and $i :: t$ is the list that starts with $i$ and carries on with the list $t$, as in Section~\ref{sec:insight}.

\begin{definition}[Certified insight event, and the three tiers]\label{def:u09-tiers}
A step from state $s$ by instruction $i$ is a \emph{certified insight event} when it turns a reading
on: either $\mathrm{addr}(s) = 0$ and $\mathrm{addr}(\mathrm{apply}(s, i)) \ne 0$, or
$\mathrm{cert}(s) = \mathrm{false}$ and $\mathrm{cert}(\mathrm{apply}(s, i)) = \mathrm{true}$.
An instruction is \emph{raw observation} when no step by it, from any state, is a certified insight event. \emph{Certified structural insight} is a certified insight event. For the third tier, runs
are taken in list order: $\mathrm{run}_\mathrm{list}([\,], s) = s$ and
$\mathrm{run}_\mathrm{list}(i :: t, s) = \mathrm{run}_\mathrm{list}(t, \mathrm{apply}(s, i))$,
with no program counter involved. \emph{Certified game-witness insight} is such a run that starts
with $\mathrm{cert} = \mathrm{false}$ and ends with $\mathrm{cert} = \mathrm{true}$ and with
$S > 2$, where $S$ is the game statistic computed from the trial tallies the machine keeps
(Section~\ref{sec:chsh}).
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[A trial is raw observation]\label{lem:u09-tier0}
Every trial step of the game is raw observation. Its charge is the cost written in the
instruction, which may be zero.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
A trial step is neither CERTIFY nor MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT, so by Theorem~\ref{thm:u17-certified} and
part (1) of Theorem~\ref{thm:u17-channel} it leaves both readings as they were, from every state.
The charge is read off the price list.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{chsh\_trial\_is\_tier0} (WitnessInsightGeneral.v); the charge is the trial step's case of
\code{instruction\_cost} (VMStep.v).

\begin{theorem}[Certified insight is not free]\label{thm:u09-nonfree}
If the step from $s$ by $i$ is a certified insight event, then $\mathrm{cost}(i) \ge 1$ and
$\mu(\mathrm{apply}(s, i)) \ge \mu(s) + 1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Two cases. If the channel turned on, $i$ is one of the five steps that reveal, emit, join,
check a formula or assert, because every other instruction leaves the channel alone (a case
split over all instructions); each of those five is priced at its declared cost plus at least
one. (By Theorem~\ref{thm:u17-channel} it is in fact MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT, but the proof only needs
the wider class.) If the flag turned on, $i$ is CERTIFY, priced at its declared
cost plus one. Either
way $\mathrm{cost}(i) \ge 1$, and conservation,
$\mu(\mathrm{apply}(s, i)) = \mu(s) + \mathrm{cost}(i)$, gives the second half.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{certified\_insight\_nonfree} (InsightTaxonomy.v), from \code{no\_free\_certification},
\code{no\_free\_certification\_certified} and their counter forms (AbstractNoFI.v), packaged there as
\code{certification\_requires\_positive\_mu}; conservation is \code{vm\_apply\_mu}
(MuLedgerConservation.v). It's parts (1) to (3) of Section~\ref{sec:isa}'s Theorem~\ref{thm:u17-nfi} said in one
breath, and part (2) of Theorem~\ref{thm:u20-assert-ok} is the same statement met in Act 3; it
gets its own block here because the third tier leans on it.

\begin{theorem}[The price of a game witness is flat]\label{thm:u09-witness}
Let $t$ be a list of instructions and $s$ a state with $\mathrm{cert}(s) = \mathrm{false}$. If
$s' = \mathrm{run}_\mathrm{list}(t, s)$ has $\mathrm{cert}(s') = \mathrm{true}$ and $S(s') > 2$,
then $\mu(s') \ge \mu(s) + 1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The hypothesis $S(s') > 2$ is not used. Induction on $t$. The empty list leaves the flag false,
which contradicts the end. For $i :: t$: if the flag is on after $i$, that step is a certified
insight event, so it raises $\mu$ by at least one (Theorem~\ref{thm:u09-nonfree}), and the rest
of the run never lowers $\mu$. If the flag is still off after $i$, the induction hypothesis
covers the rest, and the step by $i$ didn't lower $\mu$.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{witness\_insight\_nonfree\_general}, through \code{no\_free\_certification\_certified\_trace\_mu}
(WitnessInsightGeneral.v). The same lift for the assertion channel, with the extra fact that the
list contains an instruction of the five-member class, is \code{no\_free\_certified\_insight}
(InsightTaxonomy.v). The three tiers are collected as \code{witness\_insight\_complete\_taxonomy}
(WitnessInsightGeneral.v): Lemma~\ref{lem:u09-tier0}, Theorem~\ref{thm:u09-nonfree} and
Theorem~\ref{thm:u09-witness}, joined by ``and.''

So Section~\ref{sec:insight}'s two facts and a warning hold here word for word. Looking can be free. Turning a
reading on can't, and putting a game result behind it doesn't make it cost any more.

Section~\ref{sec:insight} also asked who decided the split, and said any concrete machine owes you its whole table.
This one's table is Section~\ref{sec:isa}'s. The floor sits under the whole \emph{cost-floor class}, Section~\ref{sec:isa}'s positive
class of twelve (Definition~\ref{def:u17-floor}), which is wider than the two steps that turn a
reading on, and every step outside that class costs whatever its instruction declares, which
can be zero. So the sorting into three things is by which reading moves, as it was in Section~\ref{sec:insight}. The
part of the schedule that's \emph{forced} is the floor under the flag-raisers, and Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} is the
argument for it (Theorem~\ref{thm:toll-derived}); the rest is a choice, and Section~\ref{sec:isa} defends it
under the table.

\subsection{Test, then commit, on the machine}

Section~\ref{sec:insight} put a CHECK on the paper and found nothing in the five parts that makes VOUCH wait for it
(Remark~\ref{rem:u09-no-wait}), and said a particular system could close that gap by writing it
into its step. This machine doesn't. Here's its version, the same gap with numbers on it.

The test is LASSERT, the formula check Section~\ref{sec:claims} took apart: it charges on the attempt, pass or
fail, and it raises neither certification reading. The commit is one of two other steps:
MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT, which puts a property on an arrow and sets the assertion channel, or CERTIFY,
which raises the certified flag with no arrow and no property behind it at all, the weakest
commit there is. So the honest protocol is two steps, with two separate charges, one for the
checking work and one for the flip.

And nothing in the machine makes the second step follow the first. The assertion step checks
only that the arrow it names exists. It has no way to read whether a test ran earlier in the
run on the formula the property names. A program can assert ``validated constraint'' on an
arrow with no test anywhere in its history and get the same stored value (the number worked
out from the label) for the same charge on that step. The two whole states can still differ
by whatever else the two programs did; pad the shorter program with a step that does nothing
and costs the same, and they agree. So Section~\ref{sec:insight}'s sentence holds here exactly: the receipt says a
commitment was paid for, not that it was earned. On this machine the toll prices the commit,
and whether the commit was preceded by a test is a fact about the program, not a guarantee of
the machine.

The two facts under that, exactly.

\begin{lemma}[The check commits nothing]\label{lem:u09-check-commits-nothing}
For every state $s$ and every formula-checking instruction $i$,
$\mathrm{addr}(\mathrm{apply}(s, i)) = \mathrm{addr}(s)$ and
$\mathrm{cert}(\mathrm{apply}(s, i)) = \mathrm{cert}(s)$, whether the check passes or fails.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The check is neither MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT nor CERTIFY. Apply part (1) of
Theorem~\ref{thm:u17-channel} and Theorem~\ref{thm:u17-certified}.
\end{proof}

Checked as instances of \code{non\_morph\_assert\_preserves\_cert\_addr} (RevelationRequirement.v) and
\code{vm\_apply\_certified} (PrimeAxiom.v); no theorem names the formula check's case by itself. The
same two equalities sit inside Theorem~\ref{thm:u10-lassert}, among everything else the check
leaves alone; here they stand by themselves because they're the test half of the protocol.

\begin{remark}[The commit reads no test]\label{rem:u09-commit-blind}
The assertion step's rule has one condition, that the arrow it names is in the current graph. When
it is, the new channel value is $\Sigma(\ell)$ for the instruction's label $\ell$, and the
charge is the declared cost plus one. Nothing in the rule depends on which instructions ran
before. This is read off the rule (\code{step\_morph\_assert\_ok} in VMStep.v and the matching case of
\code{vm\_apply} in SimulationProof.v); the files state no separate theorem for it.
\end{remark}

A worked chain, so the two prices have numbers. Say a register holds the address of a formula
whose declared length is four words, and another holds the address of the two rows of values
it's checked against (one meant to make it true, one meant to make it false; Section~\ref{sec:claims} laid them
out). The check,
with declared cost 0, is charged $4 \cdot 8 + (0 + 1) = 33$, pass or fail, and moves neither
reading. Then, if it passed, an assertion with declared cost 0 and the label
``validated\_\allowbreak{}constraint'' on an arrow that exists is charged $0 + 1 = 1$ and sets the channel to
the label's checksum, which isn't zero, since the label has characters with nonzero codes. The
total is 34, and the channel crossed from zero on the second step, not the first. Skip the check
and the assertion alone still costs 1 and writes the same number. These numbers are the price
function evaluated on the two instructions (\code{instruction\_cost}, VMStep.v), not a separate
theorem.

One edge the paper didn't have, because the paper's VOUCH, played from NO, always crossed: an assertion with
an empty label pays and raises nothing, because the number it stores is zero. Paid, and no
reading moved. Section~\ref{sec:insight}'s ``a crossing costs at least one'' is untouched by it; it just isn't a
crossing.

\subsection{Entitlement on the machine}

Now Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}'s count. Section~\ref{sec:entitlement} said a run is entitled to a claim when it has an object, a checked relation
and a paid event (Definition~\ref{def:u08-entitlement}), and that the leaning costs at least the
index bits of the narrowing it commits to, given lists, a tree, a covering, and a run that
paid for the tree's depth (Theorem~\ref{thm:u08-count}). On this
machine that is a theorem with a long name, \code{structural\_entitlement\_representation}, and I want
to give you its hypotheses, all of them, because the theorem is only as good as what it's
handed, and a list of hypotheses is the kind of thing that gets skimmed while the conclusion
gets quoted.

First, what ``paid step'' means here. Section~\ref{sec:entitlement} counted every step the price list charges at least one
for, and on this machine those are the cost-floor steps from a few paragraphs back: the steps
that reveal, emit, join, check a formula, read a port (take in a value from outside the
machine), certify or assert, and the checks for the two-player game of Section~\ref{sec:chsh}. Only two of them,
CERTIFY and MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT, turn a reading on. The tree is a bare shape, as in Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}, and ``no deeper than the number of
cost-floor steps'' is a count along the run that happened. It isn't a walk down the tree. In
the example below, two of the counted steps emit, and emitting raises nothing.

The theorem is handed: a decoder that turns the run's receipts into an observation (in the
files the receipts are the list of instructions the run was handed, not a log of the steps it
took); an exact equality test on observations; a posterior that's a strict subset of the prior;
one eliminated state and an observation that gives it a value no surviving state gives (the
\emph{distinguishing test}, which is Plato's third account from Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}, made into a function); a start
with the assertion channel at zero, and an end that's certified, a word the files use here for
something that never looks at the certified flag. It means three things at once: no error
latched, the posterior's membership test accepts the decoded receipts, and the assertion
channel is nonzero; a decision tree no deeper than the number of cost-floor steps the run
executed; a non-empty posterior; and a second observation function, the representative one,
with a family of fibres, one per surviving state, such that every prior state sits in the
fibre of some survivor that gives it the same representative observation. The fibre sizes
together have to add up to at least the prior's length, and no fibre may be larger than the
tree has leaves.

That last clause is Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}'s covering condition, carried by fibres, and it's the nearest thing
the record has to an anti-stopped-clock clause. I have to be exact about how near. It says
every prior state is covered by some survivor, and no survivor stands for more states than the
tree has leaves. That limits how much can be deleted per leaf you paid for. It doesn't say why
anything was deleted. The representative observation is a function somebody supplies, and one
that returns the same thing for every state makes ``same representative observation'' true of
every pair; the small two-state example below does exactly that. So the clause rules out deleting
too much for the tree you've paid for. It doesn't rule out deleting for no reason.

Given all that, the theorem concludes three things: the posterior's predicate is strictly
stronger than the prior's, an assertion event happened, and the counter rose by at least the
index bits lost. Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}'s three small prints hold here unchanged: both logarithms round up
separately and the subtraction stops at zero, the lists are lists with repeats counted, and
the difference isn't the number of questions anyone asked.

Picture that chain as three links you can hold one at a time, like three cups in a row:
narrow the list, find the step that paid, count the bill. Two of the links are their own theorems and I'll name them so you can find
them. Narrowing a list, with a test that distinguishes, makes the membership predicate
strictly stronger: \code{feasible\_strict\_subset\_implies\_strict\_predicates}, Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}'s card argument
checked on lists of this machine's states. And on this machine, reaching a certified end from
a clear start means an assertion event fired somewhere in the run:
\code{strengthening\_requires\_structure\_addition}. On that second one, one more thing about its
proof: its ``strictly stronger'' hypothesis is taken in and split. The strict half is thrown
away, and the other half only builds a premise that the last step ignores. What does the work
is ``the channel was clear at the start and set at the end,'' and the flip follows from
zero-then-nonzero. The theorem is true. Its name promises a tighter link than its proof uses.

Here is the whole chain exactly, one link at a time. First the words.

\begin{definition}[Runs, state lists, observations, predicates]\label{def:u08-lists}
A \emph{program} $p$ is a list of instructions. The run $\mathrm{run}(n, p, s)$ with fuel $n$ from
state $s$ repeats, at most $n$ times, ``fetch the instruction of $p$ at the program counter and
apply it,'' and stops early if the counter points past the end of $p$. A \emph{state list} is a
finite list $\Omega$ of states; $|\Omega|$ is its length, repeats counted. $\Omega'$ is a
\emph{strict sublist} of $\Omega$ when every member of $\Omega'$ is in $\Omega$ and some member of
$\Omega$ is not in $\Omega'$. An \emph{observation} is a function $\mathrm{obs}$ from states to
lists of instructions, and an \emph{equality test} is a Boolean function $\mathrm{eq}$ on such
lists with $\mathrm{eq}(o_1, o_2) = \mathrm{true}$ exactly when $o_1 = o_2$. A \emph{receipt predicate} is a Boolean function on lists. The \emph{membership predicate} of $\Omega$ under
$\mathrm{obs}$ is
\[
P_\Omega(o) = \mathrm{true} \iff \mathrm{eq}(\mathrm{obs}(s), o) = \mathrm{true} \text{ for some } s \in \Omega .
\]
$P$ is \emph{stronger} than $Q$ when $P(o) = \mathrm{true}$ implies $Q(o) = \mathrm{true}$ for
every $o$, and \emph{strictly stronger} when, in addition, some $o$ has $P(o) = \mathrm{false}$ and
$Q(o) = \mathrm{true}$. A state $w$ is \emph{distinguished} from $\Omega'$ by $\mathrm{obs}$ when
$\mathrm{obs}(w) \ne \mathrm{obs}(t)$ for every $t \in \Omega'$.
\end{definition}

The run with fuel is Section~\ref{sec:isa}'s (Definition~\ref{def:u17-step}), written out again here because every
block below is stated on it.

\begin{theorem}[Narrowing becomes strengthening]\label{thm:u08-narrowing}
Let $\mathrm{eq}$ be an equality test, let $\Omega'$ be a strict sublist of $\Omega$, and let
$w \in \Omega$ with $w \notin \Omega'$ be distinguished from $\Omega'$ by $\mathrm{obs}$. Then
$P_{\Omega'}$ is strictly stronger than $P_\Omega$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
``Strictly stronger'' has two parts. (a) If $P_{\Omega'}(o)$ is true, some $t \in \Omega'$ has
$\mathrm{obs}(t) = o$; that $t$ is in $\Omega$, so $P_\Omega(o)$ is true. This part is only
the inclusion. (b) Take $o = \mathrm{obs}(w)$. Since $w \in \Omega$, $P_\Omega(o)$ is true.
No member of $\Omega'$ has observation $o$, so $P_{\Omega'}(o)$ is false. The gap between the
lists would not give (b) by itself: a removed state can share its observation with a
surviving one, and then the two predicates accept the same observations. That is why the
distinguished state is a hypothesis of its own. In the Coq proof the gap witness that comes
with ``strict sublist'' is not used at all; the supplied $w$ does the work.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{feasible\_strict\_subset\_implies\_strict\_predicates}
(InformationGainToStrengthening.v), with the predicate defined as \code{omega\_predicate}; the form
that only says some strictly ordered pair of predicates exists is
\code{b4\_information\_reduction\_derives\_strict\_predicates} (HonestNoFI\_\allowbreak{}TheoremsWithoutAssumptions.v).

That's the first link: narrow the list with a test that separates, and the predicate gets
stronger. The second link needs the word ``certified'' pinned down, along with the one step
it points at.

\begin{definition}[Certified end, structure addition]\label{def:u08-certified}
Fix a \emph{decoder} $d$, a function from instruction lists to lists. The files call the program
$p$ of a run its \emph{receipts}: what the decoder reads is the list of instructions the run was
handed. The end state of a run of $p$ is \emph{certified} for a predicate $P$ when
$\mathrm{err} = \mathrm{false}$ there (the error flag is down), $P(d(p)) = \mathrm{true}$, and $\mathrm{addr} \ne 0$
there. The run $\mathrm{run}(n, p, s)$ has a \emph{structure addition} when one of the steps it
executes goes from a state with $\mathrm{addr} = 0$ to a state with $\mathrm{addr} \ne 0$.
(This is Section~\ref{sec:claims}'s structural gain, Definition~\ref{def:u10-gain}, under the name the files use
here.)
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[A certified end from a clear start has an assertion event]\label{thm:u08-structure-addition}
Let $P_\mathrm{strong}$ be strictly stronger than $P_\mathrm{weak}$, let $\mathrm{addr}(s) = 0$,
and let the end of $\mathrm{run}(n, p, s)$ be certified for $P_\mathrm{strong}$. Then the run
has a structure addition.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Only the third clause of ``certified'' is used: the channel is zero at the start and nonzero at
the end. Walk the run (induction on the fuel). At each executed step either the channel turns
nonzero, which is a structure addition, or it is still zero and the rest of the run starts
again from a clear channel. A run that stops with the channel still zero ends at zero, which
contradicts the end. The strictness hypothesis is taken apart and its pieces feed nothing the
conclusion needs. By part (3) of Theorem~\ref{thm:u17-channel}, the step found is a MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT
naming an arrow that exists, with a label of nonzero checksum.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{strengthening\_requires\_structure\_addition} (NoFreeInsight.v), through
\code{supra\_cert\_implies\_structure\_addition\_in\_run}; the step is identified by
\code{structure\_addition\_in\_run\_iff\_morph\_assert\_bridge\_pattern} (both RevelationRequirement.v).

So a certified end from a clear start always points at a step you can name. Now the count.
It needs a tree, the cost-floor steps, and the fibres.

\begin{definition}[Decision tree, cost-floor count, fibres]\label{def:u08-tree}
Decision trees, their depth and their leaf count $L(T)$ are as in
Definition~\ref{def:u08-dtree}. The \emph{cost-floor} instructions are the ones that reveal,
emit, join, check a formula, read a port, certify or assert, and the five game checks; the price
list charges
each of them its declared cost plus at least one. $c(n, p, s)$ is the number of cost-floor
instructions among the steps $\mathrm{run}(n, p, s)$ executes. The tree $T$ is \emph{realized} by
the run when $\mathrm{depth}(T) \le c(n, p, s)$. A \emph{posterior-representative reduction} of
$\Omega$ to $\Omega'$ for an observation $r$ and a tree $T$ is a function $F$ from states to
state lists (the \emph{fibres}) such that: every $s \in \Omega$ lies in $F(t)$ for some
$t \in \Omega'$ with $r(s) = r(t)$; $|\Omega| \le \sum_{t \in \Omega'} |F(t)|$; and
$|F(t)| \le L(T)$ for every $t \in \Omega'$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Paid steps cover the counter]\label{lem:u08-cert-executions}
For every run, $c(n, p, s) \le \mu(\mathrm{run}(n, p, s)) - \mu(s)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The rise of the counter over the run is exactly the sum of the charges of the executed steps
(Theorem~\ref{thm:u16-conservation}). Every cost-floor step contributes at least one to that sum,
and no step contributes less than zero.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{info\_priced\_cert\_executions\_bound} (MuShannonBridge.v), resting on
\code{cert\_setter\_cost\_pos} (VMStep.v) and \code{delta\_mu\_equals\_ledger\_sum}.

\begin{lemma}[Index bits are paid for]\label{lem:u08-index-bits}
If $T$ is realized by $\mathrm{run}(n, p, s)$, $|\Omega'| > 0$, and there is a
posterior-representative reduction of $\Omega$ to $\Omega'$ for some $r$ and $T$, then
\[
\lceil \log_2 |\Omega| \rceil \mathbin{\dot{-}} \lceil \log_2 |\Omega'| \rceil \;\le\; \mu(\mathrm{run}(n, p, s)) - \mu(s),
\]
where $\lceil \log_2 \cdot \rceil$ is the base-two logarithm rounded up and $\dot{-}$ is
subtraction on whole numbers that stops at zero.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The fibres give $|\Omega| \le \sum_{t \in \Omega'} |F(t)| \le L(T) \cdot |\Omega'|$: sort the
prior states by the survivor whose fibre holds them, and each of the $|\Omega'|$ groups has at
most $L(T)$ members. The rounded-up logarithm respects order and is subadditive on products,
$\lceil \log_2 ab \rceil \le \lceil \log_2 a \rceil + \lceil \log_2 b \rceil$, so
\[
\lceil \log_2 |\Omega| \rceil \;\le\; \lceil \log_2 L(T) \rceil + \lceil \log_2 |\Omega'| \rceil .
\]
A tree of depth $d$ has at most $2^d$ leaves (induction on the tree), so
$\lceil \log_2 L(T) \rceil \le \mathrm{depth}(T)$. Chain the rest:
\[
\lceil \log_2 |\Omega| \rceil \mathbin{\dot{-}} \lceil \log_2 |\Omega'| \rceil \;\le\; \mathrm{depth}(T) \;\le\; c(n, p, s) \;\le\; \mu(\mathrm{run}(n, p, s)) - \mu(s),
\]
the middle step being realization and the last Lemma~\ref{lem:u08-cert-executions}. The first
clause of the reduction, the one about the representative observation, is discarded by the
Coq proof; only the two counting clauses are used.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{info\_priced\_posterior\_representative\_reduction\_bound} (MuShannonBridge.v), which
goes through \code{posterior\_representative\_reduction\_implies\_fibered\_reduction},
\code{fibered\_reduction\_implies\_tree\_cover} (the bound
$|\Omega| \le L(T) \cdot |\Omega'|$, named \code{tree\_covers\_feasible\_reduction}),
\code{tree\_cover\_implies\_log2\_up\_reduction\_bound}, \code{decision\_tree\_log2\_up\_leaf\_bound} and
\code{info\_priced\_arbitrary\_feasible\_reduction\_bound}. The arithmetic is Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}'s
Theorem~\ref{thm:u08-count}, here with the fibres supplying the covering and the cost-floor
steps supplying the payment.

That's the third link: given the tree and the fibres, the counter covers the index bits the
list lost. Put the three links on one hypothesis list and you have the theorem.

\begin{theorem}[Structural entitlement, represented]\label{thm:u08-representation}
Fix fuel $n$, a program $p$, a start state $s$, a decoder $d$, two observations
$\mathrm{obs}$ and $r$, an equality test $\mathrm{eq}$, a prior $\Omega$, a posterior
$\Omega'$, and a decision tree $T$. Assume: (H1) $\mathrm{eq}$ decides equality of
observations; (H2) $\Omega'$ is a strict sublist of $\Omega$; (H3) some $w \in \Omega$ with
$w \notin \Omega'$ is distinguished from $\Omega'$ by $\mathrm{obs}$; (H4)
$\mathrm{addr}(s) = 0$; (H5) the end of $\mathrm{run}(n, p, s)$ is certified for
$P_{\Omega'}$, the membership predicate of the posterior under $\mathrm{obs}$; (H6) $T$ is
realized by the run; (H7) $|\Omega'| > 0$; (H8) there is a posterior-representative reduction
of $\Omega$ to $\Omega'$ for $r$ and $T$. Then (C1) $P_{\Omega'}$ is strictly stronger than
$P_\Omega$; (C2) the run has a structure addition; and (C3)
$\lceil \log_2 |\Omega| \rceil \mathbin{\dot{-}} \lceil \log_2 |\Omega'| \rceil \le \mu(\mathrm{run}(n, p, s)) - \mu(s)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(C1) is Theorem~\ref{thm:u08-narrowing} from (H1) to (H3). (C2) is
Theorem~\ref{thm:u08-structure-addition} from (C1), (H4) and (H5). (C3) is
Lemma~\ref{lem:u08-index-bits} from (H6) to (H8). The three conclusions share a hypothesis list
and nothing else: the proof of (C3) never looks at a membership predicate or at the channel.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{structural\_entitlement\_representation} (HonestNoFI\_\allowbreak{}TheoremsWithoutAssumptions.v).
The version with the end only required to be error-free and accepted, with no channel clause
and so no (C2), is \code{observational\_structural\_entitlement\_representation} (same file).

Hold it up against Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}'s three parts of entitlement (Definition~\ref{def:u08-entitlement}) and
they're all in the hypothesis list. The object is a pair of state lists and a decision tree.
The checked relation is the membership test with its distinguishing observation. The paid
event is a step that sets the assertion channel. That's as close as the checked work comes to
the word; the word itself stays the book's.

\begin{remark}[Why two observations]\label{rem:u08-two-observations}
The distinguishing observation and the representative one can't be the same function. If
$w \in \Omega$ is distinguished from $\Omega'$ by $\mathrm{obs}$, the reduction's first clause
puts $w$ in the fibre of some $t \in \Omega'$ with $\mathrm{obs}(w) = \mathrm{obs}(t)$, which
the distinction forbids. Checked as \code{distinguishing\_observation\_not\_posterior\_representable}
(HonestNoFI\_\allowbreak{}TheoremsWithoutAssumptions.v).
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[The complete-tree bound]\label{rem:u08-no-tree}
For any two lists with $|\Omega'| > 0$, a complete tree of depth
$d = \lceil \log_2(\lfloor |\Omega| / |\Omega'| \rfloor + 1) \rceil$ satisfies the covering
inequality (\code{exists\_covering\_tree}). So if a bounded run $\mathrm{run}(n, p, s)$ realizes the
complete tree of depth $d$ (executes at least $d$ cost-floor steps), then
$\lceil \log_2 |\Omega| \rceil - \lceil \log_2 |\Omega'| \rceil \le
\mu(\mathrm{run}(n, p, s)) - \mu(s)$
(\code{complete\_tree\_realization\_bound}, MuShannonBridge.v). The tree is still a hypothesis, the
complete one of the right depth; what the form drops is any tie between the two lists and the
run. The lists only pick which depth the run has to realize. It shows how much of (C3) is
arithmetic on lengths once the paid steps are counted. The same bound holds for lists whose
states carry whole-number weights, with total weight in place of length, given a realized
tree whose leaf count times the posterior's weight covers the prior's weight
(\code{info\_priced\_weighted\_feasible\_reduction\_bound}), and the natural fibres of an observation
give a reduction whenever they meet the counting clauses
(\code{observation\_partition\_reduction\_implies\_posterior\_representative\_reduction}).
\end{remark}

\subsection{Every sound shortcut lands here, and what that sentence is worth}

The book's big-sounding sentence in this neighbourhood is: every sound structural shortcut
lands in that bound. I want to tell you exactly what it's worth, which is less than it
sounds and more than nothing.

What's checked is a \emph{record} with fifteen fields, and here ``record'' is Coq's word for a
bundle of named slots, not the kind of record Section~\ref{sec:toll} is about: seven pieces of data (the decoder, the
observation function, a representative observation, the equality test, the prior, the
posterior, the tree) and eight proof obligations over them. ``Every sound shortcut lands here''
is the theorem that unpacks that record and applies the bound, and its proof is four short
steps (introduce, take the record apart, simplify, apply the bound), because the record was
\emph{defined} to carry exactly the bound's hypotheses. It's true by
packaging. The right word for it is ``a checklist'': a checklist for being a sound shortcut,
not a discovery about shortcuts.

And a checklist isn't nothing, which is the ``more than nothing'' half. On 30 October 1935, at
Wright Field, northeast of Dayton, Ohio, the Army was evaluating Boeing's new four-engine bomber,
the Model 299. It took off, pitched up, stalled and crashed, and two men died of their
injuries, the Army's pilot, Major Ployer Hill, and Boeing's chief test pilot, Leslie Tower. The
airplane was fine. The crew had left the gust locks on, the clamps that hold the control
surfaces still while the plane sits on the ground. A newspaper, as the story is usually told,
called it too much airplane for one man to fly. The answer wasn't more skill, it was a card: a
list of things to check, in order, every time, and the story usually told is that this is where
the pilot's checklist comes from. The airplane went on to be the B-17. Nothing on that card was a
discovery. Every item on it was something the pilots already knew. What the card did was make
sure none of it got left out when it mattered. That's what the fifteen-field record does for the
bound: it finds nothing new about shortcuts, and it makes the eight hypotheses impossible to
drop quietly.

The checklist, exactly:

\begin{definition}[Sound structural shortcut]\label{def:u08-shortcut}
For fuel $n$, a program $p$ and a start state $s$, a \emph{sound structural shortcut} is a record
of seven pieces of data, $d$, $\mathrm{obs}$, $r$, $\mathrm{eq}$, $\Omega$, $\Omega'$ and $T$,
together with proofs of the eight hypotheses (H1) to (H8) of
Theorem~\ref{thm:u08-representation} for that data: fifteen fields in all.
\end{definition}

\begin{corollary}[Every sound shortcut lands in the bound]\label{cor:u08-lands-here}
For every sound structural shortcut, conclusions (C1), (C2) and (C3) of
Theorem~\ref{thm:u08-representation} hold for its data.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Take the record apart into its fifteen fields and apply the theorem. Nothing else happens.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{every\_sound\_structural\_shortcut\_lands\_here} (HonestNoFI\_\allowbreak{}TheoremsWithoutAssumptions.v);
a record is assembled from its fifteen parts by \code{sound\_shortcut\_from\_components} (same file).

\subsection{A search whose surviving candidates can be counted}

Put three coins under three cups. Each coin is heads or tails, so there are eight possible
rows under the cups. Someone hands you two answers: heads under the first cup, tails under
the second. Lift the first cup and compare. A matching answer leaves four possible rows.
Lift the second and compare. A match leaves two. The last coin can still be either way.
The list really shrank: eight, four, two. Nothing in that count needed a claim about which
way the last coin faces.

This is a parlour game, and an old one. In \emph{A Christmas Carol}, in 1843, Scrooge's nephew
Fred plays a game called Yes and No at his Christmas party: he thinks of something, and
everybody else asks questions he may only answer yes or no. He's thinking of an animal, a
disagreeable, savage one that growls and grunts and lives in London, and the answer is Uncle
Scrooge. Most people know the game as twenty questions, and twenty is a good number for it:
each yes-or-no answer can at best cut the field in half, and twenty halvings take a million or
so possibilities, $2^{20} = 1{,}048{,}576$, down to one. Push on that, though. The halving only
happens because Fred answers truthfully about what's actually in his head. Lie once and the
count still shrinks; it shrinks around the wrong animal. That's the cups again: the four and
the two are real because you lifted the cup and compared, not because somebody told you what
was under it.

Here is that search on the machine. A candidate is a start state with an $n$-bit value in
memory, one bit per word, and the prior contains all $2^n$ such states. The program carries
$k$ supplied answers. For each one it loads the corresponding memory bit, records the
supplied answer through READ\_\allowbreak{}PORT, compares the two, and jumps to a trap if they disagree.
If all the answers match, it makes a module, gives it an identity arrow and asserts that
arrow. The answers are supplied, not discovered by an oracle inside the instruction: the
question is which possible memory states this particular answer sequence accepts.

After $j$ matching questions, the surviving candidates are exactly the values whose first
$j$ bits match those answers. There are $2^{n-j}$ of them. So the posterior is tied to what
the program actually checks: run the program on any candidate, and it ends without an
error exactly when that candidate is in the posterior.

The two observations have different jobs here. One looks at the asked bits and can tell a
rejected candidate from every survivor. The other looks at the unasked bits. For any
candidate, keep its unasked bits and replace its asked bits with the supplied answers.
That gives a survivor with the same unasked bits. Each survivor represents $2^k$ candidates,
one for every possible assignment of the asked bits. These are the fibres the bound needs.
For the three cups and two questions, the survivor with the last coin heads represents four
rows, and the survivor with the last coin tails represents the other four.

Each READ\_\allowbreak{}PORT step costs two marks with these operands. The final assertion costs one.
Everything else in this program costs zero on this ledger, so the total is $2k+1$. The
complete binary tree has depth $k$, and the run executes $k+1$ cost-floor steps. That
satisfies the representation theorem's realization condition, which counts paid steps;
it is not a separate claim that the program stores or traverses that tree.

\begin{theorem}[A checked bit search supplies the entitlement data]\label{thm:u33-bit-search}
Let $1 \le k \le n \le 64$. Let the hidden memory value have length $n$, and let the
$k$ supplied answers agree with its first $k$ bits. With the candidate start states,
asked-bit observation, unasked-bit representative observation, complete tree of depth $k$,
and program just described, all the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:u08-representation} hold.
The posterior predicate is strictly stronger, the run contains a structure addition, and
\[
\lceil\log_2 2^n\rceil - \lceil\log_2 2^{n-k}\rceil
= k \le \Delta\mu = 2k+1.
\]
For every candidate of length $n$, membership in the posterior is equivalent to the run
ending without an error. The execution budget is $5k+5$ steps.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Each successful question compares one more memory bit with its supplied answer; a mismatch
reaches the trap. Induction over the questions gives the acceptance condition and the paid
steps. Enumerating all assignments to the unasked bits gives the posterior's size.
Keeping those bits and replacing the asked ones supplies a representative for every prior
candidate, with $2^k$ candidates in each fibre. A candidate with its first bit opposite to
the first answer witnesses strictness. The honest hidden value survives and the assertion
suffix raises the channel. These facts fill the representation theorem's hypotheses; the
instruction-cost sum is $2k+1$.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{bit\_search\_entitlement}, \code{bit\_search\_bound\_reads},
\code{posterior\_is\_what\_the\_run\_certifies} (posterior membership is equivalent to an error-free run) and \code{bit\_search\_shortcut}
(BitSearchEntitlement.v).

With the three cups, two answers cost five marks and remove two index bits. This is an
example of the accounting theorem with a real candidate filter. It is not a speedup theorem,
and its prices are the chosen instruction schedule. The relation between the answers and
the candidates is proved for this program. The assertion instruction itself still accepts
a label without requiring that proof; Section~\ref{sec:smallest}'s small machine is where the check-to-commitment
rule is enforced by the step.

\subsection{A small two-state witness}

There is also a smaller witness to inhabiting the record. There's a concrete run: a twenty-three
instruction program, given a budget of thirty-three steps and ending with the counter at
nineteen. It's a factored search (find one cell in an $N$-by-$N$ grid by searching the two
coordinates separately instead of walking every cell), followed by three instructions, the
last of which asserts an arrow. It has a prior list of two states and a posterior of one, a
two-leaf tree (which I'd read as one leaf per factor), and that run is a closed term of the
record type, which is Coq for a finished value with every one of the fifteen slots filled
and nothing left open. The bound reads off it:
stronger predicate, assertion event, counter up by at least one index bit. So the class isn't
empty. One thing is written down and type-checks.

Now the honest picture of that member, because it isn't a picture of a search narrowing a
candidate set. The prior is the start state and the end state of the same run, the observation
asks whether the counter equals nineteen, and the representative observation is the constant
empty one, so the covering clause asks for nothing. The member shows the record can be
inhabited. It doesn't show a real search shrinking a real list of candidates. And there's a
boundary on the other side of it: the same factored search with only its two emitting steps and no
assertion at the end certifies the observation (no error, the posterior's test passes, the
bound's arithmetic holds) but never raises the assertion channel, so the assertion-event
conclusion doesn't apply to it. The three-instruction suffix is what closes that gap.

Here's the member laid open, all of it, because it's small enough to count. Fifteen fields:
seven data, eight proofs. The decoder is the identity on instruction lists. The program $p$ is
the twenty-instruction factored search for $N = 1$ followed by three steps that make a new
group, give it its identity arrow (Section~\ref{sec:category}'s do-nothing arrow from a module to itself, MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ID),
and assert that arrow with the label ``factorized''; the start $s$ is the machine's initial
state; the fuel is 33; the end state, call it $s_{19}$, has counter 19. The other ingredients
are these.

\begin{enumerate}
\item The prior is the two-element list $[s, s_{19}]$.
\item The posterior is the one-element list $[s_{19}]$.
\item Strict narrowing: $s_{19}$ is in both lists, and $s$ is in the prior and not the posterior.
\item The distinguishing observation returns $p$ when the counter is 19 and the empty list
otherwise. It returns $p$ at $s_{19}$ and the empty list at $s$, whose counter is 0.
\item The tree is one branch with two leaves, depth 1.
\item The tree is realized: the run executes three cost-floor steps (the two that emit and the
assertion), and $1 \le 3$. This is a count, not a walk down the tree.
\item The representative observation is written as ``if the counter equals itself then the empty
list,'' which is always the empty list, and every fibre is the whole prior.
\item The certified posterior: no error at the end, the membership predicate of $[s_{19}]$
accepts $p$, and the channel holds the checksum of ``factorized,'' which is not zero.
\item The start is clear: the initial state's channel is 0.
\end{enumerate}

The equality test is decided by \code{receipt\_list\_eqb\_spec}, the posterior is non-empty by
\code{sighted\_n1\_supra\_posterior\_nonempty}, and the fibres are \code{sighted\_n1\_supra\_representatives}.

\begin{remark}[What the member computes]\label{rem:u08-member}
Feeding these into the corollary gives a strictly stronger posterior predicate, a structure
addition, and $\lceil \log_2 2 \rceil \mathbin{\dot{-}} \lceil \log_2 1 \rceil = 1 \le 19 - 0$.
Every obligation about the run is discharged by running it inside the proof checker
(Coq's vm\_\allowbreak{}compute tactic), so the member is a computation, not an argument.
\end{remark}

Checked as \code{factored\_n1\_shortcut} and \code{factored\_n1\_shortcut\_lands\_in\_representation}
(StructuralAdvantageCertifiedShortcut.v); the version without the suffix is in
StructuralAdvantageObservedShortcut.v.

What it doesn't do, said flatly. It doesn't check that the factorisation is \emph{right}. The
assertion step certifies that an arrow was asserted with a property label; nothing ties that
label to a factorisation checker. The same goes for the formula check of Section~\ref{sec:claims}:
when it passes, it shows a formula can be made true and can also be made false, and nothing
makes the way of making it false one of the states in the prior list. Tying a check to a list takes a premise of
its own, and here that premise is the lists and observation functions somebody supplies. It's
a receipt for what the run paid, not a proof of what the run claimed. The speedup in that
example (searching the two coordinates separately, 2N steps, instead of the whole N-by-N grid,
N squared steps) is divide-and-conquer, which is as old as computing and which nobody is
selling here. And here's what's checked about it: the iteration counts are results about the
runs, for every N. The blind search over the N-by-N grid runs N squared iterations and ends
with the counter at 0; the factored one runs 2N and ends with the counter at 18. At N = 1 the
factored program is the slower one, two iterations against one. The
