point of the example is only that the shortcut's
\emph{admissibility} is on the record, with a cost, separate from its \emph{dividend}. And it is not a
result about P versus NP, and anyone who reads it as one is reading their own ambition into
the bytes. One more boundary: there is no unconditional bound on a single run's narrowing.
A single execution path doesn't carry enough information for that; the bound needs the
tree, or a per-branch account of what was ruled out, and the code refuses to claim more.

The numbers, so you can check them. The blind program, the one that walks every cell, has
every declared cost set to zero
and ends with the counter at 0. The factored one pays for two emitting steps with a one-character
payload, each charged its payload's eight bits plus one, so 18; the three-instruction suffix
adds one more for the assertion, so 19. Put a price on the counter: say one mark is worth
$\lambda$ iterations, so a run costs its iterations plus $\lambda$ times its counter. The
factored run is the cheaper one exactly when $2N + 18\lambda < N^2$, and once $N$ is at least
$18\lambda + 3$ it always is. That's the time tax in one line: the blind search pays in time,
the factored one pays a fixed eighteen marks for knowing the grid splits, and past a size you
can compute, knowing wins. The pure arithmetic around it is lopsided too: for $N \ge 6$,
$N^2 > 2N + 18$, and for every $k \ge 1$ there is an $N \ge 2$ with $N^2 \ge k \cdot 2N$, so the
ratio of the two iteration counts has no ceiling.

\begin{remark}[What the speedup theorems state]\label{rem:u08-time-tax}
Write $B_t$ for the ten-instruction blind search with target $t$ and $S_{l,r}$ for the
twenty-instruction factored search with targets $l$ and $r$, $s_0$ for the initial state,
$\mathrm{run}(F, p, s_0)$ for the program-counter runner with fuel $F$, and $r_{15}(s)$ for
register 15, which counts loop iterations.
(1) If $t + 1 < 2^{64}$ and $F \ge 5t + 8$, then $\mathrm{run}(F, B_t, s_0)$ has
$r_{15} = t + 1$, counter 0 and program counter 10.
(2) If $l + r + 2 < 2^{64}$ and $F \ge 5(l + r) + 16$, then $\mathrm{run}(F, S_{l,r}, s_0)$ has
$r_{15} = (l + 1) + (r + 1)$, counter 18 and program counter 20.
(3) For every $N \ge 1$ with $N^2 < 2^{64}$, every whole number $\lambda$, and fuel
$F_b \ge 5N^2 + 3$ and $F_s \ge 10N + 6$, let $b = \mathrm{run}(F_b, B_{N^2 - 1}, s_0)$ and
$c = \mathrm{run}(F_s, S_{N-1, N-1}, s_0)$. Then $r_{15}(b) = N^2$, $\mu(b) = 0$,
$r_{15}(c) = 2N$, $\mu(c) = 18$, and
\[
r_{15}(c) + \lambda \mu(c) < r_{15}(b) + \lambda \mu(b) \iff 2N + 18\lambda < N^2.
\]
(4) With the hypotheses of (3) and $N \ge 18\lambda + 3$ in place of $N \ge 1$,
$r_{15}(c) + \lambda \mu(c) < r_{15}(b) + \lambda \mu(b)$.
\end{remark}

\begin{proof}
(1) and (2) by a loop invariant: each pass through a loop body is five steps, adds one to
register 15 and one to the loop index, and charges nothing, because every arithmetic, load
and jump in both programs declares cost zero; the index reaches its target because the
subtraction on sixty-four-bit words is zero exactly when the two words are equal, and both
are below $2^{64}$. The exits are a few more steps each, and in the factored program each exit
runs one EMIT of a one-character payload at nine marks. Past the end of the program the runner
stops, so extra fuel changes nothing. (3) is (1) at $t = N^2 - 1$ and (2) at $l = r = N - 1$,
then arithmetic. (4) is (3), since $N \ge 18\lambda + 3$ gives
$N^2 \ge 18\lambda N + 3N > 2N + 18\lambda$.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{blind\_program\_run}, \code{sighted\_program\_run}, \code{time\_tax\_theorem} and
\code{time\_tax\_sighted\_wins} (StructuralAdvantage.v), all closed, with the loop lemmas
\code{loop\_iteration} and \code{loop\_iterations} and the word fact \code{word64\_sub\_zero\_iff}.
\code{iteration\_savings\_dwarfs\_mu\_cost} and \code{advantage\_factor\_unbounded} (same file) are the two
inequalities above, proved by arithmetic alone. The case $N = 1$ is also computed directly:
\code{blind\_halts\_in\_n\_squared} (fuel 8, register 15 holds 1, counter 0) and
\code{sighted\_halts\_in\_two\_n} (fuel 20, register 15 holds 2, counter 18).

\subsection{What landed}

So here's Section~\ref{sec:entitlement} and Section~\ref{sec:insight} on something that runs. Looking can be free: CHSH\_\allowbreak{}TRIAL moves no reading
and can cost zero. Turning a reading on can't: every one of the fifty-one instructions was
checked, and any step that does it pays at least one. A game result behind the flag adds
meaning and not a mark. The check and the commit are two steps, LASSERT and MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT,
priced separately, and nothing in the machine joins them or makes the second wait for the
first. A certified end from a clear start points at an assertion you can name, and a run that
supplies a narrowing, a tree, fibres and the cost-floor steps to cover the tree pays at least
the index bits it commits to; the record that packages all that is a checklist with one
member, and the member is honest about being small. A paid flag is still not a true claim, and
the machine still never reads either reading. Those are the parts of Section~\ref{sec:entitlement} and Section~\ref{sec:insight} this machine
witnesses. The rest of Parts II and III, the subsumption of an ordinary machine, the windows
and their collisions, the floor on all fifty-one, the finite fragment that pays for its
merges, gets the same treatment next, in Section~\ref{sec:witness}.

%===========================================================================
\section{The machine as witness}
\label{sec:witness}
%===========================================================================

Parts II and III made claims about any machine and kept saying ``when the machine exists on
the page, I'll show you.'' The machine exists, and by that I mean the big one, the
fifty-one-instruction test bench from Section~\ref{sec:onemachine} on, not the six-instruction
small machine, which keeps its own chapter and its own name. Some of the showing has happened already:
Section~\ref{sec:state} put Section~\ref{sec:counter}'s counter rule on one field, Section~\ref{sec:isa} put Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s floor on fifty-one instructions, Section~\ref{sec:separation}
showed Section~\ref{sec:windows}'s window losing the graph, and Section~\ref{sec:machine-claims} just did Section~\ref{sec:entitlement} and Section~\ref{sec:insight} whole. This section is the
rest: for each remaining claim, the theorem about \emph{this} machine, with its hypotheses and its
witness, so that the abstract parts can be checked against something that runs. I've grouped
them by the section they pay off, and where an earlier chapter of this part already stated a
fact, I point there instead of saying it again.

Fair question before any of it: why bother? Those claims were already proved for any machine
with the named parts, so what does one more machine add? Here's the worry it answers. A
theorem about every machine with some property is also true when no machine has the property.
``Every unicorn in this room is pink'' is true, and it says nothing. A witness is the cheap
insurance against that: one actual thing, every hypothesis met, that the theorem is about. And
then the next question, which is what most of this chapter turns out to be about: once a
theorem lands on a real machine, does it say what the abstract version seemed to say, or
something smaller? Sometimes it's the same. A fair number of times below it's something
smaller, and I'd rather you watch each one shrink than find out later.

\subsection{What this machine is, relative to an ordinary one (Section~\ref{sec:structure}, Section~\ref{sec:diagonal})}

An ordinary machine has arithmetic, memory, jumps, calls, ports and a halt. Of the
fifty-one instructions, twenty-nine pass the machine's own test for that
(\code{is\_classical\_opcode}), and I'd rather you see the test's answer than my description of it.
It's the same line Section~\ref{sec:isa} drew, and the twenty-two that fail are listed by name in Section~\ref{sec:isa}'s
Definition~\ref{def:u17-classical}, so I won't make you read them twice. Everything else passes: the arithmetic, the memory and heap moves, the jumps, calls and returns, the
ports, HALT and CHECKPOINT, and three that aren't plain arithmetic but pass anyway, because
they leave the structure alone: MDLACC, which only charges the ledger, and the two readers
MORPH\_\allowbreak{}GET and TENSOR\_\allowbreak{}GET, which look at the structure without changing it. Call a run
\emph{classical} when every instruction in it is one of the twenty-nine.

Two theorems say the machine contains an ordinary one without disturbing the structure.
\emph{Faithfulness}: the shadow is, by definition, six fields (registers, memory, counter,
program counter, error, certified), and a classical run leaves the graph, the assertion channel, and the flag where they were (\code{classical\_run\_shadow\_faithful}; its first half is true by
unfolding the definition, its second half is the next theorem). \emph{Conservativity}: a
classical run preserves the graph, the channel, and the flag (\code{classical\_opcodes\_preserve\_structure}, from
single-step lemmas per field). Neither says anything about the other fields (the witness
counters, the tensor, the logic accumulator, the mode word), and I won't claim more than
that. Conservativity holds both ways a program can run: as an in-order fold of the step
function over a list, and under the program-counter runner, which follows the jumps. So a
classical program that loops is inside what's proved, and Section~\ref{sec:separation}'s strictness theorem starts
from the initial state for the same reason.

Here are the test and the theorem exactly. The theorem is Section~\ref{sec:isa}'s
Theorem~\ref{thm:u17-classical} under the name the files give it; it's restated here because
this is where its partner, faithfulness, lives. For a state $s$ write $\mathrm{graph}(s)$ for its
graph, $\mathrm{chan}(s)$ for the assertion channel (Section~\ref{sec:isa} wrote it
$\mathrm{certaddr}(s)$), $\mathrm{flag}(s)$ for the certified flag (Section~\ref{sec:isa}'s
$\mathrm{cert}(s)$), and $\mu(s)$ for the counter. The shorter names are only for this
section.

\begin{definition}[Classical opcode, classical run]\label{def:u21-classical}
\code{is\_classical\_opcode} returns false on exactly the twenty-two non-classical instructions of
Definition~\ref{def:u17-classical} and
true on the other twenty-nine. A list of instructions $t$ is \emph{classical} when every member
passes. For a state $s_0$, $\mathrm{run}(t, s_0)$ applies the step function
$\mathrm{apply}$ to $s_0$ and the members of $t$ in list order, first to last; the program
counter is not consulted. For fuel $F$, $\mathrm{run}_{pc}(F, t, s_0)$ is the program-counter
runner: $F$ times, fetch the member of $t$ at the program counter and apply it, stopping
early when the program counter is past the end of $t$; jumps move the counter.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Conservativity]\label{thm:u21-conservativity}
For every classical list $t$, every state $s_0$ and every fuel $F$, with $s$ either
$\mathrm{run}(t, s_0)$ or $\mathrm{run}_{pc}(F, t, s_0)$:
$\mathrm{graph}(s) = \mathrm{graph}(s_0)$, $\mathrm{chan}(s) = \mathrm{chan}(s_0)$, and
$\mathrm{flag}(s) = \mathrm{flag}(s_0)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Induction on $t$. The empty list changes nothing. For a list $i$ followed by $t'$, three
single-step lemmas, each a case split over the instruction type, say that a classical
instruction leaves the graph, the channel and the flag as they were, and the induction
hypothesis covers $t'$. For the program-counter runner, induction on $F$: each round either
stops or fetches a member of $t$, which is classical, so the same single-step lemmas apply.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{classical\_opcodes\_preserve\_structure} (ClassicalConservativity.v), from
\code{classical\_trace\_preserves\_graph}, \code{classical\_trace\_preserves\_cert\_addr} and
\code{classical\_trace\_preserves\_certified}, and \code{classical\_opcodes\_preserve\_structure\_run\_vm} for
the program-counter runner. \code{classical\_run\_shadow\_faithful}
(TuringClassicalEmbedding.v) repeats the three equalities and adds that the shadow of
the final state is the record of its registers, memory, program counter, counter, error bit
and flag, which holds by unfolding the definition.

A third, which goes by the name ``Thiele simulates Turing'' in the files and which I'll state
for exactly what it is: there's a file-local pairing of a Turing machine's
configuration with a counter, where the lifted machine's step tracks the Turing machine's
step and adds one to the counter (two if it wrote a non-blank), and a theorem that running
the lifted machine on n units of fuel projects to running the Turing machine on n units
(\code{thiele\_simulates\_turing\_gen}, and \code{thiele\_simulates\_turing} for a start with counter
zero). The file's own scope note says not to cite it as \emph{the VM} simulating Turing machines.
It's a small lifted model, not the twelve-field state. The honest sentence is: the pattern
``an ordinary machine plus a counter that only climbs'' is instantiated once in miniature and
proved to track the ordinary machine; the twelve-field machine's relation to ordinary
computation is the faithfulness and conservativity pair.

The degenerate-projection theorem (\code{degenerate\_projection\_theorem}) packages four parts, and
this small simulation is the first. The other three are Section~\ref{sec:separation}'s quotient theorem,
Theorem~\ref{thm:u19-quotient}: two states have equal shadow exactly when they agree on the six fields, a classical run
from states that agree on the shadow, the graph and the control and status words ends at
equal shadows, and two distinct states can have equal shadow.

\subsection{The counter on this machine (Section~\ref{sec:counter})}

Section~\ref{sec:counter} argued its facts about the counter for any machine whose state carries a counter kept by a
price list (Definition~\ref{def:u06-counter}), and said the checked versions are about this
machine. Here they are. The one-step rule, counter after equals counter before plus the
instruction's cost, is Section~\ref{sec:state}'s Theorem~\ref{thm:u16-conservation}, checked by going through all
fifty-one instructions, the failure branches included; everything in this subsection stands on
it. Write $\mathrm{cost}(t)$ for the sum of the costs of a list $t$, $s_\mathrm{init}$ for the
initial state (counter 0), and call a state \emph{reachable} when it is $s_\mathrm{init}$ or
$\mathrm{apply}(s, i)$ for a reachable $s$.

One thing about the checked name of the uniqueness half, because it misleads:
\code{mu\_is\_initial\_monotone} doesn't have ``monotone'' among its hypotheses. Its two hypotheses are
that the other books start at zero and follow the schedule; climbing follows from the
schedule, since the schedule never charges a negative amount. And its conclusion holds on
reachable states only, which is what Section~\ref{sec:counter} said a receipt should promise.

\begin{theorem}[The counter on this machine]\label{thm:u21-counter}
(1) For every state $s$ and list $t$, $\mu(\mathrm{run}(t, s)) = \mu(s) + \mathrm{cost}(t)$.
(2) For every state $s$ and instruction $i$, $\mu(s) \le \mu(\mathrm{apply}(s, i))$. (3) Let
$B$ be any function from states to $\mathbb{N}$ with $B(\mathrm{apply}(s, i)) = B(s) +
\mathrm{cost}(i)$ for all $s$ and $i$. If $B(s_\mathrm{init}) = 0$, then $B(s) = \mu(s)$ for
every reachable $s$. Without the start condition, there is a nondecreasing $f$ with $B(s) =
f(\mu(s))$ for every reachable $s$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Induction on $t$, one application of the one-step rule per instruction. (2) The one-step
rule, with $\mathrm{cost}(i) \ge 0$. (3) Induction on why $s$ is reachable, exactly as in
Theorem~\ref{thm:initiality}; for the last part take $f(n) = B(s_\mathrm{init}) + n$.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{mu\_accumulates\_trace\_cost} and \code{mu\_is\_initial\_monotone} (MuInitiality.v),
\code{vm\_mu\_monotonic\_single\_step} (MuLedgerConservation.v) and \code{monotone\_factors\_through\_mu}
(MuInitiality.v), all resting on \code{vm\_apply\_mu}.

Section~\ref{sec:counter} also pointed at a universal property nearby and said exactly how far the borrowed word
``initial'' reaches. Here's the trace fold, because the word is going to get leaned on and you
should see how little is under it. A \emph{target} is any machine $M$ that takes this machine's
instructions: a set of states, a step $\mathrm{step}_M$, a cost per instruction, and a reading
that obeys the toll. Pick a state $b$ of $M$ to start from. Write $t \cdot i$ for the list $t$
with one more instruction $i$ on the end, and $F_b(t)$ for the state $M$ ends in when you walk
the list $t$ through it from $b$.

\begin{theorem}[Folding a run is the only way]\label{thm:u21-trace-fold}
For every target $M$ and starting state $b$: $F_b([\,]) = b$, and
$F_b(t \cdot i) = \mathrm{step}_M(F_b(t), i)$ for every list $t$ and instruction $i$. And any
function $g$ from instruction lists to states of $M$ with $g([\,]) = b$ and
$g(t \cdot i) = \mathrm{step}_M(g(t), i)$ for all $t$ and $i$ equals $F_b$ on every list.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The first two facts are what walking a list means. For uniqueness, induct on the list from
its end. On the empty list both give $b$. If $g(t) = F_b(t)$, then
$g(t \cdot i) = \mathrm{step}_M(g(t), i) = \mathrm{step}_M(F_b(t), i) = F_b(t \cdot i)$.
The proof never looks at the target's reading or its cost.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{thiele\_trace\_fold\_initial} (ThieleInitiality.v), which the file also exports
under the older name \code{thiele\_is\_initial\_a2\_substrate}; the file's own comment says that name
does not assert the machine's states are initial. The statement is over lists of this
machine's instructions, which is why it lives here and not in Section~\ref{sec:counter}.

Coming down from lists to states is where the borrowed word stops. Write $\mathrm{ev}(t)$ for
the state this machine is in after running $t$ from its start, and call $v$ a \emph{descended
value} at a reachable state $s$ when some list $t$ has $\mathrm{ev}(t) = s$ and $F_b(t) = v$.

\begin{theorem}[When the fold comes down to states]\label{thm:u21-descent}
Fix a target $M$ and a starting state $b$.

(1) Every reachable state has exactly one descended value if and only if, for all lists $t$
and $u$, $\mathrm{ev}(t) = \mathrm{ev}(u)$ implies $F_b(t) = F_b(u)$.

(2) Suppose some function picks, for every reachable state, a list that reaches it. Then a
map $h$ from the machine's states to $M$'s states with $h(\mathrm{ev}([\,])) = b$,
$h(\mathrm{apply}(\mathrm{ev}(t), i)) = \mathrm{step}_M(h(\mathrm{ev}(t)), i)$, and the
machine's reading at $\mathrm{ev}(t)$ equal to $M$'s reading at $h(\mathrm{ev}(t))$, for all
$t$ and $i$, exists if and only if two things hold: the condition in (1), and the machine's
reading at $\mathrm{ev}(t)$ equals $M$'s reading at $F_b(t)$ for every list $t$. Any two such
maps agree on every reachable state.

(3) A picking function as in (2) exists, so the equivalence in (2) holds with no premise
about picking.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) If equal machine states give equal target states, then $F_b(t)$ is a descended value at
$\mathrm{ev}(t)$, and any other one, $F_b(u)$ with $\mathrm{ev}(u) = \mathrm{ev}(t)$, equals
it. Conversely, if $\mathrm{ev}(t) = \mathrm{ev}(u)$, then $F_b(t)$ and $F_b(u)$ are both
descended values at that state, so they're the same one. (2) Any such map sends
$\mathrm{ev}(t)$ to $F_b(t)$, by induction on $t$ from its end, exactly as in
Theorem~\ref{thm:u21-trace-fold}; so it gives both conditions, and any two such maps agree on
reachable states. For the other direction, send each state $s$ to $F_b$ of the list picked
for $s$. The first condition makes that equal to $F_b(t)$ for every $t$ reaching $s$, which
gives the start and the step; the second gives the reading. (3) Number every list of
instructions so that every list gets a number. For a state $s$, pick the list with the first
number whose run reaches $s$, or the empty list if none does. Equality of machine states is
decidable, so each number can be checked; asking whether some number works at all is an
unbounded search, settled by the choice principle that comes with Coq's real numbers. If $s$
is $\mathrm{ev}(t)$, the number of $t$ works, so the search finds a list reaching $s$.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{trace\_descent\_unique\_value\_iff}, \code{reachable\_simulation\_exists\_iff},
\code{reachable\_simulation\_requires\_compatibility}, and \code{reachable\_simulation\_unique}
(TraceStateDescent.v); the uniqueness for maps someone supplies is also
\code{thiele\_morphism\_unique\_on\_reachable} (ThieleInitiality.v). For (3):
\code{reachable\_trace\_representative}, \code{reachable\_trace\_representative\_correct} and
\code{reachable\_representative\_exists} (ReachableTraceRepresentative.v), and
\code{generalized\_reachable\_simulation\_holds}, the equivalence of (2) for every reading, target and
starting state with the picking premise gone. Its one assumption is that choice principle,
\code{sig\_forall\_dec}, already in the standard-library set the rest of the tree uses. What it is
not: a program that rebuilds a list from a state. The picking is a search that exists, not one
anybody would run.

Three targets show where the edges are. One target has a single state and a reading that
never says yes. It obeys the toll, because nothing ever crosses, and it gets no
reading-preserving map from the machine's states at all, because the machine has a state that
reads yes (\code{no\_vm\_state\_morphism\_to\_never\_certifies}, ClaimBoundaryRegression.v). Another
keeps only one bit, whether the certified flag is up, raises it on CERTIFY, and leaves it alone
on everything else; that one comes down fine, and it reaches both no and yes
(\code{certification\_quotient\_satisfies\_descent}, TraceStateDescent.v). The third is the
interesting failure. It keeps the whole list of instructions it was handed, charges the
machine's own prices, and reads the flag with the machine's own evaluator, so its reading
agrees exactly. It still doesn't come down, because the empty list and a single zero-cost
JUMP back to where the machine already is leave the machine in the same state and leave two
different histories behind (\code{certification\_agreement\_does\_not\_imply\_descent},
TraceStateDescent.v; it comes back as part (2) of Theorem~\ref{thm:u21-history} below). The toll
plus a reading that agrees doesn't force a target to forget its history. So the fold is
unique on lists, and that's what the word ``initial'' earns here. It doesn't make this
machine's states initial among everything that obeys the toll, and I won't say it does.

Last, Section~\ref{sec:counter}'s short answer about windows, on this machine. Its \emph{full window} shows the memory,
the registers, the program counter, the counter and the certified flag. A window is
\emph{counter-complete} when some rule applied to what it shows returns the counter on every state,
and \emph{flag-complete} likewise; it \emph{forgets the counter} when changing the counter and nothing
else never changes what it shows, and likewise for the flag.

\begin{theorem}[Neither the counter nor the flag can be dropped]\label{thm:u21-neither-droppable}
The full window is both counter-complete and flag-complete. Every window on this machine's
states that forgets the counter, whatever else it shows, is not counter-complete. Every window
that forgets the flag is not flag-complete.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The full window shows both, so the rule just reads them off. For a window that forgets the
counter, take one state and set its counter to 1 and, separately, to 2. The window shows the
same thing for both, so any rule gives the same answer for both, and one of the two answers
is wrong. The flag is the same argument with yes and no.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{P\_full\_complete\_neither\_mu\_nor\_cert\_droppable}, with \code{forgets\_mu\_not\_mu\_complete}
and \code{forgets\_cert\_not\_cert\_complete} (NecessityAbstract.v; despite the file name, every
statement is over this machine's states). It says neither part can be dropped. It doesn't say
the full window is the smallest window that works, because no ordering of windows is defined
in the file, so there's nothing for it to be smallest in.

\subsection{What no window recovers (Section~\ref{sec:windows})}

Two windows, named. \code{forget} keeps the program counter, the counter, the registers, and the
memory. \code{bare\_observable} keeps the program counter, the registers, and the memory, and
drops the counter. Each is a function from the twelve-field state to a smaller record.

This is where Section~\ref{sec:windows}'s fibre fact (Theorem~\ref{thm:fibre}: a decoder has to give the same answer
on states the window can't tell apart) lands on the machine's own windows. Section~\ref{sec:separation} already stated
the three witness pairs, as Theorem~\ref{thm:u19-irrecoverable}; here they are again under Section~\ref{sec:windows}'s
name, with the two windows named. Each is listed as closed, with no axiom of any kind behind
it, in the last assumption audit (the report the Linux build writes of every axiom each
theorem leans on; Section~\ref{sec:coq} says what it covers), and together they are packaged as
\code{thiele\_content\_irrecoverable\_from\_bare\_projection}. And one fact Section~\ref{sec:separation} didn't state: \emph{every}
four-field snapshot has two distinct preimages, one certified and one not
(\code{fiber\_has\_two\_preimages}), so the many-to-one isn't a special pair; it's everywhere.

\begin{definition}[Two windows; a function of a window]\label{def:u21-windows}
For a state $s$, $\mathrm{forget}(s) = (\mathrm{pc}(s), \mu(s), \mathrm{regs}(s),
\mathrm{mem}(s))$ and $\mathrm{bare}(s) = (\mathrm{pc}(s), \mathrm{regs}(s),
\mathrm{mem}(s))$. A field $f$ of the state is \emph{a function of} a window $w$ when some
$\varphi$ has $\varphi(w(s)) = f(s)$ for every state $s$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Three fields no window recovers]\label{thm:u21-irrecoverable}
(1) $\mathrm{flag}$ is not a function of $\mathrm{forget}$. (2) $\mu$ is not a function of
$\mathrm{bare}$. (3) $\mathrm{chan}$ is not a function of $\mathrm{forget}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Each part is one pair of states written out as records. For (2) the two states agree on
every field except the counter, which is 0 in one and 1 in the other (both have program
counter 10, registers $(42, 0, 0, 0)$ and four zero memory words). Their bare images are
equal, so a $\varphi$ would have to return both 0 and 1 on the same input. Parts (1) and
(3) are the same argument with a pair whose $\mathrm{forget}$ images are equal and whose
flags, or channels, differ. Nothing in these three proofs runs the machine; the pairs are
records.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{cert\_not\_function\_of\_forget}, \code{mu\_not\_function\_of\_bare\_observable} and
\code{cert\_addr\_not\_function\_of\_forget} (ProjectionNonExistence.v, 190, 209), packaged as
\code{thiele\_content\_irrecoverable\_from\_bare\_projection}.

A fourth, from the diagonal section (Section~\ref{sec:diagonal}'s second wall): no decoder on the four-field window
agrees, on every state, with ``the assertion channel is nonzero''
(\code{structural\_shortcut\_not\_function\_of\_classical}). The two states that break every decoder
aren't hand-built records this time; they're reached from the initial state by running
programs. Both start with the same two instructions. Then one runs MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT, which
overwrites the channel with the checksum of its property string, and the other runs an
MDLACC whose charge of one matches MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT's, so the four fields agree and the channel
doesn't. Because the witnesses are reachable, the impossibility isn't about records nobody
could ever produce.

Three small theorems sit beside that one, and they're worth a sentence each because they
close off the reading a skeptic reaches for. Hand the decoder an oracle of any kind, a halting
oracle included, and it's still a function of the four-field window, so the same two states
break it (\code{structural\_axis\_survives\_any\_classical\_oracle}): information that isn't in the
input can't be supplied by an oracle. The two axes are independent in that same sense, each
not a function of the other's window (\code{axes\_mutually\_independent}). And the predicate itself
is decidable from the full state (\code{structural\_membership\_decidable}), so this is not a gap
in computability degree. It's a gap in what the window holds. The file says as much
itself, and I'd rather you didn't read the independence of the two axes as a Turing-degree
result.

One thing I have to say about how these are proved, because Section~\ref{sec:windows} stated the general fact
(\code{decoding\_requires\_fiber\_constancy}), and it's natural to say the pricing results ``are'' that
fact with a price in place of a decoder. As mathematics, fair. As a proof dependency, no:
outside its own file the general fact is used once, in the attestation fragment from Section~\ref{sec:models}, not
in any of these. These are proved directly from their witness pairs. The abstract theorem
and the concrete ones agree; neither cites the other.

\subsection{The floor, on fifty-one instructions (Section~\ref{sec:toll}, Section~\ref{sec:insight})}

Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s universal floor (Theorem~\ref{thm:universal-floor}) says: any system with the toll, any
run from uncertified to certified, paid at least one. Section~\ref{sec:isa} put the one-step form on this
machine (Theorem~\ref{thm:u17-nfi}). Here's the whole ladder of its instances, from the
narrowest to the one I'd cite if I could cite only one.

Two readings of ``certified'' run through all of this, the flag and the channel, and who
writes each is Section~\ref{sec:isa}'s Theorems~\ref{thm:u17-certified} and~\ref{thm:u17-channel}. One thing
about the channel's floor to keep in mind: its proof doesn't use the fact that only
MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT writes the channel; it uses a wider class of five instructions that may touch
the channel, and shows every one of them pays.

One step, the assertion channel: a step that takes the channel from zero to nonzero costs at
least one (\code{no\_free\_certification}; proof: only the five instructions in that class can
change it, and each has the floor). One step, the flag: same (\code{no\_free\_certification\_certified};
only CERTIFY sets it). One step, either reading: the counter rises by at least one
(\code{certification\_requires\_positive\_mu}, \code{certified\_insight\_nonfree}). Over a run, the
channel: the counter ends at least one above where it started
(\code{no\_free\_certification\_trace\_mu}), and the run contains a floor-cost instruction
(\code{no\_free\_certified\_insight}). Over a run, the flag: the counter ends at least one above
where it started (a lemma, \code{no\_free\_certification\_certified\_trace\_mu}; it doesn't also hand
you the instruction).
And the machine packaged as a certification system twice, once per reading, so that Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s
theorem applies to it directly (\code{thiele\_universal\_nfi\_cert\_addr}, \code{thiele\_universal\_nfi\_certified}).

Which is strongest? \code{universal\_nfi\_any\_substrate}, the abstract one, and the two packagings
are its instances. The per-step and counter forms are \emph{sharper} (they name the instruction,
or the counter rather than the summed cost) but narrower. No single theorem says ``either
reading, over a run'' for this machine; what exists is the one-step either-reading theorem
plus the two run theorems separately. Together they say it. There's no one name for it.

Here is the ladder as one statement, with $\mathrm{cost}$ the machine's schedule (an
instruction's declared cost, plus one for CERTIFY, MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT, LJOIN and the game checks,
plus more for LASSERT, EMIT, REVEAL and READ\_\allowbreak{}PORT; Definition~\ref{def:u17-cost}) and
$\mathrm{run}$ the in-order runner of Definition~\ref{def:u21-classical}. Parts (1) to (3) and
the channel half of (4) are Section~\ref{sec:isa}'s Theorem~\ref{thm:u17-nfi} again; the new piece is the flag
half of (4).

\begin{theorem}[The floor on this machine]\label{thm:u21-floor}
Let $s$ be a state, $i$ an instruction and $t$ a list of instructions. (1) If
$\mathrm{chan}(s) = 0$ and $\mathrm{chan}(\mathrm{apply}(s, i)) \neq 0$, then
$\mathrm{cost}(i) \ge 1$. (2) If $\mathrm{flag}(s)$ is false and
$\mathrm{flag}(\mathrm{apply}(s, i))$ is true, then $\mathrm{cost}(i) \ge 1$. (3) In either
case $\mu(\mathrm{apply}(s, i)) \ge \mu(s) + 1$. (4) If $\mathrm{chan}(s) = 0$ and
$\mathrm{chan}(\mathrm{run}(t, s)) \neq 0$, then $\mu(\mathrm{run}(t, s)) \ge \mu(s) + 1$;
the same holds when $\mathrm{flag}(s)$ is false and $\mathrm{flag}(\mathrm{run}(t, s))$ is
true.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(2) The step leaves the flag alone unless $i$ is CERTIFY, and CERTIFY with declared cost $d$
costs $d + 1$. (1) An instruction outside the class REVEAL, EMIT, LJOIN, LASSERT, MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT
leaves the channel unchanged, by a case split over the instruction type, and every member
of the class costs at least one. (3) is (1) or (2) together with conservation,
$\mu(\mathrm{apply}(s, i)) = \mu(s) + \mathrm{cost}(i)$. (4) For the channel: if no member
of $t$ were in the class, the channel would stay 0, so some member is, and the total charge
of $t$ is at least that member's charge; conservation over the run turns the total into the
rise of $\mu$. For the flag: induction on $t$, splitting on whether the flag is already up
after the first step.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{no\_free\_certification} (AbstractNoFI.v), \code{no\_free\_certification\_certified}, \code{certification\_requires\_positive\_mu}, \code{no\_free\_certification\_trace\_mu}
and the lemma \code{no\_free\_certification\_certified\_trace\_mu} (WitnessInsightGeneral.v).

\subsection{The finite fragment that pays for its merges (Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary})}

Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}'s room argument (Theorem~\ref{thm:toll-derived}: finiteness, permanence and merge pricing
force the toll) needs a finite state space, and Section~\ref{sec:state} told you the counter has no ceiling, so
the twelve-field state space is infinite. Here's how that's faced rather than hidden.

Build a finite machine: four slots times a flag, eight states. Three moves: stamp (set the
flag, go to the next slot, cost one), jump to slot a (cost two), next slot (cost zero). On
it, every one of Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}'s premises is a theorem, not a hypothesis: finite (\code{fin\_finite}),
permanent (\code{fin\_permanent}), the next-slot move forgets nothing (\code{fnext\_injective}), the
stamp and the jump merge (\code{fcertify\_merges}, \code{fjump\_merges}), merges are priced
(\code{fin\_merging\_priced}), and per halving (\code{fin\_compression\_priced}). So Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}'s two conclusions
hold on it outright (\code{fin\_a2\_from\_merging\_price}, \code{fin\_a2\_from\_compression\_price}). The
counting lemma underneath, that a duplicate-free list with at most K preimages per image has
at most K times as many members as images, is proved generically (\code{fiber\_bound\_compression}).

Then the bridge. Take a window on the twelve-field machine: the program counter modulo
four as a slot, and the certified flag. Map the three moves to CERTIFY with declared cost
zero (the floor makes the charge one, which is what the finite machine charges the stamp),
JUMP with declared cost two, and a CHECKPOINT with declared cost zero. Then for every state
and every move, the
window of the stepped state is the finite machine's step of the window
(\code{vm\_runs\_finite\_machine}), the counter rises by exactly the finite machine's cost
(\code{vm\_pays\_finite\_price}), both over runs (\code{vm\_runs\_finite\_trace}), and a run of that
fragment from unflagged to flagged raises the counter by at least one
(\code{vm\_fragment\_certification\_paid}). So Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}'s argument applies to this machine
\emph{through a window onto a finite fragment}. That's the honest form. One limit goes with it: the jump's
charge of two is a choice the program makes when it writes the instruction. The machine's
schedule allows it and doesn't force it.

\begin{theorem}[The machine runs the finite fragment]\label{thm:u21-finite-fragment}
Let $\mathrm{win}(s) = (\mathrm{pc}(s) \bmod 4, \mathrm{flag}(s))$, and send the finite moves
stamp, jump to $a$, and next to CERTIFY with declared cost 0, JUMP to $a$ with declared cost
2, and CHECKPOINT with the empty label and declared cost 0. Write $\mathrm{run}(t, s)$ for
the machine run of the images of a list $t$ of finite moves, and $\mathrm{frun}$,
$\mathrm{fcost}$ for the finite machine's run and total cost (stamp 1, jump 2, next 0). For
every $t$ and every state $s$,
\[
\mathrm{win}(\mathrm{run}(t, s)) = \mathrm{frun}(t, \mathrm{win}(s)), \qquad
\mu(\mathrm{run}(t, s)) = \mu(s) + \mathrm{fcost}(t).
\]
If moreover $\mathrm{flag}(s)$ is false and $\mathrm{flag}(\mathrm{run}(t, s))$ is true, then
$\mu(\mathrm{run}(t, s)) \ge \mu(s) + 1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
One step at a time, by computation: CERTIFY 0 moves the program counter on by one and sets
the flag, JUMP sets the program counter to $a$ and keeps the flag, CHECKPOINT moves on by one
and keeps the flag, which are the three finite moves read through the window; conservation
gives the rises 1, 2 and 0. Runs follow by induction on $t$. For the last part, the window
run goes from an unflagged to a flagged finite state, and on the finite machine every move
that raises the flag costs at least one, which is Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}'s toll proved there from finiteness,
permanence and merge pricing (all three theorems on eight states).
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{vm\_runs\_finite\_machine}, \code{vm\_pays\_finite\_price}, \code{vm\_runs\_finite\_trace} and
\code{vm\_fragment\_certification\_paid} (FiniteCertMachine.v, 265, 286, 302); the finite toll
is \code{fin\_a2\_from\_merging\_price}.

And on the full machine, Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}'s merge-or-revoke (Theorem~\ref{thm:merge-or-revoke}), directly:
any step that turns the flag on is
non-injective and costs at least one (\code{vm\_certifying\_step\_is\_priced\_merge}), \emph{and} JUMP 0 0
is non-injective and costs zero (\code{vm\_jump\_is\_free\_merge}). So the full machine prices the
certifying merge and leaves other merges free; it does \emph{not} satisfy ``every merge is
priced'' (\code{vm\_prices\_certifying\_merge\_leaves\_others\_free} states all three). That's the
sharpest sentence in this subsection and it's the one to carry: the machine's schedule
puts the floor on the flag, not on forgetting in general, and Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}'s physics premise, if you
grant it, would charge the jump too. The machine is honest about certification and silent
about everything else it forgets.

In the words of Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} (Definition~\ref{def:fin-perm-inj} and Premise~\ref{prem:merge-pricing}), on
the full machine with step $\mathrm{apply}$ and schedule $\mathrm{cost}$:

\begin{theorem}[The certifying merge is priced; a free merge exists]\label{thm:u21-merge-split}
(1) For every declared cost $d$, CERTIFY $d$ merges. (2) For every state $s$ and instruction
$i$, if $\mathrm{flag}(s)$ is false and $\mathrm{flag}(\mathrm{apply}(s, i))$ is true, then
$i$ merges and $\mathrm{cost}(i) \ge 1$. (3) JUMP to 0 with declared cost 0 merges and
$\mathrm{cost}$ of it is 0. (4) Hence the full machine does not satisfy merge pricing.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Take the initial state with the flag down and the same state with the flag up. CERTIFY
sends both to the same state: its result does not read the old flag (Coq closes this by
computation). The two starts differ, so CERTIFY is not injective. (2) Only CERTIFY turns the
flag on, so $i$ is CERTIFY $d$ for some $d$; it merges by (1) and costs $d + 1$. (3) The
initial state with program counter 0 and with program counter 1 both land at program
counter 0, with nothing charged. (4) Merge pricing applied to the jump of (3) would demand a
cost of at least one.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{vm\_certify\_merges} (FiniteCertMachine.v),
\code{vm\_certifying\_step\_is\_priced\_merge}, \code{vm\_jump\_is\_free\_merge} and
\code{vm\_prices\_certifying\_merge\_leaves\_others\_free}, which states (2), the existence of a
free merge, and (4) as one conjunction.

\subsection{Learning for free (Section~\ref{sec:narrowing})}

Section~\ref{sec:narrowing}'s demon (Theorem~\ref{thm:observer-free}: an observer can learn for free) on this machine:
load a hidden value x into register one, with the observer
watching register two. For x zero and x one the observer sees the same thing (register two
is zero either way). Now run XOR\_\allowbreak{}ADD of register one into register two at declared cost
zero: the observer sees x. The instruction's cost is zero, the counter is unchanged, both
runs started at zero (\code{vm\_observer\_narrowing\_at\_zero\_cost}, proved by computing). One bit
learned, nothing paid. Unconditional, in the sense that no physics premise is involved. I'll
also say what the theorem doesn't say: the file's small abstract demon never merges two
states, but I haven't stated that for this machine's step.

\subsection{Exact-price collisions (Section~\ref{sec:windows})}

Section~\ref{sec:windows}'s clerk (Theorem~\ref{thm:shadow-price}: no exact window price across a collision), on this
machine. From the clean state (empty registers and memory, counter
zero, uncertified), CERTIFY with declared cost zero and JUMP to one with declared cost zero
show the same \code{bare\_observable} before and the same after, and the first raises the flag
(\code{vm\_bare\_observable\_collision}). The counters differ afterwards, one against zero, because
CERTIFY pays the floor, and \code{bare\_observable} doesn't look at the counter. For \code{forget},
which keeps the counter, give the JUMP a declared cost of \emph{one} so the charges match: same
before, same after, one flips (\code{vm\_forget\_collision}). So no price computed from either window both meets the floor and
never overcharges (\code{vm\_bare\_shadow\_cannot\_price\_exactly}, \code{vm\_forget\_shadow\_cannot\_price\_exactly}).
The exact price of certification on this machine lives in the step, or in a window that
shows the flag. And the characterisation: the floor and no-overcharge hold together exactly
when the charged predicate is the flip predicate at unit price
(\code{exact\_commitment\_pricing\_characterization}).

You can run that collision at the table with two scraps of paper. On each, write the same
before-picture: program counter 0, empty registers, empty memory. Under it, on the first scrap
write CERTIFY with declared cost 0, and on the second JUMP to 1 with declared cost 0. Below
that, write the after-picture each one leaves in the bare window: program counter 1, nothing
else changed, the same on both. Fold the instruction line under, hand both scraps to someone,
and ask them to set a price from what they can see. Whatever they charge the first scrap, they
have to charge the second, because they're looking at the same two pictures. Charge one and the
jump is overcharged. Charge zero and the certification goes through free. The only way out is
to unfold the line, or to put the flag in the picture, and that's the window that shows the
flag.

The words, and then the result. Write $\mathrm{flips}(s, i)$ for ``$\mathrm{flag}(s)$ is false
and $\mathrm{flag}(\mathrm{apply}(s, i))$ is true''.

\begin{definition}[Shadow price, floor, no overcharge, collision]\label{def:u21-shadow}
Fix a window $w$. A \emph{shadow price} is a cost of the form $c(s, i) = p(w(s),
w(\mathrm{apply}(s, i)))$ for some function $p$ of the observed pair. A cost $c$
\emph{meets the floor} when $\mathrm{flips}(s, i)$ implies $c(s, i) \ge 1$, and \emph{never overcharges} when
$c(s, i) = 0$ whenever $\mathrm{flips}(s, i)$ fails. A \emph{collision} for $w$ is two steps
$(s_1, i_1)$ and $(s_2, i_2)$ with $w(s_1) = w(s_2)$, $w(\mathrm{apply}(s_1, i_1)) =
w(\mathrm{apply}(s_2, i_2))$, $\mathrm{flips}(s_1, i_1)$, and not $\mathrm{flips}(s_2, i_2)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Neither window prices certification exactly]\label{thm:u21-shadow}
(1) $\mathrm{bare}$ has a collision: from the clean state, CERTIFY with declared cost 0
against JUMP to 1 with declared cost 0. (2) $\mathrm{forget}$ has a collision: from the clean
state, CERTIFY with declared cost 0 against JUMP to 1 with declared cost 1. (3) For any
window with a collision and any $p$, the shadow price from $p$ does not both meet the floor
and never overcharge. So no shadow price from $\mathrm{bare}$, and none from
$\mathrm{forget}$, is exact.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) and (2) are computed. The clean state has program counter 0, empty registers and memory,
counter 0, and the flag down. Both steps end at program counter 1 with registers and memory
untouched; CERTIFY raises the flag and charges $0 + 1$, the jump raises nothing. In (2) the
jump charges 1, so the counters agree as well. (3) Meeting the floor charges the certifying
step at least one. The other step shows the same observed pair, so the shadow price charges
it the same amount, and not overcharging demands zero for it.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{vm\_bare\_observable\_collision}, \code{vm\_forget\_collision} (ShadowPricing.v, 154),
the general \code{shadow\_cannot\_price\_exactly}, and its two instances
\code{vm\_bare\_shadow\_cannot\_price\_exactly} and \code{vm\_forget\_shadow\_cannot\_price\_exactly}. The other direction is Theorem~\ref{thm:shadow-price}: a window that shows the flag has a shadow
price that is exact (\code{window\_showing\_reading\_prices\_exactly}) and no collision
(\code{window\_showing\_reading\_has\_no\_collision}).

\subsection{The verifier and its three escapes (Section~\ref{sec:windows})}

Section~\ref{sec:windows} told the verifier argument with a toy: two runs that leave the same transcript, one that
paid and one that didn't, and a verifier that has to give them one verdict. Here is the pair
on this machine, and the two theorems with it. Start the machine at its clean state (empty
registers and memory, counter zero, uncertified). State $A$ is where it lands after one
CERTIFY with declared cost zero, which charges one; its counter reads 1. State $B$ is where it
lands after one PNEW with an empty region (a new module with no memory cells in it), declared
at cost zero; its counter reads 0. The bare window of Definition~\ref{def:u21-windows} shows the
same thing on both runs: the same start, then the same memory, the same registers, the same
program counter. The \emph{bare transcript} $\tau$ is that pair of photographs. A \emph{verifier} $V$
takes a transcript and says accept or reject. It is \emph{sound} when every transcript it accepts
comes only from states where the claim holds, and \emph{complete} when every transcript from a
state where the claim holds is accepted. The claim is ``the counter is 1,'' and $\tau$ is
explained by exactly two states, $A$ and $B$.

\begin{theorem}[No sound and complete verifier on the bare window]\label{thm:u21-bare-verifier}
For the claim ``the counter is 1,'' with $\tau$ explained by $A$ and by $B$ and by nothing
else, no verifier on bare transcripts is both sound and complete.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Suppose $V$ were both. The counter at $A$ is 1 and $A$ explains $\tau$, so completeness says
$V$ accepts $\tau$. Now soundness, on that same accepted $\tau$: every state that explains
it satisfies the claim, and $B$ explains it. So the counter at $B$ is 1. It is 0.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{bare\_setting\_no\_sound\_complete\_verifier} (VerifierImpossibility.v), with the two
states \code{po1\_state\_A} and \code{po1\_state\_B} from NecessityOfMuLedger.v; no axioms.

Now dress the transcript up. Let $T$ be any richer kind of transcript, with a way $\pi$ to
squash one down to its bare photographs, and a relation saying which states explain which
transcripts. A verifier $V$ on $T$ \emph{factors through} $\pi$ when it only looks at the squashed
part: $V = V' \circ \pi$ for some rule $V'$ on bare transcripts (the small circle means
``squash first with $\pi$, then apply $V'$''), or equivalently, two transcripts with the same
$\pi$ always get the same answer.

\begin{theorem}[A richer verifier that only looks at the bare part does no better]\label{thm:u21-no-factor}
Suppose there are two transcripts $t_A, t_B$ in $T$ with $\pi(t_A) = \pi(t_B)$, $t_A$
explained by $A$, and $t_B$ explained by $B$. Then no verifier on $T$ that is sound and
complete for ``the counter is 1'' factors through $\pi$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If $V = V' \circ \pi$, then $V(t_A) = V'(\pi(t_A)) = V'(\pi(t_B)) = V(t_B)$. Completeness at
$t_A$, which $A$ explains with counter 1, gives $V(t_A) = $ accept. So $V(t_B) = $ accept,
and soundness at $t_B$, which $B$ explains, says the counter at $B$ is 1. It is 0.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{V\_does\_not\_factor\_through\_classical} (VerifierExhaustiveness.v), with every
premise an explicit hypothesis and the two states fixed to $A$ and $B$. The pair $t_A, t_B$ is
a premise, and it's the whole condition: the collision has to survive into the richer
transcript type. A transcript type with no such pair doesn't meet the premise, and the theorem
says nothing about it. So it doesn't classify every transcript design.

Here are the three constructions, with the relations written down. The relation matters:
it says which state a transcript is allowed to describe. If it quietly assumes a truthful
answer, the verifier has not earned the right to trust a liar.

\begin{definition}[Three richer transcripts and their explanations]\label{def:u21-escape-relations}
Keep the states $A,B$ and their shared bare transcript $\tau$ from above, with
$\mu(A)=1$ and $\mu(B)=0$. Write $E_0(s,t)$ for
$t=\tau\;\land\;(s=A\;\lor\;s=B)$. The claim remains $\mu(s)=1$.

A \emph{full-state transcript} is a finite list $t$ of machine states. Define
$E_S(s,t)$ to mean that $t$ is nonempty and its last entry is $s$.
The verifier rejects the empty list; otherwise it accepts exactly when the last
entry's counter is $1$.

A \emph{commitment transcript} is a pair $(t,b)$ of a bare transcript and a Boolean.
For any chosen explanation relation $E_C$, the \emph{commitment contract} is the pair
of implications, for all $s,t,b$:
\[
E_C(s,(t,b))\land b=\mathrm{true}\ \Longrightarrow\ \mu(s)=1,
\]
\[
E_C(s,(t,b))\land\mu(s)=1\ \Longrightarrow\ b=\mathrm{true}.
\]
These are binding and honesty, respectively. The verifier accepts exactly when
$b$ is true. One relation meeting the contract is
$E_H(s,(t,b))\iff E_0(s,t)\land(b=\mathrm{true}\iff\mu(s)=1)$.

A \emph{response transcript} is a pair $(t,r)$ of a bare transcript and a natural
number. Define $E_I(s,(t,r))\iff\mu(s)=r$. The verifier accepts exactly when
$r=1$. This relation imposes no condition on the bare component $t$; the response
alone carries its entire truth condition.

Each construction assigns verification the constant abstract cost $1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Three conditional escapes]\label{thm:u21-escapes}
The full-state verifier is sound and complete relative to $E_S$. For every $E_C$
satisfying the commitment contract, the commitment verifier is sound and complete
relative to $E_C$. The response verifier is sound and complete relative to $E_I$.
Each has cost $1$ under the stipulated cost assignment. The honest relation $E_H$
satisfies the commitment contract; the unchecked relation
$E_U(s,(t,b))\iff E_0(s,t)$ does not.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For the full-state verifier, an explaining state is precisely the last entry. Reading
that entry's counter therefore accepts exactly when the explaining state's counter is
$1$. An empty transcript is rejected and has no explaining state.

For the commitment verifier, acceptance says $b$ is true. Binding then gives the claim
for every explaining state, which is soundness. Conversely, honesty says that any
explaining state satisfying the claim has a true bit, which the verifier accepts.
The equivalence in $E_H$ gives both implications directly. Under $E_U$, however,
$B$ explains $(\tau,\mathrm{true})$ even though $\mu(B)=0$. That violates binding.

For the response verifier, explanation gives $\mu(s)=r$. Acceptance adds $r=1$,
so $\mu(s)=1$. Conversely, $\mu(s)=1$ and explanation give $r=1$, hence acceptance.
The three cost claims follow from the assigned constant.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{substrate\_escape\_succeeds} (VerifierEscape\_\allowbreak{}Substrate.v),
\code{commitment\_contract\_verifier}, \code{honest\_commitments\_satisfy\_contract},
\code{unchecked\_bit\_violates\_contract} (VerifierEscape\_\allowbreak{}Hardness.v), and
\code{interactive\_escape\_succeeds} (VerifierEscape\_\allowbreak{}Interaction.v).

The collision is gone, and no trick did it: the extra information pulls $A$ and $B$ apart.
The full-state transcript shows the counter outright. The honest commitment for $A$ carries a
true bit and the one for $B$ a false bit. The honest responses are $1$ and $0$. In none of the
three is the verifier asked to tell identical inputs apart, which was the impossible job.

Now the limit, and I'd rather say it before you find it. A list of states has no
authentication built into it, so nothing in it stops a liar from handing over whatever the
verifier wants to see. The commitment contract is assumed, and the unchecked bit above is what
happens when the assumption is dropped. The response relation only allows a truthful counter
value, so asking a question here does not buy resistance to a cheating prover. And the cost
$1$ is an abstract price I wrote down, not a measurement of what it takes to authenticate a
state, check a cryptographic proof or send a response. What these three show is which extra
distinctions a verifier can use. They are not an adversary model, a security parameter or a
hardness reduction.

So what would it take to make that commitment bit binding for real, against somebody who wants
to cheat? Cryptographers had to face that one in the open, and the place I'd point is a short
paper Manuel Blum presented at the CRYPTO meeting in 1981, ``Coin Flipping by Telephone.'' His
setup: Alice and Bob have just divorced, they live in different cities, and they want to flip a
coin over the phone for who gets the car, with nobody they both trust to do the flipping. If
Alice flips and announces, Bob has to take her word. If Bob calls it first, Alice can lie about
how it landed. Blum's way out is for one side to commit first: send something that fixes the
choice without showing it, and open it only after the other side has called. And what keeps that
commitment binding isn't anybody's promise. It's a bet that a certain kind of big number is hard
to factor. Push on that and you're standing on the honest edge of this subsection. In Blum's
protocol, binding is earned, on the condition that factoring is hard. Here it's written into the
contract and assumed outright, and the unchecked bit above shows what's left without it. That's
why I won't say these escapes beat a cheater. Blum's paper is the kind of thing it would take,
and nothing like it is in this chapter.

\subsection{Records on this machine (Section~\ref{sec:latch})}

Section~\ref{sec:latch} showed, over any base, that an honest record is a latch, and argued that two things stay
free: the price list and the event. Every checked statement of those two freedoms is about this
machine, so here they are. First the latch itself: Section~\ref{sec:latch}'s Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-latch} holds with
this machine's unbounded step as the base, for each program, halting when the program counter
is past the end (\code{record\_axis\_is\_latch\_on\_vm\_holds}, CrossBaseGranularity.v). So this machine
with an honest record is this machine plus a cup, the same as the three outside bases.

Then the strong reading of uniqueness: is every honest extension of this machine \emph{the same
machine} as this one? In the form the words suggest it's \emph{false}, and the counterexample is
Section~\ref{sec:latch}'s surcharged cup, made real. Take this machine and add a step counter to the ledger, so
every step costs one more than it did. It's honest: the toll is a \emph{floor}, and a surcharge
only raises the price. It extends the base. And it is not the same machine, because this
machine with an empty program sits still and pays nothing per step, and the billed one pays
at least one per step for sitting still (\code{adequate\_core\_uniqueness\_refuted},
\code{honest\_vm\_extension\_uniqueness\_refuted}; the counterexample is \code{BilledCore}). A machine
that charges for CPU time is honest and isn't this one. One thing about how those two theorems
are stated, so the five rules don't quietly change on you: neither is written with the five
rules of Section~\ref{sec:latch} (Definition~\ref{def:u11-honest}). The first uses a looser test of ``honest'' (a ledger that never falls, the toll, a
run that reaches the record being on, and a clause about halting: for every two-counter
machine, some start state has to halt exactly when that machine does). That's Minsky's
two-counter machine, the one Section~\ref{sec:smallest}'s small machine is built on, with its halting problem
borrowed there from the Coq undecidability library; here it only has to be matched, and Section~\ref{sec:interpreters}
runs one as an interpreter on this machine. The second is written for
machines that run this machine underneath, with a map onto its states standing in for
the ``driven by the computation'' rule. Slightly different lists, the same spirit.

Here are both lists, and the sameness they're tested against. One word in the first
definition needs saying: the machine has two step functions, and the \emph{unbounded} one keeps
every number in its registers and memory exactly, instead of cutting it to a fixed width the
way a chip has to. The files use that one here. And ``halts'' gets a convention: the program
counter has run off the end of the program with register nine reading one, which is the
``guest halted'' status the two-counter interpreter of Section~\ref{sec:interpreters} writes there, so this machine's
halting lines up with the two-counter problems in the adequacy clause. One letter, too: in
this section $M$ and $N$ are record-carrying machines in Section~\ref{sec:latch}'s sense, not the trace fold's
target from earlier in the chapter.

\begin{definition}[This machine as a record-carrying machine]\label{def:u21-thiele-core}
The \emph{Thiele core} has states $(p, s)$, a program and a machine state. Its step runs one
instruction of $p$ from $s$ on the unbounded machine, and leaves $(p, s)$ alone when the
program counter points past the end of $p$. Every state is a starting state. Its record is the
certified flag $\mathrm{cert}(s)$, its ledger is $\mu(s)$, and it halts when the program counter
equals the length of $p$ and register 9 holds $1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Adequate; same core]\label{def:u21-adequate}
A record-carrying machine $M$ is \emph{adequate} when (R2) and (R3) hold, some run from a starting
state reaches a state with the record on, and for every two-counter machine problem $P$ some
starting state $m_P$ has: $P$ halts exactly when some $\mathrm{next}_M^k(m_P)$ halts. That last
clause is an existential match, one problem at a time, not a simulation in either direction. $M$
and $N$ have the \emph{same core} when some relation $R$ between their states relates every starting
state of each to some starting state of the other, and any related $m$, $n$ have the same record,
the same next-step cost, and related next states. $R$ need not be a function, so state one
machine keeps and the other doesn't can be ignored.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Honest extension of this machine; observed sameness]\label{def:u21-vm-extension}
$M$ is an \emph{honest extension of this machine} when there is a cover of the Thiele core by $M$
(Definition~\ref{def:u11-base}, with the Thiele core as the base) and (R2) to (R5) hold. $M$ and
$N$ are \emph{observed the same} when some $R$ relates starting states both ways as above, and any
related $m$, $n$ have the same record, the same ledger value, the same halting, the same
next-step cost, and related next states.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Exact uniqueness is false]\label{thm:u21-unique-refuted}
Let the \emph{billed core} have states $(p, s, k)$, step $(p, s, k) \mapsto (p, s', k + 1)$ where
$(p, s')$ is the Thiele core's step from $(p, s)$, every state starting, record
$\mathrm{cert}(s)$, ledger $\mu(s) + k$, and the Thiele core's halting. It is adequate and it is
an honest extension of this machine, and it has neither the same core as the Thiele core nor is
it observed the same.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Every step of the billed core costs at least one. The Thiele core's starting state $([\,], s_0)$,
empty program and initial machine state, never moves and costs $0$ per step. Any relation of
either kind must relate it to some billed state, and the two must have the same next-step cost:
$0$ against at least $1$. Adequacy and honesty are checked clause by clause, the halting clause
by the two-counter interpreter that already runs on the Thiele core.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{billed\_core\_adequate}, \code{billed\_core\_honest\_extension}, \code{billed\_core\_not\_equiv},
\code{billed\_core\_not\_observed\_equiv}, \code{adequate\_core\_uniqueness\_refuted} and
\code{honest\_vm\_extension\_uniqueness\_refuted} (StructuralUniqueness.v), with the definitions
\code{Adequate}, \code{core\_equiv} (StructuralCore.v), \code{ComputationalCover}, \code{HonestVMExtension} and
\code{observed\_core\_equiv} (StructuralCoreCover.v), and the Thiele core's own adequacy
\code{thiele\_core\_adequate} (StructuralCore.v).

Keeping more history doesn't make a machine different under this sameness, and it's worth
seeing why the relation has to be allowed to forget.

\begin{theorem}[History is forgotten by the relation, and only by it]\label{thm:u21-history}
(1) The machine that runs the Thiele core and keeps a list of every state it has passed through
has the same core as the Thiele core. (2) Consider instead a target that is fed instruction
lists one instruction at a time, keeps the whole list it was fed, charges the price list, and
reads certification by running its list on this machine from the initial state. Its reading
agrees with this machine's on every list, and the price list obeys the toll on it, yet it does not
factor through this machine's state: the empty list and the list holding one free jump to
address $0$ leave this machine in the same state and leave the target in different ones.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Relate $(p, s, H)$ to $(p, s)$; records, costs and steps match because the history is never
read. (2) Call the free jump to address $0$ $j$. From the initial state it costs $0$ and sets
the program counter to the $0$ it already had, so the two lists give the same machine state, and
the target's states are the lists themselves, $[\,]$ and $[j]$, which differ.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{history\_core\_equiv\_thiele} (StructuralCore.v) and
\code{certification\_agreement\_does\_not\_imply\_descent} (TraceStateDescent.v), the third target of
Theorem~\ref{thm:u21-descent}.

So agreeing with this machine on every certification reading doesn't make a machine a function
of this machine's state. When a history-keeper counts as the same as this machine, it's because the
relation was allowed to drop the history, and for no other reason.

Back to the billed machine. It isn't a different \emph{structure}; it's the same machine with a different price list. So the claim worth keeping is uniqueness \emph{up to the price schedule}: compare two
machines by their record light, their halting, and their steps, through their maps down to
this machine, and don't compare charges. Here I have to be plain about how much that claim
says. Every machine it covers runs this one underneath, and ``the same machine'' means each state
is related only to the state of this machine that its own map assigns it. So the result says the
extra bookkeeping and the price list don't matter. It doesn't say unrelated machines
coincide. With the record fixed to \emph{this machine's own certification reading} (the certified
flag: the bit only CERTIFY sets, which carries no object and no check), uniqueness up to schedule holds (\code{cert\_record\_schedule\_uniqueness\_holds}): the billed
machine is an instance, and so is any machine that adds to the bill any amount that's a
function of the program and the current state. (The flat one-per-step bill is the separate
\code{BilledCore}.) One structure, many price lists.

\begin{definition}[The same up to the schedule]\label{def:u21-mod-schedule}
Let $M$ cover the Thiele core through $\pi$. $M$ is \emph{priced} when (R2) and (R3) hold. $M$ is
\emph{the same as the Thiele core up to the schedule} when both are priced and some relation $R$
satisfies: $R(m, t)$ only when $t = \pi(m)$; every starting state of each side is related to
some starting state of the other; and related states have the same record, the same halting,
and related next states. Charges are not compared. $M$ is an \emph{honest certification extension}
when $\mathrm{rec}(m) = \mathrm{cert}$ of $\pi(m)$ for every $m$, $M$ is priced, and (R4) and
(R5) hold. It is an \emph{honest tied extension} when instead $\mathrm{rec}(m) = g(\pi(m))$ for some
one function $g$, with the other clauses the same.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Unique up to the schedule, for the certified flag]\label{thm:u21-cert-unique}
Every honest certification extension is the same as the Thiele core up to the schedule. In
particular, so is the billed core, and so is the machine that runs the Thiele core and adds
$e(p, s)$ to a side counter at every step, with ledger $\mu(s)$ plus the side counter, for any
function $e$ from programs and machine states to whole numbers.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Take $R(m, t)$ to mean $t = \pi(m)$. The cover gives the two start conditions, halting, and the
step clause; the record clause is the hypothesis $\mathrm{rec}(m) = \mathrm{cert}$ of $\pi(m)$.
Pricedness is assumed for $M$ and proved for the Thiele core (conservation, and the toll for
the certifying step). The proof is short because the definition pins $R$ to the cover: the content is in the
hypotheses, which is the point made in the text above.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{cert\_record\_schedule\_uniqueness\_holds}, \code{billed\_core\_equiv\_mod\_schedule},
\code{surcharged\_core\_honest\_cert} and \code{surcharged\_core\_equiv\_mod\_schedule}
(StructuralScheduleUniqueness.v), with the definitions \code{record\_is\_certification}, \code{priced},
\code{HonestCertExtension}, \code{HonestTiedExtension} and \code{equiv\_mod\_schedule\_via}
(StructuralCoreSchedule.v), and \code{thiele\_core\_priced}.

And then the second free choice, Section~\ref{sec:latch}'s two cups on one die, on this machine. Let the record
be \emph{any} permanent reading that a paid step writes and that obeys the toll, instead of the
certification reading in particular. Now uniqueness \emph{fails} (\code{tied\_record\_schedule\_uniqueness\_refuted}).
The counterexample: let the record be ``the counter has reached one.'' That's permanent, a
paid step switches it on, the toll holds for it. And at a state where the counter is one and
nothing is certified, that record says on and the certification record says off. Two honest
records, same machine, disagreeing: Corollary~\ref{cor:u11-event-free} with a real machine
underneath.

\begin{theorem}[Not unique for a tied record]\label{thm:u21-tied-refuted}
Let the \emph{meter core} be the Thiele core with record ``$\mu(s) \ge 1$'' and the identity as cover.
It is an honest tied extension and it is not the same as the Thiele core up to the schedule. So
uniqueness up to the schedule fails once the record is only required to be some reading of the
computation.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The record is $g(\pi(m))$ with $g(p, s) = [\mu(s) \ge 1]$. It is priced because the ledger is
the Thiele ledger and a step that turns it on raises $\mu$ from $0$ to at least $1$; permanent
because $\mu$ never falls; and written by the certifying step from the initial state. Now take the starting
state $([\,], s_1)$ with $s_1$ the initial machine state except $\mu = 1$, flag off. Any $R$ must
relate it to some starting state of the meter core, and only to itself, since the cover is the
identity. There the meter core's record is on and the Thiele core's is off.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{meter\_core\_honest\_tied}, \code{meter\_core\_not\_equiv\_mod\_schedule} and
\code{tied\_record\_schedule\_uniqueness\_refuted} (StructuralScheduleUniqueness.v).

\subsection{Pricing and verifying on this machine (Section~\ref{sec:models})}

Section~\ref{sec:models} read five real systems at three levels (specification, transcription, wrapper) and said
some of the wrappers are written for this machine. Here they are, together with the one
sentence about pricing this machine's own flag.

First the gas wrapper's class, on this machine. Price the certified flag at one per raise and
nothing otherwise, and both halves of Section~\ref{sec:models}'s gas-schedule exactness hold, the floor and no
overcharge (\code{thiele\_vm\_commit\_pricing\_is\_exact}, GasMetering.v, through
Theorem~\ref{thm:u13-gas-exactness}). That exact schedule isn't this machine's own counter,
which also bills computation that commits nothing; on every raise the unit price is at most
what the counter charges (\code{thiele\_unit\_price\_lower\_bounds\_mu}). It's the same split the
exact-price subsection above drew with collisions: the exact price of certification lives in
the step, and the counter is a bigger bill that contains it.

The attestation wrapper is a separate file, built on the verifier pair $A$ and $B$ of the
previous subsection. A report there is a bare transcript plus one measurement register, and
an honest report of a state carries a transcript that state explains and a register equal to
its $\mu$.

\begin{theorem}[Attestation cannot factor through the bare transcript]\label{thm:u21-attestation}
Let $V$ be a verifier on reports that is sound (it accepts only reports every honest
explanation of which has $\mu = 1$) and complete (it accepts every honest report of a state
with $\mu = 1$). Then $V$ is not a function of the bare transcript: there are reports with
equal transcripts on which $V$ differs.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The pair $A$, $B$ gives two reports with the same transcript, one honestly explaining a state
that paid ($\mu = 1$) and one a state that did not ($\mu = 0$). Completeness makes $V$ accept
the first; soundness makes it reject the second.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{attestation\_cannot\_factor\_through\_bare\_transcript} (TEEAttestation.v), an
instance of \code{V\_does\_not\_factor\_through\_classical} (Theorem~\ref{thm:u21-no-factor}); the same
file has the pair itself (\code{replay\_is\_a\_two\_preimage\_witness}) and the positive side, a sound
and complete verifier at unit cost once the register is readable
(\code{measurement\_enriched\_attestation\_succeeds}). The register's faithfulness is a premise of
the model, not a fact about hardware. Section~\ref{sec:models}'s quote fragment has two more statements that lean
on this machine's transcript type: \code{quote\_projection\_faithful} says the quote, written into
the machine's bare-transcript format, loses nothing, and \code{quote\_runtime\_verifier\_separation}
says no verifier correct for the platform's runtime flag depends only on that encoding
(TPMQuoteGap.v; the separation is \code{V\_does\_not\_factor\_through\_classical} again, with the pair
$A$, $B$ as its fixed witnesses).

The transparency wrapper is Section~\ref{sec:windows}'s commitment escape in log vocabulary. Under a \emph{disclosure
contract} (a premise: the inclusion bit is set on every honest transcript of a run with
$\mu = 1$, and a set bit binds every explaining run to $\mu = 1$), there is a verifier that
reads the log's inclusion bit, is sound and complete for the claim $\mu = 1$, and costs one
unit (\code{abstract\_log\_bit\_verifier}, TransparencyLog.v). Delete the log and no verifier on the
bare transcript is sound and complete for that claim at any cost
(\code{abstract\_bare\_verifier\_impossible}, which is Theorem~\ref{thm:u21-bare-verifier} under another
name), with the collision pair behind it exhibited as \code{abstract\_mu\_collision\_witness}. The
pair has the shape of a split view, one transcript for two runs; it is not an RFC split view,
which is two inconsistent log histories: a log that shows one version of its past to you and a
different one to me, the move the certificate-transparency logs of Section~\ref{sec:models} are
built to get caught making.

The proof-carrying wrapper is Section~\ref{sec:windows}'s interaction escape. A transcript that carries the
certificate admits a checker, sound and complete for $\mu = 1$ at unit cost
(\code{proof\_rounds\_escape}, ProofCarryingVerifier.v); strip the certificate and no checker on the
bare transcript is sound and complete at any cost (\code{bare\_pcc\_impossible}). And the prover's
side has a floor. A \emph{script} is a program run from the initial state with a fixed fuel, and
it's \emph{level $k$} when it ends with the certified flag up and one of the CERTIFY steps it
executed was charged at least $k$. Then its counter rises by at least $k$, and for every
$k \ge 1$ a single CERTIFY charged $k$ does it at exactly $k$
(\code{level\_k\_verification\_floor}, \code{level\_k\_verification\_floor\_tight}). The first is
\code{level\_k\_certification\_cost\_floor} (MuHierarchyTheorem.v) by exact application, which is the
lower half of Section~\ref{sec:landauer}'s mu-hierarchy, Theorem~\ref{thm:u24-hierarchy}, so the formal statement and
proof live there. The floor prices the run's certification events. It says nothing about proof
size, prover time, or the checker's work.

In each of the three, the unit cost is stipulated, and none of them prices or verifies the
real system it borrows a name from. How to knock them down: for attestation, a sound and
complete verifier on the bare transcript; for transparency, a sound and complete verifier
that needs no log, for the same claim; for proof-carrying code, a script of level $k$ whose
counter rises by less than $k$, or a sound and complete checker with no certificate.

\subsection{The certified flag as a durable consensus (Section~\ref{sec:pointer})}

Section~\ref{sec:pointer} showed that agreement among observers doesn't buy permanence and durability does. Here's
the instance it pointed at: this machine's certified flag is the durable case.

\begin{theorem}[The certified flag is a permanent consensus]\label{thm:u21-cert-consensus}
For any $N > 0$ and any instruction $i$, the game of Definition~\ref{def:u14-game} whose states
are machine states, whose event and every view are the certified flag, and whose step is the
unbounded machine step by $i$, has a permanent event.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Authenticity holds by definition, and durability is the kernel fact that no unbounded step
turns the certified flag off; apply part (2) of Theorem~\ref{thm:u14-toggle}.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{vm\_certification\_is\_permanent\_consensus} (EcosystemGame.v); the durability fact
is \code{vm\_apply\_u\_certified\_permanent}. That one is for a run that repeats a single fixed
instruction, with every observer reading the same bit. It says nothing about the
assertion channel: no theorem says the channel stays set, and an assertion with an empty
property writes a zero to it.

\subsection{What landed}

Every pointer from Parts II and III that said ``on the machine'' has a name in this chapter. What's
\emph{not} here, and stays not here: a single either-reading run theorem; ``every merge priced'' on the
full machine (false, by the free jump); a statement of Section~\ref{sec:counter}'s counter facts or Section~\ref{sec:latch}'s two free
choices over an arbitrary base (those are argued in their chapters, checked only here); and
any claim that the small lifted model is the twelve-field machine. The machine is a witness. It's not a bigger claim than the theorems
on it.

%===========================================================================
\section{Interpreters and the guest machine}
\label{sec:interpreters}
%===========================================================================

Section~\ref{sec:diagonal} left the diagonal standing on any substrate, on a little family built to fit it, and on
L, and said the machine is one more substrate of that kind, conditionally. The machine is
on the table now, so here it is, in three pieces. First the wall pointed at the full
machine, where it is conditional on a recursion premise that can't be granted for every map and
can't hold for any class containing a correct decider's flip, and where a decider standing
outside exists and is checked. Then two interpreters, programs of the machine that run a
smaller machine handed to them as data. Then the guest, where the recursion theorem is
proved rather than assumed. I'll say which interpreter the recursion theorem lives on,
because nobody can check a claim about ``the interpreter'' if there are two.

\subsection{The diagonal, pointed at the machine}

Here's Section~\ref{sec:diagonal}'s question, asked of this machine. The machine carries a record; the record is a
latch on an event (Section~\ref{sec:latch}); for my machine the event is a certification, and Section~\ref{sec:machine-claims} said a
certification reading, with its receipt, is what lets an auditor treat a shortcut as
\emph{admissible}. So: can the machine have, as one of its own programs, a procedure that
correctly decides, for every program, ``does this program admit a sound shortcut''? That
would be autopilot. Hand it any program and it says yes or no, and it's always right.

That's the question in plain words, and the checked statement is narrower, so here it is
before the proof. In the checked work ``admits a shortcut'' is a concrete property of
programs: its bounded run from the start state ends in the same state as the bounded run of
one fixed reference program, a three-instruction one that allocates a group, makes its
identity arrow (Section~\ref{sec:structure}'s do-nothing arrow from a thing to itself), and asserts it. Two programs
that behave alike agree on the property, and there's one program that has it and one that
doesn't. The diagonal doesn't see soundness. For that one reference program the checked work
does show the property lining up with a sound-shortcut record from Section~\ref{sec:machine-claims}. For other programs it
says nothing of the kind, and a procedure that returns soundness records for some programs,
or only for restricted inputs, or with outside evidence, is not what the wall rules out.

Here is that property exactly. Write $s_\mathrm{init}$ for the machine's initial state and
$\mathrm{run}_{1000}(p, s)$ for the state the machine reaches from $s$ running $p$, cut off
after a thousand steps.

\begin{definition}[The machine's shortcut property]\label{def:u12-vm-shortcut}
Let $r$ be the three-instruction program that opens a group (a module) on cell 0, builds
