that module's identity arrow, and asserts the arrow just built; in Section~\ref{sec:isa}'s table these are PNEW, MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ID and MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT. A program $p$ \emph{admits the shortcut} when
$\mathrm{run}_{1000}(p, s_\mathrm{init}) = \mathrm{run}_{1000}(r, s_\mathrm{init})$. The
program $r$ admits it; the empty program does not.
\end{definition}

Checked as \code{vm\_admits\_shortcut\_extensional}, with \code{vm\_admits\_shortcut\_yes} and
\code{vm\_admits\_shortcut\_no} for the two witnesses (StructuralUndecidability.v; $r$ is
\code{simple\_morph\_trace} in SimpleMorphShortcut.v). The no-witness is a computation: the empty
program leaves $s_\mathrm{init}$ where it is, and $r$ does not. The link to Section~\ref{sec:machine-claims}'s record is
\code{vm\_instantiation\_target\_witnessed}: for $r$ alone, a sound-shortcut record exists.

Section~\ref{sec:diagonal}'s wall (Theorem~\ref{thm:u12-no-inside-decider}) is about any substrate: programs, a run, a
counter, an encoding of programs as data, a class of representable transformations, and a
recursion theorem for that class. The machine supplies most of that on its own. It doesn't
supply the last piece. Here's the honest form.

The \emph{concrete machine} (\code{vm\_structural\_shortcut\_undecidable}): the generic theorem applied to
my machine's bounded runs (no decider says yes exactly when a program admits the shortcut), carrying as explicit hypotheses an encoding of programs as data, a
class of representable transformations, and a recursion theorem for that class. (A companion
statement, \code{vm\_structural\_shortcut\_undecidable\_encoded}, discharges the encoding with a proved
round trip between programs and numbers, leaving only the representable class and its
recursion theorem as premises.) Asked for every map on programs, that recursion premise is false, and the reason is the
cutoff, not the size of memory: equality after a thousand steps is something you can check by
running both programs, so the flip of that check has no fixed point. So the corollary needs a
class that leaves the flip of every correct decider out, and with such a class it says exactly
that: the flip of a correct decider has no program whose thousand-step runs match its image's
from every state. The proved recursion theorem further down is for the machine's guest, a
smaller machine it runs as data, and it answers a different question.

\begin{premise}[A recursion theorem for the full machine]\label{prem:u12-vm-recursion}
A class $\mathrm{Rep}$ of maps on machine programs such that every $f$ in $\mathrm{Rep}$ has
a program $q$ with $\mathrm{run}_{1000}(q, s) = \mathrm{run}_{1000}(f(q), s)$ for every state
$s$. The class with only the identity map meets it (take $q$ empty), and so does any class of
constant maps. The class of all maps doesn't: Theorem~\ref{thm:u22-premise-refuted} names a map
with no such $q$.
\end{premise}

\begin{theorem}[The wall on the machine, conditional]\label{thm:u12-vm-wall}
For every class $\mathrm{Rep}$ satisfying Premise~\ref{prem:u12-vm-recursion}, there is no Boolean
function $d$ on machine programs such that the flip of $d$ (the empty program when $d(p)$ is
true, $r$ when it is false) is in $\mathrm{Rep}$ and, for every $p$,
$d(p) = \mathrm{true} \iff p$ admits the shortcut.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Build the substrate from the machine's bounded run, with $\mathrm{enc}(p)$ the initial state
with the number of $p$ stored in one of its number fields (the logic accumulator of Section~\ref{sec:state}) and $\mathrm{dec}$ reading it back
(the round trip between programs and numbers is proved), the given $\mathrm{Rep}$, and the
premise as its recursion theorem. The predicate of Definition~\ref{def:u12-vm-shortcut} is a shortcut
predicate with witnesses $r$ and the empty program, and it is extensional because it reads
only the run from one state. Then Theorem~\ref{thm:u12-no-inside-decider} applies.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{vm\_structural\_shortcut\_undecidable} (StructuralUndecidability.v, encoding as
hypotheses) and \code{vm\_structural\_shortcut\_undecidable\_encoded} (VMSubstrateEncoded.v, encoding
discharged by \code{vm\_encode\_decode\_concrete}). In both, the decider ruled out is one that says true
exactly when a program admits the shortcut. That the empty class meets the premise is logic,
not a stated theorem.

Now the honest part Section~\ref{sec:diagonal} did with a pencil on its little family: \emph{who counts as a decider}.
The theorem rules out a decider whose flip the machine can itself represent. It says nothing
about a decider standing \emph{outside}. And here's a thing that surprised me about my own
machine: its bounded runs (a thousand steps, then stop) make the shortcut predicate
decidable from \emph{outside}, by just running both programs and comparing. So an outside decider
exists. What the theorem says is that such a decider's flip can't be one of the machine's own
representable transformations, under the recursion premise. Same boundary as on Section~\ref{sec:diagonal}'s
family, Richard's lesson again: the language you talk about the machine in is not the
language it talks in.

\begin{theorem}[Bounded runs are decidable from outside]\label{thm:u12-outside-decider}
Let $d_\mathrm{out}(p)$ be true exactly when the two states
$\mathrm{run}_{1000}(p, s_\mathrm{init})$ and $\mathrm{run}_{1000}(r, s_\mathrm{init})$ are
equal. Then $d_\mathrm{out}$ is a total Boolean function, and $d_\mathrm{out}(p)$ is true
exactly when $p$ admits the shortcut. Moreover, let $\mathrm{Rep}$ be any class of maps on
machine programs such that every $f$ in $\mathrm{Rep}$ has a program $q$ with
$\mathrm{run}_{1000}(q, s) = \mathrm{run}_{1000}(f(q), s)$ for every state $s$. Then the flip
of $d_\mathrm{out}$ (the empty program when $d_\mathrm{out}(p)$ is true, $r$ when it is
false) is not in $\mathrm{Rep}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Equality of machine states is decidable, since a state is a finite record of numbers, lists
of numbers, and flags; comparing the two bounded runs is therefore a total function, and it
is correct by its definition. If its flip were in $\mathrm{Rep}$, then $d_\mathrm{out}$ would
be a decider of exactly the kind Theorem~\ref{thm:u12-no-inside-decider} rules out, applied to the
machine's bounded runs with that $\mathrm{Rep}$ (the instance is Theorem~\ref{thm:u12-vm-wall}).
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{vm\_bounded\_shortcut\_decide\_correct} and
\code{vm\_bounded\_decider\_flip\_not\_representable} (VMBoundedDecidability.v).

The same file says the two sentences I keep leaning on as theorems of their own, so you don't
have to take my word for how they follow.

\begin{theorem}[The full-machine recursion premise fails, and every correct flip has no fixed point]\label{thm:u22-premise-refuted}
(1) It is not the case that every map $f$ on machine programs has a program $q$ with
$\mathrm{run}_{1000}(q, s) = \mathrm{run}_{1000}(f(q), s)$ for every state $s$.
(2) Let $d$ be any Boolean function on machine programs with $d(p) = \mathrm{true} \iff p$
admits the shortcut, for every $p$, and let $f_d(q)$ be the empty program when $d(q)$ is true
and $r$ when it is false. Then there is no program $q$ with
$\mathrm{run}_{1000}(q, s) = \mathrm{run}_{1000}(f_d(q), s)$ for every state $s$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(2) If such a $q$ existed, the class whose only member is $f_d$ would satisfy
Premise~\ref{prem:u12-vm-recursion} and contain the flip of a correct decider, which
Theorem~\ref{thm:u12-vm-wall} rules out. (1) If every map had such a $q$, the class of all maps
would satisfy the premise and contain the flip of $d_\mathrm{out}$, which is correct by
Theorem~\ref{thm:u12-outside-decider}; that theorem rules this out.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{vm\_full\_recursion\_premise\_refuted} and \code{vm\_correct\_flip\_has\_no\_fixed\_point}
(VMBoundedDecidability.v), both closed under the global context. In Coq, (1) reads
\textnormal{\texttt{\textasciitilde{} (forall f, exists q, forall s, vm\_run q s = vm\_run (f q) s)}}, and (2) reads
\textnormal{\texttt{forall d, (forall p, d p = true <-> vm\_admits\_shortcut\_extensional p) -> \textasciitilde{} exists q, forall s, vm\_run q s = vm\_run (if d q then [] else simple\_morph\_trace) s}}, with \code{vm\_run} the
thousand-step run and \code{simple\_morph\_trace} the program $r$.

So the machine's property is decidable from outside, and the wall on the machine separates
nothing from classical halting: it's about bounded runs, and the premise can't be granted for
every map (part (1) of Theorem~\ref{thm:u22-premise-refuted}), and no class can both meet it and
contain a correct decider's flip (part (2)). So the machine's version can't be knocked over that way, and it doesn't
say much either: it's the diagonal applied to a property I can decide. Put plainly: against
a decider that's actually correct, the machine's conditional wall has no bite at all,
because no class it would need can hold that decider's flip.

Take the thousand-step cutoff away and the question changes shape, so here's the run with no
stopwatch on it. Unbounded halting is its own relation, and it has its own facts.

\begin{definition}[Halting without a cutoff]\label{def:u12-halts-at}
Program $p$ \emph{halts at} $r$ from $s$ when there is some number $k$ with
$\mathrm{run}_k(p, s) = r$ and the program counter of $r$ is at or past the end of $p$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[A program halts at most once]\label{thm:u12-halts-deterministic}
If $p$ halts at $r_1$ from $s$ and halts at $r_2$ from $s$, then $r_1 = r_2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let the witnesses be $k_1 \le k_2$. Once the program counter is past the end, a step changes
nothing, so $\mathrm{run}_{k_2}(p, s) = \mathrm{run}_{k_1}(p, s)$, and the two results are
equal. The other order is symmetric.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{vm\_halts\_at} and \code{vm\_halts\_at\_deterministic} (VMUnboundedExec.v). This relation
is not the bounded run of Definition~\ref{def:u12-vm-shortcut}: the bounded run always returns a state,
halted or not, and nothing identifies the two. The interpreters in the rest of this chapter
work with unbounded runs too (under a sibling step I'll flag below): programs of my machine
that run a smaller machine handed to them as data. I'll call the smaller machine the
\emph{guest}.

\subsection{Why an interpreter at all}

An interpreter is a program that reads another program as \emph{data} and does what it says. It's
one of the oldest tricks in computing, and it's the trick that makes the diagonal bite: the
Contrarian card in Section~\ref{sec:diagonal} needs ``hand me to the Checker,'' which means a program has to be able
to be \emph{handed}, as a number, to another program. On this machine, a program is a list of
instructions, and there's a proved round-trip encoding of programs as natural numbers
(\code{program\_to\_nat} and back; the wall above used it). So programs can be data. What's left is to
show that a program on the machine can \emph{run} a program given as data, and to say exactly
which programs.

How old is ``one of the oldest''? Turing's 1936 paper already has one: the universal machine,
which reads another machine's rule table off its tape and does what the table says. And the
first one people actually used came in through the side door. John McCarthy, writing up his new
language Lisp around 1960, wanted to show it was neater than Turing machines, so he wrote a
universal function for it, \emph{eval}, the language describing how to evaluate itself, and
showed it was shorter and easier to follow than a universal Turing machine. In his own history
of Lisp, that was for the paper, a thing to read; the notation for writing programs as data was
made up for the paper with no thought of using it in practice. Then S.\,R.\ Russell, Steve
Russell, noticed that eval could serve as an interpreter and coded it by hand, and there was a
running language with an interpreter that nobody had planned. McCarthy adds that the surprise
froze some decisions he'd made ``rather lightheartedly'' for the paper. So the trick has a
habit: written to be read, it ends up being run. The interpreters below go the other way round,
on purpose. They're written to run on the machine, and the proofs check that what runs is what
the page says.

A warning about what the round trip does and doesn't give you. The decoder is a Coq function,
outside the machine. The encoding the wall above uses parks the program's number in the logic
accumulator, a field no instruction ever reads, and there's a theorem that no fixed program
can then report even the encoded program's certification bit through any observation that
ignores that field (\code{no\_logic\_acc\_encoded\_interpreter}). It doesn't rule out a different
encoding. The two interpreters below are different encodings: the code arrives as an ordinary
number in an ordinary register, which is something a program can read.

Here it is exactly. Write $s[\mathrm{acc} := n]$ for the state $s$ with its logic
accumulator replaced by $n$, $\mathrm{apply}$ for the sixty-four-bit step, and
$\mathrm{run}(F, q, s)$ for the program-counter runner: $F$ times, fetch the instruction of
$q$ at the program counter and apply it, stopping early when the program counter is past the
end of $q$.

\begin{lemma}[The accumulator commutes with every step and every run]\label{lem:u22-acc-commutes}
For every state $s$, instruction $i$, number $n$, program $q$ and fuel $F$:
$\mathrm{apply}(s[\mathrm{acc} := n], i) = \mathrm{apply}(s, i)[\mathrm{acc} := n]$ and
$\mathrm{run}(F, q, s[\mathrm{acc} := n]) = \mathrm{run}(F, q, s)[\mathrm{acc} := n]$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The step form is a case split over every instruction: none reads the accumulator and none
writes it. The run form is induction on $F$, using the step form at each fetch; the fetch
reads only the program counter.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{vm\_apply\_logic\_acc\_commutes} and \code{run\_vm\_logic\_acc\_commutes} (VMEncodedInputAccess.v).

\begin{theorem}[No interpreter for the accumulator encoding]\label{thm:u22-no-acc-interpreter}
Say $q$ halts from $s$ showing $b$ under $o$, for a test $o$ from states to booleans and a
bit $b$, when for some $F$ the state $\mathrm{run}(F, q, s)$ has its program counter at or
past the end of $q$ and $o$ of it is $b$. Let $\mathrm{enc}(p)$ be the initial state with the
accumulator set to the number of $p$. For every program $I$ and every test $o$ with
$o(t[\mathrm{acc} := n]) = o(t)$ for all $t$ and $n$, it is not the case that for every
program $p$ and bit $b$, $I$ halts from $\mathrm{enc}(p)$ showing $b$ under $o$ exactly when
$p$ halts from the initial state showing $b$ under the certified flag.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Suppose $I$ did. The program consisting of CERTIFY 0 halts from the initial state with the
flag up, so $I$ halts from its encoding showing true. By Lemma~\ref{lem:u22-acc-commutes} the
run of $I$ from the encoding of the empty program is the same run with a different
accumulator, and $o$ ignores the accumulator, so $I$ also halts from the encoding of the empty
program showing true. Then the empty program would halt from the initial state with the flag
up; it halts at once with the flag down.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{vm\_apply\_logic\_acc\_commutes}, \code{run\_vm\_logic\_acc\_commutes}, \code{halts\_observes\_logic}
and \code{no\_logic\_acc\_encoded\_interpreter} (VMEncodedInputAccess.v, 33, 47, 56).

Both interpreters below run under the machine's \emph{natural-number} sibling (\code{vm\_apply\_u},
\code{run\_vm\_u}). That's a second execution model and I'll flag it: same instruction type, same
twelve-field record, but writes and arithmetic keep the exact value instead of cutting it to
sixty-four bits, and subtraction stops at zero instead of wrapping around. The guest
registers are unbounded because of it. The two steps are separate definitions, and no
theorem here ties the sixty-four-bit machine to its unbounded sibling.

\subsection{The first interpreter: a two-counter machine as guest}

A two-counter machine (Minsky's, from the 1960s) has a program counter and two counters
that hold naturals; its instructions are: halt, increment one or the other, and
``decrement-or-jump'' on one or the other (if the counter is zero, step on; otherwise
decrement and jump to a target). That's all, and once the input is encoded as a number it's
enough to compute anything a Turing machine can, which is why it's the classic small target
for undecidability proofs.

The title of Minsky's 1961 paper is the clue I can't leave alone. It's about ``Post's problem of
tag.'' Who's Post, and what's tag? Emil Post, in 1921, on a fellowship at Princeton, was playing
with about the simplest rewriting game there is. Take a word of 0s and 1s. Look at its first
letter, chop the first three letters off the front, and stick something on the end:
\texttt{00} if the letter you looked at was 0, \texttt{1101} if it was 1. Repeat, and stop when
fewer than three letters are left. Try it at the table. Start from \texttt{1000}: you get
\texttt{01101}, then \texttt{0100}, then \texttt{000}, then \texttt{00}, and it stops. Start from
\texttt{100}: you get \texttt{1101}, \texttt{11101}, \texttt{011101}, \texttt{10100},
\texttt{001101}, and then \texttt{10100} again, and it goes round forever. Post wanted a rule
that tells you, for every starting word, which of those happens. He worked at it for months and
later called it hopeless, and as far as I can tell it still is: a hundred years on, nobody knows
whether that one little game, with that one rule, can be decided. Minsky's paper showed that tag
games in general can compute anything, which is why Post's name is on it. It didn't settle Post's
own game. And the chase goes one step further. In 2008 Liesbeth De Mol turned
the famous $3n+1$ problem (halve an even number, triple an odd one and add one, and ask whether
you always get down to 1) into a small tag game of the same kind. So is Post's game secretly as
hard as everything, or just stubborn? I can't tell you, and as far as the published work goes,
nobody can yet.

None of that changes the interpreter below. It changes the picture. The two-counter machine came
out of a hunt for the smallest thing that can't be predicted, and the smallest things are exactly
where the open questions are still sitting.

The machine hosts one. Each guest instruction is packed into a word: opcode in the low three
bits, jump target in the rest, and the words are packed into one number at a width chosen
from the program. The host program is a fixed list of sixty of the machine's instructions,
all at declared cost zero, with the terminal program counter at sixty and a status register
that reads one for ``guest halted'' and two for ``malformed guest word.'' What's proved, with
none of it carrying an axiom in the last assumption audit (Section~\ref{sec:witness}): each guest step is simulated by a positive number of host steps landing
in a state that represents the new guest configuration
(\code{cm2\_uniform\_interpreter\_simulation\_total}); the guest halts with a given final
configuration if and only if some fuel brings the host to the halted status with that
result (\code{cm2\_uniform\_interpreter\_raw\_correct\_total}); the canonical encoding never reaches
the malformed status (\code{cm2\_uniform\_interpreter\_raw\_never\_malformed}); and the guest diverges if and only if the host
program counter never reaches sixty at any fuel (\code{cm2\_uniform\_interpreter\_raw\_divergence\_total}). Through that, the
two-counter halting problem maps onto ``does this host run ever reach the halted status''
(\code{mm2\_halting\_host\_iff}), and so, in the synthetic sense of the Saarland library of
undecidable problems that Section~\ref{sec:diagonal} met beside L (what ``synthetic'' buys is spelled out in the Rice part below),
``does this host run ever halt'' is undecidable (\code{actual\_unbounded\_host\_synthetic\_undecidability}). It's a reduction,
not a self-interpreter: it shows the machine can host a universal-enough guest, and it
connects the machine's halting to a known undecidable problem.

One detail here changes what counts as a guest. The two-counter machine this interpreter
runs branches when a decrement succeeds and falls through when the counter is zero. The
convention is not cosmetic: the two-instruction program ``increment counter 0, then decrement
counter 0 and jump back'' runs forever under that convention (\code{cm2\_loop\_diverges}, and the
interpreter running it never halts, \code{cm2\_loop\_host\_never\_halts}), while the same pair under
the zero-branching convention halts after two steps (\code{zero\_branch\_pair\_terminates},
VMUnboundedCM2Applicability.v). That a zero-branching guest is a weaker machine overall is
argued, not checked, and no result depends on it; the zero-branching guest is simply not used
as a witness of universality.

\subsection{The second interpreter: the machine running a piece of itself}

Now the one the recursion theorem lives on. Take a twelve-instruction fragment of the
machine's own instruction set: halt, load-immediate, transfer, add, subtract, multiply, and,
or, shift left, shift right, jump, jump-if-nonzero. Four guest registers (numbers zero to
three), unbounded values, a guest program counter, a guest ledger, and ``terminated'' meaning
the guest program counter has run off the end of the guest program. A guest program is
\emph{well-formed} when every register name is below four and every declared cost is below two
hundred and fifty-six.

The literal host listings, complete encodings and block-by-block verification are in
Appendix~\ref{sec:fixed-interpreters}. In this guest, HALT advances the program counter;
leaving the program is what ends execution.

The host is a fixed list of a hundred and twenty-two of the machine's instructions, at
declared cost zero. It keeps the guest's four registers in its registers zero to three, a
status in register nine (running, terminated, malformed), the guest ledger in register
eleven, the guest program counter in register twelve, a width in thirteen, and the packed
guest code in fourteen. The host's own counter never moves, since every host instruction is
at cost zero; the guest's ledger is just a number sitting in register eleven. Under the
hypotheses that the guest program is well-formed and fits the width: a terminating guest run gives a host run that reaches program counter one hundred
and twenty-two in the corresponding done state (\code{self\_interpreter\_complete}); any host run
that reaches one twenty-two from an encoded configuration decodes to a terminal guest run
(\code{self\_interpreter\_sound}); together, a biconditional on the final guest configuration
(\code{self\_interpreter\_correct}); the guest never terminates if and only if no fuel reaches one
twenty-two (\code{self\_interpreter\_divergence}); and for \emph{arbitrary} packed data, a fetched word
whose low four bits are thirteen, fourteen or fifteen sends the host to the end with the
malformed status and the guest registers, ledger and program counter as they were
(\code{self\_interpreter\_malformed}; opcode zero is the sentinel for ``no instruction here'', which
is how a guest ends). The guest step is proved to be the unbounded sibling's own step on the
guest fields (\code{g\_step\_is\_vm\_apply\_u}), the
code round-trips (\code{g\_decode\_guest\_code\_roundtrip}), and running the guest is actual machine
execution (\code{g\_eval\_is\_actual\_vm\_execution}).

Here's the same thing in the notation that makes it checkable and unreadable in equal
measure:

\begin{definition}[Guest configurations and runs]\label{def:u22-guest}
A guest configuration $c$ is a program counter, a ledger and four registers, all natural
numbers. A guest program $p$ is a list of the twelve guest instructions. $\mathrm{gstep}_p(c)$
executes the instruction of $p$ at $c$'s program counter on unbounded values and leaves $c$
alone when there is none; $\mathrm{grun}_p(n, c)$ is $n$ such steps. $c$ is \emph{terminal} for $p$
when its program counter is at least the length of $p$. $p$ is \emph{well-formed} when every
register field is below 4 and every declared cost below 256, and $p$ \emph{fits} the width $w$
when every packed instruction word of $p$ is below $2^w$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The self-interpreter is correct]\label{thm:u22-self-interpreter}
Let $p$ be well-formed and fit $w$, and let $U$ be the fixed host program of 122
instructions, run by the program-counter runner on the unbounded step $\mathrm{apply_u}$;
write $\mathrm{urun}(F, s)$ for $F$ steps. For a guest configuration $c$, let $H(c)$ be a host
state at host program counter 0 whose registers 0 to 3 hold $c$'s registers, register 9
holds 0, registers 11 and 12 hold $c$'s ledger and program counter, register 13 holds $w$
and register 14 holds the packed code of $p$; the seven scratch registers (4 to 8, 10 and 15), the host counter and
every other field are arbitrary. Say a host state is \emph{done for} $c'$ when it has host
program counter 122, registers 0 to 3, 11 and 12 holding $c'$, register 9 holding 1,
registers 13 and 14 as in $H(c)$, and the host counter and every field outside the registers
as in $H(c)$. Then for all $c$ and $c'$,
\[
\big(\exists n.\ \mathrm{grun}_p(n, c) = c' \text{ and } c' \text{ is terminal}\big)
\iff
\big(\exists F.\ \mathrm{urun}(F, H(c)) \text{ is done for } c'\big),
\]
and the guest run from $c$ never reaches a terminal configuration exactly when no $F$ brings
$\mathrm{urun}(F, H(c))$ to host program counter 122.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The core is a block lemma: from $H(c)$ with $c$ not terminal, a positive number of host
steps reaches $H(\mathrm{gstep}_p(c))$, with new scratch values. The block fetches the packed
word at the guest program counter (well-formedness and the width make the fetch return
exactly that instruction's word), splits it into fields with shifts and masks, dispatches on
the opcode, and performs the guest instruction on registers 0 to 3, 11 and 12; each opcode's
block is checked by computing with the host's own step. Induction on $n$ gives the forward
direction, followed by the fixed terminal sequence that sees the end sentinel and writes
status 1. The backward direction is strong induction on $F$: 122 is past the end of $U$, so
once reached the host stays there, and a block boundary has host program counter 0, so a run
that reaches 122 must pass through whole blocks. Divergence is the contrapositive of the two
directions.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{self\_interpreter\_complete}, \code{self\_interpreter\_sound}, \code{self\_interpreter\_correct}
and \code{self\_interpreter\_divergence} (VMSelfRun.v, 208, 244, 264), with \code{h\_block} and
\code{h\_simulation} (VMSelfRun.v) and the done-state definition \code{h\_done}.

So the machine runs a fragment of itself, as data, with a proof that what it computes is
what the fragment computes. Twelve of fifty-one; four registers of sixteen; and the ``itself''
is the unbounded sibling, with its saturating subtraction, not the sixty-four-bit step. A
fragment. ``Self-interpreter'' can sound as if it covered the whole instruction set. It
doesn't, and I'd rather the numbers be in front of you.

\subsection{Rice, on the guest}

With the interpreter in hand, Section~\ref{sec:diagonal}'s wall lands on the guest without any premise about
recursion. Say two guest programs \emph{behave the same} when, for every input placed in register
zero, they terminate with the same final registers and the same guest ledger, or both don't
(\code{g\_equiv}; note it sees returned registers and ledger, not the final program counter or the
step count). A property of guest programs is \emph{extensional} when well-formed programs that
behave the same agree on it. Then: for any extensional property that holds of some well-formed program
and fails of the program that jumps to itself forever, the predicate ``well-formed and has
the property'' is undecidable, in the synthetic sense the Saarland library uses (the
complement of two-counter halting reduces to its complement) (\code{self\_rice}). ``Decided'' has a
stated meaning here (\code{g\_decides}): a well-formed guest program that, given any fixed way of
numbering programs, terminates on the number of every well-formed program and reports the
property by whether register zero ends at one. A guest
program that decided such a property would make the complement of halting for single-tape Turing machines
over a two-letter alphabet enumerable (the library calls these SBTM, single-tape binary
Turing machines; the book just says single-tape) (\code{self\_rice\_representable}). ``Halts on input zero'' is a named instance. That
``undecidable'' is the library's synthetic notion, a reduction and an enumerability statement,
and not a bare negation of every decision procedure one could write in Coq.

One more word on that, because ``undecidable'' here is the Saarland library's word and it means
something exact. Inside Coq, the library doesn't say ``no algorithm decides this'' outright. It
says: if you could decide this, you could \emph{enumerate} (list, one after another, by a program)
every Turing machine that never halts. Nobody can do that: the machines that do halt can
already be listed (run them all a little at a time and write each one down when it stops), so
with both lists you could decide halting by waiting to see which list a machine turns up on,
and that's Turing's wall. So it's a reduction, a promise that a decider here would be a
decider there.

The words first, then the theorem.

\begin{definition}[Behaviour, extensional, decides, undecidable]\label{def:u22-rice}
For a guest program $p$ and input $x$, $\mathrm{beh}_p(x, g, \mu)$ holds when some
$\mathrm{grun}_p(n, c_x)$ is terminal with registers $g$ and ledger $\mu$, where $c_x$ has
program counter 0, ledger 0 and registers $(x, 0, 0, 0)$. Programs $p$ and $q$
\emph{behave the same} when $\mathrm{beh}_p(x, g, \mu) \iff \mathrm{beh}_q(x, g, \mu)$ for all $x$, $g$, $\mu$.
A property $P$ of guest programs is \emph{extensional} when $P(p)$ implies $P(q)$ for well-formed
$p$ and $q$ that behave the same. A guest program $D$ \emph{decides} $P$ under a numbering $e$ of
programs when $D$ is well-formed and for every well-formed $p$ there are $g$ and $\mu$ with
$\mathrm{beh}_D(e(p), g, \mu)$ and ($g_0 = 1 \iff P(p)$). A predicate $Q$ is \emph{undecidable},
in the library's sense, when a Coq function deciding $Q$ would make the complement of
single-tape Turing-machine halting enumerable.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Rice on the guest]\label{thm:u22-rice}
Let $P$ be extensional, let $w$ be a well-formed program with $P(w)$, and let $P$ fail for the
one-instruction program that jumps to itself. Then ``well-formed and $P$'' is undecidable. If
moreover some guest program decides $P$ under some numbering, the complement of single-tape
Turing-machine halting is enumerable.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For the first part, send a two-counter machine $m$ to a guest program that saves its input
in register 2, loads $m$'s two starting counters, runs a guest copy of $m$, puts the input
back in register 0 and clears the other three, and then runs $w$, with every instruction
before $w$ at declared cost 0. If $m$ halts, the program behaves like $w$, so it has $P$; if $m$ does not halt, it never terminates, behaves like the self-jump, and lacks
$P$. That reduces the complement of two-counter halting, undecidable in the library, to the
complement of ``well-formed and $P$'', and a predicate whose complement is undecidable is
undecidable. For the second part, a guest decider gives a Coq decider: for a well-formed $p$,
search for the least fuel at which $D$ on $e(p)$ is terminal (it exists, so the constructive
search over the naturals finds it) and read register 0.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{self\_rice} (VMSelfRiceUndec.v), \code{g\_decides\_decidable} and
\code{self\_rice\_representable} (VMSelfRiceUndec.v), with the definitions \code{g\_beh}, \code{g\_equiv}
(VMSelfRice.v, 41), \code{g\_extensional} (VMSelfRiceUndec.v) and \code{g\_decides};
\code{g\_halts\_on\_zero\_undecidable} is the instance for ``halts on input zero''. The first part
is also stated as the proposition \code{vm\_guest\_rice} (VMRecursionTarget.v), with ``fails for the
self-jump'' written as failing for \code{g\_bottom}, and proved as \code{vm\_guest\_rice\_holds}
(VMRecursionAudit.v) by \code{self\_rice}.

\subsection{The guest recursion theorem}

Here's the theorem the fragment exists for. Statement, in full, because which
transformations the guest can compute is the condition that matters. For every transformation F from guest programs to guest programs that
maps well-formed programs to well-formed programs, and every guest program D that
\emph{represents} F (D is well-formed, and run on the code of any well-formed program p, D
terminates with register zero holding the code of F applied to p), there is a well-formed
guest program p that behaves the same as F applied to p (\code{vm\_guest\_recursion\_theorem\_closed}).
Kleene's second recursion theorem, for the twelve-instruction guest, with ``the machine can
carry out the transformation'' meaning ``some guest program computes it on codes.''

The proof is a construction, which is Section~\ref{sec:diagonal}'s point about Kleene's little gem (Moschovakis's
phrase): the content is the building, and the contradiction in Section~\ref{sec:diagonal} was just the last line. The shape:
from the representing program D, build an \emph{evaluator} that reads a program's code,
specialises that program to its own code, runs D on the specialised code, and runs
the program D returns. The finite algorithm and its output encoding are given below.
Realise that evaluator as a guest program e; take the code of e; and the witness is
e \emph{specialised} to its own code by a
ten-instruction guest prefix that pairs a fixed number with the input (\code{g\_pair\_specialize}).
The prefix is the specialising step made as guest instructions (logicians call this step
s-m-n: fix one input of a program and get a new program that needs one input fewer), and the
theorem that it
specialises correctly (\code{g\_pair\_smn}, which says the specialised program on an input and the
original on the paired input finish the same way, in both directions) is what makes the witness a \emph{guest} program rather than
a Coq-level construction. So: p is e with its own code baked in; run on any input, it
evaluates D on the code of p, gets the code of F p, and runs that. It's tempting to say the
prefix pairs ``p's own code''; more exactly it pairs the code of the evaluator e, and e builds
p's code from it. So L is a tool on this route, not a source: the recursion theorem is proved
on the guest directly, and it isn't pulled back from L's own recursion theorem in Section~\ref{sec:diagonal}. The mathematical dependency is an effective translation from the computable
evaluator to a counter program and then to the guest. The checked implementation uses
L and counter-machine compilers for that translation; their role is to preserve the
input-output relation, not to supply the fixed-point argument.

Here is the statement with every word unfolded, using Definitions~\ref{def:u22-guest}
and~\ref{def:u22-rice}. Write $\ulcorner p \urcorner$ for the code of a guest program: translate
$p$ into the machine's own instructions, then take the machine's program number of that list.

\begin{definition}[Represents, pairing prefix]\label{def:u22-represents}
A guest program $D$ \emph{represents} a map $F$ from guest programs to guest programs when $D$ is
well-formed and for every well-formed $p$ there are $g$ and $\mu$ with
$\mathrm{beh}_D(\ulcorner p \urcorner, g, \mu)$ and $g_0 = \ulcorner F(p) \urcorner$. The
pairing is $\langle x, y \rangle = (2y + 1) \cdot 2^x$. For a number $x$ and a guest program
$e$, $\mathrm{spec}(e, x)$ is a fixed ten-instruction prefix, all at declared cost 0, followed
by $e$ with its jump targets moved up by ten.
\end{definition}

Here are the ten instructions themselves. Lines are numbered from zero, every
instruction has declared cost zero, and the relocated program starts at line 10.
The input is $(r_0,r_1,r_2,r_3)=(y,0,0,0)$.

\begingroup\small
\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.482\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.482\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Line} & \textbf{Operation} \\
\midrule
\endhead
\bottomrule
\endlastfoot
0 & Set $r_2:=1$. \\
1 & Set $r_0:=r_0+r_0$. \\
2 & Set $r_0:=r_0+r_2$. \\
3 & Set $r_1:=x$. \\
4 & If $r_1$ is nonzero, jump to line 7; otherwise advance. \\
5 & Set $r_2:=0$. \\
6 & Jump to line 10, the start of the relocated program. \\
7 & Set $r_0:=r_0+r_0$. \\
8 & Set $r_1:=r_1-r_2$, with natural subtraction. \\
9 & Jump to line 4. \\
\end{longtable}
\endgroup

At line 4 after $j$ turns through the loop, the registers satisfy
$r_0=(2y+1)2^j$, $r_1=x-j$, $r_2=1$, $r_3=0$, with $0\le j\le x$.
A nonzero $r_1$ doubles the first number and reduces the second by one. At $j=x$
the loop exits and clears $r_2$, leaving exactly the paired input and three zero
registers. Relocation adds 10 to every instruction address and jump target of $e$;
ordinary next-line steps and jumps therefore correspond in both directions.

\begin{lemma}[The prefix pairs]\label{lem:u22-pair-smn}
For all $e$, $x$, $y$, $g$, $\mu$:
$\mathrm{beh}_{\mathrm{spec}(e, x)}(y, g, \mu) \iff \mathrm{beh}_e(\langle x, y \rangle, g,
\mu)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The prefix doubles register 0 and adds one, then doubles it $x$ more times by a counted loop
on register 1, then clears its scratch register and jumps to the start of the moved copy of
$e$. That takes $4x + 7$ steps, charges nothing, and leaves registers
$(\langle x, y \rangle, 0, 0, 0)$, which is where a run of $e$ on $\langle x, y \rangle$
starts. A moved program runs exactly as the original with every program counter shifted.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{g\_pair\_smn} (VMGuestRecursion.v), both directions of the equivalence.

\subsection{The evaluator, without a black box}

There are two program encodings in this chapter. The interpreter appendix packs words
at a chosen fixed width for fast field selection. The recursion theorem instead
uses a self-delimiting syntax code. Mixing them would change the program being
constructed.

For the syntax code, encode a natural number $n$ as $n$ true bits followed by one false
bit. Encode an instruction by its numeric tag followed by its operands and cost,
each in that unary form. The tags are:

\begingroup\small
\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.242\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.344\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.344\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Instruction} & \textbf{Tag} & \textbf{Following fields, in order} \\
\midrule
\endhead
\bottomrule
\endlastfoot
HALT & 24 & cost \\
LOAD\_\allowbreak{}IMM & 8 & destination, immediate, cost \\
XFER & 7 & destination, source, cost \\
ADD, SUB, MUL & 11, 12, 35 & destination, first source, second source, cost \\
AND, OR, SHL, SHR & 31, 32, 33, 34 & destination, first source, second source, cost \\
JUMP & 13 & target, cost \\
JNEZ & 14 & source, target, cost \\
\end{longtable}
\endgroup

Prefix the instruction sequence with its length, also in unary. Convert the resulting
bit list to a number by $B([])=1$ and $B(b::r)=b+2B(r)$, treating false and true as
$0$ and $1$. The final leading one distinguishes the end of the bit list. Decoding
repeatedly takes parity and divides by two until that leading one is reached, then
parses the unary fields and the specified number of instructions. Reject an unknown
tag, an unfinished field or leftover bits. Encoding then decoding a guest program
returns that program: induction on each unary field gives its boundary, followed by
induction on the instruction list. This is the number $\ulcorner p\urcorner$ used
in the recursion theorem.

Fix the representing program $D$. The following finite calculation $E_D(n,z)$ either
returns a number or reports that this trial has no result:

\begin{enumerate}
\item Unpair $z$ as $\langle c,y\rangle$. For a positive $z$, repeatedly divide by two
until it is odd: the number of divisions is $c$, and the odd remainder is $2y+1$.
Decode $c$ as a guest program $e'$; a failed decode gives no result.
\item Form the actual instruction list $\mathrm{spec}(e',c)$ using the ten-instruction
prefix above and the relocated copy of $e'$. Encode that list.
\item Run $D$ on that code for $n$ guest steps. If it has not terminated, give no result.
Otherwise decode register zero as a guest program $q$; reject a failed decode.
\item Run $q$ on $y$ for $n$ guest steps. If it terminates, return the packing of its four
registers and ledger given below. Otherwise give no result.
\end{enumerate}

Only positive paired inputs are needed for the fixed point; the implementation's
unpairing convention sends zero to $(0,0)$, whose program code fails to decode.
Every trial terminates. It uses finite list operations, arithmetic and two bounded
runs. Now try $n=0,1,2,\ldots$ until a trial returns a result. This search need not
terminate, which is exactly what is needed to represent a partial computation.
Once a trial returns a result, every larger trial returns the same result: a
terminated guest run stays at its terminal configuration. If the two required runs
terminate after $n_1$ and $n_2$ steps, any $n\ge\max(n_1,n_2)$ succeeds. Conversely,
a successful trial contains those two terminating runs.

The output packing also matters because behaviour includes the ledger. For final
registers $(a,b,c,d)$ and ledger $\mu$, put
\[
s=a+b+c+d,\qquad
v=b+2^s(d+2^s c),\qquad
P(a,b,c,d,\mu)=\bigl(2((2v+1)2^s)+1\bigr)2^\mu.
\]
To decode a valid packing, first count its trailing zero bits to recover $\mu$,
remove the following odd factor's low one bit, and divide the remainder by two.
The result is $(2v+1)2^s$. Repeat the trailing-zero operation to recover $s$ and $v$.
Since each register is at most $s<2^s$, successive base-$2^s$ digits of $v$ recover
$b,d,c$, and $a=s-b-c-d$. This works also at $s=0$: all four registers are zero.

The evaluator's search is a partial recursive calculation. The compilation fact used
here is that such a calculation can be realised by a finite counter program with
its input and output represented as natural numbers. The traditional universality
constructions and the precise counter conventions are identified in
Appendix~\ref{sec:bibliography}. The implementation checks the translation through
the weak call-by-value calculus and an increment/decrement counter machine.
This is a computability result; it supplies no useful bound on the resulting
program's size or running time.

The counter program is then simulated in the four-register guest. Its administration
has declared cost zero. Its output epilogue unpacks $P$: the first trailing-zero loop
charges one per division, producing exactly $\mu$ ledger units; the second loop
and the register reconstruction charge zero. Thus the guest evaluator ends with the
actual four registers and ledger, rather than merely a code of them. The paired
input's construction and all work before that final charging loop cost zero.
This is why including the ledger in behavioural equality does not break the
fixed-point construction.

\begin{theorem}[Guest recursion theorem]\label{thm:u22-recursion}
For every map $F$ from guest programs to guest programs that sends well-formed programs to
well-formed programs, and every guest program $D$ that represents $F$, there is a
well-formed guest program $p$ that behaves the same as $F(p)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $R$ be the relation that holds of a number $z$ and an output $m$ when
$z = \langle c, y \rangle$ with $c$ the code of some program $e'$, the run of $D$ on
$\ulcorner \mathrm{spec}(e', c) \urcorner$ terminates with the code of a program $q$ in
register 0, and the run of $q$ on $y$ terminates with registers and ledger that pack to $m$.
The finite trials $E_D(n,z)$ above return exactly those outputs. Their unbounded
search, realised by the counter translation and the cost-restoring epilogue, gives a
well-formed guest evaluator $e$ with exactly this input-output behaviour.
Put $c = \ulcorner e \urcorner$ and
$p = \mathrm{spec}(e, c)$, well-formed because $e$ is. By Lemma~\ref{lem:u22-pair-smn},
$\mathrm{beh}_p(y, g, \mu) \iff \mathrm{beh}_e(\langle c, y \rangle, g, \mu)$, and by the
construction of $e$ the right side holds exactly when $F(\mathrm{spec}(e, c)) = F(p)$
terminates on $y$ with registers $g$ and ledger $\mu$. That is $p$ behaving the same as
$F(p)$. The self-reference is the prefix handing $e$ its own code; the recursion theorem for
L in Theorem~\ref{thm:u12-L} is not used.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{vm\_guest\_recursion\_theorem\_closed} (VMGuestRecursion.v), a proof of the
proposition \code{vm\_guest\_recursion\_theorem} (VMRecursionTarget.v), with
\code{g\_represents\_transformer} (VMRecursionTarget.v), \code{g\_pair\_smn} (VMGuestRecursion.v),
\code{hfun\_sem} and \code{RD\_MMA} (VMGuestEvalL.v), and \code{g\_pipeline\_beh\_pack} (VMGuestMMAPipeline.v)
for the compiled Minsky machine and its epilogue (given that every output of the Minsky
machine is a packed pair, the guest run ends with $g$ and $\mu$ exactly when the Minsky
machine outputs their packing). A guest run is the unbounded sibling's own
step on the denoted machine instructions (\code{vm\_guest\_execution\_is\_actual},
VMRecursionAudit.v). The axiom report for the theorem is the \textnormal{\texttt{Print Assumptions}} line at
the end of VMGuestRecursion.v, read from the build.

Two things it isn't. It isn't a recursion theorem for the full fifty-one-instruction
machine, and nothing can be one in the sense Premise~\ref{prem:u12-vm-recursion} asks for every
map: that premise is false (part (1) of Theorem~\ref{thm:u22-premise-refuted}). The guest theorem answers a
different question. It gives fixed points for the guest's representable transformations, under
the unbounded sibling's runs, up to equal registers and ledger, and no correspondence theorem
turns that into equal thousand-step runs of the full machine from every state. And the ledger: the
pairing prefix, the evaluator and the compiled Minsky machine all run at declared cost zero,
and a last loop charges, one cost-one instruction per unit, exactly the ledger of the program
being imitated. So the witness ends with the same registers \emph{and the same ledger} as F applied
to it, because the ledger is part of what ``behaves the same'' means. What the theorem doesn't
speak to is efficiency, how many instructions the witness executes to get there.

\subsection{What this closes}

The natural objection to a guest recursion theorem is that the evaluator and the
specialiser aren't things a guest program can call. Here they are: the specialiser is a
guest prefix and the evaluator is a compiled guest program. So the two ingredients of
Section~\ref{sec:diagonal}'s diagonal hold on this machine's guest \emph{by proof}: Rice from the interpreter, recursion
from the construction. What I haven't proved is the shortcut predicate itself on the guest;
the wall at the start of this chapter is about bounded-run equality with one reference
program on the full machine (Definition~\ref{def:u12-vm-shortcut}), and the guest results are
about behaviour on registers and ledger. On the full machine the diagonal holds under a
premise that no class containing a correct decider's flip can meet (Theorems~\ref{thm:u12-vm-wall}
and~\ref{thm:u22-premise-refuted}). Both are true; they're different sentences; and the
fragment is where the unconditional ingredients live.

Next: the one instruction family I've been pointing at since Section~\ref{sec:state} without building, the
two-player game and the integer check the machine runs on it.

%===========================================================================
\section{The CHSH check}
\label{sec:chsh}
%===========================================================================

I've pointed at a game since Section~\ref{sec:state} without building it. Here it is, built from zero, and then
the one thing my machine actually does with it, which is smaller and more exact than ``it
checks for quantum behaviour,'' a sentence that's tempting and wrong.
The short version, so you know where this is going: the machine never computes the famous
number and never writes down the famous bound. It tests seven facts about integers in eight
counters. If they pass, a certain five-by-five table has a property called positive
semidefinite, and that property forces the famous number under the famous bound. The wall
is a consequence, not an ingredient. Everything else is explaining those sentences.

\subsection{The game}

Two players, Alice and Bob, in separate rooms. A referee flips two coins and hands Alice a
question x, zero or one, and Bob a question y, zero or one. Alice answers a, zero or one;
Bob answers b. No talking during the game. They may agree on a plan beforehand, as detailed
as they like. They win a round when their answers
\emph{differ exactly when both questions were one}. In words: if either question is zero, match; if both are one, differ.

Try to win every time. A plan is a list: what Alice says to x equals zero, what she says to
x equals one, and the same two for Bob. Four bits. Now write the four requirements the
rounds impose: a0 equals b0 (both asked zero); a0 equals b1; a1 equals b0; a1 differs from
b1. Chain the first three: a0 equals b0 equals a1, and a0 equals b1, so b0 equals b1. But
the fourth says a1 differs from b1, and a1 equals b0 equals b1. Contradiction. One of the
four must break. So any plan loses at least one of the four question pairs, and if the
referee asks all four equally often, the best a plan can do is three out of four. Seventy-five percent. Do it the long way too: there are sixteen plans (four bits), and if you write
them all out and count wins you'll find eight win three rounds and eight win one, and none
wins four (the broken requirements always come in odd numbers, which you can see by adding
up the four equations: the left sides cancel to zero and the right sides to one). Sharing a
coin before the game to pick a plan at random doesn't help; a mixture of numbers no larger
than three-quarters is no larger than three-quarters. Arthur Fine proved in 1982 that the
whole ``pre-agreed answers, no influence between rooms'' story is \emph{exactly} the mixtures of
those sixteen lists, one scoreboard for all four questions at once; the sixteen are the
whole classical story.

The number. Recode answers zero and one as plus one and minus one. For each question pair,
let E be the average, over many rounds, of Alice's answer times Bob's. The CHSH quantity is
S equals E00 plus E01 plus E10 minus E11. For one fixed plan each win adds one to S and each
loss subtracts one, so S is wins minus losses: a three-win plan has S equal to two, a one-win
plan has minus two. With equal question frequencies, the win rate is one half plus S over
eight. So ``seventy-five percent'' and ``S at most two'' are the same fact, and the second is the
one that got the name.

The machine can play the three-out-of-four ceiling for free. One short program sets up two
modules and then runs four trials, one per question pair, with both players answering zero
every time. After the recoding every answer is plus one, so all four correlators are one:
the all-ones plan, which matches on every pair and so wins the three pairs that ask for a
match. Every instruction in it is declared at cost zero.

\begin{theorem}[The classical ceiling, reached at zero cost]\label{thm:u23-classical-achieved}
Let $t$ be the list PNEW, PSPLIT, and four CHSH\_\allowbreak{}TRIAL instructions, one for each question pair
$(x, y)$, each with both answers 0 and declared cost 0. The cost model's total charge for $t$
is 0, and running $t$ in order from the clean state (all registers zero, counter zero, no
trials recorded) leaves trial counters whose score
$S = E_{00} + E_{01} + E_{10} - E_{11}$, computed in rationals from the counters, equals 2.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Computation: the charge is a sum of six zeros, and running the six steps leaves one ``same''
round in each of the four pairs, so each correlator is 1 and $S = 1 + 1 + 1 - 1 = 2$.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{classical\_bound\_achieved} (ClassicalBound.v). Nothing in it says the rounds
were played; a program can tally anything at zero cost, and the theorem only shows that the
ceiling is reachable. The other side, that no finite mixture of plans beats two, is
Theorem~\ref{thm:chsh-fine} in Appendix~\ref{sec:chsh-derivation}, one direction of Fine's result.

\subsection{Where it came from, and why anyone cared}

So who started this, and why would anybody care whether two rooms can win a coin game? The
trail starts in 1935, with Einstein, Podolsky and Rosen asking whether quantum mechanics
describes everything that's real about a pair of particles. Their argument: if measuring one
particle lets you predict the other's result with certainty, the result must already have been
fixed, and the theory leaves that out. The wall they had in mind was a pre-agreed list of
answers, the plan above. And the first thing worth checking is whether the paper even says what
Einstein meant. By his own account, not quite. Podolsky did the writing, and that June Einstein
wrote to Schrödinger that the essential thing had been ``smothered by formalism.'' The person
who lays that letter out is Arthur Fine, the same Fine whose theorem closed the sixteen plans
above, in his encyclopedia entry on the argument. So even the founding paper is a lead to check,
not a verdict.

For thirty years that was philosophy. In 1964 John Bell turned it into arithmetic: if each
particle carries pre-agreed answers and nothing travels between the rooms, certain averages
can't exceed a fixed number, and quantum theory predicts they do. And where does a paper like
that get published? In a brand-new journal called \emph{Physics Physique Fizika}, which charged
authors no page fees and in fact paid them by the word, and which folded in 1968 after four
volumes. The story told in Andrew Whitaker's biography of Bell is that the journal gave out no
free copies, so Bell spent his payment buying copies of his own paper to mail to other
physicists. What his inequality rules out is the \emph{pair} of assumptions together, called
local realism (answers exist before you ask, and no influence across the gap), not either one
alone. In 1969 Clauser, Horne, Shimony and Holt rewrote it as the four-average form above, S at
most two, which could be tried in a lab with imperfect equipment.

Then the obvious next question: did anybody actually try it? Freedman and Clauser tried it in
1972; Aspect's group did it in 1982 with the measurement settings switched while the photons were
in flight. Before that, in 1975, Alain Aspect went to see Bell at CERN to tell him what he
planned, and by Aspect's own account Bell heard him out in silence and then asked, first thing,
whether he had a permanent position. Aspect did. Bell's reason, as Aspect tells it,
was that most physicists would take the experiment for a waste of time, or take him for a
crackpot. And in 2015 three groups (Hensen's in Delft with electrons a kilometre apart;
Giustina's; Shalm's) closed the two main escape routes at once. Clauser, Aspect and Zeilinger
got the 2022 Nobel for it. So in under fifty years the subject went from a question you needed a
permanent job to risk to a Nobel. The lab number sits above two. A remaining escape, that the
referee's coins were secretly correlated with the particles, is a philosophical one and I'm
not going to pretend it's closed.

What quantum play does: if the players share an entangled pair and choose what to measure
from their question, the best they can do is S equals two times the square root of two,
about 2.83, a win rate of about eighty-five percent. Boris Tsirelson showed in 1980 that
that's a \emph{ceiling}: quantum correlations violate Bell, but only up to there.

And the wall above that, which is the one I find most instructive. In 1994 Popescu and
Rohrlich asked: what if you only demand that nothing can be \emph{signalled}, that Alice's
answers on their own have the same odds whatever Bob is asked, and the other way round?
Then you can write down a ``box'' (the PR box, after their initials) that wins \emph{every} round (its answers differ exactly when
both questions are one, by fiat, each answer alone a fair coin), S equals four, and nothing
about it lets either room send a message. So relativity alone doesn't explain the quantum
ceiling; the PR box obeys relativity and beats 2.83. The order is: two for plans, 2.83 for
quantum, four for no-signalling.

And the box has the same kind of history as everything else in this book: somebody got there
first. Popescu and Rohrlich's initials stuck, but the big review of the field by Nicolas Brunner
and four coauthors credits boxes like it to Peter Rastall and, separately, to Leonid Khalfin and
Tsirelson himself, both in 1985, nine years before. Then the question that really matters: if
relativity isn't what stops things at 2.83, what is? People have tried candidates. In 2005 Wim
van Dam showed that with enough PR boxes, Bob could work out any yes-or-no function of both
their inputs after Alice sends him a single bit, which would make the whole question of how much
two parties need to talk collapse, and that's a strong hint the boxes are too good to be real.
In 2009 Marcin Pawłowski and five coauthors proposed a principle they called information
causality: Bob can't get more information about Alice's data than the bits she actually sends
him. Ordinary and quantum physics both obey it, and any theory that beats 2.83 breaks it. It
recovers part of the quantum boundary, not all of it.
Which principle fixes 2.83 is still an open question, and this book won't answer it. My
machine's check is a fence at the middle step.

\subsection{Wrong turns to take off the table}

Every one of these gets said with a straight face, and every one is easy to say by accident, so
here they are, each with what's actually true beside it.

``Faster than light.'' Nothing travels. Each room alone sees fair coins; the correlation shows
up only when you lay the two columns side by side afterward. ``Quantum means random.'' The
average S is fixed by the state; what's random is each single answer; the plans are the less
random side. ``A Bell violation proves nonlocality.'' It rules out local realism, both
assumptions together, and every real test has loopholes with names. ``A tally above two
proves nonlocality.'' No: S is a \emph{population} average, and one finite tally can land above two
by luck. Four rounds, one per question pair, with coin-flip answers, reach S equals four one
time in sixteen. That gap between a population bound and a finite sample is the problem
Zhang, Glancy and Knill work through for real Bell tests (Physical Review A, 2013), and the
book doesn't solve it. The kernel proves only the narrow thing, that a tally above two is not
explained by \emph{one fixed plan replayed every round}
(\code{chsh\_violation\_rules\_out\_locally\_factorizable\_coupling}), and that narrow thing is what
the sentence has to stay. And ``the PSD test proves the data is
quantum.'' (PSD is short for positive semidefinite, the property of the five-by-five table from
the short version; the next part builds both.) It doesn't, and the direction matters. Passing
implies the five-by-five table, pinned in a way the next part explains, is PSD, and that
implies S squared is at most eight; both are proved. Whether the
correlators of a PSD table like that are the correlators of some quantum strategy is the
cited Tsirelson, Landau and Masanes result, and I haven't proved it here. Failing says
nothing: the check is sound and not complete, and quantum behaviour can fail it. Every one
of the sixteen plans fails it, and I'll show you why. What it guarantees is in the last part
of this section.

\subsection{The five-by-five, and what positive semidefinite means}

Here's the mathematics the check rests on, and it's one idea: a table of numbers
\emph{could be a table of dot products}. Take a two-by-two symmetric table with a and c on the diagonal and b
off it. It's positive semidefinite (PSD) when a and c are at least zero and a times c minus
b squared is at least zero. Check two by hand: ones on the diagonal and one half off, the
determinant is three quarters, passes; ones on the diagonal and 1.2 off, the determinant is
negative, fails. The reading: PSD means the table could be the dot products of some arrows,
and 1.2 is too big a dot product for two arrows of length one. That's the whole idea,
generalised to bigger tables.

Now the table. Rows and columns labelled I, A0, A1, B0, B1 (the identity, Alice's two
questions, Bob's two). Diagonal all ones. The I row and column all zero (that's ``zero
marginals'': the table takes each answer alone to average to zero, a fair coin; the machine
records no marginals and doesn't test this). A0 with A1 zero, B0 with B1 zero (no round asks
Alice both questions, so no tally holds that average, and the table sets it to zero). Those
zeros are choices, they pin the table to one slice, and I'll come back to what they cost.
And the four Alice-Bob cells hold the four correlators E. That's a five-by-five with four free
numbers in it. It splits into the one in the corner and a four-by-four block made of an
identity and the two-by-two grid E of correlators, and PSD of that block is the same as
saying \emph{E shrinks every vector} (E is a contraction), which is three inequalities: one minus
E00 squared minus E10 squared at least zero; one minus E01 squared minus E11 squared at least
zero; and their product at least the square of (E00 E01 plus E10 E11).

Run it. All four correlators 0.6 except E11 at minus 0.6, S equals 2.4: the two diagonal
terms are 0.28 and 0.28, the cross term zero, passes; above two, below 2.83. All four at one
over root two (E11 negative): diagonals zero, cross term zero, passes with no slack, S equals
two root two exactly, the 2.83; nudge any entry's size up and a diagonal goes negative. The all-ones plan (one, one,
one, one): first diagonal is one minus one minus one, negative, \emph{fails}, though S equals two
and it's a perfectly legal classical play. The PR box (one, one, one, minus one): fails the
same way. A fence at the middle step, and a fence that keeps out every one of the sixteen
plans: each has all four correlators at plus or minus one, so the first diagonal is always
one minus one minus one. Only diluted mixtures of plans get through.

In 2007 Navascués, Pironio and Acín showed this is the first rung of a ladder: bigger tables
of expected products, each PSD, each a necessary condition for quantum behaviour when its
entries are left free, each rung tighter, and (their 2008 paper) converging to the quantum
set (strictly, the set from commuting operators, which can differ from the tensor-product set
in general scenarios). The machine's table is the first rung with the marginals and the two
within-party entries pinned to zero. Pinning is a stronger demand than the rung makes, so
passing puts you inside the first rung, and a quantum point can still fail. Landau in 1988 and Masanes in
2003 found the exact boundary for this two-questions-each case, and it's not a straight line
at 2.83 but a curved surface (the arc-sine form) touching it at one point. So the obvious next
question: if every rung is tighter than the last, does some rung finally land exactly on the
quantum set and stop? A 2026 paper by Chaturvedi says no: no \emph{finite} rung of the ladder
captures the whole quantum set even in
this simplest case, which is the caution this book keeps about the ladder, confirmed from
outside.

\subsection{What the machine actually does}

Eight counters (Section~\ref{sec:state}): for each of the four question pairs, one counting rounds where the
answers matched and one where they differed. One instruction, the trial, bumps one counter
per round, after checking all four inputs are bits; it checks no inequality and records no
marginals. Then one instruction, the check, reads the eight and tests seven integer facts.
For each pair, let N be same plus different and D be same minus different (so E is D over
N). The seven: the four N are strictly positive (every pair was sampled; a pair with no
rounds is rejected, not read as a correlator of zero); A, which is N00
squared N10 squared minus D00 squared N10 squared minus D10 squared N00 squared, is at least
zero; B, the same with the other column, is at least zero; and with C equal to D00 D01 N10
N11 plus D10 D11 N00 N01, C squared is at most A times B. Those are the three contraction
inequalities with the denominators cleared. No division, no reals, no square root, no S.
Try it: counters (same, different) of (4, 1), (4, 1), (4, 1), (1, 4) give E of 0.6, 0.6, 0.6,
minus 0.6; N is five and D is three (minus three for the last); A is 175, B is 175, C is zero;
passes. That's the first example above, the S equals 2.4 one, in integers.

If the seven pass, the instruction steps on: the program counter advances and the ledger
rises by the charge, and nothing else changes, not the flag, not the channel; success is
visible only as ``no trap.'' If any fails, it traps to the fixed address with the error code
and flag. Either way it costs the declared cost plus one, the floor. The theorem chain, in words: a
passed check gives PSD of the five-by-five built from the counters; contraction and PSD are
equivalent, both directions; and PSD forces S squared at most eight. The names are in the
statements below. The underlying algebra is one identity: four times the
sum of the four correlators squared, minus S squared, is a sum of six squares
(\code{chsh\_gap\_is\_sum\_of\_squares}), so if the row sums of squares are at most one, S squared is
at most eight (\code{tsirelson\_squared}), and the point one over root two reaches it
(\code{tsirelson\_tight}). That's Tsirelson's bound as \emph{algebra}, with no Hilbert space (the mathematical home of quantum states) in it.

Here is the chain as three statements. The derivations are in Appendix~\ref{sec:chsh-derivation};
this is what they prove.

\begin{definition}[Correlators from the counters; the pinned matrix]\label{def:u23-pinned}
For a state $s$ and a question pair $xy$, let
$E_{xy}(s) = (\mathrm{same}_{xy} - \mathrm{diff}_{xy}) / (\mathrm{same}_{xy} +
\mathrm{diff}_{xy})$ from its trial counters, read as 0 when both are 0. For reals $E_{xy}$,
$M(E)$ is the symmetric five-by-five matrix on $I, A_0, A_1, B_0, B_1$ with ones on the
diagonal, $E_{xy}$ in the cells $(A_x, B_y)$ and $(B_y, A_x)$, and zero everywhere else
(Definition~\ref{def:chsh-five}). $M$ is \emph{PSD} when $v^{\mathsf T} M v \ge 0$ for every real
vector $v$, and $S(E) = E_{00} + E_{01} + E_{10} - E_{11}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The gate implies the pinned matrix is PSD]\label{thm:u23-notrap-psd}
Let $s$ be a state whose error flag is false, let $d$ be a declared cost, and let $s'$ be the
result of CHSH\_\allowbreak{}LASSERT $d$ on $s$. If the error flag of $s'$ equals that of $s$, then
$M(E(s))$ is symmetric and PSD.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
When the integer check fails the step sets the error flag, which the hypotheses rule out, so
the check passed. Its four positivity facts make every denominator positive, so each
$E_{xy}(s)$ is $D_{xy}/N_{xy}$, and dividing the other three facts by positive squares turns
them into the three contraction inequalities (Lemma~\ref{lem:chsh-clear}). Contraction is
equivalent to PSD of $M(E)$ by a Schur complement on the four-by-four block
(Corollary~\ref{cor:chsh-iff}). Nothing about the program counter is needed: the error flag
alone says which branch ran.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{chsh\_lassert\_no\_trap\_implies\_npa\_psd} (QuantumPartitionPSD.v), through
\code{chsh\_lassert\_check\_implies\_npa\_psd} and \code{npa\_psd\_iff\_column\_contractive}.

\begin{theorem}[PSD forces the Tsirelson bound]\label{thm:u23-psd-tsirelson}
For all real $E_{00}, E_{01}, E_{10}, E_{11}$: if $M(E)$ is symmetric and PSD, then
$S(E)^2 \le 8$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
A PSD matrix with unit diagonal has every three-by-three principal minor at least zero. On
rows $A_0, B_0, B_1$ that minor is $1 - E_{00}^2 - E_{01}^2$, and on rows $A_1, B_0, B_1$ it
is $1 - E_{10}^2 - E_{11}^2$, so the four squares sum to at most 2. The identity
$4 \sum_{xy} E_{xy}^2 - S^2 = $ a sum of six squares then gives $S^2 \le 4 \cdot 2 = 8$.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{npa\_psd\_implies\_tsirelson\_bound} (MuLedgerQuantumBridge.v), with the row
bounds \code{npa\_psd\_zero\_marginal\_implies\_row\_bounds} and the identity
\code{chsh\_gap\_is\_sum\_of\_squares} (TsirelsonFromAlgebra.v); this is
Theorem~\ref{thm:chsh-psd-tsirelson} in the appendix.

\begin{corollary}[A passed gate means the bound]\label{cor:u23-notrap-bound}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:u23-notrap-psd}, $S(E(s))^2 \le 8$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{thm:u23-notrap-psd} supplies positive semidefiniteness of the pinned
moment matrix for these four correlators. Theorem~\ref{thm:chsh-psd-tsirelson} in the
derivation appendix applies to every such matrix and gives $S^2\le8$. Its quadratic
form calculation is printed there; no additional property of the machine is used.
\end{proof}

Checked as the composition of \code{chsh\_lassert\_no\_trap\_implies\_npa\_psd} and
\code{npa\_psd\_implies\_tsirelson\_bound}; no single Coq theorem states the two together. The
same conclusion is also proved along a parallel route,
\code{chsh\_lassert\_no\_trap\_implies\_state\_column\_contractive} followed by
\code{state\_column\_contractive\_implies\_tsirelson} (MuLedgerQuantumBridge.v).

\begin{remark}[Sound, not complete]\label{rem:u23-sound-not-complete}
The pinned matrix is stricter than the quantum question it is usually read against. PSD of
$M(E)$ gives the correlators a PSD completion, since the zeros are one choice of the two free
entries (\code{zero\_marginal\_implies\_elliptope}, ElliptopeCompletion.v). The converse fails.
The all-ones plan has a PSD completion (\code{deterministic\_strategy\_elliptope}), and every
deterministic plan is a quantum strategy, a standard fact cited and not proved here; yet its
minor on rows $A_0, B_0, B_1$ is $1 - 1 - 1 = -1$, so $M(E)$ is not PSD there, and a tally of
one matching round per pair gives $A = 1 - 1 - 1 = -1$ in the integer check, so the gate
traps. Those two failures are my arithmetic, not named theorems. So a pass proves the bound
and a trap proves nothing about the tally. The zero-cost trace of
Theorem~\ref{thm:u23-classical-achieved} is exactly such a tally: it reaches $S = 2$ and the gate
would throw it out.
\end{remark}

One thing about that trap is worth saying on its own. The check traps to the same fixed
address that LASSERT uses when a formula's certificate fails, with the same error flag and
the same rule for the charge: the attempt pays, declared cost plus one, and LASSERT more for
the formula's length. One wall comes from the moment-matrix mathematics (the table of expected products above),
which I didn't write. The other is a logical constraint a program hands to LASSERT. The step treats them the
same way: the counter charges the attempt to narrow, and it never asks whether the wall was
found or built. And that's a claim about the step, not about the chip. Four of the check
instructions below have no hardware encoding at all, and that doesn't change a word of the
step theorems. The law lives in the transition, not in the gate count.

None of that algebra is new, and I don't want it to read as if it were. Tsirelson's bound has
been formalised before, in Isabelle/HOL by Echenim and Mhalla and in Lean's Mathlib, and
Navascués, Pironio and Acín already analyse this very matrix by Schur complement and discuss
the level above it. What I think is mine here is smaller: an integer decision procedure on
the counters, living inside an instruction; a checked link from ``the instruction didn't trap''
to PSD to the bound; and a circuit proved equal to that check for thirty-two-bit counters.

So here, in one paragraph, is what the gate guarantees. If the machine steps past the
check without trapping, then every question pair was sampled, the four empirical ratios
satisfy three polynomial inequalities, hence the fixed five-by-five is PSD, hence S squared
is at most eight. It does \emph{not} guarantee that the tally came from honest play (a program
chooses its own trial inputs and can tally whatever it likes at zero cost; the kernel has a
zero-cost trace with S equals four, \code{TsirelsonUpperBound.v}, to make sure nobody forgets).
It does not guarantee any marginal is zero (the machine records no marginals and can't test
them). It does not guarantee any quantum state exists, or that the correlators lie in the
quantum set rather than a larger fence. And it traps the tally of every single plan, honest
classical play included. The check certifies a \emph{shape} of the tally. What the shape means is a question for whoever
supplied the rounds.

And the tally isn't a claim. Trials pile up for free; the counters are a record of what a
program said happened, and the ledger has no opinion about a record. The priced step is the
one that stands up and commits to something. On this machine the only instruction that can
move the assertion channel off zero is MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT: a run of a program with no
MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT in it, from channel zero, never reaches a nonzero channel
(\code{non\_morph\_assert\_trace\_cannot\_gain\_supra\_cert}, RevelationRequirement.v). A wider
theorem with a misleading name, \code{nonlocal\_correlation\_requires\_revelation}, says that
if a run from channel zero ends with it nonzero, the program contains a REVEAL, EMIT, LJOIN,
LASSERT or MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT. Its ``supra'' predicate is just ``the channel is nonzero''; it knows
nothing about CHSH, and asking for REVEAL in front of a super-quantum claim is runtime policy,
which the source says. What MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT commits to is a label on an existing arrow. Whether
the label is true of the pile of tallies is a separate question, and CHSH\_\allowbreak{}LASSERT is the
priced check that answers part of it. Statistics are free; the claim about them is what
costs.

In the chip, the check is a circuit, and the word-level circuit is proved to compute the
same seven facts as the kernel for every set of eight thirty-two-bit counters (the
intermediate products need 134 and 268 bits, which is why the circuit takes twenty-nine
firings, one hardware rule run twenty-nine times over (Section~\ref{sec:chip} says what a rule is); \code{chsh\_check\_word\_correct}, \code{chsh\_run\_result}, and, for the whole step under its
usual side conditions, \code{chsh\_lassert\_refines}). The kernel's counters are unbounded naturals
and the chip's are thirty-two bits, so the equivalence is for counters that fit. That's Section~\ref{sec:chip}'s.

\subsection{A rational stand-in for an irrational number}

One number you'll see in the files: 5657 over 2000, which is 2.8285, and two root two is
2.82842... It's the four-decimal round-up, chosen so that rational code can test ``above the
Tsirelson bound'' without square roots, and it's safe because 5657 squared is 32,001,649 and
eight times 2000 squared is 32,000,000, so the fraction sits above root eight by about seven
parts in a hundred thousand (\code{rational\_tsirelson\_bound}). It's used in a receipt-level
predicate and a few rational theorems. It is \emph{not} used in the integer gate, and the
real-number theorems use root eight. Nothing in the hardware files mentions it either: the
chip checks CHSH in integers.

\subsection{Three more tests, and how far each one is in the machine}

The second rung: a nine-by-nine table on I, the four questions, and the four Alice-Bob
\emph{products}, with the correlators and five extra free numbers for three- and four-body
entries. Its PSD is again equivalent to a contraction-like condition (\code{q1ab\_psd\_iff\_column\_contractive}),
and there are four more check instructions in the kernel for it, taking the extra numbers
as caller-supplied counters, with a cascade of two Schur steps down to a four-by-four that
Sylvester's criterion closes (\code{chsh\_lassert\_1ab\_g12345\_no\_trap\_implies\_npa\_psd\_q1ab}).
Soundness only; the interior predicates demand strict positivity, so boundary points need
another route. And a fact that's easy to list without noticing what it means: the variant
with all five extra numbers at zero certifies a strict \emph{subset of the classical set} (the
ball where the four correlators' squares sum to at most one), forcing S at most two (\code{q1ab\_check\_at\_gzero\_implies\_classical\_bound}); it can't certify
anything above the classical line. To get a point above two you have to supply the extras
(\code{q1ab\_certifies\_a\_superclassical\_chsh\_point}, S equals 2.4 with one extra at minus one
half). Those four instructions are the four with no hardware encoding (Section~\ref{sec:isa}). In order:
the one with all five extra numbers at zero, then the one with only the four-body entry
free, then three free entries (the two three-body entries and the four-body one, closed by a
four-by-four Sylvester test), then all five. Each is proved sound on its own
(\code{chsh\_lassert\_1ab\_no\_trap\_implies\_npa\_psd\_q1ab}, \code{chsh\_lassert\_1ab\_g5\_no\_trap\_implies\_npa\_psd\_q1ab},
\code{chsh\_lassert\_1ab\_g345\_no\_trap\_implies\_npa\_psd\_q1ab},
\code{chsh\_lassert\_1ab\_g12345\_no\_trap\_implies\_npa\_psd\_q1ab}, QuantumPartitionPSD\_\allowbreak{}1AB.v, 5076,
5104, 5156). Their parameter domains grow in that order. That the sets they \emph{accept} grow
too is not proved, and I won't say it. The Python side (the assembler script and the generated opcode table, Section~\ref{sec:isa}) gives them the
numbers 0x2F to 0x32; no Coq file and no hardware file uses those bytes.

The two sizes are one test, not two. A single positive-semidefinite predicate takes the size
as a parameter, and the five-by-five and the nine-by-nine are it at two sizes.

\begin{definition}[The size-generic PSD test]\label{def:u23-genrealizable}
A \emph{claim} is a top index $n$ and a matrix $M$ indexed by naturals. It is \emph{realizable} when
$M_{ij} = M_{ji}$ for all $i, j \le n$ and $\sum_{i \le n} \sum_{j \le n} v_i M_{ij} v_j \ge
0$ for every real vector $v$. The CHSH claim of $E$ is top index 4 with the matrix $M(E)$ of
Definition~\ref{def:u23-pinned}; the level-1+AB claim uses top index 8 and the nine-by-nine
matrix.
\end{definition}

\begin{corollary}[The level-1 test is the size-five case]\label{cor:u23-general}
For all real $E_{00}, E_{01}, E_{10}, E_{11}$: the three contraction inequalities hold if and
only if the CHSH claim of $E$ is realizable. The same holds at size nine for the level-1+AB
contraction condition and its claim.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Realizability at top index 4 unfolds to symmetry and PSD of the five-by-five, by computing the
finite sums, and that is equivalent to contraction by Corollary~\ref{cor:chsh-iff}. At size nine
the same unfolding meets Theorem~\ref{thm:chsh-nine-iff}. Nothing new is proved about the
matrices; the point is that one predicate covers both.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{column\_contractive\_iff\_general\_realizable} (GenRealizability.v) and
\code{column\_contractive\_q1ab\_iff\_general\_realizable}, with the machine-step form
