\code{vm\_chsh\_lassert\_step\_is\_general\_realizable}, which has the hypotheses of
Theorem~\ref{thm:u23-notrap-psd}.

The third thing: the \emph{elliptope}, the set of correlators for which \emph{some} choice of the two
missing entries (A0 with A1, B0 with B1) makes the five-by-five PSD. Every one of the
sixteen plans is inside it (\code{deterministic\_strategy\_elliptope}), mixtures stay inside
(\code{elliptope\_convex}), Tsirelson's point is inside (\code{elliptope\_tsirelson}), the PR box is out
(\code{pr\_box\_not\_elliptope}), and it's strictly bigger than the classical set
(\code{beyond\_classical\_elliptope}). There's a decider for it with a soundness proof, in two
branches: a strict Sylvester check with the completion supplied, and a rational
factorisation certificate of the completed matrix, checked in integers. What's proved is
that a pass puts the correlators inside the set and that no choice of inputs gets the PR box
through (\code{elliptope\_check\_full\_sound}, \code{elliptope\_full\_gate\_never\_accepts\_pr\_box}), and, by
computation, that some named points pass, the all-ones plan and a point that the cited arc-sine
boundary puts exactly on the quantum edge among them (\code{gate\_accepts\_all\_ones},
\code{gate\_accepts\_pythagorean\_boundary}).
The file's header also argues that every point with a rational PSD completion has such a
certificate; that is a comment, not a theorem. It is \emph{not} an
instruction. No step of the machine mentions it, and its file says the opcode and cost
schedule are not done. I may call it a decider with a soundness proof. I may not call it
part of the machine.

\subsection{What isn't proved}

The arc-sine curve. That any of these sets equals what quantum mechanics can reach. That
any state or measurement achieves 2.83. Those are the cited external results, and the files
say so in their scope notes. Also: the finite-mixture theorem (\code{fine\_theorem} in the source)
proves only one direction, that a finite local model satisfies the bound; Fine's actual
theorem is an equivalence, so ``Fine's theorem is proved'' would be wrong and I haven't said
it. And one more thing the kernel says about itself, which the guarantee paragraph above already
used: a zero-cost trace is not thereby classical (the S equals four trace). The correlators (one, one, one, minus one) are the PR box, not a
classical play; the classical vertex that fails the gate is (one, one, one, one).

That's the game, the number, the two walls, and the check. Last of the machine sections:
what all this costs against physics, and the hierarchy of what costs more.

%===========================================================================
\section{Irreversibility accounting and the mu-hierarchy}
\label{sec:landauer}
%===========================================================================

Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} did the physics argument once: on a finite machine a permanent flag merges states,
Landauer's principle (a named premise) prices merges, and the toll follows. I'm not going
to do it again. This section is about what the \emph{machine's} counter has to do with any of
that, and the answer is: less than the word ``Landauer'' in a file name suggests, and I'd
rather you hear the exact amount from me.

\subsection{A bookkeeping indicator, bounded by what it indicates}

The machine has a function that, for each instruction, returns one if the instruction's
cost is positive and zero otherwise. The source calls it \code{irreversible\_bits}, and the name
is the problem, so let me say what it is before saying what it's called. It's an \emph{indicator}: it marks cost-positive instructions. Sum it over a run and
you get the count of cost-positive instructions executed. The theorem is that this count is
at most the run's total cost (\code{total\_irreversible\_bits\_le\_cost}), and the proof is two cases
per instruction: if the cost is zero the indicator is zero; if the cost is positive the
indicator is one and one is at most the cost. A zero-one indicator bounded by what it
indicates. That's all.

What it shares with Landauer: the shape, a lower-bound quantity attached to an event. What
it doesn't share: everything else. It's not an irreversibility theorem. There's no physics
in the proof, no microscopic erasure model, no physical entropy, no Boltzmann constant. The
label ``irreversible'' on a cost-positive instruction is bookkeeping, not a proof that the
instruction erased anything or was physically irreversible. Section~\ref{sec:witness} showed you that the
machine's zero-cost JUMP \emph{does} merge states and is charged nothing. And several of the
cost-positive instructions (the check, the join, the emit) change only the program counter
and the ledger when they succeed; by the step rule they're one-to-one on the state, which I
get from reading the definition and not from a stated theorem. The indicator counts charges.
It doesn't count erasures.

\begin{definition}[The indicator]\label{def:u24-indicator}
For an instruction $i$ with schedule cost $\mathrm{cost}(i)$, let $\mathrm{ind}(i) = 0$ if
$\mathrm{cost}(i) = 0$ and $1$ otherwise. For a list $t$ of instructions,
$\mathrm{ind}(t)$ and $\mathrm{cost}(t)$ are the sums over its members.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The indicator is bounded by the cost]\label{thm:u24-indicator}
For every list of instructions $t$, $\mathrm{ind}(t) \le \mathrm{cost}(t)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Per instruction, two cases: cost zero gives $0 \le 0$, positive cost gives $1 \le
\mathrm{cost}(i)$. Induction on $t$ adds the cases up.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{irreversible\_bits\_le\_cost} and \code{total\_irreversible\_bits\_le\_cost}
(LandauerDerivation.v, 240). The source names the indicator \code{irreversible\_bits}.

\subsection{The calibration is a unit conversion}

There's a function in the source that multiplies the counter by a chosen energy per mark,
and a theorem that a state with one mark, at the scale kT ln 2 per mark, carries kT ln 2 of
energy (\code{calibrated\_mu\_landauer\_energy}, proving the predicate \code{mu\_landauer\_calibration} for
every k and T). Read that for exactly what it is: a unit conversion, true by definition,
with the scale as a free input. Nothing in it picks the scale. The theorem would be just as
true with the scale set to a dollar a mark, and I'd rather say that than let the name
``Landauer'' in it do any work. What \emph{would} connect marks to joules is the premise in Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary},
\code{landauer\_heat}, and that one is an assumption with a name that nothing proves.

Remember the constant from Boltzmann's grave in Part II, the exchange rate between a count and
heat? It has a newer chapter, and it makes the point sharper than I can. The $k_B$ in
$k_B T \ln 2$ turns a temperature into an energy, and for most of its
history it was a measured number, with error bars, pinned down by careful experiments. Since
20 May 2019 it isn't. That day the international system of units was redefined so that
Boltzmann's constant is exactly $1.380649 \times 10^{-23}$ joules per kelvin, by definition, and
the kelvin is whatever makes that true. So the conversion from temperature to energy has been a
convention since then, in the strictest sense: nobody can measure it wrong any more. What's still
physics is everything around it, whether wiping a bit at a temperature really sheds that much
heat, which is what the Lyon bead was measuring. The calibration theorem is the same kind of move
as that redefinition. It fixes a conversion, and the physics, if there is any, is somewhere else.

\begin{definition}[Energy at a scale]\label{def:u24-scale}
For a real number $c$ (joules per mark) and a state $s$, the energy of $s$ at scale $c$ is
$\mu(s) \cdot c$. The \emph{Landauer calibration} at $k_B$ and $T$ is the statement that every
state with $\mu(s) = 1$ has energy $k_B T \ln 2$ at scale $k_B T \ln 2$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The calibration is a unit conversion]\label{thm:u24-calibration}
(1) For all real $k_B$ and $T$, the Landauer calibration at $k_B$ and $T$ holds. (2) There
are two energy readings of the state, at scales 1 and 2, that disagree on every state with
one mark.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Substitute $\mu(s) = 1$: $1 \cdot k_B T \ln 2 = k_B T \ln 2$, by ring arithmetic, for any
$k_B$ and $T$, positive or not. (2) At $\mu(s) = 1$ the two readings are 1 and 2.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{calibrated\_mu\_landauer\_energy} (PricingPhysicsAudit.v), which proves
\code{mu\_landauer\_calibration} (PricingPhysicsTarget.v) for all $k_B$ and $T$, and
\code{mu\_has\_no\_intrinsic\_joule\_value} (PricingPhysicsAudit.v). The physics is the premise of
Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}, restated here once in the form the next theorems test. In words first: a \emph{dissipation}
hands each instruction a whole number of heat units, each unit worth kT ln 2. Landauer's
principle, in that currency, says an instruction that takes at least one state where some yes-or-no
property is false to a state where it's true, and never sends a true one back to false,
dissipates at least one unit. The calibration says no instruction dissipates more units than the counter charges
it. Two premises, nothing proved about either, and the only question is whether they can sit
in the same room:

\begin{premise}[Landauer, in units of the counter]\label{prem:u24-landauer-pair}
A \emph{dissipation} is a function $\delta$ from instructions to naturals, counted in units of
$k_B T \ln 2$. Landauer's principle, in this vocabulary (Premise~\ref{prem:landauer} of Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}):
every instruction that collapses a yes-or-no property has $\delta(i) \ge 1$, where $i$
\emph{collapses} $P$ when some state with $P$ false is sent to a state with $P$ true and every
state with $P$ true is sent to one with $P$ true. The \emph{calibration}: $\delta(i) \le
\mathrm{cost}(i)$ for every instruction. Neither is proved anywhere; the theorems below ask
whether they can hold together.
\end{premise}

\subsection{The premises have to be able to hold together}

Here's the one piece of this section that I think is good physics discipline, and it's a
consistency test. Suppose you want to claim the counter tracks dissipation. You need two
premises: that a positively charged step dissipates something positive, and an upper
calibration that bounds dissipation by the charge. Can those two hold at once? There's a
theorem saying exactly when (\code{calibrated\_model\_exists\_iff\_positive\_cost}): a model
satisfying both exists precisely when every operation you've chosen to count (the statement
below calls those \emph{eligible}) costs at least one. I should say how cheap that is. The model the proof builds takes the dissipation to be
the cost itself, so the theorem shows the two premises don't contradict each other, not that
the counter tracks any dissipation. Still, it does bite on a schedule: if you count a
zero-cost step, no such model can exist. The one place the tree shows the premises holding is
a one-bit reset, where resetting costs one and idling costs nothing
(\code{bit\_model\_has\_satisfiable\_calibration}); for the machine's certifying steps it follows from
that equivalence and the floor theorems of Section~\ref{sec:witness}, and I haven't stated it as a separate
theorem. The full machine fails the test, and there's a theorem that says so flatly: no
dissipation function can both charge at least one for every step that collapses two classes
of states, for any yes-or-no property of states you care to pick, and stay bounded by the
machine's cost, because JUMP to one at cost zero collapses the classes of the property
``the program counter is one'' and costs nothing (\code{landauer\_dissipation\_premises\_inconsistent}). The
premise pair fails for the whole instruction set. That's the honest shape, and it's the same
shape as Section~\ref{sec:witness}'s ``prices the certifying merge, leaves the jump free.''

\begin{theorem}[When the premises can hold together]\label{thm:u24-consistency}
(1) For any set of operations, any predicate ``eligible'' on them, and any cost, a dissipation
with $\delta(i) \ge 1$ on every eligible $i$ and $\delta(i) \le \mathrm{cost}(i)$ on every
$i$ exists if and only if every eligible operation costs at least one. (2) On a one-bit
machine with a reset of cost 1 and an idle of cost 0, taking ``eligible'' to mean ``sends two
different states to one'', such a dissipation exists. (3) On the full machine, no dissipation
satisfies Premise~\ref{prem:u24-landauer-pair} for every yes-or-no property.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) If such a $\delta$ exists, $1 \le \delta(i) \le \mathrm{cost}(i)$. Conversely, take
$\delta = \mathrm{cost}$. (2) The reset is the only operation that sends two states to one,
and it costs 1; apply (1). (3) Let $P$ be ``the program counter is 1''. JUMP to 1 with declared
cost 0 collapses $P$: it sends the initial state, where $P$ is false, to one where it is
true, and every state lands at program counter 1. So $\delta$ of that jump is at least 1 and
at most its cost, which is 0.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{calibrated\_model\_exists\_iff\_positive\_cost} (ObservationPolicy.v, with
\code{calibrated\_positive\_model} at :83), \code{bit\_model\_has\_satisfiable\_calibration} and
\code{landauer\_dissipation\_premises\_inconsistent} (LandauerDissipationStrongForm.v), with the definitions
\code{step\_collapses\_bool\_classes} (LogicalErasureCertFlip.v) and \code{cost\_dissipation\_calibrated}
(LandauerDissipationStrongForm.v).

But now the history escape from Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}, pointed at the machine. Keep the previous state in a
history list (push it onto the front each step; below, $s :: h$ is the list $h$ with $s$ put
on the front) and every fixed-instruction step becomes injective, while the step you can see
stays the same; the program counter can collapse to one place while the bigger state keeps
its past. That move applied to the zero-cost jump is a theorem
(\code{zero\_cost\_vm\_jump\_has\_injective\_history\_lift}): the free merge, lifted to a machine with
history, isn't a merge. So ``this step merged, therefore it dissipated'' is not a sentence
about the visible step alone; it's a sentence about the whole state including whatever
history is retained, and a physical model has to say what's retained. The
permanent-certificate theorem in Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} supplies that for the certifying step on finite memory.
For the rest of the machine it's unsaid.

\begin{theorem}[Keeping history makes the free merge injective]\label{thm:u24-history}
Let the history step send a pair $(s, h)$, a state and a list of past states, to
$(\mathrm{apply}(s, i), s :: h)$. For any step function, the history step with a fixed
instruction is injective, and its first component is the original step. In particular JUMP to
1 with declared cost 0 costs 0, takes the initial state with empty history to program counter
1, and its history step is injective.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Undoing the history step, by popping the list, returns the old pair, so two pairs with the same
image are equal. The rest is computation.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{retained\_history\_step\_injective} (ObservationPolicy.v) and
\code{zero\_cost\_vm\_jump\_has\_injective\_history\_lift}.

\subsection{The calorimeter protocol: a specification, not a measurement}

Here is how one \emph{would} measure this, and it's here because it makes the boundary exact. Take a two-state
register with energies zero and a gap, a population p in the excited state, and the simplest
possible rate equation for how p changes in one time step (a rate for climbing into the
excited state, a rate for falling out of it, and the length of the step). For the canonical reset
(population one half to zero, with the rates chosen so the equation closes), the heat
delivered to the bath is exactly half the gap (\code{canonical\_reset\_heat\_exact}). Choose the gap
to be twice kT ln 2 and that heat is exactly kT ln 2 (\code{selected\_gap\_gives\_landauer\_heat}).

Read that twice, because the temptation is to read it as a derivation of Landauer's number
and it's the opposite. The gap was \emph{chosen} to make the heat come out as Landauer's number.
The same populations and rates with half that gap give half the Landauer value, and there's
a theorem exhibiting identical population dynamics with different heat
(\code{master\_equation\_does\_not\_fix\_heat\_scale}). The rate equation fixes the \emph{shape}; the energy
scale is a selected Hamiltonian (the physicist's name for the rule that says what energy each
state has), and selecting it is not deriving it.

\begin{definition}[The two-state protocol]\label{def:u24-calorimeter}
For a gap $\Delta$, the register's mean energy at excited population $p$ is $\Delta \cdot p$.
One step of the rate equation is
\[
p' = p + \delta t \, \big(k_{01} (1 - p) - k_{10} \, p\big),
\]
and the heat to the bath over a step from $p$ to $p'$ is defined as $\Delta p - \Delta p'$. The
canonical reset takes $p = \tfrac12$, $\delta t = 1$, $k_{01} = 0$, $k_{10} = 1$, ending at
$p' = 0$, and counts one logical event.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The heat is fixed by the chosen gap]\label{thm:u24-calorimeter}
(1) The canonical numbers satisfy the rate equation. (2) For every $\Delta$, the canonical
reset's heat is $\Delta / 2$. (3) For all $k_B$, $T$, the gap $\Delta = 2 k_B T \ln 2$ gives
heat $k_B T \ln 2$. (4) If $k_B > 0$ and $T > 0$, the gap $k_B T \ln 2$ gives heat strictly
below $k_B T \ln 2$. (5) There are two different gaps for which the same canonical populations
satisfy the rate equation and the heats differ.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
All five are field arithmetic on the definitions: $\tfrac12 + 1 \cdot (0 - \tfrac12) = 0$;
$\Delta \cdot \tfrac12 - \Delta \cdot 0 = \Delta/2$; and $\ln 2 > 0$ for (4). For (5) take gaps
1 and 2.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{canonical\_reset\_satisfies\_master\_equation}, \code{canonical\_reset\_heat\_exact},
\code{selected\_gap\_gives\_landauer\_heat}, \code{smaller\_gap\_refutes\_unconditional\_landauer\_floor} (given
$k_B > 0$ and $T > 0$) and
\code{master\_equation\_does\_not\_fix\_heat\_scale} (CalorimeterProtocol.v, 19, 29, 41, 57), with the
definitions in CalorimeterProtocolTarget.v.

What ties it to the machine: the protocol counts one logical event (the file defines that
count as the constant one), and that equals what CERTIFY from the clean state charges, and
no step of the machine switches certification on for less
(\code{vm\_minimal\_certification\_charges\_canonical\_reset\_mu},
\code{vm\_certification\_charges\_at\_least\_canonical\_reset\_mu}, given a step that turns certification
from off to on). Both are stated for the unbounded
sibling of the step from Section~\ref{sec:interpreters}, not for the sixty-four-bit one. There is no theorem mapping the
protocol's two register states to any machine state. The file's ``heat to the bath'' is the
register's mean energy before minus after, so it also assumes the bath receives what the
register loses, and no Coq says that. So a device test would have to measure the gap, the
populations, the rates, and the bath heat independently; separately establish
thermal admissibility and detailed balance (that the up and down rates stand in the ratio the
temperature dictates); and separately establish that the device's
physical reset \emph{is} the machine's certify event. The protocol is an executable experimental
specification. It is not a measured device, and it is not an unconditional conversion of
marks to joules, and anyone who tells you otherwise is reading a file name.

\begin{theorem}[The protocol's one event against the machine's floor]\label{thm:u24-calorimeter-vm}
Write $\mathrm{apply_u}$ for the unbounded step. (1) From the clean state, whose flag is down,
CERTIFY with declared cost 0 under $\mathrm{apply_u}$ raises the flag and raises $\mu$ by
exactly 1, the protocol's count. (2) For every state $s$ with the flag down and every
instruction $i$, if $\mathrm{apply_u}(s, i)$ has the flag up then $\mu(\mathrm{apply_u}(s, i))
\ge \mu(s) + 1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) is computation. (2) is the floor for the unbounded step, only CERTIFY sets the flag and it
costs its declared cost plus one, with conservation for $\mathrm{apply_u}$.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{vm\_minimal\_certification\_charges\_canonical\_reset\_mu} and
\code{vm\_certification\_charges\_at\_least\_canonical\_reset\_mu} (CalorimeterProtocol.v, 97). No
theorem connects the protocol's two register states to any machine state.

There's one more calibration in the files, and it gets the same treatment. It feeds a chain
of files (under coq/kernel/curvature) that this book doesn't otherwise visit, so here is the
chain in plain words. In 1995 Ted Jacobson got Einstein's equation of gravity out of
thermodynamics, by asking that heat equal temperature times the change in entropy (Clausius's
old relation) across every tiny horizon, with the temperature being the one an accelerating
observer sees in empty space (Unruh's, from 1976: accelerate hard enough and the vacuum looks
warm). The files try a discrete version of that walk, starting from the counter. The
calibration is the step that ties counter marks to that Unruh heat, and the end of the chain is
a statement about curvature on graphs, a discrete form of the Gauss-Bonnet identity: a closed
surface's total curvature is fixed by its shape up to stretching, through one whole number,
the Euler characteristic, which for a closed surface is fixed by how many holes it has. The
files say plainly that this is an analogy to Einstein, not his equation recovered. The
symbols below are the ones the file uses; $\hbar$,
$c$ and $k_B$ are the usual physical constants (Planck's, the speed of light, Boltzmann's),
and $a(P)$ is an acceleration. The rest are borrowed physics words wearing very small
costumes, so here's what each one is in the files. A \emph{split} $P$ is a row of cells cut into a
left list and a right list, with some pairs of cells coupled across the cut. A \emph{support} is a
list of pairs of values, the joint states the two sides can be in together; there's one for
before and one for after. The \emph{entanglement entropy} of a support, in bits, is the base-two
logarithm, rounded up, of how many different left-side values show up in it: a counting
stand-in for the physicist's quantity, not the quantity itself. The \emph{entropy increment} is that
number of bits times the entropy per bit. A \emph{congruence}, in relativity, is a bundle of light
rays; in the files it's a record of two numbers for each split, and the \emph{focusing factor} is
the first minus the second. For the one congruence the calibration uses, the two numbers are
the split's acceleration and its boundary size, and the focusing factor comes out to exactly 1
(\code{boundary\_geodesic\_focusing\_unit}, RaychaudhuriFluxBridge.v). Small costumes, like I said.

One thing you can do at the table before the premise itself, because Unruh's formula is right
there in it and, since 2019, every constant in it is a defined number. The temperature an
accelerating observer sees is $\hbar a / (2 \pi c k_B)$. Put in the acceleration you feel
standing on the floor, about 9.8 metres per second per second, with $\hbar$ about
$1.05 \times 10^{-34}$, $c$ about $3.00 \times 10^{8}$ and $k_B$ about $1.38 \times 10^{-23}$.
You get about $4 \times 10^{-20}$ kelvin. Turn it around and ask what acceleration would make
empty space feel like a room at 300 kelvin: about $7 \times 10^{22}$ metres per second per
second, some seven thousand billion billion times what holds you in your chair. That's why the
effect is so hard to see directly, and why Jacobson's use of it is a thought about every tiny
horizon rather than a reading off a bench. It changes nothing in the files. It tells you how far
from any thermometer the word ``heat'' is in the premise below.

\begin{premise}[The Unruh-Clausius calibration]\label{prem:u24-unruh}
For constants $\hbar$, $c$, $k_B$, an entropy per bit, two states $s, s'$, a split $P$ and two
supports, \code{mu\_landauer\_unruh\_calibrated} is the equation
\[
(\mu(s') - \mu(s)) \cdot A(P) \cdot \theta(P) = T_U(P) \cdot \Delta S,
\]
where $A(P)$ is one plus the boundary size of the split, $\theta(P)$ is a focusing factor that
is 1 for the congruence used, $T_U(P) = \hbar a(P) / (2 \pi c k_B)$ is an Unruh temperature for
an acceleration $a(P)$ read off the split, and $\Delta S$ is the change in entropy increment
between the supports. It is a hypothesis of the theorems that use it, not a theorem.
\end{premise}

\begin{remark}[What the Unruh-Clausius calibration does and doesn't do]\label{rem:u24-unruh}
With $c > 0$, $k_B > 0$ and the entropy per bit set to $k_B \ln 2$, it can be derived from two
further premises: that $\hbar \ln 2 = 2 \pi c$ as numbers, which is
a choice of units, and that the change in entanglement entropy in bits between the supports
equals the change in $\mu$, which is a claim about the run
(\code{mu\_landauer\_unruh\_calibrated\_from\_constant\_and\_bit\_calibration},
BekensteinCalibration.v). So it is a unit choice plus a substantive premise, not a unit
conversion alone. What it feeds is small: when the counter goes up and the calibration holds,
the calibrated flux across the split isn't zero
(\code{nfi\_cost\_nonzero\_implies\_nontrivial\_calibration}, NoFIToEinstein.v). The curvature end of the
chain doesn't use it at all. \code{discrete\_gauss\_bonnet\_delta} (NoFIToEinstein.v) says that for two
well-formed triangulated graphs the change in total curvature equals a constant times the
change in Euler characteristic, and its only premises are the two well-formedness hypotheses:
it's the discrete Gauss-Bonnet identity \code{einstein\_emerges} (EinsteinEmergence.v) for a pair of
states. No theorem derives curvature from the counter, and none joins the cost side to the
curvature side. (\code{discrete\_einstein\_emergence\_component}, ThermoEinsteinBridge.v, takes the
Clausius data as arguments and ignores them.)
\end{remark}

There's one more limit on that chain, and it's about where the geometry lives. The curvature
files prove things about partition graphs in general, any graph you can write down. The graphs
the machine actually reaches from its initial state are much plainer, and that's proved too.

\begin{theorem}[What the machine reaches is flat]\label{thm:u24-reachable-geometry}
Let $s$ be any state reachable from the initial state. (1) The regions of distinct modules of
$s$ share no address and the module numbers are distinct, so no two distinct modules are
adjacent, every module has no neighbours and no triangles, and the face-triangle count is 0.
(2) Every module $m$ reads flat: its Laplacian is 0, its angle-defect curvature is $2\pi$ and
its calibration residual is $2\pi$. (3) So $s$ is calibrated exactly when it has no modules.
(4) If the graph of $s$ passes the triangulation test, it has no interior edges, and with $F$
triangles it has $3F$ boundary edges, $3F$ edges, $3F$ vertices and Euler characteristic $F$.
(5) That case happens: one PNEW of the cells 0, 1, 2 from the initial state reaches a
triangulated state with one triangle and Euler characteristic 1.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Start from the initial state, whose graph is well-formed with no modules: every step keeps
regions disjoint and module numbers distinct, by induction on the run, and modules adjacent by
region would have to share an address. (2) With no neighbours, the Laplacian's sum is empty,
and with no triangles no angle is taken off $2\pi$. (3) Calibrated means residual 0 at every
module, and (2) makes every residual $2\pi$. (4) Triangles that share no vertex share no edge,
so each of the $F$ triangles brings three boundary edges and three vertices of its own, and
$3F - 3F + F = F$. (5) is computed.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{vm\_reachable\_regions\_separate}, \code{reachable\_no\_adjacent\_modules},
\code{reachable\_flat\_reading}, \code{reachable\_calibrated\_iff\_no\_modules},
\code{reachable\_triangulated\_isolated} and \code{reachable\_triangulated\_exists} (ReachableGeometry.v).
The region and adjacency facts are closed; the flat reading, the calibration and the Euler
count rest on the standard real-number assumptions. So the
Gauss-Bonnet identity is a true statement about graphs, and on a running machine the surfaces
it talks about are separate triangles: every edge is a boundary edge, so no run reaches a
closed surface, let alone one with holes. The chain's theorems stay theorems; what they're
about is a graph you can write down, not one this machine has been seen to build.

That Euler characteristic is worth a side trip, because you can do it with a sugar cube. Count
the corners of a cube: eight. The edges: twelve. The faces: six. Eight minus twelve plus six is
two. Try a pyramid with a square bottom: five corners, eight edges, five faces, two again. Every
solid without a hole through it gives two. Euler announced that in a letter to Goldbach in 1750,
and what happened next is a good reason to keep history at arm's length. Descartes is sometimes
said to have had it first, in a manuscript Leibniz copied in Paris in the 1670s that turned up
again among Leibniz's papers in Hanover; a closer reading is that Descartes had facts that would
have given it to him and never took the last step. And Euler's own proof doesn't hold up by
modern standards. Then in 1963 and 1964 Imre Lakatos published a series of articles, later the
book \emph{Proofs and Refutations}, written as a classroom arguing about this one formula, with
students bringing in counterexamples and the class deciding each time whether to repair the
proof or throw the counterexample out as a monster. Here's one of the monsters, to count
yourself: a picture frame, a thick square ring. Sixteen corners, thirty-two edges, sixteen
faces. Zero. A hole costs you two.

Now the machine's case. A lone flat triangle, one face: three corners, three edges, one face, and
three minus three plus one is one. That's part (4) of the theorem above, a triangle at a time.
Separate triangles never close up into a surface, so the count is just the number of triangles,
and the cube's two and the frame's zero never show up on a running machine.

\subsection{What permanence adds to Landauer: nothing new, said plainly}

Here's a fair question: is there a prediction the permanent-certificate theorems make that
Landauer's principle alone doesn't? No, and the reason is short. The smallest case, one certified state and one
flipping in, is ``set a bit to one whatever it held,'' which is the reset Landauer described
and Bérut measured; Landauer's own name for it is ``restore to one.'' The general bound, kT ln((m plus k) over m) for squeezing m plus k
equally likely states into m, is Landauer's formula for that squeeze. What the permanence
theorems add is the \emph{derivation}: which premises about a machine (finite, permanent) make
the certifying step a reset, so that Landauer applies to it. That's a result about the
machine, not about physics, and it's the right size.

\subsection{The mu-hierarchy, and how small it is}

Computer science has a famous result called the time-hierarchy theorem: more time buys you
problems you provably couldn't solve with less. Whose is it? It's from 1965, in a paper by Juris
Hartmanis and Richard Stearns, ``On the Computational Complexity of Algorithms,'' the paper
people point to as the start of the whole study of how much computing costs, and the one that
gave the field its name. They got the Turing Award for it in 1993. I mention it so you can see
exactly whose shadow this section is standing in. The silhouette is ``more of the resource buys
something you couldn't have had.'' Here's the machine's version, and then how much smaller
the thing inside the silhouette is.

Call a run \emph{level-k certified} when it ends with the flag up and its executed instructions
include a CERTIFY whose charge (declared cost plus one) is at least k. Then for every k at
least one: there's a level-k certified run with total cost exactly k (the one-instruction
run CERTIFY with declared cost k minus one; its charge is k, it certifies, and that's the
whole bill), and any level-k certified run costs at least k (the executed CERTIFY at level
k charged at least k, everything else at least zero, and Section~\ref{sec:counter}'s conservation sums them)
(\code{mu\_hierarchy\_theorem}). Corollary: no fixed budget caps all certifications, because for
any budget B the level B plus one run exceeds it (\code{mu\_hierarchy\_no\_upper\_bound}).

\begin{definition}[Level-k certified]\label{def:u24-level}
For fuel $F$ and a program $t$, let $\mathrm{exec}(F, t)$ be the instructions the
program-counter runner actually executes from the initial state in $F$ steps, in order. The
pair is level-$k$ certified when the final state has the flag up and $\mathrm{exec}(F, t)$
contains a CERTIFY with declared cost $d$ and $d + 1 \ge k$. The \emph{cost} of the pair is the
final $\mu$ minus the initial $\mu$, and the initial one is 0.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The mu-hierarchy]\label{thm:u24-hierarchy}
For every $k \ge 1$: some pair has cost exactly $k$ and is level-$k$ certified, and every
level-$k$ certified pair has cost at least $k$. Consequently, for every budget $B$ there is a
$k \ge 1$, namely $B + 1$, such that no pair with cost at most $B$ is level-$k$ certified.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Witness: the one-instruction program CERTIFY $k - 1$, run for one step, charges $k$ and sets
the flag. Lower bound: the executed CERTIFY charged at least $k$, its charge appears in the
run's ledger entries, every other entry is at least zero, and conservation makes the final
$\mu$ the sum of the entries. The budget statement is the lower bound at $k = B + 1$.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{mu\_hierarchy\_theorem} (MuHierarchyTheorem.v), with \code{level\_k\_certified},
\code{mu\_hierarchy\_strict}, \code{mu\_hierarchy\_no\_upper\_bound} and
\code{mu\_dimension\_unbounded}.

How small is that? Very. The time-hierarchy theorem is deep because it separates
\emph{what can be computed} with more time. This separates \emph{what was charged}: a run that declared a bigger
charge was charged more. It's conservation plus the floor, and the ``level'' is defined by the
charge itself. I keep it because it's true and because the silhouette is instructive: the
counter is a resource in the formal sense that more of it is strictly more, and no budget
is enough for everything. I don't keep it because it's surprising. It isn't.

\subsection{What this section is}

A ledger that counts charges, bounded by cost; a calibration that's a premise; a
consistency check the premises pass; a measurement protocol that's a specification with a
selected scale; and a hierarchy that's arithmetic. The physics in this book is in Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}, as a
named premise with its critics named. Here there's accounting, and I've tried to call every
line by its right name. That's the end of the machine. The chip is next, and after that,
what it took to check any of this and where the checking stops.


\part{The hardware}

%===========================================================================
\section{From the proof to the chip}
\label{sec:chip}
%===========================================================================

Aristotle's bronze, from Section~\ref{sec:structure}: the same statue in three materials, and a promise I made in
Section~\ref{sec:onemachine} that I'd keep here. The materials are a step relation in Coq, a hardware model in a
language called Kami, and Verilog that a tool chain turns into a configuration file for a
programmable chip. This section walks the chain from the top down and, at every link, says
one of three words: \emph{proved}, \emph{tested}, or \emph{trusted}. The discipline is the seL4 paper's,
where a team that had just proved an operating-system kernel correct spent a
paragraph listing what they \emph{hadn't} proved (the compiler, the assembly, the hardware), and
I think that paragraph is the most important one in the paper. So here's mine, at length.

One thing about names first. The chip isn't a Thiele machine. It's hardware that implements
one, the big build, inside stated bounds: forty-seven of the fifty-one instructions have an
encoding, and its words are thirty-two bits where the kernel's are sixty-four. A laptop
implements a Turing machine the same way, with a finite memory the model doesn't have.

\subsection{Hardware as rules}

First the idea that makes any of this possible, because it's not obvious that a circuit can
be a thing you prove theorems about. In the early 2000s Arvind's group at MIT described
hardware as a set of \emph{rules}: each rule is a condition (when may I fire) and a batch of
register updates that happen all at once or not at all. The compiler's job is to build the
arbitration logic so that rules which don't conflict can fire in the same clock cycle while
the result still looks as if they fired one at a time. Bluespec is the commercial language
built on that idea; its compiler, bsc, went open source in 2020. What the idea buys: a
circuit whose behaviour is ``as if one rule at a time,'' which is a thing you can reason about
the way you reason about a program.

Then Kami, from Chlipala's and Arvind's groups in 2017: a Coq library for writing
Bluespec-style hardware \emph{inside Coq} and proving things about it as transition systems;
their case study verified a family of multicore RISC-V processors (RISC-V is an open, freely
usable instruction set). What it buys: one Kami
design refines another, checked by Coq. What it leaves trusted is the path \emph{out} of Coq: if the Bluespec compiler preserves meaning,
the circuits inherit the proofs. If.

\subsection{The chain, top to bottom}

\emph{The CPU as a Kami module.} The processor is one Kami module, with registers (sixteen
general registers of thirty-two bits, a hundred and twenty-eight words of data memory, a
hundred and twenty-eight instruction words of a hundred and twenty-eight bits each, the
partition table, the arrow tables, the tensor store, the eight counters) and rules: a main
\code{step} rule, and multi-cycle state machines for the checking step, for the two
arrow-building instructions that read memory, and for the game check (twenty-nine
firings, Section~\ref{sec:chsh}). Two methods (a method is an entry point the module offers to whatever sits
outside it) matter for what follows: \code{loadInstr}, which writes one
instruction word, and \code{start}, which clears the halted flag and sets the program counter to
zero and does nothing else. The CPU \emph{resets halted}: it comes up stopped, so a program can be
loaded before anything runs. The arrow tables are six, of sixteen slots each: arrows, coupling
descriptors, formula descriptors, certificate descriptors, descriptor metadata, and coupling
pairs. The checking step's machine keeps two buffers of sixty-four words for the formula and
its certificate. And the ledger is written by the same \code{step} rule that executes the
instruction, not by a separate datapath. (ThieleTypes.v and ThieleCPUCore.v give these
numbers.)

\emph{Start from reset: proved.} From the reset state, calling \code{start} produces exactly the
state every execution theorem begins from, calling no other method (\code{start\_from\_reset}),
and that call is a legal step in Kami's semantics (\code{start\_substep}).

\emph{Each instruction refines the specification: proved, under premises.} Three layers. A
firing of the real \code{step} rule, read through Kami's semantics, updates the registers exactly
as a Gallina function \code{step\_next} says (Gallina is the plain programming language inside Coq,
the one the kernel's step is written in) (\code{rule\_next\_correct}, \code{step\_next\_correct}). Then one
theorem per opcode, forty-eight in all and every one generated by a script: thirty-five in
one file, three for the partition instructions in a file of their own, and ten for the arrow
instructions at both encodings: if the fetched word is that opcode, the machine is live (not
halted, no error, every multi-cycle machine idle), the alarm is down (the alarm is a flag the
chip raises when the ledger falls below the tensor total), and the stated counters don't overflow thirty-two bits, then the
hardware snapshot after the step equals the abstract \code{kami\_step} of the decoded instruction
(\code{step\_add\_refines} and its siblings). The overflow premises are where the two machines meet:
the kernel's registers are sixty-four-bit words and the chip's are thirty-two. Some of these
theorems carry more premises (an address inside the active module's range, module ranges
that don't overlap, and others), so I'll stay with
``under its stated side conditions.'' The full admission catalogue, including the
different conditions on the two arrow encodings and on fault paths, is printed in
Appendix~\ref{sec:hardware-contracts}. Then the multi-cycle ones: the game check retires
through its twenty-nine firings to the same place (\code{chsh\_lassert\_refines}, with
\code{chsh\_only\_rule\_enabled} saying nothing else can fire meanwhile), the checking step through
its header and scan firings (\code{lassert\_sat\_refines}, \code{lassert\_unsat\_refines}; the scan's
premises include that the formula's clause count is at least one and at most the number of
terminator words it holds, and that the formula's addresses and the charge fit in thirty-two
bits; the abstraction function agrees with the kernel on the ledger always, and on the
program counter when the check passes, \code{logic\_engine\_equivalent\_lassert}), and the
memory-reading arrow instructions under their admission premises (table room, modules
present, pairs fit; \code{morph\_ext\_retire}, \code{compose\_ext\_retire}). A master theorem gathers
them: any instruction in an ``admitted'' list of fifty-five cases (some opcodes at two
encodings, plus fault paths) retires, meaning from a live state the scheduler picks \code{step},
every later firing runs to an idle state, and that state matches \code{kami\_step}
(\code{admitted\_retires}). The word ``admitted'' there means ``admitted under premises,'' not Coq's
\code{Admitted}, and no proof in the hardware tree ends in Coq's \code{Admitted} (the pun would have
been unfortunate). Finally \code{kami\_step} meets
the kernel's own \code{vm\_apply} through an abstraction function (\code{embed\_step\_compute}), whose
file sorts the opcodes into unconditional, preconditioned, and covered elsewhere.

The refinement theorems are equations between snapshots, field by field, which is the
stronger of the two contracts Appendix A tells apart, not a looser relation picked to make the
proofs go through. (The checking step against the kernel is weaker than that, and says
exactly where.) Here are the words and five of those theorems exactly: one per-opcode refinement, two
multi-cycle ones, the checking step against the kernel, and the master theorem.

\begin{definition}[Board state, snapshot, step firing]\label{def:u25-board}
A board state $b$ is the value of every register of the Kami module. $\mathrm{snap}(b)$ reads
off the fields the specification talks about, as natural numbers, and $\mathrm{kstep}$ is the
Gallina function \code{kami\_step} that the specification gives for one instruction on a snapshot.
$\mathrm{next}(b)$ is the board state after one firing of the \code{step} rule, the instruction
word $\mathrm{fetched}(b)$ being the one at the fetch address. $b$ is \emph{live} when it is not
halted, has no error, and every multi-cycle machine is idle; the \emph{alarm} is up when the ledger
is below the tensor total. The hardware word width is 32 bits.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[ADD refines]\label{thm:u25-add}
Let $b$ be a board state whose fetched word is an ADD word with destination $d$, sources $r_1,
r_2$ and declared cost $c$. Suppose the alarm is down, the error flag is false, the halted flag
is false, $\mathrm{pc}(b) + 1 < 2^{32}$, $\mu(b) + c < 2^{32}$, and the sum of the two source
registers is below $2^{32}$. Then $\mathrm{snap}(\mathrm{next}(b)) =
\mathrm{kstep}(\mathrm{snap}(b), \text{ADD } d\ r_1\ r_2\ c)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The step rule's writes, read through Kami's semantics, are given field by field by generated
lemmas, one per field of the snapshot: the program counter goes up by one, the ledger by $c$,
register $d$ gets the 32-bit sum, everything else is unchanged. With the three bounds, each
32-bit addition equals the natural-number addition the specification uses, and the two
snapshots agree field by field.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{step\_add\_refines} (StepRefine.v), on top of \code{rule\_next\_correct} and
\code{step\_next\_correct} (RuleStep.v, 66). The thirty-seven siblings have the same shape with
their own bounds (SUB, for instance, asks that the subtrahend not exceed the minuend).

\begin{theorem}[The game check refines]\label{thm:u25-chsh}
Let the fetched word of $b$ be CHSH\_\allowbreak{}LASSERT with declared cost $c$, the alarm down, no error,
not halted, $\mathrm{pc}(b) + 1 < 2^{32}$, $\mu(b) + c + 1 < 2^{32}$, and the trap vector equal to
the kernel's trap address. Then after the step firing and twenty-nine firings of the check
rule, the snapshot equals $\mathrm{kstep}(\mathrm{snap}(b), \text{CHSH\_LASSERT } c)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The step firing charges the ledger $c + 1$ and starts the check machine on the eight
counters. The twenty-nine firings compute the seven integer facts at the
widths of Section~\ref{sec:chsh}, and \code{chsh\_run\_result} gives the final program counter, error flag and error
code as functions of the word-level check, which \code{chsh\_check\_word\_correct} equates with the
kernel's check for every eight 32-bit counters. Every other field is untouched by the check
firings.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{chsh\_lassert\_refines} (ChshRetire.v), with \code{chsh\_run\_result} (ChshRun.v)
and \code{chsh\_only\_rule\_enabled} (ChshRetire.v).

\begin{theorem}[The satisfiable LASSERT refines]\label{thm:u25-lassert}
Let the fetched word of $b$ be LASSERT of the satisfiable kind with formula register $f$,
certificate register, length $\ell$ and declared cost $c$, and let $a$ be the value of register $f$.
Suppose the alarm is down, no error, not halted, $\mathrm{pc}(b) + 1 < 2^{32}$, the trap vector is
the kernel's trap address, the memory word at $a$ is $\ell$, $a + 3 + \ell < 2^{32}$, the clause
count $n$ stored at $a + 2$ satisfies $1 \le n \le z$, where $z$ is the number of zero
(terminator) words among the formula's literal words, and $\mu(b) + 8\ell + c + 1 < 2^{32}$.
Then there is an $m$ with $1 \le m \le \ell$ such that after the step firing, the header firing
and $m$ scan firings the check machine is idle for the first time, and the snapshot there equals
$\mathrm{kstep}(\mathrm{snap}(b), \text{LASSERT})$.
\end{theorem}

Checked as \code{lassert\_sat\_refines} (LassertRetire.v), through the scan lemma that follows.

\begin{lemma}[The hardware scan computes the kernel's checks]\label{lem:u25-scan}
For any two assignments $g_m$, $g_c$, numbers $a$, $v$, $n$ and a list of words $w$: if $1 \le
n$, $n$ is at most the number of zero words in $w$, and every word of $w$ is below $2^{32}$,
then the hardware scan of $w$ for $n$ clauses returns the conjunction of the kernel's model
check of $g_m$ and countermodel check of $g_c$ on the formula whose words are $a$, $v$,
$n$ followed by $w$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Induction on $w$. A zero word closes a clause: if it was satisfied, the scan moves to the next
clause, and the last clause ends the scan; a nonzero word is a literal, read as a signed 32-bit
number, whose truth under the assignment is the kernel's. The bound $n \le$ the number of
terminators keeps the list from running out before the last clause. For the theorem, memory
words are 32-bit by construction, and the bounds on $a$ and $\ell$ keep every address in range.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{lassert\_sat\_refines} (LassertRetire.v), \code{lassert\_unsat\_refines} for the
other kind, and \code{hw\_scan\_spec}, \code{hw\_scan\_certcheck} (LassertSpec.v, 120).

The partition-only reading $\mathrm{abs}_0$ and the full reading $\mathrm{abs}$
are defined field by field in Appendix~\ref{sec:hardware-contracts}. The first comparison
uses the partition-only reading; the later full-state theorem uses the full reading.

\begin{theorem}[The checking step against the kernel]\label{thm:u25-logic-engine}
For every snapshot $h$ and every LASSERT instruction $i$, there is a kernel state $v'$ with
$\mathrm{vm\_step}(\mathrm{abs}_0(h), i, v')$ such that $\mu(v') = \mu(\mathrm{kstep}(h, i))$; if
the kernel's check of the formula in $\mathrm{abs}_0(h)$ passes, the program counters agree too;
and the error flag of $v'$ is that of $\mathrm{abs}_0(h)$ when the check passes and true when it
fails.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Choose $v'$ to be the kernel successor of $\mathrm{abs}_0(h)$ for this LASSERT.
Both definitions add $8\ell+c+1$ to the ledger, independently of success, so their
ledgers agree. On a passing check each advances the program counter by one. The
kernel's success branch preserves the old error flag and its failure branch sets
it to true. These substitutions give the three conclusions; equality of every
state field is not asserted by this theorem.
\end{proof}

So the ledger always agrees, the program counter on a pass, and the error flag in both cases.
Checked as \code{logic\_engine\_equivalent\_lassert} (LogicEngineEquivalence.v).

\begin{definition}[Retires; admitted]\label{def:u25-retire}
An instruction $i$ \emph{retires} from $b$ to $d$ when $b$ is live, the firings that follow the
step firing (each chosen by the module's own scheduler while some machine is busy) run from
$\mathrm{next}(b)$ to $d$, $d$ is idle, and $\mathrm{snap}(d) = \mathrm{kstep}(\mathrm{snap}(b),
i)$. \emph{Admitted} means that the fetched instruction and initial board state satisfy
one of the fifty-five cases in Appendix~\ref{sec:hardware-contracts}. That catalogue gives
the common conditions, each case's ledger increment and every additional premise.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Every admitted instruction retires]\label{thm:u25-admitted}
For every $b$ and $i$, if $(b, i)$ is admitted then $i$ retires from $b$ to some $d$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
A case split over the fifty-five constructors, each closed by its own retirement lemma, which
packages a refinement theorem above with the fact that the scheduler picks \code{step} at a live
state and that the multi-cycle firings run to idle.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{admitted\_retires} (RetireMaster.v), with \code{Retire} and \code{admitted}.

And the whole-machine version, every opcode under its side conditions (\code{driven\_step\_wf}),
which, in the assumption audit (Section~\ref{sec:witness}), uses one standard axiom, functional extensionality on
dependent functions. Most of the per-rule theorems above use that one and a second, \code{eq\_rect\_eq},
the axiom form of uniqueness of identity proofs; the audit lists which. Both are standard,
and Section~\ref{sec:coq} accounts for them, along with how to rerun the audit on the sources in front of you.

The whole-machine statement compares \code{kami\_step} with the kernel's step through an abstraction
function, under a per-opcode condition, and lifts to runs.

\begin{theorem}[The specification step is the kernel step]\label{thm:u25-driven}
Let $\mathrm{abs}$ be the full snapshot reading and $\mathrm{WF}$ the per-instruction conditions printed in Appendix~\ref{sec:hardware-contracts}. (1) For every snapshot
$h$ and instruction $i$ with $\mathrm{WF}(h, i)$: $\mathrm{abs}(\mathrm{kstep}(h, i)) =
\mathrm{apply}(\mathrm{abs}(h), i)$. (2) For every fuel $F$, program $t$ and snapshot $h$ such
that $\mathrm{WF}$ holds at every state the run visits, for the instruction it fetches there:
$\mathrm{abs}$ of the specification's run of $t$ for $F$ steps from $h$ equals the kernel's
program-counter run of $t$ for $F$ steps from $\mathrm{abs}(h)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) A case split on the instruction: the opcodes with no condition go through one shared lemma
for the plain compute instructions, and each conditioned opcode has its own. (2) Induction on
$F$, using (1) at each fetched instruction; the condition is asked only of states the run
reaches.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{driven\_step\_wf} (GraphReconstructionBridge.v) and \code{driven\_trace\_commutes}, with \code{WFDrivenRun} checking \code{WFDrivenPrecondition} along the run.
The condition is True for every opcode not named here. CALL and RET need a well-formed
snapshot, with a program-counter bound for CALL. CHSH\_\allowbreak{}TRIAL needs its four operands to be
bits. LASSERT needs its length to agree with the memory header. TENSOR\_\allowbreak{}SET and TENSOR\_\allowbreak{}GET need
valid indices, and TENSOR\_\allowbreak{}GET an existing module. MORPH, COMPOSE, MORPH\_\allowbreak{}TENSOR and MORPH\_\allowbreak{}GET
need the extended table invariant; MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ID needs the empty-descriptor invariant and an
existing nonempty module; MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT and MORPH\_\allowbreak{}DELETE need a well-formed arrow table. PNEW
needs a table counter of at most sixty-four, a nonempty normalized region and a clear tensor
slot; PSPLIT and PMERGE need a well-formed partition table, live operands with nonempty ranges
(at least two cells for PSPLIT, two different modules for PMERGE) and clear fresh slots. None
of the three needs room in the table. When the module numbers run out, or a PNEW range runs
past memory, the chip traps the way the kernel does (Section~\ref{sec:state}), charges the counter and keeps
running, and the theorem covers that trap like any other branch. The chip's error word tells
the partition faults apart, 0xBADF001D for a missing module number or a range past memory and
0xBADF001E for an overlap or a merge whose ranges don't touch (\code{ERR\_PARTITION\_VAL} and
\code{ERR\_PARTITION\_OVERLAP\_VAL}, ThieleTypes.v); the kernel writes 1 for every fault. Reset doesn't make
these true forever; a run has to keep establishing them. This is a theorem about the Gallina
specification, one level above the clocked rules.

Underneath all of that sit four small files that check the floorboards: that every one of
the twelve CPU rules is something Kami's evaluator can actually run; that a run picked rule by
rule (always the first rule that's ready) really is a Kami run, with a bound on firings, an
early stop exactly when no rule is ready, and a ready rule at reset; that no register ever
changes its declared kind on any run from reset; and thirteen facts about what the registers
hold at reset. (In order, those are \code{CoreRules}, \code{CoreExecution}, \code{CoreTyping} and
\code{DispatchReset}.) What none of them pins down: fairness, the allocation invariants along a reachable run, or meaning through
the tools below Kami. One more file is worth naming so nobody leans on it:
\code{rtl\_inventory\_arithmetic} (RTLGapRegistry.v) is the equation $37 + 10 + 0 = 47$, an
inventory count of opcodes (not of the forty-eight refinement theorems above), and it would still hold if every hardware proof were deleted.

The arrow-building instructions run through a coupling state machine, and the picture is
simple: it builds a list of cell pairs, then tidies it. Descriptor zero is
reserved for the empty coupling, with base 0 and count 0 (CouplingComposeKami.v); the pair
table holds sixteen entries; and a normalization loop runs over the newly built pair range
(CouplingFsmNorm.v). Their
fault branches retire in the step firing alone with the error set
(\code{step\_morph\_ext\_fault\_refines} and its siblings, CouplingFaults.v), and their success paths
retire under the admission premises (\code{morph\_ext\_retire}, \code{compose\_ext\_retire}). From
\code{kami\_step} down to the kernel they also need the extended table invariant above.

\emph{The loader: proved for the receive, the hand-off and the report, its start discipline proved by a solver, the rest tested.} Here's the part
that answers a question worth asking in plain words: what's the point of a chip you
can't load? The answer is a second Kami module, also extracted, not hand-written: a serial
receiver. It samples one input pin through two registers (the standard way to avoid reading
a wire mid-change), reads each bit at the middle of its period, and reassembles bytes in one of the
oldest serial formats still in use: one low start bit, eight data bits least-significant first, one high
stop bit, at 115,200 bits per second. A twenty-megahertz clock gives 174 cycles per bit,
which is 0.22 percent slow, within tolerance. On top of that a small assembler takes a
two-byte count N, then N instructions of sixteen bytes each, writes each through
\code{loadInstr}, and then calls \code{start}. And a reporter sends fifteen bytes back: a header byte,
a status byte, then the program counter, the counter, and the error code as four bytes each,
and a trailer byte. That's the whole interface: one wire in, one wire out, four LEDs.

You can check that 0.22 percent at the table, and it's worth doing once, because it's the
whole trick of the format. Divide twenty million by 115,200 and you get about 173.6. A counter
can only count whole cycles, so it counts 174, and twenty million divided by 174 is about
114,943 bits per second: 0.22 percent slow. Then the obvious next question: does that matter?
The receiver lines itself up on the falling edge of the start bit and reads each bit at what it
thinks is the middle, and with every bit its idea of the middle drifts a little later. By the
middle of the stop bit, nine and a half bits in, it's about two percent of a bit late, give or
take the cycle or two the two-register sampler adds at the start. It would have to slip half a
bit before it read the wrong one. And the next start bit lines it up all over again, so the
drift never gets to pile up past one byte. That's how two machines whose clocks don't quite
agree get to talk at all.

That trick is older than any chip, and it's worth following back. Teleprinters had
the same problem: a machine at each end of a long wire, each turned by its own motor, and
keeping two motors in exact step over a long line was the hard part. The way out was to start
the receiver at the beginning of each character and let it come to rest at the end, so it only
had to keep in step for one character at a time. Howard Krum was granted a patent on a version
of that in 1918, and the unit people use for signalling speed, the baud, is named after
Émile Baudot, whose telegraph code ran over lines like those. Who had the start-stop idea
first? I can't tell you. Krum's patent has a date on it, and a patent is where somebody
stakes a claim, not where the question gets settled. None of it changes a theorem. It changes
the picture: the one input pin on this chip frames its bytes the way teleprinters framed their
characters, a start, the data, a stop, about a hundred years on.

What's proved: take any program of one to a hundred and twenty-eight instructions, start
the receiver from reset, and play on the simulated pin the serial frames of the count and
of instructions zero through k. Then the loader holds instruction k addressed to slot k,
its request flag has flipped once per instruction, and it asks for \code{start} exactly when k is
the last one (\code{serial\_program\_load}); every cycle of that run is a call of the real sample
method; the load rule passes exactly that address and word to \code{loadInstr}
(\code{load\_rule\_hands\_off}); and \code{loadInstr} puts the word at that address (\code{load\_instr\_writes}).
A program of zero instructions is a separate, smaller fact: fed straight to the assembler,
with no serial pin in between, the count bytes alone raise the start request
(\code{empty\_program\_starts}).

And the way back out is proved too. Once the CPU is halted or in error, run the loader's
report rule once per clock cycle. The pin sits high for one cycle, then carries the serial
frames of fifteen bytes: the header 0xDE, a status byte whose three low bits are halted,
error and certified, then the program counter, the counter and the CPU's error code as four
bytes each, least significant first, and the trailer 0xAD. The values are the kernel state's,
read through the same abstraction every execution theorem uses, so the bytes on the wire are
the machine's state and not a separate story. A receiver built the loader's way, started idle,
reads back exactly those fifteen bytes, and the pin stays high from then on
(\code{serial\_status\_report}). Before a halt or an error the reporter does nothing
(\code{report\_waits}). Its premise is worth saying out loud: Kami's semantics don't say when a rule
fires, so the theorem takes one firing of the report rule per clock cycle as given.

What's \emph{tested only, as far as Coq goes}: the rule that actually fires \code{start} and
the LED output. No Coq theorem names them. (The extracted circuit's start discipline has a
separate solver proof, further down, and the LEDs have only the simulations.) And one thing
the loader file says about itself that I'll repeat: Kami's semantics let a rule fire
whenever its guard holds, and the file does not prove that the load rule takes each word
before the next replaces it. That's a real gap between ``the receiver assembles the right
word'' and ``the CPU got every word,'' and only the simulations cover it, which are finite.
The solver properties don't close it either: they say the loader never writes after
\code{start}, not that every word was taken.

Here's the start, in the theorem's own words:

\begin{theorem}[Start from reset]\label{thm:u25-start}
From the reset register map, any execution of the \code{start} method calls no other method, and
its updates applied over the reset map give exactly the state every execution theorem starts
from: halted false and program counter 0, everything else at reset.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The start operation makes two assignments: clear the halted bit and set the program
counter to zero. It performs no call and preserves all other registers. Applying
those assignments to the reset map gives exactly the stated map, field by field.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{start\_from\_reset} (CPUStart.v), with \code{start\_substep} for the step of the
module.

\begin{theorem}[Serial load]\label{thm:u25-serial}
Let $w_0, \dots, w_{N-1}$ be instruction words with $1 \le N \le 128$, and $k < N$. Run the
receiver model from its reset state over the serial frames of the bytes $N$, 0, and then the
sixteen bytes of each of $w_0, \dots, w_k$. At the end, the loader holds address $k$ and word
$w_k$ for the CPU, its request flag equals ``$k$ is even'', and its start request is set exactly
when $k + 1 = N$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
One frame, a start bit, eight data bits and a stop bit, takes the receiver from idle back to
idle having delivered exactly that byte once (\code{one\_frame}, by computation). Induction over the bytes then follows the assembler: two count bytes, then
sixteen bytes per word with the address counting up, the request flag toggling per word and
the start request raised after the last.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{serial\_program\_load} (LoaderSerial.v), with \code{one\_frame} and
\code{step\_is\_rxSample}, which says each cycle of the model is a call of the real Kami
sample method. The zero-instruction case is \code{empty\_program\_starts}, in the same file.

\begin{theorem}[Hand-off and write]\label{thm:u25-handoff}
(1) If the load rule (\code{load\_rule}) runs from a register map holding request $r$, acknowledge $a$, address
$x$ and word $w$, then $r \ne a$, its only method call is \code{loadInstr} with $x$ and $w$, and its
only update sets acknowledge to $r$. (2) If \code{loadInstr} runs with $x$ and $w$, it calls no
method and its only update writes $w$ at address $x$ of instruction memory.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The load rule's guard is $r\ne a$. Once that guard holds, its action sends the stored
address and word to the instruction-memory write method and copies $r$ into the
acknowledgement register. It has no other action. The called method updates the
instruction-memory array at the supplied address to the supplied word, preserving
every other array entry and every other register; it calls nothing. These are the
two local contracts. They do not by themselves prove that every serial request
eventually receives a matching call.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{load\_rule\_hands\_off} and \code{load\_instr\_writes} (LoaderSerial.v, 695).

\begin{theorem}[Status report]\label{thm:u25-report}
Let $b$ be the CPU's registers with the halted bit $h$ or the error bit set, and let $s$ be the
kernel state they abstract to. Let $R$ be the fifteen bytes: 0xDE; the status byte
$h + 2e + 4c$, where $e$ and $c$ are the error and certified flags of $s$; the four bytes,
least significant first, of each of the program counter of $s$, the counter $\mu(s)$ and the
CPU's error code, each taken modulo $2^{32}$; and 0xAD. Start the transmitter neither active
nor done, and run the report rule once per cycle for $1 + 15 \cdot 10 \cdot 174$ cycles, the
status getters returning $b$ in the first cycle and anything afterwards. Then the pin reads
high in the first cycle and then the serial frames of $R$ in order; the loader's receiver,
started idle, decodes that sequence to exactly $R$; and for any further cycles the pin stays
high and the transmitter does not change.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
In the first cycle the guard sees halted or error, each status getter returns its register of
$b$, and the rule latches the fifteen bytes and starts sending. Each byte then goes out as a
low start bit, eight data bits least significant first and a high stop bit, 174 cycles per
bit, by induction over bytes, bits and cycles. The fifteen latched bytes equal $R$ by
computation on words. The loader's receiver turns each frame back into its byte (\code{one\_frame},
above), so it reads $R$. After the last stop bit the transmitter is done, and a done
transmitter keeps the pin high whatever the rule sees.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{serial\_status\_report} (ReportSerial.v), from \code{report\_transmits},
\code{report\_bytes\_kernel}, \code{report\_bytes\_fields}, \code{status\_byte\_value} and \code{report\_done\_stays},
with \code{report\_step\_is\_rule} (each modelled cycle is a firing of the real Kami rule, its calls the
CPU's six getters), \code{get\_tx\_is\_tx\_out} (the pin is the transmitter's output) and
\code{report\_waits} (nothing happens before a halt or an error). Assumptions: functional
extensionality and the uniqueness of equality proofs, the two Kami itself uses.

\emph{Composition: proved by reflexivity.} The system is the CPU module followed by the loader
module. The loader's calls to \code{loadInstr}, \code{start}, and the status getters are the CPU's own
methods, so they close inside the design; what's left over (sample, transmit, LEDs) becomes
the pins. A one-line theorem says the printer (the program, below, that writes the design out as
Bluespec text) receives the CPU's syntax followed by the loader's.

\emph{A second extraction, to software: tested.} Separately from the chip, Coq's extraction also
turns the kernel's step into OCaml, and a runner built on it executes programs. What Coq proves
about it is about the Coq side. For every state and instruction, the observable record taken
after one kernel step satisfies the floor (a flag that goes from down to up comes with the
counter at least one higher) and never shows the counter lower than before
(\code{ocaml\_observable\_nofi\_and\_monotone}, OCamlExtractionBridge.v). The lemma named
\code{ocaml\_runner\_observable\_defined} says only that the observable exists, which is true of
any Coq function; it is not a cross-language equivalence. That the built binary returns the
same observable is checked by a parity test suite, not proved. And the checked-in runner file
(build/extracted\_\allowbreak{}vm\_\allowbreak{}runner.ml) takes each step by calling the extracted Coq step, so the
steps themselves follow the current rules, but the code wrapped around them is its own and
differs from the kernel: it starts both graph counters at one, stops on an error, stops at
HALT and writes a status word, and steps over a CHECKPOINT written without a cost (and the
two port directives) without charging; a CHECKPOINT with a cost goes through the kernel's
step like everything else. No theorem in this book is about that runner. The board
simulations do use it as the reference they compare against, which makes those comparisons
exactly as good as the runner is, and I'd rather say that than let ``agrees with the
software machine'' sound like it names the kernel. None of the seventeen board programs
uses CHECKPOINT.

\emph{Extraction: trusted.} Coq's extraction turns the Kami syntax tree for the system into
OCaml. The stock extraction command is an unverified translator (Letouzey's 2003 design;
later work proves erasure correct, but that's not the command used here). And the step just
before it, turning Kami's module syntax into Bluespec's, is a Kami library function in a file
that contains no theorem at all. Two trusted links in a row, and I'm naming them.

\emph{Printing, patching, compiling: trusted, tested.} A vendored printer (about a thousand lines
of OCaml) prints Bluespec. A script then does things to the text that I'll list because
``nothing hand-written but clock primitives'' is a tempting sentence and it's not exact:
it strips the printer's wrapper module; rewrites one vector construction into the form the
2024 bsc accepts; turns large vector registers into register-file cells; runs bsc (2024.07)
and deletes the date line bsc stamps, so the output depends only on the input; and turns
flattened registers into Verilog arrays. For the system it also wraps the top module with an
interface made of the outermost methods, a wrapper that keeps the printed instantiation lines
verbatim and, by its own docstring, writes no expression, register, or rule. Each text
transform is audited by a script that says of itself that it is ``not a compiler correctness
proof.'' And one Bluespec library cell, a hundred-line register file in Verilog, is read by
synthesis and comes from nobody's proof. These change storage shape, not logic, by their own
account, and they're tested, not proved.

\emph{The gate that catches hand edits: tested.} The nightly full run rebuilds the extraction,
reruns the whole pipeline, and fails unless the two Verilog files it produces are
byte-for-byte identical to the tracked ones. A hand edit to the generated Verilog fails the
build. And the CPU printed inside the system must compile byte-for-byte to the CPU printed
alone, else the script exits; that's how I know the system wrapper didn't touch the CPU. Be
clear about what this gate protects: that the tracked Verilog is exactly what the extractor
prints from the current sources. It doesn't say those sources are the ones the proofs were
checked against; that's the job of the proof build on the same commit.

\emph{Simulation: tested.} The suite is seventeen programs: nine directed cases (the two
short serial tests, arithmetic-then-halt and a jump loop, are two of them) and eight
generated from a fixed random seed. The directed cases include memory reads and writes on
both sides of the sixty-four-word bank boundary, allocation past the memory limit,
overlapping partitions, splitting and merging, composition, and allocation-table exhaustion.
Each program goes in as serial frames on the board's one input pin, and the fifteen-byte
report comes back on its output pin. Three things run it. One is the netlist yosys mapped
for the chip, written back out as Verilog and simulated with yosys's models of the chip's
cells. One is the extracted Verilog of the same board top. One is the OCaml runner
extracted from the Coq step. The netlist and the Verilog must agree exactly on the report
bytes, the LEDs and every probed state field. The Verilog and the runner must agree on the
program counter, the counter, the error flag, the sixteen registers, the 128 data words,
the certified flag, the module and arrow tables and the witness counters. And each report
must match the state it reports. Every program also runs without pressing the reset
button, the netlist from its initial values and the Verilog from all zeros, so the board
wrapper's power-on reset has to do the job alone. The formal property lines ride along in
the Verilog run as checks, any failed check fails the run, and fifteen named triggers from
them must each be hit by some program. All seventeen programs and all fifteen triggers
passed in the recorded run.\footnote{Board simulation record: CI Full run 37188435151,
source revision \code{710fdaf912b0e3df1107f6a5376df0b05adb9b1c}, 4 October 2026, in which
every job passed, including the solver and netlist jobs described below. These identify the
supporting record; the comparison and its limits are stated here.}
These are finite tests on zero-delay models. The netlist they simulate is the one before
place and route; the placed and routed design itself is not simulated. Three of the chip's
cells (the input buffer, the clock synthesiser and the clock gate) are behavioural
stand-ins, and the block RAM is a functional model. So the simulations say nothing about
every program, about the analog behaviour of the clock, about physical timing, or about a
powered board. And since the runner is the reference, they are only as good as the runner.

Seventeen programs sounds like a lot until you ask how many there could be. A program here is
up to a hundred and twenty-eight instructions of a hundred and twenty-eight bits each, so the
longest ones alone come in two to the power 16,384 different bit patterns, a number about 4,900
digits long, and seventeen of them ran. Edsger Dijkstra had a sentence for this, and the
version in his 1976 book starts by admitting he'd already said it many times and written it in
many places: program testing ``can be quite effective for showing the presence of bugs, but is
hopelessly inadequate for showing their absence.'' (I'm quoting it as John Harrison quotes it,
from that book.) That's why this paragraph says \emph{tested} and not \emph{proved}, and why the
solver checks below get paragraphs of their own: they're the part that doesn't count programs
one at a time.

\emph{Safety in the extracted circuit: proved by a separate solver.} This is a different
tool pointed at the same Verilog, and it gets its own paragraph because it is the one place
where a proof reaches the circuit without going through Kami's semantics. Yosys reads the
extracted files with extra property lines added to a copy (the tracked files aren't
touched, and the added lines only watch registers, they never drive anything), and
a driver called SymbiYosys hands the questions to a solver. Each proof is an induction over every state
reachable from reset, with no bound on how long the run is. There are three.

\emph{The partition table.} The table never holds more than sixty-four slots, and the
allocation counter stays between one and sixty-four. Every slot at or above the counter is
empty. Every nonempty slot lies inside the 128-word memory, and nonempty slots never
overlap. A partition instruction that faults sends the program counter to the trap vector
and leaves the table as it was. And only PNEW, PSPLIT and PMERGE ever write the table. The
solver gets this as 321 separate obligations (a reset base, a frame step saying nothing
else touches the table, one step for each partition instruction, and the pairwise cases for
overlap), and a missing, failed or timed-out one fails the job. The memory's read signals
are left arbitrary, so the result holds for whatever the memory could return.

\emph{Control.} The error flag never clears except by reset, and nothing executes while it
is set. The arrow-table counter stays between one and sixteen, and every valid arrow slot
sits below it. The counter register changes only when the main step rule or the checking
step's scan rule fires. The halted flag clears only through \code{start}. This one runs
unbounded model checking (an engine called PDR, short for property-directed reachability) over the whole state space, so the
multi-cycle machines are inside it at every phase and every interleaving. What the list
doesn't say is that the counter never goes down. It is a thirty-two-bit register and a big
enough charge wraps it, which is exactly why the Coq theorems carry overflow premises.

\emph{The loader.} Five properties after reset: start is called only while halted;
instruction memory is never written after start; start occurs at most once; the report
begins only after start and after halt or error; and no second report begins after the
first has been sent. Six auxiliary invariants are proved with them. The induction depth of
four bounds the solver's search, not the length of the run covered, and both the reset base
and the inductive step have to pass. The check keeps the complete extracted CPU in the
system.

The two CPU proofs assume that \code{start} is called only while the CPU is halted. The
loader proof is the one that establishes that for the loader, and the loader is the only
caller, so the three fit. But they are three separate runs, and that they fit is my
reading of them, not a mechanical composition. Beside each proof sits a cover task: every
property has a named trigger event, and the task shows that a real transition of the
circuit reaches it within sixteen cycles from a state satisfying all the properties (the
CPU is not reset in those tasks). That keeps a property from being true only because its
trigger never happens. It says nothing about properties I never wrote.

What these are, and aren't. They are statements about the extracted Verilog as Yosys reads
it, checked by Yosys and its solvers, not Coq proofs of the translators. They are not the
Coq theorems either: the partition-table list says the same kind of thing as the
well-formedness premises of the refinement theorems, but nothing links the two statements
formally. They don't replace the premises of the Coq report theorem, and they don't prove
the serial input was the program the user meant. And what they read is the extracted
Verilog, not the mapped netlist that becomes the bitstream. The next check reaches part of
that gap.

\emph{The board and loader against the mapped netlist: proved, conditional on the CPU.} A
second solver check takes the netlist yosys mapped for the chip, the very file nextpnr is
handed (a digest check ties the jobs to it), and the extracted RTL of the same board top.
It proves by induction, a reset base and one arbitrary step, that the loader, the reporter
and the board wrapper's reset logic behave the same on both sides: the same serial
transmit pin, the same four LEDs, the same \code{start} and load enables, the same
connected bits of the instruction and address bus. The CPU and its memories are cut out of
the comparison. Seven signals come back from the CPU (program counter, counter, error
flag, halted flag, certified flag, error code, and whether it can take an instruction),
both sides get the same values, and the values are otherwise arbitrary. So the result
reads: if the two CPUs answer alike, the two loaders act alike. It is not a proof that the
chip's CPU matches the Verilog's. The report is stamped as component equivalence and not
