whole-chip equivalence, and the CPU and memories in the netlist are checked only by the
simulations above. The clock primitives are checked for their types and divider ratio, and
the model is synchronous and functional: no analog clock, no delays.

\emph{Synthesis, place and route, bitstream: trusted, tested.} yosys maps the Verilog to the
chip's lookup tables and flip-flops; nextpnr-xilinx places and routes it; and Project X-Ray's
tools turn the result into a bitstream, the file that fills a programmable chip's
configuration memory and makes the blank grid into this circuit. None of those three carries
a proof; yosys (2013) is a free synthesis suite covering most of Verilog, nextpnr
followed, and X-Ray documented the chip's bitstream format by building many designs with the
vendor's tool and cross-correlating the bits. Two tests sit on this link. A timing gate reads
the clock-synthesiser settings out of the board wrapper, computes the clock it produces
(twenty megahertz), and fails if nextpnr's achieved frequency is lower; the recorded run
achieved 27.22 megahertz against the 20 required. And a round trip decodes the bitstream two ways: the raw
bits must equal the frames that were encoded, and the bits decoded back to named features and
re-encoded must match too, so a bit the database can't name shows up as a mismatch.

\emph{The board wrapper: the one hand-written logic file.} It takes the
board's two-hundred-megahertz clock, which arrives as a pair of wires with opposite voltages,
and turns it into one signal; feeds that to the chip's clock synthesiser, which multiplies by
five and divides by fifty to get twenty megahertz and raises a LOCKED flag when it's
stable; drives the clock onto the chip's clock network only while locked, so the CPU never
sees a half-formed clock; and then instantiates the extracted system, ties three enables
high, and wires four LEDs. It also supplies power-on reset: a five-bit counter starts at
zero after configuration and counts the first sixteen CPU clock edges; a registered reset
keeps the system in reset until that count has completed and the reset button is released.
This matters because all-zero configuration state is not the machine's reset state.
A pin file maps the clock pair, the reset button, the LEDs, and
the two serial pins to the connector names of a specific board, a Digilent Genesys 2 (its
chip is the Kintex-7 xc7k325tffg900-2, the part the synthesis script targets), per
the file's note. The pin names match Digilent's published master constraints file for that
board.

\subsection{Why generated, and why it's the stronger artifact}

Someone will say ``it's just generated code.'' Here's why that's backwards. The generated
Verilog is the artifact the proofs are \emph{about}, one translation removed; a hand-written CPU
would carry no proof at all. The CI gate makes any hand edit fail. So generated code is the
stronger artifact, with its translators named as trusted, which is a better position than
hand-written code whose translator is a person. And ``it synthesized, so it's correct'' is
the wrong turn in the other direction: synthesis checks that the text describes \emph{some}
circuit; a wrong circuit synthesises as happily as a right one. The evidence of function is
the co-simulation, the board simulations and the solver checks, not that yosys finished.

\subsection{Thompson's knife, again}

Every link marked ``trusted'' is a place where Ken Thompson's compiler from Section~\ref{sec:diagonal} could sit
unseen: a translator that plants something and re-plants it when it translates itself.
Extraction, the printer, bsc, yosys, nextpnr, the X-Ray database. I don't believe any of them
does. I can't prove it, and the discipline of this section is to say so rather than to let
``formally verified'' cover a chain whose bottom half is trust and tests.

And a planted knife isn't the only way a trusted link goes wrong. Sometimes nobody plants
anything and the bottom row of the table, the chip itself, is just wrong. In 1994 Thomas
Nicely, a mathematics professor at Lynchburg College who was computing with twin primes and
their reciprocals, found that his new Intel Pentium got some divisions wrong. The example
everybody passes around is 4,195,835 divided by 3,145,727, which the bad chips got wrong in the
fourth decimal place. Intel's explanation was missing entries in a table inside the divider:
five of them, it said, dropped by a script. Intel set aside about \$475 million to cover it.

Push on the five, because that's the part that got retold. In 2024 Ken Shirriff went to die
photographs of an affected chip, read the table's layout off the silicon, and counted sixteen
missing entries, left out by a mistake in the table's mathematical definition, of which only
five ever mattered. So the story that got repeated for thirty years had the effect right and
the cause off, and it took somebody reading the actual silicon to say so. Floating-point
arithmetic went on to become one of the places where formal verification earned its keep in
industry; John Harrison, who did that work at Intel, brings up this very bug in a 2007 survey
of it. Does any of that touch this book's chain? The chip here was never switched on, so no.
But it's why the last row of the table says \emph{trusted, unchecked} and not something kinder.
This design runs on a chip made of lookup tables, a few hundred thousand of them, and nobody
here has read them off the silicon either.

\subsection{The numbers, true of one recorded run}

Sixteen registers of thirty-two bits; a hundred and twenty-eight words of data and of
instructions; instructions a hundred and twenty-eight bits wide; sixty-four partition
slots, the same sixty-four module numbers the kernel hands out per run (Section~\ref{sec:state}), each module
in its own slot; forty-seven of fifty-one opcodes encoded (Section~\ref{sec:isa}); fifty-five retirement cases. From the
full run 37188435151 at source revision \code{710fdaf9}, 4 October 2026: 53,117 of 407,600
lookup-table sites (thirteen percent; nextpnr counts each half of a six-input lookup table
as a site, and the datasheet lists 203,800 six-input tables), 10,390 flip-flop sites, no DSP
slices, two block RAMs, a bitstream of 11.4 megabytes whose round trip matched 2,887,071
bits by encoding and 2,887,590 by meaning, a placed and routed clock of 27.22 megahertz
against the 20 required, and every simulation and solver job in that run passing. Those
numbers belong to one run, and the gate above is what ties
any run's numbers to the sources it was built from; when the sources change, the numbers
do, and the gate says so.

\subsection{What the chip is, and isn't}

The chip is the third material. The proofs reach from the kernel's step relation to the
firing of Kami rules. Everything below that is translated by tools I trust and checked by
tests I've described in numbers. The bitstream is a wiring list, not evidence that the wiring
computes anything; the evidence is the simulations and the solver checks. And no board was ever powered on: I
don't own one, the repository records no run on one, and I'd rather end this section on that
sentence than on a flourish. What I can say is this. Any claim of the form ``the proof says
the chip does X'' has to pass through this table, and the table says exactly where the proof
stops.


\part{Checking it, and its edge}

%===========================================================================
\section{What Coq is, and why}
\label{sec:coq}
%===========================================================================

Coq is a proof assistant, which is a phrase I had to go and look up. Underneath the phrase
it's a programming language, but one whose type system is strict enough to do a thing
ordinary languages can't: you write a proof down as a program, and the compiler refuses it
unless the program genuinely matches the statement you claimed. You can't talk it into a
maybe.

The name is a joke three ways at once, and it's worth knowing before you say it out loud in
English. \emph{Coq} is French for rooster. It's also a nod to Thierry Coquand, who worked out the
logic it started from with Gérard Huet, and to that logic's initials, CoC, for the Calculus of
Constructions; and there's a French habit of naming research tools after animals. The English
slang reading did what you'd guess. By the development team's own account, some people, women
students especially, ended up never learning the tool because of its name. So in March 2025 it
got a new one, the Rocq Prover, after Rocquencourt, the Inria site where it was first built,
and after the Roc, the giant bird of legend, so the bird stayed. Everything in this book was
checked with Coq 8.18, from before the rename, so that's the name I use. The rooster changes
nothing about what got checked.

\subsection{Types as claims}

Here's the idea, and it's one idea. In a normal language a type says what kind of value a
variable holds: in Python, ``x is an int'' means x is a whole number. In Coq, types are
\emph{claims}. The type ``n is greater than zero'' is the type of \emph{proofs} that n is positive. A
function from ``n is greater than zero'' to ``n plus one is greater than zero'' is a proof that
if n is positive, n plus one is too, and the compiler checks that the function really has
that type, the way it would check that a function from integers to strings really returns
strings. This correspondence between proofs and programs has a name, Curry-Howard, after
two people who noticed it separately decades apart, and Coq's foundation, the Calculus of
Inductive Constructions, from Coquand, Huet and Paulin-Mohring in the late 1980s, is a type system built to
exploit it. The ``inductive'' part means you define your own recursive types (numbers, lists,
trees, machine states) inside the system instead of having them handed down as primitives,
so the foundation is explicit; nothing is smuggled.

``Decades apart'' undersells it, and the gap is worth a side trip. Haskell Curry noticed in 1934
that the type of a function from $A$ to $B$ reads like the claim ``$A$ implies $B$,'' and that
the types his functions could have lined up with the claims you can prove; he and Robert Feys
pushed it further in 1958. William Howard wrote the sharper version in 1969, and then it went
around as a photocopied manuscript until 1980, when it was finally printed in a collection of
essays for Curry. So the idea under the tool this book is checked with spent its first eleven
years as a stack of photocopies. Is that the bottom? No. Reading a proof of ``if $A$ then $B$''
as a method that turns any proof of $A$ into a proof of $B$ is older still: the intuitionists
had it in the 1920s and 1930s, Brouwer, Heyting and Kolmogorov, which is why people also call
it the BHK interpretation. Where it really starts I can't tell you. It changes nothing in what
the checker checks. It changes how I'd tell the story: nobody sat down one day and invented
``proofs are programs.'' It kept getting noticed, by people coming from different directions,
until somebody wrote it down plainly.

The compiler checks whether the types line up. If your proof has a hole and you write ``trust
me,'' it rejects you. But here's the part people skip, and it's the part that matters: the
compiler checks that the proof matches the \emph{statement}. It does not check that the statement
says what you \emph{meant}. Hand it a statement that means nothing and it'll prove it for you,
three characters, no complaint. So a proof being accepted is not the same as the thing being
true. It means this proof matches this statement, and whether that's the right statement is
on me, not the machine. Section~\ref{sec:toll} said a short version of this and I'm saying it again because every section
since has leaned on it: the checked names in this book are a promise that the \emph{proof} is
there, and the sentences around them are my claim about what the statement \emph{says}, and the
second can be wrong while the first is fine, which is why so many sections of this book
stop to say exactly what a statement's hypotheses are.

\subsection{Why I used it}

Not to make anything true. I used it because I don't trust my own eye to catch a gap in an
argument I want to believe. I spent months convinced by my own reasoning, pushed the proof
through, and watched a key step come apart in my hands. The machine caught where I'd fooled
myself. That's what it's for. And it's the same source the running machine and the chip are
extracted from (Section~\ref{sec:chip}), so the thing that checks the argument is the thing that becomes the
artifact. Gap-catcher and extractor. Not the proof. The proof is the argument, and an
argument has to close in a way a person can follow, or it hasn't closed at all, which is
why this book exists in prose and not as a list of theorem names.

Two precedents show that a proof assistant is a serious tool and not a
toy. CompCert, Xavier Leroy's C compiler, written and proved correct in Coq: the assembly it
emits behaves as the source does, for programs with defined behaviour. And Georges
Gonthier's 2005 proof of the four-colour theorem, a century-old problem whose first
proof (in 1976) needed a computer to check thousands of cases and was distrusted for exactly
that reason, redone in Coq so that the \emph{checker} was the small, auditable thing and the cases
were the program. That's de Bruijn's criterion from Section~\ref{sec:claims} applied to mathematics itself: the
thing you have to trust is the small kernel, not the big proof.

The 1976 proof deserves its own side trip. Kenneth Appel and Wolfgang Haken did it at the
University of Illinois, and the mathematics department changed the slogan on its postage meter
to ``Four colors suffice.'' The slogan it replaced had been on the department's mail since the
middle 1960s, and it said that $2^{11213} - 1$ is prime, a prime Don Gillies, in the same
university's computer science department, had found. Think about that for a second. For years
on end a mathematics department stamped its mail with results nobody could have checked by
hand, first one and then the other, and both were right. So was the distrust of the 1976 proof
wrong? I don't think so. The worry was never that the computer lied. It was that nobody could
read what had been checked, and a check you can't look at is hard to lean on. Gonthier's answer
was de Bruijn's: make the part you have to read small enough to read.

\subsection{What ``zero Admitted'' means}

``Zero Admitted'' is literal. Nowhere in the proof tree did I write ``trust me'' and walk on.
Every step the checker could see, it saw, end to end, with no ``and the rest is obvious.'' A
hygiene fact about the gap-catcher, not a verdict on the argument: it says I didn't let
myself skip a step where the machine was watching. It does not say the statements are the
right statements.

What it doesn't mean, listed. It doesn't mean the theorems prove physical reality; they
prove things about the machine as formalised, and whether that describes the world is
answered by experiments (Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}, Section~\ref{sec:landauer}). It doesn't mean Coq's own foundation is proved
consistent; it's believed consistent, and that can't be proved from inside, by Gödel (Section~\ref{sec:diagonal}),
so the foundation is trusted, and ``trusted'' has substance: it's the same kernel CompCert and
the four-colour proof stand on, and a bug in it would take all of them down together, which
is a kind of safety in numbers. It doesn't mean the hardware correspondence is
unconditional; Section~\ref{sec:chip}'s table says where the proof stops. And it doesn't mean no axioms: the
proofs use five standard-library assumptions, and the assumption audit names them:
functional extensionality on dependent functions (two functions that agree everywhere are
equal); uniqueness of equality proofs, in the form the standard library calls \code{eq\_rect\_eq}
(only in the hardware proofs, through the Kami library); two decidability principles that
come with the standard library's real numbers; and, in a little over a hundred theorems, the
law of excluded middle (every proposition is true or false). The count, from the full audit:
the full-corpus probe covers 14,574 named theorems across 510 files: 6,994 close under the global Coq context outright, and 7,580 use only Coq standard-library assumptions.
Zero project-local axioms appear in any of the 14,574 dependency trees.
In plain words: about fourteen thousand theorems, a little under half of them needing nothing
at all, and the rest leaning only on those standard-library assumptions, none of mine. Those
numbers belong to the audit run that produced them; the shape doesn't move between runs, the
counts do.

\subsection{What you're trusting, in one place}

If you accept every checked theorem in this book, here is what you're still taking on trust,
all of it, so you don't have to collect it from five chapters.

\begin{enumerate}
\item The statements. The checker confirms a proof proves its statement. It doesn't confirm the
statement says what my sentence about it says. That's why the book prints the important
ones in full, premises and all. A machine check supplements that reading.
\item Coq's kernel and its foundation, and the five standard assumptions above.
\item The path out of Coq. Programs pulled out of Coq as runnable code by its extraction
mechanism, and the circuit description handed to the Bluespec compiler, are trusted from
that point on. The synthesis and layout tools, the chip, and the board are trusted too, and
Section~\ref{sec:chip} lays the chain out link by link. This is the list Ken Thompson's lecture from Section~\ref{sec:diagonal} was
about. I didn't write Coq, or OCaml, or the Bluespec compiler, or yosys, so by his moral
I can't fully trust any of them, and neither can you. What I can do is keep the list
short and print it, so you know exactly which tools you're being asked to believe have no
spare key cut into them.
\item The tested parts. The Python demonstrations and the test suite are evidence that the code
does what's claimed on the runs tried, not proof that it always does.
\item The physics. Anywhere a theorem has Landauer's principle or a calorimeter in it, the
physical premise is named and assumed (Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}, Section~\ref{sec:landauer}), never derived.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{The auditor on top}

Beyond the type checker, the project has a custom proof auditor I called the Inquisitor,
because a thing that reads every proof looking for ways you've cheated deserves a name you
won't forget. It runs on every commit, and its source names about a hundred distinct rules. The main
families: no holes (no Admitted, no admit, no give-up, no unproved axiom or parameter in
project code); vacuity heuristics (no theorem whose conclusion is literally True or a
tautology; no theorem of the shape ``P implies P''; existence claims backed by a constant
witness get flagged, and a flag is a reason to look, not a verdict, since some constructions
like a fixed interpreter program are \emph{supposed} to be fixed and get judged on what they
compute); physics-definition heuristics (no physical quantity defined as a placeholder
constant, no physics claim without an invariance condition); scope enforcement (the proof
tree is split into tiers, the kernel tier may not import from research-side files, and every
active file must reach the cost or semantics foundation through its imports, or it doesn't
get to claim the kernel's pedigree); and comment hygiene (no unfinished or historical
markers in maintained source). Its rules are heuristics. They point at places to look. They don't prove
a theorem means what it should, and they can't promise every empty premise got caught.

\subsection{Checking the companion formalization}

The mathematical claims are the statements printed in this book, with their stated
hypotheses and the arguments given here. Running software is an additional way to check
their formal counterparts. It isn't a prerequisite for reading the argument.

A reproducible check needs a fixed copy of the proof sources, dependencies and probes.
Changing that copy changes the object being checked; a later software result cannot
silently revise a theorem in this edition. The procedure below describes the companion
proof build. With Python 3, GNU make, Coq 8.18 and its standard library, OCaml,
\code{ocamlfind} and CSDP installed, run this from the source snapshot's root:

\begin{verbatim}
python3 scripts/reproduce_coq.py
\end{verbatim}

That copies the sources into a fresh directory and works only from the copy: it builds the
two vendored libraries the hardware proofs use (bbv and Kami), regenerates the build file, rebuilds every proof from
source, runs the contract probes that re-check the named theorems and their assumptions, and
runs Coq's independent checker over the result. It reuses no compiled proof from the
checkout, and it writes its pass file only after every stage passes. A failed run resumes
from the snapshot it captured, and a change to the sources needs a fresh run:

\begin{verbatim}
python3 scripts/reproduce_coq.py --resume \
  --output artifacts/reproduction/RUN_DIRECTORY
\end{verbatim}

The run has to pass. Don't stop at the pass: read the theorem
types and their global dependencies, because a closed report doesn't make a theorem's own
premises go away. The hardware generation is a separate command needing the Bluespec
compiler (Section~\ref{sec:chip}), and its outputs have to name the source they were built from; a passing
proof build doesn't give you a fresh synthesis.

That's the checker. What's left is to tell you how to break what it checked.

%===========================================================================
\section{How to break this}
\label{sec:falsification}
%===========================================================================

Every main claim in this book comes with the exact shape of the thing that would kill it. I
went to the trouble on purpose. A claim you can't break is a claim that wasn't saying
anything, and I'd rather hand you a loaded gun pointed at my own work than a sentence too
vague to aim at. So these are written as instructions: here is the trace to find, the
object to build, the theorem to exhibit. Build one and the proof tree falls, and I mean that
as an invitation.

The invitation is an old one, and people have put prices on it. Donald Knuth gives the first
person to find each error in his books one hexadecimal dollar, 0x\$1.00, which is \$2.56,
deposited these days at the Bank of San Serriffe, a bank that doesn't exist, since real
checks turned out to be an open door for fraud. Why pay strangers to find your mistakes? His
own page says it plainly enough: a careful reader makes the book better for everyone who reads
it next. This chapter doesn't come with a bank, real or made up. What it comes with is, for
every claim, a description of the exact object that would make it fall, so you know before you
start what counts as winning.

\subsection{The abstract claims (Parts II and III)}

\emph{The universal floor (Section~\ref{sec:toll}).} Build a certification system that satisfies the one-step toll
and give a run from uncertified to certified with total cost zero. \code{universal\_nfi\_any\_substrate}
falls. If you instead drop the toll, you've built a free-certification system, not a
counterexample.

\emph{The toll from premises (Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}).} Exhibit a finite, duplicate-free list of every state, a
certificate no step revokes, and an \emph{injective} step that switches it on.
\code{permanent\_flip\_is\_not\_injective} falls, and the derivation of the toll with it. An infinite
state space, a revocable certificate, or an unpriced merge is not a counterexample; the file
already builds one of each. For the squeeze bound, a finite permanent machine with a cost
meeting the halving premise where one step switches k states on beside m certified ones and
two to the cost times m is less than m plus k; \code{permanent\_flips\_compression\_bound} falls.
For merge-or-revoke, a finite machine and an injective instruction that switches a reading on
without switching it off anywhere; \code{flip\_merges\_or\_revokes} falls. A move that merges and
also revokes isn't a counterexample to anything; it's the three cards.

\emph{The bill in bits (Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}).} Exhibit a finite machine with a permanent certificate, a move that
switches k states on beside m certified ones (k at least one), and a spread of probability
over those m plus k states whose image under the move has entropy above log base two of m.
\code{permanent\_step\_entropy\_ceiling} falls. For the general form, a step and a spread under which
two different states, each with some probability, land on the same state while the entropy
doesn't drop; \code{entropy\_drop\_pos\_of\_support\_merge} falls. A heat measurement on a real device
below what the bound asks doesn't touch either theorem. It refutes the premise
\code{landauer\_heat} for that device, which is Landauer's principle, and that's a fight with
physics, not with the counting. And a certifying step from a state already known that gives
off no heat isn't a counterexample: \code{known\_state\_flip\_forces\_no\_heat} says that case owes
nothing.

\emph{Learning is free (Section~\ref{sec:narrowing}).} Show that the four-state demon's measure step merges two states,
or that its observer's candidate list doesn't shrink. \code{observer\_narrowing\_can\_be\_free}
falls. A different price schedule that charges the measure step is allowed and isn't a
counterexample; the claim is ``not forced,'' not ``always free.''

\emph{The counter (Section~\ref{sec:counter}; on this machine, Section~\ref{sec:state} and Section~\ref{sec:witness}).} Find a state and an instruction such that the counter after is anything
other than the counter before plus that instruction's cost; the loud version is a counter
that goes down. \code{vm\_apply\_mu} falls. Or find two bookkeepings that both start at
zero, both follow the schedule step by step, and disagree on a reachable state;
\code{mu\_is\_initial\_monotone} falls.

\emph{Windows (Section~\ref{sec:windows}).} Exhibit a window and a price computed from the observed before and after
that meets the floor and never overcharges, on a machine where two steps share their before
and after pictures and only one certifies. \code{shadow\_cannot\_price\_exactly} falls. A window that
shows certification is not a counterexample; the theorem says exactly that such a window
prices exactly.

\emph{Entitlement (Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}; on this machine, Section~\ref{sec:machine-claims}).} Produce a strict narrowing of a candidate list, with a distinguishing
observation, that does not yield a strictly stronger membership predicate;
\code{feasible\_strict\_subset\_implies\_strict\_predicates} falls. Or exhibit a run meeting every
hypothesis of the representation theorem whose counter rose by less than the index bits
lost; \code{structural\_entitlement\_representation} falls.

\emph{The latch (Section~\ref{sec:latch}).} Exhibit an extension of a base whose record is driven by the computation
and never switches off, and which is not a latch on any event. \code{record\_axis\_is\_latch\_holds}
falls. A record that switches off, or one driven by a hidden clock, is the file's own pair of
counterexamples, not yours.

\emph{The diagonal (Section~\ref{sec:diagonal}, Section~\ref{sec:interpreters}).} Two routes. A decider for some substrate
with a shortcut predicate whose flip the substrate can represent and which answers
correctly on every program; the generic proof fails at a named step. For the nat family, a d
that correctly decides the predicate of the substrate built from d. (The concrete machine's
version offers no third route: its recursion premise is false for the class of all maps, and
given a decider correct on every program, its flip has no fixed point with equal
thousand-step runs from every state; Section~\ref{sec:interpreters} proves both, as
\code{vm\_full\_recursion\_premise\_refuted} and \code{vm\_correct\_flip\_has\_no\_fixed\_point}.) The
guest has no premise to supply, so it gets two targets of its own: a map on well-formed guest
programs that some guest program represents, with no well-formed program equivalent to its
own image, and \code{vm\_guest\_recursion\_theorem\_closed} falls; or a decider for a property of
guest programs that respects equivalence, holds of some well-formed program and fails for
JUMP 0, and \code{vm\_guest\_rice\_holds} falls.

\emph{The pointer conjecture (Section~\ref{sec:pointer}).} It's a conjecture, so the three routes are its own: a
deployed discipline pricing a non-proliferating event; a rival event proliferating as well
as certification in a real ecosystem; an honest formalisation with independence defined
where certification fails the test.

One concession goes with it, and I make it in full. The window results, the separation of
the two witness states, and the counter's uniqueness don't single out certification. Their
proofs use only that the step carries something the classical picture doesn't determine, so
the same shape of result holds for any such field. Nothing in Parts II to V proves that
certification is the one event a model is \emph{forced} to price; Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} forces a price on every
merge, certifying or not. That's the conjecture, and Section~\ref{sec:pointer} is the case I make for it.

\subsection{The machine claims (Parts IV and V)}

\emph{The small machine (Section~\ref{sec:smallest}).} Four targets. From a clean start, a
run that raises the flag without an earlier passing CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY of the same
claim, with the counter's version unchanged between the CHECK and the COMMIT;
\code{earned\_certification\_provenance} falls, and \code{earned\_commitment\_provenance} for
a COMMIT alone. From a clean start, a trace that leaves a fact in the table nobody checked;
\code{no\_forging} falls. From a clean start, a run that ends certified for a total charge
under three; \code{certified\_run\_min\_cost} falls, and a run at exactly three is not a
counterexample, it is the witness of \code{min\_cost\_tight}. A two-counter machine and a
program whose run on the small machine disagrees with it step for step, or halts when it
doesn't; \code{simulation\_step} or \code{halting\_correspondence} falls.

\emph{The partition (Section~\ref{sec:state}).} From the initial state, run any program and land on a state where two
modules share a cell, a module owns a cell numbered 128 or more, the module counter is past
sixty-four, or two modules carry one number. \code{vm\_reachable\_partition\_in\_bounds} falls (and with
the first, \code{vm\_reachable\_regions\_disjoint}). A PNEW past memory or on a spent budget that traps
isn't a counterexample; trapping is the rule doing its job.

\emph{The arrows (Section~\ref{sec:category}).} Three stored arrows with matching ends in a well-formed graph whose two
bracketings, built by COMPOSE, differ in source, target, flag, or (flag off) a pair;
\code{graph\_compose\_assoc\_stored} falls. An identity arrow from an object to itself and an arrow out
of that object whose composite isn't the same arrow, in that sense; \code{graph\_compose\_left\_identity\_stored}
falls, and the mirror for \code{graph\_compose\_right\_identity\_stored}. Or a run from the initial state
that stores a flagged arrow between two different modules, or one with pairs;
\code{vm\_reachable\_identity\_arrows\_canonical} falls. Two composites with different labels, or
different identifiers, aren't counterexamples; the sameness ignores both on purpose, and Section~\ref{sec:category}
says why.

\emph{Separation (Section~\ref{sec:separation}).} Show that the two witness states differ in one of the six shadow fields,
or that their arrow lists are the same. \code{categorical\_separation} falls. Error behaviour is
not the target; the arrow list is.

\emph{Strictness (Section~\ref{sec:separation}, Section~\ref{sec:witness}).} Exhibit a classical program (any list of the twenty-nine
classical opcodes, run as a list or by program counter with its jumps, for any fuel) whose
execution changes anything in the graph (the fresh-module counter, the arrow list, any of
it), the assertion channel or the certified flag. Or find a state some classical run reaches
from the initial state where PNEW on cell zero traps or leaves the fresh-module counter
fixed, or where the graph it produces is one a classical run from the initial state also
produces. \code{thiele\_strictly\_extends\_classical} falls, and with it
\code{pnew\_step\_separates\_thiele\_from\_classical\_reachable}. Both start from the initial state, so
there's no hand-built base to argue with.

\emph{The floor on fifty-one (Section~\ref{sec:witness}).} Find a run starting with the flag down and the counter at
zero, ending with the flag up and the counter at zero. \code{certification\_requires\_positive\_mu}
breaks at the step that prices the flip. Add the counterexample as a theorem and the build
refuses to compile on top of it.

\emph{The finite fragment (Section~\ref{sec:witness}).} Exhibit a state and one of CERTIFY at zero, JUMP at two,
CHECKPOINT at zero whose result, read as program counter modulo four and the flag, differs
from the finite machine's step, or whose counter rise differs from one, two, zero.
\code{vm\_runs\_finite\_machine} or \code{vm\_pays\_finite\_price} falls. A program using JUMP at cost zero
is outside the fragment; the full machine leaves that merge free on purpose.

\emph{The classical CHSH bound (Section~\ref{sec:chsh}).} Exhibit four fixed bits and a tally consistent with that
one plan, every pair sampled, scoring above two. \code{chsh\_violation\_rules\_out\_locally\_factorizable\_coupling}
falls, and so does known mathematics. A randomised plan landing past two by luck doesn't
count; the theorem is about one fixed plan, and Section~\ref{sec:chsh}'s coin-flip example shows the luck.

\emph{The integer gate (Section~\ref{sec:chsh}).} The game check has two walls, and here's how to knock each one
over. A correlator that passes the three contraction inequalities whose
five-by-five is not PSD (forward), or a PSD five-by-five of that shape whose correlators
aren't contractive (reverse); \code{npa\_psd\_iff\_column\_contractive} falls. A correlator whose
pinned five-by-five is PSD (contractive, by the equivalence) with S squared above eight;
\code{npa\_psd\_implies\_tsirelson\_bound} falls. The PR box and the classical mixture (1, 0, 1, 0) are
\emph{not} counterexamples to any of these. Both fail contraction by plain arithmetic (the table
in Appendix~\ref{sub:chsh-five}), which is what the theorems need them to do, not what would
break them.

\emph{The four 1+AB instructions (Section~\ref{sec:chsh}).} Four bigger checks, four targets, one per instruction.
Each of the four instructions that checks the
nine-by-nine matrix has its own theorem: from a state with no error, if the instruction
advances the program counter by one and leaves the error flag alone, the nine-by-nine matrix
at the state's correlators and the instruction's moments (all zero for the plain one; for
the other three, the free ones read from the supplied counts and the rest zero) is positive
semidefinite. Exhibit such a
run where the matrix isn't, and the matching theorem falls:
\code{chsh\_lassert\_1ab\_no\_trap\_implies\_npa\_psd\_q1ab},
\code{chsh\_lassert\_1ab\_g5\_no\_trap\_implies\_npa\_psd\_q1ab},
\code{chsh\_lassert\_1ab\_g345\_no\_trap\_implies\_npa\_psd\_q1ab}, or
\code{chsh\_lassert\_1ab\_g12345\_no\_trap\_implies\_npa\_psd\_q1ab}. A trap on a point inside the set isn't
a counterexample. The checks are sound, not complete, and the full one traps wherever its
matrix is semidefinite without being definite, because each of its tests is strict
(Appendix~\ref{sub:chsh-q1ab}).

\emph{The elliptope completion (Section~\ref{sec:chsh}).} This one's a shape, not an instruction, so you're trying
to push a point in or out of it. Three targets, one per theorem, plus the decider beside it. Signs $a_0, a_1, b_0, b_1$,
each squaring to one, and a vector on which the completed matrix of that plan goes negative;
\code{deterministic\_strategy\_elliptope} falls. A correlator with some positive semidefinite
completion and S squared above eight; \code{elliptope\_tsirelson} falls, and with it the claim that
one completion can't stretch both Cauchy-Schwarz budgets at once. Real numbers x and y that
make the PR box's completed matrix positive semidefinite; \code{pr\_box\_not\_elliptope} falls. And
for the decider that sits beside it: inputs on which it says yes while the correlators have
no PSD completion at all (S squared above eight is one way to show that);
\code{elliptope\_check\_full\_sound} falls. The all-ones plan and (1, 0, 1, 0) aren't counterexamples here either, from the other side: the
completion admits them (\code{turing\_point\_elliptope} for the second), which is what the theorems
require.

\emph{The hardware (Section~\ref{sec:chip}).} A counterexample to the whole-machine refinement (\code{driven\_step\_wf})
has to satisfy its precondition and break its stated equality. A co-simulation mismatch on a valid input
challenges the \emph{tested} transfer for that revision; then pull it apart link by link
(encoding, observation timing, extraction, printing, bsc, the harness). An input outside the
theorem's domain, or a toolchain mismatch, doesn't refute the conditional theorem. It
refutes a trusted link, which is worse for me and more useful for you. The solver checks
have a target of their own: a run from reset on the extracted circuit that breaks a
partition-table, control or loader property, which the property-carrying simulation prints
as a failed assertion and the solver would hand back as a counterexample. For the netlist
comparison, an input stream on which the loader's outputs differ in the two models while
the CPU responses agree.

\emph{The five models (Section~\ref{sec:models}; the wrappers stated on this machine, Section~\ref{sec:witness}).} Each fragment has a theorem with a named falsifier: a finality fork
with nobody slashable; a gas schedule meeting floor and no-overcharge whose charging
predicate differs from the commit predicate on some step; a sound and complete attestation
verifier that reads only the bare transcript, or a function of the quote that recovers the
unmeasured runtime flag; one of the RFC's own example proofs that the transcribed inclusion
check rejects, or an input with leaf index equal to tree size that it accepts; a program the
bounds checker accepts whose verification condition fails. Each kills one fragment. None of them, and I want this clear, says anything about the
real system beyond the fragment.

\emph{The audit (Section~\ref{sec:coq}).} Run the assumption probe on any kernel-tier theorem and find a
project-local axiom or parameter in its dependencies, and the claim of zero of them falls. Run the
Inquisitor and read what it says; it fails on high and medium findings. A new finding means
somebody looks. It doesn't automatically mean a theorem is false.

\subsection{What's mine and what isn't}

This is not a claim to have been first. Appendix~\ref{sec:whats-mine} does the sorting item by
item, with sources: what was known, what's added, and what kind of addition it is. Here's the
short form, and I'd welcome correction on any boundary.

\emph{Borrowed, with names.} As the opening chapter warned, I usually had the hunch first and
found these names after, and that order doesn't make any of it mine. Everything in Part I (every
source is cited where it's used). The
category theory (Eilenberg, Mac Lane). Turing, Church, Kleene, Rice, Cantor, Gödel, the
diagonal pattern, Lawvere's unification, and the mechanized versions of them in HOL4, Lean, and
Coq (Norrish, Carneiro, Forster, Kunze, Smolka). Bell, CHSH, Tsirelson, Wehner, NPA, Landau,
Masanes, Fine, the elliptope, and the machine-checked proofs of Tsirelson's bound that came
before mine (Echenim and Mhalla in Isabelle, and Lean's mathlib). Landauer, Bennett, Szilard,
Maxwell, and their critics. The potential method (Tarjan) and its mechanizations (Nipkow,
Charguéraud and Pottier), Lamport's clocks, Floyd and Hoare. Gettier, Necula, Cook, Hartley,
Shannon, Rissanen. Zurek. The seL4 and CompCert discipline. Kami, Bluespec, yosys with
SymbiYosys and the solvers under it, nextpnr, X-Ray. The facts under the permanence results are Landauer's own example and Shannon's
bounds, and ``set a bit to one whatever it held'' is my way of saying his RESTORE TO ONE.

\emph{Formal reconstructions.} The Coq development defines the state types, transition systems,
real-matrix predicates, encodings, and proof terms this book uses. When I say a theorem is
checked, I mean the stated proposition has a kernel-checked proof under its printed
premises. That doesn't make the underlying idea mine, and it doesn't make it new.

\emph{What this project proved, inside its stated interfaces.} The abstract floor, which is the
potential method with one particular potential. The derivation of the toll from finiteness,
permanence, and a named price, in counted states and in bits, with each premise's
counterexample built. The fixed-schedule ledger identity and uniqueness. The named projection
witnesses. The conditional representation theorem for entitlement. The latch form over any
base, with its two counterexamples and converse, and the two uniqueness results (held up to
schedule, refuted for tied records). The substrate diagonal, the L results, and the guest
recursion theorem by construction. The integer gate implying the pinned matrix is PSD (a
sufficient test, not a necessary one), the equivalence with contraction, and Tsirelson's
bound from PSD, which is known mathematics checked again here and tied to an instruction. The
per-opcode hardware refinement and the loader theorems, and the solver-checked safety
properties of the extracted circuit. All of it with premises printed. Of
that list, the toll derivation, the pricing form of the window fact, and the latch form are
the only pieces I'd call new statements, and only in the sense that I didn't find them stated
where I looked.

\emph{Interpretation, which is mine and not proved.} That structure is what a computation
establishes and the toll is the right thing to price. That certification is the pointer
event. That the record axis ``belongs in the step.'' Those are proposals, with the arguments
I've given, and the proposals are where I'd aim first if I were you.

%===========================================================================
\section{The claim ledger}
\label{sec:ledger}
%===========================================================================

Here's everything this book claims, one line each: what kind of claim it is, and where it
lives. ``Proved'' means proved under the premises printed in that section, and nothing more.
If a line here ever says more than its section does, the section is right and the line is
wrong.

Ledger is a good word for it, and it's older than bookkeeping. Around 1400 a \emph{ledger} was a
book that lay permanently in one place, a big church breviary, say, from the old verb
\emph{leggen}, to lay; the account-book sense turns up in the 1500s. A book that stays put. That's
the job here too. The home sections are long and they wander, and this is the one place where
every claim lies still, so you can come back and find it where you left it.

\subsection{Claims about the model}

First the model. Every line in this table is about any system that has the pieces the line
names: a state and a step, plus whatever the result asks for, a reading and the toll, a
counter and a price list, a window, programs. None of them is about my machine. The table
runs over several pages, in reading order.

Here's one way to use it, and it takes five minutes. Pick the sentence in this book you trust
least. Find its line. Read the Kind column before anything else. Then go to the home section
and check that the line says no more than the section does. If it says more, you've found my
mistake, and the end of this section says what I'd like done about it.

and universality is proved. Every line in the next table is about that machine and nothing
else, under the premises printed in its section.
