\subsection{What I propose and haven't proved}

And then there's what I'm proposing. These are mine. They reach further than any theorem in
here, and nothing in the tables puts an unavoidable physical price on every observable change.

\begin{itemize}
\item That the axis belongs in the step (Section~\ref{sec:scope}, Section~\ref{sec:conclusion}).
\item That the usual account of a computation is a shadow of the step (Section~\ref{sec:conclusion}).
\item That certification is the event worth recording, which is the pointer conjecture (Section~\ref{sec:pointer}).
\item That this is a structural account of computation and not just a cost model (Section~\ref{sec:scope}).
\item That the toll is the right thing to price, against a wall or a penalty for contradiction (Section~\ref{sec:models}, Section~\ref{sec:conclusion}).
\end{itemize}

And four things left open: whether Landauer's critics are right, which would leave every
theorem standing and one premise unowned by the world (Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}); whether certification really is
the pointer event (Section~\ref{sec:pointer}); whether there's a smaller start than a partition, by a ruler
someone can state (Section~\ref{sec:structure}); and whether a universal Thiele machine can
keep every foreign machine's own price list exactly; the one built in
Section~\ref{sec:universal-host} keeps a foreign machine's computation and toll and replaces
its prices.

That's the whole ledger. If you find a claim in this book that isn't on it, or a line that
says more than its home does, that's my mistake, and I'd want to hear about it.

%===========================================================================
\section{Scope}
\label{sec:scope}
%===========================================================================

This is the line around what I've proved. Inside it: an accounting law for one event, a
derivation of that law from premises each with its own counterexample, a set of windows
that provably lose it, a record axis that's a latch over any base, a diagonal that holds by
proof on a fragment of the machine, a six-instruction machine on which commitments are earned
and which computes what two counters can, an integer gate that implies a bound by algebra, and a
chain from the step relation to a wiring list with each link labelled. Outside it:
everything that follows. This is the fence. I built it myself, so lean on it before you
trust it.

G. K. Chesterton has a famous fence, in a 1929 book called \emph{The Thing}. A reformer finds a
fence across a road, can't see what it's for, and wants it cleared away; the wiser one tells
him to go off and find out why it was put there, and only then come back and argue for tearing
it down. This section runs the other way round. Every post below comes labelled with what it's
there for, the overclaim it stops, so you don't have to go off and find out first. Pull up any
post you like. Just look at what walks through the gap when you do.

\emph{Physical interpretation of the counter.} The ledger is unique once the start and schedule
are chosen. That doesn't make it entropy, and it doesn't make it energy. A physical bridge
needs a model of which states carry information, premises that can all hold at once, and a
real argument tying the formal charge to dissipation. The permanent-certificate theorems
supply the first for an abstract finite machine with a permanent reading. The two premises
are shown able to hold together only for a one-bit reset; for the machine's certifying steps
that isn't stated as a theorem. The full machine's jump merges program counters and is charged nothing, which breaks the
bridge outright (Section~\ref{sec:witness}, Section~\ref{sec:landauer}), and the calorimeter protocol shows that population
dynamics don't fix the energy scale. No joule value attaches to one mark without thermal and
device premises (Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}, Section~\ref{sec:landauer}).
In short: once you pick the start and the price list, the number is forced by arithmetic, and
it isn't energy. The rest of that paragraph is the list of what I'd need before it could be.

\emph{Class separation.} The witnesses show specific windows losing specific fields. They don't
stop a conventional simulator from keeping those fields in its encoding. No separation of
standard complexity classes follows from the collisions, or from the charge levels climbing
without bound (Section~\ref{sec:windows}, Section~\ref{sec:separation}, Section~\ref{sec:witness}, Section~\ref{sec:landauer}).
I'll be blunt about why I'm careful here. Whether P equals NP is one of the seven problems the
Clay Mathematics Institute put a million dollars on, at a meeting in Paris in May 2000. One of
the seven has been solved since, the Poincaré conjecture, by Grigori Perelman. P versus NP
hasn't. If a two-state collision on my machine settled it, somebody would be owed a million
dollars, and it wouldn't be me. A window that loses a field is a fact about that window. A
complexity class is a fact about what every possible program can do within a budget, and
nothing in these collisions reaches that far.

\emph{Trace initiality, and what it doesn't settle.} The universal property of the trace fold is
about evaluating lists of instructions: pick where a target starts, and there's exactly one
way to fold a list into it (\code{thiele\_trace\_fold\_initial}, Section~\ref{sec:witness}). The counter's uniqueness
assumes a schedule. Exact pricing assumes an event, and a reference count that says what
charging too much means (Section~\ref{sec:windows}). Those results make the construction precise. None of them
shows that the category I chose, or the event I chose, is physically necessary.

\emph{Other observables.} Certification is one worked example. A family of other observations
might turn up other structural laws, but each would need its own events, its own evidence,
and its own cost rules, justified on their own terms. The window and oracle results are
about what specific maps keep. They don't show infinitely many independent dimensions, zero
mutual information, or a cost for changing coordinates, and piling predicates on top of each
other doesn't give a topology, a metric, or independence (Section~\ref{sec:separation}).

\emph{Program predicates versus state observations.} The state-level collision (Section~\ref{sec:windows}'s wall) and
the program-level diagonal (Section~\ref{sec:diagonal}'s wall) live in different domains. Linking them would take a
theorem of its own. The nat family (Section~\ref{sec:diagonal}) and the bounded-machine theorem (Section~\ref{sec:interpreters}) keep their explicit
quantifiers and representability premises.

\emph{Entitlement bounds.} The representation theorem is handed its tree and its representative
reduction, along with the covering and payment conditions. It doesn't dig the tree out of
an arbitrary run, and it isn't a Shannon bound on every trace (Section~\ref{sec:machine-claims}).

\emph{Quantum behaviour.} The fixed-matrix equivalence is about one completion with zero
marginals and zero within-party moments. The elliptope lets the within-party moments move,
at the level of correlators. Full behaviours with marginals, and operator realisations, need
identifications this book doesn't make. A sound runtime check isn't complete for those
bigger sets, and the elliptope decider is not an instruction (Section~\ref{sec:chsh}).

\emph{The record axis.} The proved structural result is: a permanent record driven by a base
computation is a latch on an event; on finite hardware its write merges states; and the
machine's named projections don't recover it. Certification is one instance, not a theorem
selecting the unique event every system must record (Section~\ref{sec:latch}, Section~\ref{sec:pointer}). A finite monotone
multi-valued record decomposes into threshold latches, not into one Boolean latch.
Revocation, including revocation priced from the other side as in Casper, lies outside the
permanent-record axis; a price on revocation doesn't transfer to a price on the write (Section~\ref{sec:models}).
Probabilistic records don't inherit the uniqueness result either. Two honest random records
can have the same branches and the same charges and still give those branches different
weights, one choosing evenly and one two to one, so the schedule doesn't fix the
probabilities (\code{schedule\_determines\_probabilities\_refuted}). And no single deterministic
latch explains a record that can branch both ways from the same observation
(\code{deterministic\_latch\_handles\_branching\_refuted}).
Weak base equivalence is defined and is an equivalence; no two of the four bases are related
by it in the checked work, and the latch form holds on each separately, so it doesn't tell
them apart (Section~\ref{sec:latch}, Section~\ref{sec:witness}).
In short: a record that stays up is a latch, and on finite hardware its write merges states;
which event deserves the latch isn't proved; records that can come back down lie outside all
of this, and random ones lose the uniqueness.

\emph{The guest.} The twelve-instruction guest has a direct Rice reduction, numeric decoding,
verified dispatch, a guest-callable specialiser, and a recursion theorem proved by
construction. For the full fifty-one-instruction machine the recursion premise is false when asked for every
map, because equality after the thousand-step cutoff can be decided by running both programs;
the machine's wall is the diagonal applied to that decidable property, and nothing more
(\code{vm\_full\_recursion\_premise\_refuted}, \code{vm\_correct\_flip\_has\_no\_fixed\_point}, Section~\ref{sec:interpreters}).

\emph{The five models.} Each is a fragment transcribed from a specification, with a named
theorem and a named limit: the Casper transcription has no deposits or fork choice; the gas
fragment omits the refund cap; the attestation fragment has no signatures; the transparency
verifier covers control flow, not collision resistance; the proof-carrying checker is a
three-instruction role model. None is a claim about the real system beyond its fragment
(Section~\ref{sec:models}).

\emph{The two machines.} Part IV has a small machine and a big build, and they prove different
things. The small machine of Section~\ref{sec:smallest} (two counters, six instructions) is where commitments are
earned: a raised flag went through a passing check, a commitment and a certification of the
same claim, nothing is forged, and the cheapest certificate costs exactly three. It's also
where universality is proved, by matching Minsky's two-counter machines step for step and
borrowing their undecidable halting from the Coq library. Its check price is flat, its fact
table holds sixteen, and its certificate is historical (Section~\ref{sec:smallest} lists the rest). The big build of
fifty-one instructions prices every commitment and doesn't enforce that one was earned: its
check and its commit are separate steps, and nothing makes the second wait for the first
(Section~\ref{sec:machine-claims}). So ``commitments are earned'' is a theorem about the small machine, not the big one.

\emph{The comparison machines.} The small machines I built to compare against are fragments too.
The random-access memory result covers an addressed list memory with load, increment and
decrement on cells (\code{concrete\_ram\_write\_reads\_back} and its neighbours), and it's about that
machine. The register machine Section~\ref{sec:latch} puts the latch on (\code{record\_axis\_is\_latch\_on\_ram\_holds}) is
a different small machine, the one with indirect addressing, and that theorem is about it. The reversible-machine
result covers arithmetic update cores: add and subtract, each undone by the other, with or
without wrapping at a modulus (\code{janus\_like\_unbounded\_inverse}, \code{janus\_like\_bounded\_inverse}).
Neither is a theorem about real memories or full reversible languages. The cost-semantics
results are local correspondences, not full cost-framework embeddings: the trace's cost is a
writer cost and a grade, and the toll is the potential method with one potential (Section~\ref{sec:counter}).
Nobody's whole type system gets embedded either.

\emph{Outward consequences.} I looked for results about real systems that would need the record
axis. Five narrow ones are proved, each as a two-state countermodel: a certificate-transparency
client's local tree head can't decide whether the world's log is consistent
(\code{ct\_local\_view\_insufficient}); a quote check that matches only the composite digest accepts a
mismatched selection (\code{tpm\_selection\_binding\_is\_necessary}); a local suffix can't decide a
trusted anchor (\code{weak\_subjective\_suffix\_insufficient}); an acknowledgement without a durable
commit record can be lost (\code{wal\_ack\_requires\_durability}); and a current local log can't
decide what happened before it (\code{audit\_local\_snapshot\_insufficient}). Each reduces to a known
indistinguishability or durability argument. Five stronger candidates would need protocol or
hardware semantics I haven't formalised, and I've proved nothing about them. So none of this
yields a new outside result that both needs the record axis and is ready to use.

\emph{Geometry.} The curvature files prove things about partition graphs in general, and the
chain from the counter to a discrete Gauss-Bonnet identity carries its physical premises
without using them. On states the machine reaches from its initial state, modules never share
an address, every module reads flat, and every triangulation is separate triangles with Euler
characteristic equal to their count, so no run reaches a closed surface (Section~\ref{sec:landauer},
Theorem~\ref{thm:u24-reachable-geometry}).

\emph{The hardware.} The Coq refinement chain stops at Kami's semantics. Below that:
extraction, printing, bsc, yosys, nextpnr, X-Ray, and the board primitives remain trusted,
with the checks named. Beside the chain, a separate solver proves by induction that the
extracted circuit keeps its partition-table, control and loader safety properties on every
run from reset, and that the loader and board wrapper match the mapped netlist if the CPU
answers alike on both sides; no proof compares the CPU and its memories. Seventeen programs
passed the board-specific simulation across the mapped netlist (before place and route),
the extracted Verilog and the runner, including reset and power-on checks. The Coq
status-report theorem retains its premise that the report rule fires once per clock cycle.
The solver checks are not Coq theorems, and neither they nor the finite simulations prove
the translation chain correct. No physical board run is recorded (Section~\ref{sec:chip}).

\emph{Where each result lives.} Every system that follows the toll, whatever its states: the
floor, at most as many certifications as cost, and the potential-method reading. Every
finite machine whose price covers merges: the toll for permanent records, and which
instructions every such price must charge. Every finite machine paying per halving: the
machine's own narrowing bound. Every machine extending a base with a driven, permanent
record: the latch. Every window through which a certifying and a non-certifying step look
alike: no exact price from the window. This build only: the schedule and its numbers, the
collisions of its own windows, the integer gate and its PSD bridge, the hardware
correspondence, the fifty-one instructions, the finite fragment.

\emph{What I'm proposing beyond that.} That the axis belongs in the step; that certification is
the event worth recording; that this is a structural account of computation and not just a
cost model. Those reach further than any theorem here, and no theorem here puts an
unavoidable physical price on every observable change. They're the argument, and the
argument is what the rest of the book was.

%===========================================================================
\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}
%===========================================================================

I started with one word and a machine I couldn't explain. Here's where the word ended up,
and where the machine did.

Structure turned out to be relations among things, kept under chosen changes, carried by
whatever stuff, always relative to a frame. The start I chose, the smallest one by the count
of names, was a sorting of a pile, and the thing nobody I read had priced was the moment you
stand behind the sorting. That was Part I, and it ended with a question.

The question got an exact form in Part II: five parts, one rule, one theorem you proved at
the table. Then the rule stopped being only my preference. On a finite machine where the flag
stays up, raising it forgets something, and if forgetting is charged for, the way Landauer's
principle charges for it in its worst case, the toll follows. That's a derivation under three
premises you can refuse one at a time, each with its counterexample built, not a proof that
every computation has to adopt the rule; and the charge on forgetting is a named premise with
its critics named. Learning can be free; committing to a record that stays put can't be, on
those premises. That's as far as physics goes in this book, and I've tried to keep it exactly
that far.

Part III was the logic, and here's what it earned, in the order it was earned. The counter
is arithmetic once the schedule is chosen. A window in which a raising step and a quiet one
look the same can't price the raise exactly, by a fact about functions far older than the
machine. Entitlement is defined as an object, a checked relation, and a paid event; on the
machine, under the hypotheses of the representation theorem, it costs at least the index bits
it commits to; and it is a license to lean on a claim, not a proof that the claim is true.
Insight, in the sense the toll prices, is a committed relation, not a feeling, and its floor
is flat: at least one, however deep. The claim behind the flag is a formula on a group,
checked by a small checker, and the check is a different step from the commit. Over any base,
an honest record is a latch, with two free choices, the event and the price list; ``only one
substrate'' is false and ``one structure, many price lists'' is true once the event is fixed. No
procedure the substrate itself can represent decides the shortcut predicate, given a
recursion theorem, by the same diagonal that broke Frege's floor, and the machine's answer is
to record the commitment rather than automate the judgement. Of five record disciplines I
modelled in fragments, one prices the write. And which event to record is a conjecture, with
its refutations listed.

Part IV built twice. The small machine came first, two counters and six instructions, and on
it the model stands whole: a raised flag was checked, then committed, then certified, on the
same edition of the same counter, nothing gets forged, the cheapest certificate costs exactly
three, and it computes everything Minsky's two-counter machines can, so its halting is
undecidable. Earned commitments and universality are proved there. So is a universal Thiele
machine: one fixed host runs any small-machine program as a guest, mirrors the guest's
record, and pays the guest's toll in the same step the guest crosses, proved in Coq with
nothing assumed. What it covers is said plainly: guests are small-machine programs, which
compute everything, and a machine from somewhere else comes in through the two-counter
encoding with its computation and its toll kept, but not its exact prices. Then the big build, one
try, in three materials, whose job was to be the witness: every ``when the machine exists'' from
the earlier parts landed on a theorem with a name. It prices every commitment on its
fifty-one instructions and doesn't enforce that one was earned; the check and the commit stay
two separate steps there, on purpose and on the page. The
places where the machine came up short of the idea stayed on the page too: the free jump,
which has its theorem, and the four instructions with no hardware encoding. So did the near
miss: the obvious rule for composing identity arrows breaks associativity the moment two of
them meet, and the machine's rule passes the identity flag along, so the laws hold on the
arrows it stores, each one a theorem. Part V was the chain to the chip, with every link labelled
proved, tested, or trusted, and the sentence that no board was ever powered on. Part VI was
how to check it and how to break it. Every result carries the shape of the thing that would
kill it, gathered in one place (Section~\ref{sec:falsification}): a run from uncertified to certified with the counter
never rising; a contractive correlator whose pinned matrix isn't positive semidefinite; a
certification system that follows the toll and certifies at total cost zero; a function on
numbers that correctly decides the shortcut predicate of the substrate built from it. Any one
of them brings down the theorem it matches. I hunted. I came up empty.

Two things I'd point at if you asked what's sharpest.

In the build: an integer check on eight counters, run by one instruction, forces a
five-by-five matrix to be positive semidefinite, and from there the Tsirelson bound follows,
and the chain never once reaches for physics. No Hilbert space, no operators, no
observables. The route through the matrix isn't mine; it's the first rung of a ladder
Navascués, Pironio and Acín built in 2007, and the semidefinite road to Tsirelson's bound is
older than that. What's here is the check that runs in whole numbers inside an instruction,
and the checked link from ``this instruction didn't trap'' to the bound. It's algebra you can
follow line by line, and the assumption audit on that link finds exactly three standard
axioms from Coq's own library (two that come with its real numbers, and functional
extensionality) and nothing of mine, which is how anyone can see
that no physics was smuggled in.

In the model: the diagonal rules out a correct decider whenever its flip can be expressed
inside the substrate and the substrate supplies the fixed point; in L the fixed point is
proved from the reduction rules and the diagonal is Rice's theorem; and on my machine's
own guest the fixed point is proved by construction, so the wall stands there by proof
and not by premise. For the full machine the recursion premise is false when asked for every map,
because its cutoff property is decidable from outside, and the flip of every correct decider
has no fixed point; both are theorems. Those are different sentences, and sharing a vocabulary doesn't make them one.

What's open, by my count. Whether the toll is the \emph{right} thing to price, as against a
wall or a penalty for contradiction, which is what the five real systems mostly built.
Whether certification is the pointer event. Whether a universal Thiele machine can keep
every foreign machine's own price list exactly; the host in Section~\ref{sec:universal-host}
keeps a foreign machine's computation and toll, and replaces its prices. Whether Landauer's critics
are right, which would leave every theorem standing and one premise unowned by the world.
And the question I'd most like someone to take from me: is there a smaller start than a
partition, by a ruler they can state? I said in Section~\ref{sec:structure} it would change this book. It would.

And the two computers from the first pages, the sorter and the copier, holding the same bits.
Walk the warehouse again. On an ordinary machine there's still no lamp for what the sorter did,
and nothing in this book changes that. On the small machine there is one: a flag and a counter
you can read off the state, and a theorem that, from a clean start, the flag can't be up unless
a check of that very claim, about that very edition, passed first. That's the one lamp I set
out to light. Whether every machine ought to have it is the argument, not the proof.

So that's the Thiele Machine. An abstract model with five parts and one rule, an argument
made with it that the usual account of a computation is a shadow and the axis it leaves out
belongs in the step, and two builds of it to check the argument against, a small one and a
big one, the big one in three materials.
The theorems are what they are, with their premises printed. The interpretation is mine, and
I've tried to say at every turn which is which, because the first time through I was the
only one checking, and I've met me, and that's not enough people. Now there's you.


\appendix

%===========================================================================
\section{Things I had to learn first}
\label{sec:vocab}
%===========================================================================

I had been around computers my whole life and paid attention to people like John Carmack
on how graphics actually get made, but I came in with none of the formal fields this work
turned out to need. By the time the proofs compiled I'd needed enough of half a dozen of
them that I had to put down somewhere what those fields had words for. This appendix is that
place. None of it is the argument. It's what I needed to be able to make it. Everything
below is what I understood after I went and read about it; I'm not claiming to teach you
these subjects, and if you already know a part, skip it.

\subsection{Bits, bytes, and what a CPU sees}

A bit is one digit that's either zero or one, the smallest fact a machine can hold.
Everything else is bits stacked up. Eight of them make a byte, which lands you any number
from 0 to 255, and the first thing that genuinely surprised me is that the same byte is also
a letter: a convention called ASCII simply agrees to call 65 the letter A, 48 the digit 0,
32 a space. Nothing in the byte knows which it is. The meaning is a convention laid on top.

You can see the convention's seams with a pencil. Write 65 in binary: 1000001. Knock off the
first two digits and what's left, 00001, is 1, and A is the first letter. B is 66, which ends in
00010, two. Now lower case: a is 97, which is 1100001, the same pattern with one more bit
switched on, the one worth 32. Every capital and its small letter differ in exactly that bit.
That's on purpose. The first version of the code, in 1963, had no lower case at all; when lower
case arrived, in the 1967 revision, it was placed so the two cases differ by one bit, which made
matching them, and building keyboards and printers, simpler. Nothing in the byte knows it's a
letter, but somebody made the letters easy for a circuit to tell apart.

Everything in this subsection is about real CPUs and about my machine, the big build of Part
IV. None of it belongs to the abstract model, which has a kind of state and a step rule and
nothing about widths or slots.

A word is a chunk of bits the CPU treats as one unit. My machine's reference kernel (its
definition in Coq) uses 64-bit words (any number from 0 to about 18 quintillion); the
synthesised hardware uses 32-bit words (0 to about 4 billion). The abstract model doesn't
care which width.

A register is a named storage slot inside the CPU that holds one word; my machine has
sixteen, r0 through r15, and they're the fastest place to read or write. Memory is a
longer list of word-sized slots accessed by index, the address; my machine has 128 words of
it, and that's the entire address space. The program counter is one specific register that
tracks where in the program the machine is; after every instruction it moves forward by one
unless the instruction says jump. A stack pointer is a register pointing at the top of a
region used for nested calls: CALL pushes a return address there, RET pops it, and r15 is
the stack pointer by my convention. A port is a named channel for talking to the outside
world; the kernel doesn't model the outside, it charges for the communication and accepts
the value the instruction declares.

Modular arithmetic means counting wraps at a maximum: with a maximum of 16, 17 wraps to 1.
The machine wraps register indices modulo 16 and memory indices modulo 128, so r17 is r1.
Bitwise operations work on the bits of a value one position at a time: AND is 1 only when
both bits are, OR when either is, XOR (exclusive or) exactly when they differ. A shift moves
every bit left or right, which multiplies or divides by a power of two. Popcount is the
count of one-bits in a value. Hexadecimal is base 16, digits 0 to 9 then A to F, written
with a 0x prefix: 0xFF is 255.

A trap means the machine routes execution to a fixed address instead of advancing, the
hardware's ``this went wrong, go to the handler.'' An ISA, instruction set architecture, is the
list of every instruction a CPU recognises, each identified by an opcode, a numeric tag the
hardware decodes. My machine has fifty-one. The abstract model has none; it has a step rule.

\subsection{The notation the formal parts use}

I don't think in these symbols, and I had to learn to read them. The natural numbers are 0,
1, 2, and so on, written with a double-struck N; the integers add the negatives; the reals
are the whole number line. A function from a set A to a set B is written with an arrow. For
a finite set, vertical bars around it mean its size; for a number, its absolute value. A big
sigma is a sum over every member of a set. A delta before a quantity means the change in it.
An upside-down A means ``for every''; a backwards E means ``there exists.'' A double arrow is
implication; a double-headed one is ``if and only if.'' A small circle between two functions is
composition, apply the right one first. Angle brackets around a random quantity mean its
long-run average, which I picked up from the Bell-test papers. In this book a circled plus is
bitwise XOR and a circled times has one meaning, the tensor instruction's concatenation of
two coupling lists; the quantum sense of that symbol never appears, because the game section
does its work in plain integer arithmetic. A superscript T on a matrix is its transpose, rows
and columns swapped, and I with a subscript n is the identity matrix.

\subsection{Coq, in just enough detail}

Coq is a proof assistant: a programming language whose type system is expressive enough that
proofs are programs and the compiler checks them (Part VI has the long version). A Theorem is
a named statement followed by a proof; a Lemma is the same thing used for an intermediate
result; a Definition introduces a named value; an Inductive type is one with a finite list of
constructors, the only ways to build a value of it (Coq's natural numbers have two: zero, and
successor of another natural). A tactic is a step inside a proof: induction (base case, then
step), destruct (split into cases), reflexivity (prove a thing equals itself), simpl
(compute), lia and lra and nra (arithmetic solvers for integers, linear reals, and
polynomial reals), psatz (a certificate search for polynomial inequalities). Qed ends a
proof and asks Coq to check the whole chain. Admitted is the keyword for ``I claim this
without proof,'' and it appears nowhere in the active tree. A Hypothesis inside a Section is a
named premise that becomes an argument of every theorem that uses it when the Section
closes; ``closed under the global context'' doesn't make it go away. Print Assumptions lists
the global axioms a theorem depends on; on the kernel tier it shows only standard-library
ones. A total function always returns a value, and Coq requires every function to be total;
the machine's step function is, error cases included. ``Parametric in K'' means the proof
works for any K; the machine's sizes are literal constants, and the proofs are about those
literals.

\subsection{Category theory beyond Part IV}

Part IV builds objects, arrows, composition, identities, associativity, and the identity laws
from scratch. Beyond that: a functor is a structure-preserving map from one category to
another, sending objects to objects and arrows to arrows while respecting composition and
identities; think of it as a translation rule between two worlds of structure. An embedding
is a functor that throws nothing away, and faithful is the precise version for arrows: two
distinct arrows never land on one. Conservative is the version for inverses: if the
image of an arrow has an inverse, the arrow already had one, so the functor can't
manufacture an isomorphism (an arrow with an inverse) that wasn't there. The two properties
are different, and neither gives the other. Read the natural numbers under addition as a
category with one object and an arrow for each number, and the same for the integers. The
inclusion of the first into the second is faithful, since distinct naturals stay distinct
integers, but not conservative: 1 has no inverse among the naturals, and its image has one,
minus 1. The other way round, the functor from the integers onto the trivial one-arrow group
is conservative, since every arrow of the integers already has an inverse, but not faithful:
it sends every integer to the same arrow. An embedding needs faithfulness specifically. A
monoidal product combines two objects or two arrows
into one, with a unit and laws that make the combining behave; the tensor instruction is
tensor-shaped, and the checked laws for it are the interchange law under a side condition
and associativity with the empty list as unit. An initial object has exactly one arrow into
every object; the counter's uniqueness in this book is a uniqueness-on-reachable-states
fact, not a category-theoretic initial object. Yoneda's lemma is where the categorical
engine first clicked for me, the night I stopped borrowing other people's runtimes, and
nothing in the formal development uses it.

\subsection{Bell-test vocabulary}

A correlation between two outcomes is the average of their product; with outcomes plus or
minus one it lies between minus one and one, plus one meaning always match, minus one always
differ. A correlator is one such average in a labelled setting, E00 for Alice's setting 0
and Bob's 0. The marginal of a joint distribution is the distribution of one side alone with
the other averaged out; zero-marginal means each side's outcome is plus or minus one equally
often on average. A local hidden-variable model is one where both outcomes are fixed by a
shared random variable agreed before the game plus each side's own setting; Bell's theorem
says no such model produces certain correlations quantum mechanics does. No-signalling means
neither side's marginal depends on the other's setting. Quantum-realisable means compatible
with some quantum state and measurements; the NPA hierarchy gives a ladder of necessary
tests, each a positive-semidefiniteness condition on a moment matrix, and no single rung is
sufficient in general. The PR box is the no-signalling correlation that wins the game every
time, stronger than quantum mechanics allows; nature doesn't provide it. Cauchy-Schwarz is
the inequality that a dot product is bounded by the product of the lengths. The Tsirelson
bound is two root two, the largest game score quantum mechanics allows; the classical bound
is two and the PR bound is four. (If you go looking for Boris Tsirelson's 1980 paper, look
under Cirel'son, the spelling the journal printed, or you may not find it.) The elliptope is
the set of correlators that can be filled
out into a positive-semidefinite matrix.

\subsection{Hardware and synthesis vocabulary}

A hardware description language describes circuits as text; Bluespec is high-level (rules,
and the compiler builds the arbitration) and Verilog is low-level (registers and wires).
Register-transfer-level Verilog describes how data moves between registers each clock cycle
and is what synthesis tools consume. Synthesis compiles a description down to logic gates;
yosys is an open-source synthesis tool. Place-and-route assigns gates to positions on a chip
and wires them; nextpnr-xilinx does it for the chips this design targets. A bitstream is the
binary file an FPGA reads to configure itself, and the X-Ray tools produce one from the
routed design in two moves: \code{fasm2frames} packs the routed design into configuration frames,
then \code{xc7frames2bit} writes the frames out as the bitstream. An FPGA is a chip you program after manufacturing: physical gates, configurable
connections. A LUT, look-up table, is the FPGA's basic logic primitive, a small memory
programmed to implement any small Boolean function; a flip-flop is a one-bit memory cell; a
carry chain is wiring for fast addition; distributed RAM is memory built out of LUTs; block
RAM is dedicated memory; DSP slices are dedicated arithmetic. This design doesn't use the DSP
slices. Synthesis runs with yosys's \code{-nodsp} option, so the multiplier inside the game check
(one wide multiplier, shared across the phases of a multi-cycle check) is built out of LUTs.
With DSP slices the design didn't finish placing and routing inside the build's time limit;
the open-source placer stalled and the routing came out congested. It computes the same
thing either way. The choice is about what the tools can place and route, not about
correctness. A netlist is the gate-level circuit written out; a VCD waveform is a
record of every signal at every time step in a simulation; iverilog and Verilator are
open-source Verilog simulators. A bisimulation is a precise notion of two systems behaving
the same under a chosen relation on their states; field-by-field equality of states is one
particular, stronger contract, and Part V says which the hardware proofs use. A parity test
is the empirical cousin: run two implementations on the same set of inputs and check that
they agree, a correspondence earned by testing rather than by proof.

How old is the idea of a chip you wire after you buy it? Younger than you might guess. Ross
Freeman, one of the founders of Xilinx, came up with it in 1984, and the first one sold, the
XC2064, came out in 1985 with sixty-four little logic blocks in an eight-by-eight grid, each
able to compute any function of four inputs. The chip this design targets counts its lookup-table
sites in the hundreds of thousands, and this design uses about fifty-three thousand of them
(Section~\ref{sec:chip} has the numbers). Same idea, forty years on. The IEEE dedicated a
milestone plaque to it in 2026.

\subsection{Other terms I use without rebuilding}

Provenance is the recorded chain of where an object came from; on the small machine, a
commitment's provenance is the passing check that came before it (Section~\ref{sec:smallest}).
Simulation, in computer science, is one system
imitating another's input-output behaviour; a Turing machine simulates any system of the
model, my machine included, by writing the whole state out on its tape, and the difference
this book is about is what a window on that tape shows. That's real, and it's exactly what people reach for when they
want to wave the whole question away: if a tape can stand in for the state, what was the
difference? The tape carries a picture of the state, not the state, the way a photograph of
a fire keeps you exactly as warm as any other photograph. The counter and the toll live in
the step rule, not in the bytes, and an encoding copies the bytes. A Turing machine built
with the toll in its own transition table is a different case: it's an instance of the
model, not a simulation of it. What no machine can do is make a simulated rule binding just
by writing it down on tape.

Projection is a function that drops information on purpose. The bare window on my machine
keeps three things, the registers, the memory and the program counter, which are what a
Turing machine already has, and that's why projecting lands you back in ordinary
computation. It drops everything else, including the three that were doing the new work: the
counter, the certification readings, and the arrow graph. Other windows keep more: \code{forget}
also keeps the counter, and \code{shadow\_proj} keeps six fields and drops the graph. Nothing is
wrong with any of them. They're perfectly good functions. They just cost you what made the
state more than a tape. A quotient is the operation of declaring two things the same when
they agree on what you chose to look at and working with the classes instead. A projection
does exactly that: it doesn't just drop fields one at a time, it glues together states that
the dropped fields kept apart. The fibre of a function over a value is
everything the function sends to that value. An injection sends no two inputs to the same
output; a surjection covers every output. Decidable means an algorithm always halts with a
yes-or-no answer; keep the claim and the algorithm apart, since the algorithm decides the
claim only once there's a proof that its answer matches. Polynomial time means running time
bounded by a power of the input size; P is the problems solvable that way, NP the problems
where a candidate solution can be \emph{checked} that way, and whether the two are the same is
open. The two budget predicates in the checked work, \code{error\_free\_preservation\_budget} and
\code{positive\_input\_certification\_budget}, are not complexity classes. Each lets the trace be
chosen separately for every input, and the bounds they take are plain functions with no
requirement to be polynomial.

``Kernel'' wears three hats in this book, and I'd rather point that out than let it ambush
you. First, mathematics: the kernel of a map is what it sends to the identity, and for a
projection the useful version is the relation ``these two states project to the same thing.''
Second, the proofs, where the hat comes in two sizes: the kernel tier is the part of the Coq
development the main theorems live in (Section~\ref{sec:coq}), holding both the model's theorems and my
machine's definition, and the files are where the model is written down, not the model
itself;
and Coq's own kernel is the small checker that accepts or rejects every proof. Third, the
operating-system kernel, which I never use and mention only so you know it isn't meant. The
sentence around the word always says which one is.

\subsection{Matrices}

A matrix is positive semidefinite (PSD) when $v^{\mathsf T} M v \ge 0$ for every vector $v$;
the game check is all about one matrix being PSD. The determinant of a square matrix is a
single number that is zero exactly when the matrix squashes some direction flat. For a
two-by-two matrix with rows $(a, b)$ and $(c, d)$ it's $ad - bc$. For a bigger one, expand
along a row: for each entry, delete its row and column, take the determinant of what's left,
multiply by the entry, alternate the signs, and add up; the recursion bottoms out at two by
two. A principal submatrix is what you get by choosing some of the indices and keeping only
those rows and the same columns; its determinant is a principal minor. A symmetric matrix is
PSD exactly when every principal submatrix is, every one of them, and the game check uses
the three-by-three ones (Appendix~\ref{sub:chsh-five}). The Schur complement turns a question
about a block matrix into a question about a smaller one. For a symmetric block matrix with
corner block $P$, off-diagonal block $Q$ and other corner $R$, it's $R - Q^{\mathsf T} P^{-1}
Q$, and when $P$ is positive definite the whole matrix is PSD exactly when that complement is
(Lemma~\ref{lem:chsh-schur}). Positive definite matters; invertible isn't enough. Take $P = -1$
and every other entry zero: the complement is zero, which is PSD, and the whole matrix
isn't.

\subsection{Borrowed ideas the book pushes on}

These get their full story in the chapter that uses them; here's the one-line version for
when you've forgotten which one Landauer was.

The pigeonhole principle: put more pigeons than holes and some hole holds two. Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}'s room with
too few chairs is that, and so is the proof that a permanent flag can only be raised by a
step that forgets something. Landauer's principle (Rolf Landauer, 1961): a step that wipes
information, lowering the entropy of what a machine holds by some number of bits, gives off
at least Boltzmann's constant times the temperature times the natural log of two in heat per
bit. In this book it's always a premise with its name on it, never derived (Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}, Section~\ref{sec:landauer}).
Entropy, in Claude Shannon's sense: for a spread of chances over states, roughly the average number
of yes-or-no questions you'd need to pin the state down, so an even spread over $n$ states
has $\log_2 n$ bits. A spread, in this book, is just a list of chances that add up to one.
Maxwell's demon (Section~\ref{sec:narrowing}): a little creature that watches molecules and sorts fast from slow,
seemingly for free; Charles Bennett's answer was that the measuring can be free and the
wiping of the demon's notes is what costs. The potential method (Robert Tarjan, 1985): pay
for a run with a quantity stored in the state, so a step's bill plus the change in the
stored quantity is what you count; Section~\ref{sec:counter} reads the toll as that method with one particular
potential.

The halting problem (Alan Turing, 1936): no program decides, for every program and input,
whether it stops. Kleene's recursion theorem (Stephen Kleene, 1938): for any transformation
of programs that can itself be computed, some program behaves exactly like its own
transform. Rice's theorem (Henry Rice, 1953): any property that depends only on what a
program does, and isn't true of all programs or of none, can't be decided by a program. The
diagonal is the move under all three: build the thing that does the opposite of what the
table says about it (Section~\ref{sec:diagonal}). L is a small lambda calculus, a language made of nothing but
functions applied to functions, which Yannick Forster and Gert Smolka built in Coq and which
Section~\ref{sec:diagonal} and Section~\ref{sec:interpreters} use as a tool. A hash is a short fingerprint of a longer piece of data, made so
that finding two inputs with the same fingerprint is supposed to be hard; a hash chain folds
each new record into the fingerprint of the last, and a Merkle tree folds them pairwise into
one root (Section~\ref{sec:toll}, Section~\ref{sec:models}).

Extraction is Coq's mechanism for turning definitions into runnable code in another
language; nothing it produces is checked by the proofs after it leaves Coq (Section~\ref{sec:coq}). Kami is a
Coq library for writing hardware as rules and proving things about them, from Choi and
coauthors (Section~\ref{sec:chip}). A refinement proof says a lower-level step does what a higher-level
one says, under stated side conditions; Section~\ref{sec:chip}'s are per instruction.

\subsection{Words this book builds}

These are mine, or mine in the sense that I pinned them down for this book. Each is built
properly in the chapter named; this is a reminder, not the build.

A few words first, because everything else hangs off them and each has exactly one meaning.
The \emph{model} (or the abstract model) is a kind of state and a rule for stepping, plus exactly
the extra pieces a given theorem asks for: a certification reading and the toll, or a counter
and a price list, or a window, or programs written as states and a recursion theorem. The
name Thiele Machine belongs to the model. Parts I to III live there, and every claim in them
is about any system with the pieces it names. A \emph{substrate} is the model's shape with
whatever extension a theorem names, and nothing else; the word never means my machine, and
never the side of a simulation that does the stepping (\hyperref[sec:straight]{Let me be straight with you}). \emph{My machine} (also the machine I
build, the build, the big build) is the concrete machine that fills in many of those pieces at
once: its state record, its fifty-one instructions and their prices, the reference kernel in
Coq, the guest, the extracted runner, and the hardware. The \emph{small machine} (the smallest
honest machine, Section~\ref{sec:smallest}) is the other piece of scaffolding, and it comes first in Part IV. The
\emph{scaffolding} is both of them together. Parts IV and V live there. \emph{A Thiele
machine}, lower case, is any system proved to be an instance of the certification system
(Definition~\ref{def:certsys}), five parts and the toll; the paper toys are, and so are both
builds. \emph{Thiele-complete} means a Thiele machine whose base is Turing-universal, so it
computes anything a Turing machine can while carrying the record and paying the toll; the
small machine is proved Thiele-complete, and for the big build it's open. A \emph{universal}
Thiele machine runs any machine of a stated class as a guest, with the guest's record kept
and its toll collected by its own step; one is proved for the small machine's programs
(Section~\ref{sec:universal-host}), and a machine from elsewhere keeps its computation and
toll there but not its exact prices. The chip isn't a Thiele machine; it implements the big build inside
the bounds Section~\ref{sec:chip} states. When a word below belongs
to only one of the two layers, the entry says which.

A \emph{partition} is a sorting of a pile into groups, nothing in two groups and nothing left
over (Section~\ref{sec:structure}). A \emph{certification system} is a state type, moves, a step, a cost per move, and a
yes-or-no reading, plus one rule, the \emph{toll}: a move that turns the reading from no to yes
costs at least one (Section~\ref{sec:toll}). The files call that rule A2 in one of their two numbered lists
(Appendix~\ref{sec:assumptions}). A move \emph{merges} when two different starting states land on
the same end; one that never does is \emph{injective}, it forgets nothing. A reading is
\emph{permanent} when no move turns it from yes back to no (Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}).

The \emph{counter}, which I also call the \emph{ledger}: in the model, a number carried in the state
that starts at zero and that every step raises by exactly that step's charge (Section~\ref{sec:counter}). My
machine has exactly one, and the source calls it mu ($\mu$) (Section~\ref{sec:state}). Two other things get called
counters, and each chapter says which: Minsky's two bins on the small machine, and the eight witness counters that
tally the game's rounds (Section~\ref{sec:chsh}). Neither is the ledger. A \emph{price list} (on my machine,
the \emph{cost schedule}) says what each move costs; the model takes it as given, and my machine's
table of what each instruction costs is in Section~\ref{sec:isa}. A \emph{receipt} is a total that lives in the
state, only climbs, equals the sum of the charges on every path including the failures, and is
the only such total for its price list (Section~\ref{sec:counter} gives the argument for any system with a counter
and a price list; the checked theorems are about my machine, Section~\ref{sec:witness}).

These belong to my machine only, and none of them appears before Part IV. A \emph{module} is one
group in my machine's partition of its memory; its \emph{region} is the run of consecutive
data-memory addresses it owns, a base and a length, inside the hundred and twenty-eight
words; no two modules' regions overlap, and a run hands out at most sixty-four module numbers
(Section~\ref{sec:state}). An \emph{arrow} (a \emph{morphism}) goes from one module to another and carries
a \emph{coupling}, a list of pairs of cells, one from each side, plus a label (Section~\ref{sec:state}, Section~\ref{sec:category}); in Section~\ref{sec:structure},
``arrow'' means only the category theorist's general word. The \emph{certified flag} is set by
CERTIFY and nothing ever clears it; the \emph{assertion channel} is a separate number written
by MORPH\_\allowbreak{}ASSERT (Section~\ref{sec:state}, Section~\ref{sec:isa}, Section~\ref{sec:witness}). In the model there is just a \emph{certification reading}, yes or no
(Section~\ref{sec:toll}). The \emph{guest} is a twelve-instruction fragment of my machine, run as data by an
interpreter written in my machine's own instructions (Section~\ref{sec:interpreters}).

These belong to the small machine only (Section~\ref{sec:smallest}). A \emph{two-counter machine} is Minsky's: two
counters holding whole numbers with no upper limit, and two instructions: add one, and
subtract one and jump if the counter is above zero, or else go on to the next line; already enough that nobody can decide in general whether
one halts. The small machine is a two-counter machine plus HALT and three instructions for the
record, six in all: INC, DEC, HALT, CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY. A counter's \emph{version} is its
edition number: it starts at 0 and goes up by one every time the counter is written, so an
edition never comes back. A \emph{fact} is a property, a counter and a version together, such as
``$A$ is even, as of edition 3''; the properties come from a fixed language of three, \emph{is zero},
\emph{is even} and \emph{is at least $n$}. The \emph{fact table} holds up to sixteen facts, and the only way
in is a CHECK that passed; nothing ever leaves it. The small machine's \emph{channel} holds one
committed fact or nothing, and COMMIT puts a fact there only if the table has it about the
counter's current edition. The \emph{trap} is a bit that goes up when an instruction refuses, and
then nothing in the core moves again. A commitment is \emph{earned} when a passing check put its
fact in the table first, about the same edition, with no write to that counter in between; on
the small machine every flag raised from a clean start is earned, and that's a theorem there, not on my machine.
CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY cost one each and everything else costs nothing, so the cheapest
certificate costs exactly three.

A \emph{window} is any function that shows you part of a state (Section~\ref{sec:windows}); a \emph{shadow}, said loosely, is
what a window leaves you with, and \emph{the} shadow, as a named window, is my machine's six-field
one of Section~\ref{sec:separation} (registers, memory, program counter, counter, error flag, certified flag). A
\emph{collision} is two steps that look the same through a window, before and after, where one
raises the flag and the other doesn't (Section~\ref{sec:windows}). \emph{Entitlement} is what a run has when it carries an
object, a checked relation between that object and a claim, and a paid event that put the
object in place: a license to lean on the claim, not a proof that it's true (Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}). A \emph{latch} is
a record that switches on the first time some event holds and never switches off (Section~\ref{sec:latch}). The
diagonal's \emph{substrate} (Section~\ref{sec:diagonal}) is the model's shape extended with programs, a run that may give
nothing back, a counter that never falls, a way to write programs as states, the
transformations the substrate counts as its own, and its own recursion theorem for those; the
proof of the diagonal uses neither the counter nor the toll.

%===========================================================================
\section{Every assumption in one place}
\label{sec:assumptions}
%===========================================================================

This book leans on a small number of rules that nothing proves, plus a handful of record
types that carry rules as fields. I've named each one where it's used. Here they are side by
side, because a reader who wants to break this book should be able to see every place where
it says ``suppose,'' in one list, with what each ``suppose'' buys.

There's one tangle to undo first, and it's my fault. The checked work has two different
records with two different numbered lists of ``axioms,'' and both lists use the label A2 for
different things. The book uses ``the toll'' for the rule that matters and avoids
the bare labels; this appendix maps the labels for anyone reading the files.

\subsection{The records that carry a rule}

\begin{definition}[Certification system]\label{def:app-certsys}
The record \code{CertificationSystem} (UniversalCertificationCost.v) has five data fields, a state
type, a move type, a step function, a cost per move in $\mathbb{N}$, and a yes/no reading,
and one proof field, \code{cs\_cert\_costs}: a move that turns the reading from no to yes costs at
least one. This proof field is the toll of Section~\ref{sec:toll}, and in this record's
numbering it is called A2. Every result stated ``for any certification system'' assumes it,
because the record cannot be built without it.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Abstract certification machine]\label{def:app-acm}
The record \code{AbstractCertMachine} (AbstractNoFI.v) is narrower: its moves are the fifty-one
instructions of the machine in Part IV, and it has a step, a reading, and one proof field,
\code{acm\_preserve}, saying that an instruction outside a fixed list of five certification-address
setters never turns the reading from no to yes. In this record's numbering, A1 is the reading
itself, the field \code{acm\_cert}, a yes/no certification indicator on every state: the state has
to include one. Coq enforces A1 through the record type. A record with that field left out
isn't a record of this type, so A1 is discharged when the record is built. The field
\code{acm\_preserve} is A3,
the starting condition ``the reading starts at no'' is a theorem hypothesis called A2, and ``each
of the five setters costs at least one'' is a separate lemma called A4
(\code{cert\_addr\_setter\_cost\_pos}). Its theorem \code{abstract\_nfi} concludes that a run from no to yes
contains one of the five setters; it does not mention cost.
\end{definition}

So the same idea, ``the crossing costs,'' is A2 in one list and A4 in the other. The book means
the first: the field \code{cs\_cert\_costs}.

\begin{definition}[Quantitative certification system]\label{def:app-qcs}
The record \code{QuantitativeCertificationSystem} (QuantitativeNoFI.v) extends a certification
system with a \emph{witness}, a function $W$ from states to $\mathbb{N}$, and a threshold
$N \in \mathbb{N}$, and adds two proof fields:
(A3, \code{qcs\_cost\_bounds\_witness}) $W(s) + \mathrm{cost}(i) \ge W(\mathrm{step}(s, i))$, the
witness grows by at most what the move cost; and
(A5, \code{qcs\_cert\_threshold\_witness}) a state that reads yes has $W(s) \ge N$.
An optional extension, \code{QuantitativeCertificationSystem\_full}, adds
(A4, \code{qcsf\_witness\_nondecreasing}) $W(s) \le W(\mathrm{step}(s, i))$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The floor raised to a threshold]\label{thm:app-quantitative}
In a quantitative certification system, every run from a state with witness $0$ (this
starting condition is called A6) to a state that reads yes has total cost at least $N$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Adding A3 along the run telescopes: the witness at the end is at most the witness at the
start plus the total cost, so at most the total cost. A5 says the end witness is at least
$N$. Neither A4 nor the toll is used.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{universal\_nfi\_quantitative} (QuantitativeNoFI.v). A3 and A4 bound opposite
directions, and neither implies the other: witness 1, cost 0, witness 0 satisfies A3 and
breaks A4, and witness 0, cost 0, witness 1 does the reverse. Two instances are built: the
machine's assertion channel with threshold 1
(\code{thiele\_quantitative\_nfi\_cert\_addr}), and a family for the game trials of
Section~\ref{sec:chsh}, whose cost counts valid trial instructions and whose threshold is any
$N$: reaching $N$ recorded trials from none takes at least $N$ valid trial instructions
(\code{chsh\_trial\_count\_lower\_bound}).

Here are the six labels side by side, with both numberings, so none of them is left without a
meaning.

\toprule
\textbf{Label} & \textbf{In \code{AbstractCertMachine}} & \textbf{In the certification records} \\
\midrule
\endhead
\bottomrule
\endlastfoot
A1 & the reading exists: field \code{acm\_cert}, enforced by the record type & (not used) \\
A2 & the reading starts at no: a hypothesis of \code{abstract\_nfi} & the toll: field \code{cs\_cert\_costs} of \code{CertificationSystem} \\
A3 & only the five setters turn the reading on: field \code{acm\_preserve} & the witness grows by at most the cost: field \code{qcs\_cost\_bounds\_witness} \\
