\subsection{The premises the derivations take}

These are definitions used as hypotheses. Nothing proves them in general; each theorem that
uses one says so in its statement.

\begingroup\small
\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.233\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.221\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.221\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.221\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Premise} & \textbf{What it says} & \textbf{Where it's used} & \textbf{Checked name} \\
\midrule
\endhead
\bottomrule
\endlastfoot
Finite & a list with no repeats contains every state & the room argument, Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} & \code{finite\_states} \\
Permanent & no move turns the reading from yes to no & the room argument & \code{permanent} (and \code{permanent\_at} for one move) \\
Merge pricing & every move that merges costs at least one & the toll derived, Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} & \code{merging\_steps\_priced} \\
Halving price & each unit of cost pays for at most one halving of distinct states & the squeeze bound; narrowing along a run, Section~\ref{sec:narrowing} & \code{compression\_priced} \\
Entropy pricing & each move costs at least the bits it removes from any spread & the third road to the toll & \code{entropy\_priced} \\
Landauer's principle & removing $\Delta H$ bits gives off heat $\ge k_B T \ln 2 \cdot \Delta H$ & the heat floor; with $k_B T \ge 0$ (or $> 0$) as a separate hypothesis on each theorem & \code{landauer\_heat} \\
Recursion (generic) & every transformation the substrate can represent has a fixed point & the diagonal, Section~\ref{sec:diagonal} & field \code{recursion\_theorem} of the class \code{Substrate} \\
Recursion (full machine) & a fixed point for a chosen class of program transformations of the bounded machine & the machine's diagonal corollary (no decider says yes exactly when a program admits the shortcut), Section~\ref{sec:interpreters} & section hypotheses of \code{vm\_structural\_shortcut\_undecidable} \\
Commitment contract & a commitment bit is set only when the claim holds, and whenever it holds & the commitment escape, Section~\ref{sec:windows}; on the machine, Section~\ref{sec:witness} & \code{CommitmentBitContract} \\
Hardware side conditions & per-instruction preconditions (arrow-table room, modules present, no 32-bit overflow, machine live) & the hardware refinement, Section~\ref{sec:chip} & \code{WFDrivenPrecondition} and the admission premises of \code{admitted\_retires} \\
\end{longtable}
\endgroup

Three remarks on the table. First, the recursion premise for the full machine is false
when asked for every map (its thousand-step cutoff property can be decided by running both
programs), and holds for trivial classes such as the identity map and the constant maps, and for no class containing the flip of a correct decider; for the twelve-instruction guest, the corresponding statement is a theorem with no premise
(\code{vm\_guest\_recursion\_theorem\_closed}, Section~\ref{sec:interpreters}). Second, the class
\code{Substrate} (Substrate.v) carries a different rule from the toll, mu\_\allowbreak{}monotone: the counter
never goes down on a step. Neither implies the other, the diagonal uses neither, and on the
machine both hold. Third, merge pricing is Landauer's principle taken in its worst case over
what the machine might be holding: it charges every merging move, while the principle in its
general form charges only for uncertainty actually removed (Theorem~\ref{thm:known-state}).

\subsection{The axioms of the checker itself}

Beyond the premises above, the checked proofs rest on Coq's own foundation and on five
standard-library axioms, which the assumption audit lists theorem by theorem: functional
extensionality on dependent functions (the most used, across the kernel and the hardware);
uniqueness of equality proofs, \code{eq\_rect\_eq} (only in the hardware proofs); two decidability
principles for the real numbers (used wherever real analysis is, for example in the game
check of Section~\ref{sec:chsh}); and the law of excluded middle (in a little over a hundred theorems). No axiom or
parameter of the project's own appears in the audited theorems. Section~\ref{sec:coq} says what that does and
doesn't mean.

%===========================================================================
\section{What's mine, and what isn't}
\label{sec:whats-mine}
%===========================================================================

Every chapter of this book leans on somebody, and I've named them where I lean. This appendix
does a different job, and it's the one where I'd most like to be caught out early rather than
late. For each thing the book could be accused of claiming as its own, it says what was
already known, what this work actually defines, builds, proves, or connects, and what kind of
contribution that is. Six kinds, and they aren't the same claim: a \emph{new result} (a statement
nobody had); a \emph{new proof} of something known; a \emph{mechanization} (a known result checked by a
machine, here Coq); an \emph{implementation} (something built that runs); a \emph{synthesis} (known
pieces put together under one question); and a \emph{conjecture}. Every kind can be worth doing.
None of them is the others. And if you read down the list and notice that ``new result''
hardly shows up, good. You're reading it right.

Two warnings about my own evidence before the list. First, ``I didn't find it'' is a fact about
my searches, not about the literature. I searched with every tool I had, and some tools will
cheerfully invent a citation if you let them, so where it matters I say where I looked, and
you should assume it may well be sitting in a paper I'd need a few more lifetimes of homework
to read. Second, nothing below is inferred from how many theorems there
are, from the audit's clean bill, or from a good story about who came before. Those tell you
the work was checked. They don't tell you it's new. Fourteen thousand checked theorems could,
in principle, be fourteen thousand careful ways of agreeing with Tarjan.

\subsection{1. The universal floor and the potential method}

Known: the potential method of amortized analysis, a function on states whose drop bounds
the cost of a run, is Tarjan's (1985), and it has been mechanized more than once (Nipkow in
Isabelle/HOL, 2015 and 2019; Charguéraud and Pottier's time credits in Coq, 2019), built
into type systems for automatic resource analysis (Hoffmann and coauthors, 2011 onward), and
recast in cost-aware type theories (Niu, Sterling, Grodin and Harper, 2022). Mine: choosing
the potential that is one when a designated reading says no and zero when it says yes, so
that ``the crossing costs'' (the toll) and ``every run that crosses paid'' (the floor) are the
potential method's two halves (Section~\ref{sec:counter}). Kind: a mechanization of a known
technique with a particular choice of potential. The choice is the point: it makes ``was
certified'' something the account must carry. The theorem is not new mathematics. If it
looks clever, that's Tarjan's cleverness; my part was picking which number to plug in.

Go back to Tarjan's paper and there's a sentence that sits right on the line this book draws.
He opens with the dictionary (to amortize is to put money aside at intervals, as in a sinking
fund) and then gives two views of the method. In the banker's view the computer is
coin-operated, and each operation is handed credits to spend or save; in the physicist's view,
which he credits to Daniel Sleator, every state has a potential and you count its changes.
Then he stops to say that the credits are only an accounting device: the programs that actually
run contain no mention of credits or debits. That's exactly right for what he wanted, a bound
proved about a program from outside. It's also exactly the gap. In his method the coins live in
the proof. The one move I chose was to put them in the step, where no program takes a step
without it being counted. Same arithmetic, different place.

\subsection{2. The toll from finiteness, permanence, and a price on merges}

Known: that steps which merge states (no single-valued inverse) are what Landauer's principle
charges for is Landauer's (1961), sharpened by Bennett (1973, 1982, 2003; the words ``the erasure of a bit
or the merging of two computation paths'' are from the 2003 abstract); generalizations and the dependence on the input
distribution are Maroney's (2009), Sagawa's (2014), Wolpert's; the critique is Earman and
Norton's and Norton's. Write-once memory is an old topic in coding theory (Rivest and
Shamir, 1982), about reuse rather than price. Mine: the short pigeonhole argument that on a
finite machine a reading nothing can turn off can only be turned on by a merging step
(Theorem~\ref{thm:perm-flip-merges}), the merge-or-revoke dichotomy, the characterisation of the
moves every merge-pricing schedule must charge, the squeeze and entropy forms for a permanent
flip, and a built counterexample for each premise (Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}). Kind:
small new statements, I think, with mechanized proofs; the physics is a named premise and
is Landauer's. Searches: I didn't find this exact statement anywhere I looked, and nobody's
search covers a whole field, mine least of all; I found no mechanization of Landauer's principle in Coq, Isabelle, or
Lean.

\subsection{3. Learning free, committing priced}

Known: that measurement can be done at no fundamental cost and the cost sits in erasing the
record is Bennett's resolution of Maxwell's demon (1982), with the quantitative trade-off by
Sagawa and Ueda (2009). Mine: the four-state demon and the three-state ring as checked
models, and the two-state impossibility (Section~\ref{sec:narrowing}). Kind: mechanization
and illustration of a known physical point inside my ledger. Not a new physical claim.
Bennett did the hard part in 1982; I built a toy with four dots on it and got Coq to agree
with him.

\subsection{4. Windows that can't price what they hide}

Known: a function of an observation is constant on the observation's fibres; that's
elementary, and the systems version of it is Moore's distinguishing experiments (1956),
Kalman's observability (1960), and the completeness question of abstract interpretation
(Cousot and Cousot, 1977; Giacobazzi, Ranzato and Scozzari, 2000). Mine: stating the pricing
version (no window price is exact across a collision) and exhibiting colliding pairs for the
machine's two named windows (Section~\ref{sec:witness}). Kind:
mechanization of an elementary lemma, plus specific facts about this machine.

\subsection{5. Structural entitlement and its bound}

Known: decision-tree counting bounds (a tree that tells $N$ cases apart has depth at least
$\log_2 N$); certifying algorithms that hand over checkable certificates (McConnell,
Mehlhorn, Näher and Schweitzer, 2011); proof-carrying code (Necula, 1997); the gap between
justified true belief and knowledge (Gettier, 1963). Mine: the definition of entitlement as an
object, a checked relation, and a paid event on the record, and the assembled theorem that,
under its listed hypotheses, a certified strengthening on the machine pays at least the index
bits it commits to (Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}, Section~\ref{sec:machine-claims}). Kind: synthesis plus mechanization; the
counting idea is standard, the assembly and its vocabulary are this work's, and the pricing
policy is assumed, not derived.

\subsection{6. The record axis is a latch}

Known: monotone, write-once state is old: the latch (Eccles and Jordan, 1918), sticky bits
(Plotkin, 1989), grow-only state in replicated data types (Shapiro and coauthors), history
variables and stuttering in refinement (Abadi and Lamport, 1991). Mine: the exact statement
that a record driven by the computation that never switches off is, over any base, a latch
on one event, with its converse and a counterexample for each of the two conditions, and the
uniqueness-up-to-price-list result with the refutation of the stronger uniqueness
(Section~\ref{sec:latch}, Section~\ref{sec:witness}). Kind: a small structural lemma, I think not stated before in this
form (I found no prior statement in the searches I ran), built from old notions, and
mechanized.

\subsection{7. The diagonal, L, and the guest's recursion theorem}

Known: Kleene's recursion theorem and Rice's theorem; Lawvere's fixed-point form (1969) and
Yanofsky's retelling (2003); mechanized recursion theorems and Rice (Norrish in HOL4, 2011;
Carneiro in Lean; Forster, Kunze, Smolka and coauthors in Coq, including L itself, 2017, and
the Coq Library of Undecidability). Mine: the diagonal stated once over any substrate that
supplies a recursion theorem; Rice and halting proved again for L from its reduction rules;
and a recursion theorem constructed for the machine's twelve-instruction guest, ledger
included, with the evaluator compiled into guest instructions through L and the library
(Section~\ref{sec:diagonal} and Section~\ref{sec:interpreters}). Kind: checked instances, not new
theorems of computability. The guest result is an instance of a theorem that holds for any
model with universality and s-m-n; the work is in building that for this machine.

\subsection{8. The game check}

Known: that positive semidefiniteness of a correlation matrix gives the Tsirelson bound is
Tsirelson's (1980) and Wehner's semidefinite proof (2006); the moment-matrix hierarchy, the
Schur-complement analysis of this very level-one matrix, the arcsine characterization, and
the level $1+AB$ are Navascués, Pironio and Acín's (2007, 2008), with Landau (1988) and Masanes
(2003); and Tsirelson's bound has already been checked by machine, in Isabelle/HOL (Echenim
and Mhalla, 2023) and in Lean's mathlib. Rational sum-of-squares certificates are Peyrl and
Parrilo's (2008). Mine: a decision procedure in integer arithmetic on outcome counters that
runs inside one instruction; a checked chain from ``that instruction didn't trap'' to ``the
pinned level-one matrix is positive semidefinite'' to ``$S^2 \le 8$''; proofs of the
contraction equivalence by explicit test vectors; the level-$1+AB$ cascade and an
elliptope gate in whole numbers, with a soundness proof and no step of the machine
attached to it; and a circuit proved to compute the same
check on 32-bit counters (Section~\ref{sec:chsh} and its derivation appendix). Kind:
implementation and mechanization, with a new proof of a known equivalence in one slice. I
found no prior formalization taking counters as input or linking a machine instruction to the
bound, and that's a report on where I looked, not on everything that exists.

\subsection{9. The verified path to a chip}

Known: Kami (Choi, Vijayaraghavan, Sherman, Chlipala and Arvind, 2017), Kôika (Bourgeat,
Pit-Claudel, Chlipala and Arvind, 2020), the end-to-end verified stack of Erbsen and coauthors
(2021), CakeML on the verified Silver processor (Lööw and coauthors, 2019), and the discipline
of naming what isn't proved (CompCert, seL4). Mine: an instruction-by-instruction Kami
refinement for this machine, a proved serial loader, solver-checked inductions on the extracted circuit's partition-table, control and loader safety, and a labelled chain to a bitstream
(Section~\ref{sec:chip}). Kind: implementation of an established method. No new verification
method; extraction, synthesis, and the chip are trusted, and no board was run.

\subsection{10. Five record disciplines, one question}

Known: each system and its guarantee belongs to its designers: Casper (Buterin and Griffith,
2017), Ethereum's storage gas and refunds (EIP-2200, EIP-3529), extend-only TPM registers,
Certificate Transparency (RFC 9162), proof-carrying code. Mine: asking all five whether the
write is priced, with a small checked fragment of each (Section~\ref{sec:models}). Kind:
synthesis and an organizing reading; the fragments are not verifications of those systems.

\subsection{11. The pointer conjecture}

Known: Zurek's quantum Darwinism (2009), with Ollivier, Poulin and Zurek (2004) and
Blume-Kohout and Zurek (2006): preferred states are the ones whose records proliferate
redundantly in the environment. Mine: borrowing that shape for the question of which event
deserves a record, with definitions, a toy, and refutations of two stronger forms
(Section~\ref{sec:pointer}). Kind: conjecture. No claim about quantum physics.

\subsection{12. The counter as a receipt}

Known: one-way counters that give order and termination are old: Turing's 1949 note on
checking a large routine, Floyd's ranking functions (1967), Lamport's clocks (1978).
Carrying a run's cost beside its result is the writer cost of Danner and Licata and the
graded effect semantics of Katsumata (2014), with a working-language version in Orchard,
Liepelt and Eades (2019). Mine: putting three properties side by side (the total only
climbs, it equals the sum of the charges on every path including the failures, and it is
the only such total for a given price list), the argument for any system with a counter
and a price list, and the checked versions on the machine (Section~\ref{sec:counter},
Section~\ref{sec:witness}). Kind: synthesis, with mechanization on the machine; the
abstract statements are argued in the text and are not checked in Coq. Whether the counter
is an embedding of the graded frameworks or something weaker I haven't settled.

\subsection{13. Couplings and the stored-arrow laws}

Known: the category (Eilenberg and Mac Lane, 1945), and that relations compose
associatively with the diagonal as identity. Mine: the machine's rule for composing stored
arrows, which passes the identity flag along so that associativity and both identity laws
hold on the arrows it stores, each a theorem, together with the checked laws for
relational composition and for the tensor on couplings (Section~\ref{sec:category}). The
obvious rule for composing identity arrows breaks associativity, and the book says so where
it matters. Kind: implementation and mechanization of known structure on one machine. Not
a result in category theory.

\subsection{14. The small machine}

Known: two-counter machines are Minsky's (1961, 1967), and the undecidability of their
halting is checked in the Coq Library of Undecidability (Forster, Larchey-Wendling and
coauthors, 2019, 2020). Mine: a six-instruction machine on two counters, with a version
for each counter, a bounded fact table and a channel; its theorems that a committed fact
was checked first about the same edition, that nothing is forged, that nothing is evicted,
and that a certificate costs exactly three and no less; and the step-for-step match with
the library's machine, so halting is undecidable for it (Section~\ref{sec:smallest}).
Kind: implementation and mechanization of a small design. The universality and the
undecidability are borrowed, and the other properties are short consequences of the step
rule. Whether the design is new I can't say, and I make no claim beyond the proofs.

\subsection{15. The universal host}

Known: Turing's universal machine (1936), which runs any machine given as data, and the
universal register machines that run two-counter programs. Mine: a host that runs any
program of the small machine as a guest and has one extra move, a guest step that mirrors
the guest's flag and charges in the same step, with theorems that the mirror always equals
the guest's flag, that it rises only in a guest step that passed CERTIFY, for every sequence
of host moves, and that the host's ledger covers the guest's
(Section~\ref{sec:universal-host}). Kind: implementation and mechanization of a small
design. The universality is borrowed from the small machine and from Minsky. A foreign
machine's own prices are not kept, and the book says so where it states the result.

\subsection{What that adds up to}

Read straight down the list and the honest summary is this. The mathematics underneath this
book is mostly known, and some of it is very old. What's mine is the question (should an
account of computation carry what was certified and what certifying cost, as part of how it
steps), a handful of small exact statements that the question needed and that I didn't find
stated elsewhere (items 2, 4's pricing form, and 6), a large body of mechanized proof that
ties those statements to two machines that run, the small one and the big build, and my best attempt at saying which is which,
which you should check as hard as anything else in here. If someone shows me item 2, the
pricing form in item 4, or item 6 stated earlier, I'll move it up the list and be glad to,
and a little embarrassed, in that order.

\section{Every result and where it is checked}
\label{sec:crosswalk}
%===========================================================================

Every numbered result in this book is in the table below, in the order it appears, with
the Coq names that carry it, the file each lives in, and what the last full assumption
audit printed for it. ``none'' means the theorem is closed: its proof uses nothing beyond
Coq's own rules. The other entries name the standard-library assumptions it uses: FE is
functional extensionality on dependent functions, UIP is uniqueness of equality proofs
(\code{eq\_rect\_eq}), RD is the pair of decidability principles that come with the real numbers,
and EM is excluded middle. ``def'' marks a definition, which has nothing to assume.
``not probed'' marks a name the audit doesn't list, usually a local lemma; its file is still
given. A premise or a conjecture has no Coq name on purpose: it's assumed or open, and the
section that states it says so.

This table is an index of companion formalizations. The statements, hypotheses and
arguments are in the numbered sections it points to. An audit status reports the
recorded check; running a later version does not change a claim in this book.

%===========================================================================
\section{The CHSH derivation, in full}
\label{sec:chsh-derivation}
%===========================================================================

This appendix supports Section~\ref{sec:chsh}. That section tells the story; this one does the algebra. Each
item gives the exact statement with all its hypotheses, the steps a reader needs to check
it, and the Coq name with its file. Nothing here identifies any matrix with a quantum
state. Where the reading ``quantum'' appears, it is a cited result from outside the kernel.

\subsection{A. Setting and notation}
\label{sub:chsh-notation}

\begin{definition}[Settings, outcomes, correlators]\label{def:chsh-setting}
Alice receives a setting $x \in \{0,1\}$ and Bob a setting $y \in \{0,1\}$. Each answers a
bit, recoded as an outcome $a, b \in \{+1, -1\}$ (bit 0 becomes $+1$, bit 1 becomes $-1$).
The correlator $E_{xy}$ is the average of the product $ab$ over the rounds with settings
$(x, y)$. The CHSH quantity is
\[
S = E_{00} + E_{01} + E_{10} - E_{11}.
\]
I collect the four correlators into the $2 \times 2$ matrix
\[
E = \begin{pmatrix} E_{00} & E_{01} \\ E_{10} & E_{11} \end{pmatrix},
\]
whose rows are indexed by Alice's setting and whose columns by Bob's. The rows of $E$ are
$(E_{00}, E_{01})$ and $(E_{10}, E_{11})$; the columns are $(E_{00}, E_{10})$ and
$(E_{01}, E_{11})$.
\end{definition}

The same polynomial $S$ appears under three names in the source: \code{CHSH}
(kernel/quantum/TsirelsonGeneral.v), \code{CHSH\_value} (kernel/quantum/TsirelsonFromAlgebra.v)
and \code{chsh\_S} (kernel/quantum/ElliptopeCompletion.v).

\begin{definition}[Counters]\label{def:chsh-counters}
The machine keeps eight counters in the record \code{WitnessCounts}
(kernel/foundation/VMState.v): for each setting pair, $\mathrm{same}_{xy}$ counts rounds
whose two answer bits matched and $\mathrm{diff}_{xy}$ counts rounds whose bits differed.
\code{record\_trial} (kernel/foundation/VMStep.v) adds one to exactly one of the eight. Write
\[
N_{xy} = \mathrm{same}_{xy} + \mathrm{diff}_{xy}, \qquad
D_{xy} = \mathrm{same}_{xy} - \mathrm{diff}_{xy}, \qquad
E_{xy} = \frac{D_{xy}}{N_{xy}} .
\]
\end{definition}

A matched round contributes $ab = +1$ and a differing round $ab = -1$, so $D_{xy}$ is the sum
of the products and $D_{xy}/N_{xy}$ is their average. Since $|D_{xy}| \le N_{xy}$, every
correlator from counters lies in $[-1, 1]$. In Coq the integers are \code{chsh\_n\_z} and \code{chsh\_d\_z}
(kernel/foundation/VMStep.v). When a bucket is empty, the real-valued correlator
\code{state\_bucket\_correlation} (kernel/nfi/MuLedgerQuantumBridge.v) and the rational one
\code{chsh\_correlator\_q} (kernel/quantum/CHSHStatisticalBridge.v) both return 0 by
convention. The CHSH score of a tally, \code{chsh\_stat\_from\_wc} (CHSHStatisticalBridge.v),
adds the first three correlators and obtains $-E_{11}$ by swapping the two counters of the
last bucket.

\subsection{B. The classical bound}
\label{sub:chsh-classical}

\begin{lemma}[Deterministic strategies]\label{lem:chsh-deterministic}
Let $a_0, a_1, b_0, b_1 \in \{+1, -1\}$. Then
$-2 \le a_0 b_0 + a_0 b_1 + a_1 b_0 - a_1 b_1 \le 2$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Factor: $a_0 b_0 + a_0 b_1 + a_1 b_0 - a_1 b_1 = a_0(b_0 + b_1) + a_1(b_0 - b_1)$. If
$b_0 = b_1$ then $b_0 + b_1 = \pm 2$ and $b_0 - b_1 = 0$; if $b_0 \ne b_1$ the other way
round. In both cases exactly one of the two brackets is $\pm 2$ and the other is $0$, so the
expression is $\pm 2$ times a sign, which is $+2$ or $-2$. There are sixteen sign choices,
and every one of them gives exactly $\pm 2$, never $0$ or $\pm 4$.
\end{proof}

The Coq proofs do not factor; they split into the sixteen sign cases and compute. The
rational statement is \code{local\_S\_2\_deterministic} (kernel/quantum/BoxCHSH.v): for
$f_A, f_B : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Q}$ with every value $\pm 1$, the absolute value of
$f_A(0) f_B(0) + f_A(0) f_B(1) + f_A(1) f_B(0) - f_A(1) f_B(1)$ is at most 2. The real
statement is \code{deterministic\_strategy\_chsh\_bounded} (kernel/quantum/MinorConstraints.v),
with conclusion $-2 \le \cdots \le 2$.

\begin{definition}[Finite factorizable model, \code{is\_factorizable}]\label{def:chsh-factorizable}
A real-valued correlation function $E(a, b, x, y)$ is factorizable
(kernel/quantum/MinorConstraints.v) when there exist response functions $A(x, \lambda)$,
$B(y, \lambda)$, weights $p(\lambda)$ and a natural number $\lambda_{\max}$ such that:
$0 \le p(\lambda) \le 1$ for $\lambda \le \lambda_{\max}$;
$\sum_{\lambda = 0}^{\lambda_{\max}} p(\lambda) = 1$; every $A(x, \lambda)$ and every
$B(y, \lambda)$ is $-1$ or $+1$; and for all $a, b, x, y$,
$E(a, b, x, y) = \sum_{\lambda=0}^{\lambda_{\max}} p(\lambda) A(x, \lambda) B(y, \lambda)$.
The outcome arguments $a, b$ are dummies; only correlations are modelled.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[\code{fine\_theorem}, one direction only]\label{thm:chsh-fine}
If $E$ is factorizable, then $-2 \le E(0,0,0,0) + E(0,0,0,1) + E(0,0,1,0) - E(0,0,1,1) \le 2$
(kernel/quantum/MinorConstraints.v; restated as \code{factorizable\_CHSH\_classical\_bound}).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Substitute the factorization: $S = \sum_\lambda p(\lambda) S_\lambda$, where $S_\lambda$ is
the deterministic expression of Lemma~\ref{lem:chsh-deterministic} at the signs
$A(\cdot, \lambda), B(\cdot, \lambda)$. Each $S_\lambda \in [-2, 2]$, the weights are
nonnegative and sum to 1, so $-2 = \sum_\lambda p(\lambda)(-2) \le S \le
\sum_\lambda p(\lambda) \cdot 2 = 2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[What the name does and does not cover]\label{rem:chsh-fine-scope}
Fine's 1982 theorem is an equivalence between several descriptions of local models and the
Bell inequalities. \code{fine\_theorem} proves one direction: a finite factorizable model obeys
the bound. It proves no converse, and it covers only finitely many hidden states
($\lambda \le \lambda_{\max}$), not an arbitrary probability space. The transfer to rational
boxes is \code{local\_box\_CHSH\_bound} (kernel/quantum/MinorConstraints.v): if
\textnormal{\texttt{box\_correlations B}} is factorizable then the real image of $|S(B)|$ is at most 2.
\end{remark}

The finite-tally statement concerns one fixed strategy replayed on every recorded round.

\begin{definition}[\code{WCLocallyConsistent}]\label{def:chsh-wclc}
For bits $a_0, a_1, b_0, b_1 \in \{0, 1\}$ and a counter record $w$
(kernel/quantum/CHSHStatisticalBridge.v), $w$ is locally consistent with
$(a_0, a_1, b_0, b_1)$ when, for each setting pair $(x, y)$: if $a_x = b_y$ then
$\mathrm{diff}_{xy} = 0$, otherwise $\mathrm{same}_{xy} = 0$; and every bucket is sampled,
$N_{00}, N_{01}, N_{10}, N_{11} > 0$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[A tally above 2 is not one replayed strategy]\label{thm:chsh-tally}
Let $w$ be a counter record whose rational score \code{chsh\_stat\_from\_wc} $w$ is greater than 2.
Then for all bits $a_0, a_1, b_0, b_1$, $w$ is not locally consistent with
$(a_0, a_1, b_0, b_1)$. This is \code{chsh\_violation\_rules\_out\_locally\_factorizable\_coupling}
(kernel/quantum/CHSHCouplingBridge.v). Its contrapositive form,
\code{locally\_consistent\_classical\_bound}, states that a locally consistent record has
score of absolute value at most 2.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Under local consistency each sampled bucket is pure: if $a_x = b_y$ every round in the
bucket matched, so $E_{xy} = N_{xy}/N_{xy} = +1$; otherwise every round differed and
$E_{xy} = -1$. In signs, $E_{xy} = \alpha_x \beta_y$ with $\alpha_x = (-1)^{a_x}$ and
$\beta_y = (-1)^{b_y}$. The score is then the deterministic expression of
Lemma~\ref{lem:chsh-deterministic}, which is at most 2 in absolute value. A score above 2
contradicts this.
\end{proof}

The theorem rules out one explanation, a single four-bit plan used on every round. It says
nothing about a local model that redraws its hidden state every round; Section~\ref{sec:chsh} gives a four-round
coin-flip tally with score 4.

\subsection{C. Tsirelson's bound from algebra}
\label{sub:chsh-tsirelson-algebra}

\begin{lemma}[The six-square identity, \code{chsh\_gap\_is\_sum\_of\_squares}]\label{lem:chsh-sos}
For all real $a, b, c, d$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
&4(a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2) - (a + b + c - d)^2 \\
&\quad = (a-b)^2 + (a-c)^2 + (a+d)^2 + (b-c)^2 + (b+d)^2 + (c+d)^2 .
\end{aligned}
\]
(kernel/quantum/TsirelsonFromAlgebra.v, closed by \code{ring}.)
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Expand the square on the left:
$(a+b+c-d)^2 = a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2 + 2ab + 2ac - 2ad + 2bc - 2bd - 2cd$. So the left side is
\[
3(a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2) - 2ab - 2ac + 2ad - 2bc + 2bd + 2cd .
\]
On the right, each variable appears in exactly three of the six brackets ($a$ in
$a-b$, $a-c$, $a+d$; $b$ in $a-b$, $b-c$, $b+d$; $c$ in $a-c$, $b-c$, $c+d$; $d$ in $a+d$,
$b+d$, $c+d$), so the squared terms add to $3(a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2)$. The cross terms are
$-2ab$ from $(a-b)^2$, $-2ac$ from $(a-c)^2$, $+2ad$ from $(a+d)^2$, $-2bc$ from $(b-c)^2$,
$+2bd$ from $(b+d)^2$ and $+2cd$ from $(c+d)^2$. Both sides agree term by term.
\end{proof}

Since the right side is a sum of squares, $S^2 \le 4 \sum_{xy} E_{xy}^2$ for any four reals;
this is \code{cauchy\_schwarz\_chsh} (TsirelsonFromAlgebra.v).

\begin{theorem}[Row-bound form of Tsirelson's bound]\label{thm:chsh-row-tsirelson}
For all real $E_{00}, E_{01}, E_{10}, E_{11}$ with $E_{00}^2 + E_{01}^2 \le 1$ and
$E_{10}^2 + E_{11}^2 \le 1$, $S^2 \le 8$. This is \code{tsirelson\_squared}
(kernel/quantum/TsirelsonFromAlgebra.v) and \code{tsirelson\_from\_row\_bounds}
(kernel/quantum/TsirelsonGeneral.v). The absolute form $|S| \le \sqrt 8 = 2\sqrt 2$ is
\code{tsirelson\_bound\_abs} (TsirelsonGeneral.v).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Adding the two row bounds gives $\sum_{xy} E_{xy}^2 \le 2$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:chsh-sos},
$S^2 \le 4 \sum_{xy} E_{xy}^2 \le 8$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Tightness]\label{thm:chsh-tight}
The point $E_{00} = E_{01} = E_{10} = 1/\sqrt 2$, $E_{11} = -1/\sqrt 2$ satisfies both row
bounds and has $S = \sqrt 8$. This is \code{tsirelson\_tight} (TsirelsonFromAlgebra.v) and
\code{tsirelson\_achievable} (TsirelsonGeneral.v).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Each row has squared length $1/2 + 1/2 = 1$, and $S = 4/\sqrt 2 = 2\sqrt 2 = \sqrt 8$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Where equality can happen]\label{rem:chsh-equality}
This step is argued here, not checked in Coq. Equality $S^2 = 8$ under the row bounds forces
equality in both steps of the proof above: the six squares must all vanish, which gives
$a = b = c = -d$, and the rows must be tight, which gives $2a^2 = 1$. So the point of
Theorem~\ref{thm:chsh-tight} and its negative are the only places the bound is reached.
\end{remark}

\begin{lemma}[A rational constant above the bound, \code{rational\_tsirelson\_bound}]\label{lem:chsh-rational}
$\sqrt 8 < 5657/2000$ (kernel/quantum/TsirelsonFromAlgebra.v).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Both numbers are positive, so it suffices to compare squares. $5657^2 = 32{,}001{,}649$ and
$8 \cdot 2000^2 = 32{,}000{,}000$, so $(5657/2000)^2 = 32{,}001{,}649/4{,}000{,}000 > 8 =
(\sqrt 8)^2$. If $\sqrt 8 \ge 5657/2000$ held, squaring both nonnegative sides would give
$8 \ge (5657/2000)^2$, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

The constant is the four-decimal round-up of $2\sqrt 2 = 2.8284271\ldots$; the gap is about
$7.3 \times 10^{-5}$. It lets rational code test ``above the Tsirelson bound'' without a square
root. It plays no part in the integer check of item E.

\subsection{D. The zero-marginal 5x5 moment matrix}
\label{sub:chsh-five}

\begin{definition}[The pinned level-1 matrix]\label{def:chsh-five}
\code{zero\_marginal\_npa} (kernel/quantum/NPAMomentMatrix.v) fills the general record
\code{NPAMomentMatrix} with all four one-party entries and both within-party entries set
to zero, and \code{npa\_to\_matrix} lays it out on rows and columns
$I, A_0, A_1, B_0, B_1$:
\end{definition}

\[
M(E) \;=\;
\begin{array}{c@{\quad}c}
 & \begin{array}{ccccc} I & A_0 & A_1 & B_0 & B_1 \end{array} \\
\begin{array}{c} I \\ A_0 \\ A_1 \\ B_0 \\ B_1 \end{array} &
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 1 & 0 & E_{00} & E_{01} \\
0 & 0 & 1 & E_{10} & E_{11} \\
0 & E_{00} & E_{10} & 1 & 0 \\
0 & E_{01} & E_{11} & 0 & 1
\end{pmatrix}
\end{array}
\]

Positive semidefiniteness in the source is defined by quadratic forms, not eigenvalues:
\code{PSD5} (kernel/quantum/ConstructivePSD.v) says $v^{\mathsf T} M v \ge 0$ for every
$v \in \mathbb{R}^5$, and \code{npa\_psd} (NPAMomentMatrix.v) is ``symmetric and \code{PSD5}''.
In block form,

\[
M(E) \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & G \end{pmatrix},
\qquad
G \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} I_2 & E \\ E^{\mathsf T} & I_2 \end{pmatrix}.
\]

The corner $1$ is decoupled, so $M(E)$ is PSD exactly when $G$ is.

\begin{lemma}[Schur complement, the standard form]\label{lem:chsh-schur}
Let $P$ be symmetric positive definite. The symmetric block matrix
$\begin{pmatrix} P & Q \\ Q^{\mathsf T} & R \end{pmatrix}$ is PSD if and only if
$R - Q^{\mathsf T} P^{-1} Q$ is PSD.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For $u, w$ of the right sizes,
\[
\begin{pmatrix} u \\ w \end{pmatrix}^{\!\mathsf T}
\begin{pmatrix} P & Q \\ Q^{\mathsf T} & R \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} u \\ w \end{pmatrix}
= (u + P^{-1} Q w)^{\mathsf T} P \,(u + P^{-1} Q w)
+ w^{\mathsf T} (R - Q^{\mathsf T} P^{-1} Q)\, w .
\]
The first term is never negative because $P$ is positive definite, and it is zero at
$u = -P^{-1} Q w$. So the form is nonnegative for all $(u, w)$ exactly when the second term
is nonnegative for all $w$.
\end{proof}

The Coq proofs do not invoke this lemma abstractly. They carry out its one instance with
$P = I_2$, $Q = E$, $R = I_2$, where the complement is
\[
I_2 - E^{\mathsf T} E =
\begin{pmatrix}
1 - E_{00}^2 - E_{10}^2 & -(E_{00} E_{01} + E_{10} E_{11}) \\
-(E_{00} E_{01} + E_{10} E_{11}) & 1 - E_{01}^2 - E_{11}^2
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The diagonal of $E^{\mathsf T} E$ holds the squared lengths of the columns of $E$, which is
why the conditions below are column conditions.

\begin{definition}[Column contractive, \code{zero\_marginal\_column\_contractive}]\label{def:chsh-cc}
(kernel/nfi/MuLedgerQuantumBridge.v) Write
$p = 1 - E_{00}^2 - E_{10}^2$, $q = 1 - E_{01}^2 - E_{11}^2$ and
$s = E_{00} E_{01} + E_{10} E_{11}$. The correlators are column contractive when
\[
p \ge 0, \qquad q \ge 0, \qquad p\,q - s^2 \ge 0 .
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[The 2x2 test, \code{psd2\_quadratic\_form\_nonneg}]\label{lem:chsh-psd2}
(kernel/nfi/MuLedgerQuantumBridge.v) If $\alpha \ge 0$, $\delta \ge 0$ and
$\alpha\delta - \beta^2 \ge 0$, then $\alpha u^2 + 2\beta u w + \delta w^2 \ge 0$ for all real
$u, w$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
If $w = 0$ the form is $\alpha u^2 \ge 0$. Otherwise put $t = u/w$, so the form is
$w^2(\alpha t^2 + 2\beta t + \delta)$. If $\alpha = 0$, then $-\beta^2 \ge 0$ forces
$\beta = 0$ and the bracket is $\delta \ge 0$. If $\alpha > 0$,
$\alpha t^2 + 2\beta t + \delta = \alpha (t + \beta/\alpha)^2 + (\alpha\delta - \beta^2)/\alpha$,
a sum of two nonnegative terms.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Contractive implies PSD]\label{thm:chsh-cc-psd}
If $p \ge 0$, $q \ge 0$ and $pq - s^2 \ge 0$, then \code{PSD5} holds of $M(E)$.
This is \code{zero\_marginal\_npa\_column\_contractive\_implies\_psd}
(kernel/nfi/MuLedgerQuantumBridge.v).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write $v = (v_0, x_0, x_1, y_0, y_1)$. Reading off the entries of $M(E)$,
\[
v^{\mathsf T} M(E)\, v = v_0^2 + x_0^2 + x_1^2 + y_0^2 + y_1^2
+ 2x_0(E_{00} y_0 + E_{01} y_1) + 2x_1(E_{10} y_0 + E_{11} y_1).
\]
Complete the squares in $x_0$ and $x_1$:
\[
\begin{aligned}
v^{\mathsf T} M(E)\, v ={}& v_0^2 + (x_0 + E_{00} y_0 + E_{01} y_1)^2
+ (x_1 + E_{10} y_0 + E_{11} y_1)^2 \\
&+ p\, y_0^2 - 2 s\, y_0 y_1 + q\, y_1^2 .
\end{aligned}
\]
To check the last three terms, expand the two squares: they contribute
$(E_{00} y_0 + E_{01} y_1)^2 + (E_{10} y_0 + E_{11} y_1)^2$ beyond the cross terms, which is
$(E_{00}^2 + E_{10}^2) y_0^2 + 2 s\, y_0 y_1 + (E_{01}^2 + E_{11}^2) y_1^2$; subtracting it
from $y_0^2 + y_1^2$ leaves $p\, y_0^2 - 2 s\, y_0 y_1 + q\, y_1^2$. The first three terms are
squares. The last is the $2 \times 2$ form with $\alpha = p$, $\beta = -s$, $\delta = q$,
nonnegative by Lemma~\ref{lem:chsh-psd2}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Discriminant, \code{quadratic\_nonneg\_discriminant}]\label{lem:chsh-discriminant}
(kernel/quantum/ConstructivePSD.v) If $a + 2bt + ct^2 \ge 0$ for every real $t$, then
$b^2 \le ac$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
If $c < 0$ the quadratic tends to $-\infty$, so $c \ge 0$. If $c = 0$, the line
$a + 2bt$ is nonnegative for every $t$ only if $b = 0$, and then $b^2 = 0 = ac$. If $c > 0$,
evaluate at $t = -b/c$: $a - b^2/c \ge 0$, so $b^2 \le ac$. (The Coq proof is the same case
analysis, with explicit witnesses $t$ for the contradictions.)
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[PSD implies contractive]\label{thm:chsh-psd-cc}
If \code{PSD5} holds of $M(E)$, then $p \ge 0$, $q \ge 0$ and $pq - s^2 \ge 0$. This is
\code{npa\_psd\_implies\_column\_contractive} (kernel/quantum/QuantumPartitionPSD.v).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Feed the quadratic form three test vectors, written in the order
$(I, A_0, A_1, B_0, B_1)$; their values are the lemmas \code{npa\_quad5\_test\_col0},
\code{npa\_quad5\_test\_col1} and \code{npa\_quad5\_test\_schur} (QuantumPartitionPSD.v).
Each is the choice $x = -E y$ that zeroes both completed squares in the proof of
Theorem~\ref{thm:chsh-cc-psd}, so only $y^{\mathsf T}(I_2 - E^{\mathsf T} E) y$ is left.

First, $v = (0, -E_{00}, -E_{10}, 1, 0)$ gives $v^{\mathsf T} M v = p$, so $p \ge 0$.

Second, $v = (0, -E_{01}, -E_{11}, 0, 1)$ gives $v^{\mathsf T} M v = q$, so $q \ge 0$.

Third, for each real $t$, $v(t) = (0, -(E_{00} t + E_{01}), -(E_{10} t + E_{11}), t, 1)$
gives $v(t)^{\mathsf T} M v(t) = p\,t^2 - 2 s\,t + q \ge 0$. Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:chsh-discriminant}
with $a = q$, $b = -s$, $c = p$: $s^2 \le pq$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The equivalence]\label{cor:chsh-iff}
For all real $E_{00}, E_{01}, E_{10}, E_{11}$, \code{PSD5} of $M(E)$ holds if and only if the
correlators are column contractive: \code{npa\_psd\_iff\_column\_contractive}
(kernel/quantum/QuantumPartitionPSD.v). With symmetry packaged in,
\code{column\_contractive\_iff\_npa\_psd} states contractivity if and only if \code{npa\_psd} holds
of \code{zero\_marginal\_npa} at the four correlators.
\end{corollary}

The bound itself goes through rows rather than columns.

\begin{theorem}[PSD implies Tsirelson]\label{thm:chsh-psd-tsirelson}
If \code{npa\_psd} holds of \code{zero\_marginal\_npa} at $E_{00}, E_{01}, E_{10}, E_{11}$, then $S^2 \le 8$, and
$|S| \le \sqrt 8$. These are \code{npa\_psd\_implies\_tsirelson\_bound} and
\code{npa\_psd\_implies\_tsirelson\_bound\_abs} (kernel/nfi/MuLedgerQuantumBridge.v).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\code{psd\_3x3\_determinant\_nonneg} (kernel/quantum/ConstructivePSD.v) says a symmetric PSD
matrix with unit diagonal has every $3 \times 3$ principal minor
$1 - x^2 - y^2 - z^2 + 2xyz \ge 0$. On rows $A_0, B_0, B_1$ the entries are
$x = E_{00}$, $y = E_{01}$, $z = 0$, so $E_{00}^2 + E_{01}^2 \le 1$. On rows $A_1, B_0, B_1$
the same gives $E_{10}^2 + E_{11}^2 \le 1$. This is
\code{npa\_psd\_zero\_marginal\_implies\_row\_bounds} (MuLedgerQuantumBridge.v). Then
Theorem~\ref{thm:chsh-row-tsirelson} applies, through \code{tsirelson\_from\_minors}
(kernel/quantum/TsirelsonGeneral.v).
\end{proof}

Here are the three conditions and the score at a few points, all by direct arithmetic.
In this table, $a = 3/5$, $b = 4/5$ and $t = 1/\sqrt 2$.

\begingroup\small
\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.214\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.122\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.122\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.122\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.122\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.122\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{point $(E_{00}, E_{01}, E_{10}, E_{11})$} & \textbf{$S$} & \textbf{$p$} & \textbf{$q$} & \textbf{$pq - s^2$} & \textbf{contractive} \\
\midrule
\endhead
\bottomrule
\endlastfoot
$(0, 0, 0, 0)$ & 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 & yes \\
$(0.6, 0.6, 0.6, -0.6)$ & 2.4 & 0.28 & 0.28 & 0.0784 & yes \\
$(a, b, b, -a)$ & 2.8 & 0 & 0 & 0 & yes, with no slack \\
$(t, t, t, -t)$ & $2\sqrt 2$ & 0 & 0 & 0 & yes, with no slack \\
